section: 1.11 Elementary row operations and the invariance of rank
text:
1.11 Elementary row operations and the invariance of rank
In practice rank, bases of the four subspaces, and solutions of systems are computed by Gaussian elimination, which transforms a matrix by elementary row operations. We record why these operations leave rank unchanged. There are three:

swapping two rows;
multiplying a row by a nonzero scalar;
adding a scalar multiple of one row to another.

Each is realized by left multiplication by an elementary matrix \(E\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\), obtained by performing the operation on \(I_m\). Each elementary matrix is invertible, its inverse being the elementary matrix of the reverse operation (swap the same rows back; scale by the reciprocal; subtract the same multiple). The key fact is that multiplying by any invertible matrix preserves rank.

Lemma 1.13 (Invertible factors preserve rank) Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\). If \(P\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) is invertible then \(\operatorname{rank}(PA)=\operatorname{rank}(A)\), and if \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is invertible then \(\operatorname{rank}(AQ)=\operatorname{rank}(A)\). In particular elementary row operations preserve rank, and they preserve the null space \(\mathcal{N}(A)\) exactly.


Proof. Left multiplication. The map \(\mathbf{v}\mapsto P\mathbf{v}\) is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb{R}^m\) (invertible, hence bijective and linear). We have \(\mathcal{C}(PA)=\{PA\mathbf{x}:\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\}=P\big(\{A\mathbf{x}\}\big)=P\,\mathcal{C}(A)\), the image of \(\mathcal{C}(A)\) under the isomorphism \(P\). An isomorphism maps a basis of a subspace to a basis of its image (it preserves independence and spanning), so \(\dim P\,\mathcal{C}(A)=\dim\mathcal{C}(A)\), giving \(\operatorname{rank}(PA)=\operatorname{rank}(A)\). Moreover, since \(P\) is invertible, \(PA\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\iff A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\), so \(\mathcal{N}(PA)=\mathcal{N}(A)\) exactly.
Right multiplication. Because \(Q\) is invertible, the map \(\mathbf{x}\mapsto Q\mathbf{x}\) is onto \(\mathbb{R}^n\), so as \(\mathbf{x}\) ranges over \(\mathbb{R}^n\) so does \(Q\mathbf{x}\); hence \(\mathcal{C}(AQ)=\{A(Q\mathbf{x})\}=\{A\mathbf{u}:\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^n\}=\mathcal{C}(A)\), and a fortiori the dimensions agree. Elementary row operations are left multiplications by invertible elementary matrices, so they preserve both rank and null space. \(\square\)

By Gaussian elimination, every matrix can be brought by elementary row operations to a row-echelon form. Two terms suffice. A pivot is the first (leftmost) nonzero entry of a nonzero row. A matrix is in row-echelon form when it is a staircase: every pivot sits strictly to the right of the pivot in the row above, and any all-zero rows are at the bottom. It is in reduced row-echelon form (RREF) when, in addition, every pivot equals \(1\) and is the only nonzero entry in its column. The pivots fall in certain columns of the original matrix, called the pivot columns. The existence of these forms is the elimination algorithm; we take it as standard and refer the reader to Strang (2016) for the procedure. What matters here is that the pivots count the rank, which we first see on a concrete matrix and then prove.

Example 1.7 (Rank, null space, and a column-space basis by elimination) Take \[
B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&2\\1&2&3\\2&3&5\end{pmatrix}.
\] Eliminate below the first pivot (the \(1\) in position \(1,1\)): replace row \(2\) by (row \(2\) \(-\) row \(1\)) and row \(3\) by (row \(3\) \(-2\cdot\) row \(1\)), \[
\begin{pmatrix}1&1&2\\1&2&3\\2&3&5\end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow
\begin{pmatrix}1&1&2\\0&1&1\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\] Now eliminate below the second pivot (the \(1\) in position \(2,2\)): replace row \(3\) by (row \(3\) \(-\) row \(2\)), giving the row-echelon form \[
U=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&2\\0&1&1\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\] There are two pivots, in columns \(1\) and \(2\), so \(\operatorname{rank}(B)=2\) and (by Theorem 1.3) \(\dim\mathcal{N}(B)=3-2=1\). Clearing above the second pivot (row \(1\) \(-\) row \(2\)) reaches the reduced form \[
R=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Null space. Column \(3\) has no pivot, so \(x_3\) is a free variable. Reading \(R\), the equations are \(x_1+x_3=0\) and \(x_2+x_3=0\), so \(x_1=-x_3\) and \(x_2=-x_3\). Setting \(x_3=1\) gives the basis \(\mathcal{N}(B)=\operatorname{span}\{(-1,-1,1)^\top\}\), of dimension \(1\), as predicted.
Column-space basis. The pivot columns are columns \(1\) and \(2\), so the corresponding columns of the original \(B\), namely \((1,1,2)^\top\) and \((1,2,3)^\top\), form a basis of \(\mathcal{C}(B)\). (This is the deletion scan of Lemma 1.7 in action: column \(3\) is discarded because \((2,3,5)^\top=(1,1,2)^\top+(1,2,3)^\top\) lies in the span of its predecessors.)
Row-space basis. The nonzero rows of \(U\), namely \((1,1,2)\) and \((0,1,1)\), form a basis of the row space \(\mathcal{C}(B^\top)\), again of dimension \(2=\operatorname{rank}(B)\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Proposition 1.3 (Rank equals the number of pivots) Let \(U\) be a row-echelon form of \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), obtained by elementary row operations. Then the nonzero rows of \(U\) form a basis of the row space \(\mathcal{C}(A^\top)\), and consequently \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\) equals the number of pivots (nonzero rows) of \(U\).


Proof. Row operations are invertible left multiplications, so by the argument of Lemma 1.13 applied to \(A^\top\) they do not change the row space: the rows of \(U\) and the rows of \(A\) span the same subspace \(\mathcal{C}(A^\top)\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). (Each row of \(U\) is a linear combination of rows of \(A\) and vice versa, since the operations are reversible.) Hence the nonzero rows of \(U\) span \(\mathcal{C}(A^\top)\).
They are also independent. Suppose \(\mathbf{u}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{u}^{(s)}\) are the nonzero rows, with the pivot of \(\mathbf{u}^{(t)}\) in column \(p_t\), where \(p_1<p_2<\dots<p_s\) by the echelon staircase. Suppose \(\sum_{t=1}^s c_t\mathbf{u}^{(t)}=\mathbf{0}\). Look at column \(p_1\), the leftmost pivot column: only \(\mathbf{u}^{(1)}\) has a nonzero entry there (every later row has zeros in all columns up to and including its predecessors’ pivots, in particular in column \(p_1\)), so the \(p_1\)-entry of the combination is \(c_1\,U_{1,p_1}=0\) with \(U_{1,p_1}\neq 0\), forcing \(c_1=0\). With \(c_1=0\), repeat at column \(p_2\) to get \(c_2=0\), and so on; all \(c_t=0\). Thus the nonzero rows are independent and form a basis of \(\mathcal{C}(A^\top)\), whose dimension is \(\operatorname{rank}(A^\top)=\operatorname{rank}(A)\) by Theorem 1.4. The number of nonzero rows is the number \(s\) of pivots. \(\square\)

Why this matters. This is the practical face of rank. To find how many independent effects a design can resolve, run elimination and count pivots; the pivot columns name a non-redundant set of model columns, and the free (non-pivot) columns are exactly the redundant ones responsible for any non-identifiability. The next time software reports a “rank-deficient model matrix,” it has found fewer pivots than columns.

title: 1  Linear Algebra I: Vector Spaces, Linear Maps, and Rank
text:
1.12 Characterizations of invertibility
A square matrix is invertible when it has a two-sided multiplicative inverse. For square matrices a remarkable collapse occurs: a long list of a priori distinct conditions, about solutions, columns, rank, and one-sided inverses, are all equivalent. This theorem is used constantly, for instance to certify that the normal-equations matrix \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) of regression can be inverted.

Definition 1.11 (Invertible matrix) A matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is invertible (or nonsingular) if there exists \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) with \(AB=BA=I_n\). Such a \(B\) is unique when it exists: if \(AB=BA=I_n\) and \(AB'=B'A=I_n\) then \(B=BI_n=B(AB')=(BA)B'=I_nB'=B'\). We write \(B=A^{-1}\).

What this means. “Invertible” means the matrix can be perfectly undone: \(A^{-1}\) exactly reverses what \(A\) does, so \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) can always be solved by \(\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}\). The synonym nonsingular means precisely the same thing; this book uses “invertible” throughout, and the two words may be read interchangeably whenever a source you consult prefers the other.
The next theorem lists ten conditions that are all equivalent to invertibility. That is a lot to hold in mind at once, so before the statement here is a map. The conditions fall into four groups that say the same thing in four languages, and the proof links the groups along a short cycle of implications.








Group
Conditions
What the group says




Inverse conditions
(1), (2), (3), (10)
a genuine inverse exists (two-sided, or one-sided; and \(A^\top\) inverts too)


Rank conditions
(4), (5), (6), (7)
the columns are independent and span; the rank is full


Solution conditions
(8), (9)
every system \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) has exactly one solution; the map is a bijection



The proof establishes the arrows in the following table; together they form cycles that link all ten conditions, so any one implies every other.







Implication proved
Role




(4) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (5) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (7) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (6)
the rank group is internally equivalent


(4),(6) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (9) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (8)
ties the rank group to the solution group


(9) \(\Rightarrow\) (1)
a bijection has a linear inverse matrix


(1) \(\Rightarrow\) (2) and (1) \(\Rightarrow\) (3)
a genuine inverse is in particular one-sided


(2) \(\Rightarrow\) (4)
a left inverse kills the null space


(3) \(\Rightarrow\) (6)
a right inverse forces the columns to span


(1) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (10)
transpose




Theorem 1.6 (Characterizations of invertibility) For a square matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), the following are equivalent.

\(A\) is invertible.
\(A\) has a left inverse: \(BA=I_n\) for some \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\).
\(A\) has a right inverse: \(AC=I_n\) for some \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\).
\(\mathcal{N}(A)=\{\mathbf{0}\}\); equivalently \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\) has only the trivial solution.
The columns of \(A\) are linearly independent.
The columns of \(A\) span \(\mathbb{R}^n\), that is, \(\mathcal{C}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\) (\(A\) has full rank).
For every \(\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the system \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) has a unique solution.
The linear map \(T_A\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is a bijection.
\(A^\top\) is invertible.

Each of these is moreover equivalent to \(\det(A)\neq 0\); we take this last equivalence from the theory of determinants (Strang (2016), Chapter 5) rather than reproving it here.


Proof. We first establish the equivalence of (4) through (9), which is pure rank-nullity, and then close the loop through the inverse conditions (1), (2), (3), and (10).
(4) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (5) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (7) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (6). By Proposition 1.2(3), \(\mathcal{N}(A)=\{\mathbf{0}\}\) is the same statement as the columns being independent, giving (4) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (5). The matrix rank-nullity theorem Theorem 1.3 for the square \(A\) reads \(\operatorname{rank}(A)+\dim\mathcal{N}(A)=n\), so \(\mathcal{N}(A)=\{\mathbf{0}\}\) if and only if \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\), giving (4) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (7). Finally \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=\dim\mathcal{C}(A)\) and \(\mathcal{C}(A)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), so \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\) if and only if \(\mathcal{C}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n\) (a subspace of full dimension is the whole space), giving (7) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (6).
(4),(6) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (9) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (8). The map \(T_A\) is injective if and only if \(\ker T_A=\mathcal{N}(A)=\{\mathbf{0}\}\) (Lemma 1.10), that is, condition (4); it is surjective if and only if \(\operatorname{im}T_A=\mathcal{C}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n\), that is, condition (6). Hence \(T_A\) is bijective, condition (9), if and only if both (4) and (6) hold; but we have just shown (4) and (6) are equivalent to each other, so any one of them is equivalent to (9). Bijectivity of \(T_A\) is the statement that \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) has exactly one solution for each \(\mathbf{b}\), condition (8). Thus (8) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (9).
(9) \(\Rightarrow\) (1). If \(T_A\) is a bijection it has an inverse function \(T_A^{-1}\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\). This inverse is linear: for \(\mathbf{u}=T_A\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{v}=T_A\mathbf{y}\), \(T_A^{-1}(a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{v})=T_A^{-1}\big(T_A(a\mathbf{x}+b\mathbf{y})\big)=a\mathbf{x}+b\mathbf{y}
=a\,T_A^{-1}\mathbf{u}+b\,T_A^{-1}\mathbf{v}\). By Proposition 1.1 it is \(T_B\) for a matrix \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\). Then \(T_A\circ T_B=T_B\circ T_A=\mathrm{id}\), and by Theorem 1.2 this says \(AB=BA=I_n\). So \(A\) is invertible.
(1) \(\Rightarrow\) (2) and (1) \(\Rightarrow\) (3). Immediate: \(A^{-1}\) is both a left and a right inverse.
(2) \(\Rightarrow\) (4). Suppose \(BA=I_n\). If \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\) then \(\mathbf{x}=I_n\mathbf{x}=BA\mathbf{x}=B\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{0}\), so \(\mathcal{N}(A)=\{\mathbf{0}\}\).
(3) \(\Rightarrow\) (6). Suppose \(AC=I_n\). For any \(\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(A(C\mathbf{b})=(AC)\mathbf{b}=I_n\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}\), so \(\mathbf{b}\in\mathcal{C}(A)\); hence \(\mathcal{C}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n\).
These implications close the loop. Indeed (2) \(\Rightarrow\) (4) \(\Rightarrow\) (9) \(\Rightarrow\) (1) \(\Rightarrow\) (2), so (1), (2), (4), (9) are equivalent; and (3) \(\Rightarrow\) (6) \(\Rightarrow\) (9) \(\Rightarrow\) (1) \(\Rightarrow\) (3), folding in (3). Together with the chain of the first two paragraphs, all of (1) through (9) are equivalent.
(1) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (10). If \(AB=BA=I_n\), transpose: \(B^\top A^\top=A^\top B^\top=I_n^\top=I_n\), so \(A^\top\) is invertible with \((A^\top)^{-1}=(A^{-1})^\top\). The converse applies the same to \(A^\top\), whose transpose is \(A\). (Equivalently, \(\operatorname{rank}(A^\top)=\operatorname{rank}(A)\) by Theorem 1.4, so \(A\) has full rank if and only if \(A^\top\) does, conditions (7) for each.) \(\square\)

Why this matters. This theorem is the workhorse behind “the treatment effect is uniquely estimable.” In Chapter 6 the least-squares coefficients solve \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\), which has a unique solution exactly when the \(p\times p\) matrix \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) is invertible, that is (condition 7) when it has full rank, which Exercise Exercise 1.13 shows happens precisely when \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank. So “the columns of the design are independent” (no dummy-variable trap) and “the treatment effect has a unique estimate” are, through this chain of equivalences, the same statement.

Remark. Two observations sharpen the theorem. First, for square matrices a one-sided inverse is automatically two-sided: if \(BA=I_n\) then, by the proof, \(A\) is invertible, and \(B=B(AA^{-1})=(BA)A^{-1}=A^{-1}\), so \(B\) is the genuine inverse; symmetrically for a right inverse. This is special to square matrices and fails for rectangular ones. Second, the determinant condition links to the spectral theory of Chapter 3: \(A\) is invertible if and only if \(0\) is not an eigenvalue, because \(\mathcal{N}(A)\neq\{\mathbf{0}\}\) is exactly the existence of a nonzero \(\mathbf{x}\) with \(A\mathbf{x}=0\cdot\mathbf{x}\). The singular value decomposition Theorem 3.7 makes the same statement through singular values: \(A\) is invertible if and only if all \(n\) singular values are positive.

section: 1.13 A worked example: the two-arm design matrix
text:
1.13 A worked example: the two-arm design matrix
We close by analyzing in full the very matrix that opened the chapter in Section 1.2, now with every tool in hand. The computation can be verified entirely by hand and previews the regression machinery of Chapter 6. Recall the tiny clinical comparison: four patients, the first two on control and the last two on an active treatment. We model an outcome with an intercept (a common baseline) and a treatment indicator. The design matrix, with first column the intercept \(\mathbf{1}_4\) and second column the treatment indicator \(\mathbf{t}=(0,0,1,1)^\top\), is \[
\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\\1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 2},
\qquad
\boldsymbol\beta=\begin{pmatrix}\beta_0\\\beta_1\end{pmatrix},
\] so that \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_0,\beta_0+\beta_1,\beta_0+\beta_1)^\top\): every control patient is predicted to have outcome \(\beta_0\) and every treated patient \(\beta_0+\beta_1\), making \(\beta_1\) the treatment effect.

Example 1.8 (Four subspaces of a two-arm design) We compute, for the matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) above (here \(m=4\), \(n=p=2\)), all four fundamental subspaces, the rank, and the consequences for solving \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf{y}\).
Rank. The two columns \(\mathbf{1}_4\) and \(\mathbf{t}\) are not scalar multiples of each other, so they are linearly independent and \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X})=2\). As \(n=p=2\), the matrix has full column rank.
Column space. \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{1}_4,\mathbf{t}\}\subseteq
\mathbb{R}^4\) is two-dimensional. A vector \(\mathbf{v}=(v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4)^\top\) lies in it if and only if \(\mathbf{v}=\beta_0\mathbf{1}_4+\beta_1\mathbf{t}\) for some scalars, that is, \(v_1=v_2=\beta_0\) and \(v_3=v_4=\beta_0+\beta_1\). So the column space is exactly the set of vectors that are constant within each treatment group.
Null space. Solve \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf{0}\). Reading the rows, \(\beta_0=0\) and \(\beta_0+\beta_1=0\), hence \(\beta_0=\beta_1=0\). Thus \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})=\{\mathbf{0}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\), of dimension \(0\). Rank-nullity checks out: \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X})+\dim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})=2+0=2=p\).
Row space. \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\) is spanned by the rows \((1,0)\) and \((1,1)\) (the distinct rows of \(\mathbf{X}\)). These are independent, so the row space is all of \(\mathbb{R}^2\), of dimension \(2=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X})\), as Theorem 1.5 requires.
Left null space. By Equation 1.5 its dimension is \(m-r=4-2=2\). A vector \(\mathbf{y}=(y_1,y_2,y_3,y_4)^\top\) lies in \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top)\) if and only if it is orthogonal to both columns: \(\mathbf{1}_4^\top\mathbf{y}=y_1+y_2+y_3+y_4=0\) and \(\mathbf{t}^\top\mathbf{y}=y_3+y_4=0\). The second equation gives \(y_4=-y_3\), and substituting into the first gives \(y_1+y_2=0\), so \(y_2=-y_1\). Hence \[
\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top)=\operatorname{span}\Big\{(1,-1,0,0)^\top,\ (0,0,1,-1)^\top\Big\},
\] the within-group mean-zero contrasts. One verifies directly that each basis vector is orthogonal to \(\mathbf{1}_4\) and to \(\mathbf{t}\), confirming \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top)=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})^\perp\) of Equation 1.6.
Solvability. By Proposition 1.2(1), \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf{y}\) has a solution if and only if \(\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})\), that is, if and only if \(y_1=y_2\) and \(y_3=y_4\). Real outcome data almost never satisfy this, which is the whole reason we project the data onto \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})\) and solve in the least-squares sense; that projection is the subject of Chapter 2, and the resulting estimator is the ordinary least squares estimator of Chapter 6. When a solution does exist it is unique here, because \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})=\{\mathbf{0}\}\) (Proposition 1.2(3)).
The normal-equations matrix. Anticipating Chapter 6, compute the Gram matrix \[
\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}=
\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{1}_4^\top\mathbf{1}_4 & \mathbf{1}_4^\top\mathbf{t}\\
\mathbf{t}^\top\mathbf{1}_4 & \mathbf{t}^\top\mathbf{t}\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \det(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=4\cdot 2-2\cdot 2=4\neq 0 .
\] Because \(\det\neq 0\), the matrix is invertible by Theorem 1.6, with \[
(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\-2&4\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac12 & -\tfrac12\\[2pt] -\tfrac12 & 1\end{pmatrix}.
\] (One checks \(\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac12&-\tfrac12\\-\tfrac12&1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) by hand.) The invertibility of \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) is no accident: it holds exactly because \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank, the equivalence proved in general in Exercise Exercise 1.13. This is the precise condition under which the regression coefficients, and hence the treatment effect \(\beta_1\), are uniquely estimable. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark (Collinearity and non-identifiability). Suppose we had instead included a redundant third column, the control indicator \(\mathbf{c}=(1,1,0,0)^\top=\mathbf{1}_4-\mathbf{t}\), forming \(\mathbf{X}'=[\mathbf{1}_4\ \ \mathbf{t}\ \ \mathbf{c}]\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 3}\). Now the columns satisfy the linear dependence \(\mathbf{1}_4-\mathbf{t}-\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{0}\), so \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}')\ni(1,-1,-1)^\top\neq\mathbf{0}\) and one computes \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}')=\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1,-1)^\top\}\), of dimension \(1\). By rank-nullity \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}')=3-1=2\): adding the column did not raise the rank. Consequently \(\mathbf{X}'^\top\mathbf{X}'\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}\) has rank \(2<3\) and is not invertible, so the normal equations no longer pin down a unique coefficient vector. Concretely, as computed in Example 1.6, the distinct coefficient vectors \((0,1,0)^\top\) and \((1,0,-1)^\top\) produce the identical fitted values \((0,0,1,1)^\top\), so no data can choose between them. This is the “dummy variable trap”: the intercept and the two group indicators are collinear, and the treatment effect is identifiable only as the contrast \(\beta_{\text{trt}}-\beta_{\text{ctrl}}\), a linear functional that is constant along the null direction \((1,-1,-1)^\top\). The remedy practiced everywhere in this book, dropping one indicator, is exactly the restoration of full column rank. Identifiability in indirect comparison is, at bottom, this same statement about null spaces.

title: 1  Linear Algebra I: Vector Spaces, Linear Maps, and Rank
text:
1.14 Notes and references
The development of vector spaces, bases, and dimension through the Steinitz exchange theorem (Theorem 1.1) is classical and is treated in any linear-algebra text; we follow the spirit of Strang (2016), the standard reference for the applied theory and the origin of the “four fundamental subspaces” organizing picture (Definition 1.10, Theorem 1.5). The rank factorization Equation 1.4 used to prove that row rank equals column rank (Theorem 1.4) is standard; the proof given here is self-contained. The rank-nullity theorem (Theorem 1.3) is the load-bearing result of the chapter and is proved in full; everything in later chapters that counts degrees of freedom, from the residual degrees of freedom of regression to the dimension of an estimable contrast space, is an application of it.
We have stated the orthogonality of the four subspaces (Equation 1.6) and proved the elementary set-equalities, but deferred the projection geometry that realizes the orthogonal decomposition \(\mathbb{R}^n=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)\oplus\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})\) to the orthogonal projection theorem Theorem 2.5 and the Gram-Schmidt construction Theorem 2.3 of Chapter 2. The existence and algorithm of (reduced) row-echelon form, used in Proposition 1.3, and the determinant characterization of invertibility in Theorem 1.6, are taken from Strang (2016) rather than reproved; full determinant theory is not needed in this book beyond this one equivalence, and the eigenvalue and singular-value characterizations of invertibility are returned to in Chapter 3 (Theorem 3.2, Theorem 3.7, Theorem 3.3). The design-matrix example of Section 1.13 is the seed of the linear-model theory developed from first principles in Chapter 6 (Definition 6.1, Theorem 6.1, Definition 6.3); the invertibility of \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) under full column rank, previewed there and proved in Exercise Exercise 1.13, is the algebraic precondition for the existence and uniqueness of the least-squares estimator.
This chapter has no counterpart in the ITC_Coq development and therefore carries no machine-checked tags.

title: 1  Linear Algebra I: Vector Spaces, Linear Maps, and Rank
text:
1.15 Exercises
Exercises marked with a star (\(\star\)) have a full worked solution in Appendix F. The tag after each title flags its flavor: warm-up and interpretation exercises need only the ideas, not heavy algebra, and are the place to start; computation exercises ask you to grind a small example by hand; proof and starred challenge exercises build machinery used later in the book. Begin with the warm-ups, which use the running two-arm trial of Section 1.2.

Exercise 1.1 (Fitted values by hand (warm-up)) Using the running two-arm design \(\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\\1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) of Section 1.2 and the coefficient vector \(\boldsymbol\beta=(5,3)^\top\): (a) compute the fitted-value vector \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\) by hand. (b) Which patients share a predicted outcome, and why? (c) What is the predicted treatment effect, that is, the predicted treated outcome minus the predicted control outcome?


Exercise 1.2 (Spotting a redundant column (warm-up)) Consider the three columns \(\mathbf{1}_4=(1,1,1,1)^\top\), \(\mathbf{t}=(0,0,1,1)^\top\), and \(\mathbf{c}=(1,1,0,0)^\top\). (a) Write \(\mathbf{c}\) as a linear combination of \(\mathbf{1}_4\) and \(\mathbf{t}\). (b) Explain in one sentence why a design built from all three columns has rank \(2\), not \(3\). (c) In plain words, what goes wrong if you try to estimate a separate intercept, control effect, and treatment effect from these three columns?


Exercise 1.3 (Which effect can you estimate? (interpretation)) A trialist fits an outcome model with an intercept, a control-group indicator, and a treatment-group indicator, and is surprised the software cannot return unique estimates of the three coefficients. (a) Identify the null-space direction responsible (see Section 1.10.1). (b) Explain which single quantity built from the coefficients is determined by the data, and why, referring to Example 1.6. (c) State the one-line fix and say what, if anything, is lost.


Exercise 1.4 (Computing the four subspaces (computation)) Let \[
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\2&4&3\\3&6&4\end{pmatrix}.
\] (a) Show that \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=2\) by exhibiting a dependence among the rows and among the columns. (b) Find a basis and the dimension of each of \(\mathcal{C}(A)\), \(\mathcal{C}(A^\top)\), \(\mathcal{N}(A)\), and \(\mathcal{N}(A^\top)\). (c) Verify the dimension counts of Theorem 1.5 and check explicitly that your null-space basis vector is orthogonal to your row-space basis vectors.


Exercise 1.5 (Rank by elimination (computation)) Bring the matrix \(A\) of Exercise 1.4 to reduced row-echelon form by elementary row operations, and confirm that the number of pivots equals the rank you found, as guaranteed by Proposition 1.3. Use the pivot columns to read off a basis of \(\mathcal{C}(A)\) consisting of columns of \(A\). (Worked template: Example 1.7.)


Exercise 1.6 (Intersections, unions, and sums of subspaces (proof)) Let \(U\) and \(W\) be subspaces of a vector space \(V\). (a) Prove that \(U\cap W\) is a subspace. (b) Give an explicit example of two subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) whose union is not a subspace. (c) Prove that the sum \(U+W=\{\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}:\mathbf{u}\in U,\ \mathbf{w}\in W\}\) is a subspace, and is the smallest subspace containing \(U\cup W\).


Exercise 1.7 (The dummy-variable trap (computation and interpretation)) For the augmented design \(\mathbf{X}'=[\mathbf{1}_4\ \ \mathbf{t}\ \ \mathbf{c}]\) of the remark in Section 1.13, with \(\mathbf{t}=(0,0,1,1)^\top\) and \(\mathbf{c}=(1,1,0,0)^\top\): (a) verify that \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}')=\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1,-1)^\top\}\); (b) compute \(\mathbf{X}'^\top\mathbf{X}'\) and show it is singular by exhibiting a nonzero vector in its null space; (c) explain, using Proposition 1.2, why the individual coefficients are not identifiable while the contrast \(\beta_{\mathbf{t}}-\beta_{\mathbf{c}}\) is.


Exercise 1.8 (Rank of a product (proof)) Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\). (a) Prove that \(\mathcal{C}(AB)\subseteq\mathcal{C}(A)\) and \(\mathcal{N}(B)\subseteq\mathcal{N}(AB)\). (b) Deduce \(\operatorname{rank}(AB)\le\min\{\operatorname{rank}(A),\operatorname{rank}(B)\}\). (c) Show that if \(A\) has full column rank (its columns independent) then \(\operatorname{rank}(AB)=\operatorname{rank}(B)\), and if \(B\) has full row rank then \(\operatorname{rank}(AB)=\operatorname{rank}(A)\).


Exercise 1.9 (Rank-one matrices (proof)) Let \(\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonzero. (a) Prove that the outer product \(\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank exactly \(1\), and describe its column space and row space. (b) Conversely, prove that every matrix of rank \(1\) can be written as \(\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top\) for some nonzero \(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\). (Hint for (b): a rank-one matrix has a one-dimensional column space spanned by some \(\mathbf{u}\); express each column as a multiple of \(\mathbf{u}\).)


Exercise 1.10 (One-sided inverses of a square matrix (proof)) Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\). Prove directly from Theorem 1.6 that if \(A\) has a right inverse \(C\) with \(AC=I_n\), then \(A\) is invertible and \(C=A^{-1}\). Then give a \(2\times 3\) matrix \(A\) and a \(3\times 2\) matrix \(C\) with \(AC=I_2\) but \(CA\neq I_3\), showing that the square hypothesis is essential.


Exercise 1.11 (Linear maps are matrices (proof)) Without appealing to Proposition 1.1, prove from Lemma 1.11 that every linear map \(T\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) equals \(T_A\) for a unique \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and identify the columns of \(A\). Then prove that \(T\) is injective if and only if the columns of \(A\) are independent, and surjective if and only if they span \(\mathbb{R}^m\).


Exercise 1.12 (Dimension of a sum (starred challenge)) \(\star\) Let \(U\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional subspaces of a vector space \(V\). Prove the dimension formula \[
\dim(U+W)=\dim U+\dim W-\dim(U\cap W).
\] (Hint: start from a basis of \(U\cap W\) and extend it, using Lemma 1.8, to a basis of \(U\) and separately to a basis of \(W\); prove that the combined list is a basis of \(U+W\).) A solution appears in Appendix F.


Exercise 1.13 (The Gram matrix and full column rank (starred challenge)) \(\star\) Let \(\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\). (a) Prove that \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})\). (Hint: if \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\), consider \(\mathbf{v}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}\|_2^2\).) (b) Deduce that \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X})\), and hence that the \(p\times p\) Gram matrix \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) is invertible if and only if \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank \(p\). (c) Conclude that the normal-equations system \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\) has a unique solution exactly when \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank, the algebraic foundation of ordinary least squares developed in Chapter 6. A solution appears in Appendix F.





Strang, Gilbert. 2016. Introduction to Linear Algebra. 5th ed. Wellesley-Cambridge Press.

title: 2  Linear Algebra II: Orthogonality and the Projection Theorem
text:
2.1 Why orthogonality is the engine of indirect comparison
Almost every method in this book ends, at its computational core, in a least-squares problem: fit a linear or generalized-linear model to data, read off a contrast of coefficients, and propagate its uncertainty. Simulated treatment comparison (STC) fits an outcome regression and predicts into a target population; multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR) fits a shared regression across studies; matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) reweights one trial so that its covariate moments match another, which is again a constrained least-squares idea in disguise. Underneath all of them sits one geometric fact: the best approximation of a data vector by the vectors a model can produce is the orthogonal projection of the data onto the model’s column space, and the error of that approximation is orthogonal to everything the model can explain.
This chapter develops that fact from the ground up. Chapter 1 gave us vector spaces, linear maps, the column space Definition 1.10, and the rank-nullity theorem Theorem 1.3. Here we add length and angle through an inner product, prove the two inequalities that make geometry work (Cauchy-Schwarz and the triangle inequality), and build orthonormal bases with the Gram-Schmidt process. The centerpiece is the projection theorem Theorem 2.5: in a finite-dimensional subspace there is a unique closest point to any target vector, and it is characterized by the residual being orthogonal to the subspace. From this single theorem we derive the normal equations Theorem 2.7, the algebraic identity that Chapter 6 turns into the ordinary-least-squares estimator, and the QR factorization Theorem 2.8, the numerically sound way software actually solves them. Every result that later chapters lean on is proved here in full.

title: 2  Linear Algebra II: Orthogonality and the Projection Theorem
text:
2.1.1 Typeface conventions and symbols recalled from Chapter 1
Throughout, vectors are bold lowercase (\(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{q}\)). For matrices we follow two typeface conventions of Notation, and it is worth fixing them now because both kinds can appear on the same line later. A matrix that holds data or model structure is bold uppercase (\(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{R},\mathbf{X}\)). A matrix whose job is to act on vectors as an operator is set in light (non-bold) uppercase (\(I_n\) the identity, \(P_{\mathcal{M}}\) a projection, \(H\) the hat matrix). For example, in the hat matrix \(H=\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\) the data matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) is bold while the operator it builds, \(H\), is light. A quick test settles every case: if you could fill the entries from a spreadsheet of patients and covariates, the matrix is bold; if its entire purpose is to turn one vector into another, it is light.








Typeface
Symbols
What the matrix is




Bold uppercase
\(\mathbf{A},\ \mathbf{X},\ \mathbf{Q},\ \mathbf{R}\)
data or factor matrices; entries come from a dataset or a factorization


Light uppercase
\(I_n,\ P_{\mathcal{M}},\ H,\ M\)
operator matrices; they map vectors to vectors



We work over the real field \(\mathbb{R}\) throughout. This chapter also reuses five symbols from Chapter 1. Here is a one-line reminder of each; if any is unfamiliar, the cross-reference points to its full definition, and you do not need anything else from Chapter 1 to read on.








Symbol
Read as
Meaning (from Chapter 1)




\(\operatorname{span}(S)\)
“span of \(S\)”
all linear combinations of the vectors in \(S\)


\(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})\)
“rank of \(\mathbf{A}\)”
the number of linearly independent columns of \(\mathbf{A}\) (Theorem 1.3)


\(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})\)
“column space of \(\mathbf{A}\)”
all vectors \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\): everything the columns can build (Definition 1.10)


\(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\)
“null space of \(\mathbf{A}\)”
all \(\mathbf{x}\) with \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\) (Theorem 1.3)


\(\dim\mathcal{M}\)
“dimension of \(\mathcal{M}\)”
the number of vectors in any basis of the subspace \(\mathcal{M}\)





2.1.2 A trial we will carry through the chapter
The next three sections build a small vocabulary: length, angle, perpendicularity, and a way to manufacture perpendicular reference directions. The single purpose of that vocabulary is to make the phrase “the prediction closest to the data” mean something exact. To keep that goal in sight, we open with a concrete trial and return to it after every new tool, finishing it once the projection theorem is in hand.

Example 2.1 (A two-arm trial we will carry through the chapter) Four patients enter a trial; the first two receive control and the last two receive the active treatment. Their outcomes (say a symptom score, where higher is worse) are \[
\mathbf{y}=(1,\,3,\,6,\,8)^\top .
\] A model that allows a separate mean in each arm has the design matrix of Chapter 1’s Example 1.8: an intercept column \(\mathbf{1}_4=(1,1,1,1)^\top\) and a treatment indicator \(\mathbf{t}=(0,0,1,1)^\top\), \[
\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\\1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\boldsymbol\beta=\begin{pmatrix}\beta_0\\\beta_1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=\begin{pmatrix}\beta_0\\\beta_0\\\beta_0+\beta_1\\\beta_0+\beta_1\end{pmatrix}.
\] Every prediction the model can make is constant within each arm: control patients all receive \(\beta_0\), treated patients all receive \(\beta_0+\beta_1\). The set of all such prediction vectors is exactly the column space \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})\) of Chapter 1, the “vectors the model can produce.”
The data \(\mathbf{y}=(1,3,6,8)^\top\) is not constant within each arm, so no choice of \(\boldsymbol\beta\) reproduces it exactly. The question this chapter answers is: among all constant-within-arm prediction vectors, which one is closest to \(\mathbf{y}\), and how would we recognize it? Intuition says “use each arm’s average,” giving control mean \(2\) and treated mean \(7\), hence the prediction \((2,2,7,7)^\top\) and an estimated treatment effect \(\hat\beta_1=7-2=5\). We will not assume this. We will prove that the arm means are the unique closest prediction, that the leftover errors \((-1,1,-1,1)^\top\) are perpendicular to everything the model can produce, and that this perpendicularity is the same statement as the familiar fact that least-squares residuals sum to zero within each group. Each section advances this example one step; Section 2.8 finishes it. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. A picture to hold onto (in place of a figure). Throughout the chapter, keep this mental image. The data vector \(\mathbf{v}\) is a point in space. The model’s reachable predictions \(\mathcal{M}\) form a flat sheet through the origin: a line, a plane, or a higher-dimensional flat. The best prediction is the point of the sheet directly “below” \(\mathbf{v}\), reached by dropping a perpendicular from \(\mathbf{v}\) to the sheet. The perpendicular segment is the residual; the foot of the perpendicular is the fitted value. Every theorem in this chapter is a precise statement about that perpendicular drop. The book targets a portable PDF engine, so figures are described in words rather than drawn; the numerical examples are chosen so you can sketch each picture yourself. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 2  Linear Algebra II: Orthogonality and the Projection Theorem
text:
2.2 Inner product spaces and norms
An abstract vector space in the sense of Definition 1.1 has addition and scaling but no notion of length or perpendicularity. An inner product supplies both. We front-load three definitions and two inequalities here; to keep them from feeling weightless, the section ends with a numerical example (Example 2.2) showing that “perpendicular” depends on which inner product you choose, the very idea that underlies MAIC’s matching geometry.

Definition 2.1 (Inner product space) Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(\mathbb{R}\). An inner product on \(V\) is a map \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}\) such that for all \(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\in V\) and all \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\):

(Symmetry) \(\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle=\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{u}\rangle\);
(Linearity in the first argument) \(\langle a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\rangle=a\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w}\rangle+b\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\rangle\);
(Positive definiteness) \(\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{u}\rangle\ge 0\), with equality if and only if \(\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0}\).

A real vector space carrying an inner product is an inner product space. By symmetry, linearity holds in the second argument as well, so \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) is bilinear, meaning linear in each slot separately when the other slot is held fixed.

Reader translation. An inner product is a numerical “agreement meter” between two vectors: large and positive when they point the same way, zero when they are perpendicular, negative when they oppose. It is the single extra ingredient that turns a bare vector space into one with lengths and angles, and therefore with a meaningful notion of “closest.” For data, \(\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle\) is the engine behind correlations, residual checks, and least squares.
The motivating example, and the default of Notation, is the Euclidean inner product on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), namely \(\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle=\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{y}=\sum_{i=1}^n x_iy_i\). Axioms (1) and (2) are immediate from the algebra of the transpose, and (3) holds because \(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}=\sum_i x_i^2\ge 0\) vanishes only when every \(x_i=0\).

Remark. Weighted inner products and the Mahalanobis distance. This is the most ITC-relevant idea in the section, so we develop it slowly. Call a symmetric matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) positive definite, written \(A\succ 0\), when \(\mathbf{x}^\top A\,\mathbf{x}>0\) for every \(\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}\); the full theory of such matrices is the business of Chapter 3 (Theorem 3.3), but that one-line definition is all we need here. For such an \(A\), the map \(\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle_A:=\mathbf{x}^\top A\,\mathbf{y}\) is an inner product: symmetry uses \(A^\top=A\), bilinearity is clear, and positive definiteness is exactly \(\mathbf{x}^\top A\,\mathbf{x}>0\) for \(\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}\). Its induced norm is the quadratic-form norm \(\|\mathbf{x}\|_A=\sqrt{\mathbf{x}^\top A\,\mathbf{x}}\) of Notation, so called because \(\mathbf{x}^\top A\,\mathbf{x}\) is a degree-two polynomial (a quadratic form) in the entries of \(\mathbf{x}\).
Taking \(A=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\), the inverse covariance of a covariate distribution, gives the Mahalanobis distance. In plain terms, the Mahalanobis distance of a patient’s covariate vector from the average patient measures how far that patient is from the center in standard-deviation-like units, after accounting for how spread out and how correlated the covariates are. A direction in which the population naturally varies a great deal is down-weighted (a large gap there is unremarkable); a direction in which patients barely vary is up-weighted (a small gap there is striking). Concretely, suppose age varies widely across a trial but a biomarker barely varies. Two patients who differ by ten years of age but share the biomarker are close in Mahalanobis distance, because age scatter is expected; two patients of the same age who differ sharply on the biomarker are far, because biomarker scatter is not. This is the geometry that MAIC uses to decide which trial population a reweighted sample resembles, developed in Part IV, and that the distance-matching methods of Part VI reuse. Everything proved in this chapter for a general inner product applies verbatim to these weighted geometries. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

A norm records the length of a vector. We define it abstractly, then attach one to every inner product.

Definition 2.2 (Norm and induced norm) A norm on a real vector space \(V\) is a function \(\|\cdot\|:V\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying, for all \(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in V\) and \(a\in\mathbb{R}\):

(Positivity) \(\|\mathbf{u}\|\ge 0\), with equality if and only if \(\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0}\);
(Absolute homogeneity) \(\|a\mathbf{u}\|=|a|\,\|\mathbf{u}\|\);
(Triangle inequality) \(\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\|\le\|\mathbf{u}\|+\|\mathbf{v}\|\).

The norm induced by an inner product is \(\|\mathbf{u}\|:=\sqrt{\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{u}\rangle}\), which is well defined because \(\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{u}\rangle\ge 0\).

Reader translation. A norm is just “length.” The induced norm measures a vector’s length as the square root of its inner product with itself, so \(\|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{m}\|\) is the straight-line distance from the data \(\mathbf{v}\) to a candidate prediction \(\mathbf{m}\). Minimizing that distance over all candidate predictions is precisely least squares.
The induced norm satisfies (1) and (2) at once: positivity is axiom (3) of Definition 2.1, and \(\|a\mathbf{u}\|=\sqrt{\langle a\mathbf{u},a\mathbf{u}\rangle}=\sqrt{a^2\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{u}\rangle}
=|a|\,\|\mathbf{u}\|\) by bilinearity. The triangle inequality is the only property requiring work, and it follows from the single most important inequality in the subject.

Theorem 2.1 (Cauchy-Schwarz inequality) For all vectors \(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\) in an inner product space, \[
|\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle|\le\|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|,
\tag{2.1}\] with equality if and only if \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) are linearly dependent.

The idea of the proof is worth stating before the symbols arrive. The quantity \(\|\mathbf{u}-t\mathbf{v}\|^2\) can never be negative, so as a quadratic in the real variable \(t\) it cannot dip below zero; a parabola opening upward that never goes negative has discriminant at most zero, and that discriminant turns out to be exactly the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The proof below makes that precise by plugging in the value of \(t\) that minimizes the quadratic.

Proof. If \(\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\) then both sides equal \(0\), and the pair \(\{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{0}\}\) is linearly dependent, so the statement holds. Assume \(\mathbf{v}\ne\mathbf{0}\), so \(\|\mathbf{v}\|^2>0\). For every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), positive definiteness gives \[
0\le\|\mathbf{u}-t\mathbf{v}\|^2
=\langle\mathbf{u}-t\mathbf{v},\,\mathbf{u}-t\mathbf{v}\rangle
=\|\mathbf{u}\|^2-2t\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle+t^2\|\mathbf{v}\|^2,
\] where the expansion uses bilinearity and symmetry. The right-hand side is a quadratic in \(t\) with positive leading coefficient. Differentiating it with respect to \(t\) and setting the derivative \(-2\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle+2t\|\mathbf{v}\|^2\) to zero shows it is minimized at \(t^\star=\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle/\|\mathbf{v}\|^2\). Substituting \(t^\star\) gives \[
0\le\|\mathbf{u}\|^2-\frac{\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle^2}{\|\mathbf{v}\|^2},
\] which rearranges to \(\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle^2\le\|\mathbf{u}\|^2\|\mathbf{v}\|^2\). Taking nonnegative square roots yields Equation 4.12.
For the equality case, the inequality above is an equality exactly when \(\|\mathbf{u}-t^\star\mathbf{v}\|^2=0\), that is, by positive definiteness, when \(\mathbf{u}=t^\star\mathbf{v}\); then \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) are linearly dependent. Conversely, if they are dependent and \(\mathbf{v}\ne\mathbf{0}\), then \(\mathbf{u}=c\mathbf{v}\) for some scalar \(c\), and both sides of Equation 4.12 equal \(|c|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|^2\). \(\square\)

Why this matters. Cauchy-Schwarz is the guardrail that makes “angle” and “distance” behave. Without it the cosine defined in the next section could exceed \(1\), and the triangle inequality (hence the very word “norm,” hence the meaning of “closest point”) would fail. Every least-squares, MAIC-balancing, and distance-matching argument in this book silently relies on having a genuine norm, which is what this one inequality secures.

Corollary 2.1 (Triangle inequality) For all \(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\) in an inner product space, \(\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\|\le\|\mathbf{u}\|+\|\mathbf{v}\|\). Consequently the induced norm of Definition 2.2 is a genuine norm.


Proof. Expanding and applying Theorem 2.1 to the cross term, \[
\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\|^2
=\|\mathbf{u}\|^2+2\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle+\|\mathbf{v}\|^2
\le\|\mathbf{u}\|^2+2\|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|+\|\mathbf{v}\|^2
=\bigl(\|\mathbf{u}\|+\|\mathbf{v}\|\bigr)^2 .
\] Both sides are nonnegative, so taking square roots gives the triangle inequality. Together with the positivity and homogeneity noted after Definition 2.2, this shows the induced norm satisfies all three norm axioms. \(\square\)

Picture in words. Draw the vector \(\mathbf{u}\), then draw \(\mathbf{v}\) starting where \(\mathbf{u}\) ends. The single arrow from the start of \(\mathbf{u}\) to the tip of \(\mathbf{v}\) is \(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\). The triangle inequality says the direct route (\(\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\|\)) is never longer than the two-leg detour (\(\|\mathbf{u}\|+\|\mathbf{v}\|\)): a straight line is the shortest path. When the two legs are perpendicular the triangle is a right triangle, and the inequality becomes the Pythagorean equality of Theorem 2.2 below.
A useful corollary of homogeneity is the reverse triangle inequality \(\bigl|\,\|\mathbf{u}\|-\|\mathbf{v}\|\,\bigr|\le\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\|\), obtained by applying Corollary 2.1 to \(\mathbf{u}=(\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v})+\mathbf{v}\) and symmetrically; we record it for later use without separate proof.
We can now make the promise of the section concrete: which vectors count as “perpendicular” depends on the inner product, not on the vectors alone.

Example 2.2 (Perpendicular depends on the inner product) Work in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and compare the Euclidean inner product with the weighted one \(\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle_A=\mathbf{x}^\top A\,\mathbf{y}\) for the positive definite diagonal matrix \[
A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\] Take \(\mathbf{x}=(1,1)^\top\) and \(\mathbf{y}=(1,-1)^\top\). Under the Euclidean inner product \(\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle=1\cdot1+1\cdot(-1)=0\), so the two vectors are perpendicular: the Euclidean angle is \(90^\circ\). Under the weighted inner product, \[
\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle_A=\mathbf{x}^\top A\,\mathbf{y}
=(1,1)\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}
=(1,1)\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\end{pmatrix}=2-1=1\ne 0,
\] so they are not perpendicular in the weighted geometry. Their weighted lengths are \(\|\mathbf{x}\|_A=\sqrt{2+1}=\sqrt3\) and \(\|\mathbf{y}\|_A=\sqrt{2+1}=\sqrt3\), so the weighted angle \(\vartheta_A\) satisfies \(\cos\vartheta_A=1/(\sqrt3\cdot\sqrt3)=\tfrac13\), about \(70.5^\circ\). Reweighting the first coordinate (here doubling its importance) literally bends the angles. This is exactly what a covariance weighting does in MAIC and in Mahalanobis matching: it changes which patients count as “close” and which directions of difference count as “large.” \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 2  Linear Algebra II: Orthogonality and the Projection Theorem
text:
2.3 Orthogonality and orthonormal sets
ITC connection. The orthonormal directions built in this section and the next are the reference axes in which the regression and matching solves of Parts IV and V become numerically stable; the same directions make a vector’s coordinates trivial to read off.
Cauchy-Schwarz lets us define the angle \(\vartheta\) between nonzero vectors by \(\cos\vartheta=\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle/(\|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|)\). This definition makes sense precisely because Theorem 2.1 guarantees the ratio lies in \([-1,1]\): indeed \(|\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle|\le\|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|\) is the statement that the ratio is between \(-1\) and \(1\), so its arccosine \(\vartheta\) exists. The single most useful angle is the right angle.

Definition 2.3 (Orthogonality) Two vectors are orthogonal, written \(\mathbf{u}\perp\mathbf{v}\), when \(\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle=0\). A set \(S\subseteq V\) is orthogonal when its elements are pairwise orthogonal, and orthonormal when additionally every element has unit norm, that is, \(\langle\mathbf{q}_i,\mathbf{q}_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\) for the members \(\mathbf{q}_i\) of \(S\), where \(\delta_{ij}=1\) if \(i=j\) and \(\delta_{ij}=0\) otherwise (the Kronecker delta). A vector is orthogonal to a subspace \(\mathcal{M}\), written \(\mathbf{u}\perp\mathcal{M}\), when \(\mathbf{u}\perp\mathbf{m}\) for every \(\mathbf{m}\in\mathcal{M}\).

Reader translation. Orthogonal means perpendicular: a zero inner product. An orthonormal set is a collection of perpendicular unit-length directions, the cleanest possible reference frame. For data, a residual being orthogonal to the model will mean the error carries no pattern the model could have used, which is exactly the optimality condition for least squares.

Theorem 2.2 (Pythagorean theorem) If \(\mathbf{u}\perp\mathbf{v}\) then \(\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\|^2=\|\mathbf{u}\|^2+\|\mathbf{v}\|^2\). More generally, if \(\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_k\) are pairwise orthogonal, then \[
\Bigl\|\sum_{i=1}^k\mathbf{u}_i\Bigr\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^k\|\mathbf{u}_i\|^2.
\tag{2.2}\]


Proof. By bilinearity, \(\bigl\|\sum_i\mathbf{u}_i\bigr\|^2=\sum_{i}\sum_{j}\langle\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{u}_j\rangle\). Every term with \(i\ne j\) vanishes by pairwise orthogonality, leaving \(\sum_i\langle\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{u}_i\rangle=\sum_i\|\mathbf{u}_i\|^2\). \(\square\)

Why this matters. Squared lengths of mutually perpendicular pieces simply add. This is the engine behind “total variation = explained variation + unexplained variation,” the decomposition that defines \(R^2\) in Chapter 6 and that the projection theorem will deliver for free.
Orthonormality is a strong form of independence and makes coordinates trivial to read off.

Lemma 2.1 (Orthonormal sets are linearly independent) Every orthonormal set \(\{\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_k\}\) is linearly independent.


Proof. Suppose \(\sum_{i=1}^k c_i\mathbf{q}_i=\mathbf{0}\). Taking the inner product of both sides with \(\mathbf{q}_j\) and using \(\langle\mathbf{q}_i,\mathbf{q}_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\) gives \(0=\sum_i c_i\langle\mathbf{q}_i,\mathbf{q}_j\rangle=c_j\). As \(j\) was arbitrary, every \(c_j=0\). \(\square\)


Proposition 2.1 (Coordinates in an orthonormal basis) Let \(\{\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_k\}\) be an orthonormal basis of a subspace \(\mathcal{M}\). Then every \(\mathbf{m}\in\mathcal{M}\) satisfies \[
\mathbf{m}=\sum_{i=1}^k\langle\mathbf{m},\mathbf{q}_i\rangle\,\mathbf{q}_i,
\qquad
\|\mathbf{m}\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^k\langle\mathbf{m},\mathbf{q}_i\rangle^2 .
\tag{2.3}\]


Proof. Because \(\{\mathbf{q}_i\}\) is a basis of \(\mathcal{M}\), write \(\mathbf{m}=\sum_i c_i\mathbf{q}_i\) for unique scalars \(c_i\). Taking the inner product with \(\mathbf{q}_j\) gives \(\langle\mathbf{m},\mathbf{q}_j\rangle=\sum_i c_i\langle\mathbf{q}_i,\mathbf{q}_j\rangle=c_j\), which is the first identity. The second (Parseval’s identity) is the Pythagorean theorem Theorem 2.2 applied to the pairwise orthogonal vectors \(c_i\mathbf{q}_i\), using \(\|c_i\mathbf{q}_i\|^2=c_i^2\). \(\square\)

Reader translation. In an orthonormal basis the coordinate of \(\mathbf{m}\) along direction \(\mathbf{q}_i\) is nothing more than the inner product \(\langle\mathbf{m},\mathbf{q}_i\rangle\): no linear system to solve, just one dot product per axis. That is what “orthonormality makes coordinates trivial to read off” means, and it is why software prefers orthonormal bases when fitting models.

title: 2  Linear Algebra II: Orthogonality and the Projection Theorem
text:
2.4 The Gram-Schmidt process
ITC connection. MAIC and ML-NMR both fit models by solving normal equations; the orthonormal basis built here is what lets software solve those equations stably, through the QR factorization of Section 2.9.
The coordinate formulas above presuppose an orthonormal basis. Gram-Schmidt manufactures one from any linearly independent list, one vector at a time, by subtracting off the part already explained. The single sentence to keep in mind: at each step we take the next input vector and remove its shadow on the directions already built, leaving a piece that points in a genuinely new direction.

Theorem 2.3 (Gram-Schmidt orthonormalization) Let \(\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_p\) be linearly independent vectors in an inner product space. Define recursively \[
\mathbf{u}_1=\mathbf{a}_1,
\qquad
\mathbf{u}_k=\mathbf{a}_k-\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\frac{\langle\mathbf{a}_k,\mathbf{u}_i\rangle}{\langle\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{u}_i\rangle}\,\mathbf{u}_i
\quad(2\le k\le p),
\qquad
\mathbf{q}_k=\frac{\mathbf{u}_k}{\|\mathbf{u}_k\|}.
\tag{2.4}\] Then for every \(k\in\{1,\dots,p\}\): \(\mathbf{u}_k\ne\mathbf{0}\) (so \(\mathbf{q}_k\) is defined), \(\{\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_k\}\) is orthonormal, and \(\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_k\}=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_k\}\).

In words, each term in the sum subtracts the component of \(\mathbf{a}_k\) already lying in the directions we have built: the fraction \(\langle\mathbf{a}_k,\mathbf{u}_i\rangle/\langle\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{u}_i\rangle\) is exactly the amount of \(\mathbf{u}_i\) contained in \(\mathbf{a}_k\) (the coefficient of the projection of \(\mathbf{a}_k\) onto \(\mathbf{u}_i\)). Removing all of those leaves \(\mathbf{u}_k\) pointing in a direction orthogonal to everything before it; dividing by its length makes it a unit vector. Before the induction, it helps to run the recursion once on two vectors.

Example 2.3 (Gram-Schmidt on two vectors) Take \(\mathbf{a}_1=(3,0)^\top\) and \(\mathbf{a}_2=(1,2)^\top\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Then \(\mathbf{u}_1=\mathbf{a}_1=(3,0)^\top\) and \(\mathbf{q}_1=\tfrac13(3,0)^\top=(1,0)^\top\). The amount of \(\mathbf{u}_1\) inside \(\mathbf{a}_2\) is \(\langle\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{u}_1\rangle/\langle\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_1\rangle=3/9=\tfrac13\), so \[
\mathbf{u}_2=\mathbf{a}_2-\tfrac13\mathbf{u}_1=(1,2)^\top-\tfrac13(3,0)^\top=(0,2)^\top,
\] and \(\mathbf{q}_2=(0,1)^\top\). Geometrically we removed the horizontal shadow of \(\mathbf{a}_2\), leaving its purely vertical part. One checks \(\langle\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2\rangle=0\), as the theorem promises, and \(\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2\}=\mathbb{R}^2=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Proof. We argue by strong induction on \(k\), proving simultaneously the three claims labeled below: \(\mathbf{u}_k\ne\mathbf{0}\) (nonzero); \(\mathbf{u}_k\perp\mathbf{u}_j\) for all \(j<k\) (orthogonal); and the span equality (span). The reader can follow one claim at a time; the induction hypothesis supplies all three claims for every index below \(k\).
Base case \(k=1\). Linear independence forces \(\mathbf{a}_1\ne\mathbf{0}\), so \(\mathbf{u}_1=\mathbf{a}_1\ne\mathbf{0}\) and \(\mathbf{q}_1=\mathbf{u}_1/\|\mathbf{u}_1\|\) has unit norm. There are no pairs to check, and \(\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{q}_1\}=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{a}_1\}\) since the two vectors are nonzero scalar multiples of each other.
Inductive step. Fix \(k\ge 2\) and assume the three claims for all indices \(<k\). By the induction hypothesis \(\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_{k-1}\) are nonzero and pairwise orthogonal, so the coefficients in Equation 2.4 are well defined.
Claim 1 (nonzero): \(\mathbf{u}_k\ne\mathbf{0}\). If instead \(\mathbf{u}_k=\mathbf{0}\), then Equation 2.4 expresses \(\mathbf{a}_k\) as a linear combination of \(\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_{k-1}\), hence of \(\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_{k-1}\) by the induction hypothesis on spans. That contradicts the linear independence of \(\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_k\). So \(\mathbf{u}_k\ne\mathbf{0}\) and \(\mathbf{q}_k\) is defined with unit norm.
Claim 2 (orthogonal): \(\mathbf{u}_k\perp\mathbf{u}_j\) for each \(j<k\). Using bilinearity and the orthogonality of \(\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_{k-1}\) from the induction hypothesis (so \(\langle\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{u}_j\rangle=0\) whenever \(i\ne j\) with \(i,j<k\)), \[
\langle\mathbf{u}_k,\mathbf{u}_j\rangle
=\langle\mathbf{a}_k,\mathbf{u}_j\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\frac{\langle\mathbf{a}_k,\mathbf{u}_i\rangle}{\langle\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{u}_i\rangle}\langle\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{u}_j\rangle
=\langle\mathbf{a}_k,\mathbf{u}_j\rangle-\frac{\langle\mathbf{a}_k,\mathbf{u}_j\rangle}{\langle\mathbf{u}_j,\mathbf{u}_j\rangle}\langle\mathbf{u}_j,\mathbf{u}_j\rangle
=0 .
\] The only term of the sum that survives is the one with \(i=j\), because every other inner product \(\langle\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{u}_j\rangle\) (with \(i\ne j\)) is zero by the induction hypothesis; and that surviving term cancels \(\langle\mathbf{a}_k,\mathbf{u}_j\rangle\) exactly. Dividing by the positive norms shows \(\langle\mathbf{q}_k,\mathbf{q}_j\rangle=0\); with the unit-norm property this makes \(\{\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_k\}\) orthonormal.
Claim 3 (span): \(\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_k\}=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_k\}\). From Equation 2.4, \(\mathbf{u}_k\) is \(\mathbf{a}_k\) plus a combination of \(\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_{k-1}\), and each \(\mathbf{q}_i\) is a scalar multiple of \(\mathbf{u}_i\); hence \(\mathbf{u}_k\in\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_k\}\) and \(\mathbf{q}_k\in\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_k\}\). Conversely, solving Equation 2.4 for \(\mathbf{a}_k\) shows \(\mathbf{a}_k\in\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_k\}
=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_k\}\). Combined with the induction hypothesis \(\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_{k-1}\}=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_{k-1}\}\), both spanning sets contain each other’s generators, so they are equal. This closes the induction. \(\square\)


Remark. The list \(\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_p\) produced before normalization is an orthogonal (not yet orthonormal) basis. In floating-point arithmetic the form in Equation 2.4 loses orthogonality when the \(\mathbf{a}_k\) are nearly dependent; the algebraically identical modified Gram-Schmidt, which subtracts each projection immediately as it is computed, is markedly more stable, as is the Householder approach to the QR factorization in Section 2.9. We prove the classical form because its induction is the most transparent, and because modified Gram-Schmidt produces the same vectors in exact arithmetic, this proof covers it as well. See Strang (2016) for both. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Corollary 2.2 (Existence of orthonormal bases) Every finite-dimensional inner product space, and every finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space, has an orthonormal basis.


Proof. A finite-dimensional space (or subspace) has a basis \(\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_p\) by Definition 1.5. Applying Theorem 2.3 produces an orthonormal set \(\{\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_p\}\) with the same span. The set has \(p=\dim\) elements and is linearly independent by Lemma 2.1, so it is a basis. \(\square\)

title: 2  Linear Algebra II: Orthogonality and the Projection Theorem
text:
2.5 Orthogonal complement and orthogonal decomposition
ITC connection. The residual of every regression in this book lives in an orthogonal complement; this section gives that “leftover space” its structure and ties it back to the four fundamental subspaces of Chapter 1.

Definition 2.4 (Orthogonal complement) For a subset \(S\) of an inner product space \(V\), the orthogonal complement of \(S\) is \[
S^\perp=\{\mathbf{v}\in V:\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{s}\rangle=0\ \text{for all}\ \mathbf{s}\in S\}.
\tag{2.5}\]

Reader translation. \(S^\perp\) (read “\(S\) perp”) is the set of all vectors perpendicular to everything in \(S\). If \(S\) is the set of predictions a model can make, then \(S^\perp\) is the space of “directions the model cannot see,” and the least-squares residual will live there.

Lemma 2.2 (Elementary properties of the complement) Let \(S,T\subseteq V\) and let \(\mathcal{M}\) be a subspace. Then:

\(S^\perp\) is a subspace of \(V\);
\(S^\perp=(\operatorname{span} S)^\perp\);
if \(S\subseteq T\) then \(T^\perp\subseteq S^\perp\);
\(\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{M}^\perp=\{\mathbf{0}\}\).



Proof. 

The zero vector lies in \(S^\perp\) because \(\langle\mathbf{0},\mathbf{s}\rangle=0\). If \(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\in S^\perp\) and \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\), then for every \(\mathbf{s}\in S\), \(\langle a\mathbf{v}+b\mathbf{w},\mathbf{s}\rangle=a\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{s}\rangle+b\langle\mathbf{w},\mathbf{s}\rangle=0\), so \(a\mathbf{v}+b\mathbf{w}\in S^\perp\).
Since \(S\subseteq\operatorname{span}S\), part (3) gives \((\operatorname{span}S)^\perp\subseteq S^\perp\). Conversely, if \(\mathbf{v}\in S^\perp\) and \(\mathbf{s}=\sum_i c_i\mathbf{s}_i\) is a combination of elements of \(S\), then \(\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{s}\rangle=\sum_i c_i\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{s}_i\rangle=0\), so \(\mathbf{v}\in(\operatorname{span}S)^\perp\).
If \(\mathbf{v}\perp T\) and \(S\subseteq T\), then in particular \(\mathbf{v}\perp S\).
If \(\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{M}^\perp\), then \(\mathbf{v}\) is orthogonal to itself, so \(\|\mathbf{v}\|^2=\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{v}\rangle=0\), whence \(\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\) by positive definiteness. \(\square\)


The next theorem is the structural heart of the chapter: a finite-dimensional subspace splits the whole space cleanly into itself and its complement.

Theorem 2.4 (Orthogonal decomposition) Let \(\mathcal{M}\) be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space \(V\). Then every \(\mathbf{v}\in V\) admits a unique decomposition \[
\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{m}+\mathbf{w},\qquad \mathbf{m}\in\mathcal{M},\ \ \mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{M}^\perp .
\tag{2.6}\] Equivalently, \(V=\mathcal{M}\oplus\mathcal{M}^\perp\) (an internal direct sum).

Reader translation. Every vector splits, in exactly one way, into an “explainable” part lying in \(\mathcal{M}\) and a “leftover” part lying in \(\mathcal{M}^\perp\), with no overlap between the two pieces. The symbol \(\oplus\) (read “direct sum”) records two facts at once: the two subspaces together span the whole space, and they meet only at \(\mathbf{0}\). The word internal simply means the two pieces live inside the same space \(V\) and add up to it, as opposed to being glued together from separate spaces; you do not need the external notion anywhere in this book. For a regression, the explainable part will be the fitted values and the leftover part the residual.

Proof. Existence. By Corollary 2.2 choose an orthonormal basis \(\{\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_k\}\) of \(\mathcal{M}\). Set \[
\mathbf{m}=\sum_{i=1}^k\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{q}_i\rangle\,\mathbf{q}_i\in\mathcal{M},
\qquad
\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{m}.
\] To see \(\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{M}^\perp\) it suffices, by Lemma 2.2(2), to check orthogonality against each basis vector \(\mathbf{q}_j\): \[
\langle\mathbf{w},\mathbf{q}_j\rangle
=\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{q}_j\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^k\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{q}_i\rangle\langle\mathbf{q}_i,\mathbf{q}_j\rangle
=\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{q}_j\rangle-\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{q}_j\rangle=0 .
\] Thus \(\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{m}+\mathbf{w}\) with \(\mathbf{m}\in\mathcal{M}\) and \(\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{M}^\perp\).
Uniqueness. Suppose \(\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{m}+\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{m}'+\mathbf{w}'\) with \(\mathbf{m},\mathbf{m}'\in\mathcal{M}\) and \(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{w}'\in\mathcal{M}^\perp\). Then \(\mathbf{m}-\mathbf{m}'=\mathbf{w}'-\mathbf{w}\). The left side lies in \(\mathcal{M}\) and the right side in \(\mathcal{M}^\perp\), so this common vector lies in \(\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{M}^\perp=\{\mathbf{0}\}\) by Lemma 2.2(4). Hence \(\mathbf{m}=\mathbf{m}'\) and \(\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{w}'\). The two properties, \(\mathcal{M}+\mathcal{M}^\perp=V\) and \(\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{M}^\perp=\{\mathbf{0}\}\), are exactly the definition of the internal direct sum \(V=\mathcal{M}\oplus\mathcal{M}^\perp\). \(\square\)

Why this matters. This unique split is the abstract form of “data = fit + residual.” Once we know the split exists and is unique, the projection theorem just identifies the fit as the closest point, and every later decomposition (explained versus unexplained variation, anchored versus unanchored contrasts) is a special case.

Example 2.4 (A subspace and its complement, with numbers) In \(\mathbb{R}^3\) let \(\mathcal{M}=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{e}_1,\mathbf{e}_2\}\) be the \(xy\)-plane. A vector is orthogonal to both \(\mathbf{e}_1=(1,0,0)^\top\) and \(\mathbf{e}_2=(0,1,0)^\top\) exactly when its first two entries vanish, so \(\mathcal{M}^\perp=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{e}_3\}\) is the \(z\)-axis. Decompose \(\mathbf{v}=(3,4,5)^\top\): its \(\mathcal{M}\)-part is \(\mathbf{m}=(3,4,0)^\top\) and its \(\mathcal{M}^\perp\)-part is \(\mathbf{w}=(0,0,5)^\top\). They are perpendicular, and the squared-length split of Theorem 2.5 is visible already, \(\|\mathbf{v}\|^2=9+16+25=50=25+25=\|\mathbf{m}\|^2+\|\mathbf{w}\|^2\). Here \(\dim\mathcal{M}+\dim\mathcal{M}^\perp=2+1=3=\dim\mathbb{R}^3\), the dimension identity of the next corollary. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Corollary 2.3 (Dimension and the double complement) Let \(\mathcal{M}\) be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space \(V\). Then \[
\dim\mathcal{M}+\dim\mathcal{M}^\perp=\dim V,
\qquad
(\mathcal{M}^\perp)^\perp=\mathcal{M}.
\tag{2.7}\]


Proof. The direct sum \(V=\mathcal{M}\oplus\mathcal{M}^\perp\) from Theorem 2.4 gives the dimension identity once we check that a basis \(\{\mathbf{m}_1,\dots,\mathbf{m}_a\}\) of \(\mathcal{M}\) together with a basis \(\{\mathbf{w}_1,\dots,\mathbf{w}_b\}\) of \(\mathcal{M}^\perp\) forms a basis of \(V\). Independence: suppose \(\sum_i \alpha_i\mathbf{m}_i+\sum_j\beta_j\mathbf{w}_j=\mathbf{0}\). Then \(\sum_i\alpha_i\mathbf{m}_i=-\sum_j\beta_j\mathbf{w}_j\), and the left side lies in \(\mathcal{M}\) while the right side lies in \(\mathcal{M}^\perp\); by Lemma 2.2(4) both equal \(\mathbf{0}\). Independence of each individual basis then forces every \(\alpha_i=0\) and every \(\beta_j=0\). Spanning: every \(\mathbf{v}\in V\) decomposes as \(\mathbf{m}+\mathbf{w}\) by Theorem 2.4, and each piece is a combination of its own basis, so the union spans. Hence the union is a basis and \(\dim V=a+b=\dim\mathcal{M}+\dim\mathcal{M}^\perp\).
For the double complement, every \(\mathbf{m}\in\mathcal{M}\) is orthogonal to all of \(\mathcal{M}^\perp\), so \(\mathcal{M}\subseteq(\mathcal{M}^\perp)^\perp\). Applying the dimension identity twice, \(\dim(\mathcal{M}^\perp)^\perp=\dim V-\dim\mathcal{M}^\perp=\dim\mathcal{M}\). A subspace contained in another of equal finite dimension must equal it, so \((\mathcal{M}^\perp)^\perp=\mathcal{M}\). \(\square\)

Specializing to \(V=\mathbb{R}^n\) with the Euclidean inner product ties the complement to the four fundamental subspaces of Chapter 1 (Theorem 1.5).

Proposition 2.2 (Orthogonality of the fundamental subspaces) For \(\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), with the Euclidean inner product, \[
\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})^\perp=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}^\top)\ \ \text{in }\mathbb{R}^m,
\qquad
\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})^\perp=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A}^\top)\ \ \text{in }\mathbb{R}^n .
\tag{2.8}\]


Proof. Write the columns of \(\mathbf{A}\) as \(\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_n\), so \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_n\}\) by Definition 1.10. By Lemma 2.2(2), \(\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})^\perp\) if and only if \(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{a}_j=0\) for every \(j\), that is, if and only if \(\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{0}\), which says \(\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}^\top)\). This proves the first identity. Applying it to \(\mathbf{A}^\top\) in place of \(\mathbf{A}\) gives \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A}^\top)^\perp=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})\). Now apply \((\cdot)^\perp\) to both sides and invoke the double-complement identity \((\mathcal{M}^\perp)^\perp=\mathcal{M}\) from Equation 2.7, here with \(\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A}^\top)\): the left side becomes \(\bigl(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A}^\top)^\perp\bigr)^\perp=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A}^\top)\) and the right side becomes \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})^\perp\), yielding \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A}^\top)=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A})^\perp\). \(\square\)

The proposition says the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix come in two orthogonal-complement pairs. With \(r=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})\), the bookkeeping is worth tabulating once.

Why this matters. The top row is the workhorse: a least-squares residual is orthogonal to the column space, so it lands in the left null space \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}^\top)\). In the two-arm trial of Example 2.1 this left null space is the set of within-group mean-zero contrasts (computed in Chapter 1’s Example 1.8), which is precisely why the residuals \((-1,1,-1,1)^\top\) there sum to zero inside each arm.
