\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}&\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\end{pmatrix}\). If \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}=0\), then \(\mathbf{X}_1\perp\mathbf{X}_2\).


Proof. Write \(\mathbf{t}=(\mathbf{t}_1,\mathbf{t}_2)\) conformably. When \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}=0\) (hence \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}^{\top}=0\)), the quadratic form in Equation 4.13 splits, \(\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{t}
=\mathbf{t}_1^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}\mathbf{t}_1+\mathbf{t}_2^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\mathbf{t}_2\), and the linear form splits as \(\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbf{t}_1^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\mathbf{t}_2^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_2\). Hence the joint MGF factors, \[
M_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{t}_1,\mathbf{t}_2)
=\exp\!\Bigl(\mathbf{t}_1^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\tfrac12\mathbf{t}_1^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}\mathbf{t}_1\Bigr)
\exp\!\Bigl(\mathbf{t}_2^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_2+\tfrac12\mathbf{t}_2^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\mathbf{t}_2\Bigr)
=M_{\mathbf{X}_1}(\mathbf{t}_1)\,M_{\mathbf{X}_2}(\mathbf{t}_2),
\] where the marginal MGFs are read off from Theorem 4.14. By the factorization criterion of Theorem 4.11, \(\mathbf{X}_1\perp\mathbf{X}_2\). \(\square\)


Theorem 4.15 (Conditional distribution of a multivariate normal) Partition \(\mathbf{X}\sim\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) as above with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\succ 0\). Then the conditional distribution of \(\mathbf{X}_1\) given \(\mathbf{X}_2=\mathbf{x}_2\) is multivariate normal, \[
\mathbf{X}_1\mid\mathbf{X}_2=\mathbf{x}_2\ \sim\
\mathcal{N}\Bigl(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2),
\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}\Bigr).
\tag{4.15}\] The conditional covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1\mid 2}:=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}\) is the Schur complement of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\) (the residual covariance left in \(\mathbf{X}_1\) after subtracting the part linearly explained by \(\mathbf{X}_2\)) and does not depend on \(\mathbf{x}_2\).


Proof. Define the regression residual \(\mathbf{U}:=\mathbf{X}_1-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{X}_2\). The pair \((\mathbf{U},\mathbf{X}_2)\) is the affine image of \(\mathbf{X}\) under \[
\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{U}\\\mathbf{X}_2\end{pmatrix}
=\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}I&-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\\0&I\end{pmatrix}}_{=:A}
\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{X}_1\\\mathbf{X}_2\end{pmatrix},
\] so by Theorem 4.14 it is jointly multivariate normal. Its cross-covariance vanishes: \[
\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{U},\mathbf{X}_2)
=\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{X}_1,\mathbf{X}_2)-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{X}_2,\mathbf{X}_2)
=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}=0,
\] so \(\mathbf{U}\perp\mathbf{X}_2\) by Lemma 4.3. The mean and covariance of \(\mathbf{U}\) are \[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{U}]=\boldsymbol{\mu}_1-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_2,
\qquad
\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{U})=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}-2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}
+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}
=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1\mid 2},
\] the cross terms combining because \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}^{\top}\). Now recover \(\mathbf{X}_1=\mathbf{U}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{X}_2\) and compute the conditional MGF given \(\mathbf{X}_2=\mathbf{x}_2\). Since the factor \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{X}_2\) becomes the constant \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{x}_2\) under the conditioning, and since \(\mathbf{U}\perp\mathbf{X}_2\) implies \(\mathbb{E}[e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}\mathbf{U}}\mid\mathbf{X}_2]=\mathbb{E}[e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}\mathbf{U}}]\) (this is the one step that genuinely uses normality: for a general distribution \(\mathbf{U}\) could be uncorrelated with \(\mathbf{X}_2\) yet still dependent, but Lemma 4.3 upgrades the vanishing cross-covariance to full independence, so conditioning on \(\mathbf{X}_2\) leaves the law of \(\mathbf{U}\) untouched), \[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_1}\,\big|\,\mathbf{X}_2=\mathbf{x}_2\bigr]
=e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{x}_2}\,
\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}\mathbf{U}}\bigr]
=\exp\!\Bigl(\mathbf{t}^{\top}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2)\bigr)
+\tfrac12\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1\mid 2}\mathbf{t}\Bigr),
\] where the last step substitutes the MGF Equation 4.13 of \(\mathbf{U}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{U}],\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1\mid 2})\) and collects the linear terms. This is the MGF of the normal law on the right of Equation 4.15, so by Theorem 4.11 the conditional law is as claimed. \(\square\)

The conditional mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2)\) is an affine function of the conditioning value, the population analogue of a linear regression of \(\mathbf{X}_1\) on \(\mathbf{X}_2\), and the conditional covariance is constant in \(\mathbf{x}_2\). These two features, linear conditional mean and homoskedastic conditional covariance, are the exact distributional content of the linear model of Chapter 6 and recur in every normal-approximation likelihood used in the network meta-analysis chapters.

Remark. Why this matters. The conditional mean of a multivariate normal is linear in the conditioning value, the population blueprint of linear regression: the regression coefficients are the population object \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\). For indirect comparison this is the object we integrate over a target population’s covariate distribution to produce a population-average prediction, the move at the heart of ML-NMR in Part V. The constant (homoskedastic) conditional covariance is why the normal-theory likelihoods of network meta-analysis can carry a single residual variance.

title: 4  Probability and Distributions
text:
4.13 A fully worked example
Where the toy trial of Example 4.1 gave us a discrete thread, we now run a continuous one. We carry a single bivariate normal through every theorem of Section 4.9 and Section 4.12, with arithmetic the reader can reproduce by hand, and then verify the Poisson binomial mass function of Definition 4.11 on a small example.

4.13.1 A bivariate normal
Let \(\mathbf{X}=(X_1,X_2)^{\top}\sim\mathcal{N}_2(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) with \[
\boldsymbol{\mu}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Positive definiteness (Theorem 4.9). The matrix is symmetric. Its eigenvalues solve \(\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}-\lambda I)=(2-\lambda)(1-\lambda)-1=\lambda^2-3\lambda+1=0\), giving \(\lambda=\tfrac{3\pm\sqrt5}{2}\approx 2.618\) and \(0.382\), both positive, so \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ 0\); its determinant is \(\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=2\cdot 1-1\cdot 1=1\). We may also confirm positive semidefiniteness through Equation 4.4 on a specific direction: for \(\mathbf{a}=(1,-1)^{\top}\), \[
\mathbf{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{a}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}=1
=\mathrm{Var}(X_1-X_2)=\mathrm{Var}(X_1)+\mathrm{Var}(X_2)-2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=2+1-2=1\ge 0,
\] where \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{a}=(2-1,\,1-1)^{\top}=(1,0)^{\top}\).
Marginals and correlation (Theorem 4.14, Theorem 4.7). Reading off the diagonal, \(X_1\sim\mathcal{N}(1,2)\) and \(X_2\sim\mathcal{N}(2,1)\). The correlation is \(\rho=\mathrm{Cov}(X_1,X_2)/\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X_1)\mathrm{Var}(X_2)}=1/\sqrt{2\cdot 1}=1/\sqrt2\approx 0.707\), and Cauchy-Schwarz is the statement \(\mathrm{Cov}(X_1,X_2)^2=1\le 2=\mathrm{Var}(X_1)\,\mathrm{Var}(X_2)\), that is \(\rho^2=\tfrac12\le 1\).
An affine map (Theorem 4.14). Let \(Y=X_1+X_2=B\mathbf{X}\) with \(B=(1,\ 1)\). Then \(Y\sim\mathcal{N}(B\boldsymbol{\mu},B\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{\top})\) with mean \(B\boldsymbol{\mu}=1+2=3\) and variance \(B\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{\top}=(1,1)\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}(1,1)^{\top}=(3,2)(1,1)^{\top}=5\), so \(Y\sim\mathcal{N}(3,5)\). The direct check is \(\mathrm{Var}(X_1+X_2)=2+1+2\cdot 1=5\).
The conditional distribution (Theorem 4.15). With \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}=2\), \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}=1\), \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}=1\), the conditional law of \(X_1\) given \(X_2=x_2\) has mean \(\mu_1+\Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(x_2-\mu_2)=1+1\cdot(x_2-2)=x_2-1\) and variance \(\Sigma_{11}-\Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}=2-1\cdot 1\cdot 1=1\). Hence \[
X_1\mid X_2=x_2\ \sim\ \mathcal{N}(x_2-1,\ 1),\qquad\text{and at }x_2=4,\quad X_1\mid X_2=4\sim\mathcal{N}(3,1).
\] Note that the conditional variance \(1\) is smaller than the marginal variance \(2\): conditioning on the correlated \(X_2\) removes part of the uncertainty in \(X_1\). This is the law of total variance Corollary 4.2 in action, \[
\mathrm{Var}(X_1)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(X_1\mid X_2)]+\mathrm{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X_1\mid X_2])
=1+\mathrm{Var}(X_2-1)=1+1=2,\ \checkmark
\] because \(\mathrm{Var}(X_1\mid X_2)\equiv 1\) is constant and \(\mathbb{E}[X_1\mid X_2]=X_2-1\) has variance \(\mathrm{Var}(X_2)=1\).
The density (Proposition 4.2). Since \(\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=1\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\) (one checks \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}=I\)), the density is \[
f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{2\pi}\exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac12\bigl[(x_1-1)^2-2(x_1-1)(x_2-2)+2(x_2-2)^2\bigr]\Bigr),
\] and at the mean \(\mathbf{x}=\boldsymbol{\mu}=(1,2)^{\top}\) this is \(f_{\mathbf{X}}(\boldsymbol{\mu})=1/(2\pi)\approx 0.159\).
The Jensen gap (Theorem 4.6). Apply the convex \(\varphi(u)=u^2\) to \(X_1\sim\mathcal{N}(1,2)\). The left side of Equation 4.11 is \(\varphi(\mathbb{E}[X_1])=1^2=1\); the right side is \(\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_1)]=\mathbb{E}[X_1^2]=\mathrm{Var}(X_1)+(\mathbb{E}X_1)^2=2+1=3\). The Jensen gap is \(3-1=2\), which is exactly \(\mathrm{Var}(X_1)\), as anticipated after Theorem 4.6.


4.13.2 A Poisson binomial count
Take \(n=3\) trials with heterogeneous success probabilities \(\mathbf{p}=(0.2,\,0.5,\,0.8)\), so \(X\sim\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf{p})\) with failure probabilities \((0.8,\,0.5,\,0.2)\). The mass function of Definition 4.11 enumerates subsets: \[
\begin{aligned}
P(X=0)&=0.8\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.2=0.08,\\
P(X=1)&=0.2\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.2+0.8\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.2+0.8\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.8=0.02+0.08+0.32=0.42,\\
P(X=2)&=0.2\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.2+0.2\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.8+0.8\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.8=0.02+0.08+0.32=0.42,\\
P(X=3)&=0.2\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.8=0.08,
\end{aligned}
\] which sum to \(1\). The mean is \(\mathbb{E}[X]=0.2+0.5+0.8=1.5\), confirmed from the mass function as \(0(0.08)+1(0.42)+2(0.42)+3(0.08)=1.5\). The variance is \(\mathrm{Var}(X)=0.2(0.8)+0.5(0.5)+0.8(0.2)=0.16+0.25+0.16=0.57\), confirmed as \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]-(\mathbb{E}X)^2=(0.42+4\cdot 0.42+9\cdot 0.08)-1.5^2=2.82-2.25=0.57\). For contrast, a binomial \(\mathrm{Bin}(3,0.5)\) has the same mean \(1.5\) but the larger variance \(3(0.5)(0.5)=0.75\); spreading the per-trial risks apart, at fixed total risk, has reduced the dispersion of the count, in keeping with the convexity remark after Definition 4.11.

title: 4  Probability and Distributions
text:
4.14 Notes and references
The measure-theoretic framework of Definition 4.1 is Kolmogorov’s; the closure properties (Lemma 4.1), the pushforward law (Proposition 4.1), the convergence theorems (Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.2), conditional expectation through the Radon-Nikodym theorem (Definition 4.4), Fubini-Tonelli (Theorem 4.8), and the uniqueness and continuity theorems for moment generating functions (Theorem 4.11, Theorem 4.13) are standard and are proved in Billingsley (1995) and Williams (1991), which we cite for the results stated without proof. The load-bearing results of the chapter, the tower property (Theorem 4.4), Jensen’s inequality (Theorem 4.6) with its supporting-line lemma (Lemma 4.2), the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for expectations (Theorem 4.7), the positive semidefiniteness of covariance matrices (Theorem 4.9), and the multivariate normal calculus (Theorem 4.14, Lemma 4.3, Theorem 4.15), are proved here in full, the last group resting on the spectral theorem Theorem 3.2 and the positive-definiteness characterization Theorem 3.3 of Chapter 3. The multivariate normal theory follows the treatment in Bingham and Fry (2010), which we recommend for the linear-models reader; the causal framing of conditional independence and the role of expectation in identification is from Hernán and Robins (2020).
The development corresponds to results A.1 through A.10 of the proof catalogue: A.1 (Definition 4.1, Lemma 4.1), A.2 (Definition 4.2, Proposition 4.1), A.3 (Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.2), A.4 (Theorem 4.3, Theorem 4.4), A.5 (Definition 4.4), A.6 (Definition 4.6, Theorem 4.5), A.7 (Theorem 4.6), A.8 (Theorem 4.7), A.9 (Corollary 4.1), and A.10 (Theorem 4.8). The asymptotic tools A.11 through A.13, the delta method, Slutsky’s theorem, and the continuous mapping theorem, belong to the inference chapter that follows. The graphoid axioms Theorem 4.5 have a machine-checked counterpart in the companion Coq development: the lemmas cond_indep_symmetry and cond_indep_decomposition and the theorems cond_indep_weak_union and cond_indep_contraction of theories/ConditionalIndep.v verify (G1) through (G4) for a discrete joint model. The foundational facts of Section 4.3 through Section 4.6 are accepted in that development as axioms imported from the mathcomp-analysis library rather than reproved, as documented in its AXIOMS.md; the mathematical content here is the classical pen-and-paper version.

title: 4  Probability and Distributions
text:
4.15 Exercises
A starred exercise, marked \(\star\), has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first four exercises are warm-ups and interpretation; the proof-heavy and starred ones follow.

Exercise 4.1 (Warm-up: reweight two strata) In Example 4.1 the control-arm risks are \(0.20\) for low-risk patients and \(0.50\) for high-risk patients. The source trial has severity shares \((0.6,0.4)\), while a target population has shares \((0.3,0.7)\). Using Corollary 4.1, compute the marginal control response rate in the source and in the target, and explain in one sentence why they differ even though the within-stratum risks are identical.


Exercise 4.2 (Interpretation: average risk versus risk of the average) Two equally sized subgroups have event risks \(0.2\) and \(0.8\). Compute the population-average risk, and separately compute the inverse-logit of the average log-odds. Which is larger, and which one should a decision maker report as the population risk? Relate your answer to Example 4.4 and Theorem 4.6.


Exercise 4.3 (Interpretation: which independence is ignorability?) Let \(T\) be treatment, \(X\) baseline covariates, and \(Y(0),Y(1)\) the potential outcomes. Using the notation of Definition 4.6, write the conditional-independence statement expressing “a covariate-adjusted trial assigns treatment without regard to prognosis once covariates are fixed.” Explain in words why \(T\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\) without conditioning is a stronger statement, and which one a covariate-adjusted analysis actually needs.


Exercise 4.4 (Computation: a heterogeneous event count) Three patients have event risks \(\mathbf{p}=(0.1,0.4,0.6)\). Using Definition 4.11, write out the full mass function of the event count \(X\sim\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf{p})\), and verify from it that \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_i p_i\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X)=\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)\). Compare the variance with that of \(\mathrm{Bin}(3,\bar p)\) at the same mean \(\bar p=\tfrac13\sum_i p_i\).


Exercise 4.5 (Closure and a tail event) Using Lemma 4.1, show that for events \(\{A_n\}\) the event “\(A_n\) occurs for infinitely many \(n\)” equals \(\limsup_n A_n\) and lies in \(\mathcal{F}\). Show further that if \(\sum_n P(A_n)<\infty\) then \(P(\limsup_n A_n)=0\). (This is the first Borel-Cantelli lemma; use \(P(\limsup_n A_n)\le P(\bigcup_{n\ge m}A_n)\le\sum_{n\ge m}P(A_n)\) and let \(m\to\infty\).)


Exercise 4.6 (Variance algebra) For \(X,Y\in L^2\) and constants \(a,b,c\), prove from Definition 4.3 that \(\mathrm{Var}(aX+bY+c)=a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)+b^2\mathrm{Var}(Y)+2ab\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)\), and deduce that the correlation coefficient lies in \([-1,1]\) using Theorem 4.7.


Exercise 4.7 (Jensen at work) Let \(X\) be a positive random variable in \(L^1\) with \(\log X\in L^1\). Using Theorem 4.6 with a suitable convex or concave \(\varphi\), prove the inequality \(\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log X])\le\mathbb{E}[X]\), the probabilistic form of the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality. Identify the convex function you used and state when equality holds.


Exercise 4.8 (Uncorrelated but dependent) Let \(Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and set \(X=Z\), \(Y=Z^2\). Show that \(\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0\) yet \(X\) and \(Y\) are not independent. Explain why this does not contradict Lemma 4.3. (Hint: \((X,Y)\) is not jointly normal.)


Exercise 4.9 (Sums of Poissons) Using Theorem 4.12 and Definition 4.10, prove that if \(X\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\) and \(Y\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\nu)\) are independent then \(X+Y\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda+\nu)\). Then, using Theorem 4.14, prove the normal analogue: independent \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)\) and \(Y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)\) have \(X+Y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_1+\mu_2,\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)\).


Exercise 4.10 (Bivariate conditioning by hand) For the bivariate normal of Section 4.13.1, derive the conditional distribution of \(X_2\) given \(X_1=x_1\) using Theorem 4.15, and verify directly that \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X_2\mid X_1]]=\mathbb{E}[X_2]=2\) via Corollary 4.1. Compute the conditional variance and confirm the law of total variance Corollary 4.2 for \(X_2\).


Exercise 4.11 (Realizing a covariance (starred)) \(\star\) Let \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix}\) with \(\rho\in(-1,1)\). Using Theorem 4.9, exhibit an explicit random vector with this covariance as a linear image of a standard normal pair, computing \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\) from the spectral decomposition Theorem 3.2. Determine for which \(\rho\) the matrix fails to be positive definite and interpret the degenerate case via Lemma 4.3 and Theorem 4.15.


Exercise 4.12 (The need for positivity (starred)) \(\star\) The intersection axiom (G5) of Theorem 4.5 can fail without the positivity hypothesis. Construct a joint distribution of binary \((X,Y,Z,W)\), for instance one in which \(X=Y\) deterministically and \(W\) is degenerate, such that \(X\perp Y\mid(Z,W)\) and \(X\perp W\mid(Z,Y)\) both hold but \(X\perp(Y,W)\mid Z\) fails. Explain precisely which step of a positivity-based proof breaks down.





Billingsley, Patrick. 1995. Probability and Measure. 3rd ed. Wiley.


Bingham, N. H., and John M. Fry. 2010. Regression: Linear Models in Statistics. Springer Undergraduate Mathematics Series. Springer.


Hernán, Miguel A., and James M. Robins. 2020. Causal Inference: What If. Chapman & Hall/CRC.


Williams, David. 1991. Probability with Martingales. Cambridge University Press.

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
5.1 Statistical models, estimators, and risk
Every indirect treatment comparison reduces, in the end, to a statement about numbers we estimated from finite data and the uncertainty attached to them. A network meta-analysis combines log odds ratios, each of which is a nonlinear function of fitted model parameters; its credible or confidence intervals come from the curvature of a likelihood. A matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC, Notation) solves a system of weighting equations and then reports a standard error that must remain valid even though the weighting model is almost certainly misspecified. Multilevel network meta-regression fits a likelihood over individual and aggregate data and inverts the Fisher information to quantify precision. None of these methods can be stated, let alone trusted, without the machinery of estimation theory: what an estimator is, when it is unbiased, how its variance behaves, what the likelihood and the score and the Fisher information are, and how an estimator behaves as the sample grows.
This chapter builds that machinery from first principles. We define statistical models and estimators and the three numbers that summarize an estimator’s accuracy (bias, variance, mean squared error). We introduce the likelihood, the score function, and the Fisher information, and prove the information equality that ties them together. We define the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE), prove its functional invariance, and then prove the two results on which all asymptotic inference rests: the MLE is consistent and asymptotically normal. We prove the Cramér-Rao lower bound, which says no unbiased estimator can beat the inverse Fisher information, and we show the MLE attains it asymptotically. We prove the three asymptotic tools used throughout the book: the continuous mapping theorem, Slutsky’s theorem, and the delta method (catalogue results A.13, A.12, A.11). We then generalize from maximum likelihood to M-estimation and define the sandwich variance estimator, the robust standard error that Chapter 18 needs for MAIC. We close with the Wald, score, and likelihood-ratio tests and the confidence intervals obtained by inverting them.
Throughout, the data are \(X_1, \dots, X_n\), modeled as independent and identically distributed (iid) draws from a distribution indexed by a parameter \(\boldsymbol\theta\). The reader should keep one picture in mind: the log-likelihood is a random function of \(\boldsymbol\theta\); its slope (the score) vanishes at the MLE; its curvature (the information) determines how sharply the data pin down the parameter; and asymptotic normality is the statement that, viewed through a magnifying glass of width \(1/\sqrt n\), this random function looks like a parabola whose vertex is Gaussian.
That picture, drawn once, is worth carrying through the whole chapter:
Everything that follows attaches a name and a theorem to one feature of this curve. The table below is a preview and a reference: each row is defined precisely in the section listed, and you can return to it whenever a symbol feels unfamiliar.
A word on the data. We write the observations as \(X_1, \dots, X_n\), but a single \(X_i\) can be many things depending on the model: one yes/no outcome (did patient \(i\) respond?), a covariate vector (age, sex, biomarker), or an entire patient record (covariates, treatment arm, and outcome together). The theory below never cares which; it only needs the \(X_i\) to be iid draws from \(f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta_0)\).
We work on a probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal F, P)\) in the sense of Definition 4.1. A statistical model is a family of candidate distributions for the data, indexed by a parameter.
The bias and the variance measure two different failures: bias is a systematic offset, variance is random scatter. The MSE combines them, and the decomposition below shows exactly how.
Two notions of “the estimator gets it right as data accumulate” recur throughout the book. The first is asymptotic and concerns a sequence of estimators.

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
Example 5.1 (A running example: a two-arm trial and an indirect comparison) We return to one concrete study at every step. A randomized trial of a new treatment records, for each of \(n = 25\) patients, whether the patient responded (\(X_i = 1\)) or not (\(X_i = 0\)):














Patient \(i\)

Response \(X_i\)

\(\sum_i X_i = 10\)



Ten of the \(25\) patients respond. The single number we want is the response probability \(p\), together with an honest measure of how uncertain our estimate of \(p\) is. Every tool in this chapter is, in the end, a way to answer one of two questions about this trial: what is our best guess for \(p\)? (estimation) and how far off could that guess be? (uncertainty).
The destination is an indirect treatment comparison. Imagine a second trial of a different treatment against the same control, reporting its own response probabilities. Neither trial compares the two new treatments head to head, yet we will want the contrast between them on the log-odds scale, with a valid standard error. By the end we assemble exactly that (Example 5.3), using the likelihood to estimate each \(p\), the Fisher information for its precision, and the delta method to move to the log-odds scale and combine the two trials. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Definition 5.1 (Parametric statistical model) Let \(\mathcal X\) be a sample space carrying a \(\sigma\)-finite dominating measure \(\nu\) (Lebesgue measure for continuous data, counting measure for discrete data). A parametric statistical model is a family \[
\mathcal F = \bigl\{\, f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta \,\bigr\},
\qquad \Theta \subseteq \mathbb R^{p},
\] where each \(f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta)\) is a probability density (or mass) function with respect to \(\nu\). The set \(\Theta\) is the parameter space. The model is identifiable if the map \(\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta)\) is injective, that is, if \(\boldsymbol\theta \ne \boldsymbol\theta'\) implies \(f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta) \ne
f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta')\) on a set of positive \(\nu\)-measure.
We observe \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) iid with common density \(f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) for some unknown true parameter \(\boldsymbol\theta_0 \in \Theta\), and write \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\), \(\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\), \(P_{\boldsymbol\theta}\) for expectation, variance, and probability computed under \(f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta)\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. A statistical model is a menu of candidate distributions for the data, one for each value of \(\boldsymbol\theta\); estimation is the job of picking the menu item that best matches what we saw. Two pieces of jargon in the definition:

A \(\sigma\)-finite dominating measure \(\nu\) is just a fixed reference yardstick that lets the word “density” mean something. For continuous data it is ordinary length or area (Lebesgue measure), so a density is the height of a curve; for discrete data it is counting measure, so a “density” is simply a probability mass \(P(X = x)\). You never have to choose \(\nu\) in practice: it is Lebesgue for continuous outcomes and counting for counts or yes/no data.
Identifiable says the map \(\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta)\) is injective (different inputs give different outputs): no two parameter values produce the same distribution of observable data. If two did, no amount of data could ever tell them apart. For a non-identifiable example, suppose a model only ever affects the data through a product \(\mu = \alpha\beta\) but carries \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) separately; then \((\alpha,\beta) = (2,3)\) and \((6,1)\) give identical data distributions and are indistinguishable.

A note on \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\). Calling it the true parameter assumes the model is correctly specified, that the data really were generated by some member of the menu. Real outcome models are usually simplifications. We keep the clean “true parameter” language while developing maximum likelihood, and in Section 5.8 we drop it: there the target becomes whatever parameter our estimating equation aims at, whether or not any menu item is exactly right. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Definition 5.2 (Estimator, bias, variance, mean squared error) An estimator of a quantity \(g(\boldsymbol\theta) \in \mathbb R\) is a measurable function \(T_n = T(X_1, \dots, X_n)\) of the data alone (it may not depend on \(\boldsymbol\theta\)). Its bias, variance, and mean squared error (MSE) at \(\boldsymbol\theta\) are \[
\mathrm{Bias}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T_n] - g(\boldsymbol\theta),
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n),
\qquad
\mathrm{MSE}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\bigl[(T_n - g(\boldsymbol\theta))^2\bigr].
\] The estimator is unbiased if \(\mathrm{Bias}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n) = 0\) for every \(\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta\). For a vector estimator \(\mathbf T_n\) of \(g(\boldsymbol\theta) \in \mathbb R^q\), the variance is replaced by the covariance matrix \(\mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T_n)\) and the MSE by the matrix \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[(\mathbf T_n - g)(\mathbf T_n - g)^\top]\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. An estimator is a recipe that turns the data into a guess, with no peeking at the unknown \(\boldsymbol\theta\). In the running example the obvious estimator of \(p\) is the sample proportion \(\hat p = \tfrac1n\sum_i X_i = 10/25 = 0.40\). Bias is the systematic part of the error (does the recipe aim at the right target on average?), variance is the random scatter from sample to sample, and mean squared error combines the two. These three numbers are exactly how competing estimators are graded in the simulation studies of Chapter 29. \(\blacktriangleleft\)



Proposition 5.1 (Bias-variance decomposition) For any estimator \(T_n\) with \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T_n^2] < \infty\), \[
\mathrm{MSE}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n)
= \mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n) + \bigl(\mathrm{Bias}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n)\bigr)^2 .
\tag{5.1}\] For a vector estimator \(\mathbf T_n\) of \(g(\boldsymbol\theta)\in\mathbb R^q\), the matrix MSE equals \(\mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T_n) + \mathbf b\,\mathbf b^\top\) with \(\mathbf b = \mathrm{Bias}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T_n)\), and taking traces gives the scalar identity \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\|\mathbf T_n - g\|_2^2 = \mathrm{tr}\,\mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T_n) + \|\mathbf b\|_2^2\).


Proof. Write \(m = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T_n]\) and \(b = m - g(\boldsymbol\theta)\). Then \[
\mathrm{MSE}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n)
= \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl[(T_n - m + b)^2\bigr]
= \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl[(T_n - m)^2\bigr] + 2 b\, \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T_n - m] + b^2 .
\] The cross term vanishes because \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T_n - m] = 0\), and the first term is \(\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n)\) by definition, giving Equation 5.1. The vector statement is identical with \(\mathbf m = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\mathbf T_n]\) and \(\mathbf b = \mathbf m - g\): expand \((\mathbf T_n - g)(\mathbf T_n - g)^\top = (\mathbf T_n - \mathbf m)(\mathbf T_n - \mathbf m)^\top + (\mathbf T_n - \mathbf m)\mathbf b^\top + \mathbf b(\mathbf T_n - \mathbf m)^\top + \mathbf b\mathbf b^\top\) and take \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\); the two middle terms vanish. The trace identity follows from \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf b\mathbf b^\top) = \|\mathbf b\|_2^2\) and linearity of the trace. \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters. The decomposition is the rule for trading bias against variance. A more complicated adjustment model (more covariates in a regression, a more flexible weighting model in MAIC) usually lowers bias but raises variance; Equation 5.1 is the scoreboard on which that trade is settled, and it is why a slightly biased estimator can be the more accurate one (Exercise 5.6). \(\blacktriangleleft\)



Definition 5.3 (Consistency) A sequence of estimators \(T_n\) is (weakly) consistent for \(g(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) if \(T_n \xrightarrow{p} g(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) as \(n \to \infty\), that is, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), \(P_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\!\bigl(|T_n - g(\boldsymbol\theta_0)| > \varepsilon\bigr) \to 0\). It is strongly consistent if \(T_n \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} g(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. Consistency is the promise that with enough data the estimator lands on the truth. Weak consistency (convergence in probability) is all we use in this book; strong consistency (almost-sure convergence, from Chapter 4) is the stronger statement that the estimator settles down for almost every possible infinite data stream, not merely with high probability at each \(n\). For the running example, consistency is the guarantee that \(\hat p \to p\) as the trial grows; in later chapters it is the guarantee that network meta-analysis and MAIC estimates stop being systematically wrong as studies get larger. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Unbiasedness and consistency are logically independent. The sample mean \(\bar X_n\) of iid data with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance is both unbiased (\(\mathbb E[\bar X_n] = \mu\)) and consistent (by the weak law of large numbers below). But \(T_n = X_1\) is unbiased for \(\mu\) yet not consistent, and a biased estimator whose bias and variance both vanish (for example a shrunken mean \(\tfrac{n}{n+1}\bar X_n\)) is consistent: its bias is \(\tfrac{n}{n+1}\mu - \mu = -\mu/(n+1) \to 0\) and its variance is \(\bigl(\tfrac{n}{n+1}\bigr)^2 \sigma^2/n \to 0\), so by Equation 5.1 its MSE vanishes. The MSE in Equation 5.1 is the right single-number summary of finite-sample accuracy, because \(\mathrm{MSE}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n)\to 0\) is equivalent to \(L^2\) convergence, which implies consistency by Chebyshev’s inequality. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 5  Statistical Inference
section: 5.2 Asymptotic tools: continuous mapping, Slutsky, and the delta method
text:
5.2 Asymptotic tools: continuous mapping, Slutsky, and the delta method
Why this section, and why now. Here is the concrete problem these three tools solve. In the running example we will estimate \(p\), but a network meta-analysis never reports a probability; it reports a log odds ratio, a nonlinear function of fitted probabilities. So the real question is: given the uncertainty in \(\hat p\), what is the uncertainty in \(\log\frac{\hat p}{1 - \hat p}\), or in a contrast of two such quantities across trials? The delta method below is the machine that answers this, and it is the single most-used result of the chapter, because every effect measure in the book (log odds ratio, log hazard ratio, risk difference) is a smooth function of fitted parameters. The continuous mapping theorem and Slutsky’s theorem are the two lemmas the delta method (and the later limit theory of the MLE) is built from. If you read this section for one thing, read it for the delta method and Example 5.3. One honest word about ordering: we prove these tools before we have an estimator in hand because the consistency and normality proofs will call them repeatedly; keep the running example’s \(\hat p\) in mind as the thing they will eventually be applied to.
Before we can analyze any estimator as \(n \to \infty\) we need three theorems about how limits in distribution interact with continuous functions and with constants. We will use them constantly, so we prove them here, near the front. We take as given two classical results from probability, which belong to the foundations of Chapter 4 and which we cite rather than reprove; see Bingham and Fry (2010) and a standard graduate probability text for proofs.

Remark (Prerequisites cited from probability). We use the following standard facts about iid random vectors \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) in \(\mathbb R^p\).

Weak law of large numbers (WLLN). If \(\mathbb E\|X_1\| < \infty\) with mean \(\boldsymbol\mu\), then \(\bar X_n = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\mu\).
Multivariate central limit theorem (CLT). If, in addition, \(X_1\) has finite covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\), then \(\sqrt n\,(\bar X_n - \boldsymbol\mu) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \boldsymbol\Sigma)\).
Portmanteau theorem. \(X_n \xrightarrow{d} X\) if and only if \(\mathbb E[h(X_n)] \to \mathbb E[h(X)]\) for every bounded continuous \(h\); equivalently, if and only if \(\mathbb E[h(X_n)] \to \mathbb E[h(X)]\) for every bounded function \(h\) that is continuous at \(P_X\)-almost every point.
Cramér-Wold device. \(X_n \xrightarrow{d} X\) in \(\mathbb R^p\) if and only if \(\mathbf t^\top X_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathbf t^\top X\) in \(\mathbb R\) for every \(\mathbf t \in \mathbb R^p\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)



Remark (The \(O_p\) and \(o_p\) shorthand (read once, use everywhere)). Two of the proofs below use a compact notation for “stochastically small” and “stochastically bounded,” listed in Notation. A sequence of random vectors \(V_n\) is \(o_p(1)\) if \(V_n \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf 0\) (it vanishes), and \(O_p(1)\) if it is bounded in probability: for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is a constant \(K\) with \(\sup_n P(\|V_n\| > K) < \varepsilon\) (it does not run off to infinity). Three rules are all we need, and each is elementary:

A sequence that converges in distribution is \(O_p(1)\) (a convergent limit law cannot put mass at infinity).
\(o_p(1) \times O_p(1) = o_p(1)\): something vanishing times something bounded vanishes.
\(o_p(1) + o_p(1) = o_p(1)\) and \(O_p(1) + O_p(1) = O_p(1)\).

These are exactly the steps that let us discard remainder terms in the delta method and in Wilks’ theorem. You do not need their proofs to follow the chapter; treat them as arithmetic for random sequences. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The first tool says continuous functions preserve convergence in distribution. It corresponds to A.13 in the proof catalogue.

Theorem 5.1 (Continuous mapping theorem) Let \(X_n, X\) be random vectors in \(\mathbb R^p\) and let \(g : \mathbb R^p \to \mathbb R^q\) be measurable. Let \(D_g\) be the set of discontinuity points of \(g\) and suppose \(P(X \in D_g) = 0\). Then:

\(X_n \xrightarrow{d} X \;\Rightarrow\; g(X_n) \xrightarrow{d} g(X)\);
\(X_n \xrightarrow{p} X \;\Rightarrow\; g(X_n) \xrightarrow{p} g(X)\);
\(X_n \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} X \;\Rightarrow\; g(X_n) \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} g(X)\).



Proof. (i) Let \(h : \mathbb R^q \to \mathbb R\) be bounded and continuous. The composition \(h \circ g\) is bounded by \(\|h\|_\infty\), and it is continuous at every point where \(g\) is continuous, hence at every point of \(\mathbb R^p \setminus D_g\), a set of \(P_X\)-probability one. By the second (almost-everywhere) form of the Portmanteau theorem, \(\mathbb E[h(g(X_n))] = \mathbb E[(h\circ g)(X_n)] \to \mathbb E[(h\circ g)(X)] = \mathbb E[h(g(X))]\). As \(h\) was an arbitrary bounded continuous function, the first form of Portmanteau gives \(g(X_n) \xrightarrow{d} g(X)\).
(iii) If \(X_n(\omega) \to X(\omega)\) and \(X(\omega) \notin D_g\), then \(g(X_n(\omega)) \to g(X(\omega))\) by continuity of \(g\) at \(X(\omega)\). This holds for all \(\omega\) outside the union of the null set \(\{X_n \not\to X\}\) and the null set \(\{X \in D_g\}\), which is null; hence \(g(X_n) \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} g(X)\).
(ii) Suppose \(g(X_n) \overset{p}{\nrightarrow} g(X)\). Then there exist \(\varepsilon, \eta > 0\) and a subsequence along which \(P(\|g(X_n) - g(X)\| > \varepsilon) > \eta\). Along that subsequence \(X_n \xrightarrow{p} X\) still holds, so it has a further subsequence with \(X_{n_k} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} X\) (a standard fact: convergence in probability implies almost-sure convergence along a subsequence; see Bingham and Fry (2010)). Intuitively, a sequence converges in probability if and only if every subsequence contains a further subsequence that converges almost surely, and the contradiction we now derive exploits exactly that escape hatch. By part (iii), \(g(X_{n_k}) \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} g(X)\), hence \(g(X_{n_k}) \xrightarrow{p} g(X)\), contradicting \(P(\|g(X_{n_k}) - g(X)\| > \varepsilon) > \eta\). \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters. This is the “plug-in” theorem: if an estimate converges, a continuous transformation of it converges too. It is what lets us pass from a converging \(\hat p\) to a converging odds \(\hat p/(1 - \hat p)\), or from a converging log odds ratio to its converging exponential, the odds ratio. One-line example: if \(\bar X_n \xrightarrow{p} \mu\) then \(\bar X_n^2 \xrightarrow{p} \mu^2\). What to remember: continuity transfers convergence, provided the function is well behaved at the limit. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The second tool lets us combine a sequence that converges in distribution with one that converges to a constant. It corresponds to A.12.

Theorem 5.2 (Slutsky’s theorem) Let \(X_n \xrightarrow{d} X\) in \(\mathbb R^p\) and let \(Y_n \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf c\) for a constant \(\mathbf c \in \mathbb R^p\) (respectively a constant matrix \(C_n \xrightarrow{p} C\)). Then \[
X_n + Y_n \xrightarrow{d} X + \mathbf c,
\qquad
Y_n^\top X_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathbf c^\top X,
\qquad
C_n X_n \xrightarrow{d} C\,X .
\] If \(p = 1\) and \(\mathbf c \ne 0\), then \(X_n / Y_n \xrightarrow{d} X/\mathbf c\).


Proof. The key step is that joint convergence holds: \((X_n, Y_n) \xrightarrow{d} (X, \mathbf c)\) in \(\mathbb R^{2p}\). To see this, take a bounded uniformly continuous \(h:\mathbb R^{2p}\to\mathbb R\) with modulus of continuity \(\omega_h(\delta) = \sup\{|h(u)-h(v)| : \|u-v\|\le\delta\}\), which satisfies \(\omega_h(\delta) \to 0\) as \(\delta \downarrow 0\). For any \(\delta > 0\), \[
\bigl|\mathbb E[h(X_n, Y_n)] - \mathbb E[h(X_n, \mathbf c)]\bigr|
\le \omega_h(\delta) + 2\|h\|_\infty\, P(\|Y_n - \mathbf c\| > \delta).
\] This inequality splits the difference by where \(Y_n\) lands. On the good event \(\{\|Y_n - \mathbf c\| \le \delta\}\) the two points \((X_n, Y_n)\) and \((X_n, \mathbf c)\) are within \(\delta\) of each other, so \(h\) differs between them by at most the modulus \(\omega_h(\delta)\). On the bad event \(\{\|Y_n - \mathbf c\| > \delta\}\) we cannot control the difference, but \(h\) is bounded by \(\|h\|_\infty\), so the difference is at most \(2\|h\|_\infty\), weighted by the probability \(P(\|Y_n - \mathbf c\| > \delta)\) of that event. Letting \(n \to \infty\) and using \(Y_n \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf c\) kills the last term, leaving \(\limsup_n |\mathbb E[h(X_n, Y_n)] - \mathbb E[h(X_n, \mathbf c)]| \le \omega_h(\delta)\); since \(\delta\) is arbitrary, the limsup is zero. Meanwhile \(\mathbb E[h(X_n, \mathbf c)] \to \mathbb E[h(X, \mathbf c)]\) because \(u \mapsto h(u, \mathbf c)\) is bounded and continuous and \(X_n \xrightarrow d X\). Hence \(\mathbb E[h(X_n, Y_n)] \to \mathbb E[h(X, \mathbf c)]\) for all bounded uniformly continuous \(h\), which by the Portmanteau theorem (uniformly continuous test functions suffice) gives \((X_n, Y_n) \xrightarrow{d} (X, \mathbf c)\).
Now apply the continuous mapping theorem (Theorem 5.1). The maps \((x, y) \mapsto x + y\), \((x, y) \mapsto y^\top x\), and (matrix version) \((x, C) \mapsto C x\) are continuous everywhere, so \(X_n + Y_n \xrightarrow{d} X + \mathbf c\), \(Y_n^\top X_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathbf c^\top X\), and \(C_n X_n \xrightarrow{d} C X\). The map \((x, y) \mapsto x/y\) is continuous on \(\mathbb R \times (\mathbb R \setminus \{0\})\), and the limit \((X, \mathbf c)\) lands in that set with probability one when \(\mathbf c \ne 0\), so \(X_n/Y_n \xrightarrow{d} X/\mathbf c\). \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters. Slutsky lets us replace an unknown constant by a consistent estimate without changing a limiting distribution. This is why a \(z\)- or \(t\)-statistic still works when we plug an estimated standard error into the denominator: the numerator has a central limit theorem, the denominator converges to a constant, and Slutsky glues them. One-line example: if \(\sqrt n(\bar X_n - \mu) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) and \(S_n \xrightarrow{p} \sigma\), then \(\sqrt n(\bar X_n - \mu)/S_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N(0, 1)\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The third tool transfers a \(\sqrt n\) central limit theorem through a smooth transformation. It is the single most-used result of this chapter in later applications, because every effect measure in the book (log odds ratio, log hazard ratio, risk difference) is a smooth function of fitted parameters. It corresponds to A.11.

Theorem 5.3 (Delta method) Let \(\mathbf T_n\) be a sequence of \(\mathbb R^p\)-valued estimators and \(\boldsymbol\theta \in \mathbb R^p\) a constant with \[
\sqrt n\,(\mathbf T_n - \boldsymbol\theta) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \boldsymbol\Sigma).
\] Let \(g : \mathbb R^p \to \mathbb R^q\) be differentiable at \(\boldsymbol\theta\) with Jacobian matrix \(\mathbf D = \bigl[\partial g_a / \partial \theta_b\bigr]_{a,b}\) evaluated at \(\boldsymbol\theta\). Then \[
\sqrt n\,\bigl(g(\mathbf T_n) - g(\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr)
\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_q\!\bigl(\mathbf 0,\; \mathbf D\,\boldsymbol\Sigma\,\mathbf D^\top\bigr).
\tag{5.2}\] In the scalar case \(p = q = 1\) this reads \(\sqrt n\,(g(T_n) - g(\theta)) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N\!\bigl(0,\, g'(\theta)^2 \sigma^2\bigr)\).


Proof. First note that \(\sqrt n\,(\mathbf T_n - \boldsymbol\theta) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \boldsymbol\Sigma)\) implies \(\mathbf T_n - \boldsymbol\theta = n^{-1/2}\bigl[\sqrt n(\mathbf T_n - \boldsymbol\theta)\bigr] \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf 0\) by Slutsky (Theorem 5.2) with the constant sequence \(n^{-1/2} \to 0\); hence \(\mathbf T_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta\).
Differentiability of \(g\) at \(\boldsymbol\theta\) means \[
g(\mathbf t) = g(\boldsymbol\theta) + \mathbf D\,(\mathbf t - \boldsymbol\theta) + R(\mathbf t),
\qquad
\frac{\|R(\mathbf t)\|}{\|\mathbf t - \boldsymbol\theta\|} \to 0 \ \text{ as } \mathbf t \to \boldsymbol\theta,
\] with the convention \(R(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathbf 0\). Define the function \(\rho(\mathbf t) = \|R(\mathbf t)\| / \|\mathbf t - \boldsymbol\theta\|\) for \(\mathbf t \ne \boldsymbol\theta\) and \(\rho(\boldsymbol\theta) = 0\); then \(\rho\) is continuous at \(\boldsymbol\theta\). Multiplying the expansion at \(\mathbf t = \mathbf T_n\) by \(\sqrt n\), \[
\sqrt n\,\bigl(g(\mathbf T_n) - g(\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr)
= \mathbf D\,\underbrace{\sqrt n\,(\mathbf T_n - \boldsymbol\theta)}_{=:\,\mathbf Z_n}
\;+\; \sqrt n\, R(\mathbf T_n).
\] The remainder is controlled by \(\|\sqrt n\,R(\mathbf T_n)\| = \rho(\mathbf T_n)\,\|\mathbf Z_n\|\). Since \(\mathbf T_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta\) and \(\rho\) is continuous at \(\boldsymbol\theta\) with \(\rho(\boldsymbol\theta) = 0\), the continuous mapping theorem (Theorem 5.1) gives \(\rho(\mathbf T_n) \xrightarrow{p} 0\); and \(\|\mathbf Z_n\| \xrightarrow{d} \|\mathbf Z\|\) where \(\mathbf Z \sim \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \boldsymbol\Sigma)\), so \(\|\mathbf Z_n\| = O_p(1)\) (rule 1 of the \(O_p/o_p\) remark above: a convergent-in-distribution sequence is bounded in probability). Hence \(\sqrt n\,R(\mathbf T_n) = \rho(\mathbf T_n)\,\|\mathbf Z_n\| \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf 0\), the product of an \(o_p(1)\) and an \(O_p(1)\) sequence (rule 2). Applying Slutsky once more, \[
\sqrt n\,\bigl(g(\mathbf T_n) - g(\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr)
= \mathbf D\,\mathbf Z_n + o_p(1) \xrightarrow{d} \mathbf D\,\mathbf Z .
\] Finally \(\mathbf D \mathbf Z \sim \mathcal N_q(\mathbf 0, \mathbf D\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf D^\top)\) because an affine image of a Gaussian is Gaussian with the transformed covariance (Theorem 4.14). This is Equation 5.2. \(\square\)


Remark. The hypothesis \(g'(\theta) \ne 0\) (more generally, \(\mathbf D\) of full row rank) is what makes the limit nondegenerate. If \(g'(\theta) = 0\) the first-order term vanishes and the correct rate is \(n\) rather than \(\sqrt n\), with a \(\chi^2\)-type limit driven by the second derivative; this second-order delta method underlies the asymptotics of the likelihood-ratio statistic in Section 5.9. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why this matters. This is the result that produces a standard error for almost every effect measure you will report. When you fit a model and then transform a coefficient (a probability into a log odds, a rate into a log rate, two coefficients into a ratio), the delta-method formula Equation 5.2 gives the variance of the transform: multiply the variance of the fitted parameter by the squared derivative (scalar case), or sandwich the covariance between the Jacobian \(\mathbf D\) and its transpose (vector case). It is the source of the familiar “standard error of a log odds ratio” and, in Example 5.3, of the standard error of an indirect comparison. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Example 5.2 (Delta method for a log odds (a first taste)) Anticipating the running example, the central limit theorem for a proportion gives \(\sqrt n\,(\hat p - p) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N(0,\, p(1 - p))\). We want the uncertainty of the log odds \(g(p) = \log\frac{p}{1 - p}\), whose derivative is \(g'(p) = \frac{1}{p(1 - p)}\). The scalar delta method (Theorem 5.3) gives \[
\sqrt n\,\bigl(g(\hat p) - g(p)\bigr) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N\!\Bigl(0,\; g'(p)^2\, p(1 - p)\Bigr)
= \mathcal N\!\Bigl(0,\; \tfrac{1}{p(1 - p)}\Bigr),
\] so \(\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\bigl(g(\hat p)\bigr) \approx \frac{1}{n\,\hat p(1 - \hat p)} = \frac{1}{n\hat p} + \frac{1}{n(1 - \hat p)} = \frac{1}{\#\text{responders}} + \frac{1}{\#\text{non-responders}}\). For our trial (\(n = 25\), \(10\) responders) this is \(\tfrac1{10} + \tfrac1{15} = 0.1\overline 6\), so the log odds has standard error \(\sqrt{0.1\overline 6} = 0.408\). The reading is concrete: a parameter on an awkward scale (a probability, bounded in \([0,1]\)) is moved to a convenient unbounded scale (the log odds) and its standard error comes along for free. The full computation, with confidence intervals, returns in Example 5.4. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Example 5.3 (A toy indirect treatment comparison) Here is the chapter’s subject in miniature. Two randomized trials share a common control \(A\). Trial 1 compares a new treatment \(B\) against \(A\); trial 2 compares a different treatment \(C\) against \(A\). No trial compares \(B\) with \(C\), yet we want that contrast on the log-odds-ratio scale.

Each arm gives a log odds \(\log\frac{\hat p}{1 - \hat p}\) whose variance, by Example 5.2, is (\(1/\text{responders} + 1/\text{non-responders}\)). A log odds ratio is a difference of two independent arm log odds, so its variance is the sum of the four reciprocals. For the direct contrasts, \[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat d_{BA} &= \log\tfrac{20/30}{10/40} = \log\tfrac{20\cdot 40}{30\cdot 10} = 0.9808, &
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\widehat d_{BA}) &= \tfrac1{20} + \tfrac1{30} + \tfrac1{10} + \tfrac1{40} = 0.20833,\\
\widehat d_{CA} &= \log\tfrac{18/42}{15/45} = \log\tfrac{18\cdot 45}{42\cdot 15} = 0.2513, &
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\widehat d_{CA}) &= \tfrac1{18} + \tfrac1{42} + \tfrac1{15} + \tfrac1{45} = 0.16825.
\end{aligned}
\] The indirect contrast of \(B\) versus \(C\) is the difference \(\widehat d_{BC} = \widehat d_{BA} - \widehat d_{CA} = 0.9808 - 0.2513 = 0.7295\). Because the two trials are independent, the variances add (there is no covariance term across independent studies in Equation 5.2): \(\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\widehat d_{BC}) = 0.20833 + 0.16825 = 0.37658\), so the standard error is \(\sqrt{0.37658} = 0.6137\). A 95% interval is \(0.7295 \pm 1.96 \times 0.6137 = (-0.4733,\, 1.9323)\), and on the odds-ratio scale \((e^{-0.4733}, e^{1.9323}) = (0.62,\, 6.91)\). The interval covers \(1\), so the indirect comparison is inconclusive; and note its standard error (\(0.61\)) exceeds either direct one (\(0.46\) and \(0.41\)): combining two estimates adds uncertainty. This is the Bucher indirect comparison, developed in full in Chapter 14; every number above came from the delta method plus the independence of the two trials. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
5.3 Likelihood, score, and Fisher information
The likelihood reverses the usual reading of a density. Where \(f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\) is, for fixed \(\boldsymbol\theta\), a function of the data \(x\), the likelihood fixes the observed data and varies the parameter.

Definition 5.4 (Likelihood and log-likelihood) Given observed data \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) from the model Definition 5.1, the likelihood function is \[
L_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} f(X_i;\boldsymbol\theta),
\qquad \boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta,
\] viewed as a (random) function of \(\boldsymbol\theta\). The log-likelihood is \[
\ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \log L_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log f(X_i;\boldsymbol\theta).
\] For a single observation we write \(\ell(\boldsymbol\theta; x) = \log f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\), so \(\ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \sum_i \ell(\boldsymbol\theta; X_i)\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. The likelihood asks, of each candidate \(\boldsymbol\theta\), “how probable were the data we actually saw, if this were the parameter?” High likelihood means good fit. Taking logs turns the product over independent patients into a sum, which is why every formula below is additive over the sample. For the running example, \(\ell_n(p) = \bigl(\textstyle\sum_i X_i\bigr)\log p + \bigl(n - \textstyle\sum_i X_i\bigr)\log(1 - p) = 10\log p + 15\log(1 - p)\), a function of \(p\) alone once the data are in hand. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The slope of the log-likelihood in \(\boldsymbol\theta\) is the score; the MLE is found by setting it to zero.

Definition 5.5 (Score function) The (per-observation) score is the gradient of the single-observation log-likelihood in the parameter, \[
\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; x) = \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\,\log f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)
= \frac{\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta} f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)}{f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)} \in \mathbb R^{p},
\] defined wherever \(f(x;\boldsymbol\theta) > 0\). The sample score is \[
\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\,\ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta)
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X_i).
\tag{5.3}\] \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. The score \(\mathbf s_n\) is the slope of the log-likelihood hill in the parameter (\(\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\) is the gradient, the vector of partial derivatives in each coordinate of \(\boldsymbol\theta\)). It points in the direction that would increase the fit, and it is zero exactly at the top of the hill, the MLE. Read it as “how strongly, and in which direction, the data push each parameter.” We compute the Bernoulli score just below, in Lemma 5.1. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

All of the clean identities about the score require an interchange of differentiation and integration, which is not automatic. We isolate the needed conditions in one definition and refer back to it.

Definition 5.6 (Regularity conditions) The model Definition 5.1 is regular at an interior point \(\boldsymbol\theta \in \mathrm{int}\,\Theta\) if:
(R1) Common support. The set \(\{x : f(x;\boldsymbol\theta) > 0\}\) does not depend on \(\boldsymbol\theta\).
(R2) Smoothness. For \(\nu\)-almost every \(x\), the map \(\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\) is twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(\boldsymbol\theta\).
(R3) Differentiation under the integral. The first two derivatives in \(\boldsymbol\theta\) of \(\int f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\,d\nu(x) = 1\) may be taken inside the integral; concretely there are \(\nu\)-integrable envelopes dominating \(\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta} f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\|\) and \(\|\nabla^2_{\boldsymbol\theta} f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\|\) uniformly in a neighborhood, so the dominated convergence theorem applies.
(R4) Finite, positive-definite information. The Fisher information Definition 5.7 exists, is finite, and is positive definite at \(\boldsymbol\theta\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation: what R1-R4 are for. These are safety checks that make the log-likelihood smooth enough, and its tails light enough, for calculus to behave. R1 (common support) says the set of possible outcomes does not move as \(\boldsymbol\theta\) changes: true for the Bernoulli, where outcomes are always \(\{0, 1\}\), but false for Uniform\((0,\theta)\), whose range grows with \(\theta\) (Exercise 5.8). R2 (smoothness) says the log-likelihood has a well-defined slope and curvature. R3 (differentiation under the integral) is the license to swap a derivative with an integral, which is what every score identity below secretly uses; the “integrable envelopes” are a domination condition that makes the swap legal. R4 (positive-definite information) says no direction of the parameter is left totally undetermined by the data. Read R1-R4 as “the curve is smooth, its tails are tame, and the parameter is locally pinned down”; the rest is the machinery that turns those words into theorems. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Under (R1)-(R3) the score has mean zero. This is the cornerstone identity from which everything else (the information equality, the Cramér-Rao bound, the asymptotics of the MLE) follows.

Lemma 5.1 (The score has mean zero) If the model is regular (Definition 5.6) at \(\boldsymbol\theta\), then \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl[\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\bigr] = \mathbf 0\).


Proof. Because \(f(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta)\) integrates to \(1\) for every \(\boldsymbol\theta\), differentiating the identity \(\int f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x) = 1\) and moving the gradient inside the integral (licensed by (R3)), \[
\mathbf 0 = \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta} \int f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)
= \int \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta} f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)
= \int \frac{\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta} f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)}{f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)}\, f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)
= \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl[\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\bigr],
\] where the third equality multiplies and divides by \(f\) on the set \(\{f > 0\}\), which carries all the mass by (R1). Condition (R1) is doing real work here: because the support \(\{f > 0\}\) does not move with \(\boldsymbol\theta\), differentiating the integral produces no extra term from a \(\boldsymbol\theta\)-moving boundary, and the interchange of \(\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\) with the integral is clean. (When the support does move with \(\boldsymbol\theta\), as for Uniform\((0,\theta)\) in Exercise 5.8, this lemma fails.) \(\square\)


Remark. What this means, and the Bernoulli score. The score is the slope of the log-likelihood. Saying its average is zero at the truth means: the true parameter is, on average, the value at which the data give no reason to nudge the estimate up or down. That is exactly why the MLE, found by setting the score to zero, aims at the truth. For the running example the single-observation log-likelihood is \(\ell(p; x) = x\log p + (1 - x)\log(1 - p)\), so the score is \[
s(p; x) = \frac{x}{p} - \frac{1 - x}{1 - p} = \frac{x - p}{p(1 - p)},
\] and since \(\mathbb E[X] = p\) its mean is \(\mathbb E[s(p; X)] = (p - p)/(p(1 - p)) = 0\), confirming Lemma 5.1. The numerator \(x - p\) shows the score is positive when a success pushes the estimate up and negative when a failure pulls it down. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Since the score has mean zero, its covariance is just its second moment. That second moment is the Fisher information.

Definition 5.7 (Fisher information) For a regular model the Fisher information matrix (in one observation) at \(\boldsymbol\theta\) is the covariance of the score, \[
\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)
= \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl(\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\bigr)
= \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\bigl[\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\,\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)^\top\bigr]
\in \mathbb R^{p\times p}.
\tag{5.4}\] The information in the full sample of size \(n\) is \(\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta))\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. Fisher information measures how much one observation tells you about \(\boldsymbol\theta\). There are two equivalent readings, made precise in Theorem 5.4 below: it is the variance of the score (how much the slope of the log-likelihood jumps around from sample to sample) and it is the average curvature of the log-likelihood (how sharply peaked it is). A sharply peaked log-likelihood pins down the parameter tightly, so large information means small standard error. For the Bernoulli, \(\mathcal I(p) = 1/[p(1 - p)]\), which is smallest at \(p = 1/2\) (a 50/50 outcome is the least informative) and blows up near \(0\) or \(1\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Fisher information is always positive semidefinite (it is a covariance matrix, Theorem 4.9), and (R4) asks that it be strictly positive definite, which is the analytic statement that the parameter is locally identifiable: no nonzero direction leaves the log-likelihood flat in expectation.

Theorem 5.4 (Information equality) If the model is regular (Definition 5.6) at \(\boldsymbol\theta\), then the Fisher information equals minus the expected Hessian of the log-likelihood: \[
\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)
= \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\bigl[\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\,\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)^\top\bigr]
= -\,\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\bigl[\nabla^2_{\boldsymbol\theta}\,\ell(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\bigr].
\tag{5.5}\]


Proof. The first equality is Equation 5.4 together with Lemma 5.1 (mean-zero makes the second moment equal the covariance). For the second, start from \(\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; x) = \nabla f / f\) and compute the Hessian of \(\ell(\boldsymbol\theta; x) = \log f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\) by the quotient rule for gradients (the vector version of the scalar quotient rule; if it helps, read the display one component of \(\boldsymbol\theta\) at a time, with \(\nabla^2\) the Hessian, the matrix of second partial derivatives): \[
\nabla^2_{\boldsymbol\theta}\,\ell(\boldsymbol\theta; x)
= \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\left(\frac{\nabla f}{f}\right)
= \frac{\nabla^2 f}{f} - \frac{(\nabla f)(\nabla f)^\top}{f^2}
= \frac{\nabla^2 f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)}{f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)} - \mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; x)\,\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; x)^\top,
\] using \(\nabla f / f = \mathbf s\) in the last term. Take \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\) of both sides. The first term integrates to zero: \[
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\left[\frac{\nabla^2 f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)}{f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)}\right]
= \int \frac{\nabla^2 f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)}{f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)}\, f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)
= \int \nabla^2 f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)
= \nabla^2 \int f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x) = \nabla^2 (1) = \mathbf 0,
\] where the second-derivative interchange is licensed by (R3). Therefore \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\nabla^2 \ell(\boldsymbol\theta; X)] = \mathbf 0 - \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\mathbf s \mathbf s^\top] = -\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)\), which rearranges to Equation 5.5. \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters. The information equality is a duality: how variable the slope of the log-likelihood is across samples (the score variance, left side) equals how curved the log-likelihood is on average (minus the expected Hessian, right side). This is the hinge of the whole chapter. It is why the same matrix \(\mathcal I\) appears both as the variance in the central limit theorem for the score and as the curvature that converts that noise into estimator noise; it makes the MLE’s variance equal to \(\mathcal I^{-1}\) (Theorem 5.6), it powers the Cramér-Rao bound, and its failure under misspecification is exactly what forces the sandwich variance of Section 5.8. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The information in independent data adds. This additivity is why precision scales linearly with sample size, and it is the reason the per-observation information \(\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)\) is the natural unit.

Corollary 5.1 (Additivity of information) For iid data the sample score \(\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \sum_i \mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X_i)\) has mean zero and \[
\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl(\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr)
= n\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta).
\]


Proof. By Lemma 5.1 each summand has mean zero, so \(\mathbb E[\mathbf s_n] = \mathbf 0\). The summands are iid, hence uncorrelated, so the covariance of the sum is the sum of the covariances: \(\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf s_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X_i)) = n\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)\) by Definition 5.7. \(\square\)


Remark (Per-observation information versus sample information (a common source of confusion)). Two informations are now in play, and standard errors depend on getting the factor of \(n\) right. Keep them straight with this table.









Symbol
Name
Formula
Refers to




\(\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)\)
per-observation information
\(\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X))\)
a single observation


\(\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta)\)
sample information
\(n\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)\)
the whole sample of size \(n\)



The variance of the MLE is governed by the sample information: in large samples \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) \approx \mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1} = \tfrac1n\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1}\), and the standard error is the square root of a diagonal entry. The per-observation \(\mathcal I\) is the fixed “information rate”; multiplying by \(n\) and inverting is what makes the standard error shrink like \(1/\sqrt n\). For the running example, \(\mathcal I(p) = 1/[p(1 - p)]\), the sample information is \(\mathcal I_n(p) = n/[p(1 - p)]\), and \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat p) \approx p(1 - p)/n\). At \(\hat p = 0.4\), \(n = 25\): \(\mathcal I_n(\hat p) = 25/0.24 = 104.17\) and \(\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat p) = 0.24/25 = 0.0096\). A recurring novice slip is to invert \(\mathcal I\) instead of \(\mathcal I_n\), which inflates the standard error by a factor of \(\sqrt n\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
5.4 Maximum likelihood and its invariance

Definition 5.8 (Maximum likelihood estimator) A maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) is any parameter value maximizing the likelihood, equivalently the log-likelihood, \[
\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}} = \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n
\in \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta} L_n(\boldsymbol\theta)
= \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta} \ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta).
\] When \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) lies in the interior of \(\Theta\) and \(\ell_n\) is differentiable there, \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) solves the likelihood (score) equations \(\mathbf s_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathbf 0\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. The MLE is the parameter value under which the data we actually saw would have been most probable: the top of the log-likelihood hill, where the score (slope) is zero. For the running example this is just \(\hat p = \bar X_n = 0.40\), the sample proportion. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Maximization is invariant under reparameterization, which is one of the most useful practical properties of the MLE: to estimate any function of the parameter by maximum likelihood, just plug in.

Proposition 5.2 (Invariance of the MLE) Let \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) be an MLE of \(\boldsymbol\theta\).

If \(h : \Theta \to \mathrm H\) is a bijection and the model is reparameterized by \(\boldsymbol\eta = h(\boldsymbol\theta)\), then \(h(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\) is an MLE of \(\boldsymbol\eta\).
For an arbitrary (not necessarily injective) function \(h : \Theta \to \mathrm H\), define the induced (profile) likelihood \(L_n^{*}(\boldsymbol\eta) = \sup\{L_n(\boldsymbol\theta) : h(\boldsymbol\theta) = \boldsymbol\eta\}\). Then \(h(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\) maximizes \(L_n^{*}\); we call \(h(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\) the MLE of \(\boldsymbol\eta = h(\boldsymbol\theta)\).



Proof. (i) Write the likelihood in the new parameterization as \(\tilde L_n(\boldsymbol\eta) = L_n(h^{-1}(\boldsymbol\eta))\). Since \(h^{-1}\) is a bijection of \(\mathrm H\) onto \(\Theta\), ranging \(\boldsymbol\eta\) over \(\mathrm H\) ranges \(h^{-1}(\boldsymbol\eta)\) over all of \(\Theta\), so \(\sup_{\boldsymbol\eta} \tilde L_n(\boldsymbol\eta) = \sup_{\boldsymbol\theta} L_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = L_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\), and the supremum is attained at \(\boldsymbol\eta = h(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\) because \(\tilde L_n(h(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)) = L_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\).
(ii) By construction \(L_n^{*}(\boldsymbol\eta) \le \sup_{\boldsymbol\theta} L_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = L_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\) for every \(\boldsymbol\eta\), since each \(L_n^{*}(\boldsymbol\eta)\) is a supremum over a subset of \(\Theta\). Evaluating at \(\boldsymbol\eta^{*} = h(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\), the defining set \(\{\boldsymbol\theta : h(\boldsymbol\theta) = \boldsymbol\eta^{*}\}\) contains \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\), so \(L_n^{*}(\boldsymbol\eta^{*}) \ge L_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\). The two inequalities force \(L_n^{*}(\boldsymbol\eta^{*}) = L_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \max_{\boldsymbol\eta} L_n^{*}(\boldsymbol\eta)\), so \(\boldsymbol\eta^{*} = h(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\) maximizes \(L_n^{*}\). \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters, and what “profile” means. Part (i) is the workhorse behind every transformed estimate in the book: to get the MLE of an odds ratio, a risk ratio, a hazard ratio, or a marginal effect, you fit the model once and plug the MLE into the transformation; no separate maximization is needed. Part (ii) handles the case where the transformation \(h\) throws away some parameters (nuisance parameters). The profile likelihood \(L_n^{*}(\boldsymbol\eta)\) is built by maximizing out everything except the target \(\boldsymbol\eta\), tracing a one-dimensional ridge (“profile”) across the full likelihood surface; it is the object inverted to get the profile-likelihood confidence intervals of Section 5.9, which is why we record it now even though we do not use it until then. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
5.5 Consistency of the MLE
Why prove this? As a practitioner you may take for granted that more data means a better estimate. Consistency is the theorem that makes that faith legitimate: it is the guarantee that, as trials grow, the MLE, and with it the network meta-analysis and MAIC estimates of later chapters, stops being systematically wrong and settles on the true value. Without it, none of the asymptotic standard errors below would describe anything real.
We now prove that the MLE converges to the truth. The argument has three clean pieces: a population criterion uniquely maximized at \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\) (the information inequality), a uniform law of large numbers transferring the sample criterion to the population one, and an argmax-continuity lemma. The first piece relies on Jensen’s inequality (Theorem 4.6).

Lemma 5.2 (Information inequality) Let \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\) be the true parameter and suppose the model is identifiable (Definition 5.1). For every \(\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta\) with \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\bigl|\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr| < \infty\), \[
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\!\bigl[\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta_0)\bigr]
\;\ge\;
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\!\bigl[\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr],
\] with equality if and only if \(\boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol\theta_0\). Equivalently, the Kullback-Leibler divergence \(\mathrm{KL}(f_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\,\|\,f_{\boldsymbol\theta}) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[\log(f(X;\boldsymbol\theta_0)/f(X;\boldsymbol\theta))]\) is nonnegative and vanishes only at \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\).


Proof. Consider the ratio \(r(X) = f(X;\boldsymbol\theta) / f(X;\boldsymbol\theta_0)\), defined where \(f(X;\boldsymbol\theta_0) > 0\). The function \(\varphi(u) = -\log u\) is strictly convex on \((0,\infty)\). By Jensen’s inequality (Theorem 4.6), \[
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\!\bigl[-\log r(X)\bigr]
\;\ge\; -\log \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[r(X)].
\] The right-hand expectation is \[
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[r(X)]
= \int_{\{f_{\boldsymbol\theta_0} > 0\}} \frac{f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)}{f(x;\boldsymbol\theta_0)}\, f(x;\boldsymbol\theta_0)\, d\nu(x)
= \int_{\{f_{\boldsymbol\theta_0} > 0\}} f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x) \le 1,
\] so \(-\log \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[r(X)] \ge 0\). Therefore \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[-\log r(X)] = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta_0)] - \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)] \ge 0\), which is the claimed inequality and shows \(\mathrm{KL} \ge 0\).
For equality: strict convexity of \(\varphi\) makes Jensen an equality only if \(r(X)\) is \(P_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\)-almost surely constant, say \(r(X) = c\). Then \(f(X;\boldsymbol\theta) = c\, f(X;\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) a.s., and integrating both sides forces \(c = 1\) (both are densities), so \(f(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta) = f(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) \(\nu\)-almost everywhere. By identifiability this means \(\boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol\theta_0\). Conversely \(\boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol\theta_0\) gives equality trivially. \(\square\)

The population criterion is \(M(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)]\) and the sample criterion is \(M_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \tfrac1n \ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \tfrac1n \sum_i \log f(X_i;\boldsymbol\theta)\). For each fixed \(\boldsymbol\theta\) the WLLN gives \(M_n(\boldsymbol\theta) \xrightarrow{p} M(\boldsymbol\theta)\); to control the maximizer we need this uniformly in \(\boldsymbol\theta\). We state the uniform law as a cited prerequisite.

Lemma 5.3 (Uniform law of large numbers) Let \(\Theta\) be compact, let \(\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto \log f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\) be continuous for \(\nu\)-almost every \(x\), and suppose the envelope condition \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\bigl[\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta} |\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)|\bigr] < \infty\) holds. Then \(M\) is continuous on \(\Theta\) and \[
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta} \bigl|M_n(\boldsymbol\theta) - M(\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr|
\xrightarrow{p} 0 .
\]


Proof. This is a standard consequence of compactness, almost-everywhere continuity, and the integrable envelope; the proof covers \(\Theta\) by finitely many small balls, applies the pointwise WLLN at the centers, and controls the oscillation inside each ball with the envelope and dominated convergence. See Bingham and Fry (2010) and a standard text on asymptotic statistics; we take it as given. \(\square\)


Lemma 5.4 (Argmax consistency) Let \(M : \Theta \to \mathbb R\) be continuous on a compact set \(\Theta\) with a unique maximizer \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\). Let \(M_n\) be random functions with \(\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta} |M_n(\boldsymbol\theta) - M(\boldsymbol\theta)| \xrightarrow{p} 0\), and let \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \in \arg\max_{\boldsymbol\theta} M_n(\boldsymbol\theta)\). Then \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta_0\).


Proof. Fix \(\varepsilon > 0\) and let \(B_\varepsilon = \{\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta : \|\boldsymbol\theta - \boldsymbol\theta_0\| \ge \varepsilon\}\). This set is closed, hence compact, so the continuous \(M\) attains its maximum over \(B_\varepsilon\) at some point; because \(\boldsymbol\theta_0 \notin B_\varepsilon\) and \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\) is the unique maximizer of \(M\), this maximum is strictly below \(M(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\). Set \[
\delta = M(\boldsymbol\theta_0) - \sup_{\boldsymbol\theta \in B_\varepsilon} M(\boldsymbol\theta) > 0 .
\] Let \(U_n = \sup_{\boldsymbol\theta} |M_n(\boldsymbol\theta) - M(\boldsymbol\theta)|\) and work on the event \(\{U_n < \delta/2\}\). On this event, for any \(\boldsymbol\theta \in B_\varepsilon\), \[
M_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) \ge M_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0) > M(\boldsymbol\theta_0) - \tfrac{\delta}{2}
= \sup_{B_\varepsilon} M + \tfrac{\delta}{2} \ge M(\boldsymbol\theta) + \tfrac{\delta}{2} > M_n(\boldsymbol\theta),
\] using, in order, that \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) maximizes \(M_n\), the bound \(U_n < \delta/2\) at \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\), the definition of \(\delta\), and again \(U_n < \delta/2\) at \(\boldsymbol\theta\). Thus no point of \(B_\varepsilon\) can be the maximizer of \(M_n\), so \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \notin B_\varepsilon\), that is \(\|\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0\| < \varepsilon\). Hence \[
P\bigl(\|\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0\| \ge \varepsilon\bigr)
\le P\bigl(U_n \ge \tfrac{\delta}{2}\bigr) \to 0 ,
\] by the uniform convergence hypothesis. As \(\varepsilon\) was arbitrary, \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta_0\). \(\square\)


Theorem 5.5 (Consistency of the MLE) Suppose \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) are iid from \(f(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) and:
(C1) \(\Theta \subseteq \mathbb R^p\) is compact and \(\boldsymbol\theta_0 \in \Theta\);
(C2) the model is identifiable (Definition 5.1);
(C3) \(\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto \log f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\) is continuous for \(\nu\)-almost every \(x\);
(C4) the envelope condition \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\bigl[\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}|\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)|\bigr] < \infty\) holds.
Then any MLE sequence \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) satisfies \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta_0\).


Proof. The MLE maximizes \(M_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \tfrac1n \ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta)\) (dividing the log-likelihood by \(n\) does not move the argmax). By Lemma 5.2 and identifiability (C2), the population criterion \(M(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)]\) has a unique maximizer at \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\); the envelope (C4) makes \(M\) finite, and with (C3) it is continuous by Lemma 5.3, which simultaneously gives the uniform convergence \(\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta}|M_n(\boldsymbol\theta) - M(\boldsymbol\theta)| \xrightarrow{p} 0\). Compactness (C1), continuity, the unique maximum, and uniform convergence are exactly the hypotheses of Lemma 5.4, which yields \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta_0\). \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters, with the running example. For the Bernoulli the hypotheses are easy to check: \(\Theta = [0, 1]\) is compact (C1), the model is identifiable since different \(p\) give different distributions (C2), \(\log f(x; p)\) is continuous in \(p\) (C3), and the envelope holds, so the theorem gives \(\hat p_n \xrightarrow{p} p_0\). In words, the trial’s response rate converges to the true response rate. Translated to the book’s subject, this is what guarantees that, with enough patients, an indirect comparison built from such estimates converges to the true contrast rather than to a biased value. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Compactness of \(\Theta\) (C1) is the only restrictive condition, and it can be relaxed. The standard device is to show the log-likelihood is eventually larger at \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\) than outside a compact set (so the maximizer cannot escape to the boundary), then apply the theorem on the compact core. Alternatively, the Cramér approach abandons the global maximizer and proves that the score equation \(\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathbf 0\) has, with probability tending to one, a root within \(O_p(n^{-1/2})\) of \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\); that local root is consistent and asymptotically normal even when the global MLE is ill-behaved. We use the global form here for definiteness. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
5.6 Asymptotic normality of the MLE
Consistency says the MLE lands near \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\).
