Asymptotic normality describes the distribution of the residual error \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0\), rescaled by \(\sqrt n\). The proof is the canonical “Taylor-expand the score” argument: the score vanishes at the MLE, expand it about the truth, and read off a ratio of a central-limit term over an information term.

Theorem 5.6 (Asymptotic normality of the MLE) Suppose \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta_0\) (for instance by Theorem 5.5), and in addition:
(A1) \(\boldsymbol\theta_0 \in \mathrm{int}\,\Theta\) and the model is regular (Definition 5.6) on a neighborhood of \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\), so \(\ell(\boldsymbol\theta; x)\) is twice continuously differentiable there;
(A2) the Fisher information \(\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) is finite and positive definite;
(A3) the Hessian satisfies a local uniform law of large numbers: there is a neighborhood \(\mathcal U\) of \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\) with \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\bigl[\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathcal U}\|\nabla^2\ell(\boldsymbol\theta;X)\|\bigr] < \infty\), so that \(\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathcal U}\|\tfrac1n\sum_i \nabla^2\ell(\boldsymbol\theta;X_i) - \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[\nabla^2\ell(\boldsymbol\theta;X)]\| \xrightarrow{p} 0\).
Then, with probability tending to one \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) solves \(\mathbf s_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathbf 0\), and \[
\sqrt n\,\bigl(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0\bigr)
\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_p\!\bigl(\mathbf 0,\; \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr).
\tag{5.6}\]


Proof. Step 1 (the estimator solves the score equation). Since \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta_0\) and \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\) is interior (A1), with probability tending to one \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) lies in the open neighborhood \(\mathcal U\) where \(\ell_n\) is differentiable and is an interior maximizer, so the first-order condition \(\mathbf s_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \nabla\ell_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathbf 0\) holds. We work on this event henceforth.
Step 2 (exact first-order expansion with integral remainder). Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus to the gradient field \(\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto \mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta)\) along the segment from \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\) to \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\), both eventually in \(\mathcal U\). (This is the fundamental theorem of calculus applied to each component of the vector field \(\mathbf s_n\) along the path; the bracketed matrix \(\bar{\mathbf H}_n\) is the Hessian averaged over the segment, playing the role of the mean-value remainder familiar from the scalar Taylor expansion.) With \(\mathbf H_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \nabla^2 \ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \nabla \mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta)\), \[
\mathbf 0 = \mathbf s_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)
= \mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0) + \underbrace{\left[\int_0^1 \mathbf H_n\bigl(\boldsymbol\theta_0 + t(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)\bigr)\, dt\right]}_{=:\; \bar{\mathbf H}_n}\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0).
\] Define \(\mathbf A_n = -\tfrac1n \bar{\mathbf H}_n\). Then, multiplying by \(-1/n\) and rearranging, \[
\mathbf A_n\,\sqrt n\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)
= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\,\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0).
\tag{5.7}\]
Step 3 (the score term is asymptotically normal). Write \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0) = \sqrt n\,\bigl(\tfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta_0; X_i) - \mathbf 0\bigr)\). The per-observation scores \(\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta_0; X_i)\) are iid with mean \(\mathbf 0\) (Lemma 5.1) and covariance \(\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) (Definition 5.7), finite by (A2). The multivariate CLT gives \[
\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\,\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0) \xrightarrow{d} \mathbf Z, \qquad \mathbf Z \sim \mathcal N_p\bigl(\mathbf 0,\, \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\bigr).
\tag{5.8}\]
Step 4 (the averaged Hessian converges to the information). Each intermediate point \(\boldsymbol\theta_0 + t(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)\) lies between \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\), hence converges in probability to \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\) uniformly in \(t \in [0,1]\). By the local uniform law (A3), the map \(\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto -\tfrac1n\sum_i \nabla^2\ell(\boldsymbol\theta; X_i)\) converges in probability, uniformly over \(\mathcal U\), to the continuous limit \(\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto -\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[\nabla^2\ell(\boldsymbol\theta; X)]\), which at \(\boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol\theta_0\) equals \(\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) by the information equality (Theorem 5.4). Combining uniform convergence with \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\theta_0\) and continuity of the limit, \[
\mathbf A_n = -\tfrac1n \int_0^1 \mathbf H_n\bigl(\boldsymbol\theta_0 + t(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)\bigr)\, dt
\xrightarrow{p} \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0).
\tag{5.9}\]
Step 5 (solve and apply Slutsky). By (A2) the limit \(\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) is invertible. Matrix inversion is continuous at any nonsingular matrix, so the continuous mapping theorem (Theorem 5.1) gives \(\mathbf A_n^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\) (in particular \(\mathbf A_n\) is invertible with probability tending to one). Solving Equation 5.7 and applying Slutsky (Theorem 5.2) to the product of the convergent-in-probability matrix \(\mathbf A_n^{-1}\) and the convergent-in-distribution vector Equation 5.8, \[
\sqrt n\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)
= \mathbf A_n^{-1}\, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0)
\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\,\mathbf Z .
\] Finally, the affine (here linear) image of a Gaussian is Gaussian (Theorem 4.14): with \(\mathbf B = \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\) and \(\mathbf Z \sim \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0))\), \[
\mathbf B\mathbf Z \sim \mathcal N_p\bigl(\mathbf 0,\; \mathbf B\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\,\mathbf B^\top\bigr)
= \mathcal N_p\bigl(\mathbf 0,\; \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr)
= \mathcal N_p\bigl(\mathbf 0,\; \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr),
\] using the symmetry of \(\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\). This is Equation 5.6. \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters. This theorem is the source of the ubiquitous “estimate \(\pm 1.96\) standard errors” interval. It says the MLE is approximately \(\mathcal N_p(\boldsymbol\theta_0,\, \tfrac1n\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1})\) in large samples, so every Wald confidence interval and \(z\)-test in a regression printout is an application of Equation 5.6. The idea behind the proof, stripped of detail: at the maximum the slope (score) is zero; near the truth the slope is approximately linear, with slope equal to the curvature (information); solving that linear relation turns the central-limit noise in the score into Gaussian noise in the estimator, scaled by the inverse information. For the running example, \(\sqrt n(\hat p - p) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N(0,\, p(1 - p))\) because \(\mathcal I(p)^{-1} = p(1 - p)\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark (Estimating the asymptotic variance). Equation 5.6 says \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) is approximately \(\mathcal N_p(\boldsymbol\theta_0,\, \tfrac1n \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1})\) in large samples, so a standard error for the \(b\)-th coordinate is the square root of the \((b,b)\) entry of \(\tfrac1n \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\). In practice \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\) is unknown, so one of two consistent plug-ins is used: the expected information evaluated at the estimate, \(\mathcal I(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\), or the observed information \(\mathbf J_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = -\nabla^2 \ell_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\), which by Step 4 satisfies \(\tfrac1n \mathbf J_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) \xrightarrow{p} \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\). Either yields a valid asymptotic variance estimate by Slutsky; the observed information requires no expectation and is what most software reports. The two agree in large samples; they can differ in small samples or under departures from the model, where the observed form uses the actual curvature at your estimate while the expected form averages curvature over hypothetical datasets. Concretely, what software prints as a “standard error” is the square root of a diagonal entry of the inverted observed information \(\mathbf J_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)^{-1}\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 5  Statistical Inference
section: 5.7 The Cramér-Rao lower bound and efficiency
text:
5.7 The Cramér-Rao lower bound and efficiency
Why a lower bound matters for indirect comparisons. Every method in this book reports a standard error, and a natural question is whether it could have done better with the same data. The Cramér-Rao bound is the yardstick: it is the smallest variance any unbiased estimator can achieve under a correctly specified regular model, so when MAIC or a network meta-analysis reports a precision you can ask whether it is near this optimum or is leaving information on the table. It is a theoretical benchmark, not something you compute on each dataset, but it explains why the inverse Fisher information is the natural ideal variance.
How small can the variance of an unbiased estimator be? The Cramér-Rao bound answers: no smaller than the inverse Fisher information. The proof is a single application of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (Theorem 2.1), using that the score has mean zero.

Theorem 5.7 (Cramér-Rao lower bound) Let the model be regular (Definition 5.6) at \(\boldsymbol\theta\), and let \(T = T(X)\) be a statistic with \(\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T) < \infty\) whose mean \(g(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T]\) is differentiable with the differentiation passing under the integral sign.

Scalar parameter (\(p = 1\)). Then \[
\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T) \;\ge\; \frac{g'(\boldsymbol\theta)^2}{\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)} .
\tag{5.10}\] In particular, if \(T\) is unbiased for \(\boldsymbol\theta\) (so \(g(\boldsymbol\theta) = \boldsymbol\theta\), \(g' = 1\)), then \(\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T) \ge 1/\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)\). Equality holds if and only if \(T - g(\boldsymbol\theta)\) is, almost surely, a (deterministic) multiple of the score \(\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\).
Vector parameter. If \(\mathbf T\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\boldsymbol\theta \in \mathbb R^p\), then in the Loewner (positive-semidefinite) order \[
\mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T) \;\succeq\; \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1} ,
\tag{5.11}\] that is, \(\mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T) - \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1}\) is positive semidefinite. Here \(A \succeq B\) (the Loewner order) means \(A - B\) is positive semidefinite; concretely it says every scalar combination \(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf T\) has variance at least \(\mathbf v^\top\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1}\mathbf v\), so the estimator beats the bound in no direction.



Proof. (i) Differentiate the identity \(g(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T] = \int T(x)\, f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)\) under the integral sign: \[
g'(\boldsymbol\theta) = \int T(x)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol\theta} f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)
= \int T(x)\, \mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; x)\, f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)
= \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl[T\,\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\bigr],
\] using \(\partial_{\boldsymbol\theta} f = \mathbf s\, f\). Because the score has mean zero (Lemma 5.1), \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T\,\mathbf s] = \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T, \mathbf s)\), so \(g'(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T, \mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X))\). The space of mean-zero square-integrable random variables under \(P_{\boldsymbol\theta}\) is an inner product space with \(\langle U, V\rangle = \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(U, V)\); applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (Theorem 2.1) to \(T - g(\boldsymbol\theta)\) and the score, \[
g'(\boldsymbol\theta)^2 = \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T, \mathbf s)^2
\le \mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T)\,\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf s)
= \mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T)\, \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta) .
\] Dividing by \(\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta) > 0\) gives Equation 5.10. Cauchy-Schwarz is an equality exactly when the two vectors are linearly dependent, that is when \(T - g(\boldsymbol\theta) = a(\boldsymbol\theta)\,\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\) almost surely for some constant \(a(\boldsymbol\theta)\).
(ii) Let \(\mathbf s = \mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\) and center \(\mathbf U = \mathbf T - \boldsymbol\theta\) (mean zero by unbiasedness). The componentwise version of the scalar computation gives, for each pair \((a, b)\), \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[U_a\, s_b] = \partial_{\theta_b}\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T_a] = \partial_{\theta_b}\theta_a = \mathbb 1\{a = b\}\), so the cross-covariance is the identity: \(\mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T, \mathbf s) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\mathbf U \mathbf s^\top] = I_p\). Stack \(\mathbf U\) and \(\mathbf s\) into a \(2p\)-vector; its covariance matrix is positive semidefinite (Theorem 4.9): \[
\mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf U \\ \mathbf s\end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T) & I_p \\[2pt] I_p & \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta) \end{pmatrix}
=: \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma_T & I_p \\ I_p & \mathcal I \end{pmatrix} \succeq 0 .
\] Since \(\mathcal I \succ 0\), evaluate the quadratic form of this block matrix on the cleverly chosen vector \((\,\mathbf v^\top,\; -(\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf v)^\top)^\top\) for arbitrary \(\mathbf v \in \mathbb R^p\). The second block \(-\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf v\) is engineered so that the identity cross-blocks cancel, leaving only the difference \(\Sigma_T - \mathcal I^{-1}\); this cancellation is the algebraic content of the Schur complement of the \(\mathcal I\) block: \[
0 \le \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf v \\ -\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf v\end{pmatrix}^{\!\top}\!
\begin{pmatrix} \Sigma_T & I_p \\ I_p & \mathcal I \end{pmatrix}\!
\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf v \\ -\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf v\end{pmatrix}
= \mathbf v^\top \Sigma_T \mathbf v - 2\,\mathbf v^\top \mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf v + \mathbf v^\top \mathcal I^{-1}\mathcal I\,\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf v
= \mathbf v^\top\bigl(\Sigma_T - \mathcal I^{-1}\bigr)\mathbf v .
\] As \(\mathbf v\) was arbitrary, \(\Sigma_T - \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1} \succeq 0\), which is Equation 5.11. (This is precisely the Schur-complement positivity of the block matrix.) \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters. Read the scalar bound Equation 5.10 as: precision is capped by information. You cannot make an unbiased estimator arbitrarily precise; the best achievable variance is \(1/\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = 1/[n\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)]\), which is why “more information” and “more data” both mean “smaller standard error.” When a later method attains this bound (the MLE does, asymptotically), you know no regular competitor can do better with the same model and data. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The bound motivates a precise notion of “best possible” estimator.

Definition 5.9 (Efficiency and asymptotic efficiency) An unbiased estimator \(T\) of a scalar \(g(\boldsymbol\theta)\) is (Cramér-Rao) efficient if it attains the bound Equation 5.10 with equality for all \(\boldsymbol\theta\). A consistent estimator sequence \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) with \(\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \mathbf V(\boldsymbol\theta_0))\) is asymptotically efficient if \(\mathbf V(\boldsymbol\theta_0) = \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\), the smallest asymptotic covariance permitted (in the Loewner order) for regular estimators. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Corollary 5.2 (The MLE is asymptotically efficient) Under the hypotheses of Theorem 5.6, the MLE is asymptotically efficient: its asymptotic covariance \(\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\) equals the per-observation Cramér-Rao bound.


Proof. Immediate by comparing Equation 5.6 with Definition 5.9: the asymptotic covariance of \(\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)\) is \(\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\). \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters. Asymptotic efficiency is the precise sense in which maximum likelihood is “as good as it gets”: no regular estimator can have a smaller asymptotic variance than the MLE’s \(\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\). The practical payoff is reassurance: when a systematic review uses likelihood-based methods (most network meta-analyses, and ML-NMR), it is not leaving precision on the table relative to any competing regular estimator built from the same model. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. The matrix bound Equation 5.11 is a finite-sample statement about unbiased estimators, while Definition 5.9’s asymptotic optimality is a statement about the limiting distribution of possibly biased estimators. The rigorous bridge that no regular estimator can have asymptotic covariance below \(\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\) is the Hájek-Le Cam convolution theorem and the local asymptotic minimax theorem; we cite these (see Bingham and Fry (2010) and the asymptotic-statistics literature) rather than prove them, as they require the local asymptotic normality framework beyond this chapter. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
5.8 M-estimation and the sandwich variance
Maximum likelihood is the special case, with \(\boldsymbol\psi\) equal to the score, of a far more general construction: define an estimator as the solution of an estimating equation. This generality is exactly what later chapters need. A MAIC estimator (Chapter 18) solves a weighting equation that is not the score of any correctly specified likelihood, yet it is asymptotically normal, and its correct standard error is the sandwich variance defined below.

Definition 5.10 (M-estimator and estimating equation) Let \(\boldsymbol\psi(x; \boldsymbol\theta) \in \mathbb R^p\) be a known estimating function. An M-estimator \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) is a solution of the estimating equation \[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \boldsymbol\psi(X_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathbf 0 .
\tag{5.12}\] The target (or estimand) is the value \(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}\) solving the population equation \(\mathbb E_{P}[\boldsymbol\psi(X; \boldsymbol\theta^{*})] = \mathbf 0\), where \(P\) is the true data-generating distribution, which need not belong to the working model. The MLE is the M-estimator with \(\boldsymbol\psi = \mathbf s\), the score, in which case \(\boldsymbol\theta^{*} = \boldsymbol\theta_0\) under correct specification. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. An M-estimator is defined not by maximizing something but by solving an equation \(\sum_i \boldsymbol\psi(X_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathbf 0\). Choosing \(\boldsymbol\psi\) to be the score recovers maximum likelihood, but \(\boldsymbol\psi\) can be any sensible estimating function, even one with no likelihood behind it. The crucial shift is the target \(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}\): it is whatever value the equation aims at in the real world \(P\), which need not be the “true parameter” of any correct model. This is the honest setting for MAIC, whose weighting equation is a computational device, not a believed model. A one-covariate MAIC balancing equation has the schematic form \(\sum_i w_i(\boldsymbol\theta)\,(x_i - \bar x^{*}) = 0\), “choose weights so the weighted covariate mean equals the target population mean \(\bar x^{*}\)”; Chapter 18 makes this precise. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The asymptotic distribution of an M-estimator follows the same Taylor expansion as the MLE, but the variance no longer collapses to a single information matrix; it is a sandwich of two matrices.

Theorem 5.8 (Asymptotic normality of M-estimators) Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be iid from \(P\), let \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) solve Equation 5.12, and suppose \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta^{*}\), where \(\mathbb E_P[\boldsymbol\psi(X; \boldsymbol\theta^{*})] = \mathbf 0\). Assume \(\boldsymbol\psi(x; \cdot)\) is continuously differentiable near \(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}\), the matrix \[
\mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}) = -\,\mathbb E_P\!\bigl[\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\boldsymbol\psi(X; \boldsymbol\theta^{*})\bigr]
\quad(\text{the ``bread''})
\] is nonsingular, the matrix \(\mathbf B(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}) = \mathbb E_P\!\bigl[\boldsymbol\psi(X; \boldsymbol\theta^{*})\,\boldsymbol\psi(X; \boldsymbol\theta^{*})^\top\bigr]\) (the ``meat’’) is finite, and \(\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\boldsymbol\psi\) obeys a local uniform law of large numbers near \(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}\): there is a neighborhood \(\mathcal U^{*}\) of \(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}\) with \(\mathbb E_P\bigl[\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathcal U^{*}}\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\boldsymbol\psi(X;\boldsymbol\theta)\|\bigr] < \infty\) and \(\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathcal U^{*}}\bigl\|\tfrac1n\sum_i \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\boldsymbol\psi(X_i;\boldsymbol\theta) - \mathbb E_P[\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\boldsymbol\psi(X;\boldsymbol\theta)]\bigr\| \xrightarrow{p} 0\), exactly parallel to (A3) of Theorem 5.6. Then \[
\sqrt n\,\bigl(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta^{*}\bigr)
\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_p\!\Bigl(\mathbf 0,\; \mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})^{-1}\,\mathbf B(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})\,\mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})^{-\top}\Bigr) ,
\tag{5.13}\] where \(\mathbf A^{-\top}\) abbreviates \((\mathbf A^{-1})^\top = (\mathbf A^\top)^{-1}\).


Proof. Write \(\boldsymbol\Psi_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol\psi(X_i; \boldsymbol\theta)\), so \(\boldsymbol\Psi_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathbf 0\). As in Step 2 of Theorem 5.6, the fundamental theorem of calculus along the segment from \(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}\) to \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) gives \[
\mathbf 0 = \boldsymbol\Psi_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)
= \boldsymbol\Psi_n(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}) + \Bigl[\textstyle\int_0^1 \nabla\boldsymbol\Psi_n\bigl(\boldsymbol\theta^{*} + t(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta^{*})\bigr)\, dt\Bigr](\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta^{*}),
\] hence with \(\mathbf A_n = -\tfrac1n\int_0^1 \nabla\boldsymbol\Psi_n(\boldsymbol\theta^{*} + t(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta^{*}))\,dt\), \[
\mathbf A_n\,\sqrt n\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta^{*}) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\,\boldsymbol\Psi_n(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}).
\] The summands \(\boldsymbol\psi(X_i; \boldsymbol\theta^{*})\) are iid with mean \(\mathbf 0\) (by the definition of \(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}\)) and covariance \(\mathbf B(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})\), so the multivariate CLT gives \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\boldsymbol\Psi_n(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \mathbf B(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}))\). By consistency, the local uniform law, and continuity (exactly as in Step 4 of Theorem 5.6), \(\mathbf A_n \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})\), which is nonsingular, so \(\mathbf A_n^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})^{-1}\) by continuous mapping (Theorem 5.1). Slutsky (Theorem 5.2) and Theorem 4.14 give \[
\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta^{*}) = \mathbf A_n^{-1}\,\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\boldsymbol\Psi_n(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})
\xrightarrow{d} \mathbf A^{-1}\mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \mathbf B)
= \mathcal N_p\bigl(\mathbf 0, \mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf B\,\mathbf A^{-\top}\bigr),
\] which is Equation 5.13. \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters, and the “bread”/“meat” nicknames. When the model may be wrong, the MLE variance \(\mathcal I^{-1}\) is no longer correct; the right variance is the sandwich \(\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf B\,\mathbf A^{-\top}\). The names are conventional and purely mnemonic, not technical terms: \(\mathbf A\) (the “bread”) measures how sensitive the estimating equation is to the parameter (the average slope of \(\boldsymbol\psi\)), while \(\mathbf B\) (the “meat”) measures how variable the estimating equation itself is (the covariance of \(\boldsymbol\psi\)). The two outer copies of \(\mathbf A^{-1}\) are the bread, the central \(\mathbf B\) is the meat; together they describe the shape \(\mathbf A^{-1}\,\mathbf B\,\mathbf A^{-\top}\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Definition 5.11 (Sandwich (robust) variance estimator) Under Theorem 5.8, the sandwich variance estimator of \(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\) is the empirical plug-in of Equation 5.13, \[
\widehat{\mathbb V}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)
= \tfrac1n\,\widehat{\mathbf A}_n^{-1}\,\widehat{\mathbf B}_n\,\widehat{\mathbf A}_n^{-\top},
\tag{5.14}\] with \[
\widehat{\mathbf A}_n = -\tfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\boldsymbol\psi(X_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n),
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf B}_n = \tfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol\psi(X_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\,\boldsymbol\psi(X_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)^\top .
\] The name records the structure \(\widehat{\mathbf A}_n^{-1}\) (bread), \(\widehat{\mathbf B}_n\) (meat), \(\widehat{\mathbf A}_n^{-\top}\) (bread). Under the regularity above, the law of large numbers and the continuous mapping theorem give \(\widehat{\mathbf A}_n \xrightarrow{p}\mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})\) and \(\widehat{\mathbf B}_n \xrightarrow{p}\mathbf B(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})\), so \(n\,\widehat{\mathbb V}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) \xrightarrow{p}\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf B\,\mathbf A^{-\top}\): the sandwich estimator is consistent for the true asymptotic variance even when the working model is misspecified. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation, with a picture. The estimator is three matrices multiplied in a row: plug in the empirical bread \(\widehat{\mathbf A}_n\) and meat \(\widehat{\mathbf B}_n\) computed from the data at the fitted \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\), and you get a standard error valid even when the working model is wrong.
                                A^{-1}        B          A^{-T}
   Var-hat(theta_hat)  =  (1/n) [ bread ] [  meat  ] [  bread  ]
                                sensitivity  variability  sensitivity
                                of the eqn   of the eqn   of the eqn
When the model is right, the information equality forces bread \(=\) meat \(= \mathcal I\) and the sandwich collapses to \(\mathcal I^{-1}\), the ordinary inverse-information variance (next corollary). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The information equality is exactly the statement that, under correct specification, the sandwich collapses to the familiar inverse-information variance.

Corollary 5.3 (Correct specification collapses the sandwich) Suppose \(\boldsymbol\psi = \mathbf s\) is the score of a correctly specified regular model, so \(P = f(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) and \(\boldsymbol\theta^{*} = \boldsymbol\theta_0\). Then \(\mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta_0) = \mathbf B(\boldsymbol\theta_0) = \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\), and the sandwich variance Equation 5.13 reduces to \(\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\), recovering Theorem 5.6.


Proof. The meat is \(\mathbf B(\boldsymbol\theta_0) = \mathbb E[\mathbf s\,\mathbf s^\top] = \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) by Definition 5.7. The bread is \(\mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta_0) = -\mathbb E[\nabla\mathbf s] = -\mathbb E[\nabla^2 \ell] = \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) by the information equality (Theorem 5.4). Hence \(\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf B\,\mathbf A^{-\top} = \mathcal I^{-1}\mathcal I\,\mathcal I^{-1} = \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\). \(\square\)


Remark (The sandwich and MAIC). When the model is misspecified, \(\mathbf A \ne \mathbf B\) in general, and using the naive inverse-bread or inverse-information variance understates (or overstates) the truth. The sandwich Equation 5.14 is the universal fix.
This is the precise reason Chapter 18 reports robust standard errors for MAIC. In a matching-adjusted indirect comparison the individual-level study fits weights \(w_i = \exp(\alpha + \boldsymbol\beta^\top \mathbf x_i)\) by an estimating equation that forces the weighted covariate means to match the aggregate target population, schematically \(\sum_i w_i(\boldsymbol\beta)\,(\mathbf x_i - \bar{\mathbf x}^{*}) = \mathbf 0\); the treatment effect is then estimated on the weighted sample. The “working model” here is the weighting scheme together with the outcome model on the reweighted data, and there is no reason for it to be correctly specified: the weights are a device for balancing covariates, not a belief about how the data arose. Maximum-likelihood (inverse-information) standard errors would therefore be wrong, and only the sandwich form, with \(\boldsymbol\psi\) stacking the weighting equations and the outcome equation, is guaranteed consistent for the sampling variance of the population-adjusted effect. Carry this picture into Chapter 18: weights solve an estimating equation, the model is a working approximation, and the sandwich is the honest standard error. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
5.9 Tests and confidence intervals
We close with the three classical large-sample tests of a null hypothesis \(H_0 : \boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol\theta_0\) (or, after reparameterization, a value of a subvector), and the confidence intervals obtained by inverting them. All three statistics have the same limiting \(\chi^2_p\) distribution and are first-order equivalent; they differ in whether they need the estimate, the null value, or both. Throughout, \(\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = n\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)\) is the sample information (Corollary 5.1).
In a health application the practical question is which test to report for an indirect comparison. The short answer: the three agree in large samples (Theorem 5.9), but near a boundary or in small studies the likelihood-ratio and score versions are usually preferred (see the remark after Theorem 5.9). The table contrasts what each test looks at.










Test
What it evaluates
Needs the MLE \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\)?
Needs the null fit?
Intuitive question




Wald
distance of \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) from \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\), scaled by curvature at \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\)
yes
no
“How many standard errors is the estimate from the null?”


Score (Rao)
slope of the log-likelihood evaluated at \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\)
no
yes
“Is the log-likelihood still climbing steeply at the null?”


Likelihood ratio
drop in log-likelihood from \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) down to \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\)
yes
yes
“How much worse does the null fit than the best fit?”




Definition 5.12 (Wald, score, and likelihood-ratio statistics) For testing \(H_0 : \boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol\theta_0\) with MLE \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\):

the Wald statistic is \[
W_n = (\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)^\top\, \mathcal I_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0);
\tag{5.15}\]
the score (Rao) statistic is \[
R_n = \mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^\top\, \mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\, \mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0);
\tag{5.16}\]
the likelihood-ratio statistic is \[
\Lambda_n = 2\bigl[\ell_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) - \ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\bigr] .
\tag{5.17}\] \(\blacktriangleleft\)



Remark. Reader translation. All three compare a null value \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\) to what the data prefer, using the geometry of the log-likelihood near its peak (recall the parabola picture from the start of the chapter). Wald measures the horizontal distance from the peak to the null; the score measures the slope at the null; the likelihood ratio measures the vertical drop in height. Near the peak a smooth function looks like a parabola, and for a parabola these three are the same measurement up to scaling, which is why Theorem 5.9 finds them asymptotically equal. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Theorem 5.9 (Limiting null distribution (Wilks)) Under \(H_0\) and the hypotheses of Theorem 5.6, each of \(W_n\), \(R_n\), and \(\Lambda_n\) converges in distribution to \(\chi^2_p\), and the three are asymptotically equivalent: \(W_n - \Lambda_n \xrightarrow{p} 0\) and \(R_n - \Lambda_n \xrightarrow{p} 0\).


Proof. Abbreviate \(\mathcal I = \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) and let \(\mathbf Z_n = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0) \xrightarrow{d} \mathbf Z \sim \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \mathcal I)\) by Equation 5.8. From the proof of Theorem 5.6, \[
\sqrt n\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0) = \mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z_n + o_p(1).
\tag{5.18}\]
Score statistic. Directly, \(R_n = \mathbf Z_n^\top (\tfrac1n \mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0))^{-1}\mathbf Z_n = \mathbf Z_n^\top \mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z_n\), and by continuous mapping (Theorem 5.1) applied to the continuous map \(\mathbf z \mapsto \mathbf z^\top\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf z\), \(R_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathbf Z^\top \mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z\). Writing \(\mathbf Z = \mathcal I^{1/2}\mathbf G\) with \(\mathbf G \sim \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, I_p)\) (the symmetric PSD square root, Theorem 4.9), \(\mathbf Z^\top\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z = \mathbf G^\top\mathbf G = \|\mathbf G\|_2^2 \sim \chi^2_p\). Hence \(R_n \xrightarrow{d}\chi^2_p\).
Wald statistic. Since \(\tfrac1n\mathcal I_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathcal I(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) \xrightarrow{p}\mathcal I\) (continuity of \(\mathcal I\) and consistency), substituting Equation 5.18, \[
W_n = \bigl[\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)\bigr]^\top \mathcal I(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\bigl[\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)\bigr]
= (\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z_n + o_p(1))^\top \mathcal I (\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z_n + o_p(1)) = \mathbf Z_n^\top\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z_n + o_p(1),
\] using Slutsky to absorb the \(o_p(1)\) terms (the leading factors are \(O_p(1)\)). Thus \(W_n = R_n + o_p(1)\), so \(W_n \xrightarrow{d}\chi^2_p\) and \(W_n - R_n \xrightarrow{p} 0\).
Likelihood-ratio statistic. Take a second-order Taylor expansion of \(\ell_n\) about \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\), using \(\mathbf s_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathbf 0\) and the integral form of the remainder: \[
\ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0) = \ell_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) + \mathbf 0 + \tfrac12 (\boldsymbol\theta_0 - \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)^\top \mathbf H_n(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)(\boldsymbol\theta_0 - \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n),
\] for \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) on the segment, so \[
\Lambda_n = 2[\ell_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) - \ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0)]
= (\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)^\top\bigl[-\mathbf H_n(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\bigr](\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0).
\] Now \(-\tfrac1n \mathbf H_n(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) \xrightarrow{p}\mathcal I\) (Step 4 of Theorem 5.6, since \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\theta_0\)), so \(\Lambda_n = [\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)]^\top(-\tfrac1n\mathbf H_n)[\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)] = \mathbf Z_n^\top\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z_n + o_p(1)\) by the same substitution (both the averaged Hessian at \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) here and the one at \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\) in the Wald step converge in probability to the same \(\mathcal I\), because \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\theta_0\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\theta_0\), and we substitute Equation 5.18 for \(\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)\)). Therefore \(\Lambda_n = R_n + o_p(1) \xrightarrow{d}\chi^2_p\), and \(\Lambda_n - R_n \xrightarrow{p} 0\), \(\Lambda_n - W_n \xrightarrow{p} 0\). \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters. All three tests give the same answer in large samples, so for a single large indirect comparison it rarely matters which you quote. What to remember: they are the three natural ways to ask “is the effect different from the null,” and a confidence interval is simply the set of null values that none of them rejects (next remark). The picture is the parabola: the distance, slope, and height of a parabola all encode the same curvature, which is why the statistics coincide. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark (Confidence intervals by inversion). A level-\(\alpha\) test of \(H_0 : \boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol\theta_0\) rejects when the statistic exceeds the upper-\(\alpha\) quantile \(\chi^2_{p, 1-\alpha}\). The set of null values not rejected is a \((1-\alpha)\) confidence region. For a scalar parameter the Wald region is the familiar interval \[
\hat\theta_n \pm z_{1 - \alpha/2}\,\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat\theta_n),
\qquad \widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat\theta_n) = \bigl(\mathcal I_n(\hat\theta_n)\bigr)^{-1/2},
\] where \(z_{1-\alpha/2} = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha/2)\) and \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function (Notation). Inverting the likelihood-ratio test instead gives the profile-likelihood interval \(\{\theta : 2[\ell_n(\hat\theta_n) - \ell_n(\theta)] \le \chi^2_{1, 1-\alpha}\}\), which respects the shape of the log-likelihood and is not forced to be symmetric. The three intervals agree to first order by Theorem 5.9 but can differ markedly in small samples or near a boundary, where the likelihood-ratio and score intervals are generally preferred. Concretely, to build a confidence interval by hand you can sweep candidate null values \(\theta_0\), run the test at each, and keep those it does not reject; the retained values form the interval. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
5.10 A fully worked example
We tie the chapter together on the simplest nontrivial model, the Bernoulli, where every quantity can be computed by hand, and then illustrate the sandwich variance on a deliberately misspecified model. Most pieces have already appeared in context, threaded through the running example: the score in Lemma 5.1, the information in Corollary 5.1, the log-odds delta method in Example 5.2, and the indirect comparison in Example 5.3. Here we assemble them on the one dataset \(n = 25\), \(\sum_i X_i = 10\).

Example 5.4 (Maximum likelihood for a Bernoulli proportion) Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be iid \(\mathrm{Ber}(p)\) with \(\theta = p \in (0,1)\). Suppose we observe \(n = 25\) trials with \(\sum_i X_i = 10\) successes.
Likelihood, score, MLE. The single-observation density is \(f(x; p) = p^x(1-p)^{1-x}\), so \[
\ell_n(p) = \Bigl(\textstyle\sum_i X_i\Bigr)\log p + \Bigl(n - \textstyle\sum_i X_i\Bigr)\log(1-p) = 10\log p + 15\log(1-p)
\] (dropping the constant binomial coefficient, which does not depend on \(p\)). The score is \[
s_n(p) = \frac{10}{p} - \frac{15}{1-p}, \qquad s_n(p) = 0 \iff 10(1-p) = 15 p \iff \hat p = \tfrac{10}{25} = 0.40 .
\] This matches Definition 5.8: \(\hat p_{\mathrm{MLE}} = \bar X_n\).
Fisher information and standard error. The per-observation score is \(s(p; x) = x/p - (1-x)/(1-p)\), and by the information equality (Theorem 5.4), with \(\partial_p^2 \log f = -x/p^2 - (1-x)/(1-p)^2\) and \(\mathbb E[X] = p\), \[
\mathcal I(p) = -\mathbb E_p\bigl[\partial_p^2 \log f\bigr] = \frac{p}{p^2} + \frac{1-p}{(1-p)^2} = \frac1p + \frac{1}{1-p} = \frac{1}{p(1-p)} .
\] At \(\hat p = 0.4\), \(\mathcal I(\hat p) = 1/(0.4\cdot 0.6) = 1/0.24 = 4.1\overline{6}\), the sample information is \(\mathcal I_n(\hat p) = 25 \times 4.1\overline 6 = 104.1\overline 6\), and the asymptotic variance of \(\hat p\) is \[
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat p) = \frac{1}{\mathcal I_n(\hat p)} = \frac{\hat p(1 - \hat p)}{n} = \frac{0.24}{25} = 0.0096,
\qquad \widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat p) = \sqrt{0.0096} = 0.09798 .
\] The Wald 95% confidence interval (Section 5.9) is \(0.40 \pm 1.96 \times 0.09798 = 0.40 \pm 0.19204 = (0.2080,\, 0.5920)\).
Delta method for the log-odds. The log-odds is \(g(p) = \log\!\frac{p}{1-p}\) with \(g'(p) = \frac{1}{p(1-p)}\). By the delta method (Theorem 5.3), \[
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\bigl(g(\hat p)\bigr) = g'(\hat p)^2\,\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat p)
= \Bigl(\frac{1}{p(1-p)}\Bigr)^2 \cdot \frac{p(1-p)}{n} = \frac{1}{n\,p(1-p)}\Big|_{p = \hat p} = \frac{1}{25 \times 0.24} = \frac16 = 0.1\overline 6 .
\] Notice the algebra collapses to \(\tfrac{1}{n\hat p(1-\hat p)} = \tfrac{1}{n\hat p} + \tfrac{1}{n(1-\hat p)} = \tfrac{1}{\#\text{success}} + \tfrac{1}{\#\text{fail}} = \tfrac{1}{10} + \tfrac{1}{15} = 0.1\overline 6\), the textbook standard error of an empirical log-odds. Thus \(g(\hat p) = \log(0.4/0.6) = -0.40546\) with \(\widehat{\mathrm{se}} = \sqrt{1/6} = 0.40825\), giving a 95% interval for the log-odds of \(-0.40546 \pm 1.96 \times 0.40825 = (-1.2056,\, 0.3947)\) and, exponentiating, an odds-ratio-scale interval \((e^{-1.2056}, e^{0.3947}) = (0.2995,\, 1.4830)\).
Three tests of \(H_0 : p = 0.5\). Using Definition 5.12 with \(\boldsymbol\theta_0 = 0.5\):

Score test. \(s_n(0.5) = 10/0.5 - 15/0.5 = -10\) and \(\mathcal I_n(0.5) = 25/(0.5\cdot 0.5) = 100\), so \(R_n = (-10)^2/100 = 1.000\).
Wald test. \(W_n = (\hat p - 0.5)^2\,\mathcal I_n(\hat p) = (-0.1)^2 \times 104.1\overline 6 = 0.01/0.0096 = 1.0417\).
Likelihood-ratio test. \(\ell_n(0.4) = 10\log 0.4 + 15\log 0.6 = -9.16291 - 7.66238 = -16.82529\) and \(\ell_n(0.5) = 25\log 0.5 = -17.32868\), so \(\Lambda_n = 2(-16.82529 + 17.32868) = 2 \times 0.50339 = 1.0068\).

All three statistics cluster near \(1.0\), confirming the first-order equivalence of Theorem 5.9. Against the critical value \(\chi^2_{1, 0.95} = 3.841\), none rejects \(H_0 : p = 0.5\); equivalently, \(0.5\) lies inside the Wald interval \((0.208, 0.592)\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Example 5.5 (When the model is wrong: the sandwich earns its name) Suppose we estimate a population mean \(\mu\) by fitting a working model that treats the data as \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) with the variance fixed (incorrectly) at \(1\), while the true distribution \(P\) has mean \(\mu_0\) and variance \(\sigma_0^2 \ne 1\). The working score is \(\psi(x; \mu) = \partial_\mu\bigl[-\tfrac12(x - \mu)^2\bigr] = x - \mu\), so the estimating equation \(\sum_i (X_i - \hat\mu_n) = 0\) yields the M-estimator \(\hat\mu_n = \bar X_n\), which targets \(\mu^{*} = \mu_0\).
By Theorem 5.8, the bread and meat are \[
\mathbf A = -\mathbb E_P[\partial_\mu \psi] = -\mathbb E_P[-1] = 1,
\qquad
\mathbf B = \mathbb E_P[\psi^2] = \mathbb E_P[(X - \mu_0)^2] = \sigma_0^2,
\] so the correct asymptotic variance is \(\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf B\,\mathbf A^{-1}/n = \sigma_0^2/n\), exactly the variance of \(\bar X_n\). The naive model-based variance, which trusts the working model and uses the inverse working information \(\mathbf A^{-1}/n = 1/n\), is wrong by the factor \(\sigma_0^2\).
Concrete numbers. Take \(n = 40\) observations with sample mean \(\bar X_n = 2.5\) and \(\sum_i (X_i - \bar X_n)^2 = 160\). Then \(\widehat{\mathbf A}_n = 1\), \(\widehat{\mathbf B}_n = 160/40 = 4.0\), and the sandwich variance Equation 5.14 is \[
\widehat{\mathbb V}(\hat\mu_n) = \tfrac1n\,\widehat{\mathbf A}_n^{-1}\,\widehat{\mathbf B}_n\,\widehat{\mathbf A}_n^{-1} = \frac{4.0}{40} = 0.10,
\qquad \widehat{\mathrm{se}}_{\text{robust}} = \sqrt{0.10} = 0.3162,
\] whereas the naive standard error is \(\sqrt{1/40} = 0.1581\), understating the true uncertainty by a factor of \(\sqrt{\widehat{\mathbf B}_n} = 2\). This is the mechanism, in miniature, that makes the sandwich estimator mandatory for MAIC in Chapter 18: the weighting “model” is a computational device, not a believed truth, and only the robust variance is consistent. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
5.11 Notes and references
The estimation theory of this chapter is classical and is developed, with the regression emphasis this book shares, in Bingham and Fry (2010); the worked Bernoulli example and the three-test comparison follow that source’s treatment of likelihood inference. The notation for likelihood, score, Fisher information, the MLE, and the sandwich variance matches Notation.
The asymptotic tools of Section 5.2 correspond to the proof catalogue: the delta method is A.11, Slutsky’s theorem is A.12, and the continuous mapping theorem is A.13 (corresponds to A.11-A.13 in the proof catalogue). Our statements and proofs align with the companion manuscript’s treatment in manuscript/01_probability.md; we have expanded the catalogue’s one-line sketches into full proofs and have generalized the delta method and Slutsky’s theorem to the multivariate case via the Cramér-Wold device. The continuous mapping and Slutsky proofs rest on the Portmanteau theorem, which we cite as a standard result of weak-convergence theory.
The consistency proof (Theorem 5.5) is the Wald argmax argument: the Kullback-Leibler information inequality (Lemma 5.2, a consequence of Jensen’s inequality Theorem 4.6) identifies \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\) as the unique maximizer of the population log-likelihood, a uniform law of large numbers (Lemma 5.3, cited) transfers this to the sample, and the argmax-continuity lemma (Lemma 5.4, proved in full) concludes. The asymptotic-normality proof (Theorem 5.6) is the standard Taylor expansion of the score, assembled from the information equality (Theorem 5.4), the multivariate central limit theorem, and Slutsky’s theorem, with the affine-image property of the multivariate normal (Theorem 4.14 from Chapter 4) delivering the Gaussian limit. The Cramér-Rao bound (Theorem 5.7) is proved via the covariance Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (Theorem 2.1), with the matrix version following from positive-semidefiniteness of a joint covariance (Theorem 4.9) and a Schur-complement computation.
M-estimation and the sandwich variance (Definition 5.11) generalize maximum likelihood; the collapse of the sandwich to the inverse information under correct specification (Corollary 5.3) is a direct corollary of the information equality, and is the conceptual bridge to the robust variance used for MAIC in Chapter 18. The convolution-theorem justification of asymptotic efficiency is cited, not proved, as it requires the local asymptotic normality machinery outside the scope of a foundations chapter.
No result in this chapter is tagged machine-checked. The companion Coq development depends on mathcomp-analysis for measure-theoretic foundations and, per the manuscript, treats the asymptotic results A.11-A.13 at the level of cited library facts rather than re-derived theorems; the pen-and-paper proofs here are the authoritative versions. Candidates for future formalization are the information equality and the M-estimator sandwich, both of which are purely algebraic given the differentiation-under-the-integral hypotheses.

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
5.12 Exercises
The exercises progress from warm-ups and interpretation to computation and proof. A starred exercise (\(\star\)) has a full worked solution in Appendix F; the first warm-up below is solved inline so you can calibrate your approach before attempting the rest.

Exercise 5.1 (Warm-up (solved): a log odds and its interval from one arm) In a single-arm cohort, \(20\) of \(50\) patients respond. (a) Give the MLE \(\hat p\). (b) Give the log odds \(g(\hat p) = \log\frac{\hat p}{1 - \hat p}\) and its delta-method standard error. (c) Report a 95% confidence interval on the log-odds scale and on the odds scale.
Solution. (a) \(\hat p = 20/50 = 0.40\). (b) The log odds is \(g(\hat p) = \log(0.40/0.60) = \log(0.6667) = -0.4055\). By Example 5.2 the variance of an empirical log odds is \(\tfrac{1}{\#\text{responders}} + \tfrac{1}{\#\text{non-responders}} = \tfrac1{20} + \tfrac1{30} = 0.08333\), so the standard error is \(\sqrt{0.08333} = 0.2887\). (c) On the log-odds scale, \(-0.4055 \pm 1.96 \times 0.2887 = (-0.9713,\, 0.1603)\); exponentiating gives the odds-scale interval \((e^{-0.9713}, e^{0.1603}) = (0.379,\, 1.174)\). The interval includes odds \(1\) (probability \(0.5\)), so the data are consistent with a coin-flip response rate. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Exercise 5.2 (Warm-up (interpretation): where is a proportion hardest to estimate?) Using \(\mathcal I(p) = 1/[p(1 - p)]\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat p) \approx p(1 - p)/n\): (a) for fixed \(n\), at what value of \(p\) is \(\hat p\) most variable, and where is it most precise? (b) A trial wants the standard error of \(\hat p\) below \(0.02\) when the true \(p\) is near \(0.5\); roughly how many patients are needed? (c) In one sentence, relate your answer to why the Fisher information is largest near \(p = 0\) or \(p = 1\).


Exercise 5.3 (Interpretation: the cost of going indirect) In Example 5.3 the direct contrasts had standard errors \(0.456\) and \(0.410\), while the indirect contrast of \(B\) versus \(C\) had standard error \(0.614\). (a) Show that the indirect variance is the sum of the two direct variances and confirm the number. (b) Explain in one sentence why an indirect comparison is necessarily less precise than the direct comparisons it is built from. (c) If a third trial directly compared \(B\) and \(C\) with standard error \(0.30\), which estimate would you trust more, and why?


Exercise 5.4 (Poisson information and efficiency) Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be iid \(\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\). (a) Derive the MLE \(\hat\lambda_n\). (b) Compute the score, show it has mean zero, and compute the Fisher information \(\mathcal I(\lambda)\) two ways (as the variance of the score and as minus the expected second derivative), confirming the information equality. (c) Show \(\hat\lambda_n\) is unbiased and attains the Cramér-Rao bound exactly, hence is efficient.


Exercise 5.5 (Reparameterization and invariance) Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be iid Exponential with rate \(\lambda > 0\), density \(f(x;\lambda) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) on \(x > 0\). (a) Find the MLE of \(\lambda\). (b) Using invariance (Proposition 5.2), write down the MLE of the mean \(\eta = 1/\lambda\) and of the median \(m = (\log 2)/\lambda\). (c) Use the delta method (Theorem 5.3) to give the asymptotic variance of \(\hat\eta_n\), and verify it equals the Cramér-Rao bound for estimating \(\eta\).


Exercise 5.6 (Bias can lower MSE) For iid \(\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) data with known \(\sigma^2\), consider the shrinkage estimator \(\hat\mu_c = c\,\bar X_n\) for a constant \(c \in [0,1]\). (a) Using Proposition 5.1, write \(\mathrm{MSE}_\mu(\hat\mu_c)\) as a function of \(c\). (b) Minimize over \(c\) and show the optimal \(c^{*}\) is strictly less than \(1\) whenever \(\mu \ne 0\), so a biased estimator strictly beats the unbiased \(\bar X_n\) in MSE. (c) Explain why this does not contradict the Cramér-Rao bound.


Exercise 5.7 (Score versus Wald in finite samples) Repeat the three tests of Example 5.4 for the data \(n = 25\), \(\sum_i X_i = 10\) against the null \(H_0 : p = 0.3\). Report \(W_n\), \(R_n\), and \(\Lambda_n\) to three decimals and state which (if any) reject at level \(0.05\). Comment on the ordering \(W_n\), \(R_n\), \(\Lambda_n\) you observe.


Exercise 5.8 (Where the information equality fails (\(\star\))) The information equality (Theorem 5.4) requires regularity (Definition 5.6), in particular a common support not depending on the parameter. Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be iid Uniform\((0, \theta)\), whose support \((0, \theta)\) does depend on \(\theta\). (a) Show that the naive score \(\partial_\theta \log f = -1/\theta\) has nonzero expectation, so Lemma 5.1 fails. (b) Show the MLE is \(\hat\theta_n = \max_i X_i\), that \(n(\theta - \hat\theta_n)/\theta \xrightarrow{d} \mathrm{Exp}(1)\), and hence the rate is \(n\) rather than \(\sqrt n\) and the limit is not normal. (c) Explain precisely which hypotheses of Theorem 5.6 are violated. (Solution in Appendix F.)


Exercise 5.9 (Sandwich variance for a misspecified Poisson (\(\star\))) Suppose the true data are overdispersed counts with mean \(\mu_0\) and variance \(v_0 = \kappa\,\mu_0\) for some \(\kappa > 1\) (so \(\kappa = 1\) would be Poisson), but we fit a working Poisson model with log-likelihood contribution \(x\log\mu - \mu\). (a) Show the working score is \(\psi(x;\mu) = x/\mu - 1\) and the M-estimator is \(\hat\mu_n = \bar X_n\), targeting \(\mu^{*} = \mu_0\). (b) Compute the bread \(\mathbf A(\mu_0)\) and meat \(\mathbf B(\mu_0)\) and show the sandwich asymptotic variance is \(\kappa\,\mu_0/n\), whereas the naive model-based variance is \(\mu_0/n\). (c) Conclude that the naive Poisson standard error understates the truth by the factor \(\sqrt\kappa\), and relate this to Corollary 5.3. (Solution in Appendix F.)


Exercise 5.10 (Multivariate delta method for a ratio) Let \((\hat\alpha_n, \hat\beta_n)\) be jointly asymptotically normal, \(\sqrt n\bigl((\hat\alpha_n, \hat\beta_n) - (\alpha, \beta)\bigr) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_2(\mathbf 0, \boldsymbol\Sigma)\) with \(\boldsymbol\Sigma = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} \sigma_\alpha^2 & \sigma_{\alpha\beta} \\ \sigma_{\alpha\beta} & \sigma_\beta^2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\) and \(\beta \ne 0\). Using Theorem 5.3, derive the asymptotic variance of the ratio \(\hat\rho_n = \hat\alpha_n / \hat\beta_n\). Specialize to the independent case \(\sigma_{\alpha\beta} = 0\) and comment on the well-known instability when \(\beta\) is near zero.





Bingham, N. H., and John M. Fry. 2010. Regression: Linear Models in Statistics. Springer Undergraduate Mathematics Series. Springer.

title: 6  Linear Regression from First Principles
text:
6.1 Introduction
Every method in this book that adjusts an indirect comparison for differences between trial populations is, at its core, a regression. Simulated treatment comparison fits an outcome model on individual patient data and then evaluates it at a comparator population; multilevel network meta-regression writes the linear predictor of every arm as a regression on covariates; and matching-adjusted indirect comparison reweights individuals to balance covariates, a procedure we will see (Chapter 18) is closely tied to a weighted regression. Before any of that can be made rigorous we must understand the simplest and most important regression model completely: the linear model, fit by ordinary least squares. This chapter builds that theory from the ground up and proves every statement it makes.
The questions we answer are the following. Given data, what does “the line of best fit” mean precisely, and what formula produces it? In what sense is that formula optimal, and under what assumptions? If we repeated the experiment, how would the estimate vary, and how do we quantify our uncertainty about it with a confidence interval or a test? Finally, the philosophical question that justifies the whole enterprise: why squares? Why minimize the sum of squared residuals rather than, say, the sum of absolute residuals? We preview the answer at once, so the reader does not spend the chapter wondering: under Gaussian errors, minimizing the sum of squares is exactly maximum likelihood (proved in Section 6.8); minimizing the sum of absolute residuals would instead be maximum likelihood under a different, Laplace-shaped error model. The choice of squares is therefore a statement about the assumed shape of the noise, not an arbitrary convention.
We will see that under the assumption of normal, homoskedastic (equal-variance), independent errors the least-squares estimator is selected by four different optimality principles at once:
These are four genuinely different statements: (i) is geometric, (ii) ranges over linear estimators assuming only two moments, (iii) is likelihood-based, and (iv) ranges over all unbiased estimators. That they select the same estimator is the reason linear regression is the workhorse of applied statistics, and it is the foundation on which the later chapters build.
How to read this chapter. Every result is proved in full, because every later chapter leans on these facts and we want nothing downstream to be a black box. On a first reading you may take the formulas on trust and skip the proofs without losing the through-line; the prose around each result tells you what it means and why it matters for indirect comparison. The chapter is built in four layers, summarized here so you always know which layer you are in.
The development is self-contained but rests on the linear algebra of Chapters 1 to 3 (column spaces, Theorem 2.5, the Theorem 3.2) and the probability and inference of Chapters 4 and 5 (the multivariate normal, Definition 4.7, Theorem 5.7). We recall what we use and prove everything that is specific to regression.

Projection (pure geometry). The fitted vector is the point of the model space closest to the data. This uses only linear algebra, no probability (Section 6.3).
Best linear unbiased estimator, BLUE (Gauss-Markov). Among all estimators that are linear in the data and unbiased, ordinary least squares has the smallest variance. This uses only the first two moments of the errors, not their shape (Theorem 6.3).
Maximum likelihood estimator, MLE. Under Gaussian errors, least squares is the coefficient value that makes the observed data most probable (Theorem 6.11).
Uniformly minimum-variance unbiased estimator, UMVU (Cramér-Rao). Under Gaussian errors, least squares beats every unbiased estimator, even nonlinear ones (Corollary 6.2).

text:
6.2 The linear model and its assumptions
Before the abstractions arrive, here is the concrete example we will return to at every transition.

Example 6.1 (A running example: a small two-arm trial) Six patients in a trial are randomized to a control arm or an active arm. For each patient we record the change in HbA1c (a continuous glycemic outcome, where a more negative change is better) together with the patient’s baseline disease severity. To model the expected change we use three regressors: a constant term, a treatment indicator \(T\) (equal to \(1\) on the active arm and \(0\) on control), and the mean-centered baseline severity \(z\). In words, \[
\mathbb{E}[\text{change}]=\beta_0\cdot 1+\beta_1\cdot T+\beta_2\cdot z .
\] Each regressor is one column of the design matrix, and each carries a clinical role:









Column of \(\mathbf{X}\)
Meaning
Coefficient
Clinical role




\(\mathbf{1}\)
constant (intercept)
\(\beta_0\)
mean outcome in the reference arm at average covariates


\(T\)
treatment indicator
\(\beta_1\)
the adjusted treatment effect we care about


\(z\)
baseline severity, centered
\(\beta_2\)
a prognostic-covariate adjustment


(\(\mathrm{age}\))
(a further covariate)
(\(\beta_3\))
(a further adjustment, omitted below for hand arithmetic)



Taking three patients per arm at centered baseline values \(z=-1,0,1\), the design matrix and response are \[
\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&-1\\1&0&0\\1&0&1\\1&1&-1\\1&1&0\\1&1&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{y}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\2\\-1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix},
\] the first three rows being the control arm and the last three the active arm. We compute the fit in Example 6.2 and reuse this design when we reach the Gauss-Markov theorem and the variance formulas. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

We observe a response vector \(\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and, for each of the \(n\) units, the values of \(p\) regressors collected as the rows of a known matrix \(\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\). The model asserts that, up to random error, \(\mathbf{y}\) lies in the column space \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})\).

Definition 6.1 (The linear model) The linear model for a response \(\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with design matrix \(\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\) (\(p\le n\)) is \[
\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon},
\tag{6.1}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^p\) is an unknown vector of coefficients and \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is an unobserved random error vector. The Gauss-Markov assumptions are
(G1) zero mean, \(\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}]=\mathbf{0}_n\);
(G2) homoskedasticity and no correlation, \(\mathrm{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})=\sigma^2 I_n\) for some unknown \(\sigma^2>0\), that is, \(\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\sigma^2\) for every \(i\) and \(\mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_k)=0\) for \(i\ne k\).
The model has full column rank when \(\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p\). For the exact distributional theory of Section 6.5 onward we add
(G3) normality, \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}_n(\mathbf{0}_n,\sigma^2 I_n)\),
which (with G1, G2) is equivalent to \(\mathbf{y}\sim\mathcal{N}_n(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2
I_n)\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Reader translation. The model says the response is a straight-line combination of the regressors, \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\), plus random noise \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) that on average is zero (G1), has the same spread for every patient and does not link patients together (G2), and, when we want exact tests, follows a bell curve (G3). In the running example \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is the part of a patient’s HbA1c change explained by their arm and baseline severity, and \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) is everything else.
A recurring source of confusion is the difference between the error and the residual. The table below fixes the roles of the symbols used throughout the chapter.









Symbol
Name
Observed?
Meaning




\(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\)
error (disturbance)
no

\(\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}\)

yes

\(\boldsymbol{\beta}\)

no

\(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\)

yes

\(\sigma^2\)

no

\(s^2\)

yes

yes

The left-hand quantities \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon},\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\) are unknown features of the population we never see; the right-hand quantities \(\mathbf{r},\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},s^2\) are things we compute. Estimation is the act of guessing the first column from the second.
A few words on the content of the assumptions. Assumption G1 says the regressors capture the systematic part of the response, so that the model \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}]=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is correct on average; it forces \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}]\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})\). Assumption G2 is two assumptions in one: equal variances across units (homoskedasticity) and uncorrelated errors. It is what makes ordinary, unweighted least squares the right procedure; when it fails one uses weighted or generalized least squares, and the robust “sandwich” variance of Definition 5.11 repairs the inference. Assumption G3 is needed only for exact, finite-sample tests and intervals; the point estimator and the Gauss-Markov optimality of Section 6.4 require only G1 and G2.

Remark. What homoskedasticity looks like, and when it fails. Homoskedasticity (G2, first half) means every patient’s outcome scatters around the regression line by the same amount. Picture the data points: under homoskedasticity they form a band of constant vertical thickness around the fitted line; heteroskedasticity is a band that fans out, for example wider scatter at higher baseline severity. A health researcher should expect G2 to fail when outcomes are recorded on different scales or in clusters: sicker patients often vary more than healthy ones, and patients within the same hospital are correlated (the second half of G2, no correlation, then also fails). When G2 fails, the point estimate \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is still unbiased, but its reported standard errors are wrong. Two standard repairs exist: weighted or generalized least squares (developed in Exercise 6.8), which models the unequal variances directly, and the robust “sandwich” variance estimator of Definition 5.11, which estimates the uncertainty of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) without assuming the tidy \(\sigma^2 I_n\) covariance structure at all. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reading the coefficients in health terms. The coefficient \(\beta_k\) is the conditional effect on \(\mathbb{E}[y_i]\) of a one-unit change in the \(k\)-th regressor with all others held fixed. The three roles a column can play, which recur throughout the book, are visible already in the running example.

The coefficient on the treatment indicator, \(\beta_1\), is the adjusted treatment effect: the expected difference in outcome between the active and control arms for two patients with the same baseline severity. This is the quantity every indirect comparison ultimately targets.
The coefficient on baseline severity, \(\beta_2\), is a prognostic effect: severity predicts the outcome regardless of treatment. A covariate that influences the outcome but not the treatment effect is a prognostic variable (Definition 11.5); you do not need the formal definition yet, only the picture of a covariate that shifts everyone’s outcome.
If we added a treatment-by-severity product column, its coefficient would measure how the treatment effect itself changes with severity. A covariate that changes the treatment effect is an effect modifier (Definition 11.3). Effect modifiers are the central obstacle in indirect comparison: two trials with different severity mixes can report different treatment effects even when nothing else differs. We meet them properly in Part II.

On the identity link used here, this conditional reading is also the marginal (population-averaged) one, so the distinctions stay simple. For the nonlinear links of Chapter 7 the conditional and marginal effects diverge, a phenomenon named Definition 7.7. The clean behavior of the identity-link linear model is exactly why it is the right place to learn the machinery before meeting its complications. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Throughout Section 6.3 to Section 6.7 we assume full column rank, \(\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p\). In plain terms this means no regressor column can be reconstructed as a combination of the others, so each coefficient is separately identifiable: the data can tell the columns apart. The assumption fails in familiar situations, for example when a categorical predictor is coded with an intercept and a separate indicator for every level, so that the indicators add up to the intercept column. We treat that rank-deficient case fully in Section 6.9, where the geometry survives intact and only the coordinate vector \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) becomes non-unique; a reader who meets a coding problem of this kind in practice can jump ahead to that section without loss. The following small lemma is the algebraic hinge of the full-rank theory: it is what makes \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) invertible.

Lemma 6.1 (Null space of the Gram matrix) For any \(\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\), \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})\) and \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)\); consequently \(\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})\). In particular \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) is invertible if and only if \(\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p\), in which case it is positive definite.


Proof. We argue in four short steps.
Step 1 (the two null spaces are equal). If \(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\) then \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\), so \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})\subseteq\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})\). Conversely, if \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\) then \[
0=\mathbf{v}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v})^\top(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v})
=\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}\|_2^2,
\] whence \(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\) (a vector of norm zero is the zero vector); thus \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})\subseteq\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})\) and the two null spaces are equal.
Step 2 (the ranks are equal). Apply the rank-nullity theorem (Theorem 1.3) to the \(p\times p\) matrix \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) and to \(\mathbf{X}\), both of which have \(p\) columns. Rank-nullity says (number of columns) \(=\) rank \(+\) nullity, so \[
\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=p-\dim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})
=p-\dim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X}),
\] the middle equality being Step 1.
Step 3 (the column spaces are equal). The inclusion \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})\subseteq\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)\) is immediate, because every column of \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{X})\) is \(\mathbf{X}^\top\) times a column of \(\mathbf{X}\). To upgrade this inclusion to equality it suffices to show the two spaces have the same dimension. The dimension of \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})\) is \(\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X}^\top
\mathbf{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})\) by Step 2, while the dimension of \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)\) is \(\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X}^\top)\), and a basic fact of linear algebra is that a matrix and its transpose have the same rank, \(\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X}^\top)=\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})\) (this is part of the fundamental theorem of the four subspaces, Theorem 1.5; row rank equals column rank). The two dimensions match, so the inclusion is an equality.
Step 4 (definiteness and invertibility). The matrix \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) is symmetric with \(\mathbf{v}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}\|_2^2\ge 0\), so it is positive semidefinite. It is positive definite exactly when \(\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}\|_2^2>0\) for every \(\mathbf{v}\ne\mathbf{0}\), that is, when \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})=\{\mathbf{0}\}\), equivalently \(\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p\) (Theorem 3.3). A positive definite matrix is invertible. \(\square\)

Reader translation. The Gram matrix \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) inherits exactly the non-redundancy of \(\mathbf{X}\): it is invertible if and only if the regressors are not redundant. This is the single fact that lets us write down the closed-form estimator Equation 6.3 below; when it fails we are in the rank-deficient world of Section 6.9.
