Definition 7.5 (Saturated model) The saturated model for responses \(y_1,\dots,y_n\) is the GLM with one free mean parameter per observation, fitted at \(\tilde\mu_i=y_i\) for every \(i\), with natural parameter \(\tilde\theta_i=\theta(y_i)\). It attains the largest log-likelihood achievable by any model in the family for the given data, because each term \(y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)\) in Equation 7.10 is maximized over \(\theta_i\) where its derivative vanishes, \(\frac{d}{d\theta_i}\bigl[y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)\bigr]=y_i-b'(\theta_i)=0\), that is at \(b'(\theta_i)=y_i\), i.e. at \(\theta_i=\tilde\theta_i\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Definition 7.6 (Deviance and residual deviance) Let \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) be the fitted coefficients of a GLM, with fitted means \(\hat\mu_i\) and natural parameters \(\hat\theta_i=\theta(\hat\mu_i)\). The scaled deviance is twice the log-likelihood gap between the saturated model and the fitted model, \[
D^\ast(\mathbf y;\hat{\boldsymbol\mu})=2\bigl[\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}(\mathbf y)-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})\bigr]
=\frac{2}{\phi}\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\Bigl[y_i(\tilde\theta_i-\hat\theta_i)-b(\tilde\theta_i)+b(\hat\theta_i)\Bigr],
\tag{7.19}\] and the deviance is its dispersion-free numerator \[
D(\mathbf y;\hat{\boldsymbol\mu})=\phi\,D^\ast(\mathbf y;\hat{\boldsymbol\mu})
=2\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\Bigl[y_i(\tilde\theta_i-\hat\theta_i)-b(\tilde\theta_i)+b(\hat\theta_i)\Bigr]
=\sum_{i=1}^n d_i.
\tag{7.20}\] The value of \(D\) at the fitted model is the residual deviance; the deviance residual of observation \(i\) is \(r_i^D=\mathrm{sign}(y_i-\hat\mu_i)\sqrt{d_i}\), so that \(\sum_i(r_i^D)^2=D\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Reader translation. The deviance is one number saying how far the fitted model sits from a flawless fit: large deviance, poor fit; zero deviance, perfect fit. The scaled deviance simply divides by the dispersion \(\phi\) (for the binomial and Poisson \(\phi=1\), so the two coincide). The deviance residuals \(r_i^D\) are the GLM’s stand-ins for the ordinary residuals \(y_i-\hat\mu_i\) of Chapter 6: they carry the sign of the raw residual, and their squares sum to the total deviance, exactly as squared residuals summed to the residual sum of squares.

Remark (Bregman divergence (a named building block)). The proof of the next proposition uses one recurring construction, so we name it once here rather than mid-argument. For a smooth strictly convex function \(b\), the Bregman divergence from \(v\) to \(u\) is \[
D_b(u,v)=b(u)-b(v)-b'(v)(u-v),
\] the gap at the point \(u\) between \(b\) itself and its tangent line drawn at \(v\). Because a convex function lies on or above each of its tangents, \(D_b(u,v)\ge0\), with equality only when \(u=v\); this single inequality is what forces the deviance to be nonnegative. No prior acquaintance with the term is assumed: it is just a name for “function minus its own tangent line.” \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Proposition 7.3 (The deviance is a sum of nonnegative Bregman divergences) Each deviance contribution satisfies \(d_i\ge0\), with \(d_i=0\) if and only if \(\hat\mu_i=y_i\). Hence \(D\ge0\), and \(D=0\) if and only if the fit is saturated. For the normal linear model with identity link, \(D=\sum_i(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2\) is the residual sum of squares of Chapter 6.


Proof. Fix \(i\) and write \(u=\hat\theta_i\), \(v=\tilde\theta_i\). Since \(\tilde\mu_i=y_i=b'(\tilde\theta_i)=b'(v)\), \[
\tfrac12\,d_i/w_i=y_i(v-u)-b(v)+b(u)=b'(v)(v-u)-b(v)+b(u)=b(u)-b(v)-b'(v)(u-v)=:D_b(u,v).
\] The quantity \(D_b(u,v)\) is exactly the Bregman divergence of the convex function \(b\) just defined: by Taylor’s theorem with the Lagrange form of the remainder there is \(\xi\) between \(u\) and \(v\) with \(D_b(u,v)=\tfrac12 b''(\xi)(u-v)^2\ge0\), since \(b''>0\). It is zero exactly when \(u=v\), i.e. \(\hat\theta_i=\tilde\theta_i\), equivalently \(\hat\mu_i=b'(\hat\theta_i)=b'(\tilde\theta_i)=y_i\). Thus \(d_i=2w_iD_b(u,v)\ge0\) with equality iff \(\hat\mu_i=y_i\), and summing gives \(D\ge0\) with equality iff the fit is saturated. For the normal model \(b(\theta)=\theta^2/2\), \(\theta=\mu\), \(w_i=1\), so \(d_i=2[y_i(y_i-\hat\mu_i)-\tfrac12y_i^2+\tfrac12\hat\mu_i^2]=y_i^2-2y_i\hat\mu_i+\hat\mu_i^2=(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2\), and \(D=\sum_i(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2=\mathrm{RSS}\). \(\square\)

The deviance specializes to clean closed forms for the discrete families, which are the ones used in practice.

Example 7.4 (Poisson and binomial deviance) Poisson. With \(b(\theta)=e^\theta\), \(\theta=\log\mu\), \(w_i=1\), the \(i\)-th contribution is \(d_i=2[y_i\log y_i-y_i-y_i\log\hat\mu_i+\hat\mu_i]=2[y_i\log(y_i/\hat\mu_i)-(y_i-\hat\mu_i)]\), so \[
D_{\mathrm{Poisson}}=2\sum_{i=1}^n\Bigl[y_i\log\frac{y_i}{\hat\mu_i}-(y_i-\hat\mu_i)\Bigr],
\] with the convention \(0\log0=0\). If the model has an intercept then \(\sum_i\hat\mu_i=\sum_iy_i\) by Corollary 7.1, and the second term vanishes, leaving \(D=2\sum_iy_i\log(y_i/\hat\mu_i)\).
Binomial proportion. With \(y_i=R_i/n_i\), \(\hat\mu_i=\hat p_i\), \(w_i=n_i\), and writing the fitted counts \(\hat R_i=n_i\hat p_i\), the contribution is \(d_i=2n_i[y_i\log(y_i/\hat p_i)+(1-y_i)\log((1-y_i)/(1-\hat p_i))]\), so in count form \[
D_{\mathrm{binom}}=2\sum_{i=1}^n\Bigl[R_i\log\frac{R_i}{\hat R_i}+(n_i-R_i)\log\frac{n_i-R_i}{n_i-\hat R_i}\Bigr].
\] \(\blacktriangleleft\)


7.6.1 Deviance for model comparison
The deviance is to GLMs what the residual sum of squares is to linear models: the basis of the goodness-of-fit and nested-model tests. The key fact is that a difference of scaled deviances is exactly a likelihood ratio statistic.

Theorem 7.4 (Analysis of deviance) Let \(M_0\subset M_1\) be nested GLMs with the same EDF, the same link, and the same known dispersion \(\phi\), with \(p_0<p_1\) parameters, fitted by maximum likelihood with residual deviances \(D_0\ge D_1\). Then the scaled deviance difference equals the likelihood ratio statistic for \(M_0\) within \(M_1\), \[
\frac{D_0-D_1}{\phi}=2\bigl[\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_1)-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_0)\bigr],
\tag{7.21}\] and under \(M_0\), as \(n\to\infty\), \[
\frac{D_0-D_1}{\phi}\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi^2_{\,p_1-p_0}.
\tag{7.22}\] When \(\phi\) is unknown (as for the normal or gamma families) it is replaced by a consistent estimator \(\hat\phi\) and \((D_0-D_1)/\{\hat\phi(p_1-p_0)\}\) is referred to an \(F_{p_1-p_0,\,n-p_1}\) distribution.


Proof. By Equation 7.19 the scaled deviance of a model is \(D^\ast=2[\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})]\), and the saturated log-likelihood \(\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}(\mathbf y)\) does not depend on which fitted model is used. Subtracting, \[
\frac{D_0-D_1}{\phi}=D_0^\ast-D_1^\ast
=2[\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_0)]-2[\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_1)]
=2[\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_1)-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_0)],
\] which is Equation 7.21: the saturated term cancels and what remains is twice the maximized log-likelihood gap between the two models, i.e. the log likelihood ratio statistic for testing \(M_0\) inside \(M_1\). Under \(M_0\) this statistic converges in distribution to \(\chi^2_{p_1-p_0}\) by Wilks’s theorem (Theorem 5.9), the number of degrees of freedom being the difference \(p_1-p_0\) in the number of free parameters. The \(F\) reference distribution for unknown \(\phi\) follows from writing the statistic as a ratio of the deviance difference to an independent estimator of \(\phi\) scaled by its degrees of freedom, exactly as the linear-model \(F\)-test of Chapter 6 arises from the ratio of two sums of squares. \(\square\)


Remark (Reading an analysis-of-deviance table). Theorem Theorem 7.4 licenses the standard workflow: fit a sequence of nested models, tabulate their residual deviances, and test each added term by referring the drop in deviance to a chi-square (or \(F\)) distribution on the added degrees of freedom. This is the GLM counterpart of the analysis-of-variance \(F\)-test used for the linear model of Chapter 6: the drop in deviance plays the role of the extra regression sum of squares, and for the normal family with the identity link the deviance test reduces to exactly that \(F\)-test. The residual deviance of a single model, compared to its degrees of freedom \(n-p\), is itself a rough absolute goodness-of-fit check, because under a correctly specified model with \(\phi\) known the residual deviance is approximately \(\chi^2_{n-p}\) in favorable (large per-group count) regimes. The worked example of Section 7.8 carries this out by hand. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 7  Generalized Linear Models
section: 7.7 Non-collapsibility of the odds ratio and the hazard ratio
text:
7.7 Non-collapsibility of the odds ratio and the hazard ratio
We now reach the phenomenon that distinguishes nonlinear-link GLMs from the linear model and that reverberates through the rest of the book. In a linear model the coefficient of a treatment indicator is both the effect within every covariate stratum and the effect on the population average, because expectation is linear. For the odds ratio and the hazard ratio this is false: an effect that is constant across strata need not equal the effect computed from the population-averaged risks. The marginal and the conditional effect are different numbers, and the difference is not bias from confounding but an arithmetic consequence of the nonlinearity of the link.
To see why the linear model is the special case, write the marginal treatment effect on the identity scale as the average of the stratum-specific effects. With no confounding, \[
\mathbb E_X[\mu_1(X)]-\mathbb E_X[\mu_0(X)]=\mathbb E_X\bigl[\mu_1(X)-\mu_0(X)\bigr]=\delta,
\] so if the within-stratum difference is a constant \(\delta\), the population-average difference is that same \(\delta\). Linearity of the expectation is doing all the work; the odds ratio and hazard ratio break precisely because their scales are nonlinear.
For a health researcher the phenomenon is concrete before it is formal. Suppose a trial reports a conditional odds ratio of \(3.5\) for an active drug versus control, and that this same \(3.5\) holds in both younger and older patients, so there is no effect modification by age. Yet when the two age groups are pooled and a single odds ratio is computed from the combined response rates, the answer is about \(3.14\), not \(3.5\). Nothing was confounded and no subgroup interaction was hidden; the pooled number simply differs from the common stratum number by arithmetic. The whole of this section formalizes that observation, and its consequence for a systematic review is immediate: an odds ratio reported by a trial is a conditional effect tied to the covariates in that trial’s model, whereas an indirect comparison may need a marginal effect for a target population, and the two are not interchangeable even under flawless randomization. The numbers \(3.5\) and \(3.14\) reappear, computed exactly, in Example 7.5.

7.7.1 A precise definition
We work with two treatments, indexed by the potential outcomes \(Y(0),Y(1)\) of Notation, and a baseline covariate \(X\) that stratifies the population. Write \(\mu_t(x)=\mathbb E[Y(t)\mid X=x]\) for the stratum-specific mean outcome under treatment \(t\), and assume throughout this section the no-confounding identity \(\mathbb E[Y(t)]=\mathbb E_X[\mu_t(X)]\), so that the marginal mean is the average of the conditional means. We compare effects measured on the scale of a strictly increasing transform \(g\), the effect measure’s link (logit for the odds ratio).

Definition 7.7 (Collapsibility and non-collapsibility of an effect measure) For a strictly increasing transform \(g\) define the conditional effect in stratum \(x\) and the marginal effect by \[
\psi_g(x)=g(\mu_1(x))-g(\mu_0(x)),
\qquad
\psi_g^{\mathrm M}=g\bigl(\mathbb E_X[\mu_1(X)]\bigr)-g\bigl(\mathbb E_X[\mu_0(X)]\bigr).
\tag{7.23}\] The effect measure based on \(g\) is collapsible over \(X\) if, whenever the conditional effect is constant in \(x\) (no effect modification on the \(g\)-scale), \(\psi_g(x)\equiv\psi_g\), the marginal effect equals that common value, \(\psi_g^{\mathrm M}=\psi_g\), for every distribution of \(X\) and every pair of stratum means \(\mu_0(\cdot),\mu_1(\cdot)\) consistent with it. The measure is non-collapsible if it is not collapsible, that is, if there exist stratum means with constant conditional effect for which \(\psi_g^{\mathrm M}\neq\psi_g\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

In plain terms, a measure is collapsible when a conditional effect that is identical in every stratum is inherited unchanged by the pooled population, no matter how large or small the strata are; it is non-collapsible when pooling can move that common number even though nothing modifies the effect from one stratum to the next.
The definition isolates the question cleanly: collapsibility is the statement that the link commutes with averaging across strata when the conditional effect is constant. For some scales it does.

Proposition 7.4 (The risk difference and the risk ratio are collapsible) The identity-scale effect measure (the risk difference, \(g(\mu)=\mu\)) and the log-scale effect measure (the risk ratio, \(g(\mu)=\log\mu\)) are collapsible over \(X\).
[machine-checked: theories/STC.v, Lemma STC_collapse_linear]


Proof. Risk difference. Suppose \(\psi_{\mathrm{id}}(x)=\mu_1(x)-\mu_0(x)\equiv\delta\). By linearity of expectation, \[
\psi_{\mathrm{id}}^{\mathrm M}=\mathbb E_X[\mu_1(X)]-\mathbb E_X[\mu_0(X)]=\mathbb E_X[\mu_1(X)-\mu_0(X)]=\mathbb E_X[\delta]=\delta.
\] Risk ratio. Suppose \(\psi_{\log}(x)=\log\mu_1(x)-\log\mu_0(x)\equiv\rho\), equivalently \(\mu_1(x)=e^\rho\mu_0(x)\) for all \(x\). Taking expectations, \(\mathbb E_X[\mu_1(X)]=e^\rho\mathbb E_X[\mu_0(X)]\), so \[
\psi_{\log}^{\mathrm M}=\log\frac{\mathbb E_X[\mu_1(X)]}{\mathbb E_X[\mu_0(X)]}=\log e^\rho=\rho.
\] In both cases the marginal effect equals the common conditional effect for every distribution of \(X\), so the measure is collapsible. The mean-difference (identity-link) case is the one verified in the Coq development, where it is proved from linearity of expectation alone, exactly the property that the nonlinear logit lacks. \(\square\)



7.7.2 The odds ratio is non-collapsible
The contrast with the logit scale is sharp, and a single explicit example proves non-collapsibility.

Example 7.5 (A two-stratum non-collapsible odds ratio) Read \(X\) as an age group (\(0\) for younger, \(1\) for older patients), split evenly across the trial, and read each pair of numbers below as the probability of response under control and under an active drug in that age group. Let \(X\in\{0,1\}\) be this binary prognostic covariate with \(P(X=0)=P(X=1)=\tfrac12\), and let the stratum-specific outcome probabilities under control and treatment be \[
\mu_0(0)=0.3,\quad \mu_1(0)=0.6,\qquad \mu_0(1)=0.6,\quad \mu_1(1)=0.84.
\] The conditional log odds ratio is the same in both strata. In stratum \(X=0\), \[
\psi_{\mathrm{logit}}(0)=\mathrm{logit}(0.6)-\mathrm{logit}(0.3)
=\log\frac{0.6/0.4}{0.3/0.7}=\log\frac{1.5}{0.428571\ldots}=\log 3.5=1.25276\ldots,
\] and in stratum \(X=1\), \[
\psi_{\mathrm{logit}}(1)=\mathrm{logit}(0.84)-\mathrm{logit}(0.6)
=\log\frac{0.84/0.16}{0.6/0.4}=\log\frac{5.25}{1.5}=\log 3.5=1.25276\ldots .
\] So the conditional effect is constant, \(\psi_{\mathrm{logit}}(x)\equiv\log 3.5\), with conditional odds ratio \(3.5\) and no effect modification on the logit scale.
The marginal risks are the stratum averages, \[
\mathbb E[Y(0)]=\tfrac12(0.3+0.6)=0.45,\qquad \mathbb E[Y(1)]=\tfrac12(0.6+0.84)=0.72,
\] and the marginal log odds ratio is \[
\psi_{\mathrm{logit}}^{\mathrm M}=\mathrm{logit}(0.72)-\mathrm{logit}(0.45)
=\log\frac{0.72/0.28}{0.45/0.55}=\log\frac{2.571429\ldots}{0.818182\ldots}=\log 3.142857\ldots=1.14513\ldots .
\] The marginal odds ratio is \(\tfrac{22}{7}=3.142857\ldots\), strictly less than the conditional odds ratio \(3.5\). Therefore \[
\psi_{\mathrm{logit}}^{\mathrm M}=1.14513\ldots\;\neq\;1.25276\ldots=\psi_{\mathrm{logit}},
\] so the odds ratio is non-collapsible, proving the negative half of Definition 7.7. The marginal odds ratio is attenuated toward the null value \(1\) relative to the conditional odds ratio \(3.5\). This direction is not an accident of the chosen numbers: whenever the conditional odds ratio exceeds \(1\) and the baseline risks genuinely differ across strata, the marginal odds ratio falls strictly between \(1\) and the conditional value, so it is always pulled toward the null. The general statement, and its proof from the convexity of the logit (Jensen’s inequality, Theorem 4.6), are the content of the starred Exercise 7.12; the mechanism is unpacked in the remark just below. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark (Non-collapsibility is not confounding). The example is engineered so that there is no confounding: we specified the potential-outcome stratum means \(\mu_t(x)\) directly and used \(\mathbb E[Y(t)]=\mathbb E_X[\mu_t(X)]\) to form the marginal risks, as would hold in a randomized trial where \(X\) is a pure prognostic factor balanced across arms. No backdoor path, no omitted common cause, and yet the marginal and conditional odds ratios differ. The mechanism is Jensen’s inequality (Theorem 4.6): the marginal effect applies the nonlinear logit to the average risk, \(g(\mathbb E_X[\mu_t(X)])\), whereas the constant conditional effect lives on the average of the logits; for a nonaffine \(g\) these disagree, \[
g\bigl(\mathbb E_X[\mu_t(X)]\bigr)\neq\mathbb E_X\bigl[g(\mu_t(X))\bigr],
\] and the two halves of the contrast fail to cancel. The risk difference and risk ratio escape this fate because, as Proposition 7.4 shows, their links interact linearly with the averaging. \(\blacktriangleleft\)



7.7.3 The hazard ratio, and why this seeds later chapters
The same mechanism afflicts the hazard ratio of survival analysis. A precise treatment requires the survival function and the proportional-hazards model, which we develop later, but the statement and its cause can be recorded now. If the cause-specific hazard under treatment \(t\) in stratum \(x\) is \(h_t(x)\) with a constant conditional hazard ratio \(h_1(x)/h_0(x)\equiv r\), the marginal hazard ratio, formed from the population-averaged survival functions \(\bar S_t(u)=\mathbb E_X[\exp(-\int_0^u h_t(x)\,ds)]\), is in general not equal to \(r\) and moreover drifts with time \(u\). The reason is again a nonlinear averaging: survival is an exponential functional of the integrated hazard, and the population average of an exponential is not the exponential of the average. Concretely, writing the integrated hazard \(H_t(x,u)=\int_0^u h_t(x)\,ds\), Jensen’s inequality (Theorem 4.6) applied to the strictly convex map \(v\mapsto e^{-v}\) gives \[
\bar S_t(u)=\mathbb E_X\!\bigl[e^{-H_t(X,u)}\bigr]\;>\;e^{-\mathbb E_X[H_t(X,u)]},
\] so the population survival curve is not the survival curve of the average patient, and the marginal hazard \(-\tfrac{d}{du}\log\bar S_t(u)\) it induces is not \(r\) times any baseline hazard. This subsection is only a conceptual preview: the survival function, the integrated hazard, and the proportional-hazards model are developed in later chapters, and the full non-collapsibility proof for the hazard ratio is deferred to that machinery (flagged again in Section 7.9). Thus the hazard ratio, like the odds ratio, is non-collapsible; this is exactly why the cloglog GLM of Section 7.4.3, which encodes a conditional proportional-hazards model, cannot be read marginally without care.

Remark (Consequences threaded through the book). This single section seeds three later developments. In Chapter 11 collapsibility and effect modification are separated as the two distinct reasons a stratified and a pooled analysis can disagree, with the odds ratio’s non-collapsibility as the running example. In Chapter 17 the choice between a conditional and a marginal estimand becomes the central design decision of a population-adjusted indirect comparison, precisely because on the non-collapsible logit and log-hazard scales the two estimands differ even under perfect adjustment. In Chapter 19 the simulated treatment comparison is shown to have two flavors, a conditional and a marginal version, that disagree by exactly the gap exhibited in Example 7.5, which is why a naive plug-in of covariate means into a fitted logistic model targets the wrong estimand. The network meta-analysis of Dias et al. (2018) sidesteps the issue by combining evidence on the conditional log-odds scale and never marginalizing, and multilevel network meta-regression resolves it by integrating the inverse link over the covariate distribution rather than evaluating it at the mean. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 7  Generalized Linear Models
section: 7.8 A fully worked example: logistic regression by hand
text:
7.8 A fully worked example: logistic regression by hand
We carry out a complete logistic regression on a small grouped data set, computing the maximum likelihood estimate in closed form, executing one iteration of IRLS by hand to see the machinery move, and testing the slope with an analysis of deviance. Every number can be reproduced with a calculator.
The data. Two groups defined by a binary covariate \(x\in\{0,1\}\), each of \(n=10\) trials, with observed successes \[
x_1=0:\;\; R_1=2 \text{ of } n_1=10,\qquad
x_2=1:\;\; R_2=7 \text{ of } n_2=10,
\] so the observed proportions are \(y_1=0.2\) and \(y_2=0.7\). The model is logistic with linear predictor \(\eta_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\), design matrix and prior weights \[
\mathbf X=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad w_1=w_2=10,\qquad\phi=1.
\]
Closed-form maximum likelihood estimate. The model has two parameters and two groups, so it is saturated: the score equations Equation 7.13 force \(\hat p_i=y_i\), the observed proportions. Hence \[
\hat\beta_0=\mathrm{logit}(0.2)=\log\frac{0.2}{0.8}=\log 0.25=-1.38629,
\] \[
\hat\beta_1=\mathrm{logit}(0.7)-\mathrm{logit}(0.2)=\log\frac{0.7/0.3}{0.2/0.8}=\log\frac{2.33333}{0.25}=\log 9.33333=2.23359.
\] The fitted odds ratio for the covariate is \(e^{\hat\beta_1}=9.3333=\tfrac{(7/3)}{(2/8)}\), the cross-product ratio of the two-by-two table, as it must be for a saturated logistic model.
One iteration of IRLS from \(\boldsymbol\beta^{(0)}=(0,0)^\top\). At the start the linear predictors are \(\eta_i^{(0)}=0\), so \(p_i^{(0)}=\tfrac12\) for both groups, and the logit-link quantities are \(d\mu/d\eta=p(1-p)=0.25\) and \(g'(\mu)=1/(p(1-p))=4\). The working response Equation 7.17 and the working weights Equation 7.14 are \[
z_i^{(0)}=\eta_i^{(0)}+\frac{y_i-p_i^{(0)}}{p_i^{(0)}(1-p_i^{(0)})},
\qquad
W_i^{(0)}=n_i\,p_i^{(0)}(1-p_i^{(0)}).
\] Group 1: \(z_1=0+\dfrac{0.2-0.5}{0.25}=-1.2\), \(\;W_1=10(0.25)=2.5\). Group 2: \(z_2=0+\dfrac{0.7-0.5}{0.25}=0.8\), \(\;W_2=10(0.25)=2.5\). The weighted least squares step Equation 7.16 solves \(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\,\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf z\) with \[
\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X=\begin{pmatrix}W_1+W_2&W_2\\W_2&W_2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5&2.5\\2.5&2.5\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf z=\begin{pmatrix}W_1z_1+W_2z_2\\W_2z_2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1.0\\2.0\end{pmatrix}.
\] Subtracting the second equation from the first eliminates \(\beta_1\): \(2.5\,\beta_0=-1.0-2.0=-3.0\), so \(\beta_0^{(1)}=-1.2\); back-substituting, \(2.5(-1.2)+2.5\,\beta_1=2.0\) gives \(\beta_1^{(1)}=2.0\). Thus \[
\boldsymbol\beta^{(1)}=(-1.2,\;2.0)^\top.
\] One step has moved the estimate from \((0,0)\) a large fraction of the way to the maximum likelihood value \((-1.386,\,2.234)\). A second IRLS iteration, evaluated at \(\boldsymbol\beta^{(1)}\) where \(p_1^{(1)}=1/(1+e^{1.2})=0.2315\) and \(p_2^{(1)}=1/(1+e^{-0.8})=0.6900\), yields \(\boldsymbol\beta^{(2)}=(-1.377,\,2.224)^\top\), and the iterates converge to the closed-form estimate above. This illustrates Theorem 7.3 concretely: each step is an ordinary weighted least squares fit of the synthetic response \(\mathbf z\) on \(\mathbf X\).
Testing the slope by analysis of deviance. The fitted (saturated) two-parameter model has residual deviance \(D_1=0\) by Proposition 7.3, since \(\hat p_i=y_i\). Compare it to the null, intercept-only model \(\mathrm{logit}(p)=\beta_0\), whose maximum likelihood estimate is the pooled proportion \(\hat p=(R_1+R_2)/(n_1+n_2)=9/20=0.45\), giving fitted counts \(\hat R_i=n_i\hat p=4.5\) in each group. Its residual deviance from the binomial formula of Example 7.4 is \[
D_0=2\sum_{i=1}^2\Bigl[R_i\log\frac{R_i}{\hat R_i}+(n_i-R_i)\log\frac{n_i-R_i}{n_i-\hat R_i}\Bigr].
\] Group 1 (\(R_1=2\)): \(2\log\frac{2}{4.5}+8\log\frac{8}{5.5}=2(-0.81093)+8(0.37469)=-1.62186+2.99753=1.37567\). Group 2 (\(R_2=7\)): \(7\log\frac{7}{4.5}+3\log\frac{3}{5.5}=7(0.44183)+3(-0.60614)=3.09282-1.81841=1.27441\). Summing and doubling, \(D_0=2(1.37567+1.27441)=2(2.65008)=5.30016\).
The analysis-of-deviance statistic for testing \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) is, by Theorem 7.4 with \(\phi=1\), \[
D_0-D_1=5.30016-0=5.300\;\;\text{on}\;\;p_1-p_0=1\;\text{degree of freedom}.
\] Referred to the \(\chi^2_1\) distribution, whose \(95\%\) quantile is \(3.841\), the observed value \(5.300\) exceeds the critical value, so \(H_0\) is rejected at the \(5\%\) level; the upper-tail probability is \(P(\chi^2_1>5.300)=0.0213\). The covariate is associated with the outcome, with estimated odds ratio \(e^{2.234}=9.33\). This is the complete logistic-regression workflow, estimate, algorithm, and test, carried out by hand.

title: 7  Generalized Linear Models
text:
7.9 Notes and references
The exponential dispersion family and the unifying GLM framework are due to McCullagh and Nelder (1989), whose Chapters 2 and 4 contain the mean-variance identity Theorem 7.1, the score equations Theorem 7.2, the iteratively reweighted least squares algorithm Theorem 7.3, and the deviance Definition 7.6; our development gives full proofs of statements that the monograph often presents as calculations. The cumulant-generating-function proof of Theorem 7.1 follows the exponential family tradition and uses the moment results of Chapter 4 (Definition 4.7, Theorem 4.10). The asymptotic normality of the estimator, Corollary 7.2, is the specialization to the GLM of the general maximum likelihood theory of Chapter 5 (Theorem 5.6, Definition 5.7, Theorem 5.4); the analysis-of-deviance test Theorem 7.4 rests on Wilks’s theorem (Theorem 5.9). The IRLS connection to weighted least squares ties the chapter back to the normal equations of Chapter 6 (Theorem 6.1) and the projection geometry of Definition 6.3.
The treatment of GLMs as the outcome models of indirect comparison, with the linear predictor written as a study baseline plus relative treatment effects on the link scale, is the framework of Dias et al. (2018), whose Chapter 4 develops logistic, Poisson, and other GLM likelihoods for trial data and combines them on the conditional log-odds and log-rate scales. The non-collapsibility of the odds ratio (Example 7.5) is a classical fact of categorical data analysis; the numerical example here is the one used in the companion proof catalogue (catalogue result B.13). The collapsibility of the mean-difference (identity-link) effect, Proposition 7.4, has a machine-checked counterpart in the Coq development at theories/STC.v, Lemma STC_collapse_linear, which proves marginal equals conditional for linear models from linearity of expectation alone; the proof there isolates exactly the property that the nonlinear logit lacks. The non-collapsibility of the hazard ratio is stated here and proved in full once the survival machinery is available; this is the one result of the chapter left as a forward reference rather than proved in place.

title: 7  Generalized Linear Models
text:
7.10 Exercises
A starred exercise, marked \(\star\), has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first four exercises are low-barrier warm-ups and interpretation questions; the remainder mix computation and proof.

Exercise 7.1 (Warm-up.) From linear predictor to fitted probability. A logistic model gives a patient the linear predictor \(\eta=-0.4\). Compute the fitted probability \(p=g^{-1}(\eta)=e^\eta/(1+e^\eta)\). If a treatment indicator has coefficient \(\beta_1=\log 2\), by what multiplicative factor do the patient’s odds of response change on treatment, and what is the treated fitted probability? (Use Equation 7.7 and Equation 7.8.)


Exercise 7.2 (Interpretation.) Reading a coefficient as an odds ratio. A trial arm reports \(R=18\) responders out of \(n=60\), as in Example 7.1. (a) Compute the observed proportion, the odds, and the log odds. (b) An intercept-only logistic fit returns \(\hat\beta_0\) equal to this log odds; state its numerical value. (c) A second arm has fitted log odds larger by \(0.2\). Write the odds ratio between the two arms, and say in one sentence what “\(e^{\beta}\) is a conditional odds ratio” means to a clinician.


Exercise 7.3 (Warm-up.) Name the family, link, and variance function. For each trial outcome, state the natural EDF member, its canonical link, and its variance function \(V(\mu)\), reading them from the summary table in Section 7.3: (a) the number responding out of a fixed number randomized; (b) the count of adverse events over a fixed person-time; (c) a continuous biomarker modeled as normal.


Exercise 7.4 (Interpretation.) Conditional versus marginal, in words. Without any algebra, explain to a colleague why a logistic-regression odds ratio that is identical in every age stratum can differ from the odds ratio computed after pooling the ages, and why this is neither confounding nor effect modification. Then state which of the two, the conditional or the marginal odds ratio, a network meta-analysis working on the log-odds scale actually combines. (See Section 7.7 and Example 7.5.)


Exercise 7.5 Gamma as an EDF. Starting from the gamma density with mean \(\mu\) and shape \(\nu\), verify the entries of the summary table in Section 7.3: that \(\theta=-1/\mu\), \(b(\theta)=-\log(-\theta)\), \(\phi=1/\nu\), and \(V(\mu)=\mu^2\). Confirm \(\mathbb E[Y]=\mu\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu^2/\nu\) from Equation 7.3, and identify the canonical link.


Exercise 7.6 Canonical links from the cumulant function. For each of the Bernoulli, Poisson, and gamma families, compute \(b'(\theta)\), invert it to obtain \(\theta(\mu)=(b')^{-1}(\mu)\), and confirm that the canonical link \(g_{\mathrm c}=\theta(\cdot)\) is the logit, the log, and the reciprocal respectively.


Exercise 7.7 Poisson score equations. Write out the score equations Equation 7.11 for Poisson regression with the log link, and show they reduce to \(\sum_i(y_i-\hat\mu_i)\mathbf x_i=\mathbf 0\). Deduce that a Poisson log-linear model with an intercept reproduces the total count, \(\sum_i\hat\mu_i=\sum_iy_i\). Relate this to Corollary 7.1.


Exercise 7.8 (\(\star\)) IRLS for the probit link. For binary data with the non-canonical probit link \(g(\mu)=\Phi^{-1}(\mu)\), derive the working weights and working response of Theorem 7.3 explicitly in terms of \(\Phi\) and its derivative \(\Phi'\). Show that the working weight is \(W_i=n_i\,\Phi'(\eta_i)^2/\{\Phi(\eta_i)(1-\Phi(\eta_i))\}\). Then show that for a non-canonical link the observed information differs from the expected information, so Fisher scoring and Newton-Raphson are not identical, in contrast to Lemma 7.1.


Exercise 7.9 Poisson deviance by hand. Three Poisson observations \(y=(3,5,10)\) are fitted by an intercept-only log-linear model. Compute \(\hat\mu\), then the residual deviance using the Poisson formula of Example 7.4, and the three deviance residuals. Verify that the deviance residuals satisfy \(\sum_i(r_i^D)^2=D\).


Exercise 7.10 Deviance generalizes the residual sum of squares. Prove from Definition 7.6 that for a normal-response GLM with the identity link the deviance equals the residual sum of squares, \(D=\sum_i(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2\), recovering the central quantity of Chapter 6. Identify what plays the role of \(\phi\) and explain why the deviance test of Theorem 7.4 reproduces the linear-model \(F\)-test in this case.


Exercise 7.11 Offsets and rate ratios. A Poisson regression models event counts \(y_i\) accrued over person-times \(t_i\) with \(\log\mathbb E[y_i]=\log t_i+\beta_0+\beta_1 x_i\). Show that \(\beta_1\) is a log incidence rate ratio, that the offset \(\log t_i\) enters as a regressor with coefficient fixed at one, and that the score equation for \(\beta_0\) equates the total observed count to the total fitted count.


Exercise 7.12 (\(\star\)) Constructing and bounding a non-collapsible odds ratio. Let \(X\in\{0,1\}\) with \(P(X=1)=\pi\), and let the conditional odds ratio be a constant \(\omega>1\) on the logit scale, with baseline risks \(\mu_0(0)\neq\mu_0(1)\). (a) Construct a numerical example, different from Example 7.5, in which the marginal odds ratio is strictly between \(1\) and \(\omega\). (b) Prove in general that, under the no-confounding identity of Section 7.7 and with \(\omega>1\) and genuinely unequal baseline risks, the marginal odds ratio lies strictly between \(1\) and the conditional odds ratio \(\omega\); conclude that the odds ratio is attenuated toward the null. (Hint: write the marginal odds ratio as a function of \(\pi\) and use the strict convexity of the logistic transform, i.e. Theorem 4.6.)


Exercise 7.13 Wald interval for an odds ratio. In the worked example of Section 7.8, the estimated information for the saturated model is \(\mathbf X^\top\hat{\mathbf W}\mathbf X\) with \(\hat W_i=n_i\hat p_i(1-\hat p_i)\). Compute \(\hat{\mathbf W}\) at the maximum likelihood estimate, invert \(\mathbf X^\top\hat{\mathbf W}\mathbf X\), read off \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\), and use the delta method (Theorem 5.3) to give a \(95\%\) confidence interval for the odds ratio \(e^{\beta_1}\).


Exercise 7.14 Complementary log-log and grouped survival. For the cloglog link \(g(\mu)=\log(-\log(1-\mu))\) with inverse \(g^{-1}(\eta)=1-\exp(-e^\eta)\), compute \(d\mu/d\eta\) and the IRLS working weight. Show that if a continuous event time has hazard scaled by \(e^{\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta}\), then the probability of an event in a fixed interval follows a cloglog GLM with covariate coefficients \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and a baseline offset, and explain why this makes the cloglog coefficient a conditional log hazard ratio.





Dias, Sofia, A. E. Ades, Nicky J. Welton, Jeroen P. Jansen, and Alexander J. Sutton. 2018. Network Meta-Analysis for Decision-Making. Statistics in Practice. Wiley.


McCullagh, Peter, and John A. Nelder. 1989. Generalized Linear Models. 2nd ed. Chapman & Hall/CRC.

title: 8  Hierarchical Models, Shrinkage, and Bayesian Inference
text:
8.1 Exchangeability and the rationale for hierarchical models
An indirect treatment comparison never rests on a single study. It assembles effect estimates from a collection of trials that are similar but not identical: different sites, different eligibility criteria, different calendar years, possibly different versions of an outcome scale. Two extreme ways to handle such a collection are both wrong. We could analyze each trial in isolation, treating its effect as an unrelated unknown constant; this throws away the obvious fact that the trials inform one another and leaves each estimate as noisy as its own small sample allows. Or we could pool everything, pretending the trials estimate one common effect; this ignores genuine heterogeneity and reports a false precision. The hierarchical model threads between these extremes. It treats the study-specific true effects as a sample from a common population, so that each study’s estimate is pulled toward the others by an amount that the data themselves calibrate. The resulting estimator, the posterior mean, is a partial pooling that borrows strength across studies; the amount it borrows is the shrinkage factor.
This chapter builds that machinery from the ground up and then develops the Bayesian inference and computation that make it operational. We begin with exchangeability, the symmetry assumption that licenses pooling, and de Finetti’s theorem, which shows that for an exchangeable sequence the hierarchical “conditionally independent given a latent parameter” structure is not a modeling choice but a representation theorem. We then specify the normal-normal hierarchical model, distinguish random effects from fixed effects, and derive the shrinkage estimator as a posterior mean, with the James-Stein phenomenon as its frequentist shadow. Restricted maximum likelihood and empirical Bayes supply the variance components. The second half of the chapter is the Bayesian toolkit on which Bayesian network meta-analysis (Part III) and multilevel network meta-regression (Part V) rest: Bayes’ theorem for parameters, conjugate analysis, the posterior predictive distribution, credible intervals, Markov chain Monte Carlo with a full proof that detailed balance forces the target to be stationary, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and the No-U-Turn Sampler, and the marginal likelihood and Bayes factors. Every load-bearing result is proved in full.
Throughout we follow the notation of Notation: \(\boldsymbol\xi\) is the full parameter vector, \(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi)\) a prior density, \(p(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol\xi)\) a likelihood, and \(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathbf y)\) a posterior density. In the hierarchical sections we write \(\theta_j\) for the true effect in study \(j\), \(\mu\) and \(\tau^2\) for the population mean and variance of those effects, and \(s_j^2\) for the (known) within-study sampling variance of the estimate \(y_j\).
How to read this chapter. Two kinds of material are interleaved, and it helps to know which is which. The essential thread, which every applied reader should master, is short: what a hierarchical model is, why related trials borrow strength, how shrinkage and the heterogeneity \(\tau^2\) work, what a posterior and a credible interval mean, and what the draws returned by Bayesian software represent. The justification thread proves that this machinery is forced and correct: de Finetti’s representation theorem, the measure-theoretic form of Bayes’ theorem, the James-Stein phenomenon, and the detailed-balance and volume-preservation arguments behind the samplers. The table sorts the sections; on a first reading you may skim the right column and come back to it once the essentials are secure.
We will not stay abstract for long. Before any theory, here is the concrete object the whole chapter serves; we return to it at every transition.
The notation is dense, so here is the cast in one place; each row is pinned down precisely where indicated, and you can return here whenever a symbol feels unfamiliar.
One clarification the chapter relies on. The hyperparameter \(\boldsymbol\phi = (\mu, \tau^2)\) is the part of the model the studies have in common, and it is one piece of the full Bayesian parameter vector \(\boldsymbol\xi\), which also contains the study effects \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_J\). So \(\boldsymbol\phi\) is contained in \(\boldsymbol\xi\); when a later section writes \(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathbf y)\) it includes the posterior for \(\mu\) and \(\tau^2\) as well as for each \(\theta_j\).
The premise that several studies “estimate related quantities” must be made precise before it can do any work. The right formalization is a symmetry: before seeing the data, we have no reason to label one study as systematically different from another, so our joint model for their true effects should be invariant to relabeling. That symmetry is exchangeability.
Exchangeability is strictly weaker than independence and identical distribution. Independent and identically distributed (iid) variables are exchangeable, because the joint density factors into a product that any permutation leaves unchanged. But exchangeable variables need not be independent: the defining symmetry permits the kind of positive dependence we expect among related studies, where learning the effect in one study revises our belief about the others. The following lemma is the source of every example of exchangeable-but-dependent variables we shall use.
The hierarchical model is exactly the structure of Lemma 8.1 read as a generative recipe: draw a latent \(\theta\), then draw conditionally iid data. The remarkable content of de Finetti’s theorem is that, for infinite sequences, this is the only structure an exchangeable law can have. We state the binary case, which is cleanest, prove the direction we shall use, and cite the converse.
Before the formal statement, the idea in one sentence: if you genuinely cannot tell the units apart before seeing data, then they must share something, and that “something” can always be written as a single hidden parameter which, once fixed, makes the units independent and identically distributed. The hierarchical “draw \(\theta\), then draw data” recipe is therefore not one modeling option among many; for an exchangeable sequence it is forced. This is precisely the license a health researcher needs for random-effects meta-analysis: treating the study effects as a sample drawn from a population of effects is not a convenience, it is the only coherent way to encode “the trials are exchangeable.” Everything after the hidden parameter is bookkeeping.
A two-point mixing distribution makes the representation concrete and the dependence visible by hand.
For a finite meta-analysis the practical reading is this. de Finetti’s theorem is the idealized justification, stated for an infinite exchangeable population; real evidence synthesis has a finite number of studies, which we treat as exchangeable conditional on shared hyperparameters and as a sample from a conceptual population of possible studies. The infinite theorem tells us the right shape for the model (a latent population parameter with conditionally independent studies); the finite model of Definition 8.2, with its hyperprior, is that shape made operational and honest about uncertainty in the hyperparameters.
We can now define the object the theorem motivates.
Stage 2 of Definition 8.2 encodes exactly the exchangeability of the unit parameters: given \(\boldsymbol\phi\) they are iid, so unconditionally they are exchangeable by Lemma 8.1. The hyperparameter \(\boldsymbol\phi\) is what the units have in common, and the hyperprior expresses our uncertainty about it. Inference for any single \(\theta_j\) now flows through the others, because the data from all units inform \(\boldsymbol\phi\), which in turn informs each \(\theta_j\). This is the mechanism of borrowing strength, and the rest of the chapter makes it quantitative.

title: 8  Hierarchical Models, Shrinkage, and Bayesian Inference
text:
Definition 8.1 (Exchangeability) A finite collection of random variables \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) (each taking values in a measurable space \(\mathcal{S}\)) is exchangeable if for every permutation \(\sigma\) of \(\{1, \dots, n\}\), \[
(X_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, X_{\sigma(n)}) \stackrel{d}{=} (X_1, \dots, X_n),
\] that is, the two random vectors have the same joint distribution. An infinite sequence \((X_i)_{i \ge 1}\) is (infinitely) exchangeable if \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) is exchangeable for every \(n \ge 1\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. The symbol \(\stackrel{d}{=}\) means “has the same distribution as”: the two random vectors it joins are not equal value by value, but they follow the identical joint law. So exchangeability says that shuffling the labels of the variables leaves their joint distribution untouched. For an indirect comparison this is the precise version of a familiar judgment: the trials of treatment A versus B that we are about to combine are exchangeable if, before seeing any data, we have no reason to single out one trial’s true effect as larger or smaller than another’s. We are not claiming the trials are identical; we are claiming our ignorance about them is symmetric. That is exactly the state of mind in which pooling is defensible. \(\blacktriangleleft\)



Remark. A primer on the measure-theoretic words (skim once, then refer back). The next few proofs use a handful of terms from measure-theoretic probability. They make the statements airtight, but the modeling lessons survive without them, so on a first pass read the plain gloss and move on; nothing later in the chapter requires you to manipulate these objects by hand.

A density with respect to a measure generalizes “probability density.” A dominating measure \(\nu\) is the yardstick the density is measured against: Lebesgue measure (ordinary length or area) for continuous data, counting measure for discrete data. “\(f\) is a density with respect to \(\nu\)” just means probabilities are recovered by integrating \(f\) against \(\nu\), which is an ordinary integral for continuous data and a sum for discrete data.
\(\sigma\)-finite is a mild technical condition on \(\nu\) (the space is a countable union of pieces of finite measure) that every measure in this book satisfies; you may ignore it.
The product measure \(\nu^{\otimes n}\) is the yardstick for \(n\) independent coordinates at once; a joint density “with respect to \(\nu^{\otimes n}\)” is the ordinary joint density of \((x_1,\dots,x_n)\).
Integrating against a distribution \(\Pi\), written \(\int \cdots \, d\Pi(\theta)\), is averaging over a random parameter \(\theta \sim \Pi\). It is more general than \(\int \cdots f(\theta)\,d\theta\) because \(\Pi\) need not have a density (it could place point masses), but when \(\Pi\) does have a density it is the familiar weighted average.
The Radon-Nikodym theorem is the guarantee that the densities we write down exist; Tonelli’s and Fubini’s theorems are the guarantees that we may swap the order of a double integral (Tonelli for nonnegative integrands, Fubini once absolute integrability is checked). Disintegration is the formal name for “conditional density”: it is what makes \(p(x,y) = p(x \mid y)\,p(y)\) rigorous in general.
A martingale (used once, in the de Finetti converse) is a running average or running total that, on average, neither grows nor shrinks given the past; such sequences converge under mild conditions, which is why an empirical frequency settles down to a limit.
The kernel of a density is its shape as a function of the unknown, dropping any constant that does not depend on the unknown. Two densities with the same kernel are the same distribution, because the constant is forced by the requirement that the density integrate to \(1\). We use this constantly: recognizing a kernel lets us read off a posterior without computing any normalizing integral.

\(\blacktriangleleft\)


Lemma 8.1 (Mixtures of iid sequences are exchangeable) Let \(\Theta\) be a random parameter with distribution \(\Pi\) on a space \(\mathcal{T}\), and suppose that conditional on \(\Theta = \theta\) the variables \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) are iid with density \(f(\cdot \mid
\theta)\) with respect to a dominating measure \(\nu\) on \(\mathcal{S}\). Then \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) is exchangeable.


Proof. The joint density of \((X_1, \dots, X_n)\) with respect to \(\nu^{\otimes n}\) is obtained by integrating the conditional joint density against \(\Pi\): \[
p(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \int_{\mathcal{T}} \prod_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i \mid \theta) \, d\Pi(\theta).
\] For any permutation \(\sigma\), the product \(\prod_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i \mid \theta)\) is unchanged when the arguments \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) are permuted, since multiplication is commutative; this holds for every fixed \(\theta\), hence after integration \(p(x_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n)}) = p(x_1, \dots, x_n)\). Equal joint densities give equal joint distributions, so the collection is exchangeable. \(\square\)




Theorem 8.1 (de Finetti representation (binary case)) Let \((X_i)_{i \ge 1}\) be an infinitely exchangeable sequence of \(\{0,1\}\)-valued random variables. Then there is a unique probability measure \(\Pi\) on \([0,1]\) such that for every \(n\) and every \((x_1, \dots, x_n) \in \{0,1\}^n\) with \(s = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\), \[
P(X_1 = x_1, \dots, X_n = x_n) = \int_0^1 \theta^{s}(1-\theta)^{n-s} \, d\Pi(\theta).
\tag{8.1}\] Equivalently, there is a random variable \(\Theta \sim \Pi\) such that, conditional on \(\Theta = \theta\), the \(X_i\) are iid \(\mathrm{Ber}(\theta)\); moreover \(\Theta = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
X_i\) almost surely.


Proof. The direction we use in modeling, that any law of the form Equation 8.1 is exchangeable, is immediate from Lemma 8.1 with \(f(x \mid \theta) = \theta^x (1-\theta)^{1-x}\): the right side of Equation 8.1 depends on \((x_1, \dots, x_n)\) only through \(s\), which is permutation-invariant. The converse, that every infinitely exchangeable binary law admits the representation Equation 8.1 with a unique mixing measure \(\Pi\), is the substantive half of the theorem; it is proved by showing that the empirical frequencies \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\le n} X_i\) form a bounded martingale (a running average that, given the past, neither drifts up nor down) and therefore converge almost surely to a limit \(\Theta\) whose distribution is the required \(\Pi\); the hidden parameter is thus literally the long-run frequency of successes, and the finite-dimensional probabilities match Equation 8.1 in the limit. We cite this converse to the standard literature (Hewitt and Savage 1955; see the work log) rather than reproduce its measure-theoretic apparatus here. \(\square\)


Remark. The general (real-valued) de Finetti theorem of Hewitt and Savage replaces \(\mathrm{Ber}(\theta)\) by an arbitrary sampling distribution and \([0,1]\) by an abstract parameter space: an infinitely exchangeable sequence of random variables is a mixture of iid sequences. This is the precise sense in which “exchangeable units” and “conditionally iid given a latent parameter” coincide for infinite populations. Finite exchangeable sequences are only approximately of this form, which matters little for our applications because the latent parameter is the quantity of scientific interest and the number of studies, though finite, is treated as a sample from a conceptual super-population of studies. \(\blacktriangleleft\)



Example 8.2 (de Finetti with a hand calculation) Imagine binary responses from a population that is half “low responders” and half “high responders”: with probability \(\tfrac12\) the latent rate is \(\theta = 0.3\) and with probability \(\tfrac12\) it is \(\theta = 0.7\), so \(\Pi\) puts mass \(\tfrac12\) at each. Given \(\theta\), responses are iid \(\mathrm{Ber}(\theta)\). For three patients, the probability of any pattern with \(s = 2\) successes is, by Equation 8.1, \[
\int_0^1 \theta^{2}(1-\theta)^{1}\, d\Pi(\theta)
= \tfrac12\,(0.3)^2(0.7) + \tfrac12\,(0.7)^2(0.3) = \tfrac12(0.063) + \tfrac12(0.147) = 0.105.
\] The answer depends on the data only through \(s = 2\), not on which two patients responded: that is exchangeability, confirmed numerically. The variables are not independent, though. A single response has \(P(X_1 = 1) = \mathbb{E}[\theta] = \tfrac12(0.3) + \tfrac12(0.7) = 0.5\), yet two responses have \(P(X_1 = 1, X_2 = 1) = \mathbb{E}[\theta^2] = \tfrac12(0.09) + \tfrac12(0.49) = 0.29\), which exceeds \(0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25\). Seeing one success raises the chance of a second, because it nudges our belief about \(\theta\) toward \(0.7\). The hidden \(\theta\) is exactly the engine of borrowing strength: data on some units inform the others only through what they reveal about \(\theta\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)




Definition 8.2 (Bayesian hierarchical model) A two-level Bayesian hierarchical model for units \(j = 1, \dots, J\) consists of:

a sampling distribution for the data, \(y_j \mid \theta_j \sim p(y_j \mid \theta_j)\), independent across \(j\) given the unit parameters;
a population distribution (second-level prior) for the unit parameters, \(\theta_j \mid
\boldsymbol\phi \sim p(\theta_j \mid \boldsymbol\phi)\), iid across \(j\) given a hyperparameter \(\boldsymbol\phi\); and
a hyperprior \(\boldsymbol\phi \sim p(\boldsymbol\phi)\).

The joint density factors as \[
p(\mathbf y, \boldsymbol\theta, \boldsymbol\phi)
= p(\boldsymbol\phi) \prod_{j=1}^{J} p(\theta_j \mid \boldsymbol\phi)\, p(y_j \mid \theta_j),
\tag{8.2}\] where \(\boldsymbol\theta = (\theta_1, \dots, \theta_J)\) and \(\mathbf y = (y_1, \dots, y_J)\). Models with further levels (units nested in groups nested in populations) are defined by iterating the construction. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. The three stages name three different things, and keeping them apart is most of the battle. The sampling distribution (stage 1) is what each trial observed: its estimate \(y_j\) given its own true effect \(\theta_j\). The population distribution (stage 2) is what the trials share: the \(\theta_j\) are drawn from one population governed by the hyperparameter \(\boldsymbol\phi\) (for us \(\boldsymbol\phi = (\mu, \tau^2)\)). The hyperprior (stage 3) is our uncertainty about that shared population before any data. In one line: stage 1 is observed, the \(\theta_j\) are latent, and \(\boldsymbol\phi\) is shared. This is the skeleton of every Bayesian network meta-analysis in Part III, where the unit parameters are study-level treatment contrasts and the shared \(\boldsymbol\phi\) is the pooled effect plus the heterogeneity. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 8  Hierarchical Models, Shrinkage, and Bayesian Inference
section: 8.2 The normal-normal model: random effects versus fixed effects
text:
8.2 The normal-normal model: random effects versus fixed effects
The canonical instance of Definition 8.2, and the workhorse of meta-analysis, is Gaussian at both levels. Suppose study \(j\) reports an effect estimate \(y_j\) (for concreteness, a log odds ratio) together with its standard error, so that the within-study sampling variance \(s_j^2\) is known to good approximation. The two-level model is \[
y_j \mid \theta_j \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_j, s_j^2), \qquad
\theta_j \mid \mu, \tau^2 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \tau^2), \qquad j = 1, \dots, J,
\tag{8.3}\] with hyperparameters \(\boldsymbol\phi = (\mu, \tau^2)\). Here \(\theta_j\) is the true effect in study \(j\), \(\mu\) is the population mean effect, and \(\tau^2\) is the between-study variance that measures heterogeneity. The distinction between the two ways of reading \(\theta_j\) is the distinction between fixed and random effects.
The same five objects, read in the language of the running example of Example 8.1, are the following.









Object
Symbol
Trial 1 value
Reading




observed estimate
\(y_j\)
\(0.0\)
what trial \(j\) reported (a log OR)


standard error
\(s_j\)
\(0.5\)
how precise that report is


within-study variance
\(s_j^2\)
\(0.25\)
squared standard error, treated as known


true study effect
\(\theta_j\)
unknown
what trial \(j\) would report with infinite data


population mean
\(\mu\)
unknown
the average true effect across trials


heterogeneity
\(\tau^2\)
unknown
how widely the \(\theta_j\) scatter around \(\mu\)



A feel for \(\tau^2\) is worth having now, because it governs everything downstream. On the log-OR scale a between-study standard deviation \(\tau = 0.5\) (so \(\tau^2 = 0.25\)) means a typical trial’s true effect lies within roughly \(\pm 1\) of \(\mu\) on the log-OR scale, that is, within a factor of about \(e^{\pm 1} \approx (0.37,\, 2.7)\) on the odds-ratio scale: real, substantial heterogeneity. A value such as \(\tau^2 = 0.01\) (\(\tau = 0.1\)) would mean the trials nearly agree, and \(\tau^2 \to 0\) would force them to share one true effect. The whole job of Section 8.6 is to let the data estimate this number rather than guess it.

Definition 8.3 (Fixed effects and random effects) In a model with unit parameters \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_J\) for the data \(y_j \mid \theta_j \sim p(y_j
\mid \theta_j)\):

the parameters are fixed effects if they are treated as unrelated unknown constants, each estimated only from its own unit (formally, the joint model places no second-level distribution linking them, so inference for \(\theta_j\) uses \(y_j\) alone); and
the parameters are random effects if they are modeled as an exchangeable sample from a common population distribution \(\theta_j \mid \boldsymbol\phi \sim p(\cdot \mid \boldsymbol\phi)\), so that information is shared across units through the common hyperparameter \(\boldsymbol\phi\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)



Remark. A terminology warning you will be glad to have. The words “fixed” and “random effects” mean different things in different fields, and meta-analysis is the worst trap. In regression and mixed-model language, which Definition 8.3 follows, fixed effects are unrelated unknown constants estimated each from its own unit (no link, the \(\tau^2 \to \infty\) extreme). But in meta-analysis software (RevMan, the R package metafor) a fixed-effect model, increasingly called a common-effect model, means the opposite extreme: there is one single true effect shared by every study, \(\theta_1 = \dots = \theta_J =
\mu\), which is complete pooling, the \(\tau^2 \to 0\) case. So the meta-analysis “fixed-effect model” is this chapter’s complete pooling, not its fixed effects. The table reconciles the three usages.








Term (and field)
Meaning here
Limit




fixed effects (regression, mixed models)
unrelated unknown constants, each from its own unit
\(\tau^2 \to \infty\) (no link)


fixed-effect or common-effect model (meta-analysis)
one shared true effect \(\theta_1 = \dots = \theta_J = \mu\)
\(\tau^2 = 0\) (complete pooling)


random-effects model (both fields)
true effects are an exchangeable sample from a population
\(0 < \tau^2 < \infty\) (partial pooling)



The practical choice is simple to state. If you believe every trial estimates the same underlying drug effect, the common-effect (meta-analysis “fixed-effect”) model is appropriate. If you believe each trial has its own true effect drawn from a population of trial effects, use random effects. The random-effects model of Equation 8.3 contains both beliefs as the extremes \(\tau^2 = 0\) and \(\tau^2 \to \infty\), and lets the data choose where between them to sit. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The two readings are genuinely different probability models, and the difference is visible in the marginal law of the data. Under fixed effects the \(y_j\) are independent with means \(\theta_j\) that bear no stated relation. Under random effects, integrating out \(\theta_j\) in Equation 8.3 gives a marginal model in which every observation carries information about the shared \((\mu, \tau^2)\), hence about every other unit; we compute that marginal in Proposition 8.2. The fixed-effects analysis is the \(\tau^2 \to \infty\) limit of the random-effects analysis (an improper flat population that links nothing), and the complete-pooling analysis \(\theta_1 = \dots = \theta_J = \mu\) is the \(\tau^2 \to 0\) limit (a degenerate population that forces equality). The random-effects model contains both as extreme cases and lets the data choose where between them to sit, by estimating \(\tau^2\). Three estimators of the study effects correspond to the three regimes: \[
\underbrace{\hat\theta_j = y_j}_{\text{no pooling}\;(\tau^2 = \infty)}, \qquad
\underbrace{\hat\theta_j = \bar y_w}_{\text{complete pooling}\;(\tau^2 = 0)}, \qquad
\underbrace{\hat\theta_j = \text{posterior mean}}_{\text{partial pooling}\;(0 < \tau^2 < \infty)},
\] where \(\bar y_w\) is a precision-weighted average. To compute the partial-pooling estimator we need Bayes’ theorem and the normal-normal conjugate update, which we now develop in general before returning to specialize them in Section 8.5.

title: 8  Hierarchical Models, Shrinkage, and Bayesian Inference
text:
8.3 Bayes’ theorem for parameters
Bayesian inference treats the parameter as a random variable, assigns it a prior distribution, and updates that distribution by conditioning on the data. The update is Bayes’ theorem. Five distributions recur from here on; they are worth fixing in a table before any algebra.








Distribution
Symbol
The question it answers




prior
\(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi)\)
what we believe about the parameter before data


likelihood
\(p(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol\xi)\)
how probable the observed data are for each parameter value


posterior
\(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathbf y)\)
what we believe about the parameter after data


marginal likelihood
\(p(\mathbf y)\)
how probable the data are overall, averaging the likelihood over the prior


posterior predictive
\(p(\tilde{\mathbf y} \mid \mathbf y)\)
what future data should look like, given the data so far



The working content of Bayes’ theorem is a single proportionality, posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior, and it needs nothing measure-theoretic. The simplest possible instance uses pure arithmetic.

Example 8.3 (A one-line Bayes update with no calculus) Before a trial we entertain just two possibilities for a treatment’s true response probability: a “modest” rate \(p = 0.3\) and a “strong” rate \(p = 0.6\), judged equally likely, so the prior is \(\pi(0.3) = \pi(0.6) = 0.5\). One patient is treated and responds (\(y = 1\)). The likelihood of this datum is \(p(y = 1 \mid p) = p\), so by posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior, \[
\pi(0.3 \mid y) \propto 0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.15, \qquad \pi(0.6 \mid y) \propto 0.6 \times 0.5 = 0.30.
\] Normalizing so the two add to \(1\) (dividing by \(0.15 + 0.30 = 0.45\)) gives \(\pi(0.3 \mid y) = \tfrac13\) and \(\pi(0.6 \mid y) = \tfrac23\). The single success has shifted belief from \(50{:}50\) toward the stronger rate, exactly as intuition demands, and the only operation was “multiply, then rescale to sum to one.” Bayes’ theorem below is this same recipe with a sum replaced by an integral. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The theorem states the recipe in full generality, for parameters living in continuous spaces where the “rescale to one” step is an integral and densities must be handled with care. Its content is interpretive and computational, not analytical: in practice you use the proportional form above. The proof that follows is the measure-theoretic guarantee that the proportional form is legitimate even when the parameter has no density in the elementary sense; a reader meeting measure theory for the first time may take the boxed primer on faith and skim the proof, losing nothing needed for the rest of the chapter.

Theorem 8.2 (Bayes’ theorem (densities)) Let \(\boldsymbol\xi\) take values in a measurable space \((\Xi, \mathcal{G})\) with prior density \(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi)\) with respect to a \(\sigma\)-finite dominating measure \(\mu\), and let the data \(\mathbf y\) take values in \((\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{B})\) with conditional density \(p(\mathbf y \mid
\boldsymbol\xi)\) with respect to a \(\sigma\)-finite measure \(\nu\). Define the marginal likelihood \[
p(\mathbf y) = \int_{\Xi} p(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol\xi)\, \pi(\boldsymbol\xi) \, d\mu(\boldsymbol\xi).
\] Then for every \(\mathbf y\) with \(p(\mathbf y) > 0\), a version of the posterior density of \(\boldsymbol\xi\) given \(\mathbf y\) (with respect to \(\mu\)) is \[
\pi(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathbf y) = \frac{p(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol\xi)\, \pi(\boldsymbol\xi)}{p(\mathbf y)}.
\tag{8.4}\]


Proof. By construction the pair \((\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf y)\) has joint density \(p(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf y) =
p(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol\xi)\,\pi(\boldsymbol\xi)\) with respect to the product measure \(\mu \otimes
\nu\); the existence of these densities is the Radon-Nikodym theorem applied to the assumed dominated families. The marginal density of \(\mathbf y\) is \(p(\mathbf y) = \int_\Xi p(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf y)\,
d\mu(\boldsymbol\xi)\), by Tonelli’s theorem applied to the nonnegative integrand. Fix \(\mathbf y\) with \(p(\mathbf y) > 0\) and let \(g\) denote the right side of Equation 8.4, a nonnegative function of \(\boldsymbol\xi\) with \(\int_\Xi g\, d\mu = p(\mathbf y)/p(\mathbf y) = 1\), hence a probability density with respect to \(\mu\). To see that \(g(\cdot \mid \mathbf y)\) is a version of the conditional density, we verify the defining disintegration property: for every bounded measurable \(h: \Xi \to \mathbb{R}\) and every \(B \in \mathcal{B}\), \[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[h(\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathbf 1_B(\mathbf y)\right]
= \int_B \left( \int_\Xi h(\boldsymbol\xi)\, g(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathbf y)\, d\mu(\boldsymbol\xi) \right) p(\mathbf y)\, d\nu(\mathbf y).
\] Indeed, writing the left side through the joint density and substituting \(p(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf y) =
g(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathbf y)\, p(\mathbf y)\), \[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[h(\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathbf 1_B(\mathbf y)\right]
= \int_B \int_\Xi h(\boldsymbol\xi)\, p(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf y)\, d\mu(\boldsymbol\xi)\, d\nu(\mathbf y)
= \int_B \int_\Xi h(\boldsymbol\xi)\, g(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathbf y)\, p(\mathbf y)\, d\mu(\boldsymbol\xi)\, d\nu(\mathbf y),
\] which is the asserted identity by Fubini’s theorem (the integrand is \(\nu \otimes \mu\)-integrable since \(h\) is bounded and \(p(\boldsymbol\xi,\mathbf y)\) integrates to \(1\)). The disintegration identity characterizes the conditional density up to \(\mu\)-null sets, so \(g(\cdot \mid \mathbf y) =
\pi(\cdot \mid \mathbf y)\) is the posterior density. \(\square\)


Remark. Three points organize everything that follows. First, the denominator \(p(\mathbf y)\) does not depend on \(\boldsymbol\xi\), so up to a normalizing constant Equation 8.4 reads “posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior,” and every method that needs only the shape of the posterior (conjugate updating, Markov chain Monte Carlo) can ignore \(p(\mathbf y)\). Second, the same \(p(\mathbf y)\) is the central object of model comparison (Section 8.10), where its dependence on the model, not on \(\boldsymbol\xi\), is exactly the point. Third, Bayes’ theorem is a statement about densities; its use is a modeling decision, namely to regard \(\boldsymbol\xi\) as random and to report \(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi \mid
\mathbf y)\) as the inference. (Corresponds to L.1 in the proof catalogue.) \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why this matters. Every Bayesian network meta-analysis in this book is this one update applied to study-level treatment contrasts: a prior on the pooled effects and heterogeneity, a binomial or normal likelihood from the trials, and a posterior that the software reports. The proportional form posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior is all that the Markov chain Monte Carlo of Section 8.8 ever needs, because the unknown constant \(p(\mathbf y)\) cancels in every ratio it computes. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 8  Hierarchical Models, Shrinkage, and Bayesian Inference
text:
8.4 Conjugate analysis
A prior family is conjugate to a likelihood when the posterior stays in the family, with updated hyperparameters. Conjugacy turns Equation 8.4 into algebra, gives closed-form posteriors that we can read and check, and supplies the building blocks of both the shrinkage estimator and the Gibbs updates inside samplers. We prove the two pairs we use in full and state the third.

8.4.1 Normal-normal conjugacy

Theorem 8.3 (Normal-normal conjugacy) Let \(y \mid \theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma^2 > 0\) known, and let the prior be \(\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \tau_0^2)\). Then the posterior is \[
\theta \mid y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \tau_1^2), \qquad
\frac{1}{\tau_1^2} = \frac{1}{\tau_0^2} + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}, \qquad
\mu_1 = \tau_1^2 \left( \frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2} + \frac{y}{\sigma^2} \right).
\tag{8.5}\] If instead we observe an iid sample \(y_1, \dots, y_n \mid \theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, \sigma^2)\), the same conclusion holds with \(y\) replaced by \(\bar y = \frac1n \sum_i y_i\) and \(\sigma^2\) replaced by \(\sigma^2/n\), so that \(\tau_1^{-2} = \tau_0^{-2} + n\sigma^{-2}\).


Proof. By Bayes’ theorem in proportional form (Theorem 8.2), the posterior density is proportional in \(\theta\) to the product of the likelihood and the prior: \[
\pi(\theta \mid y) \propto \exp\!\left(-\frac{(y - \theta)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
\exp\!\left(-\frac{(\theta - \mu_0)^2}{2\tau_0^2}\right)
= \exp\!\left(-\frac12 Q(\theta)\right),
\] where, collecting the two quadratics, \[
Q(\theta) = \frac{(\theta - y)^2}{\sigma^2} + \frac{(\theta - \mu_0)^2}{\tau_0^2}
= \left(\frac{1}{\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{\tau_0^2}\right)\theta^2
- 2\theta\left(\frac{y}{\sigma^2} + \frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2}\right) + \text{const}.
\] Write \(\tau_1^{-2} = \sigma^{-2} + \tau_0^{-2}\) for the coefficient of \(\theta^2\) and \(\mu_1 = \tau_1^2(
y\sigma^{-2} + \mu_0\tau_0^{-2})\). Completing the square, \[
Q(\theta) = \frac{1}{\tau_1^2}\bigl(\theta^2 - 2\theta\mu_1\bigr) + \text{const}
= \frac{(\theta - \mu_1)^2}{\tau_1^2} + \text{const},
\] where the constant absorbs all terms free of \(\theta\). Hence \(\pi(\theta \mid y) \propto \exp(-(\theta -
\mu_1)^2/(2\tau_1^2))\), which is the kernel of the \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \tau_1^2)\) density; since a density is determined by its kernel (Proposition 4.2), the posterior is \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \tau_1^2)\). For the iid sample, the likelihood factor is \(\prod_i \exp(-(y_i - \theta)^2/(2\sigma^2)) =
\exp(-\sum_i (y_i - \theta)^2/(2\sigma^2))\), and \(\sum_i (y_i - \theta)^2 = n(\bar y - \theta)^2 +
\sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2\); the second term is free of \(\theta\), so the sample enters exactly as a single observation \(\bar y\) with variance \(\sigma^2/n\). \(\square\)


Remark. Equation Equation 8.5 is the rule “precisions add, and the posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of prior mean and data.” Writing the precision \(\tau_1^{-2}\) as the sum of the prior precision \(\tau_0^{-2}\) and the data precision \(\sigma^{-2}\) makes the update additive in information, and exhibits the posterior mean \(\mu_1 = (\tau_0^{-2}\mu_0 + \sigma^{-2} y)/(\tau_0^{-2} +
\sigma^{-2})\) as a weighted average with weights proportional to those precisions. This is the analytic heart of shrinkage. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why this matters. This single update is what a Bayesian network meta-analysis performs for each study-level treatment contrast: the prior mean \(\mu_0\) is the pooled effect, the datum \(y\) is one trial’s log odds ratio, and the posterior mean \(\mu_1\) is that trial’s shrunken contrast. Read the update with \(\mu_0\) as the network’s pooled effect and you are looking at the engine of Part III. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The same computation runs in any dimension and is the bridge to the multivariate normal of Chapter 4. We need the multivariate version because a network meta-analysis estimates a whole vector of pooled contrasts at once (treatment \(B\) versus \(A\), \(C\) versus \(A\), and so on), correlated through the studies they share; the update below is the joint version of the scalar shrinkage above, applied to that vector of effects.

Corollary 8.1 (Multivariate normal-normal conjugacy) Let \(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol\theta \sim \mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol\theta, \boldsymbol\Sigma)\) with \(\boldsymbol\Sigma \succ 0\) known, and let \(\boldsymbol\theta \sim \mathcal{N}_p(\mathbf m_0,
\boldsymbol\Omega_0)\) with \(\boldsymbol\Omega_0 \succ 0\). Then \[
\boldsymbol\theta \mid \mathbf y \sim \mathcal{N}_p(\mathbf m_1, \boldsymbol\Omega_1), \qquad
\boldsymbol\Omega_1^{-1} = \boldsymbol\Omega_0^{-1} + \boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}, \qquad
\mathbf m_1 = \boldsymbol\Omega_1\bigl(\boldsymbol\Omega_0^{-1}\mathbf m_0 + \boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf y\bigr).
\]


Proof. The posterior is proportional in \(\boldsymbol\theta\) to \(\exp(-\tfrac12 Q(\boldsymbol\theta))\) with \[
Q(\boldsymbol\theta) = (\mathbf y - \boldsymbol\theta)^\top \boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf y - \boldsymbol\theta)
+ (\boldsymbol\theta - \mathbf m_0)^\top \boldsymbol\Omega_0^{-1}(\boldsymbol\theta - \mathbf m_0)
= \boldsymbol\theta^\top \boldsymbol\Omega_1^{-1}\boldsymbol\theta - 2\boldsymbol\theta^\top
\bigl(\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf y + \boldsymbol\Omega_0^{-1}\mathbf m_0\bigr) + \text{const},
\] using symmetry of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\) and \(\boldsymbol\Omega_0^{-1}\) to combine the cross terms. The matrix \(\boldsymbol\Omega_1^{-1} = \boldsymbol\Omega_0^{-1} + \boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\) is the sum of two positive definite matrices, hence positive definite and invertible (Theorem 3.3), so \(\boldsymbol\Omega_1\) is well defined and \(\succ 0\). With \(\mathbf m_1 = \boldsymbol\Omega_1(
\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf y + \boldsymbol\Omega_0^{-1}\mathbf m_0)\), completing the square in the \(\boldsymbol\Omega_1^{-1}\) quadratic form (Definition 3.6) gives \(Q(\boldsymbol\theta) =
(\boldsymbol\theta - \mathbf m_1)^\top \boldsymbol\Omega_1^{-1}(\boldsymbol\theta - \mathbf m_1) +
\text{const}\), the kernel of \(\mathcal{N}_p(\mathbf m_1, \boldsymbol\Omega_1)\). \(\square\)


Remark. The same posterior can be read off without algebra by stacking \((\boldsymbol\theta, \mathbf y)\) into a joint Gaussian and applying the conditioning formula Theorem 4.15: with \(\boldsymbol\theta \sim
\mathcal{N}_p(\mathbf m_0, \boldsymbol\Omega_0)\) and \(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol\theta \sim
\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol\theta, \boldsymbol\Sigma)\), the pair is jointly normal, and the conditional of \(\boldsymbol\theta\) given \(\mathbf y\) is normal with the stated mean and covariance. The two routes agree, which is a useful check on Theorem 4.15. \(\blacktriangleleft\)



8.4.2 Beta-binomial conjugacy

Theorem 8.4 (Beta-binomial conjugacy) Let \(y \mid p \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n, p)\) and let the prior be \(p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b)\) with \(a, b > 0\). Then \[
p \mid y \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a + y, \, b + n - y),
\tag{8.6}\] and the posterior mean is the convex combination \[
\mathbb{E}[p \mid y] = \frac{a + y}{a + b + n}
= \frac{a + b}{a + b + n}\cdot \frac{a}{a + b} + \frac{n}{a + b + n}\cdot \frac{y}{n}.
\]


Proof. The likelihood is \(p(y \mid p) = \binom{n}{y} p^y (1 - p)^{n - y} \propto p^y (1 - p)^{n - y}\) as a function of \(p\), and the prior density is \(\pi(p) = \frac{1}{B(a,b)} p^{a-1}(1 - p)^{b-1} \propto
p^{a-1}(1 - p)^{b-1}\) on \((0,1)\), where \(B(a,b) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b)\) is the beta function. By Theorem 8.2, \[
\pi(p \mid y) \propto p^{y}(1 - p)^{n - y} \cdot p^{a-1}(1 - p)^{b-1}
= p^{(a + y) - 1}(1 - p)^{(b + n - y) - 1},
\] which is the kernel of the \(\mathrm{Beta}(a + y, b + n - y)\) density. A density is determined by its kernel and its total mass \(1\); the unique normalizing constant making the displayed kernel integrate to \(1\) is \(1/B(a + y, b + n - y)\), so the posterior is \(\mathrm{Beta}(a + y, b + n - y)\). The mean of a \(\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)\) variable is \(\alpha/(\alpha + \beta)\); substituting \(\alpha = a + y\) and \(\beta = b + n - y\) gives \((a + y)/(a + b + n)\), and splitting the numerator as \(a + y\) and writing the denominator as \((a + b) + n\) produces the stated convex combination of the prior mean \(a/(a+b)\) and the maximum likelihood estimate \(y/n\). \(\square\)


Remark. The posterior mean again shrinks the data estimate \(y/n\) toward the prior mean \(a/(a + b)\), with weight \(n/(a + b + n)\) on the data growing to \(1\) as \(n \to \infty\). The hyperparameters \(a\) and \(b\) act as prior “pseudo-counts” of successes and failures; this is the discrete-data analogue of the precision-weighting in Equation 8.5. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

A number makes the update tangible, and event counts are the data a health researcher actually holds.

Example 8.4 (A treatment-response update by hand) One trial arm treats \(n = 8\) patients and \(y = 7\) respond, a raw response rate of \(7/8 = 0.875\). Before the trial we hold a weakly informative prior \(p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(2, 2)\), centered at \(0.5\) and worth two pseudo-successes and two pseudo-failures. By Theorem 8.4 the posterior is \[
p \mid y \sim \mathrm{Beta}(2 + 7, \; 2 + 1) = \mathrm{Beta}(9, 3),
\] with posterior mean \(9/12 = 0.75\). The observed \(0.875\) has been pulled toward the prior mean \(0.5\); the pull is exactly the “four prior pseudo-patients out of twelve total” weight, \(4/12 = \tfrac13\) toward \(0.5\) and \(8/12 = \tfrac23\) toward the data. Only two integers changed, \(a \mapsto a + y\) and \(b \mapsto
b + (n - y)\): Bayesian updating with event counts is bookkeeping on responders and non-responders. \(\blacktriangleleft\)



8.4.3 Gamma-Poisson conjugacy
We state the third standard pair, with its one-line proof, for completeness; it is the conjugate analysis behind count-data meta-analysis.

Proposition 8.1 (Gamma-Poisson conjugacy) Let \(y_1, \dots, y_n \mid \lambda \sim \mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\) iid, and let \(\lambda \sim
\mathrm{Gamma}(a, b)\) with shape \(a > 0\) and rate \(b > 0\) (so \(\mathbb{E}[\lambda] = a/b\)). Then \[
\lambda \mid \mathbf y \sim \mathrm{Gamma}\!\left(a + \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n y_i, \; b + n\right).
\]


Proof. The likelihood is \(\prod_i e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{y_i}/y_i! \propto \lambda^{\sum_i y_i} e^{-n\lambda}\), and the prior density is \(\propto \lambda^{a-1} e^{-b\lambda}\) on \(\lambda > 0\). Their product is \(\propto \lambda^{(a + \sum_i y_i) - 1} e^{-(b + n)\lambda}\), the kernel of \(\mathrm{Gamma}(a + \sum_i
y_i, \, b + n)\). \(\square\)
