title: 12  Transportability: The Estimand-Based Theory
section: 12.7 Why a shared effect modifier assumption is not enough
text:
12.7 Why a shared effect modifier assumption is not enough
For a non-collapsible measure the cancellation of Theorem 12.5 happens on the linear-predictor scale but does not survive the passage to the margin, because marginalization and the link do not commute. The result is that the marginal odds ratio, even with SEMA and alignment in force and the conditional odds ratio held perfectly constant, drifts with the covariate distribution. This is catalogue result N.11, the insufficiency of SEMA, and it rests on the strict convexity that defines non-collapsibility.

Theorem 12.6 (SEMA and alignment are sufficient if and only if the measure is collapsible) Consider the anchored model Equation 12.10 under SEMA Equation 12.11 and scale alignment \(h=g\), so that the conditional active versus active contrast is the constant \(c=\gamma_B-\gamma_C\) (Theorem 12.4(i)). The marginal active versus active effect \(d_{BC(\mathcal P)}\) is directly transportable across all populations if and only if the effect measure is collapsible on scale \(g\).
In particular, for the odds ratio (logit link) and the hazard ratio (log-hazard link), which are non-collapsible (Theorem 11.2), the marginal effect is not directly transportable under SEMA and alignment: there exist populations \(\mathcal P_1\ne\mathcal P_2\) with \(d_{BC(\mathcal P_1)}\ne d_{BC(\mathcal P_2)}\). Concretely, when the conditional log odds ratio is the nonzero constant \(c\) and the reference risk \(\mu_C(X)\) is non-degenerate, the marginal log odds ratio is strictly attenuated, \[
0<\big|\,\mathrm{logit}\,m_B(\mathcal P)-\mathrm{logit}\,m_C(\mathcal P)\,\big|<|c|,
\tag{12.14}\] and its value depends on the distribution of \(\mu_C(X)\).

Reader translation. The odds ratio is a curved (nonlinear) summary of risks. Averaging risks across a population and then forming the odds ratio is not the same as forming the odds ratio in each stratum and then averaging; the curvature opens a gap, and the size of the gap depends on how spread out the risks are, which is a property of the population. So even with the conditional odds ratio pinned to a constant, the marginal odds ratio drifts as the covariate distribution changes. The proof turns this into an exact strict inequality using Jensen’s inequality.

Proof. Sufficiency (collapsible \(\Rightarrow\) transportable). This is Theorem 12.5: with the conditional contrast constant at \(c\) and the measure collapsible, \(d_{BC(\mathcal P)}=c\) for every \(\mathcal P\).
Necessity (non-collapsible \(\Rightarrow\) not transportable), shown for the odds ratio. Work on the logit scale, \(g=h=\mathrm{logit}\). SEMA and alignment give a constant conditional log odds ratio \(\mathrm{logit}\,\mu_B(x)-\mathrm{logit}\,\mu_C(x)=c\) for all \(x\), equivalently \[
\mu_B(x)=\varphi\big(\mu_C(x)\big),\qquad \varphi(p):=\mathrm{expit}\big(\mathrm{logit}\,p+c\big)=\frac{e^{c}p}{1+(e^{c}-1)p},
\] the map that adds \(c\) on the logit scale. We show \(\varphi\) is strictly concave on \((0,1)\) when \(c>0\). Writing \(k=e^{c}>1\), \(\varphi(p)=kp/(1+(k-1)p)\), so \[
\varphi'(p)=\frac{k}{\big(1+(k-1)p\big)^{2}}>0,\qquad
\varphi''(p)=\frac{-2k(k-1)}{\big(1+(k-1)p\big)^{3}}<0,
\] since \(k>1\) makes the numerator of \(\varphi''\) negative and the denominator positive on \((0,1)\). Thus \(\varphi\) is strictly increasing and strictly concave. Now compute the marginal means. With \(m_C=\mathbb E_{X\sim\mathcal P}[\mu_C(X)]\) and \(m_B=\mathbb E_{X\sim\mathcal P}[\mu_B(X)]
=\mathbb E_{X\sim\mathcal P}[\varphi(\mu_C(X))]\), strict Jensen’s inequality (Theorem 4.6) applied to the strictly concave \(\varphi\) and the non-degenerate random variable \(\mu_C(X)\) gives a strict inequality \[
m_B=\mathbb E\big[\varphi(\mu_C(X))\big]<\varphi\big(\mathbb E[\mu_C(X)]\big)=\varphi(m_C)=\mathrm{expit}\big(\mathrm{logit}\,m_C+c\big).
\] Applying the strictly increasing logit to both sides, \(\mathrm{logit}\,m_B<\mathrm{logit}\,m_C+c\), that is, the marginal log odds ratio satisfies \(\mathrm{logit}\,m_B-\mathrm{logit}\,m_C<c\). For the lower bound, \(c>0\) and \(\varphi(p)>p\) on \((0,1)\) give \(m_B=\mathbb E[\varphi(\mu_C(X))]>\mathbb E[\mu_C(X)]=m_C\), hence \(\mathrm{logit}\,m_B>\mathrm{logit}\,m_C\) and the marginal log odds ratio is positive. Together these are the strict attenuation Equation 12.14 (the case \(c<0\) is symmetric, with \(\varphi\) strictly convex).
Finally, the marginal log odds ratio depends on the covariate distribution. Take \(\mathcal P_1\) degenerate at a single covariate value \(x_0\): then \(\mu_C(X)=\mu_C(x_0)\) is constant, Jensen holds with equality, and \(\mathrm{logit}\,m_B-\mathrm{logit}\,m_C=c\). Take \(\mathcal P_2\) any non-degenerate distribution of \(\mu_C(X)\): then the strict inequality gives \(\mathrm{logit}\,m_B-\mathrm{logit}\,m_C<c\). Hence \(d_{BC(\mathcal P_1)}=c\ne d_{BC(\mathcal P_2)}\), so \(d_{BC}\) is not directly transportable, proving necessity for the odds ratio. The hazard ratio is non-collapsible by the same mechanism, with the mixture-of-survival argument of Theorem 11.2 playing the role of strict Jensen; we do not repeat it. \(\square\)

Why this matters. This is why two HTA submissions built on the very same trials can report different odds ratios and both be correct: SEMA makes the conditional odds ratio portable, but HTA usually reports the marginal odds ratio, and that one is not portable. The attenuation formula Equation 12.14 is not a rounding artifact; it is structural, and it says the reported number belongs to the population it was averaged in.
Why prove necessity, not just show an example? A single counterexample would establish only that the marginal odds ratio can fail to transport. Necessity says something stronger: under SEMA and alignment, for a non-collapsible measure there is no configuration, no clever choice of constants, that rescues marginal transport, because the obstruction is the curvature of \(\varphi\) itself, which SEMA cannot touch. That is the difference between “sometimes fails” and “must fail,” and it is why the result is stated as an if and only if.
The proof locates the obstruction precisely. The strict concavity of the logit-shift map \(\varphi\) is the analytic essence of odds-ratio non-collapsibility, and it is what forces a strict Jensen gap between the marginal mean \(m_B\) and the value \(\varphi(m_C)\) that a collapsible measure would have produced. The size of that gap is governed by the spread of \(\mu_C(X)\), which is a property of the covariate distribution, so the marginal log odds ratio is a function of the population. There is no choice of \(c\), no shared effect modifier structure, that removes the curvature of \(\varphi\). SEMA controls the conditional effect; it has no purchase on the marginalization.
Collecting Theorem 12.5, Corollary 12.1, and Theorem 12.6 gives the clean characterization, catalogue results N.8 to N.10.

Proposition 12.1 (Transportability of common effect measures under SEMA) Assume SEMA and structural invariance. For each effect measure below, with its natural model link, the conditional active versus active effect is directly transportable when SEMA and scale alignment hold, and the marginal active versus active effect is directly transportable when in addition the measure is collapsible. Proof. Each row is an instance of the three theorems. A “yes” in the conditional column is Corollary 12.1, valid whenever the measure is scale aligned (so that SEMA makes the conditional contrast constant). A “yes” in the marginal column additionally requires collapsibility, by Theorem 12.5; a “no” in the marginal column with alignment present is the non-collapsibility obstruction of Theorem 12.6 (odds ratio, hazard ratio rows). Why this matters. This one table is the chapter’s practical output: for any effect measure it tells you whether you may carry the number to a new population unchanged. The two rows HTA cares about most, the log odds ratio and the log hazard ratio, sit in the “no” column for marginal transport. Read the table before trusting any indirect-comparison number that has crossed populations.
The table exhibits the paradox in its starkest form. The mean difference, risk ratio, and rate ratio, all collapsible and naturally aligned, transport both conditionally and marginally under SEMA. The log odds ratio and log hazard ratio, the two effect measures that dominate HTA, transport conditionally under SEMA but not marginally, because non-collapsibility breaks the third condition. And a risk difference computed from a logistic model, or a restricted mean survival time computed from a proportional-hazards model, fails to transport at all, because scale misalignment breaks the first. The measures we report most are the measures that travel least.

title: 12  Transportability: The Estimand-Based Theory
text:
12.8 Worked examples
We exhibit all three phenomena with a single covariate structure, a binary effect modifier \(X\in\{0,1\}\) distributed differently in two populations, \(\mathcal P_1\) with \(P(X=1)=0.1\) and \(\mathcal P_2\) with \(P(X=1)=0.9\). In every example SEMA holds and the scales are arranged so that the conditional active versus active effect, \(B\) versus \(C\), is constant across \(x\). The question is whether the marginal effect is the same in \(\mathcal P_1\) and \(\mathcal P_2\). The continuous case says yes; the binary and survival cases say no, for the two distinct reasons of Theorem 12.6 and Theorem 12.4(ii).

12.8.1 Continuous outcome: the mean difference transports
Let the outcome be continuous with an identity-link model and a binary effect modifier. Take conditional means under the comparator \(C\) equal to \(\mu_C(0)=2\), \(\mu_C(1)=7\), and a constant active versus active benefit of \(\gamma_B-\gamma_C=3\) on the identity scale, so \(\mu_B(x)=\mu_C(x)+3\), giving \(\mu_B(0)=5\), \(\mu_B(1)=10\). SEMA holds because the active versus active contrast carries no interaction; the conditional mean difference is \(d_{BC}(x)=\mu_B(x)-\mu_C(x)=3\) for both \(x\). The identity scale is aligned and collapsible, so Theorem 12.5 predicts the marginal mean difference equals \(3\) in every population. Verify by hand. In \(\mathcal P_1\), \[
m_C(\mathcal P_1)=0.9(2)+0.1(7)=2.5,\quad m_B(\mathcal P_1)=0.9(5)+0.1(10)=5.5,\quad d_{BC(\mathcal P_1)}=5.5-2.5=3.
\] In \(\mathcal P_2\), \[
m_C(\mathcal P_2)=0.1(2)+0.9(7)=6.5,\quad m_B(\mathcal P_2)=0.1(5)+0.9(10)=9.5,\quad d_{BC(\mathcal P_2)}=9.5-6.5=3.
\] The marginal mean difference is \(3\) in both populations, as it must be, since \(d_{BC(\mathcal P)}=\mathbb E_{\mathcal P}[\mu_B(X)-\mu_C(X)]=\mathbb E_{\mathcal P}[3]=3\) for any covariate distribution. The collapsible aligned measure transports.
What a researcher would report. The mean difference is \(3\) units, and it is the same \(3\) in the index population \(f_{AB}\), the comparator population \(f_{AC}\), and the decision population \(\mathcal P^{*}\). For this collapsible, aligned measure the analyst can report a single number and attach it to any of the three populations without qualification; nothing goes wrong when it is carried to the decision population. This is the best case, and it is why mean differences and risk ratios are the easy measures for indirect comparison.


12.8.2 Binary outcome: the marginal odds ratio does not transport
Keep the same binary \(X\) and the same two populations, but now a binary outcome with a logit-link model. On the logit scale set the comparator linear predictors \(\eta_C(0)=-3\), \(\eta_C(1)=3\) (a strong prognostic gradient: the covariate raises the log-odds by \(6\)), and a constant active versus active log odds ratio \(c=\gamma_B-\gamma_C=2\), so \(\eta_B(x)=\eta_C(x)+2\), giving \(\eta_B(0)=-1\), \(\eta_B(1)=5\). SEMA holds and the logit scale is aligned, so the conditional log odds ratio is the constant \(c=2\), an odds ratio of \(e^{2}=7.389\), at both covariate values. The risks \(\mu_k(x)=\mathrm{expit}(\eta_k(x))\) are \[
\mu_C(0)=0.047426,\quad \mu_C(1)=0.952574,\quad \mu_B(0)=0.268941,\quad \mu_B(1)=0.993307,
\] each \(\mathrm{expit}(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\) computed to six places. Now marginalize. In \(\mathcal P_1\), \(P(X=1)=0.1\): \[
m_C(\mathcal P_1)=0.9(0.047426)+0.1(0.952574)=0.137941,\qquad
m_B(\mathcal P_1)=0.9(0.268941)+0.1(0.993307)=0.341378.
\] The marginal log odds ratio is \[
d_{BC(\mathcal P_1)}=\mathrm{logit}(0.341378)-\mathrm{logit}(0.137941)=(-0.65716)-(-1.83250)=1.17534,
\] a marginal odds ratio of \(e^{1.17534}=3.239\). In \(\mathcal P_2\), \(P(X=1)=0.9\): \[
m_C(\mathcal P_2)=0.1(0.047426)+0.9(0.952574)=0.862060,\qquad
m_B(\mathcal P_2)=0.1(0.268941)+0.9(0.993307)=0.920871,
\] \[
d_{BC(\mathcal P_2)}=\mathrm{logit}(0.920871)-\mathrm{logit}(0.862060)=2.45423-1.83250=0.62173,
\] a marginal odds ratio of \(e^{0.62173}=1.862\). The conditional odds ratio is \(7.389\) in both populations, yet the marginal odds ratio is \(3.24\) in \(\mathcal P_1\) and \(1.86\) in \(\mathcal P_2\). SEMA holds, the scale is aligned, the conditional effect is pinned to a constant, and still the marginal effect nearly halves when the covariate distribution shifts. Both marginal values lie strictly between \(1\) (log odds ratio \(0\)) and \(7.389\) (log odds ratio \(2\)), the strict attenuation Equation 12.14 of Theorem 12.6, and they differ from each other because the spread of \(\mu_C(X)\) differs between the populations. This single calculation is the chapter’s central message in numbers: a marginal odds ratio is not a property the treatments carry from population to population.
What a researcher would report, and what would go wrong. A MAIC or STC standardizing the index trial to the comparator population \(f_{AC}\) (here \(P(X=1)=0.9\)) would report a marginal odds ratio of about \(1.86\). That number is correct for \(f_{AC}\). Carried unchanged to a younger decision population like \(f_{AB}\) (here \(P(X=1)=0.1\)) it is simply wrong: the right marginal odds ratio there is \(3.24\). Nothing was mis-estimated; the number was moved to a population it does not describe. A report should therefore state which population its odds ratio belongs to, and either argue that the decision population matches it or redo the standardization for the decision population.

Remark (What a degenerate population shows). The proof of Theorem 12.6 predicts that a population concentrated at one covariate value recovers the conditional value. Check it: at the point mass \(X\equiv 0\), the marginal log odds ratio is \(\mathrm{logit}(\mu_B(0))-\mathrm{logit}(\mu_C(0))=\eta_B(0)-\eta_C(0)=(-1)-(-3)=2=c\), and at \(X\equiv 1\) it is \(\eta_B(1)-\eta_C(1)=5-3=2=c\). Only when the covariate genuinely varies, as in \(\mathcal P_1\) and \(\mathcal P_2\), does the Jensen gap open and the marginal effect attenuate below \(c\) and become population dependent. \(\blacktriangleleft\)



12.8.3 Time-to-event outcome: scale misalignment breaks transport
Finally a survival outcome modeled by proportional hazards, where the effect is reported as a difference in restricted mean survival time (RMST). This is the misaligned case of Theorem 12.4(ii): SEMA is imposed on the log-hazard scale, but RMST lives on the time scale, and \(h\circ g^{-1}\) is not the identity. Take an exponential baseline so the integrals are elementary. Let the comparator hazards at the two covariate values be \(\lambda_C(0)=0.5\) and \(\lambda_C(1)=2.0\), and let \(B\) halve the hazard, a constant hazard ratio of \(0.5\), so \(\lambda_B(x)=0.5\,\lambda_C(x)\), giving \(\lambda_B(0)=0.25\), \(\lambda_B(1)=1.0\). On the log-hazard scale the active versus active contrast is \(\log 0.5=-0.69315\) at both covariate values: SEMA holds and the conditional hazard ratio is the constant \(0.5\). Restrict at time \(\tau=2\). For an exponential hazard \(\lambda\) the survival is \(S(t)=e^{-\lambda t}\) and the RMST is \[
\mathrm{RMST}(\lambda)=\int_0^{\tau}e^{-\lambda t}\,dt=\frac{1-e^{-\lambda\tau}}{\lambda}.
\] Watch for the following, because it is the whole point and it happens before any marginalization: the conditional hazard ratio is a constant \(0.5\) at both covariate values, yet we are about to find that the conditional RMST difference is already unequal at \(x=0\) and \(x=1\). The misaligned scale has made the reported conditional contrast covariate dependent on its own, with no help from the covariate distribution. In the binary example the conditional contrast stayed constant and only marginalization broke transport; here the breakage is visible one step earlier. Compute the four conditional RMSTs: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{RMST}_C(0)&=\tfrac{1-e^{-1.0}}{0.5}=1.264241, & \mathrm{RMST}_B(0)&=\tfrac{1-e^{-0.5}}{0.25}=1.573877,\\
\mathrm{RMST}_C(1)&=\tfrac{1-e^{-4.0}}{2.0}=0.490842, & \mathrm{RMST}_B(1)&=\tfrac{1-e^{-2.0}}{1.0}=0.864665.
\end{aligned}
\] The conditional RMST difference is therefore \[
d_{BC}(0)=1.573877-1.264241=0.309636,\qquad d_{BC}(1)=0.864665-0.490842=0.373823,
\] not constant in \(x\), even though the conditional hazard ratio is the constant \(0.5\). This is exactly Theorem 12.4(ii): the nonlinear map from log-hazard to RMST refuses to cancel the covariate, which enters through the prognostic gradient \(\lambda_C(0)\ne\lambda_C(1)\). Because the conditional RMST difference varies in \(x\), the marginal RMST difference depends on the population. The RMST difference is collapsible, so the marginal is the population-average of the conditional (each marginal RMST is the average of the conditional survival curves integrated, by Fubini), and we average: \[
d_{BC(\mathcal P_1)}=0.9(0.309636)+0.1(0.373823)=0.316055,\qquad
d_{BC(\mathcal P_2)}=0.1(0.309636)+0.9(0.373823)=0.367404.
\] The marginal RMST difference is \(0.316\) in \(\mathcal P_1\) and \(0.367\) in \(\mathcal P_2\): a collapsible measure that still fails to transport, because the misaligned scale has manufactured effect modification on the reported scale. The contrast with the binary example is instructive. There, the conditional effect was constant and the failure came from non-collapsibility of the marginalization (Theorem 12.6); here, the measure is collapsible and the marginalization is innocent, but the conditional effect is itself covariate dependent because of scale misalignment (Theorem 12.4). Two different theorems, two different mechanisms, the same operational conclusion: the effect is comparator-population specific and the Step 2 transport of Theorem 12.3 is not free.
What a researcher would report. An RMST difference standardized to \(f_{AC}\) is about \(0.367\) units of extra event-free time; standardized to \(f_{AB}\) it is about \(0.316\). Even though RMST is collapsible, the number is population-specific, because the proportional-hazards model was fitted on the log-hazard scale while the effect is reported on the time scale. Reporting an RMST difference from a hazard model therefore carries the same “which population?” caveat as an odds ratio, for a different underlying reason.

title: 12  Transportability: The Estimand-Based Theory
text:
12.9 Notes and references
The estimand-based theory of transportability for population-adjusted indirect comparisons developed here is that of Chandler and Ishak (2026), which reframes MAIC, STC, and their kin as solving a transportability problem and isolates the three conditions, SEMA, scale alignment, and collapsibility, that govern direct transportability of a marginal relative effect. The chapter expands every result of that paper’s estimand-based core into a full proof: Theorem 12.2 (the transport g-formula), Theorem 12.3 (the two-step decomposition and bias split), Theorem 12.5 and Corollary 12.1 (the positive transport results), Theorem 12.4 (the role of scale alignment), and Theorem 12.6 (the insufficiency of SEMA for non-collapsible marginal effects). These correspond, in order, to catalogue results N.3, N.4, N.6 with N.8, N.9, N.7, and N.8 with N.11 in proofs/N_transportability.md; Definition 12.2 and Definition 12.3 formalize N.1 and N.2, Lemma 12.1 and Proposition 12.1 cover N.5 and N.10, and the HTA discussion threaded through Section 12.5 and Section 12.7 is N.12.
The identification scaffolding is from Hernán and Robins (2020), whose chapters on transportability use a population indicator \(S\) and a transport g-formula identical in structure to Equation 12.6; the within-population identification it rests on, Theorem 9.2, Definition 9.7, Definition 9.8, Theorem 10.4, and Theorem 10.3, is proved in Chapters 9 and 10, and the doubly robust augmentation alluded to after Theorem 12.2 is Theorem 10.5. The collapsibility facts, Definition 11.6, Definition 7.7, Example 7.5, and the non-collapsibility of the odds ratio and hazard ratio Theorem 11.2, are from Chapters 7 and 11; the strict-concavity argument used in Theorem 12.6 is the quantitative form of that non-collapsibility and rests on Jensen’s inequality Theorem 4.6. The constancy of relative effects that unanchored and standard indirect comparisons assume, Definition 14.2, is direct transportability of the relative effect in the sense of Theorem 12.1, and its failure under effect modification is the subject of Theorem 16.1 and the ecological bias of Definition 16.2 in Chapter 16. The shared effect modifier assumption itself is developed as part of the population adjustment theory of Chapter 17; here it is used as a stated structural condition, Equation 12.11, and the methods that operationalize the transport g-formula, MAIC, STC, and ML-NMR, are the subjects of Chapters 18 to 23. The current NICE Decision Support Unit and EU joint guidance that treat SEMA as sufficient for transport are documented in Phillippo et al. (2016); Theorem 12.6 is the precise sense in which that treatment is incomplete for non-collapsible marginal effects, and Phillippo et al. (2020) is the modeling framework that makes the target population, and hence the Step 2 transport, explicit.
Machine-checked status. In one sentence for readers outside formal methods: none of this chapter’s own results have yet been checked by the companion computer-proof system, and this paragraph only records which neighboring facts have been. None of this chapter’s owned results has a counterpart in the ITC_Coq development. The Coq tree formalizes the algebraic core of indirect comparison, Bucher’s identity and unbiasedness in theories/Bucher.v, propensity-score balancing, inverse-probability and doubly robust estimation, and the anchored cancellation of prognostic variables in theories/EffectModifiers.v, but the transportability propositions here, which combine SEMA, collapsibility, and scale alignment across populations, are pen-and-paper by design, as the companion manuscript notes. The closest machine-checked relative is the collapsibility of the linear-model effect, Lemma STC_collapse_linear in theories/STC.v, which proves the identity-scale case of Lemma 12.1(1) from linearity of expectation; it is owned and tagged by Chapter 19. No tag is added to any result in this chapter.

title: 12  Transportability: The Estimand-Based Theory
text:
12.10 Exercises
A starred exercise, marked \(\star\), has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The unstarred exercises are arranged from applied identification and interpretation, through computation, to proof, so a reader can stop at the level that suits them.

Exercise 12.1 (Warm-up, interpretation) Name the three populations. A sponsor submits an indirect comparison of drug \(B\) against drug \(C\), both anchored on a common comparator \(A\). The sponsor owns individual patient data from a trial of \(A\) versus \(B\) that enrolled mostly younger, biologic-naive patients, and uses published aggregate results from a trial of \(A\) versus \(C\) that enrolled mostly older, biologic-experienced patients. The national HTA body must decide about all label-eligible patients, a mix of both. (a) Identify, in the language of this chapter, the source population, the comparator population, and the decision population, and say which supplies IPD and which supplies AgD. (b) Using Theorem 12.3, state which population the standard pairwise PAIC estimand \(d_{BC(AC)}\) is attached to. (c) In one sentence, say what extra information the sponsor would need before claiming the result applies to the decision population.


Exercise 12.2 (Interpretation) Reading a MAIC report. A submitted MAIC reports a marginal odds ratio for \(B\) versus \(C\) “standardized to the comparator trial population,” and a reviewer asks whether it applies to the national decision population. (a) Using the two-step decomposition Equation 12.9, explain which of the two terms the MAIC has controlled and which it has left untouched. (b) Explain, citing Theorem 12.6, why “the shared effect modifier assumption holds, so the odds ratio is the same in any population” is not a valid answer for a marginal odds ratio. (c) State one condition on the two populations under which the reported number would in fact apply unchanged to the decision population.


Exercise 12.3 (Computation) Direct transportability of a constant conditional effect. Suppose the conditional mean difference is the constant \(\tau(x)=4\) for all \(x\), and a covariate \(X\) has mean \(\bar x_1=0\) in population \(\mathcal P_1\) and \(\bar x_2=10\) in population \(\mathcal P_2\). Using Theorem 12.1, show that the marginal mean difference is \(4\) in both populations, and explain why the difference in covariate means is irrelevant. Then show by counterexample that the same conclusion fails for the marginal odds ratio when the model is logistic with the same constant conditional log odds ratio.


Exercise 12.4 (Computation) Transport g-formula and weights. Let \(X\in\{0,1\}\) with source probabilities \(P_{\mathcal P}(X=1)=0.3\) and target probabilities \(P_{\mathcal P^{*}}(X=1)=0.6\), and let the source conditional means under treatment \(t\) be \(\mu_t(0)\) and \(\mu_t(1)\). (a) Write the transportability weights \(w(0),w(1)\) as density ratios and verify \(\mathbb E_{X\sim\mathcal P}[w(X)]=1\). (b) Show by direct computation that the re-weighting identity Equation 12.7 and the g-formula Equation 12.6 give the same target marginal mean \(m_t(\mathcal P^{*})\). (c) Explain what the overlap condition (iv) of Theorem 12.2 requires here and what goes wrong if \(P_{\mathcal P}(X=1)=0\).


Exercise 12.5 (Interpretation) The two sponsors. Two sponsors each compare \(B\) versus \(C\) anchored on \(A\), using comparator trials with covariate distributions \(f_{AC}^{(1)}\) and \(f_{AC}^{(2)}\) that differ. The conditional log odds ratio of \(B\) versus \(C\) is the constant \(c=0.7\) (SEMA and alignment hold). Using Theorem 12.3 and Theorem 12.6, explain why the two sponsors’ marginal log odds ratios \(d_{BC(AC^{(1)})}\) and \(d_{BC(AC^{(2)})}\) can differ, identify which of the two bias terms in Equation 12.9 is responsible, and state what additional information would be needed to transport either estimate to a third, decision-relevant population.


Exercise 12.6 (Computation) Risk ratio transports where the odds ratio does not. Consider a log-link binomial model with a binary \(X\), constant conditional log risk ratio \(\log R\) for \(B\) versus \(C\), and reference risks \(\mu_C(0)=0.05\), \(\mu_C(1)=0.20\). (a) Show that the marginal risk ratio equals \(R\) in every population, using Lemma 12.1(2). (b) Take \(R=1.5\) and the two populations \(P(X=1)=0.1\) and \(P(X=1)=0.9\); compute the marginal risks under \(B\) and \(C\) and confirm the marginal risk ratio is \(1.5\) in both. (c) Contrast this with Section 12.8.2 and explain in one sentence why the odds ratio behaves differently.


Exercise 12.7 (\(\star\), proof) Strict attenuation of the marginal odds ratio. Let the conditional log odds ratio be the constant \(c>0\), so \(\mu_B(x)=\varphi(\mu_C(x))\) with \(\varphi(p)=\mathrm{expit}(\mathrm{logit}\,p+c)\). (a) Prove that \(\varphi\) is strictly increasing and strictly concave on \((0,1)\) by computing \(\varphi'\) and \(\varphi''\). (b) Using Jensen’s inequality Theorem 4.6, prove the strict attenuation \(0<\mathrm{logit}\,m_B-\mathrm{logit}\,m_C<c\) whenever \(\mu_C(X)\) is non-degenerate. (c) Show that the attenuation gap \(c-(\mathrm{logit}\,m_B-\mathrm{logit}\,m_C)\) increases as the spread of \(\mu_C(X)\) increases, in the sense that it is zero for a point mass and positive otherwise, and use this to conclude that the marginal log odds ratio is population dependent. (d) Verify (b) numerically on the \(\mathcal P_1,\mathcal P_2\) of Section 12.8.2.


Exercise 12.8 (\(\star\), computation and proof) Scale misalignment manufactures effect modification. Consider a logistic model (\(g=\mathrm{logit}\)) with no interactions at all, \(\eta_k(x)=\alpha+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_k\), so that SEMA holds trivially, and report the effect as a risk difference (\(h=\mathrm{id}\)). (a) Show \(h\circ g^{-1}=\mathrm{expit}\) and that the conditional risk difference \(\mathrm{expit}(\eta_B(x))-\mathrm{expit}(\eta_C(x))\) is non-constant in \(x\) whenever \(\boldsymbol\beta_1\ne\mathbf 0\), instantiating Theorem 12.4(ii). (b) With scalar \(x\in\{0,1\}\), \(\alpha=-2\), \(\beta_1=3\), \(\gamma_C=0\), \(\gamma_B=1.5\), compute the conditional risk differences at \(x=0\) and \(x=1\) and the marginal risk differences in \(P(X=1)=0.2\) and \(P(X=1)=0.8\). (c) Explain why this failure occurs even though the risk difference is a collapsible measure.


Exercise 12.9 (Proof) RMST transport under an RMST-scale assumption. The last row of Proposition 12.1 claims that an RMST difference transports if SEMA is imposed on the RMST (time) scale rather than the log-hazard scale. (a) State precisely what “RMST-scale SEMA” means for the conditional RMST difference \(d_{BC}(x)\). (b) Prove that under it the marginal RMST difference is directly transportable, citing Theorem 12.5 and the collapsibility of the RMST difference. (c) Explain why this structural assumption is restrictive in practice: what would have to be true of the baseline hazard and the covariate effects for a proportional-hazards model to also satisfy RMST-scale SEMA?


Exercise 12.10 (Interpretation) The conditional advantage. Using Corollary 12.1 and Theorem 12.6, explain why an analysis targeting the population-average conditional log odds ratio needs only SEMA and scale alignment to transport, while one targeting the marginal log odds ratio additionally needs collapsibility, which the odds ratio lacks. Then state the scientific cost of preferring the conditional estimand: what question does it answer, and why is it not interchangeable with the marginal estimand a decision maker may actually want?

title: 12  Transportability: The Estimand-Based Theory
text:
Recall the two inverse maps of logistic regression: \(\mathrm{logit}(p)=\log\{p/(1-p)\}\) sends a probability in \((0,1)\) to a real number, and its inverse \(\mathrm{expit}(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\) sends a real number back to a probability. Both are used throughout this chapter.↩︎
Labels such as N.1, N.3, and N.4 point to numbered results in the companion proof catalogue for this Part; they let the formal development be cross-checked against the chapter. A first-time reader can safely ignore the codes.↩︎
An anchored indirect comparison of \(B\) versus \(C\) runs through a comparator \(A\) present in both trials, so study-level factors that shift both arms cancel; an unanchored comparison pits single arms against each other with no shared comparator and must assume far more. Anchoring is developed in Chapter 14.↩︎
Named after the statistician Jaroslav Hájek; “self-normalized” means dividing by the sum of the weights, so only the relative weights matter and any unknown overall scale cancels.↩︎
Restricted mean survival time up to a horizon \(\tau\) is the expected event-free time in \([0,\tau]\), equivalently the area under the survival curve out to \(\tau\). An RMST difference is measured in units of time and is often easier for patients and payers to interpret than a hazard ratio.↩︎

title: 13  Pairwise Meta-Analysis
text:
13.1 The fixed-effect model and inverse-variance weighting
Meta-analysis is the arithmetic of evidence synthesis. Several studies have each estimated the same treatment effect, and we wish to combine their estimates into one summary that is more precise than any single trial and that lays bare whether the studies agree. This chapter develops that arithmetic from first principles. It is the foundation of every later chapter: the indirect comparison of Chapter 14 is a meta-analysis of contrasts, the network meta-analysis of Chapter 15 is a multivariate meta-analysis, and the population-adjusted methods of Parts IV and V are meta-analyses in which the within-study estimates are first recalibrated to a common population. Master the pairwise case and the rest is structure built on top of it.
We work throughout with the two-stage view. In the first stage, each study \(i\) has been analyzed on its own and has produced a point estimate \(\hat\theta_i\) of an effect (a log odds ratio, a log hazard ratio, a mean difference, whatever the outcome scale demands) together with an estimate \(s_i^2\) of the variance of that point estimate. In the second stage, which is the subject of this chapter, we treat the pairs \((\hat\theta_i, s_i^2)\), \(i = 1, \dots, k\), as the data and combine them. The within-study variances \(s_i^2\) are treated as known constants. This is an idealization: in reality \(s_i^2\) is itself estimated from the \(n_i\) patients of study \(i\). The idealization is excellent when the \(n_i\) are large, because then \(s_i^2\) is estimated with negligible relative error, and it is the standard convention in the meta-analysis and network meta-analysis literature (Dias et al. (2018)). We adopt it and flag, where it matters, what changes when it is relaxed.
Two orientations before the mathematics begins, both aimed at a reader who runs meta-analyses in software but has not seen one built from the ground up.
Reader translation of the two-stage view. Stage 1 happens inside each trial: a statistician fits a model (a logistic regression for a binary outcome, a Cox model for time to event, a linear model for a continuous outcome) and reports two numbers, a point estimate \(\hat\theta_i\) and its standard error. Squaring the standard error gives \(s_i^2\). Stage 2, the whole of this chapter, never revisits the patients; it works only with the pairs \((\hat\theta_i, s_i^2)\). So \(s_i^2\) is “the square of the standard error you read off the trial report,” and treating it as known is the statement that we trust each trial’s own reported precision. The one place this idealization bites is the Hartung-Knapp interval of Section Section 13.7, which exists precisely because pretending we know more than we do makes intervals too narrow when the trials are few.
Why we pool on the link (log) scale. The estimate \(\hat\theta_i\) is almost never an odds ratio or a hazard ratio itself; it is the logarithm of one, or a raw mean difference. There are two reasons, one statistical and one mathematical. Statistically, a log odds ratio is far closer to normally distributed, and its confidence interval far more symmetric, than the odds ratio itself, so the Gaussian machinery below is trustworthy on the log scale and not on the ratio scale. Mathematically, the odds ratio and hazard ratio are non-collapsible: the population-average ratio is not the average of subgroup ratios, so averaging ratios directly does not even estimate a well-defined effect (Definition 11.6, Theorem 11.2). Throughout the chapter \(\theta\) is a contrast on the linear-predictor scale (the “link scale”); the word contrast simply means a difference of two effects, here two linear predictors. Keep in mind that the pooled \(\theta\) inherits whatever scale the inputs were on, and that this choice of scale is exactly what the later ITC chapters must respect.
A forest plot draws each estimate as a point with its \(95\%\) confidence interval \(\hat\theta_i \pm 1.96\, s_i\), stacking the trials with the pooled estimate at the foot; it is the picture every health researcher already reads. For the five trials:
The vertical bar marks no effect (log OR \(= 0\), odds ratio \(1\)). Study \(C\) has the shortest interval, so it is the most precise (\(s_C^2 = 0.01\)), and it sits lowest; studies \(D\) and \(E\) are higher and wider. The two pooled markers, fixed-effect (FE) and random-effects (RE), are what the chapter will compute and compare.
Terms you will meet. A little vocabulary recurs. Each term is also defined in line where it is first used; the table is only for quick reference.
Roadmap. The chapter runs in a straight line. Section Section 13.1 pools under the assumption of a single common effect and proves the inverse-variance weights optimal. Section Section 13.2 asks whether that assumption holds, through Cochran’s \(Q\). Sections Section 13.3 through Section 13.6 quantify and then estimate the heterogeneity (\(I^2\), then the variance \(\tau^2\) by two methods). Section Section 13.7 fixes the interval when trials are few, Section Section 13.8 gives the Bayesian version that later networks generalize, and Section Section 13.9 checks the evidence base for small-study bias. Everything feeds the indirect comparison of Chapter 14 and the network of Chapter 15.
The simplest assumption is that every study estimates one and the same effect \(\theta\), and that the studies differ only through sampling error.
Write \(\mathbf{w} = (w_1, \dots, w_k)\) for the inverse-variance weights \[
w_i = \frac{1}{s_i^2}, \qquad W = \sum_{i=1}^k w_i ,
\] and define the inverse-variance-weighted (IVW) estimator \[
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k w_i \hat\theta_i}{\sum_{i=1}^k w_i}
= \frac{1}{W}\sum_{i=1}^k w_i \hat\theta_i .
\tag{13.2}\]
The next theorem is the meta-analytic incarnation of the Gauss-Markov theorem (Theorem 6.3): among all unbiased estimators that are linear in the data, the IVW estimator has the smallest variance.
The same conclusion has a one-line elementary proof by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, which also pins down the equality case; we record it because it is so transparent.
Under the Gaussian version of Equation 13.1 the IVW estimator is more than best linear unbiased: it is fully efficient, coinciding with the maximum likelihood estimator and attaining the Cramer-Rao bound.

title: 13  Pairwise Meta-Analysis
text:
Definition 13.1 (Fixed-effect meta-analysis model) The fixed-effect model for \(k\) study estimates is \[
\hat\theta_i = \theta + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i] = 0, \qquad
\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = s_i^2, \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon_i, \varepsilon_j) = 0 \ (i \ne j),
\tag{13.1}\] where \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\) is the common effect and the within-study variances \(s_i^2 > 0\) are known. When distributional results are needed we add the Gaussian assumption \(\varepsilon_i \sim
\mathcal{N}(0, s_i^2)\), independently across \(i\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. The fixed-effect model makes a strong claim: there is one number \(\theta\) (say, one true log odds ratio for \(B\) versus \(A\)), and the five trials differ only because each saw a finite sample. A fair question is “the same effect for whom, and on what scale?” The answer is: the same effect on the chosen link scale, in whatever common population the trials are taken to share. If that claim is false, the model is misspecified, and the rest of the chapter (Cochran’s \(Q\), then random effects) is the diagnosis and the repair. \(\blacktriangleleft\)



Remark. Why these weights? (intuition before the theorem.) Inverse-variance weighting says: trust each trial in proportion to \(1/s_i^2\), its precision. Why the reciprocal variance, rather than the reciprocal standard error, the sample size, or a quality score? Because variance is the currency in which independent estimates combine. If you average with weights \(a_i\) summing to one, the variance of the average is \(\sum_i a_i^2 s_i^2\), and minimizing that forces \(a_i \propto 1/s_i^2\). Concretely, in the running trio study \(C\) has \(s_C^2 = 0.01\) and study \(D\) has \(s_D^2 = 0.04\): \(D\)’s estimate is four times as variable, so \(C\) earns four times the weight (\(w_C = 100\) versus \(w_D = 25\)). In standard-error units \(C\) fluctuates half as much as \(D\) (\(0.10\) versus \(0.20\)), and squaring that halving is exactly the factor of four; reciprocal standard error would give \(C\) only twice \(D\)’s weight, which does not minimize the variance. On the running trio \(C, D, E\) the total weight is \(W = 137.5\) and \[
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}} = \frac{100(0.15) + 25(0.60) + 12.5(0.50)}{137.5} = \frac{36.25}{137.5} = 0.264,
\] with standard error \(1/\sqrt{137.5} = 0.085\): the precise study \(C\) alone carries \(100/137.5 = 73\%\) of the weight and pulls the summary down toward its own \(0.15\). The next theorem makes “minimizes the variance” precise and proves these weights optimal. \(\blacktriangleleft\)



Theorem 13.1 (Inverse-variance weighting is best linear unbiased) Under the fixed-effect model Equation 13.1, consider the class of linear estimators \(\hat\theta = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i \hat\theta_i\) with fixed coefficients \(a_i\). Such an estimator is unbiased for \(\theta\) for every value of \(\theta\) if and only if \(\sum_i a_i = 1\). Among all linear unbiased estimators, the IVW estimator Equation 13.2 is the unique minimizer of the variance, and \[
\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}) = \frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^k w_i} = \frac{1}{W} .
\tag{13.3}\] (Corresponds to C.1 in the proof catalogue.)


Remark. Why this matters, and how to read the proof. “Best linear unbiased” (BLUE) is the principled answer to “why these weights and not others”: among all ways of averaging the trials without introducing bias, inverse-variance weighting is the uniquely most precise. This is why the inverse-variance default in standard meta-analysis software is not arbitrary, and it is the very same optimality that will justify the contrast weights of the Bucher indirect comparison in Chapter 14 and the network estimator of Chapter 15. Two proofs follow. The second, by Cauchy-Schwarz, is the short transparent one, and a reader meeting this material for the first time may prefer to read it first. The first connects the result to the regression theory of Part I, and uses three pieces of vocabulary worth pinning down in advance: \(\mathbf{1}_k\) is the \(k\)-vector of all ones (the design matrix of a single common mean); “\(\mathbf{S}
\succ 0\)” means the covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) is positive definite, which here just says every \(s_i^2 > 0\); and to whiten is to rescale each study’s equation by \(1/s_i\) so every error has variance \(1\), converting the unequal-variance (heteroscedastic) problem into the equal-variance one that Gauss-Markov handles. The step calling \(\mathbf{a} \mapsto \mathbf{S}^{1/2}\mathbf{a}\) a “bijection” is only saying the rescaling is invertible, so every estimator before whitening corresponds to exactly one after and nothing is gained or lost by working in the whitened data. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Proof. Unbiasedness holds iff \(\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta] = \sum_i a_i \theta = \theta\) for all \(\theta\), that is iff \(\sum_i a_i = 1\). We prove optimality by reducing the problem to ordinary least squares and applying Theorem 6.3, the route that exhibits the result as a genuine Gauss-Markov statement.
Collect the data into \(\mathbf{y} = (\hat\theta_1, \dots, \hat\theta_k)^\top\). Model Equation 13.1 reads \(\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{1}_k \theta + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) with \(\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}]
= \mathbf{0}\) and \(\mathrm{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}) = \mathbf{S} := \mathrm{diag}(s_1^2, \dots,
s_k^2) \succ 0\). This is a linear model with design matrix \(\mathbf{1}_k\), but with heteroscedastic errors, so Theorem 6.3 does not apply directly. We whiten the errors. Let \(\mathbf{S}^{-1/2} =
\mathrm{diag}(s_1^{-1}, \dots, s_k^{-1})\) and set \[
\tilde{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{S}^{-1/2}\mathbf{y}, \qquad \tilde{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{S}^{-1/2}\mathbf{1}_k
= (s_1^{-1}, \dots, s_k^{-1})^\top, \qquad \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}} = \mathbf{S}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
\] Then \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}} = \tilde{\mathbf{X}}\theta + \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\) with \(\mathrm{Cov}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}) = \mathbf{S}^{-1/2}\mathbf{S}\,\mathbf{S}^{-1/2} = I_k\), so the whitened model satisfies the Gauss-Markov hypotheses G1 and G2 of Definition 6.1 with error covariance \(\sigma^2 I_k\), \(\sigma^2 = 1\), and full column rank \(\mathrm{rank}(\tilde{\mathbf{X}}) = 1\).
The whitening is an invertible linear change of data: \(\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{S}^{1/2}\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\), and a linear estimator \(\sum_i a_i \hat\theta_i = \mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{y} = (\mathbf{S}^{1/2}\mathbf{a})^\top
\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\) is a linear function of \(\mathbf{y}\) if and only if it is a linear function of \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\), the map \(\mathbf{a} \mapsto \mathbf{S}^{1/2}\mathbf{a}\) being a bijection of \(\mathbb{R}^k\). Likewise it is unbiased in one parameterization iff in the other. Hence the class of linear unbiased estimators of \(\theta\) is identical whether expressed in \(\mathbf{y}\) or in \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\), and minimizing variance over the class is the same problem either way. By Theorem 6.3 the unique minimum-variance linear unbiased estimator in the whitened model is the OLS estimator \[
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}} = (\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^\top\tilde{\mathbf{X}})^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^\top
\tilde{\mathbf{y}} = \frac{\mathbf{1}_k^\top \mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{y}}{\mathbf{1}_k^\top\mathbf{S}^{-1}
\mathbf{1}_k} = \frac{\sum_i \hat\theta_i / s_i^2}{\sum_i 1/s_i^2} = \frac{\sum_i w_i \hat\theta_i}{\sum_i w_i},
\] which is Equation 13.2. Its variance is, by Theorem 6.2 specialized here or by direct computation, \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}) = (\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^\top\tilde{\mathbf{X}})^{-1} =
(\mathbf{1}_k^\top\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{1}_k)^{-1} = 1/\sum_i w_i\), which is Equation 13.3. Uniqueness in Theorem 6.3 transfers through the bijection. \(\square\)



Remark. Cauchy-Schwarz proof and the equality case. For any unbiased weights, \(\sum_i a_i = 1\). The variance is \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) = \sum_i a_i^2 s_i^2\). By Cauchy-Schwarz applied to the vectors \((a_i s_i)_i\) and \((1/s_i)_i\), \[
1 = \Big(\sum_i a_i\Big)^2 = \Big(\sum_i (a_i s_i)\cdot \tfrac{1}{s_i}\Big)^2
\le \Big(\sum_i a_i^2 s_i^2\Big)\Big(\sum_i \tfrac{1}{s_i^2}\Big)
= \mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta)\cdot W ,
\] so \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) \ge 1/W\), with equality iff \((a_i s_i)_i \propto (1/s_i)_i\), that is iff \(a_i \propto 1/s_i^2 = w_i\). The normalization \(\sum_i a_i = 1\) then forces \(a_i = w_i/W\), the IVW weights. \(\blacktriangleleft\)



Proposition 13.1 (IVW is the Gaussian MLE and attains the Cramer-Rao bound) Under Equation 13.1 with \(\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, s_i^2)\) independent, the maximum likelihood estimator of \(\theta\) is \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}\), the Fisher information for \(\theta\) is \(\mathcal{I}(\theta) = \sum_i w_i = W\), and \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}) = 1/W\) equals the Cramer-Rao lower bound, so \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}\) is the minimum-variance unbiased estimator among all (not merely linear) unbiased estimators.


Proof. The log-likelihood is \(\ell(\theta) = -\tfrac12 \sum_i \log(2\pi s_i^2) - \tfrac12 \sum_i (\hat\theta_i -
\theta)^2/s_i^2\). The score is \(\ell'(\theta) = \sum_i (\hat\theta_i - \theta)/s_i^2 = \sum_i w_i
(\hat\theta_i - \theta)\), which vanishes exactly at \(\theta = \sum_i w_i \hat\theta_i/\sum_i w_i =
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}\); since \(\ell''(\theta) = -\sum_i w_i < 0\), this is the maximizer. The Fisher information (Definition 5.7) is \(\mathcal{I}(\theta) = -\mathbb{E}[\ell''(\theta)] = \sum_i w_i =
W\). The Cramer-Rao bound (Theorem 5.7) for an unbiased estimator of \(\theta\) is therefore \(1/\mathcal{I}(\theta) = 1/W\), which Equation 13.3 shows \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}\) attains. An unbiased estimator attaining the Cramer-Rao bound is minimum-variance unbiased. \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters. Under the Gaussian model, inverse-variance weighting is not merely best among linear estimators; it is best among all unbiased estimators and coincides with maximum likelihood. So there is nothing cleverer to be attempted: the standard pooled estimate is already fully efficient. The two Part I ingredients are Definition 5.7, the Fisher information (the curvature of the log-likelihood, a measure of how sharply the data pin down \(\theta\)), and Theorem 5.7, the Cramer-Rao bound (no unbiased estimator can have variance below \(1/\mathcal{I}(\theta)\)). All of this still rests on the fixed-effect premise of a single \(\theta\); the next section puts that premise on trial. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 13  Pairwise Meta-Analysis
section: 13.2 Cochran’s \(Q\) and the test for heterogeneity
text:
13.2 Cochran’s \(Q\) and the test for heterogeneity
If the fixed-effect model holds, the studies should agree up to their sampling errors, and the weighted spread of the \(\hat\theta_i\) about \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}\) should be no larger than sampling noise predicts. Cochran’s \(Q\) measures that spread.

Definition 13.2 Cochran’s \(Q\) statistic is \[
Q = \sum_{i=1}^k w_i (\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}})^2, \qquad w_i = \frac{1}{s_i^2}.
\tag{13.4}\]


Remark. Reader translation, and where this is going. Once we commit to a single common effect and estimate it by \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}\), we look at what is left over: how far does each trial sit from the pooled value? Cochran’s \(Q\) adds up those gaps, each squared and weighted by the trial’s precision. It is exactly a weighted residual sum of squares after fitting one mean, the meta-analytic twin of the residual sum of squares in regression, so it should behave like one: on \(k\) studies, one degree of freedom is spent locating the common effect and \(k - 1\) independent disagreements remain. Knowing its distribution is what turns “do the trials agree?” into a heterogeneity \(p\)-value. On the running trio, \[
Q = 100(0.15 - 0.264)^2 + 25(0.60 - 0.264)^2 + 12.5(0.50 - 0.264)^2 = 4.82,
\] against an expected \(k - 1 = 2\): the trio disagrees by more than sampling error alone would predict. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

We first isolate the linear-algebra fact that drives its distribution: a quadratic form in independent standard normals, with an orthogonal projector in the middle, is chi-squared with degrees of freedom equal to the rank of the projector. This is the same mechanism behind the residual sum of squares in regression (Theorem 6.6); we state it once, cleanly, for reuse.
Two reminders make the lemma readable. A matrix \(P\) is idempotent if \(P^2 = P\); such a \(P\) is a projection, and its rank equals its trace (if \(P^2 = P\), then each eigenvalue \(\lambda\) satisfies \(\lambda^2 = \lambda\), forcing \(\lambda \in \{0, 1\}\), so the number of nonzero eigenvalues, the rank, is their sum, the trace). The spectral theorem (Theorem 3.2) writes a symmetric matrix as \(Q\Lambda Q^\top\) with \(Q\) orthogonal and \(\Lambda\) the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues, and Lemma 6.3 says a linear image \(A\mathbf{Z}\) of a Gaussian vector is again Gaussian with covariance \(A A^\top\) (an orthogonal \(Q^\top\) leaves the standard covariance \(I_k\) unchanged).

Lemma 13.1 (Chi-squared law of a projected Gaussian) Let \(\mathbf{Z} \sim \mathcal{N}_k(\mathbf{0}, I_k)\) and let \(P \in \mathbb{R}^{k\times k}\) be symmetric and idempotent, \(P = P^\top = P^2\), with \(\mathrm{rank}(P) = r\). Then \(\mathbf{Z}^\top P \mathbf{Z} \sim
\chi^2_r\).


Proof. By the spectral theorem (Theorem 3.2) write \(P = Q\Lambda Q^\top\) with \(Q\) orthogonal and \(\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)\). Idempotence forces \(\lambda_i^2 = \lambda_i\), hence \(\lambda_i \in \{0, 1\}\); the number of unit eigenvalues equals \(\mathrm{rank}(P) = r\) (equivalently \(\mathrm{tr}(P) = r\), the rank of an idempotent matrix equaling its trace). Reorder so that \(\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(I_r, \mathbf{0})\). Put \(\mathbf{U} = Q^\top\mathbf{Z}\). By Lemma 6.3, \(\mathbf{U} \sim \mathcal{N}_k(\mathbf{0}, Q^\top I_k Q) = \mathcal{N}_k(\mathbf{0}, I_k)\), so its coordinates are independent standard normals. Then \[
\mathbf{Z}^\top P \mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{Z}^\top Q\Lambda Q^\top \mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{U}^\top\Lambda\mathbf{U}
= \sum_{i=1}^r U_i^2 ,
\] a sum of \(r\) independent squared standard normal variables, which by definition has the \(\chi^2_r\) distribution. \(\square\)


Remark. Reader translation. The lemma is the engine of the whole section: pass a standard Gaussian vector through a projection and take its squared length, and the result is chi-squared with degrees of freedom equal to the dimension the projection keeps. Cochran’s \(Q\) is precisely of this form, with the projection removing the one dimension used up by estimating the common effect. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Theorem 13.2 (Distribution of Cochran’s \(Q\) under homogeneity) Under the fixed-effect model Equation 13.1 with Gaussian errors \(\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, s_i^2)\), \[
Q \sim \chi^2_{k-1}.
\] (Corresponds to C.2 in the proof catalogue.)


Proof. Standardize each study: \(Z_i := \sqrt{w_i}\,(\hat\theta_i - \theta) = (\hat\theta_i - \theta)/s_i\). Under the Gaussian fixed-effect model the \(Z_i\) are independent \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\), so \(\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1,
\dots, Z_k)^\top \sim \mathcal{N}_k(\mathbf{0}, I_k)\), and \(\hat\theta_i - \theta = Z_i/\sqrt{w_i}\). Subtracting the common \(\theta\) from numerator and denominator leaves the IVW deviation unchanged, \[
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}} - \theta = \sum_i \frac{w_i}{W}(\hat\theta_i - \theta) = \frac{1}{W}\sum_i w_i
\cdot \frac{Z_i}{\sqrt{w_i}} = \frac{1}{W}\sum_i \sqrt{w_i}\,Z_i .
\] Introduce the unit vector \(\mathbf{u}\) with components \(u_i = \sqrt{w_i/W}\); then \(\sum_i u_i^2 = \sum_i
w_i/W = 1\), and \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}} - \theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{W}}\sum_i u_i Z_i =
\frac{1}{\sqrt{W}}\,\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{Z}\). Therefore \[
\sqrt{w_i}\,(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}) = \sqrt{w_i}\,(\hat\theta_i - \theta) -
\sqrt{w_i}\,(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}} - \theta) = Z_i - \frac{\sqrt{w_i}}{\sqrt{W}}\,\mathbf{u}^\top
\mathbf{Z} = Z_i - u_i\,\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{Z} = \big[(I_k - \mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^\top)\mathbf{Z}\big]_i .
\] Squaring and summing, \[
Q = \sum_i w_i(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}})^2 = \sum_i \big[(I_k - \mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^\top)
\mathbf{Z}\big]_i^2 = \big\|(I_k - \mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^\top)\mathbf{Z}\big\|_2^2 = \mathbf{Z}^\top
(I_k - \mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^\top)\mathbf{Z},
\] the last step using that \(P := I_k - \mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^\top\) is symmetric and idempotent (\(P^2 = I_k -
2\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^\top + \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{u})\mathbf{u}^\top = I_k -
\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^\top\) because \(\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{u} = 1\)). Its rank is \(\mathrm{tr}(P) = k -
\|\mathbf{u}\|_2^2 = k - 1\). By Lemma 13.1, \(Q \sim \chi^2_{k-1}\). \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters. This distribution is what makes \(Q\) usable. Under homogeneity \(Q \sim \chi^2_{k-1}\), so a value in the upper tail is evidence that the trials disagree by more than chance, and the tail probability \(P(\chi^2_{k-1} > Q_{\mathrm{obs}})\) is the classical heterogeneity \(p\)-value. The \(k - 1\) has the plain reading promised above: of the \(k\) standardized deviations, one linear combination is spent locating the common effect \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}\), leaving \(k - 1\) free to disagree. For the running trio, \(Q = 4.82\) on \(k - 1 = 2\) degrees of freedom gives \(P(\chi^2_2 > 4.82) = 0.09\): suggestive but not decisive with only three trials, which is typical. For indirect comparison this test is the first alarm bell, because heterogeneity in a direct \(A\)-versus-\(C\) or \(B\)-versus-\(C\) comparison is exactly what threatens the transitivity that Chapter 14 relies on. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The mean of the \(\chi^2_{k-1}\) law is \(k - 1\), so under homogeneity we expect \(Q \approx k - 1\). A value of \(Q\) far above \(k - 1\) is evidence that the studies disagree by more than sampling error allows, that is, evidence of heterogeneity. To quantify “far above,” we need the behavior of \(Q\) when the effects genuinely differ. The following second-moment computation requires no Gaussianity and is the engine behind both the \(I^2\) statistic and the DerSimonian-Laird estimator.

Proposition 13.2 (Expected value of \(Q\) under heterogeneity) Suppose the study-specific effects vary: \(\hat\theta_i = \theta + b_i + \varepsilon_i\) where the \(b_i\) have mean \(0\) and variance \(\tau^2\), the \(\varepsilon_i\) have mean \(0\) and variance \(s_i^2\), and all \(2k\) variables \(b_1, \dots, b_k, \varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_k\) are uncorrelated. With the fixed-effect weights \(w_i = 1/s_i^2\) used in \(Q\), \[
\mathbb{E}[Q] = (k - 1) + \tau^2 c, \qquad c := \sum_i w_i - \frac{\sum_i w_i^2}{\sum_i w_i} = W -
\frac{\sum_i w_i^2}{W} .
\tag{13.5}\] Moreover \(c > 0\) whenever \(k \ge 2\).


Proof. Let \(\delta_i = \hat\theta_i - \theta = b_i + \varepsilon_i\), so \(\mathbb{E}[\delta_i] = 0\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(\delta_i) = \tau^2 + s_i^2\). The common \(\theta\) cancels in the deviations, \(\hat\theta_i -
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}} = \delta_i - \bar\delta_w\) with \(\bar\delta_w = \frac{1}{W}\sum_j w_j \delta_j\). The weighted sum-of-squares identity gives \[
Q = \sum_i w_i(\delta_i - \bar\delta_w)^2 = \sum_i w_i \delta_i^2 - W \bar\delta_w^2 ,
\] which is the weighted version of the familiar identity. Expanding the square and using \(\sum_i w_i
\delta_i = W\bar\delta_w\) (the definition of \(\bar\delta_w\)) together with \(\sum_i w_i = W\), \[
\sum_i w_i(\delta_i - \bar\delta_w)^2 = \sum_i w_i \delta_i^2 - 2\bar\delta_w \sum_i w_i \delta_i +
\bar\delta_w^2 \sum_i w_i = \sum_i w_i \delta_i^2 - 2\bar\delta_w(W\bar\delta_w) + W\bar\delta_w^2 =
\sum_i w_i \delta_i^2 - W\bar\delta_w^2 .
\]
Take expectations term by term. First, using \(w_i s_i^2 = 1\), \[
\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_i w_i \delta_i^2\Big] = \sum_i w_i(\tau^2 + s_i^2) = \tau^2 W + \sum_i w_i s_i^2 =
\tau^2 W + k .
\] Second, \(\mathbb{E}[\bar\delta_w] = 0\), so \(\mathbb{E}[W\bar\delta_w^2] = W\,\mathrm{Var}(\bar\delta_w)\), and by uncorrelatedness, using \(w_j^2 s_j^2 = w_j\), \[
\mathrm{Var}(\bar\delta_w) = \frac{1}{W^2}\sum_j w_j^2 \mathrm{Var}(\delta_j) = \frac{1}{W^2}\sum_j w_j^2
(\tau^2 + s_j^2) = \frac{\tau^2 \sum_j w_j^2 + \sum_j w_j}{W^2} = \frac{\tau^2\sum_j w_j^2 + W}{W^2}.
\] Hence \(\mathbb{E}[W\bar\delta_w^2] = \tau^2 \frac{\sum_j w_j^2}{W} + 1\). Subtracting, \[
\mathbb{E}[Q] = \big(\tau^2 W + k\big) - \Big(\tau^2 \tfrac{\sum_j w_j^2}{W} + 1\Big) = (k - 1) + \tau^2
\Big(W - \tfrac{\sum_j w_j^2}{W}\Big),
\] which is Equation 13.5. Finally \(c = (W^2 - \sum_i w_i^2)/W\), and since \(W^2 = (\sum_i w_i)^2 = \sum_i
w_i^2 + \sum_{i \ne j} w_i w_j\) with all \(w_i > 0\), the cross sum is strictly positive once \(k \ge 2\), so \(c > 0\). \(\square\)


Remark. Reader translation. This is the first point in the chapter where trials are allowed to genuinely differ: the term \(b_i\), with variance \(\tau^2\), is the real effect difference of trial \(i\) (its population, protocol, or setting), as opposed to the sampling noise \(\varepsilon_i\). The formula \(\mathbb{E}[Q] = (k - 1) + \tau^2 c\) says \(Q\) carries a signal (\(\tau^2 c\)) sitting on a baseline (\(k - 1\)): with no heterogeneity \(Q\) averages \(k - 1\), and each unit of heterogeneity variance \(\tau^2\) inflates it by the known constant \(c\). Solving that relation for \(\tau^2\) is exactly how the DerSimonian-Laird estimator of Section Section 13.5 will work. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Setting \(\tau^2 = 0\) recovers \(\mathbb{E}[Q] = k - 1\), consistent with Theorem 13.2. The coefficient \(c\) depends only on the known weights, a fact we exploit repeatedly below.

title: 13  Pairwise Meta-Analysis
text:
13.3 The \(I^2\) statistic
Cochran’s \(Q\) has a defect as a description of heterogeneity: its size grows with the number of studies, so a large \(Q\) may reflect many studies rather than severe heterogeneity. Higgins and Thompson proposed a scale-free and dimension-free summary.
From detection to description to estimation. The next three sections form one arc, and it helps to name the three roles up front. \(Q\) answers yes or no; \(I^2\) puts the answer on a \(0\) to \(100\%\) scale that does not grow with the number of studies; and \(\tau^2\) is the quantity the random-effects model actually needs.








Statistic
Section
What it does




Cochran’s \(Q\)
Section 13.2
detects excess disagreement (is there heterogeneity?)


\(I^2\)
Section 13.3
describes its share (what fraction of variability is heterogeneity?)


\(\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}\), \(\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{REML}}\)
Section 13.5, Section 13.6
estimate the between-study variance \(\tau^2\)




Definition 13.3 (The \(I^2\) and \(H^2\) heterogeneity statistics) Given Cochran’s \(Q\) on \(k\) studies, define \[
H^2 = \frac{Q}{k - 1}, \qquad I^2 = \max\!\left\{0,\; \frac{Q - (k - 1)}{Q}\right\} = \max\!\left\{0,\;
1 - \frac{1}{H^2}\right\}.
\tag{13.6}\] The statistic \(I^2\), usually reported as a percentage, lies in \([0, 1]\) and is interpreted as the proportion of the total variability in the effect estimates that is due to between-study heterogeneity rather than to within-study sampling error. (Corresponds to C.3 in the proof catalogue.)


Remark. Reader translation, and a notation warning. \(I^2\) rescales \(Q\) so that it no longer grows merely because there are more studies: it reports the share of the observed variability that exceeds what sampling error alone would produce. Note a symbol clash: the \(H^2\) here is the Higgins-Thompson heterogeneity ratio, unrelated to the hat matrix \(H\) of Chapter 6. The letters collide but the meanings do not. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. What \(I^2\) is not. \(I^2\) is not the probability that heterogeneity exists, not the percentage of trials that are biased or discordant, not the amount by which the pooled effect is wrong, and not a decision rule on its own. An \(I^2\) of \(30\%\) does not mean “\(30\%\) of the studies disagree”; it means that, of the spread seen among the estimates, roughly \(30\%\) is in excess of sampling error. With few studies \(I^2\) is itself estimated very imprecisely, so the conventional \(25/50/75\%\) labels are rough descriptions, not test thresholds. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The interpretation is made precise by replacing the random quantity \(Q\) with its expectation and reading off a variance-ratio.

Proposition 13.3 (\(I^2\) as a variance ratio) Under the heterogeneity model of Proposition 13.2 with \(\tau^2 \ge 0\) and \(k \ge 2\), define the typical within-study variance \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{typ}} = (k - 1)/c\), with \(c\) as in Equation 13.5. Replacing \(Q\) by \(\mathbb{E}[Q]\) in Equation 13.6 gives the population analogue \[
I^2_{\ast} := \frac{\mathbb{E}[Q] - (k - 1)}{\mathbb{E}[Q]} = \frac{\tau^2 c}{(k - 1) + \tau^2 c}
= \frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2 + \sigma^2_{\mathrm{typ}}} .
\tag{13.7}\] Thus \(I^2_\ast\) is the fraction of total variance \(\tau^2 + \sigma^2_{\mathrm{typ}}\) attributable to the between-study component \(\tau^2\). It equals \(0\) when \(\tau^2 = 0\), increases monotonically in \(\tau^2\), and tends to \(1\) as \(\tau^2 \to \infty\).


Proof. By Equation 13.5, \(\mathbb{E}[Q] - (k - 1) = \tau^2 c\), so \(I^2_\ast = \tau^2 c/((k-1) + \tau^2 c)\). Dividing numerator and denominator by \(c\) and writing \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{typ}} = (k - 1)/c\) gives the middle and right expressions of Equation 13.7. The map \(t \mapsto t/(t + \sigma^2_{\mathrm{typ}})\) is strictly increasing on \([0, \infty)\) with value \(0\) at \(t = 0\) and limit \(1\) at infinity, applied at \(t = \tau^2\). \(\square\)


Remark. The quantity \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{typ}} = (k-1)/c\) is a weighted-harmonic-type average of the \(s_i^2\), and in the special case of equal within-study variances \(s_i^2 \equiv s^2\) one computes \(c = (k - 1)/s^2\), whence \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{typ}} = s^2\) exactly: \(I^2_\ast = \tau^2/(\tau^2 + s^2)\) is then literally the intraclass correlation of the random-effects model. The conventional benchmarks are \(I^2 \approx 25\%\) low, \(50\%\) moderate, \(75\%\) high; they are descriptive rules of thumb, not test thresholds, and \(I^2\) itself is estimated with considerable uncertainty when \(k\) is small. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. Read Equation 13.7 as \(I^2_\ast = \tau^2 / (\tau^2 + \sigma^2_{\mathrm{typ}})\), the between-study variance divided by the total. The denominator’s second piece, \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{typ}} = (k-1)/c\), is just a single “typical” within-study variance standing in for the whole collection of \(s_i^2\): when the \(s_i^2\) are all equal to \(s^2\) it is \(s^2\), and in general it is a precision-weighted average of them (the subscript “typ” is only a label for that stand-in, nothing deeper). On the running trio, \(Q = 4.82\) gives \[
I^2 = \frac{Q - (k-1)}{Q} = \frac{4.82 - 2}{4.82} = 0.585,
\] about \(59\%\): a moderate-to-high share, consistent with the visibly scattered forest plot. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 13  Pairwise Meta-Analysis
text:
13.4 The random-effects model
When \(Q\) signals heterogeneity, the fixed-effect premise that all studies estimate one \(\theta\) is untenable. The random-effects model lets each study have its own effect, drawn from a common distribution.
Fixed effect versus random effects: the contrast that matters most. Before the definition, it is worth stating plainly what changes, because this is the distinction a health researcher most needs and the one on which the later ITC methods hinge.








Aspect
Fixed-effect model
Random-effects model




Assumption
one common true effect \(\theta\) for all trials
each trial has its own effect \(\theta_i\), drawn from a distribution


What is pooled
that single \(\theta\)
the mean \(\theta\) of the distribution of trial effects


Weight for trial \(i\)
\(w_i = 1/s_i^2\)
\(\tilde w_i = 1/(s_i^2 + \tau^2)\)


Meaning of the summary
the effect, estimated more precisely
the average effect across the population of trial settings


When heterogeneity is large
untenable; interval too narrow
weights flatten, interval widens honestly


Why it matters for ITC
licenses transitivity: one effect transports
forces the question which population’s effect (Chapters 12, 15)



The mathematical content of the right-hand column is one sentence: adding \(\tau^2\) to every \(s_i^2\) shrinks the weights toward equality, so a single dominant precise trial no longer controls the pooled estimate, the summary widens to admit real between-trial variation, and the target of inference changes from “the common effect” to “the mean of the trial-specific effects.” That last change is not cosmetic: a mean of effects is an average over some population of trials, and pinning down which population is the whole subject of Part IV.

Definition 13.4 (Random-effects meta-analysis model) The random-effects model for \(k\) study estimates is the two-level Gaussian hierarchy \[
\hat\theta_i \mid \theta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_i, s_i^2), \qquad \theta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta,
\tau^2), \qquad i = 1, \dots, k,
\tag{13.8}\] with the \(\theta_i\) independent of one another and of the sampling errors, and the \(s_i^2 > 0\) known. Here \(\theta\) is the mean effect across the population of studies and \(\tau^2 \ge 0\) is the between-study variance (heterogeneity variance). Marginalizing over the study effects, \[
\hat\theta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, s_i^2 + \tau^2) \quad \text{independently across } i.
\tag{13.9}\] This is the meta-analytic instance of the general random-effects construction of Definition 8.3; the fixed-effect model Equation 13.1 is the boundary case \(\tau^2 = 0\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. The two lines of Equation 13.8 read: within trial \(i\), the estimate scatters around that trial’s own true effect \(\theta_i\) with variance \(s_i^2\); and the trial’s own effect scatters around a grand mean \(\theta\) with variance \(\tau^2\). Marginally, each estimate then has variance \(s_i^2 + \tau^2\), its own sampling error plus the heterogeneity. So random-effects weighting is just inverse-variance weighting again, with the enlarged variance \(s_i^2 + \tau^2\) in place of \(s_i^2\). Setting \(\tau^2 = 0\) collapses everything back to the fixed-effect model, and the target \(\theta\) is now the mean of the trial effects, an average over some population of trial settings, not a single shared value. Which population that is becomes a central question for the transportability of Chapter 12 and the networks of Chapter 15. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Writing \(\tilde w_i = 1/(s_i^2 + \tau^2)\) for the random-effects weights, the marginal log-likelihood of \((\theta, \tau^2)\) from Equation 13.9 is \[
\ell(\theta, \tau^2) = -\frac12 \sum_{i=1}^k \log\!\big(2\pi(s_i^2 + \tau^2)\big) - \frac12 \sum_{i=1}^k
\frac{(\hat\theta_i - \theta)^2}{s_i^2 + \tau^2} .
\tag{13.10}\] Before estimating the parameters we must check they are identifiable, that is, that distinct parameter values give distinct data distributions. Otherwise no amount of data could distinguish them.

Proposition 13.4 (Identifiability of the random-effects parameters) Fix known \(s_1^2, \dots, s_k^2 > 0\) with \(k \ge 1\). The map \[
\Psi: (\theta, \tau^2) \in \mathbb{R}\times[0, \infty) \longmapsto \bigotimes_{i=1}^k \mathcal{N}(\theta,
s_i^2 + \tau^2)
\] is injective. Hence \((\theta, \tau^2)\) is identifiable from the joint law of \((\hat\theta_1, \dots,
\hat\theta_k)\). (Corresponds to C.4 in the proof catalogue.)


Proof. Suppose \(\Psi(\theta, \tau^2) = \Psi(\theta', \tau'^2)\). Equality of the joint laws implies equality of every marginal. The first marginal is \(\mathcal{N}(\theta, s_1^2 + \tau^2) = \mathcal{N}(\theta', s_1^2 +
\tau'^2)\); equating means gives \(\theta = \theta'\), and equating variances gives \(s_1^2 + \tau^2 = s_1^2
+ \tau'^2\), hence \(\tau^2 = \tau'^2\). Thus \((\theta, \tau^2) = (\theta', \tau'^2)\), and \(\Psi\) is injective. \(\square\)


Remark. Identifiability is not estimability, and the role of known \(s_i^2\). The proposition says the parameters are determined by the data distribution; it does not say they can be estimated well from a single realization. With \(k = 1\), \(\tau^2 = \mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_1) - s_1^2\) is identified, yet one draw of \(\hat\theta_1\) carries essentially no information about its own variance, so no consistent estimator of \(\tau^2\) exists. Consistency of the moment and likelihood estimators below requires \(k \to \infty\); in practice \(\tau^2\) is estimated stably only with \(k \gtrsim 5\) studies, and the catalogue’s working condition “\(k \ge 2\) with the \(s_i^2\) not all equal” is the practical requirement for \(\hat\tau^2\) to draw on more than a single contrast and to behave well. The hypothesis that the \(s_i^2\) are known is essential to the proof: if the within-study variances were free parameters, only the sums \(s_i^2 + \tau^2\) would be identified from Equation 13.9 and \(\tau^2\) would be confounded with the \(s_i^2\). Meta-analysis breaks the confounding by estimating each \(s_i^2\) within study \(i\) from its \(n_i\) patients, where it is consistent as \(n_i \to \infty\), and then treating it as fixed. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation, concretely. “Identifiable but not estimable” is less mysterious than it sounds. With a single trial you could write down \(\hat\tau^2 = \hat\theta_1^2 - s_1^2\) as a formal solution, but one number cannot estimate a variance: you need several trials to see the spread that \(\tau^2\) describes. This is why heterogeneity is genuinely hard to estimate in the small meta-analyses typical of health technology assessment, and why the rules of thumb (roughly \(k \gtrsim 5\) trials for a stable \(\hat\tau^2\), and at least \(k \ge 2\) with unequal \(s_i^2\) for the estimator to draw on more than a single comparison) are practical guidance rather than theorems; the “\(5\)” is an empirical convention from simulation studies, not a derived constant. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

We now turn to estimating \(\tau^2\). Two estimators dominate practice: the closed-form method-of-moments estimator of DerSimonian and Laird, and the restricted maximum likelihood estimator.
