title: 13  Pairwise Meta-Analysis
text:
13.5 Estimating the heterogeneity variance: DerSimonian-Laird
The method of moments equates the observed \(Q\) to its expected value Equation 13.5 and solves for \(\tau^2\).
The idea in one line: the DerSimonian-Laird estimator converts the excess of \(Q\) over its null mean into an estimate of \(\tau^2\). Since Equation 13.5 says \(\mathbb{E}[Q] = (k-1) + \tau^2 c\), the excess \(Q - (k-1)\) is on average \(\tau^2 c\), so dividing the observed excess by the known constant \(c\) inverts the relation. Here \(c\) is the conversion factor between excess \(Q\) and heterogeneity variance; it depends only on the weights, so the same excess \(Q\) implies more or less \(\tau^2\) according to how precise the trials are.

Theorem 13.3 (The DerSimonian-Laird estimator) Under the random-effects model Equation 13.8, the method-of-moments estimator obtained by equating \(Q\) to \(\mathbb{E}[Q] = (k - 1) + \tau^2 c\) is \[
\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}} = \max\!\left\{0,\; \frac{Q - (k - 1)}{c}\right\}, \qquad c = \sum_i w_i -
\frac{\sum_i w_i^2}{\sum_i w_i}, \quad w_i = \frac{1}{s_i^2}.
\tag{13.11}\] The untruncated version \(\tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}} = (Q - (k-1))/c\) is exactly unbiased for \(\tau^2\), and the truncated estimator Equation 13.11 is biased upward. (Corresponds to C.5 in the proof catalogue.)


Proof. Solving \(Q = (k - 1) + \tau^2 c\) for \(\tau^2\) gives \(\tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}} = (Q - (k - 1))/c\); the truncation \(\max\{0, \cdot\}\) enforces the constraint \(\tau^2 \ge 0\). Since \(c\) depends only on the known weights and is therefore a constant, Equation 13.5 gives \[
\mathbb{E}[\tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}] = \frac{\mathbb{E}[Q] - (k - 1)}{c} = \frac{\big((k - 1) + \tau^2
c\big) - (k - 1)}{c} = \tau^2 ,
\] so the untruncated estimator is exactly unbiased; note this uses only the second-moment assumptions of Proposition 13.2, not Gaussianity. The truncated estimator satisfies \(\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}} =
\max\{0, \tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}\} \ge \tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}\) pointwise, with strict inequality on the event \(\{\tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}} < 0\}\), which has positive probability whenever \(\tau^2\) is small. Taking expectations, \(\mathbb{E}[\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}] \ge \mathbb{E}[\tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}] =
\tau^2\), with strict inequality there, so truncation introduces upward bias. \(\square\)


Remark. The DerSimonian-Laird estimator is the historical default and remains ubiquitous because it is non-iterative. Its exact unbiasedness before truncation is a genuine finite-sample property, not merely asymptotic. Consistency as \(k \to \infty\) holds under mild conditions on the weights (for example \(w_i\) bounded above and below by positive constants), since then \(\mathrm{Var}(\tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}})
\to 0\); we cite DerSimonian and Laird (1986) for the original argument and Dias et al. (2018) for the meta-analytic context. The price of the closed form is statistical: in small samples DL can be inefficient relative to likelihood-based estimators, which motivates REML. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation, and the running trio. DerSimonian-Laird is the non-iterative default: compute \(Q\), subtract its null mean \(k - 1\), divide by \(c\), and floor at zero. For the running trio, \(c = W - \sum_i w_i^2/W = 137.5 - 10781.25/137.5 = 59.1\), so \[
\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}} = \frac{Q - (k-1)}{c} = \frac{4.82 - 2}{59.1} = 0.048 .
\] Feeding this back as \(\tilde w_i = 1/(s_i^2 + 0.048)\) shrinks the weights toward one another: study \(C\)’s share of the total weight falls from \(73\%\) (fixed-effect) to \(47\%\) (random-effects), and the pooled estimate moves from \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}} = 0.264\) up to \(\hat\theta_R = 0.365\), no longer dragged so hard toward the one precise trial. This down-weighting of the dominant trial is the entire practical meaning of “random effects gives smaller trials more say.” \(\blacktriangleleft\)
crumbs: Part III: Meta-Analysis and Network Meta-Analysis

title: 13  Pairwise Meta-Analysis
text:
13.6 Estimating the heterogeneity variance: REML
Maximizing the marginal likelihood Equation 13.10 jointly in \((\theta, \tau^2)\) gives the maximum likelihood estimator of \(\tau^2\), which is biased downward because it ignores the degree of freedom spent estimating \(\theta\), exactly the \(n\)-versus-\((n-1)\) phenomenon of the ordinary sample variance. Restricted maximum likelihood (REML, Definition 8.4) removes the bias by basing inference for the variance on error contrasts, linear combinations of the data orthogonal to the mean, whose distribution is free of \(\theta\).
What REML is trying to fix (read this before the derivation). Plain maximum likelihood maximizes Equation 13.10 in \(\theta\) and \(\tau^2\) at once. The trouble is that it estimates \(\theta\) from the same data and then acts as if \(\theta\) were known, spending a degree of freedom it does not pay for; the result is a \(\tau^2\) biased downward, exactly as the naive sample variance \(\frac1n \sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2\) underestimates the truth and must be corrected to the \(\frac{1}{n-1}\) version. A downward-biased \(\tau^2\) is dangerous for a decision-maker because it makes the pooled interval too narrow, overstating confidence. REML fixes this by estimating \(\tau^2\) from error contrasts, combinations of the data that carry no information about \(\theta\) because they are orthogonal to the mean, so no degree of freedom is silently spent. The payoff is visible in the sanity check right after the theorem: when all trials have equal variance, REML reproduces the honest \(\frac{1}{k-1}\) divisor exactly. The derivation below is the densest in the chapter, but the single fact that makes it work is that the random-effects-weighted residuals sum to zero, which annihilates the awkward chain-rule term. Read the equal-variance remark first if the general algebra feels like a wall.

Theorem 13.4 (REML estimator of the heterogeneity variance) Consider the random-effects model Equation 13.8, written as \(\mathbf{y} \sim \mathcal{N}_k(\mathbf{1}_k
\theta, \mathbf{V})\) with \(\mathbf{y} = (\hat\theta_1, \dots, \hat\theta_k)^\top\) and \(\mathbf{V} =
\mathrm{diag}(s_i^2 + \tau^2)\). Writing \(\tilde w_i = 1/(s_i^2 + \tau^2)\) and \(\hat\theta_R(\tau^2) =
\sum_i \tilde w_i \hat\theta_i / \sum_i \tilde w_i\), the restricted log-likelihood of \(\tau^2\) is, up to an additive constant, \[
\ell_R(\tau^2) = -\frac12 \sum_{i=1}^k \log(s_i^2 + \tau^2) - \frac12 \log\!\Big(\sum_{i=1}^k \tilde w_i
\Big) - \frac12 \sum_{i=1}^k \tilde w_i \big(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R(\tau^2)\big)^2 .
\tag{13.12}\] Its maximizer \(\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{REML}}\) (truncated at \(0\)) solves the estimating equation \[
\sum_{i=1}^k \tilde w_i^2 \big(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R\big)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^k \tilde w_i -
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \tilde w_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^k \tilde w_i},
\tag{13.13}\] equivalently the fixed point \[
\tau^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \tilde w_i^2 \big[(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R)^2 - s_i^2\big]}{\sum_{i=1}^k
\tilde w_i^2} + \frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^k \tilde w_i} .
\tag{13.14}\] (Corresponds to C.6 in the proof catalogue.)


Proof. For the Gaussian linear model \(\mathbf{y} \sim \mathcal{N}_k(\mathbf{X}\theta, \mathbf{V})\) with \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{1}_k\), the general restricted log-likelihood established for Definition 8.4 is, up to an additive constant, \[
\ell_R = -\frac12 \log\det\mathbf{V} - \frac12 \log\det(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}) -
\frac12 (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat\theta_R)^\top \mathbf{V}^{-1}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat\theta_R),
\] with \(\hat\theta_R = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{y}\) the generalized least squares estimator. Specialize to \(\mathbf{V} = \mathrm{diag}(s_i^2 + \tau^2)\), \(\mathbf{V}^{-1} = \mathrm{diag}(\tilde w_i)\), and \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{1}_k\). Then \(\log\det\mathbf{V} =
\sum_i \log(s_i^2 + \tau^2)\); \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{1}_k^\top
\mathrm{diag}(\tilde w_i)\mathbf{1}_k = \sum_i \tilde w_i\), so \(\log\det(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}
\mathbf{X}) = \log(\sum_i \tilde w_i)\); the GLS estimator is \(\hat\theta_R = \sum_i \tilde w_i \hat\theta_i
/\sum_i \tilde w_i\); and the quadratic form is \(\sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R)^2\). Substituting yields Equation 13.12.
Now differentiate Equation 13.12 in \(\tau^2\). Abbreviate \(v_i = s_i^2 + \tau^2\), so \(\tilde w_i =
v_i^{-1}\) and \(\mathrm{d}\tilde w_i/\mathrm{d}\tau^2 = -\tilde w_i^2\), and write \(r_i = \hat\theta_i -
\hat\theta_R\) and \(S_1 = \sum_i \tilde w_i\), \(S_2 = \sum_i \tilde w_i^2\). The three terms differentiate as follows.
First term. Since \(\mathrm{d}\log v_i/\mathrm{d}\tau^2 = \tilde w_i\), \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\tau^2}\Big(-\tfrac12 \sum_i \log v_i\Big) = -\tfrac12 \sum_i \tilde w_i =
-\tfrac12 S_1 .
\]
Second term. Since \(\mathrm{d}S_1/\mathrm{d}\tau^2 = \sum_i (-\tilde w_i^2) = -S_2\), \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\tau^2}\Big(-\tfrac12 \log S_1\Big) = -\tfrac12 \frac{-S_2}{S_1} = \tfrac12
\frac{S_2}{S_1} .
\]
Third term. Here \(r_i = \hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R(\tau^2)\) depends on \(\tau^2\) through \(\hat\theta_R\). Differentiating, \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\tau^2}\Big(-\tfrac12 \sum_i \tilde w_i r_i^2\Big) = -\tfrac12 \sum_i\Big[
\frac{\mathrm{d}\tilde w_i}{\mathrm{d}\tau^2} r_i^2 + \tilde w_i \cdot 2 r_i \frac{\mathrm{d}r_i}
{\mathrm{d}\tau^2}\Big] = -\tfrac12\Big[ -\sum_i \tilde w_i^2 r_i^2 - 2\frac{\mathrm{d}\hat\theta_R}
{\mathrm{d}\tau^2}\sum_i \tilde w_i r_i\Big].
\] The crucial simplification is that the chain-rule term through \(\hat\theta_R\) vanishes: by the very definition of the GLS estimator, the random-effects-weighted residuals sum to zero, \[
\sum_i \tilde w_i r_i = \sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R) = \sum_i \tilde w_i \hat\theta_i -
\hat\theta_R \sum_i \tilde w_i = 0 ,
\] so regardless of \(\mathrm{d}\hat\theta_R/\mathrm{d}\tau^2\) the second summand is \(0\). Hence the third term contributes \(+\tfrac12 \sum_i \tilde w_i^2 r_i^2 = \tfrac12 \sum_i \tilde w_i^2 r_i^2\).
Adding the three contributions, the REML score is \[
\ell_R'(\tau^2) = -\tfrac12 S_1 + \tfrac12 \frac{S_2}{S_1} + \tfrac12 \sum_i \tilde w_i^2 r_i^2 .
\] Setting \(\ell_R'(\tau^2) = 0\) gives \(\sum_i \tilde w_i^2 r_i^2 = S_1 - S_2/S_1\), which is Equation 13.13. To reach the fixed-point form, multiply the target identity \(\tau^2 = \frac{1}{S_2}\sum_i \tilde w_i^2
(r_i^2 - s_i^2) + 1/S_1\) by \(S_2\) and use \(s_i^2 + \tau^2 = 1/\tilde w_i\): \[
\tau^2 S_2 + \sum_i \tilde w_i^2 s_i^2 - \frac{S_2}{S_1} = \sum_i \tilde w_i^2(\tau^2 + s_i^2) -
\frac{S_2}{S_1} = \sum_i \tilde w_i^2 \cdot \frac{1}{\tilde w_i} - \frac{S_2}{S_1} = S_1 - \frac{S_2}{S_1},
\] so \(\sum_i \tilde w_i^2 r_i^2 = S_1 - S_2/S_1\) is equivalent to Equation 13.14. The estimating equation Equation 13.13 is solved by iterating Equation 13.14, recomputing \(\tilde w_i\) and \(\hat\theta_R\) at each step from the current \(\tau^2\), starting from a nonnegative value such as \(\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}\), and truncating any negative iterate at \(0\). \(\square\)


Remark. Equal-variance check. When the within-study variances are equal, \(s_i^2 \equiv s^2\), all random-effects weights coincide, \(\tilde w_i \equiv \tilde w = 1/(s^2 + \tau^2)\), and \(\hat\theta_R =
\bar{\hat\theta} = \frac1k\sum_i \hat\theta_i\). Then Equation 13.13 reads \(\tilde w^2 \sum_i (\hat\theta_i -
\bar{\hat\theta})^2 = k\tilde w - (k\tilde w^2)/(k\tilde w) = (k - 1)\tilde w\), that is \[
s^2 + \tau^2 = \frac{1}{\tilde w} = \frac{1}{k - 1}\sum_{i=1}^k (\hat\theta_i - \bar{\hat\theta})^2 ,
\qquad \text{so} \qquad \hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{REML}} = \frac{1}{k - 1}\sum_{i=1}^k (\hat\theta_i -
\bar{\hat\theta})^2 - s^2 .
\] The divisor is \(k - 1\), not \(k\): REML reproduces the unbiased sample-variance correction, exactly the one-sample phenomenon of Theorem 8.8 with \(n - 1 = k - 1\) degrees of freedom. This is the sanity check that REML has done its job. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. REML by iteration, on the running trio. The fixed point Equation 13.14 is solved by starting from a nonnegative guess and recomputing. Take the trio \(C, D, E\) and start at the DerSimonian-Laird value \(\tau^2_{(0)} = 0.048\). Each step recomputes the weights \(\tilde w_i = 1/(s_i^2 + \tau^2)\), then \(\hat\theta_R = \sum_i \tilde w_i \hat\theta_i / \sum_i \tilde w_i\), then the right-hand side of Equation 13.14. Iterating gives approximately \[
\tau^2_{(0)} = 0.048 \;\to\; 0.046 \;\to\; 0.0454 \;\to\; 0.0452 \;\to\; \hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{REML}}
\approx 0.045,
\] converging in a handful of steps. Here REML settles just below DerSimonian-Laird, and the two agree to the second decimal; the point is only that “solve the estimating equation” is a short loop, not a mystery. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 13  Pairwise Meta-Analysis
text:
13.7 The Hartung-Knapp adjustment
Once \(\tau^2\) has been estimated, the random-effects summary is the IVW estimator with random-effects weights, \[
\hat\theta_R = \frac{\sum_i \tilde w_i \hat\theta_i}{\sum_i \tilde w_i}, \qquad \tilde w_i = \frac{1}
{s_i^2 + \hat\tau^2}, \qquad \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\theta_R) = \frac{1}{\sum_i \tilde w_i}.
\] The conventional Wald interval \(\hat\theta_R \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\theta_R)}\) treats the weights as known and the Gaussian quantile as exact; both approximations fail when \(k\) is small, and the interval is then too narrow. The Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustment fixes the calibration by estimating an overall scale and switching to a \(t\) reference distribution.
The idea first (why the usual interval is too narrow). When only a few trials are available, two things the Wald interval pretends to know are actually uncertain: the heterogeneity \(\tau^2\) baked into the weights, and the assumption that a normal quantile is exact. Pretending we know them makes the interval too short, so its true coverage falls below the advertised \(95\%\); and few trials is the typical case in health technology assessment. Hartung-Knapp repairs the calibration with a device from ordinary regression. It treats the random-effects fit as a one-parameter working model \(\hat\theta_i = \theta + e_i\) with \(\mathrm{Var}(e_i) = \sigma^2/\tilde w_i\), in which the trials share one unknown overall scale \(\sigma^2\); the real random-effects model is the special case \(\sigma^2 = 1\). Instead of imposing \(\sigma^2 = 1\) (the Wald choice), it estimates \(\sigma^2\) from the weighted residuals, exactly as a regression estimates its error variance, and pays for that estimate by widening the quantile from the normal \(z\) to a Student \(t_{k-1}\). That is the whole idea; the theorem shows the resulting interval is exact under the working model.

Theorem 13.5 (Exactness of the Hartung-Knapp \(t\) interval under a working model) Suppose \(\hat\theta_i = \theta + e_i\) with \(e_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2/\tilde w_i)\) independent, \(i = 1, \dots, k \ge 2\), where the weights \(\tilde w_i > 0\) are known and \(\sigma^2 > 0\) is an unknown common scale. Then, with \[
\hat\theta_R = \frac{\sum_i \tilde w_i \hat\theta_i}{\sum_i \tilde w_i}, \qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{HK}}(\hat\theta_R) = \frac{1}{k - 1}\,\frac{\sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i
- \hat\theta_R)^2}{\sum_j \tilde w_j},
\tag{13.15}\] the Hartung-Knapp statistic has an exact Student distribution, \[
T_{\mathrm{HK}} = \frac{\hat\theta_R - \theta}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{HK}}(\hat\theta_R)}}
\sim t_{k-1},
\] so \(\hat\theta_R \pm t_{k-1,\,1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{HK}}(\hat\theta_R)}\) is an exact \(1 - \alpha\) confidence interval for \(\theta\). (Corresponds to C.7 in the proof catalogue.)


Proof. Whiten the working model. Put \(\tilde y_i = \sqrt{\tilde w_i}\,\hat\theta_i\) and \(x_i = \sqrt{\tilde w_i}\), and let \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}} = (\tilde y_1, \dots, \tilde y_k)^\top\), \(\mathbf{X} = (x_1, \dots, x_k)^\top
\in \mathbb{R}^{k\times 1}\). Multiplying \(\hat\theta_i = \theta + e_i\) by \(\sqrt{\tilde w_i}\) gives \[
\tilde y_i = \theta\, x_i + \tilde e_i, \qquad \tilde e_i = \sqrt{\tilde w_i}\, e_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,
\sigma^2) \ \text{independent},
\] which is the Gaussian linear model of Definition 6.1 with \(n = k\) observations, \(p = 1\) coefficient \(\theta\), homoscedastic variance \(\sigma^2\), and full column rank. Here \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} =
\sum_i \tilde w_i\) and \(\mathbf{X}^\top\tilde{\mathbf{y}} = \sum_i \tilde w_i \hat\theta_i\), so the OLS estimator is \(\hat\theta_R = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\tilde{\mathbf{y}} = \sum_i
\tilde w_i \hat\theta_i/\sum_i \tilde w_i\), matching the stated \(\hat\theta_R\). The residual sum of squares is \[
\mathrm{RSS} = \sum_i (\tilde y_i - \hat\theta_R x_i)^2 = \sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R)^2,
\] and the unbiased error-variance estimate (Theorem 6.4) is \(s^2 = \mathrm{RSS}/(k - 1) =
\frac{1}{k-1}\sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R)^2\), with \(\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{HK}}
(\hat\theta_R) = s^2 \,(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1} = s^2/\sum_i \tilde w_i\), which is Equation 13.15. Applying the \(t\)-statistic theorem Theorem 6.8 with contrast \(\mathbf{c} = 1\) (a scalar) gives directly \[
\frac{\hat\theta_R - \theta}{s\sqrt{(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}}} = \frac{\hat\theta_R - \theta}
{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{HK}}(\hat\theta_R)}} = T_{\mathrm{HK}} \sim t_{k-1}.
\] Inverting the two-sided \(t\) test yields the stated confidence interval. \(\square\)


Remark. Why this calibrates the random-effects interval. The actual random-effects model Equation 13.8, with \(\tau^2\) replaced by its estimate, corresponds to the working model with the “true” scale \(\sigma^2 = 1\), because then \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_i) = 1/\tilde w_i\). The Wald interval imposes \(\sigma^2 = 1\) and uses a normal quantile. Hartung-Knapp instead estimates \(\sigma^2\) from the weighted residuals and uses a \(t_{k-1}\) quantile, exactly as one estimates the error variance in a regression rather than assuming it. Writing \(q = \frac{1}{k-1}\sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R)^2\) for the estimated scale, the two variance estimators are related by \[
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{HK}}(\hat\theta_R) = q \cdot \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\theta_R), \qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\theta_R) = \frac{1}{\sum_i \tilde w_i},
\] so Hartung-Knapp rescales the Wald variance by the data-driven factor \(q\) and widens the quantile from \(z\) to \(t_{k-1}\). When the random-effects model fits, \(q \approx 1\) and the adjustment is mild for large \(k\); for small \(k\) the wider \(t\) quantile restores coverage that the Wald interval loses. The factor \(q\) can fall below \(1\), occasionally yielding a Hartung-Knapp interval narrower than the Wald interval; a common conservative safeguard takes \(\max\{1, q\}\). The method is recommended whenever \(k \le 10\) (Dias et al. (2018)). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Running trio: the interval to report. With only \(k = 3\) trials the difference is dramatic. The trio’s random-effects fit gives \(\hat\theta_R = 0.365\) with \(\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\theta_R) = 1/\sum_i
\tilde w_i = 0.027\), so the Wald interval is \(0.365 \pm 1.96\sqrt{0.027} = (0.04, 0.69)\). The scale factor is \(q = \frac{1}{k-1}\sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R)^2 = 0.79\), giving \(\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{HK}} = q\,\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\theta_R) = 0.0215\). Even though \(q < 1\) shrinks the variance a little, the Student quantile \(t_{2,\,0.975} = 4.303\) (a heavy penalty for having only two degrees of freedom) dominates, and the interval \[
0.365 \pm 4.303\sqrt{0.0215} = (-0.27,\, 1.00)
\] is far wider than the Wald interval, and honest about how little three trials pin down. A cautious analyst reports the wider one. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 13  Pairwise Meta-Analysis
text:
13.8 Bayesian meta-analysis
The Bayesian treatment places priors on the parameters and reports the posterior. It is the framework that generalizes most cleanly to networks (Chapter 15) and to the multilevel models of Part V, and it handles the uncertainty in \(\tau^2\) coherently rather than by plug-in. We work the conjugate core: with \(\tau^2\) fixed, the mean effect has a closed-form Gaussian posterior.
Concretely, the network meta-analysis models of Chapter 15 and the multilevel models of Part V are Bayesian hierarchical models fit by Markov chain Monte Carlo; the conjugacy proved here is the one piece of them that can be done by hand, and it is worth seeing once in closed form before the machine takes over.

Theorem 13.6 (Normal-normal conjugacy for the mean effect) Take the random-effects model Equation 13.8 with the conjugate prior \(\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_0,
\sigma_0^2)\) on the mean effect and any prior \(\pi(\tau^2)\) on the heterogeneity variance. Conditional on \(\tau^2\) and the data, the posterior of \(\theta\) is Gaussian, \[
\theta \mid \hat\theta_1, \dots, \hat\theta_k, \tau^2 \sim \mathcal{N}(m_\ast, v_\ast), \qquad
\frac{1}{v_\ast} = \frac{1}{\sigma_0^2} + \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{1}{s_i^2 + \tau^2}, \qquad
m_\ast = v_\ast\Big(\frac{\theta_0}{\sigma_0^2} + \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{\hat\theta_i}{s_i^2 + \tau^2}\Big).
\tag{13.16}\] (Corresponds to C.8 in the proof catalogue.)


Proof. Given \(\tau^2\), the marginal model Equation 13.9 makes the \(\hat\theta_i\) independent with \(\hat\theta_i \mid \theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, s_i^2 + \tau^2)\) and known variances \(v_i := s_i^2 +
\tau^2\). We process the observations sequentially and invoke normal-normal conjugacy Theorem 8.3 at each step. Start from the prior \(\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu^{(0)}, \varsigma^{(0)2})\) with \(\mu^{(0)} = \theta_0\) and \(\varsigma^{(0)2} = \sigma_0^2\). Suppose after incorporating \(\hat\theta_1,
\dots, \hat\theta_{i-1}\) the posterior is \(\mathcal{N}(\mu^{(i-1)}, \varsigma^{(i-1)2})\). Treating this as the prior and observing \(\hat\theta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, v_i)\), Theorem 8.3 gives the updated posterior \(\mathcal{N}(\mu^{(i)}, \varsigma^{(i)2})\) with \[
\frac{1}{\varsigma^{(i)2}} = \frac{1}{\varsigma^{(i-1)2}} + \frac{1}{v_i}, \qquad \frac{\mu^{(i)}}
{\varsigma^{(i)2}} = \frac{\mu^{(i-1)}}{\varsigma^{(i-1)2}} + \frac{\hat\theta_i}{v_i} .
\] These recursions are additive, so after all \(k\) updates \[
\frac{1}{\varsigma^{(k)2}} = \frac{1}{\sigma_0^2} + \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{1}{v_i}, \qquad \frac{\mu^{(k)}}
{\varsigma^{(k)2}} = \frac{\theta_0}{\sigma_0^2} + \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{\hat\theta_i}{v_i} .
\] Identifying \(v_\ast = \varsigma^{(k)2}\) and \(m_\ast = \mu^{(k)}\) gives Equation 13.16. The conclusion that the posterior is exactly Gaussian at each step, hence at the last, is the content of Theorem 8.3. \(\square\)


Remark. Reader translation. Read Equation 13.16 as precision bookkeeping: a Gaussian prior contributes precision \(1/\sigma_0^2\) centered at \(\theta_0\), each trial contributes precision \(1/(s_i^2 + \tau^2)\) centered at \(\hat\theta_i\), the posterior precision is their sum, and the posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of all of them. Theorem 8.3 is the fact that a normal prior and normal data give a normal posterior, so the update is exact rather than approximate. Numerically, for the running trio with \(\tau^2\) fixed at the DerSimonian-Laird value \(0.048\) and a vague prior, the posterior is \(\mathcal{N}(0.365,\, 0.027)\), matching the frequentist random-effects estimate and its Wald variance exactly, which is the content of the next remark. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Flat-prior limit and the frequentist tie. Let the prior become uninformative, \(\sigma_0^2 \to
\infty\). Then \(v_\ast^{-1} \to \sum_i \tilde w_i\) and \(m_\ast \to \sum_i \tilde w_i \hat\theta_i/\sum_i
\tilde w_i = \hat\theta_R\), with \(v_\ast \to 1/\sum_i \tilde w_i = \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\theta_R)\). The conditional Bayesian posterior mean and variance coincide exactly with the random-effects point estimate and its Wald variance. The Bayesian and frequentist random-effects analyses agree at the conditional level; they differ in how they propagate the uncertainty in \(\tau^2\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. The full posterior and the link to REML. With \(\tau^2\) unknown there is no conjugate prior for it in this model, so the joint posterior \(\pi(\theta, \tau^2 \mid \text{data}) \propto \pi(\tau^2)\,\pi(\theta)
\prod_i \mathcal{N}(\hat\theta_i; \theta, s_i^2 + \tau^2)\) is computed numerically, typically by Markov chain Monte Carlo (Chapter 24) with a half-normal or half-\(t\) prior on \(\tau\), which behave better than inverse-gamma priors when \(\tau\) may be near zero. Integrating \(\theta\) out of the likelihood under the improper flat prior \(\pi(\theta) \propto 1\) gives, by the Gaussian integral (obtained by completing the square in \(\theta\)) \(\int \exp(-\tfrac12 \sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i - \theta)^2)\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \sqrt{2\pi/\sum_i
\tilde w_i}\,\exp(-\tfrac12 \sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R)^2)\), the marginal likelihood \[
L_R(\tau^2) = \int \prod_i \mathcal{N}(\hat\theta_i; \theta, s_i^2 + \tau^2)\,\mathrm{d}\theta \;\propto\;
\Big(\prod_i (s_i^2 + \tau^2)\Big)^{-1/2}\Big(\sum_i \tilde w_i\Big)^{-1/2}\exp\!\Big(-\tfrac12 \sum_i
\tilde w_i (\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R)^2\Big),
\] whose logarithm is exactly Equation 13.12. The REML estimator of \(\tau^2\) is therefore the Bayesian marginal-likelihood (type-II maximum likelihood, that is, maximizing the likelihood after integrating the mean \(\theta\) out) estimator under a flat prior on the mean effect, which is why REML and the marginal posterior mode of \(\tau^2\) so often agree. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 13  Pairwise Meta-Analysis
text:
13.9 Egger’s test for small-study effects
Small studies are more prone to selective reporting than large ones, and the resulting small-study effects distort the pooled estimate. The funnel plot displays \(\hat\theta_i\) against its precision; under no bias it is symmetric, and asymmetry signals small-study effects. Egger’s test quantifies the asymmetry by a regression.
The funnel plot, and what “precision” means. Plot each trial as a point: its effect estimate \(\hat\theta_i\) on the horizontal axis, its precision \(1/s_i\) (large for big, tight trials; small for little, noisy ones) on the vertical axis. Large precise trials sit near the top and, if all is well, cluster tightly around the pooled effect; small imprecise trials sit near the bottom and scatter widely to both sides. The cloud then resembles an inverted funnel that is symmetric about the pooled effect when there is no bias. Asymmetry, small trials leaning to one side, is the signature of small-study effects, for instance small trials with unimpressive results going unpublished. For the running example’s five trials:
  precision
  10.00 |           C      :
   7.07 |              A   :
   5.00 |                  :                     D
   4.47 |                  :           B
   3.54 |                  :              E
        ++------------+------------+------------+------
         0.0          0.2          0.4          0.6        log OR
The pooled value sits at the dotted line. The tightest trial \(C\) falls to its left while the looser trials \(B, D, E\) lean right, a left-leaning asymmetry. Egger’s test replaces this eyeballing with a regression line through the plot and tests whether it is level.

Theorem 13.7 (Egger’s regression test) Define the standardized effect \(z_i = \hat\theta_i/s_i\) and the precision \(p_i = 1/s_i\), and consider the ordinary least squares regression \[
z_i = \alpha + \beta\, p_i + u_i .
\tag{13.17}\] Two facts hold.

Null behavior. Under the fixed-effect model Equation 13.1 with no small-study effects, \(z_i = \theta
p_i + u_i\) with \(u_i = \varepsilon_i/s_i\) having mean \(0\) and variance \(1\); the population regression Equation 13.17 then has intercept \(\alpha = 0\) and slope \(\beta = \theta\).
Algebraic identity. The fitted Egger intercept \(\hat\alpha\) equals the slope coefficient in the precision-weighted (weights \(w_i = 1/s_i^2\)) regression of the effect \(\hat\theta_i\) on its standard error \(s_i\); and the fitted Egger slope \(\hat\beta\) equals the intercept of that weighted regression.

Consequently the test of \(H_0: \alpha = 0\), carried out as the usual \(t\) test on the intercept of Equation 13.17 with \(k - 2\) degrees of freedom, is a test for a linear dependence of the effect estimate on its standard error, that is, for funnel-plot asymmetry. (Corresponds to C.9 in the proof catalogue.)


Proof. 

Under Equation 13.1, \(\hat\theta_i = \theta + \varepsilon_i\) with \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i] = 0\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = s_i^2\). Divide by \(s_i\): \[
z_i = \frac{\hat\theta_i}{s_i} = \frac{\theta}{s_i} + \frac{\varepsilon_i}{s_i} = \theta\, p_i + u_i,
\qquad u_i := \frac{\varepsilon_i}{s_i},
\] and \(\mathbb{E}[u_i] = 0\), \(\mathrm{Var}(u_i) = s_i^2/s_i^2 = 1\), so the errors are homoscedastic. Hence the data-generating line through the origin has intercept \(0\) and slope \(\theta\); the population least squares fit of Equation 13.17 recovers \(\alpha = 0\), \(\beta = \theta\).
Egger’s regression minimizes \(\sum_i (z_i - \alpha - \beta p_i)^2\) over \((\alpha, \beta)\). Substitute \(z_i = \hat\theta_i/s_i\) and \(p_i = 1/s_i\) and factor out \(1/s_i^2\): \[
\sum_i (z_i - \alpha - \beta p_i)^2 = \sum_i \Big(\frac{\hat\theta_i}{s_i} - \alpha - \frac{\beta}{s_i}
\Big)^2 = \sum_i \frac{1}{s_i^2}\big(\hat\theta_i - \beta - \alpha\, s_i\big)^2 = \sum_i w_i\big(\hat
\theta_i - (\beta + \alpha s_i)\big)^2 .
\] The right-hand side is precisely the objective of the weighted least squares regression of \(\hat\theta_i\) on the covariate \(s_i\) with weights \(w_i = 1/s_i^2\), where the role of the intercept is played by \(\beta\) and the role of the slope on \(s_i\) by \(\alpha\). Minimizing the identical objective produces identical minimizers, so the weighted regression of \(\hat\theta_i\) on \(s_i\) has intercept \(\hat\beta\) and slope \(\hat\alpha\). This is the claimed identity. Inference on \(\hat\alpha\) uses the standard normal-theory \(t\) statistic for a regression coefficient (Theorem 6.8) with \(n = k\) points and \(p = 2\) parameters, hence \(k - 2\) degrees of freedom. \(\square\)



Remark. The identity (ii) is the conceptual content of the test. A nonzero intercept \(\alpha\) means the effect estimate \(\hat\theta_i\) varies systematically with its standard error \(s_i\): large, imprecise studies sit at a different effect level than small, precise ones, which is exactly funnel asymmetry. The weighted intercept \(\hat\beta\), the extrapolation of the effect to \(s_i = 0\) (infinite precision), is the “precision-effect test” estimate of the bias-adjusted effect. Egger’s test has low power for \(k < 10\) studies and conflates genuine small-study reporting effects with ordinary between-study heterogeneity, since heterogeneity also breaks the homoscedasticity assumed in part (i); trim-and-fill, the funnel plot itself, and the PET-PEESE family are common complements. We include the test for completeness; it is diagnostic, not confirmatory. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why this matters for ITC. An indirect comparison is only as trustworthy as the direct comparisons it is built from. If the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) evidence is distorted by small-study effects, the Bucher contrast \(\hat d_{AB} = \hat d_{AC} - \hat d_{BC}\) of Chapter 14 and the network estimates of Chapter 15 inherit that distortion. Screening each pairwise contrast for funnel asymmetry is therefore part of judging whether the evidence base is solid enough to compare treatments indirectly at all. The caution above applies with force: with few trials the test is underpowered and confounds reporting bias with ordinary heterogeneity, so it informs judgment rather than deciding it. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Fixed-effect estimate. By Equation 13.2 and Equation 13.3, \[
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}} = \frac{55.25}{207.5} = 0.2663, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}) =
\frac{1}{207.5} = 0.004819, \qquad \mathrm{SE} = 0.0694 .
\] The precise study C (\(w_C = 100\)) carries nearly half the weight and pulls the summary toward \(0.15\).
Cochran’s \(Q\) and \(I^2\). Using Equation 13.4, \[
Q = 50(0.20 - 0.2663)^2 + 20(0.45 - 0.2663)^2 + 100(0.15 - 0.2663)^2 + 25(0.60 - 0.2663)^2 + 12.5(0.50 -
0.2663)^2 = 5.714 .
\] With \(k - 1 = 4\) degrees of freedom, the upper-tail probability is \(P(\chi^2_4 > 5.714) = 0.222\), so \(Q\) is not significant at the usual levels, yet it exceeds its null mean of \(4\). The heterogeneity summaries Equation 13.6 are \[
H^2 = \frac{5.714}{4} = 1.428, \qquad I^2 = 1 - \frac{4}{5.714} = 0.300 = 30.0\% ,
\] a low-to-moderate level: about \(30\%\) of the variability is in excess of sampling error.

\] noticeably wider than the Wald interval \((0.127, 0.481)\), driven mainly by the \(t_4\) quantile \(2.776\) replacing \(1.96\). With only \(k = 5\) studies this is the interval to trust.
Egger’s test. Forming \(z_i = \hat\theta_i/s_i\) and \(p_i = 1/s_i\) and fitting Equation 13.17 by least squares gives intercept \(\hat\alpha = 2.634\) with standard error \(0.815\), so \(t = 2.634/0.815 = 3.23\) on \(k - 2 = 3\) degrees of freedom, two-sided \(p = 0.048\). The algebraic identity of Theorem 13.7 is visible in the companion weighted regression of \(\hat\theta_i\) on \(s_i\): its slope is \(2.634\) (equal to \(\hat\alpha\)) and its intercept is \(-0.116\) (equal to \(\hat\beta\)). Taken at face value the test flags asymmetry, but with \(k = 5\) it is severely underpowered and unstable; the “signal” is essentially the single precise low-effect study C, and no conclusion about reporting bias is warranted from five trials. The example shows both the mechanics and the fragility of the test.
Decision impact: which interval, and why. It is worth stating what a decision-maker would actually conclude from these five trials, because the three analyses tell noticeably different stories. The fixed-effect interval \(0.266 \pm 1.96(0.069) = (0.130, 0.402)\) is the narrowest, but it excludes no effect only because it assumes the five trials share one effect, which the \(I^2\) of \(30\%\) already questions. The random-effects Wald interval \((0.127, 0.481)\) widens to admit heterogeneity, yet still trusts a normal quantile and a plug-in \(\tau^2\). The Hartung-Knapp interval \((0.058, 0.550)\) is wider still and is the only one whose stated \(95\%\) coverage survives having just \(k = 5\) trials. All three keep the effect positive here, but the strength of that conclusion weakens as the interval widens; a cautious analyst reports the Hartung-Knapp interval and treats the fixed-effect interval as an optimistic bound. This is the pattern to expect whenever heterogeneity is present and trials are few, which is the normal situation in health technology assessment, and it is the same caution that will attend every indirect comparison built on these pooled inputs.

title: 13  Pairwise Meta-Analysis
text:
13.11 Notes and references
This chapter expands items C.1 through C.9 of the companion proof catalogue into complete proofs in the notation of this book, and adds the worked example and exercises. The primary reference for the random-effects model, its estimation, and the Bayesian formulation is Dias et al. (2018), which is also the source for the bridge from pairwise to network meta-analysis taken up in Chapters 14 and 15. The method-of-moments heterogeneity estimator Equation 13.11 is from DerSimonian and Laird (1986); we sharpened the catalogue’s asymptotic statement by proving exact unbiasedness of the untruncated estimator (Theorem 13.3), which holds under second moments alone.
Several attributions rely on sources not yet in the bibliography, listed with full data in the work log for the orchestrator to merge: Higgins and Thompson (2002) for \(H^2\) and \(I^2\) (Definition 13.3, Proposition 13.3); Hartung (1999), Hartung and Knapp (2001), and Sidik and Jonkman (2002) for the \(t\) adjustment (Theorem 13.5), with IntHout et al. (2014) for its small-\(k\) recommendation; Viechtbauer (2005) and the metafor package (Viechtbauer 2010) for the REML estimating equation and its iterative solution (Theorem 13.4); Egger et al. (1997) for the regression test (Theorem 13.7), with Sterne and Egger and the PET-PEESE literature for the complements noted there; Gelman (2006) for half-normal and half-\(t\) priors on \(\tau\); and Veroniki et al. (2016) for the modern comparison of \(\tau^2\) estimators.
The proofs lean on Part I: the Gauss-Markov theorem and the linear-model machinery (Theorem 6.3, Definition 6.1, Theorem 6.8, Theorem 6.4, Theorem 6.6, Lemma 6.3) carry the fixed-effect optimality, Cochran’s \(Q\), and the Hartung-Knapp result; the spectral theorem (Theorem 3.2) underlies Lemma 13.1; Fisher information and the Cramer-Rao bound (Definition 5.7, Theorem 5.7) give the efficiency of inverse-variance weighting; restricted maximum likelihood (Definition 8.4, Theorem 8.8) is specialized to the heterogeneity variance; and normal-normal conjugacy (Theorem 8.3) gives the Bayesian posterior. The random-effects model Definition 13.4 is the meta-analytic case of the hierarchical construction Definition 8.3.
No result in this chapter carries a machine-checked tag. The companion Coq development under theories/ formalizes the identification and algebraic content of the indirect-comparison methods (propensity scores, the Bucher contrast, outcome regression, doubly robust estimation, MAIC), not the classical estimation theory of meta-analysis: there is no Coq counterpart to inverse-variance weighting, Cochran’s \(Q\), or the heterogeneity-variance estimators, a scope decision recorded in the companion manuscript. The cleanest candidates for future formalization are the purely algebraic identities here, namely the best-linear-unbiased property of inverse-variance weights (Theorem 13.1) and the expected value of \(Q\) (Proposition 13.2).
Forward connections. The fixed-effect contrast estimator and its variance Equation 13.3 are the inputs to the Bucher indirect comparison of Chapter 14 (Theorem 14.1) under the transitivity assumption (Definition 14.3); the random-effects structure of Definition 13.4 becomes the multivariate random effect of network meta-analysis, where contrasts sharing a comparator acquire the characteristic correlation of Theorem 15.4; and Cochran’s \(Q\) generalizes to the network heterogeneity and inconsistency statistics of Chapter 15. The within-study effects pooled here live on the linear-predictor (link) scale, which is why their collapsibility properties (Definition 11.6, Theorem 11.2) matter for what the pooled \(\theta\) means.

title: 13  Pairwise Meta-Analysis
text:
13.12 Exercises
Exercises marked with a star (\(\star\)) have a complete worked solution in Appendix F. Start with the two warm-ups, which need only the running example and a calculator; the later exercises build toward the proofs.

Exercise 13.1 (Which trial gets more weight? (warm-up)) Two trials estimate the same log odds ratio: trial \(P\) reports \(\hat\theta_P = 0.30\) with \(s_P^2 = 0.01\), and trial \(R\) reports \(\hat\theta_R = 0.10\) with \(s_R^2 = 0.04\). (a) Compute the inverse-variance weights \(w_P\) and \(w_R\), and state in words how many times more weight the more precise trial receives and why. (b) Compute the fixed-effect estimate \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}\) and check that it lies closer to the more precise trial. (c) Without recomputing from scratch, describe what happens to the two weights and to their ratio if a heterogeneity variance \(\tau^2 = 0.03\) is added to each \(s_i^2\), and connect this to the random-effects reweighting of Section Section 13.4.


Exercise 13.2 (Interpreting \(I^2\) (interpretation)) A meta-analysis of \(k = 8\) trials reports \(I^2 = 60\%\). For each statement, say whether it is true or false and why. (a) “\(60\%\) of the eight trials are biased.” (b) “There is a \(60\%\) probability that heterogeneity is present.” (c) “About \(60\%\) of the observed variability among the estimates exceeds what sampling error alone would produce.” (d) “The pooled effect is wrong by \(60\%\).” (e) “A fixed-effect analysis is therefore the safe choice.” Justify each answer from Definition 13.3 and Proposition 13.3.


Exercise 13.3 (Fixed-effect pipeline by hand (\(\star\))) Three trials report a mean difference: \(\hat\theta_1 = 1.2\) with \(s_1^2 = 0.16\), \(\hat\theta_2 = 0.8\) with \(s_2^2 = 0.09\), \(\hat\theta_3 = 1.5\) with \(s_3^2 = 0.25\). (a) Compute the inverse-variance weights, the fixed-effect estimate \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}\), and its standard error. (b) Compute Cochran’s \(Q\), state its null distribution, and compute \(I^2\). (c) Compute the constant \(c\) of Equation 13.5 and the DerSimonian-Laird estimate \(\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}\). (d) Recompute the pooled estimate and its standard error under the random-effects weights \(\tilde w_i = 1/(s_i^2 + \hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}})\).


Exercise 13.4 (Optimality and the equality case) Prove from scratch, using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, that any linear unbiased estimator \(\sum_i a_i \hat\theta_i\) of \(\theta\) under Equation 13.1 has variance at least \(1/\sum_i w_i\), and that equality holds if and only if \(a_i = w_i/\sum_j w_j\). Then show, without Lagrange multipliers, that the same conclusion follows by writing \(a_i = w_i/W + d_i\) with \(\sum_i d_i = 0\) and expanding the variance. Hint. For the first route, apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the vectors \((a_i s_i)_i\) and \((1/s_i)_i\) exactly as in the remark after Theorem 13.1. For the second, expand \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) = \sum_i
a_i^2 s_i^2\) with \(a_i = w_i/W + d_i\); the cross term vanishes because \(\sum_i d_i = 0\), leaving \(1/W\) plus a nonnegative remainder \(\sum_i d_i^2 s_i^2\) that is zero only when every \(d_i = 0\).


Exercise 13.5 (Exact unbiasedness and truncation bias of DerSimonian-Laird)  

Using only the second-moment assumptions of Proposition 13.2, prove that the untruncated estimator \(\tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}} = (Q - (k-1))/c\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[\tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}] = \tau^2\).
Deduce that the truncated estimator Equation 13.11 has \(\mathbb{E}[\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}] \ge \tau^2\), with strict inequality whenever \(P(\tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}} < 0) > 0\). (c) Explain why the truncation bias is largest when the true \(\tau^2\) is near zero and negligible when \(\tau^2\) is large.



Exercise 13.6 (REML reproduces the \((k-1)\) divisor (\(\star\))) Suppose all within-study variances are equal, \(s_i^2 \equiv s^2\). Starting from the REML estimating equation Equation 13.13, show that \(\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{REML}} = \frac{1}{k-1}\sum_i (\hat\theta_i -
\bar{\hat\theta})^2 - s^2\) (truncated at \(0\)), where \(\bar{\hat\theta}\) is the unweighted mean. Compare with the maximum likelihood estimator, which would divide by \(k\), and explain the discrepancy in terms of the degree of freedom spent on \(\theta\), referencing Theorem 8.8. Hint. Set all \(\tilde w_i\) equal in Equation 13.13; the right-hand side collapses to \((k-1)\tilde w\) and \(\hat\theta_R\) becomes the unweighted mean \(\bar{\hat\theta}\), as in the equal-variance remark after Theorem 13.4.


Exercise 13.7 (The Hartung-Knapp scale factor) Within the working model of Theorem 13.5, let \(q = \frac{1}{k-1}\sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i -
\hat\theta_R)^2\). (a) Show that \(\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{HK}}(\hat\theta_R) = q\,
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\theta_R)\) with \(\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\theta_R) = 1/\sum_i \tilde w_i\). (b) Show \(\mathbb{E}[q] = 1\) under the working model with \(\sigma^2 = 1\), using \((k-1)q = \sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R)^2\) and Theorem 13.2 applied to the weights \(\tilde w_i\). (c) Explain why the Hartung-Knapp interval can be narrower than the Wald interval, and what the \(\max\{1, q\}\) safeguard does. Hint for (b). Under the working model with \(\sigma^2 = 1\) the variables \(\sqrt{\tilde w_i}(\hat\theta_i - \theta)\) are standard normal, so \((k-1)q = \sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R)^2\) is exactly the Cochran statistic of Theorem 13.2 formed with the weights \(\tilde w_i\), and that statistic has mean \(k - 1\).


Exercise 13.8 (Bayesian study-specific effects and shrinkage) In the random-effects model Equation 13.8 with \(\tau^2\) and \(\theta\) known, derive the posterior of an individual study effect \(\theta_i\) given \(\hat\theta_i\) using Theorem 8.3, and show it is \[
\theta_i \mid \hat\theta_i \sim \mathcal{N}\big(B_i \theta + (1 - B_i)\hat\theta_i,\; (1 - B_i)s_i^2\big),
\qquad B_i = \frac{s_i^2}{s_i^2 + \tau^2}.
\] Interpret \(B_i\) as a shrinkage factor: less precise studies (large \(s_i^2\)) are pulled harder toward the mean \(\theta\). Connect this to the shrinkage estimator Theorem 8.5 of Chapter 8.


Exercise 13.9 (Egger’s intercept as a weighted slope) For the data of Exercise 13.3, (a) fit Egger’s regression Equation 13.17 and report \(\hat\alpha\) and its \(t\) statistic on \(k - 2 = 1\) degree of freedom. (b) Fit the precision-weighted regression of \(\hat\theta_i\) on \(s_i\) with weights \(1/s_i^2\), and verify numerically that its slope equals \(\hat\alpha\) and its intercept equals \(\hat\beta\), as Theorem 13.7 asserts. (c) Comment on why a test on a single residual degree of freedom is uninformative. Hint. Reuse the algebraic identity of Theorem 13.7: Egger’s regression and the weighted regression of \(\hat\theta_i\) on \(s_i\) minimize the same objective, so their fitted coefficients swap roles. With \(k = 3\) points and \(p = 2\) parameters there are \(k - 2 = 1\) residual degrees of freedom.





DerSimonian, Rebecca, and Nan Laird. 1986. “Meta-Analysis in Clinical Trials.” Controlled Clinical Trials 7 (3): 177–88.


Dias, Sofia, A. E. Ades, Nicky J. Welton, Jeroen P. Jansen, and Alexander J. Sutton. 2018. Network Meta-Analysis for Decision-Making. Statistics in Practice. Wiley.

title: 14  Indirect Comparison and Bucher’s Theorem
text:
14.1 Introduction
A health technology assessment routinely faces a question that the available trials never asked. A regulator must decide whether a new drug \(A\) is better than an established drug \(B\), but the two have never been compared head to head. To keep a concrete picture in view throughout the chapter, let \(A\) be a new statin and \(B\) an established statin, each tested in its own randomized trial against the same comparator \(C\) (a placebo or standard of care), with an unfavorable cardiovascular event as the outcome. What does exist is a trial of \(A\) against \(C\), and a separate trial of \(B\) against the same comparator \(C\). The clinical question is about \(A\) versus \(B\); the evidence speaks only about \(A\) versus \(C\) and \(B\) versus \(C\). The task of this chapter is to make precise the simplest device that bridges the gap: the anchored indirect comparison, and the theorem of Bucher et al. (1997) that governs it.
The idea is disarmingly simple. If the effect of \(A\) relative to \(C\) is \(d_{AC}\) and the effect of \(B\) relative to \(C\) is \(d_{BC}\), both measured on a scale where contrasts add, then the effect of \(A\) relative to \(B\) ought to be the difference \(d_{AC}-d_{BC}\), because the common comparator \(C\) cancels. Replacing the unknown true effects by their trial estimates gives the Bucher estimator \(\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}\). The algebra is the algebra of a triangle. What makes the chapter a piece of mathematics rather than a piece of arithmetic is the question of when the algebra is licensed. The estimator is unbiased only if the true effect of \(A\) versus \(C\) is the same quantity in the \(A\) versus \(C\) trial as it would be in the (hypothetical) population where we want to report \(A\) versus \(B\), and likewise for \(B\) versus \(C\). That requirement is the transitivity assumption, equivalently the constancy of relative effects. It is the load-bearing hypothesis of every method in this book, and the rest of the book is, in a precise sense, the study of what to do when it fails.
We prove four things in full. First, that the relative effects on a fixed scale obey an antisymmetry law and an additivity law within any single population, so that \(d_{AC}-d_{BC}=d_{AB}\) is a tautology inside one population (Lemma 14.1). Second, that under transitivity the same identity holds across the three trial populations, which is the content of constancy (Proposition 14.2). Third, that the Bucher estimator is then unbiased for the cross-population contrast (Theorem 14.1), with variance equal to the sum of the two direct variances under independence (Theorem 14.2). Fourth, that the common comparator is exactly what cancels the study-specific baselines, so that the anchored comparison is protected against a bias that destroys the naive single-arm comparison (Proposition 14.4, Proposition 14.5). A fully worked example on the log odds-ratio scale, computed from raw two-by-two tables, closes the development.
Throughout we use the relative-effect notation of Notation: \(d_{ab(\mathcal P)}\) is the marginal effect of treatment \(b\) versus treatment \(a\) in population \(\mathcal P\), on a stated scale, and \(\hat d_{ab(j)}\) is its estimator from study \(j\). The potential-outcome machinery of Chapter 9 (Definition 9.1, Definition 9.4, Theorem 9.3) supplies the meaning of a single trial’s relative effect; the inference tools of Chapter 5 (Theorem 5.3, Theorem 5.6) supply its standard error. This chapter corresponds to results D.1 to D.4 of the proof catalogue.

section: 14.2 A running example and a map of the argument
text:
14.2 A running example and a map of the argument
Before any formalism, fix the picture we will return to at every turn. Two randomized trials share the comparator \(C\) (placebo):

Trial \(AC\) compares the new statin \(A\) with placebo \(C\) and reports an odds ratio of the cardiovascular event of \(2\) for \(C\) versus \(A\); on the log scale, \(\hat d_{AC}=\log 2\approx 0.69\). In words, placebo patients had twice the odds of the event, so \(A\) is protective.
Trial \(BC\) compares the established statin \(B\) with placebo \(C\) and reports an odds ratio of \(1.5\) for \(C\) versus \(B\); on the log scale, \(\hat d_{BC}=\log 1.5\approx 0.41\). Placebo patients had one and a half times the odds, so \(B\) is protective too, but less so.

We will compute the full example from raw counts in Section 14.11; the two trials there produce exactly these numbers.
What “population” means here. By a population we do not mean the specific people enrolled, but the distribution of their baseline characteristics: the mix of ages, disease severities, and risk factors a trial would draw from. Formally it is a probability distribution over the covariate space \(\mathcal X\). The two trials draw from two different such distributions, \(\mathcal P_{AC}\) and \(\mathcal P_{BC}\), and we will also speak of a third, \(\mathcal P_{AB}\): the population in which we actually want the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) answer, typically the patients who would receive the drug in routine care. No trial was ever run in \(\mathcal P_{AB}\) for \(A\) against \(B\); that absence is the entire reason an indirect comparison is needed.
Two recurring words. A contrast is a difference of two positions on the chosen scale, such as \(\eta_B-\eta_A\); it is the mathematical form of the phrase “relative effect.” The link scale is the transformed scale (log-odds for a probability, log for a rate or hazard, or the untransformed mean for a continuous outcome) on which we agree to do all subtraction, chosen precisely so that contrasts add along a path.
The available and missing comparisons form a triangle:
              A  - - - - - - - - -  B        target contrast d_AB
               \                   /            (dashed: NO A-vs-B trial)
                \                 /
          d_AC   \               /   d_BC
       (trial AC) \             / (trial BC)
                   \           /
                    \         /
                     \       /
                        C                     common comparator (the anchor)
The two solid legs \(A\!-\!C\) and \(B\!-\!C\) are the trials we have; the dashed edge \(A\!-\!B\) is the comparison we want. Bucher walks the triangle: go from \(A\) down to \(C\), then from \(C\) up to \(B\), and the detour through \(C\) recovers the missing edge.

Remark. The object, stated once, up front. Everything below serves one formula. Writing \(\hat d_{AC}\) and \(\hat d_{BC}\) for the two trials’ estimated log-scale effects against the shared comparator \(C\), the Bucher estimator of the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) effect is the single subtraction \[
\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC},
\] with standard error \(\sqrt{\mathrm{SE}_{AC}^2+\mathrm{SE}_{BC}^2}\) when the two trials are independent. In the running example \(\hat d_{AC}=\log 2\) and \(\hat d_{BC}=\log 1.5\), so \(\hat d_{AB}=\log 2-\log 1.5=\log\tfrac43\approx 0.29\): the indirect odds ratio of the event for \(B\) versus \(A\) is \(\tfrac43\). The rest of the chapter answers one question: when is this subtraction allowed? \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Orientation, once and for all. The single most common source of confusion in indirect comparison is sign. We follow Notation: \(d_{ab}=\eta_b-\eta_a\) places the reference treatment first and the active treatment second. Because the outcome is unfavorable, a positive contrast flags higher, hence worse, odds for the treatment in the second slot. title: 14  Indirect Comparison and Bucher’s Theorem
section: 14.3 The relative effect and its scale
text:
14.3 The relative effect and its scale
The goal of this section is modest but easy to lose sight of: we want to put every treatment arm on a single additive scale, a number \(\eta_k\) we can subtract, so that “effect” becomes “difference.” Everything in the section is machinery for doing that honestly when the outcome is binary or a survival time rather than a plain average.
Fix three treatments \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) and a strictly increasing, differentiable link function \(g\) (Definition 7.2) that maps a mean outcome to a “linear-predictor” scale on which effects are to be reported: the logit for binary outcomes (giving log odds ratios), the log for rates and hazards (giving log rate or hazard ratios), and the identity for continuous outcomes (giving mean differences). For a treatment \(k\in\{A,B,C\}\) write \(\mu_k(x)=\mathbb E[Y(k)\mid X=x]\) for the conditional mean of the potential outcome under \(k\) (Definition 9.1), as a function of the baseline covariates \(x\in\mathcal X\).

Definition 14.1 (Marginal link-scale position) Let \(\mathcal P\) be a population with covariate density \(f_{\mathcal P}\). The marginal mean of treatment \(k\) in \(\mathcal P\) is \(\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P)}=\int \mu_k(x)\,f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx\), and its marginal link-scale position is \[
\eta_{k(\mathcal P)} \;=\; g\!\left(\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P)}\right)
\;=\; g\!\left(\int \mu_k(x)\,f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx\right).
\tag{14.1}\] The marginal relative effect of treatment \(b\) versus treatment \(a\) in \(\mathcal P\) (Definition 11.2) is the contrast of link-scale positions, \[
d_{ab(\mathcal P)} \;=\; \eta_{b(\mathcal P)}-\eta_{a(\mathcal P)}
\;=\; g\!\left(\bar\mu_{b(\mathcal P)}\right)-g\!\left(\bar\mu_{a(\mathcal P)}\right).
\tag{14.2}\] \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. The phrase “link-scale position” is jargon coined here; take it to mean “the arm’s adjusted location on the report scale, before we subtract two arms.” The object \(\eta_{k(\mathcal P)}\) is a two-step recipe. Step one: in population \(\mathcal P\), work out the average outcome you would see if everyone took treatment \(k\); this is the inner integral \(\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P)}\), an ordinary population mean. Step two: push that single average through the link \(g\) to land on the additive scale (the logit of a probability, the log of a rate). The relative effect \(d_{ab(\mathcal P)}\) is then just the gap between two such numbers. One notational caution: \(\eta_{k(\mathcal P)}\) is a population-level (marginal) quantity indexed by a treatment and a population; it is not the individual-level linear predictor \(\eta_{ijk}\) of Notation, which carries a person, study, and arm subscript. Same Greek letter, a coarser object. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Two further points of interpretation deserve emphasis before we use Equation 14.2.

Remark. Marginal, not conditional. Equation Equation 14.2 marginalizes the conditional means first (the inner integral) and applies the link second. This is the effect a trial reports when it compares arm-level summaries: the marginal odds ratio, the marginal hazard ratio. It is in general not equal to the conditional effect \(g(\mu_b(x))-g(\mu_a(x))\) averaged over \(x\), because a nonlinear \(g\) does not commute with averaging. Here is the phenomenon in one line of arithmetic: if half a population has event probability \(0.9\) and half has \(0.1\), the average probability is \(0.5\) with logit \(0\), whereas the average of the two logits is \(\tfrac12\operatorname{logit}(0.9)+\tfrac12\operatorname{logit}(0.1)=0\) only by the symmetry of this toy case; shift the split to \(0.8\) and \(0.1\) and \(g\) of the average (\(\operatorname{logit}0.45=-0.20\)) no longer equals the average of the \(g\)’s (\(\tfrac12\operatorname{logit}0.8+\tfrac12\operatorname{logit}0.1\approx-0.40\)). For the identity link the two always coincide; for the logit and log links they differ, the phenomenon of non-collapsibility (Definition 7.7, Definition 11.6, Theorem 11.2). The Bucher construction operates on whatever marginal effects the trials report, and the transitivity assumption below is a statement about those marginal effects. We return to the interaction between non-collapsibility and indirect comparison in Chapter 16. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why a scale on which contrasts add. The whole construction lives on the link scale precisely because on that scale a relative effect is a difference of two positions, and differences subtract cleanly. On the natural outcome scale the same information is multiplicative: an odds ratio of \(A\) versus \(C\) times the odds ratio of \(C\) versus \(B\) gives the odds ratio of \(A\) versus \(B\). Taking logarithms turns the product into the sum Equation 14.2. The risk difference is the one common effect measure that adds on the identity scale directly. We make the additive structure a lemma in Section 14.4. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


14.3.1 The single trial as a source of an unbiased contrast
A randomized trial comparing two of the treatments in a population \(\mathcal P\) delivers an (approximately) unbiased estimator of the corresponding marginal relative effect Equation 14.2. We record this as the input to everything that follows; the proof is the identification argument of Chapter 9. The reader who wants only the upshot may read the proposition, skip its proof, and note the plain-language remark that follows it.

Proposition 14.1 (A randomized trial estimates its own marginal contrast) Let study \(j\) randomize patients drawn from population \(\mathcal P_j\) between arms \(a\) and \(b\), with randomization probability \(P(T=b\mid X=x)=\pi\in(0,1)\) independent of \(x\). Then the arms satisfy ignorability and positivity (Definition 9.7, Definition 9.8) by design, the arm means identify the marginal potential-outcome means \(\bar\mu_{a(\mathcal P_j)}\) and \(\bar\mu_{b(\mathcal P_j)}\) (Theorem 9.3), and any estimator \(\hat d_{ab(j)}\) formed by applying \(g\) to consistent arm-mean estimators is consistent for \(d_{ab(\mathcal P_j)}\), with \(\mathbb E[\hat d_{ab(j)}]\to d_{ab(\mathcal P_j)}\).


Proof. Randomization makes the treatment indicator \(T\) independent of the potential outcomes \((Y(a),Y(b))\) and of the covariates \(X\); in particular \(T\perp (Y(a),Y(b))\mid X\) holds with the conditioning on \(X\) vacuous, which is ignorability (Definition 9.7), and \(\pi\in(0,1)\) is positivity (Definition 9.8). By the identification theorem (Theorem 9.3) applied within \(\mathcal P_j\), the observed mean in arm \(a\), namely \(\mathbb E[Y\mid T=a]\), equals \(\mathbb E[Y(a)]=\bar\mu_{a(\mathcal P_j)}\), and likewise for \(b\). An estimator that plugs consistent arm-mean estimators \(\widehat{\bar\mu}_{a(j)},\widehat{\bar\mu}_{b(j)}\) into \(g\) and differences them is, by the continuous mapping theorem and the differentiability of \(g\), consistent for \(g(\bar\mu_{b(\mathcal P_j)})-g(\bar\mu_{a(\mathcal P_j)})=d_{ab(\mathcal P_j)}\); its bias vanishes in the limit, and to first order in the delta-method expansion of Section 14.10 it is unbiased. \(\square\)


Remark. What the proof said, in plain words. Ignorability means that, thanks to randomization, which treatment a patient received tells you nothing about how they would have fared under either treatment; the two arms are exchangeable. Because the coin flip is independent of everything about the patient, the conditioning on \(X\) is “vacuous,” that is, unnecessary. Positivity is just \(\pi\in(0,1)\): everyone had a genuine chance of either arm. Together these are what a randomized trial buys you by design, so the arm averages estimate the population averages you would have seen if everyone had taken that treatment. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Consistent, and unbiased to first order. A subtlety worth stating plainly: the empirical log odds-ratio is not exactly unbiased in a finite sample. What Proposition 14.1 delivers is (i) consistency, meaning that as the arm sizes grow, \(\hat d_{ab(j)}\) converges in probability to the true contrast, and (ii) first-order (asymptotic) unbiasedness, meaning the leading term of its bias vanishes as the sample grows. Every use of the word “unbiased” in this chapter, including in the statement of Bucher’s theorem below, is meant in this large-sample sense, which is the scale on which all Bucher calculations operate. For trials of realistic size the distinction is harmless; we flag it only so the word is not over-read. A separate warning about the word consistent: in Proposition 14.1 it is the statistical sense (an estimator converging to its target); in Equation 14.6 below it is the network-meta-analysis sense (direct and indirect estimates agreeing). The two senses are unrelated; context disambiguates. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The phrase “unbiased estimator of \(d_{AC}\)” in Bucher’s theorem is shorthand for the conclusion of Proposition 14.1: each trial estimates its own population’s marginal contrast without (first-order) bias. The entire subtlety of indirect comparison is that the trial estimates the contrast in its population \(\mathcal P_j\), whereas we wish to combine the trials into a statement about a single contrast. Bridging the populations is the work of the transitivity assumption.

14  Indirect Comparison and Bucher's Theorem

title: 14  Indirect Comparison and Bucher’s Theorem
text:
14.4 The algebra of contrasts
Inside a single population the relative effects Equation 14.2 are differences of three numbers \(\eta_{A},\eta_{B},\eta_{C}\) (suppressing the population subscript), and therefore satisfy two elementary laws. They are the entire algebraic content of Bucher’s identity; the statistics enters only through Proposition 14.1 and the variance bookkeeping of Section 14.8.
It is fair to ask why a book states a theorem for something so elementary. The reason is that this trivial algebra is the entire mathematical skeleton of the Bucher estimator: the variance result (Theorem 14.2), the cancellation of baselines (Proposition 14.4), and the unbiasedness theorem (Theorem 14.1) all reduce to the two laws below applied on the right scale. Naming them now lets those later proofs cite them by name rather than re-derive them.

Lemma 14.1 (Antisymmetry and additivity of contrasts) Fix a population \(\mathcal P\) and let \(d_{ab}=\eta_{b}-\eta_{a}\) for \(a,b\in\{A,B,C\}\) as in Equation 14.2. Then for all treatments \(a,b,c\):

Antisymmetry (reversal): \(d_{ab}=-d_{ba}\), and in particular \(d_{aa}=0\).
Additivity (the triangle identity): \[
d_{ac} \;=\; d_{ab}+d_{bc}, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad d_{ab}=d_{ac}-d_{bc}.
\tag{14.3}\]



Proof. Both laws are immediate from the representation \(d_{ab}=\eta_b-\eta_a\). For antisymmetry, \(d_{ab}=\eta_b-\eta_a=-(\eta_a-\eta_b)=-d_{ba}\), and setting \(b=a\) gives \(d_{aa}=\eta_a-\eta_a=0\). For additivity, \[
d_{ab}+d_{bc}=(\eta_b-\eta_a)+(\eta_c-\eta_b)=\eta_c-\eta_a=d_{ac}.
\] Adding \(-d_{bc}\) to both sides of \(d_{ac}=d_{ab}+d_{bc}\) and using antisymmetry rearranges this to \(d_{ab}=d_{ac}-d_{bc}\). The middle term \(\eta_b\) cancels because it enters \(d_{ab}\) with a plus sign and \(d_{bc}\) with a minus sign; this cancellation of the intermediate treatment’s link-scale position is the algebraic seed of the indirect comparison. \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters. Read the triangle identity with the roles of the running example: setting \(a=A,b=C,c=B\) in \(d_{ab}=d_{ac}-d_{bc}\) gives exactly \(d_{AB}=d_{AC}-d_{BC}\), the Bucher combination. The lemma says this is a tautology whenever all three contrasts live in one population; the whole difficulty, taken up next, is that our three contrasts come from three different populations. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. A note on index order and the clinical convention. With the convention of Notation, \(d_{ab}=\eta_b-\eta_a\) places the reference treatment first and the active treatment second. The common comparator of an anchored comparison is \(C\), so the two trial contrasts that involve \(C\) are \(d_{AC}=\eta_C-\eta_A\) and \(d_{BC}=\eta_C-\eta_B\), in which \(C\) occupies the second slot; the target contrast between the two new treatments is \(d_{AB}=\eta_B-\eta_A\). Much applied writing uses the opposite order, “\(A\) versus \(C\),” and reports \(-d_{AC}=\eta_A-\eta_C\). By the antisymmetry law Lemma 14.1(1) the two orderings differ only by an overall sign and carry identical information; the indirect identity \(d_{AB}=d_{AC}-d_{BC}\) holds verbatim in either bookkeeping, because reversing all three contrasts negates both sides. The practical rule to remember, tabulated in Section 14.2: with an unfavorable outcome, a positive \(d_{ab}\) means the second-slot treatment has the higher (worse) odds. We keep the Notation order and let the reader translate by the reversal law where a “\(A\) versus \(C\)” phrasing is more natural. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The additivity law Equation 14.3 is a tautology when all three contrasts live in one population, where the \(\eta\)’s are three fixed numbers. The trials, however, live in three different populations \(\mathcal P_{AB}\), \(\mathcal P_{AC}\), \(\mathcal P_{BC}\), each with its own \(\eta\)’s. To carry Equation 14.3 across populations we need exactly the assumption that the relevant contrasts do not depend on which population we evaluate them in.

title: 14  Indirect Comparison and Bucher’s Theorem
section: 14.5 Constancy of relative effects and transitivity
text:
14.5 Constancy of relative effects and transitivity
Before the formal definitions, the assumption in plain terms, because it is the most important idea in the chapter. The two trials were run in different populations. Anchoring (Section Section 14.9) will handle any difference in baseline risk for free. What it cannot handle is a difference in the size of a treatment effect between the populations. A covariate that changes the size of a treatment effect is an effect modifier (Definition 11.3); a covariate that shifts outcomes but leaves treatment effects unchanged is a prognostic variable (Definition 11.5). Transitivity is the assumption that the trial populations are alike in their effect modifiers, and it allows them to differ freely in everything else.







Question about the trial populations
Answer under transitivity




What must be similar?
The distribution of any effect modifier of the relevant relative effects, that is, any covariate that changes the size of a treatment effect.


What is allowed to differ?
Baseline risk and purely prognostic factors, which shift outcomes but not treatment effects; the anchor cancels these (Proposition 14.4).


What cannot be repaired by more data?
Bias from an imbalance in effect modifiers. It is a bias, not a variance, so a larger trial does not shrink it.




Remark. A clinical instance, before the algebra. Return to the two statin trials. Suppose age modifies the effect of statin \(B\) versus placebo \(C\): the reduction in cardiovascular events is larger in older patients. If the \(BC\) trial enrolled a substantially younger population than the one in which we want to report \(A\) versus \(B\), then \(\hat d_{BC}\) estimates \(B\)’s effect in a younger population, and subtracting it from \(\hat d_{AC}\) silently mixes two different populations; transitivity fails. If instead age only predicts cardiovascular risk but does not change the size of the statin effect, then age is a prognostic variable, not an effect modifier: it shifts a study’s baseline but not its treatment effect, and anchoring absorbs the difference at no cost. Transitivity is thus a statement about effect modifiers, not about baseline comparability. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Definition 14.2 (Constancy of relative effects) Let a network of studies be given, study \(j\) having population \(\mathcal P_j\) with covariate density \(f_j\). The marginal relative effect of \(b\) versus \(a\) in \(\mathcal P_j\) on the scale \(g\) is, as in Equation 14.2, \[
d_{ab(\mathcal P_j)}=g\!\left(\int \mu_b(x)\,f_j(x)\,dx\right)-g\!\left(\int \mu_a(x)\,f_j(x)\,dx\right).
\] The constancy of relative effects assumption asserts that this quantity does not depend on the population: for every ordered pair of treatments \((a,b)\) and all studies \(j,j'\), \[
d_{ab(\mathcal P_j)} \;=\; d_{ab(\mathcal P_{j'})} \;=:\; d_{ab}.
\tag{14.4}\] The common value \(d_{ab}\) is then a population-free network contrast. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. Constancy says every relative effect in the network is a single number that does not care which study you look at, so “the effect of \(b\) versus \(a\)” is well defined without naming a population. It is the general network assumption. Transitivity, defined next, is its restriction to the one triangle \(\{A,B,C\}\) we need for a single Bucher comparison: constancy for the whole network, transitivity for the triangle. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Constancy Equation 14.4 is a property of every pair of treatments across every study. For a single indirect comparison we need only its restriction to the triangle \(\{A,B,C\}\) and the three populations in play. That restriction is the transitivity assumption.

Definition 14.3 (Transitivity (for the anchored triangle)) Let \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) be three treatments studied in populations \(\mathcal P_{AB}\), \(\mathcal P_{AC}\), \(\mathcal P_{BC}\) (the population of a hypothetical direct \(A\)-versus-\(B\) trial, and the populations of the available \(A\)-versus-\(C\) and \(B\)-versus-\(C\) trials). The transitivity assumption asserts that each of the three relative effects takes the same value in every one of the three populations: \[
d_{AB(\mathcal P_{AB})}=d_{AB(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{AB(\mathcal P_{BC})}=:d_{AB},
\tag{14.5}\] and likewise \(d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AB})}=d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=:d_{AC}\) and \(d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})}=d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=:d_{BC}\). Equivalently, transitivity is the restriction of constancy Equation 14.4 to the treatment triangle \(\{A,B,C\}\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)
[machine-checked: theories/Bucher.v, Definition transitivity]


Remark. Reader translation. Transitivity says: the number you would call “the effect of \(B\) versus \(C\)” is the same number whether you measure it in the \(A\)-vs-\(C\) trial’s population, the \(B\)-vs-\(C\) trial’s population, or the target population where you actually want the answer, and likewise for the other two contrasts. It does not require the populations to be alike in every way; it requires them to be alike in the ingredients that change treatment effects, the effect modifiers. It is the population-level cousin of “no unmeasured confounding”: ignorability (Definition 9.7) lets one study impersonate a randomized experiment, and transitivity lets three studies impersonate one connected experiment run in a single population. In practice a reviewer checks it not from the data but from the trial reports, by asking whether the trials enrolled comparable patients with respect to known effect modifiers of the outcome; it is a judgment about clinical similarity, informed by subject-matter knowledge, that the data alone cannot confirm. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The next proposition makes the bridge precise: under transitivity the additivity law Equation 14.3, a tautology inside one population, becomes a genuine relation among the three well-defined network contrasts.

Proposition 14.2 (Transitivity yields the population consistency equation) Under transitivity (Definition 14.3), the network contrasts satisfy the consistency equation \[
d_{AB} \;=\; d_{AC}-d_{BC}.
\tag{14.6}\] Conversely, if the relative effects in each population obey the within-population additivity law Equation 14.3 and the consistency equation Equation 14.6 holds for the common values, then the three contrasts are mutually consistent in the sense required by Definition 14.3.
[machine-checked: theories/Bucher.v, Lemma transitivity_subtract, Lemma subtract_transitivity]


Proof. By Definition 14.3 the three symbols \(d_{AB},d_{AC},d_{BC}\) are well defined, each being the common value of a relative effect across the three populations. Evaluate the within-population additivity law Lemma 14.1(2) in, say, the population \(\mathcal P_{AC}\): \[
d_{AB(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AC})}.
\] Transitivity replaces each population-specific effect on the right and the left by its common value, \(d_{AB(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{AB}\), \(d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{AC}\), \(d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{BC}\), giving \(d_{AB}=d_{AC}-d_{BC}\), which is Equation 14.6. The same conclusion follows from evaluating the additivity law in any of the three populations, since transitivity forces them to agree.
For the converse, suppose each population obeys Equation 14.3 and the common values obey Equation 14.6. Then in any population \(\mathcal P_j\) the additivity law reads \(d_{AB(\mathcal P_j)}=d_{AC(\mathcal P_j)}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_j)}\); if two of the three contrasts are constant across populations the third is forced to equal \(d_{AC}-d_{BC}=d_{AB}\), the common value, in every population, which is Definition 14.3. \(\square\)


Remark. Reading the two directions. The forward direction is the one an analyst uses; the table records both.









Direction
Assume
Conclude
Who uses it




Forward
transitivity (Definition 14.3)
consistency equation Equation 14.6
Theorem 14.1, the whole method


Converse
within-population additivity plus consistency of the common values
transitivity
bookkeeping only



The converse is a consistency check, not something a data analyst invokes: it says the three contrasts cannot be defined inconsistently. “If two of the three are constant across populations, the third is forced” because inside each population the three already satisfy \(d_{AB}=d_{AC}-d_{BC}\) by pure algebra (Lemma 14.1), so fixing any two of them across populations pins the third by subtraction. Which two does not matter; the algebra is symmetric. A first-time reader can take the forward direction and move on. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. The Coq development encodes transitivity in the equivalent additive form \(d_{AC}=d_{AB}+d_{BC}\) (Definition transitivity) and proves the two implications \(d_{AC}=d_{AB}+d_{BC}\Rightarrow d_{AB}=d_{AC}-d_{BC}\) (Lemma transitivity_subtract) and its converse (Lemma subtract_transitivity); these are precisely the two directions of Proposition 14.2, stripped to their field algebra. \(\blacktriangleleft\)
