title: 14  Indirect Comparison and Bucher’s Theorem
text:
14.6 The anchored indirect comparison
We can now name the estimator and the contrasting naive alternative it improves upon.

Definition 14.4 (Anchored indirect comparison) Suppose study \(AC\) provides an estimator \(\hat d_{AC}\) of the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) network contrast and study \(BC\) provides an estimator \(\hat d_{BC}\) of the \(B\)-versus-\(C\) network contrast, the two studies sharing the common comparator \(C\). The anchored indirect comparison of \(A\) and \(B\), or Bucher estimator, is \[
\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}} \;:=\; \hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}.
\tag{14.7}\] The comparison is called anchored because the within-study contrasts to the shared comparator \(C\) (the anchor) are differenced, rather than the bare arm-level outcomes. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation and orientation. The estimator subtracts the two “versus \(C\)” log-effects. In the chapter’s orientation the result estimates \(d_{AB}=\eta_B-\eta_A\), so a positive Bucher estimate means \(B\) has the higher (with an unfavorable outcome, worse) odds, hence \(A\) is the better treatment. In the running example \(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}=\log 2-\log 1.5=\log\tfrac43>0\): \(B\) carries slightly higher event odds than \(A\). Always restate the direction when reporting: “\(B\) versus \(A\), higher is worse.” \(\blacktriangleleft\)

We also name the wrong thing to do, because seeing why it is wrong is the fastest route to seeing why anchoring works. The following naive comparison is a foil: it is what you get if you ignore the common comparator and simply compare the two active arms across studies. It is used in practice only as a last resort, for disconnected networks (Chapter 26); here it is the cautionary contrast that makes the value of the anchor visible.

Definition 14.5 (Unanchored (naive single-arm) comparison) With the same two studies, the unanchored comparison discards the comparator arms and contrasts the two active arms directly across studies: \[
\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{naive}} \;:=\; \hat\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{AC})}-\hat\eta_{B(\mathcal P_{BC})},
\tag{14.8}\] where \(\hat\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{AC})}\) is the estimated link-scale outcome of arm \(A\) in study \(AC\), and \(\hat\eta_{B(\mathcal P_{BC})}\) that of arm \(B\) in study \(BC\). This comparison ignores the anchor \(C\) entirely. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. The unanchored estimator throws away the placebo arms and directly compares the new statin’s event rate in one trial to the established statin’s event rate in the other. That is exactly what you would do if you had two single-arm studies with no common comparator. The comparison looks tempting because it seems to use the arms you care about, but it silently assumes the two trials had the same baseline risk, which they almost never do; Proposition 14.5 makes the error precise and Example 14.1 shows it as a number. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Section Section 14.9 shows that the unanchored comparison carries a bias equal to the difference of the two study baselines, a bias that the anchored comparison removes by construction. The distinction between anchored and unanchored comparison organizes the whole of population-adjusted indirect comparison: anchored methods (Chapters 17 to 20) repair residual bias in Equation 14.7, while unanchored methods (Chapter 26) confront the baseline bias of Equation 14.8 head on.

title: 14  Indirect Comparison and Bucher’s Theorem
text:
14.7 Bucher’s theorem: unbiasedness
The next two results look almost the same, and it helps to say up front how they differ. First we prove the deterministic identity: if the trials reported the true contrasts with no sampling error at all, the subtraction lands exactly on the target (Proposition 14.3). Then we reintroduce sampling error and show that the subtraction is still right on average (Theorem 14.1). The first is arithmetic; the second is arithmetic plus one line of expectation.

Proposition 14.3 (Bucher’s identity (exact estimates)) If \(\hat d_{AC}=d_{AC}\) and \(\hat d_{BC}=d_{BC}\) hold exactly and transitivity (Definition 14.3) holds, then \(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}=d_{AB}\).


Proof. Substitute the exact values into the estimator Equation 14.7 and apply the consistency equation Equation 14.6 of Proposition 14.2: \[
\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}=d_{AC}-d_{BC}=d_{AB}. \qquad\square
\]

[machine-checked: theories/Bucher.v, Theorem bucher_identity]
The stochastic version replaces exact equality by unbiasedness and the substitution by linearity of expectation. This is the theorem of Bucher et al. (1997).

Theorem 14.1 (Bucher’s theorem (unbiasedness)) Suppose two studies provide estimators of pairwise relative effects of the form \[
\hat d_{AC}=d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}+\varepsilon_{AC},\qquad
\hat d_{BC}=d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}+\varepsilon_{BC},
\] with mean-zero errors \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_{AC}]=\mathbb E[\varepsilon_{BC}]=0\), so that \(\hat d_{AC}\) and \(\hat d_{BC}\) are unbiased for the relative effects in their own trial populations (Proposition 14.1). Assume transitivity (Definition 14.3). Then the Bucher estimator Equation 14.7 is unbiased for the network contrast \(d_{AB}\): \[
\mathbb E\!\left[\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\right]=d_{AB}.
\]

[machine-checked: theories/Bucher.v, Theorem bucher_unbiased]

Remark. Why this matters. This is the license for the whole method: provided transitivity holds, the one-line subtraction \(\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}\) targets the right quantity, so an indirect estimate is a legitimate answer to the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) question. The theorem localizes all the risk in a single assumption, which the remainder of the chapter, and much of the book, learns to inspect. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Proof. Linearity of expectation applied to Equation 14.7 gives \[
\mathbb E\!\left[\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\right]
=\mathbb E[\hat d_{AC}]-\mathbb E[\hat d_{BC}].
\] By the unbiasedness hypothesis the two expectations equal the trial-population relative effects, \[
\mathbb E[\hat d_{AC}]=d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})},\qquad
\mathbb E[\hat d_{BC}]=d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}.
\] Transitivity (Definition 14.3) identifies each trial-population effect with the corresponding network contrast, \(d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{AC}\) and \(d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=d_{BC}\), so \[
\mathbb E\!\left[\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\right]=d_{AC}-d_{BC}.
\] Finally the consistency equation Equation 14.6, which Proposition 14.2 derives from transitivity, gives \(d_{AC}-d_{BC}=d_{AB}\). Chaining the three displays yields \(\mathbb E[\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}]=d_{AB}\). \(\square\)


Remark. Where each hypothesis is spent. The proof uses each assumption exactly once and at a distinct step. Unbiasedness of the trial estimators converts expectations into trial-population effects; this is a property of randomization within each trial and uses no cross-trial information. Transitivity converts trial-population effects into network contrasts; this is the only cross-population assumption and is the one that can fail. The consistency equation converts the difference of network contrasts into the target; this is pure algebra (Lemma 14.1) and never fails. The theorem is therefore as strong as its weakest hypothesis, and the weakest is invariably transitivity. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. The estimator is trivial; the assumption is not. Equation Equation 14.7 is one subtraction, and one might wonder why it warrants a theorem. The answer is that the subtraction is licensed only on the consistency-constrained set where Equation 14.6 holds, and membership in that set is the substantive scientific claim. Every population-adjusted method in Parts IV and V is, in the end, a device for making Equation 14.6 hold after a correction, or for quantifying the error when it does not. The simplicity of Bucher’s formula is exactly why the assumption that underwrites it must be stated with care. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

14  Indirect Comparison and Bucher's Theorem

title: 14  Indirect Comparison and Bucher’s Theorem
text:
14.8 The Bucher variance
We already know from Theorem 14.1 that the indirect estimate is centered correctly. The question now is how precise it is, and the headline is simple: an indirect estimate is built from two uncertain inputs, so its uncertainty is larger than either. The estimator Equation 14.7 is a linear combination of two trial summaries, so its variance is a two-line consequence of the bilinearity of covariance. We first record the general identity, valid whether or not the trials are independent, because the general form is what later chapters need when a multi-arm trial makes the two contrasts dependent.

Lemma 14.2 (Variance of a difference) For any two square-integrable random variables \(U,V\) (that is, random variables with finite variance), \[
\mathrm{Var}(U-V)=\mathrm{Var}(U)+\mathrm{Var}(V)-2\,\mathrm{Cov}(U,V).
\tag{14.9}\]


Proof. Write \(\mathrm{Var}(U-V)=\mathbb E\big[(U-V-\mathbb E[U-V])^2\big]\) and put \(\tilde U=U-\mathbb E[U]\), \(\tilde V=V-\mathbb E[V]\), so \(U-V-\mathbb E[U-V]=\tilde U-\tilde V\). Expanding the square and using linearity of expectation, \[
\mathbb E\big[(\tilde U-\tilde V)^2\big]
=\mathbb E[\tilde U^2]-2\,\mathbb E[\tilde U\tilde V]+\mathbb E[\tilde V^2]
=\mathrm{Var}(U)-2\,\mathrm{Cov}(U,V)+\mathrm{Var}(V),
\] which is Equation 14.9. The covariance is a symmetric bilinear form on centered variables, the same form whose positive semidefiniteness is recorded in Theorem 4.9. \(\square\)


Theorem 14.2 (The Bucher variance) Let \(\hat d_{AC}\) and \(\hat d_{BC}\) have variances \(v_{AC}=\mathrm{Var}(\hat d_{AC})\) and \(v_{BC}=\mathrm{Var}(\hat d_{BC})\). If the two estimators are uncorrelated, \(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat d_{AC},\hat d_{BC})=0\) (as holds when they come from disjoint sets of trials), then the Bucher estimator Equation 14.7 has variance \[
\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\right)=v_{AC}+v_{BC}.
\tag{14.10}\] In general, without the independence assumption, \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}})=v_{AC}+v_{BC}-2\,\mathrm{Cov}(\hat d_{AC},\hat d_{BC})\).

[machine-checked: theories/Bucher.v, Theorem bucher_variance]

Remark. Why this matters, and a picture. Indirect evidence is real evidence, but it is more expensive: its uncertainty is the sum of the two direct uncertainties. Independent uncertainties add in quadrature, exactly as independent errors combine by the Pythagorean rule, so the indirect standard error is the hypotenuse \(\sqrt{\mathrm{SE}_{AC}^2+\mathrm{SE}_{BC}^2}\) of the two direct standard errors. A practical consequence, made concrete in Section 14.11: an indirect comparison anchored on a tiny \(B\)-versus-\(C\) trial can be uninformative even when both direct trials are individually significant, because the small trial’s large variance is added in. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Proof. Apply Lemma 14.2 with \(U=\hat d_{AC}\) and \(V=\hat d_{BC}\): \[
\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\right)
=v_{AC}+v_{BC}-2\,\mathrm{Cov}(\hat d_{AC},\hat d_{BC}),
\] which is the general formula. Under the independence hypothesis the covariance term is zero, leaving \(v_{AC}+v_{BC}\), equation Equation 14.10. \(\square\)

The independence hypothesis holds in the canonical Bucher setting, where the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) evidence and the \(B\)-versus-\(C\) evidence come from separate trials. It fails when a single multi-arm trial contributes to both contrasts through a shared comparator arm: then the shared arm’s sampling error enters both \(\hat d_{AC}\) and \(\hat d_{BC}\) with the same sign, inducing a positive covariance. Intuitively, the shared comparator’s error is partly subtracted away rather than counted twice, so a positive covariance reduces the Bucher variance below the sum Equation 14.10. The standard homoskedastic random-effects model (a model in which every contrast is given the same variance) makes that correlation exactly one half; the intuition is that two contrasts sharing one of their two arms overlap in half of their sampling error, and we compute it exactly in Theorem 15.4. Because the covariance is positive, treating correlated contrasts as independent overstates the variance, which is conservative for this comparison.

Corollary 14.1 (The price of indirectness) Under the independence hypothesis of Theorem 14.2, the standard error of the Bucher estimate strictly exceeds the standard error of either direct contrast it is built from: \[
\mathrm{SE}\!\left(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\right)=\sqrt{v_{AC}+v_{BC}}
\;>\;\max\!\left(\sqrt{v_{AC}},\,\sqrt{v_{BC}}\right),
\] whenever both \(v_{AC}>0\) and \(v_{BC}>0\).


Proof. Since \(v_{AC},v_{BC}>0\), we have \(v_{AC}+v_{BC}>v_{AC}\) and \(v_{AC}+v_{BC}>v_{BC}\); taking square roots, which is monotone on the nonnegative reals, gives \(\sqrt{v_{AC}+v_{BC}}>\sqrt{v_{AC}}\) and \(>\sqrt{v_{BC}}\), hence the inequality with the maximum. \(\square\)

The corollary quantifies a fact of evidence synthesis: an indirect comparison is less precise than either of the direct comparisons it rests on, because it accumulates the uncertainty of both. Indirect evidence is genuine evidence, but it is statistically more expensive than a head-to-head trial of the same size. This is one half of the case for direct trials; the other half, that indirect evidence can be biased when transitivity fails, is the subject of Section 14.12.

title: 14  Indirect Comparison and Bucher’s Theorem
section: 14.9 The common comparator cancels baseline differences
text:
14.9 The common comparator cancels baseline differences
We now make precise the sense in which the anchor \(C\) protects the comparison. Decompose each arm’s link-scale position into a study-specific baseline and a treatment-specific effect. Under transitivity the treatment effects are population-free; the baselines are not, and they are exactly what the anchoring removes.

Definition 14.6 (The additive arm decomposition) Write the marginal link-scale position of arm \(k\) in study \(j\) as \[
\eta_{k(\mathcal P_j)} \;=\; \mu_j+\alpha_k,
\tag{14.11}\] where \(\mu_j\) is a study-specific baseline and \(\alpha_k\) is a treatment-specific shift shared across studies, with the reference treatment normalized to \(\alpha_{\mathrm{ref}}=0\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation, with a picture. The decomposition splits each arm’s position into “where the study starts” plus “how far the treatment moves it.” Concretely, normalizing the comparator as reference, \(\alpha_C=0\), so \(\mu_j=\eta_{C(\mathcal P_j)}\) is literally the placebo arm’s link-scale outcome in study \(j\):
   position eta_k(P_j)  =  mu_j (study baseline)  +  alpha_k (treatment shift)

   study AC:   arm C:  mu_AC + 0            study BC:   arm C:  mu_BC + 0
               arm A:  mu_AC + alpha_A                  arm B:  mu_BC + alpha_B

   mu_AC, mu_BC differ across studies      (different baseline risk)
   alpha_A, alpha_B, alpha_C are SHARED     (constancy of relative effects)
Read \(\mu_j\) as “how risky study \(j\)’s population is under the reference treatment,” its baseline log-odds of the event; read \(\alpha_k\) as “how much treatment \(k\) moves that risk on the link scale,” the same move in every study. This \(\mu_j\) is exactly the study-\(j\) baseline (intercept) of Notation; the reuse of the symbol is deliberate, not a clash. Because both trials share \(C\), the two baselines \(\mu_{AC}\) and \(\mu_{BC}\) are the same kind of quantity, the placebo log-odds, measured in two different populations, and they will differ. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. The decomposition encodes constancy. The decomposition Equation 14.11 is precisely the fixed-effect network model in the reference-treatment parameterization (Definition 15.3). The same \(\alpha_k\) appears in every study, so the contrast \(\alpha_k-\alpha_{k'}\) is the population-free network effect \(d_{k'k}\): under Equation 14.11, \(d_{ab(\mathcal P_j)}=\eta_{b(\mathcal P_j)}-\eta_{a(\mathcal P_j)}=\alpha_b-\alpha_a\), free of \(\mu_j\). This is the model form of transitivity, and it is the bridge to the network meta-analysis of Chapter 15, where the same \(\mu_j\)-plus-\(\alpha_k\) structure is fitted to a whole network at once. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Proposition 14.4 (Anchoring removes both the baselines and the comparator) Assume the additive decomposition Equation 14.11 with a common comparator \(C\) present in both studies. Then the Bucher estimand is free of the study baselines \(\mu_{AC},\mu_{BC}\) and of the comparator effect \(\alpha_C\): \[
d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=(\alpha_C-\alpha_A)-(\alpha_C-\alpha_B)=\alpha_B-\alpha_A=d_{AB}.
\] Each direct contrast already cancels its own study baseline, and the difference of contrasts then cancels the shared comparator effect \(\alpha_C\).


Proof. In study \(AC\) the two arms have positions \(\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{AC})}=\mu_{AC}+\alpha_A\) and \(\eta_{C(\mathcal P_{AC})}=\mu_{AC}+\alpha_C\) by Equation 14.11. Their contrast is \[
d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}=\eta_{C(\mathcal P_{AC})}-\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{AC})}=(\mu_{AC}+\alpha_C)-(\mu_{AC}+\alpha_A)=\alpha_C-\alpha_A,
\] the baseline \(\mu_{AC}\) cancelling because it is common to both arms of the same study. This is the within-study cancellation effected by randomization. Identically, study \(BC\) gives \(d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=\alpha_C-\alpha_B\). Subtracting, \[
d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=(\alpha_C-\alpha_A)-(\alpha_C-\alpha_B)=\alpha_B-\alpha_A,
\] the comparator effect \(\alpha_C\) cancelling because it is common to both contrasts. The result \(\alpha_B-\alpha_A\) equals \(d_{AB}\) by Equation 14.11. \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters. This is the precise sense in which the anchor earns its keep. Differencing within each trial before differencing across trials deletes the study baselines \(\mu_j\) in two stages, so the anchored comparison is immune to the baseline-risk differences that sink the naive comparison. It does not, however, protect against differences in the treatment shifts \(\alpha_k\) across populations; that is the province of transitivity, and its failure is Section 14.12. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The contrast with the unanchored comparison is now sharp. The naive estimator Equation 14.8 forgoes the within-study cancellation and inherits the difference of baselines as outright bias.

Proposition 14.5 (The unanchored comparison is biased by the baseline difference) Under the additive decomposition Equation 14.11, the unanchored estimand Equation 14.8 is \[
\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{AC})}-\eta_{B(\mathcal P_{BC})}=(\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC})+(\alpha_A-\alpha_B)=(\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC})-d_{AB},
\] so, taking \(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{naive}}\) as an estimate of \(-d_{AB}\) (the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) contrast in the reversed orientation), its bias is the difference of study baselines: \[
\text{bias}\;=\;\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC}.
\tag{14.12}\] The bias vanishes only in the special case \(\mu_{AC}=\mu_{BC}\), that is, only when the two studies happen to share the same baseline link-scale outcome.


Proof. By Equation 14.11, \(\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{AC})}=\mu_{AC}+\alpha_A\) and \(\eta_{B(\mathcal P_{BC})}=\mu_{BC}+\alpha_B\). Subtracting, \[
\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{AC})}-\eta_{B(\mathcal P_{BC})}=(\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC})+(\alpha_A-\alpha_B).
\] By Equation 14.11 again, \(\alpha_A-\alpha_B=-(\alpha_B-\alpha_A)=-d_{AB}\). Hence the estimand equals \((\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC})-d_{AB}\), an estimate of \(-d_{AB}\) offset by \(\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC}\), which is the claimed bias. It is zero precisely when \(\mu_{AC}=\mu_{BC}\). \(\square\)


Example 14.1 (Anchored versus unanchored, on the same data) Use the two trials of the running example (computed in full in Section 14.11). The placebo (arm \(C\)) log-odds were \(\hat\eta_C^{(AC)}=\log 0.5=-0.693\) in trial \(AC\) and \(\hat\eta_C^{(BC)}=\log 0.375=-0.981\) in trial \(BC\); normalizing \(\alpha_C=0\) makes these the two baselines, \[
\mu_{AC}=-0.693,\qquad \mu_{BC}=-0.981,\qquad \mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC}=0.288.
\] The two statin arms happened to have identical event rates, \(\hat\eta_A=\hat\eta_B=\log 0.25=-1.386\), so the two analyses disagree sharply:

The naive comparison concludes the two statins are identical (\(\mathrm{OR}=1\)), because their event rates look the same. But they are not comparable: statin \(B\) was tested against a placebo population with a lower event rate (\(27\%\) versus \(33\%\)), so \(B\) merely had an easier comparator. The anchored comparison corrects for this and finds \(B\) carries \(\tfrac43\) the event odds of \(A\). The entire discrepancy, \(0.288\), is precisely the gap between the two placebo baselines, exactly as Equation 14.12 predicts. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why anchoring matters. The baseline \(\mu_j\) absorbs everything about study \(j\)’s population that shifts the absolute outcome level: disease severity, follow-up duration, the prevalence of prognostic variables (Definition 11.5). Two trials of different drugs are run in different places at different times and essentially never share a baseline, so \(\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC}\) is essentially never zero, and the unanchored estimator Equation 14.8 is essentially always biased, as Example 14.1 just showed. The anchored estimator Equation 14.7 removes this bias for free, by differencing within each study before differencing across studies. This is the whole reason anchored indirect comparison is the default and unanchored comparison a last resort reserved for disconnected networks (Chapter 26), where it must be propped up by strong additional assumptions to control Equation 14.12. Crucially, anchoring does not protect against differences in the treatment effects \(\alpha_k\) across populations; that is the province of transitivity, and its failure is Section 14.12. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

section: 14.10 The variance of an empirical log-odds
text:
14.10 The variance of an empirical log-odds
To turn the worked example into honest numbers we need the standard error of a single trial’s log odds-ratio. It follows from the delta method (Theorem 5.3), and it is the standard error every applied Bucher computation uses.

Remark. You may skip the proof on a first reading. The only thing the worked example needs from this section is the boxed formula Equation 14.13: the estimated variance of a log odds-ratio is the sum of the reciprocals of the four cell counts of its two-by-two table. A reader in a hurry can take this on faith and go straight to Section 14.11; the delta-method derivation below merely justifies it, repeating the machinery of Chapter 5 (Theorem 5.3). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Proposition 14.6 (Large-sample variance of an empirical log-odds and log odds-ratio) Let an arm enroll \(n\) patients of whom \(r\) experience the event, with \(r\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\) and \(0<p<1\). Let \(\hat p=r/n\) and let the empirical log-odds be \(\hat\eta=\operatorname{logit}(\hat p)=\log\frac{\hat p}{1-\hat p}\). Then, to first order, \[
\mathrm{Var}(\hat\eta)\approx\frac{1}{np(1-p)},\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\eta)=\frac{1}{r}+\frac{1}{n-r}.
\tag{14.13}\] Consequently the empirical log odds-ratio contrasting two independent arms, with event counts \(r_1,r_2\) out of \(n_1,n_2\), has estimated variance \(\big(\tfrac1{r_1}+\tfrac1{n_1-r_1}\big)+\big(\tfrac1{r_2}+\tfrac1{n_2-r_2}\big)\), the sum of the inverse cell counts of the underlying two-by-two table.


Proof. The logit \(g(p)=\log p-\log(1-p)\) has derivative \(g'(p)=\frac1p+\frac1{1-p}=\frac{1}{p(1-p)}\). Since \(\hat p\) is the mean of \(n\) independent Bernoulli\((p)\) variables, \(\mathbb E[\hat p]=p\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat p)=p(1-p)/n\), and by the central limit theorem \(\sqrt n(\hat p-p)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,p(1-p))\). The delta method (Theorem 5.3) applied to \(g\) gives \[
\sqrt n\big(g(\hat p)-g(p)\big)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N\!\big(0,\,[g'(p)]^2\,p(1-p)\big),
\qquad [g'(p)]^2\,p(1-p)=\frac{p(1-p)}{p^2(1-p)^2}=\frac{1}{p(1-p)},
\] so \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\eta)\approx\frac{1}{np(1-p)}\). Substituting the plug-in estimate \(\hat p=r/n\), \[
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\eta)=\frac{1}{n\hat p(1-\hat p)}=\frac{1}{n\cdot\frac{r}{n}\cdot\frac{n-r}{n}}
=\frac{n}{r(n-r)}=\frac{(n-r)+r}{r(n-r)}=\frac1r+\frac1{n-r},
\] which is Equation 14.13. The two arms are independent, so by Lemma 14.2 (with zero covariance) the variance of their difference of log-odds is the sum of the two arm variances; collecting the four reciprocals gives the stated table formula. The normal approximation underlying a Wald interval is justified by the asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator (Theorem 5.6), of which \(\hat\eta\) is an instance. \(\square\)

text:
14.11 A worked Bucher comparison on the log odds-ratio scale
We carry a complete example from raw counts to a confidence interval, so that every number can be checked by hand. The event is an unfavorable outcome (a cardiovascular event); larger log-odds means worse.

Remark. Recipe: Bucher from published trials. Most of the time you will not have raw counts but a reported estimate and interval. The five-step recipe is then:

Recover each standard error from a reported \(95\%\) interval on the log scale: \(\mathrm{SE}=(\text{upper}-\text{lower})/(2\times 1.96)\), both endpoints on the log scale.
Line up the orientation: express both direct effects as “versus the common comparator \(C\)” on the same log scale (log OR, log RR, or log HR), so that \(\hat d_{AC}\) and \(\hat d_{BC}\) mean \(\eta_C-\eta_A\) and \(\eta_C-\eta_B\).
Subtract: \(\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}\).
Add variances (if the trials are independent): \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat d_{AB})=\sqrt{\mathrm{SE}_{AC}^2+\mathrm{SE}_{BC}^2}\).
Interval, then back-transform: form a Wald interval on the log scale, then exponentiate the estimate and both interval endpoints to report a ratio.

The example below runs this recipe starting one step earlier, from the raw tables. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Example 14.2 (Indirect comparison of \(A\) and \(B\) through a common comparator \(C\)) Orientation check. We report on the chapter’s \(d_{ab}=\eta_b-\eta_a\) scale. The event is unfavorable, so a positive contrast flags higher, worse odds. We expect both statins to beat placebo, so we expect \(\hat d_{AC}=\eta_C-\eta_A>0\) and \(\hat d_{BC}=\eta_C-\eta_B>0\) (placebo worse than each statin), and the target is \(d_{AB}=\eta_B-\eta_A\), “\(B\) versus \(A\), higher is worse.”
Two randomized trials report the following two-by-two tables.
Study \(AC\) (treatment \(A\) versus comparator \(C\)):

Step 1: arm log-odds. With \(\hat\eta=\log\frac{r}{n-r}\), \[
\hat\eta_A=\log\tfrac{30}{120}=\log 0.25=-1.38629,\qquad
\hat\eta_C^{(AC)}=\log\tfrac{50}{100}=\log 0.5=-0.69315,
\] \[
\hat\eta_B=\log\tfrac{40}{160}=\log 0.25=-1.38629,\qquad
\hat\eta_C^{(BC)}=\log\tfrac{60}{160}=\log 0.375=-0.98083.
\]
Step 2: direct contrasts. Using the Notation order \(d_{kC}=\eta_C-\eta_k\), \[
\hat d_{AC}=\hat\eta_C^{(AC)}-\hat\eta_A=-0.69315-(-1.38629)=0.69315=\log 2,
\] \[
\hat d_{BC}=\hat\eta_C^{(BC)}-\hat\eta_B=-0.98083-(-1.38629)=0.40546=\log 1.5.
\] Both are positive, as the orientation check anticipated. On the odds-ratio scale the comparator \(C\) has twice the event odds of \(A\) and one and a half times the event odds of \(B\); equivalently \(A\) and \(B\) are both protective relative to \(C\), with \(A\) the more so.
Step 3: direct variances by Proposition 14.6, summing inverse cell counts, \[
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat d_{AC})=\tfrac1{30}+\tfrac1{120}+\tfrac1{50}+\tfrac1{100}=0.071667,\qquad
\mathrm{SE}=0.26771,
\] \[
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat d_{BC})=\tfrac1{40}+\tfrac1{160}+\tfrac1{60}+\tfrac1{160}=0.054167,\qquad
\mathrm{SE}=0.23274.
\]
Step 4: the Bucher estimate. By Equation 14.7 and Equation 14.10, \[
\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}=0.69315-0.40546=0.28768=\log\tfrac43,
\] \[
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\!\left(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\right)=0.071667+0.054167=0.125833,\qquad
\mathrm{SE}=0.35473.
\]
Step 5: interval and back-transformation. A \(95\%\) Wald interval on the log scale is \(0.28768\pm 1.95996\times 0.35473=0.28768\pm 0.69526=(-0.40758,\,0.98293)\). Exponentiating, the indirect odds ratio of the event comparing \(B\) to \(A\) is \[
\widehat{\mathrm{OR}}_{AB}=e^{0.28768}=1.3333=\tfrac43,\qquad
95\%\ \mathrm{CI}=(e^{-0.40758},\,e^{0.98293})=(0.665,\,2.672).
\] \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Final interpretation, in both orientations. On this chapter’s \(d_{AB}=\eta_B-\eta_A\) scale, the event odds for statin \(B\) are estimated as \(1.33\) times those for statin \(A\); equivalently, the event odds for \(A\) are \(1/1.33=0.75\) times those for \(B\). Either way, the point estimate favors \(A\) as the better statin. But the \(95\%\) interval for the odds ratio, \((0.67,\,2.67)\), comfortably includes \(1\), so on this evidence the difference is not statistically distinguishable from no difference. And the estimate is trustworthy only under transitivity: it assumes the two trials’ populations shared the distribution of any covariate that modifies the statin effect on the log odds-ratio scale. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Three further features of the example repay attention.

Remark. Ratios divide; logs subtract. The indirect odds ratio \(\tfrac43\) is exactly the ratio of the two reported odds ratios, \(2/1.5=\tfrac43\), which is the multiplicative face of the additive identity \(\log\tfrac43=\log 2-\log 1.5\). Had we (wrongly) subtracted the odds ratios, \(2-1.5=0.5\), we would have produced a number with no meaning. The additive scale of Lemma 14.1 is not optional bookkeeping; it is where the cancellation lives. The same arithmetic works verbatim on any additive scale: if a rheumatoid-arthritis network instead reported \(\hat d_{AC}=-0.40\) and \(\hat d_{BC}=-0.15\) as log hazard ratios of disease progression, then \(\hat d_{AB}=-0.40-(-0.15)=-0.25\), a hazard ratio \(e^{-0.25}=0.78\); only the name of the scale changed. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. The price of indirectness, concretely. The Bucher standard error \(0.355\) exceeds both direct standard errors \(0.268\) and \(0.233\), as Corollary 14.1 guarantees. The effect on inference is stark. The direct \(A\)-versus-\(C\) contrast is significant (\(z=0.69315/0.26771=2.59\)), the direct \(B\)-versus-\(C\) contrast borderline (\(z=0.40546/0.23274=1.74\)), yet the indirect \(A\)-versus-\(B\) contrast is firmly inconclusive (\(z=0.28768/0.35473=0.81\), two-sided \(p\approx 0.42\)), its \(95\%\) interval for the odds ratio running from \(0.67\) to \(2.67\) and comfortably including \(1\). Two informative direct comparisons can combine into an uninformative indirect one. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. What the number means, and what it assumes. The estimate \(\widehat{\mathrm{OR}}_{AB}=\tfrac43\) is unbiased for the true \(A\)-versus-\(B\) odds ratio only under transitivity: the populations of the two trials must share the distribution of any covariate that modifies the treatment effect on the log odds-ratio scale. If, for instance, study \(BC\) enrolled younger patients and age modifies the effect of \(B\), then \(\hat d_{BC}\) estimates the effect in a younger population than the one in which \(\hat d_{AC}\) estimates the effect of \(A\), and the subtraction mixes populations. No amount of data fixes this; it is a bias, not a variance, and it is invisible in the standard error \(0.355\). Diagnosing and repairing it is the subject of node-splitting (Definition 15.4), a diagnostic that splits a comparison into its direct and indirect parts and checks whether they agree, and of population adjustment (Parts IV and V). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

14  Indirect Comparison and Bucher's Theorem

title: 14  Indirect Comparison and Bucher’s Theorem
text:
14.12 When transitivity fails
Bucher’s theorem is exact under its hypotheses, so every difficulty with indirect comparison is a difficulty with a hypothesis. The variance hypothesis (independence) is mild and is relaxed by an honest covariance term, Theorem 14.2. The unbiasedness hypothesis (randomization) holds by design in the trials that anchored comparisons are built from. The hypothesis that bears the weight is transitivity, and it fails for a definite mechanism: an effect modifier (Definition 11.3) whose distribution differs between the trial populations.
To see the mechanism, suppose a binary covariate \(Z\) modifies the \(B\)-versus-\(C\) effect, so that the conditional contrast \(d_{BC}(z)\) takes one value at \(z=0\) and another at \(z=1\). The marginal effect Equation 14.2 is then a weighted average of \(d_{BC}(0)\) and \(d_{BC}(1)\) with weights given by the prevalence of \(Z\) in the population. If study \(BC\) has a different prevalence of \(Z\) than the population in which we wish to report \(A\) versus \(B\), the marginal \(d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}\) differs from \(d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})}\), transitivity Equation 14.5 is violated, the consistency equation Equation 14.6 no longer holds, and the Bucher estimator Equation 14.7 is biased by exactly the discrepancy \(d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})}\).

Example 14.3 (A transitivity failure as a specific number) Let \(Z\) be presence of diabetes, an effect modifier of the statin-\(B\) effect. On the log odds-ratio scale, the conditional \(B\)-versus-\(C\) contrast is \(d_{BC}(Z=0)=0.4\) in non-diabetics and \(d_{BC}(Z=1)=1.0\) in diabetics (statin \(B\) is more protective in diabetics). Diabetes is more common in the \(BC\) trial than in the target population where we want the answer:

The marginal \(B\)-versus-\(C\) effects are the prevalence-weighted averages \[
\begin{aligned}
d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})} &= 0.4\times 0.4 + 1.0\times 0.6 = 0.76,\\
d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})} &= 0.4\times 0.8 + 1.0\times 0.2 = 0.52.
\end{aligned}
\] Suppose the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) effect is unaffected by \(Z\) and equals \(d_{AC}=0.6\) in every population. The true target contrast is \(d_{AB}=d_{AC}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})}=0.6-0.52=0.08\). The Bucher estimand, however, subtracts the \(BC\) trial’s own marginal effect, \(d_{AC}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=0.6-0.76=-0.16\). The bias is \[
-0.16-0.08=-0.24=-\big(d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})}\big),
\] a log-odds-ratio error of \(-0.24\), a multiplicative error of \(e^{-0.24}\approx 0.79\) in the odds ratio, about \(21\%\). It does not shrink as the trials grow: it is a bias, not a variance, and it is invisible in any standard error. This is the mechanism the rest of the book is built to detect and repair. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Chapter 16 makes this calculation general and names the resulting failure (Theorem 16.1), and shows how it compounds with the non-collapsibility of the odds ratio and with ecological bias (Definition 16.2), the bias that arises when a relationship estimated at the trial-average level does not hold at the individual level. The point to carry forward is structural: prognostic variables that are not effect modifiers do not break transitivity, because they shift the baselines \(\mu_j\), which Proposition 14.4 already cancels; only effect modifiers, which alter the \(\alpha_k\) across populations, can break it.
When both direct and indirect evidence exist for the same contrast, the consistency equation becomes testable by comparing them: this is node-splitting (Definition 15.4, Theorem 15.1), the diagnostic developed in Chapter 15 that splits a comparison into its direct and indirect parts and checks whether they agree. A significant discrepancy is the empirical signature of a transitivity failure and the trigger for the population-adjustment methods that occupy the remainder of the book.
Transitivity is also the assumption that connects this chapter to the transportability framework of Chapter 12. Transportability asks when a relative effect measured in one population may be carried to another; transitivity is exactly the special case, direct transportability (Definition 12.3, Theorem 12.1), in which the relative effect is assumed to transport unchanged from each trial population to the target. In the language of Example 14.3, transportability would have us reweight the conditional contrasts \(d_{BC}(z)\) to the target prevalence of \(Z\) before subtracting; the population-adjustment methods of Parts IV and V are precisely the machinery that performs that reweighting when it is needed. Transitivity is the assumption that it is not needed, and the bridge to Chapter 12 is the tool for the cases where it is.

title: 14  Indirect Comparison and Bucher’s Theorem
text:
14.13 Notes and references
The anchored indirect comparison and the estimator Equation 14.7 are due to Bucher et al. (1997), who introduced the difference of log relative effects and its variance Equation 14.10 as the basis for indirect comparison in meta-analysis of randomized trials. The framing in terms of constancy of relative effects and transitivity, and the embedding of the estimator in the network model with the reference-treatment decomposition Equation 14.11, follows Dias et al. (2018) and the thesis of Phillippo (2019) (Eq. 1.2 for constancy, Eq. 1.3 for the indirect estimator). The two-layer cancellation argument of Section 14.9, separating the within-study cancellation of baselines from the across-study cancellation of the comparator, is the algebraic core of why anchored comparisons are preferred to unanchored ones; the bias formula Equation 14.12 for the naive comparison is the quantity that unanchored population adjustment (Chapter 26) must control. The delta-method variance of the empirical log-odds (Proposition 14.6) is classical; the sum-of-inverse-cell-counts form is the standard error reported by every two-by-two table routine.
This chapter corresponds to results D.1 (transitivity), D.2 (Bucher’s theorem), D.3 (the Bucher variance), and D.4 (constancy of relative effects) of the proof catalogue in proofs/D_network_meta_analysis.md. The network-level material that builds on Bucher’s identity, namely the parameterizations (Definition 15.2, Definition 15.3), identifiability via the graph incidence rank (Theorem 15.3), the random-effects contrast correlation (Theorem 15.4), the consistency closure and node-splitting (Theorem 15.1, Definition 15.4), and goodness-of-fit (Definition 15.5, Definition 15.6), is developed in Chapter 15; the breakdown of transitivity under effect modification (Theorem 16.1, Definition 16.2) is developed in Chapter 16. When the two direct contrasts are themselves pooled over several trials, the pooling is the pairwise meta-analysis of Chapter 13 (Theorem 13.1 for the fixed-effect inverse-variance estimate, Theorem 13.3 for the random-effects estimate), and Bucher’s identity operates on the pooled summaries. The connection to transportability (Definition 12.3, Theorem 12.1) is developed in Chapter 12.
Three results of this chapter have machine-checked counterparts in the companion Coq development, in theories/Bucher.v. The exact identity Proposition 14.3 is Theorem bucher_identity; the unbiasedness theorem Theorem 14.1 is Theorem bucher_unbiased; the variance theorem Theorem 14.2 is Theorem bucher_variance. The transitivity definition Definition 14.3 and the equivalence Proposition 14.2 are formalized as Definition transitivity together with Lemma transitivity_subtract and Lemma subtract_transitivity. The Coq development treats expectation, variance, and covariance as abstract operators satisfying linearity and the difference identity Equation 14.9, exactly the structure used in the proofs above, so that the formalization captures the algebraic content of Bucher’s theorem while leaving the measure-theoretic construction of those operators to the caller.

title: 14  Indirect Comparison and Bucher’s Theorem
text:
14.14 Exercises
The exercises progress from warm-up to challenge, and are tagged by kind. An exercise marked \(\star\) has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first two are gentle checks of orientation and interpretation; the later ones build toward the network theory of Chapters 15 and 16.

Exercise 14.1 Warm-up. Identify, orient, compute. A health technology assessment has two independent trials against a common comparator \(C\) (placebo). Trial \(AC\) reports the effect of a new drug on the log odds-ratio scale as \(\hat d_{AC}=\eta_C-\eta_A=0.50\) with \(\mathrm{SE}=0.20\); trial \(BC\) reports \(\hat d_{BC}=\eta_C-\eta_B=0.30\) with \(\mathrm{SE}=0.15\). The outcome is unfavorable, so higher odds is worse. (a) Name the common comparator and the target contrast. (b) State whether a positive \(\hat d_{AC}\) means the new drug \(A\) is better or worse than \(C\), and why. (c) Compute the Bucher estimate \(\hat d_{AB}\) and its standard error. (d) Back-transform to an odds ratio for \(B\) versus \(A\) and say, in one sentence, which drug the point estimate favors. (e) State the transitivity assumption you relied on, in one plain sentence.


Exercise 14.2 Interpretation. What breaks it, and what does not. In the setting of Exercise 14.1, suppose you learn that trial \(BC\) enrolled much older patients than trial \(AC\). (a) If age strongly modifies the effect of drug \(B\), is the age difference a threat to the Bucher comparison, and which assumption does it threaten? (b) Would enrolling more patients in each trial remove the threat? Explain in one sentence why or why not. (c) Now suppose instead that age predicts the outcome but does not change the size of any treatment effect. Explain why the anchored comparison is then unharmed, naming the result (Proposition 14.4) that does the work.


Exercise 14.3 Computation. A Bucher computation from summaries. Two trials report log hazard ratios on the proportional-hazards scale: \(\hat d_{AC}=-0.51\) with \(\mathrm{SE}=0.18\), and \(\hat d_{BC}=-0.22\) with \(\mathrm{SE}=0.13\), the contrasts being independent. Compute the indirect log hazard ratio of \(A\) versus \(B\), its standard error, a \(95\%\) confidence interval, and the back-transformed hazard ratio with interval. State the transitivity assumption you are relying on in words.


Exercise 14.4 Computation. From raw tables. Repeat the worked example Example 14.2 with the tables: study \(AC\) has \(A:24/120\) and \(C:48/160\); study \(BC\) has \(B:20/100\) and \(C:30/150\). Report the two direct log odds-ratios with standard errors, the Bucher estimate with standard error, and the indirect odds ratio with \(95\%\) interval. Verify that the indirect odds ratio equals the ratio of the two direct odds ratios.


Exercise 14.5 Proof. Additivity holds on the right scales. Prove that the antisymmetry and additivity laws Lemma 14.1 hold for the log risk-ratio contrast \(d_{ab}=\log\bar\mu_b-\log\bar\mu_a\) and for the mean-difference contrast \(d_{ab}=\bar\mu_b-\bar\mu_a\), and show by a numerical counterexample that they fail for the risk-ratio contrast taken on the ratio scale itself, \(\bar\mu_b/\bar\mu_a\) (that is, that \(\bar\mu_C/\bar\mu_A\ne(\bar\mu_C/\bar\mu_B)\cdot\text{(something additive)}\) unless one first takes logarithms). Conclude that Bucher’s subtraction is a statement about the link scale.


Exercise 14.6 Computation. The cost of dropping the anchor. Using the additive decomposition Equation 14.11, suppose \(\mu_{AC}=-1.2\), \(\mu_{BC}=-1.8\), \(\alpha_A=-0.7\), \(\alpha_B=-0.4\), \(\alpha_C=0\) on the logit scale. Compute the true network contrast \(d_{AB}\), the anchored estimand \(d_{AC}-d_{BC}\), and the unanchored estimand Equation 14.8, and verify that the unanchored estimand is off by exactly \(\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC}\) as Proposition 14.5 predicts. Comment on which of the five parameters an anchored comparison is immune to.


Exercise 14.7 Proof. A longer chain. Generalize Bucher’s identity to a path of comparators \(A\to C\to D\to B\), in which trial \(AC\) estimates \(d_{AC}\), trial \(CD\) estimates \(d_{CD}\), and trial \(DB\) estimates \(d_{DB}\), all independent. Using Lemma 14.1, derive the chained indirect estimator of \(d_{AB}\) as a signed sum of the three direct contrasts, prove it unbiased under transitivity along the path, and show its variance is the sum of the three direct variances. Explain why each additional link strictly inflates the variance.


Exercise 14.8 (\(\star\), challenge) Correlated contrasts from a three-arm trial. Suppose a single three-arm trial reports both \(\hat d_{AC}\) and \(\hat d_{BC}\) (arms \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) in one study), so the shared comparator arm makes the two contrasts correlated with \(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat d_{AC},\hat d_{BC})=\rho\sqrt{v_{AC}v_{BC}}\) for some \(\rho>0\). Using the general formula in Theorem 14.2, write the variance of the Bucher estimate of \(d_{AB}\) and show it is strictly smaller than \(v_{AC}+v_{BC}\). For the homoskedastic structure in which both contrasts share a comparator arm of variance \(\sigma^2\) and have arm-level variance \(\sigma^2\) in each non-comparator arm, show \(\rho=\tfrac12\) and recover the variance of the within-study \(A\)-versus-\(B\) contrast directly; reconcile your answer with Theorem 15.4.


Exercise 14.9 (\(\star\), interpretation) Quantifying a transitivity failure. A binary effect modifier \(Z\) acts on the \(B\)-versus-\(C\) contrast so that the conditional log odds-ratios are \(d_{BC}(Z=0)=0.2\) and \(d_{BC}(Z=1)=0.8\) (on the link scale, treating these conditional contrasts as collapsible for simplicity). Study \(BC\) has \(\Pr(Z=1)=0.7\), while the target population \(\mathcal P_{AB}\) in which we wish to report \(A\) versus \(B\) has \(\Pr(Z=1)=0.3\). The \(A\)-versus-\(C\) contrast is unaffected by \(Z\) and equals \(d_{AC}=0.6\) in every population. Compute the marginal \(d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}\) and \(d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})}\), the true target contrast \(d_{AB}\), the Bucher estimand \(d_{AC}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}\), and hence the bias of the unadjusted indirect comparison. Identify which quantity an effect-modifier adjustment (Chapter 17 onward) must reweight to remove the bias, and explain why a prognostic variable that shifted only the baseline would have created no bias at all.





Bucher, Heiner C., Gordon H. Guyatt, Lauren E. Griffith, and Stephen D. Walter. 1997. “The Results of Direct and Indirect Treatment Comparisons in Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.” Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 50 (6): 683–91.


Dias, Sofia, A. E. Ades, Nicky J. Welton, Jeroen P. Jansen, and Alexander J. Sutton. 2018. Network Meta-Analysis for Decision-Making. Statistics in Practice. Wiley.


Phillippo, David Mark. 2019. “Calibration of Treatment Effects in Network Meta-Analysis Using Individual Patient Data.” PhD thesis, University of Bristol.

title: 15  Network Meta-Analysis: Models and Identifiability
text:
15.1 Introduction
The previous chapter built an indirect comparison from a single triangle: a study of \(A\) against a common comparator \(C\), a study of \(B\) against the same \(C\), and the subtraction \(\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}\) that the algebra of contrasts licenses under transitivity (Theorem 14.1). A health technology assessment is rarely so tidy. It must usually weigh a dozen treatments compared in a scatter of trials, some two-armed and some multi-armed, some sharing comparators and some not, with the same pairwise contrast occasionally informed by both a direct head-to-head trial and one or more indirect paths. Network meta-analysis (NMA) is the apparatus that pools all of this evidence at once into a single coherent set of relative effects, estimating every pairwise contrast in the network, including contrasts never studied head to head, while honoring the correlations that multi-arm trials and shared comparators impose.
Why pool everything into one model instead of running a separate Bucher comparison for each pair of treatments? Three reasons, each made precise in this chapter. First, pooling borrows strength: a contrast with no direct head-to-head trial is still estimated, informed by every indirect path through the network, and a contrast carrying both direct and indirect evidence combines the two efficiently rather than discarding either. Second, pooling respects structure: a three-arm trial is one randomized experiment, not three independent two-arm trials, and a single model preserves the correlations that such shared-comparator designs impose, correlations that separate pairwise calculations would silently throw away. Third, pooling makes coherence testable: isolated pairwise comparisons cannot notice that the whole web of relative effects must fit together, whereas the network can check whether the direct and indirect routes to a contrast agree, and flag them when they do not. Chapter 14 gave the single triangle; this chapter gives the whole web, together with the tools to decide which of its contrasts a reader may trust.
This chapter develops the standard NMA model as a piece of mathematics. The organizing idea is that an NMA is a generalized linear model (Definition 7.4): each trial arm contributes one observation, the link-scale arm means are a linear function \(\boldsymbol\theta=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\) of a parameter vector \(\boldsymbol\beta\) through a design matrix \(\mathbf X\), and the entire analytic content of the method, its estimability and its assumptions, is read off from the structure of \(\mathbf X\). Bucher’s estimator is then visible as the special case in which \(\mathbf X\) encodes one triangle and two studies, and the question “which contrasts can the network estimate?” becomes the linear-algebra question “which columns of \(\mathbf X\) are independent?”
We prove, in full, the results that make this picture rigorous. We give the two standard parameterizations of the arm means, the baseline-shift form (Definition 15.2) that names a separate contrast inside each study and the reference-treatment form (Definition 15.3) that names a single network-wide contrast per treatment, and we prove they describe the same model exactly on the subspace where the consistency equations hold (Theorem 15.2). We prove that the network contrasts are identifiable if and only if the treatment graph is connected, by computing the rank of the design matrix through the rank of a graph incidence matrix (Theorem 15.3). We derive the characteristic one-half correlation between two contrasts that share an arm in a multi-arm trial, and we show that the one-half is not an arbitrary modeling choice but the unique value that makes the heterogeneity variance independent of which arm is called the baseline (Theorem 15.4). We prove the algebraic closure of the consistency equations (Theorem 15.1), which says that the \(\binom{K}{2}\) pairwise contrasts of a \(K\)-treatment network are generated by \(K-1\) basis contrasts and constrained by exactly \(\binom{K-1}{2}\) loop identities, the very identities that node-splitting (Definition 15.4) tests for inconsistency. We extend the model to individual patient data and prove the identifiability of the network meta-regression (Theorem 15.5), the springboard for the population-adjustment methods of Parts IV and V. We close the theory with the goodness-of-fit machinery the applied literature reports for these models, the residual deviance (Definition 15.5) and the deviance information criterion (Definition 15.6). A fully worked triangle-plus-extra-arm network, carried from a design matrix to fitted contrasts, standard errors, a node-split, and a residual deviance, makes every formula concrete.
Throughout we use the notation of Notation: \(j\) indexes studies, \(k\) indexes treatments and arms, \(\theta_{jk}\) is the link-scale mean of arm \(k\) in study \(j\), \(\mu_j\) is a study baseline, \(d_{ab}\) is the network contrast of treatment \(b\) versus treatment \(a\), and \(\delta_{j,\,t_1 t_k}\) is a study-level contrast. The chapter corresponds to results D.5 through D.14 of the proof catalogue in proofs/D_network_meta_analysis.md, and it builds directly on the Bucher development of Chapter 14 (Definition 14.3, Definition 14.2, Theorem 14.1, Theorem 14.2) and the pairwise meta-analysis of Chapter 13 (Theorem 13.1, Theorem 13.3, Definition 13.3).

text:
15.2 A running example and a reader’s toolkit
The formal development below moves quickly into design matrices, graphs, and rank conditions. To keep it anchored, we fix one small clinical network now and carry it through every section. A reader who holds this picture in mind can translate each abstract step back into trials and drugs.

Example 15.1 (Three treatments, four trials) A health technology assessment compares three treatments for a single condition:

treatment \(1\) = placebo (the network reference),
treatment \(2\) = Drug A,
treatment \(3\) = Drug B.

Four randomized trials are available. Each reports a relative effect on the log-odds scale (a log odds ratio); a positive value means the second-named treatment raises the odds of a good outcome.









Study \(j\)
Arms
Design
Comparison(s) it reports




1
placebo, Drug A
two-arm
Drug A vs placebo


2
placebo, Drug B
two-arm
Drug B vs placebo


3
Drug A, Drug B
two-arm (head-to-head)
Drug B vs Drug A


4
placebo, Drug A, Drug B
three-arm
Drug A vs placebo, and Drug B vs placebo



Drawing a dot for each treatment and a line for each within-study comparison gives the treatment-comparison graph:
                  (2) Drug A
                  /         \
       studies 1, 4          study 3
                /             \
   (1) placebo  --------------  (3) Drug B
                studies 2, 4
Three facts can be read straight off the picture, and the rest of the chapter turns each one into a theorem.

Direct versus indirect evidence. Every pair is compared directly by at least one trial: placebo vs Drug A (studies 1 and 4), placebo vs Drug B (studies 2 and 4), Drug A vs Drug B (study 3). Drug A vs Drug B is also estimable indirectly, by chaining Drug A vs placebo with placebo vs Drug B.
Connectedness. One can travel from any treatment to any other along the lines. This is what lets the network estimate every relative effect, including ones with no direct trial; Theorem 15.3 makes it precise.
A loop. The three edges \(1\)-\(2\), \(2\)-\(3\), \(1\)-\(3\) close a triangle. That loop is what makes it possible to test whether the direct and indirect routes to Drug A vs Drug B agree; Theorem 15.1 and Section 15.10 build the test. A tree-shaped network with no loop offers nothing to test.

Study \(4\), the three-arm trial, is the source of most of the subtlety in this chapter. Its full numerical analysis is completed in Example 15.2. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The picture uses standard graph words. Here is the whole vocabulary in trial language; keep it nearby.







Graph term
What it means for the evidence




vertex (node)
a treatment


edge
one within-study comparison (a single randomized contrast)


path
a chain of comparisons linking two treatments


connected
every treatment is reachable from every other by comparisons


connected component
a maximal cluster of treatments joined by comparisons


loop (cycle)
a closed chain: both a direct and an indirect route between two treatments


direct evidence (on \(a\) vs \(b\))
a trial that randomized patients between \(a\) and \(b\)


indirect evidence (on \(a\) vs \(b\))
an estimate of \(a\) vs \(b\) obtained through a path via other treatments



Four quantities recur throughout, and beginners routinely blend them. The next table previews them with plain meanings and a running-example instance; the precise definitions follow in Section 15.3 and Section 15.4, so nothing here is used before it is defined later.








Symbol

\(\theta_{jk}\)
outcome level of arm \(k\) in study \(j\), on the link scale
log-odds of a good outcome on the Drug A arm of study \(1\)


\(\mu_j\)
study \(j\) baseline: its reference arm’s level
log-odds on the placebo arm of study \(1\)


\(\delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}k}\)
a study-specific contrast: treatment \(k\) vs that study’s own baseline arm
Drug A vs placebo as measured inside study \(1\)


\(d_k\)

Drug A vs placebo, pooled across all trials


\(d_{ab}=d_b-d_a\)

Drug B vs Drug A, pooled

\(\tilde{\mathbf d}=(0,d_2,d_3)\)



The single most common conceptual slip is to confuse a study-specific contrast \(\delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}k}\) (one study’s answer) with a network contrast \(d_k\) or \(d_{ab}\) (the pooled answer). The whole point of an NMA is to build the network contrasts out of the study-specific ones.

Remark. Reading the sign of a contrast. The convention \(d_{ab}=d_b-d_a\) means “treatment \(b\) versus treatment \(a\)”, with \(b\) in the favored-if-positive direction. On the logit scale a contrast is a log odds ratio: \(d_{ab}>0\) says \(b\) raises the odds of the outcome relative to \(a\), and the odds ratio is \(\mathrm{OR}_{ab}=e^{d_{ab}}\). Reversing the order flips the sign and inverts the odds ratio: \(d_{ba}=-d_{ab}\) and \(\mathrm{OR}_{ba}=1/\mathrm{OR}_{ab}\). For instance a log-odds contrast of \(0.5\) is an odds ratio \(e^{0.5}\approx1.65\); the same comparison written the other way is \(-0.5\), an odds ratio \(e^{-0.5}\approx0.61\). Applied papers are inconsistent about direction, so always check which treatment is named first. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 15  Network Meta-Analysis: Models and Identifiability
section: 15.3 The network as a generalized linear model
text:
15.3 The network as a generalized linear model
A network of evidence is a finite collection of randomized studies. Study \(j\in\{1,\dots,J\}\) randomizes patients among a set of arms \(\mathcal A_j\subseteq\{1,\dots,K\}\), where \(\{1,\dots,K\}\) enumerates the treatments under comparison and treatment \(1\) is a fixed network reference (often placebo or standard of care). We write \(A_j=|\mathcal A_j|\ge 2\) for the number of arms in study \(j\), and we designate one arm \(t_{j,1}\in\mathcal A_j\) as the study baseline; nothing of substance depends on which arm is chosen as \(t_{j,1}\), a freedom we exploit in Section 15.7. The total number of arms in the network is \[
N \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{J} A_j ,
\tag{15.1}\] and the total number of within-study contrasts, one fewer than the arm count in each study, is \[
C \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{J} (A_j-1) \;=\; N - J .
\tag{15.2}\]
The treatments that are compared, directly or by sharing a trial, form a graph.

Definition 15.1 (The arm-based network model) The treatment-comparison graph \(G=(\mathcal V,\mathcal E)\) has vertex set \(\mathcal V=\{1,\dots,K\}\), one vertex per treatment, and one edge for each within-study contrast: study \(j\) with baseline \(t_{j,1}\) contributes the \(A_j-1\) edges \(\{t_{j,1},k\}\) for \(k\in\mathcal A_j\setminus\{t_{j,1}\}\). Parallel edges from different studies are kept distinct, so \(G\) is in general a multigraph with \(|\mathcal E|=C\) edges.
For a chosen link function \(g\) (Definition 7.2), let \(\theta_{jk}=g(\bar\mu_{jk})\) be the link-scale mean outcome of arm \(k\) in study \(j\), where \(\bar\mu_{jk}\) is the marginal mean response in that arm. The arm-based network model writes the vector \(\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathbb R^{N}\) of all arm means as a linear predictor \[
\boldsymbol\theta \;=\; \mathbf X\,\boldsymbol\beta ,
\tag{15.3}\] for a design matrix \(\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{N\times p}\) and a parameter vector \(\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb
R^{p}\). Coupled with a response distribution from an exponential family (Definition 7.1), for instance \(r_{jk}\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n_{jk},g^{-1}(\theta_{jk}))\) for binary outcomes under the logit link, Equation 15.3 makes the network a generalized linear model. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader’s translation of the arm model. Stack all the trial arms into one tall column \(\boldsymbol\theta\), one entry per arm. In the running example the arms are placebo and Drug A (study \(1\)), placebo and Drug B (study \(2\)), Drug A and Drug B (study \(3\)), and placebo, Drug A, Drug B (study \(4\)), so \(\boldsymbol\theta\) has \(N=9\) entries; for example \(\theta_{4,2}\) is the log-odds of a good outcome on the Drug A arm of the three-arm study \(4\). The model Equation 15.3 says every one of these arm levels is assembled from a handful of shared ingredients, the study baselines and the treatment effects, through the table \(\mathbf X\). The two appearances of the link, \(\theta_{jk}=g(\bar\mu_{jk})\) in the definition and \(g^{-1}(\theta_{jk})\) in the binomial example, are the same map read in opposite directions: \(\theta\) is the arm’s outcome level moved onto the additive scale where treatment effects add up, and \(g^{-1}\) moves it back to a probability. With the logit link, \(\theta_{jk}=0.5\) corresponds to a response probability \(g^{-1}(0.5)=1/(1+e^{-0.5})\approx0.62\). The treatment-comparison graph is nothing more than the picture of Example 15.1: a dot per treatment, a line per within-study comparison. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Multi-arm trials: clinical pairs versus contrast rows. A three-arm trial such as study \(4\) compares all three treatment pairs within one randomized experiment, so clinically it carries direct evidence on placebo vs Drug A, placebo vs Drug B, and Drug A vs Drug B. The graph definition, however, gives it only \(A_j-1=2\) edges: after we name one arm the study baseline (here placebo), we keep the \(2\) contrasts to that baseline and treat the third pairwise comparison, Drug A vs Drug B, as their difference. This is no loss of information. The omitted contrast is recovered exactly by subtraction, \(\delta_{\text{A vs B}}=\delta_{\text{placebo vs B}}-\delta_{\text{placebo vs A}}\), and it is correlated with the two kept contrasts because all three share the placebo arm. Keeping \(A_j-1\) independent contrasts rather than all \(\binom{A_j}{2}\) pairwise comparisons is what keeps the rows of the design linearly independent; carrying their correlation, computed in Theorem 15.4, is what keeps the standard errors honest. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Equation Equation 15.3 is the entire formal commitment of an NMA: a single linear predictor across all studies, tying the arms together through shared treatment parameters. Two specifications of \((\mathbf X,\boldsymbol\beta)\) are in standard use, and the bulk of this chapter studies them and their consequences. Before naming them we record the sense in which the chapter generalizes the last one.

Remark. Bucher as a two-study, one-triangle network. Recall the Bucher triangle of Chapter 14: two active treatments each compared against a common comparator. Relabel that comparator as the network reference, treatment \(1\), and the two actives as treatments \(2\) and \(3\). With two two-arm studies, one on \(\{1,2\}\) and one on \(\{1,3\}\), we have \(K=3\), \(N=4\), \(J=2\), and \(C=(2-1)+(2-1)=2\) within-study contrasts; the graph \(G\) is the path \(2-1-3\). The arm-based model has one baseline and one contrast per study, and eliminating the two baselines leaves exactly the contrasts \(d_{12}\) and \(d_{13}\), whose difference \(d_{13}-d_{12}=d_{23}\) is the Bucher estimator (Theorem 14.1). The graph is connected but contains no cycle, so there is direct evidence on \(2\) versus \(1\) and on \(3\) versus \(1\) but only indirect evidence on \(3\) versus \(2\); there is nothing to test for inconsistency. Adding a third study on \(\{2,3\}\) closes the triangle into a cycle and creates the direct-versus-indirect tension that node-splitting (Definition 15.4) adjudicates. The running example of Example 15.1 is this closed triangle with one further multi-arm trial, and everything in this chapter is the systematic version of this enlargement. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Arm-based and contrast-based likelihoods. The model Equation 15.3 is arm-based: the observations are the \(N\) arms. An equivalent contrast-based form, used for estimation and in the worked example of Section 15.13, takes as data the \(C\) within-study contrast estimates \(y_{j,\,t_{j,1}k}=\hat\theta_{jk}-\hat\theta_{j,t_{j,1}}\). In large samples each contrast estimate is approximately normal about the true contrast by the delta method (Theorem 5.3), and two contrasts that share the baseline arm of a multi-arm study are correlated because the shared arm’s sampling error enters both; Theorem 15.4 computes that correlation. Passing from the arm-based to the contrast-based likelihood is exactly the elimination of the per-study baselines \(\mu_j\), which appear in each study’s arms alike and cancel in within-study differences. Concretely, in a two-arm study with baseline arm \(1\), the two arm means are \(\theta_{j1}=\mu_j\) and \(\theta_{j2}=\mu_j+\delta_{j,12}\); subtracting the baseline arm removes \(\mu_j\) and leaves the contrast \(\delta_{j,12}=\theta_{j2}-\theta_{j1}\). The recipe is the same in general: (i) start from the \(N\) arms; (ii) in each study pick a baseline arm \(t_{j,1}\); (iii) subtract that arm’s estimate from the others; (iv) keep the resulting \(A_j-1\) within-study contrasts; (v) carry their covariance, which within a multi-arm study has the shared-arm correlation of Theorem 15.4. Steps (i) to (iv) turn \(N\) arm observations into \(C\) contrast observations by discarding the \(J\) baselines; step (v) is the price of that convenience. We develop both views and prove the identifiability theory on the arm-based design, where the baselines are explicit. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

section: 15.4 Two parameterizations of the arm means
text:
15.4 Two parameterizations of the arm means
The arm means \(\boldsymbol\theta\) carry two layers of information: the level of each study’s outcomes, which is a nuisance reflecting that study’s population and baseline risk, and the contrasts between treatments, which are the quantities of interest. The two standard parameterizations split these layers in two different ways.

Definition 15.2 (Baseline-shift parameterization) The baseline-shift parameterization (corresponds to D.5 in the proof catalogue) writes each arm mean as the study baseline plus a study-specific contrast to that baseline: \[
\theta_{jk} \;=\; \mu_j^{\mathrm{BS}} \;+\; \delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}k},
\qquad k\in\mathcal A_j,
\tag{15.4}\] with the convention \(\delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}t_{j,1}}=0\) for the baseline arm, so that \(\mu_j^{\mathrm{BS}}=\theta_{j,t_{j,1}}\). The free parameters are the \(J\) baselines \(\mu_j^{\mathrm{BS}}\) and the \(C=N-J\) within-study contrasts \(\delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}k}\) for the non-baseline arms \(k\ne t_{j,1}\), a total of \(J+C=N\) parameters. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

In words, the baseline-shift form gives every study its own private answer: it names a separate contrast \(\delta_{j,t_{j,1}k}\) inside every study. It places no restriction on the arm means at all: there are as many parameters, \(N\), as arms, and Equation 15.4 is simply a relabeling of the \(N\) numbers \(\theta_{jk}\) into \(J\) baselines and \(C\) within-study differences. Its virtue is that each \(\delta_{j,t_{j,1}k}\) is the natural target of a random effect in the random-effects model of Section 15.9. Its defect is that it does not, by itself, tie studies together: the contrast \(\delta_{j,t_{j,1}k}\) of study \(j\) and the contrast \(\delta_{j',t_{j',1}k}\) of study \(j'\) for the very same pair of treatments are, a priori, distinct parameters. Tying them together is the content of the consistency assumption, which the second parameterization builds in from the start.

Definition 15.3 (Reference-treatment parameterization) Fix the network reference treatment \(1\) and a vector of network contrasts \(\mathbf d=(d_2,\dots,d_K)^\top\in\mathbb R^{K-1}\), where \(d_k\) is the relative effect of treatment \(k\) versus the reference on the link scale, with the convention \(d_1=0\). The reference-treatment parameterization (corresponds to D.6 in the proof catalogue) writes \[
\theta_{jk} \;=\; \mu_j \;+\; \bigl(d_k - d_{t_{j,1}}\bigr),
\qquad k\in\mathcal A_j,
\tag{15.5}\] where \(\mu_j=\theta_{j,t_{j,1}}\) is the study-\(j\) baseline. The free parameters are the \(J\) baselines \(\mu_j\) and the \(K-1\) network contrasts \(d_2,\dots,d_K\), a total of \(J+K-1\) parameters. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

In the reference-treatment form a treatment carries a single contrast \(d_k\) for the whole network. In words, this form gives each treatment one number, its effect versus the reference, good for the entire network; every study comparing two treatments must then show the same gap between them. The reference treatment \(1\) is only a coordinate origin, like the choice of where to put zero on a thermometer: it is usually placebo for readability, but any treatment could serve, and the network’s answers (any \(d_{ab}\)) do not depend on the choice. The within-study contrast of treatment \(k\) versus the study baseline is forced to be \[
\delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}k} \;=\; \theta_{jk}-\theta_{j,t_{j,1}} \;=\; d_k - d_{t_{j,1}} ,
\tag{15.6}\] the same expression in every study that compares those two treatments. Equation Equation 15.6 is the consistency constraint: it is automatic in the reference-treatment parameterization and is the formal statement that the relative effects are constant across the network, the population-level constancy of Definition 14.2 rendered as an algebraic identity among parameters. A caution on the word: consistency here is a property of a whole network of relative effects (direct and indirect routes agree), and it is unrelated to the SUTVA consistency of Chapter 9, which links an observed outcome to a potential outcome. The two ideas share only a name. The two parameterizations therefore differ in their parameter counts, \(N\) for baseline-shift against \(J+K-1\) for reference-treatment, and they agree precisely when the within-study contrasts obey Equation 15.6. Making that statement exact is the work of Section 15.7; first we study the algebra of the network contrasts themselves.

title: 15  Network Meta-Analysis: Models and Identifiability
section: 15.5 Consistency equations and their algebraic closure
text:
15.5 Consistency equations and their algebraic closure
The reference-treatment parameterization defines a contrast only against the reference. The contrast between any two treatments is recovered by subtraction, and the resulting family of \(\binom{K}{2}\) pairwise contrasts is highly redundant. The next theorem makes the redundancy precise: the family is generated by \(K-1\) free numbers and is pinned down by a definite number of loop constraints. These constraints are what an inconsistency analysis tests.
Before the general statement, here is the identity in the running example. Suppose the pooled effects come out as Drug A vs placebo \(d_{12}=0.5\) and Drug B vs placebo \(d_{13}=1.0\) on the log-odds scale. Then consistency forces the Drug B vs Drug A contrast to be \(d_{23}=d_{13}-d_{12}=0.5\): it is not free to take any other value. If a head-to-head trial instead reported Drug B vs Drug A as \(0.1\), the gap between the forced \(0.5\) and the observed \(0.1\) is exactly the disagreement that node-splitting (Section 15.10) measures. The next theorem shows that this triangle identity, and its \(K\)-treatment generalizations, are the only constraints the network imposes on its pairwise effects.

Theorem 15.1 (Closure of the consistency equations) Define, from a network-contrast vector \(\mathbf d=(d_1,\dots,d_K)\) with \(d_1=0\), the full family of pairwise network contrasts \[
d_{ab} \;:=\; d_b - d_a, \qquad a,b\in\{1,\dots,K\}.
\tag{15.7}\] Then the following hold (corresponds to D.10 in the proof catalogue).

Antisymmetry. \(d_{ab}=-d_{ba}\) for all \(a,b\), and \(d_{aa}=0\).
Additivity (the triangle, or loop, identity). For all \(a,b,c\), \[
d_{ab} + d_{bc} \;=\; d_{ac}, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad d_{ac}-d_{bc}=d_{ab}.
\tag{15.8}\]
Generation. Every pairwise contrast is determined by the \(K-1\) basis contrasts \(d_2,\dots,d_K\) through \(d_{ab}=d_{1b}-d_{1a}=d_b-d_a\).
Converse and uniqueness. Conversely, let \((e_{ab})_{a,b}\) be any family of real numbers satisfying the additivity identity Equation 15.8 for all triples. Then \(e\) is antisymmetric, and there is a unique vector \(\mathbf d\) with \(d_1=0\) such that \(e_{ab}=d_b-d_a\) for all \(a,b\), namely \(d_k=e_{1k}\).
Count. The set of consistent contrast families, those of the form Equation 15.7, is a linear subspace of dimension \(K-1\) inside the \(\binom{K}{2}\)-dimensional space of antisymmetric families. The additivity identities therefore impose exactly \[
\binom{K}{2}-(K-1)=\binom{K-1}{2}
\tag{15.9}\] independent constraints.



Proof. Parts 1 and 2 are immediate from Equation 15.7 and reproduce, for the network contrasts, the antisymmetry and additivity of relative effects proved within a single population in Chapter 14 (Lemma 14.1). For antisymmetry, \(d_{ab}=d_b-d_a=-(d_a-d_b)=-d_{ba}\), and \(d_{aa}=0\). For additivity, \(d_{ab}+d_{bc}=(d_b-d_a)+(d_c-d_b)=d_c-d_a=d_{ac}\); the middle term \(d_b\) cancels, and subtracting \(d_{bc}\) from both sides rearranges to \(d_{ac}-d_{bc}=d_{ab}\). Part 3 is the definition Equation 15.7 read with \(a\) or \(b\) equal to \(1\): \(d_{1b}=d_b-d_1=d_b\) and \(d_{ab}=d_b-d_a=d_{1b}-d_{1a}\).
For part 4, suppose \((e_{ab})\) satisfies Equation 15.8 for all triples. Because the identity holds for every triple, we are free to choose convenient ones. Plugging the same index into all three slots, \(a=b=c\), gives \(e_{aa}+e_{aa}=e_{aa}\), so \(e_{aa}=0\): the diagonal vanishes. Choosing \(c=a\) gives \(e_{ab}+e_{ba}=e_{aa}=0\), so \(e_{ba}=-e_{ab}\) and \(e\) is antisymmetric. Define \(d_k:=e_{1k}\); then \(d_1=e_{11}=0\). Apply additivity to the triple \((a,1,b)\): \(e_{a1}+e_{1b}=e_{ab}\), and using antisymmetry \(e_{a1}=-e_{1a}=-d_a\), so \(e_{ab}=-d_a+d_b=d_b-d_a\), as claimed. Uniqueness: if \(e_{ab}=d_b-d_a=d_b'-d_a'\) for all \(a,b\) with \(d_1=d_1'=0\), then taking \(a=1\) gives \(d_b=e_{1b}=d_b'\) for every \(b\).
For part 5, let \(\mathcal A\cong\mathbb R^{\binom{K}{2}}\) be the vector space of antisymmetric families, coordinatized by the values \(e_{ab}\) for \(a<b\), and let \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{cons}}\subseteq\mathcal A\) be the subset satisfying all additivity identities, the consistent families. The map \(T:\mathbb R^{K-1}\to\mathcal A\) sending \((d_2,\dots,d_K)\mapsto (e_{ab})\) with \(e_{ab}=d_b-d_a\) (and \(d_1=0\)) is linear. It is injective: if \(d_b-d_a=0\) for all \(a,b\), then taking \(a=1\) gives \(d_b=0\) for all \(b\). By parts 3 and 4 its image is exactly \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{cons}}\). Hence \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{cons}}\) is a linear subspace with \(\dim\mathcal D_{\mathrm{cons}}=\dim\mathbb R^{K-1}=K-1\), and its codimension in \(\mathcal A\) is \(\binom{K}{2}-(K-1)\). The arithmetic \(\binom{K}{2}-(K-1)=\tfrac{K(K-1)}{2}-(K-1)=(K-1)\tfrac{K-2}{2}=\binom{K-1}{2}\) gives Equation 15.9. \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters, and how loops carry the constraints. In evidence-synthesis terms: of all the pairwise relative effects in a network, only \(K-1\) are genuinely free; every other is forced by the ones already chosen, and the forcing identities are the loop equations. Those loop equations are the only places inconsistency can surface, so a network can be checked for coherence exactly where it contains a loop, and nowhere else. The count Equation 15.9 has a matching graph-theoretic reading. On the complete graph \(K_K\) a spanning tree has \(K-1\) edges and contains no cycle; the contrasts along the tree edges are free and generate all others, which is part 3. Each of the remaining \(\binom{K}{2}-(K-1)=\binom{K-1}{2}\) edges closes exactly one independent cycle, and that cycle is one additivity identity, an equation of the form \(d_{a_1a_2}+d_{a_2a_3}+\cdots+d_{a_m a_1}=0\). The number of independent constraints equals the cycle rank of the complete graph, and a contrast is testable for inconsistency precisely when the evidence contains an independent cycle, that is, both a direct edge and an indirect path between its endpoints. A tree-shaped network, such as the Bucher triangle-as-path of Section 15.3, has no cycle and nothing to test. \(\blacktriangleleft\)
