title: 18  Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison
section: 18.8 MAIC weights are logistic inverse-probability weights
text:
18.8 MAIC weights are logistic inverse-probability weights
The exponential form Equation 18.5 is not an accident of the entropy objective; it is the functional form of an inverse probability-of-selection weight. Making the connection precise places MAIC inside the inverse-probability-weighting framework of Chapter 10 and the transportability framework of Chapter 12, and it explains both why MAIC works and what it assumes.
The idea in one sentence, before the algebra. Imagine pooling the \(AC\) and \(BC\) patients and fitting a model that predicts, from covariates alone, which trial a patient came from. A patient who “looks like a \(BC\) patient” gets a high predicted probability of \(BC\) membership. MAIC upweights exactly those \(AC\) patients, the ones who resemble the comparator population, and downweights the \(AC\) patients who look distinctively like the index trial. The theorem below shows that the entropy weights we derived are these inverse-membership-odds weights, so MAIC is quietly doing propensity weighting for trial membership, the same machinery as inverse probability weighting in Chapter 10, but pointed at “which population” instead of “which treatment.” The only twist is that we never see the individual \(BC\) patients, so we cannot fit the membership model by ordinary likelihood; we fit it by matching moments instead.
Introduce a binary selection indicator \(S\) that labels which trial an individual came from: \(S=1\) for the index (\(AC\)) trial and \(S=0\) for the comparator (\(BC\)) trial. Posit a logistic model for trial membership given covariates, \[
\operatorname{logit}P(S=1\mid\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})
=\log\frac{P(S=1\mid\mathbf{x})}{P(S=0\mid\mathbf{x})}
=\tilde\alpha+\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top\mathbf{x}.
\tag{18.15}\]

Theorem 18.3 (Equivalence of MAIC weights and logistic inverse-odds weights) Under the trial-membership model Equation 18.15, the density ratio that transports an index-population average to the comparator population is the inverse selection odds, \[
\frac{f_{BC}(\mathbf{x})}{f_{AC}(\mathbf{x})}
=\frac{P(S=0)}{P(S=1)}\cdot\frac{P(S=0\mid\mathbf{x})}{P(S=1\mid\mathbf{x})}
=\frac{P(S=0)}{P(S=1)}\,\exp\!\big(-\tilde\alpha-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top\mathbf{x}\big),
\tag{18.16}\] which, as a function of \(\mathbf{x}\), is proportional to the MAIC weight Equation 18.5 under the identification \(\boldsymbol{\beta}=-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\). Consequently the MAIC estimator of the comparator-population mean of arm \(A\), \[
\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}
=\frac{\sum_{i}w_i^{*}\,\mathbf{1}\{T_i=A\}\,Y_i}{\sum_{i}w_i^{*}\,\mathbf{1}\{T_i=A\}},
\tag{18.17}\] is the inverse-probability-weighting (Horvitz-Thompson) estimator of Theorem 10.3 applied to the transport problem from \(\mathcal{P}_{AC}\) to \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\), with selection weights estimated by the moment conditions Equation 18.10 rather than by logistic maximum likelihood.


Proof. The density ratio is the inverse odds. By Bayes’ theorem applied within each trial, the covariate density given membership is \(f_{AC}(\mathbf{x})=P(\mathbf{x}\mid S=1)\) and \(f_{BC}(\mathbf{x})=P(\mathbf{x}\mid S=0)\). (In this line \(P(\mathbf{x})\) and \(P(\mathbf{x}\mid S=s)\) are covariate densities, whereas \(P(S=s)\) and \(P(S=s\mid\mathbf{x})\) are membership probabilities; Bayes’ theorem is what links the two.) Writing \(P(\mathbf{x}\mid S=s)=P(S=s\mid\mathbf{x})\,
P(\mathbf{x})/P(S=s)\) and taking the ratio, the marginal covariate density \(P(\mathbf{x})\) cancels: \[
\frac{f_{BC}(\mathbf{x})}{f_{AC}(\mathbf{x})}
=\frac{P(S=0\mid\mathbf{x})/P(S=0)}{P(S=1\mid\mathbf{x})/P(S=1)}
=\frac{P(S=0)}{P(S=1)}\cdot\frac{P(S=0\mid\mathbf{x})}{P(S=1\mid\mathbf{x})}.
\] Under Equation 18.15 the conditional odds is \(P(S=1\mid\mathbf{x})/P(S=0\mid\mathbf{x})=
\exp(\tilde\alpha+\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top\mathbf{x})\), so its reciprocal is \(\exp(-\tilde\alpha-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top\mathbf{x})\), giving Equation 18.16. As a function of \(\mathbf{x}\) this equals a positive constant times \(\exp(-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top\mathbf{x})\), which matches \(\exp(\alpha+\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC}))\) up to a positive constant exactly when \(\boldsymbol{\beta}=-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\). The constant is irrelevant to Equation 18.17 because it cancels between numerator and denominator.
Recognition as inverse-probability weighting. Transporting the index-population conditional mean to \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\) means computing \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_{BC}}[\mu_A(\mathbf{X})]=\int
\mu_A(\mathbf{x})f_{BC}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}\). Writing \(f_{BC}=(f_{BC}/f_{AC})\,f_{AC}\), this is \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_{AC}}[(f_{BC}/f_{AC})(\mathbf{X})\,\mu_A(\mathbf{X})]\), an index-population expectation of the outcome weighted by the density ratio. Estimating it by the self-normalized weighted average over the arm-\(A\) index patients (self-normalized meaning we divide the weighted sum of outcomes by the sum of the weights, so the weights behave like proportions that add to one, and any constant scaling of the weights cancels), with the density ratio Equation 18.16 replaced by the MAIC weight Equation 18.5, is exactly Equation 18.17. This is the inverse-probability-weighting estimator of Theorem 10.3, transposed from “probability of treatment within a population” to “probability of selection into a population,” which is the transportability weighting of Definition 12.3 and Theorem 12.2. The selection weights play the role of the balancing score (Definition 10.1): a function of \(\mathbf{x}\) that, used as a weight, renders the index covariate distribution equal to the comparator’s. \(\square\)


Remark. Method of moments versus maximum likelihood. The only difference between MAIC and a textbook logistic inverse-probability weighting is the estimation criterion for \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\). Ordinary IPW fits the logistic model by maximum likelihood on a sample with individual \(S\)-labels. MAIC has no individual labels from the \(BC\) trial, only its reported moments, so it cannot write a logistic likelihood; instead it chooses \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) to make the weighted index moments equal the reported comparator moments, which is Equation 18.10. The two criteria target the same population density ratio and coincide asymptotically when the log-odds is genuinely linear in \(\mathbf{x}\); MAIC is thus the method-of-moments implementation of logistic IPW adapted to aggregate comparator data. Its consistency inherits the inverse-probability-weighting requirement that the weight model be correct, here that the density ratio is log-linear in the matched features, which is the same linearity condition that governed the choice of moments in Section 18.4. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The equivalence, and the one place the two methods part company, is worth a side-by-side.









Standard logistic IPW
MAIC




Data needed
individual trial labels \(S\) for every patient
index IPD plus comparator summary moments only


Weight form
inverse odds \(\exp(-\tilde\alpha-\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}^\top\mathbf x)\)
\(\exp(\alpha+\boldsymbol\beta^\top(\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}))\), the same shape


How \(\boldsymbol\beta\) is fit
maximum likelihood on labeled data
moment matching (Equation 18.10)


Target it estimates
density ratio \(f_{BC}/f_{AC}\)
the same density ratio


Agree asymptotically when
the membership log-odds is truly linear in \(\mathbf x\)
the same linearity holds



The reason MAIC exists as a separate method is the first row: in an indirect comparison we almost never have the comparator’s patient-level data, only a published table, so maximum likelihood is off the table and moment matching is the best we can do.
This result corresponds to F.5 in the proof catalogue.

title: 18  Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison
text:
18.9 Consistency of anchored MAIC
We now establish that the anchored MAIC estimator targets the right quantity. MAIC is a particular population-adjusted indirect comparison (PAIC), so its consistency is an instance of the general anchored PAIC theorem of Chapter 17 (Theorem 17.1); we give the weighting-specific argument in full and invoke the general theorem for the scale-alignment step that handles non-collapsible measures.
The anchored MAIC estimator combines the reweighted index contrast with the published comparator contrast: \[
\hat d_{AB}^{\mathrm{MAIC,anch}}
:=\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}-\hat d_{BC}^{\mathrm{AgD}},
\qquad
\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=g(\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{MAIC}})-g(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}),
\tag{18.18}\] with \(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}\) as in Equation 18.17 and \(\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{MAIC}}\) its arm-\(C\) analogue, on the link scale \(g\).
A word on sign. We write each contrast as comparator-minus-active on the link scale, for example \(\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=g(\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{MAIC}})-g(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}})\), so that when the active treatment improves the outcome (a lower severity score, a lower event risk) the contrast comes out positive and reads as “how much better \(A\) is than \(C\).” Orient this to your own outcome: if higher is better, flip the sign. In the running Example 18.1 the benefit \(\mu_C-\mu_A=4+2x\) is positive because lower severity is better and \(A\) lowers it.
Why this matters, and what to watch. This theorem is the payoff: it says the reweight-then-subtract recipe recovers the true \(A\)-versus-\(B\) effect in the comparator population \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\), the population we could not re-analyze directly. But it does so only under a stack of assumptions, and a health researcher’s real job is to know which of them are checkable and which are acts of faith. The next table is that map; the formal statement and proof follow, and the remark after the proof (Section 18.9, “Where each hypothesis is spent”) revisits each assumption in prose. The one genuinely new idea in the assumption list is shared effect modification (SEMA, Definition 17.6): in plain terms, a covariate such as severity must bend the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) effect in the same way it bends the \(B\)-versus-\(C\) effect, so that the published \(BC\) result can be read as the comparator-population \(B\)-versus-\(C\) effect without our re-estimating it from \(BC\)’s (unavailable) patient data.









Assumption
Plain meaning
Checkable from the two trials?
What goes wrong if it fails




(i) Randomized index trial
the \(A\) and \(C\) arms are comparable without adjustment
Yes, it is a design fact
nothing, if the trial was truly randomized


(ii) Conditional constancy + SEMA
the \(A\)-vs-\(C\) effect is the same function of covariates in both trials, and modifiers act alike on \(A\)-vs-\(C\) and \(B\)-vs-\(C\)
No, untestable from two trials
the carried and published effects do not describe \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\); residual bias


(iii) All imbalanced effect modifiers measured and balanced
every covariate that changes the \(A\)-vs-\(C\) effect and differs between trials is in \(\mathbf{x}\) and balanced
Partly: you can see imbalance, not prove completeness
leftover confounding-by-population, the Bucher failure MAIC was built to fix


(iv) Overlap
the comparator mean lies inside the index covariate cloud
Yes, compare covariate ranges
weights diverge; estimator undefined or unstable


(v) Right moments for the scale
first moments suffice on a linear scale; higher moments needed on nonlinear ones
Partly, from the link and the reported summaries
mismatch on nonlinear scales; ecological bias




Theorem 18.4 (Consistency of anchored MAIC) Fix a link scale \(g\) and report the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) contrast in the comparator population \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\). Assume:

(Randomization.) The index trial \(AC\) is randomized, so within \(\mathcal{P}_{AC}\), \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=t,\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}]=\mu_t(\mathbf{x})\) for \(t\in\{A,C\}\).
(Conditional constancy of relative effects, Definition 17.4, with shared effect modification, Definition 17.6.) The conditional \(A\)-versus-\(C\) contrast on scale \(g\) is the same function of \(\mathbf{x}\) in \(\mathcal{P}_{AC}\) and \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\), and the effect modifiers and their interaction coefficients are shared across \(A\) and \(B\) relative to \(C\), so that \(\hat d_{BC}^{\mathrm{AgD}}\) is consistent for the \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\) marginal contrast \(d_{BC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}\).
(Complete, balanced effect modifiers.) Every covariate that modifies the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) contrast on scale \(g\) and is imbalanced between \(\mathcal{P}_{AC}\) and \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\) is included in \(\mathbf{x}\) and balanced by the matched moments.
(Overlap.) \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC}\in\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf{x}_i\}\), so finite positive weights exist (Theorem 18.2), and the effective sample size grows without bound, \(\mathrm{ESS}\to\infty\), as \(n\to\infty\).
(Sufficiency of the matched moments.) The conditional means \(\mu_A(\cdot),\mu_C(\cdot)\) entering the estimand are affine in the matched features (first moments for the identity scale; augmented with the balanced higher moments otherwise), so that weighted index means converge to \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\) marginal means.

Then the anchored MAIC estimator Equation 18.18 is consistent for the target contrast, \[
\hat d_{AB}^{\mathrm{MAIC,anch}}\;\xrightarrow{\ p\ }\;d_{AB(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}.
\] This is consistency, not finite-sample unbiasedness: the weights are estimated from \(\{\mathbf{x}_i\}\), so \(\hat d_{AB}^{\mathrm{MAIC,anch}}\) carries an \(O(1/n)\) finite-sample bias that vanishes in the limit. The reason for the bias is that the same patients are used twice, once to choose the weights and once to average the outcomes, so a chance covariate imbalance in a finite sample nudges the weights and the weighted mean in correlated ways; as \(n\) grows the fitted weights settle to their true values and the correlation washes out, which is why consistency survives even though exact unbiasedness does not.


Proof. Step 1 (exact balance at finite \(n\)). By (iv) and Theorem 18.2 the weights \(w_i^{*}=\exp(\hat\alpha+\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i)\) exist, are finite and positive, and by construction satisfy the moment constraint Equation 18.2 exactly, so the weighted index covariate mean equals \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC}\) for every \(n\).
Step 2 (the weighted arm mean targets the comparator marginal mean). Consider arm \(A\). By (i), for \(T_i=A\) write \(Y_i=\mu_A(\mathbf{x}_i)+\varepsilon_i\) with \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,
T_i=A]=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,T_i=A)\le\sigma^2<\infty\). Then \[
\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}
=\underbrace{\frac{\sum_{i:T_i=A}w_i^{*}\,\mu_A(\mathbf{x}_i)}{\sum_{i:T_i=A}w_i^{*}}}_{\text{(signal)}}
+\underbrace{\frac{\sum_{i:T_i=A}w_i^{*}\,\varepsilon_i}{\sum_{i:T_i=A}w_i^{*}}}_{\text{(noise)}}.
\] Under (v), \(\mu_A(\mathbf{x})=a_0+\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x}\) is affine, so the signal term equals \(a_0+\mathbf{a}^\top\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{A}_{w}\), where \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{A}_{w}\) is the weighted covariate mean over arm \(A\). Randomization (i) makes the covariate distribution in arm \(A\) identical to the overall index covariate distribution, and the weights depend only on \(\mathbf{x}\), so the within-arm weighted covariate mean converges to the overall weighted covariate mean, which by Step 1 equals \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC}\); hence the signal term converges to \(a_0+\mathbf{a}^\top\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC}\). By conditional constancy (ii) the function \(\mu_A\) is the same in \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\), so \(a_0+\mathbf{a}^\top\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_{BC}}[\mu_A(\mathbf{X})]=
\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}\). The noise term has conditional mean zero and conditional variance bounded by \(\sigma^2\sum_{i:T_i=A}(w_i^{*})^2/(\sum_{i:T_i=A}w_i^{*})^2=\sigma^2/\mathrm{ESS}_A\), which tends to zero by (iv); by Chebyshev’s inequality the noise term converges to zero in probability. Therefore \(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}\xrightarrow{p}\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}\). The same argument gives \(\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{MAIC}}\xrightarrow{p}\bar\mu_{C(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}\).
Step 3 (the reweighted contrast). The link \(g\) is continuous, so by the continuous mapping theorem \[
\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=g(\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{MAIC}})-g(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}})
\xrightarrow{p} g(\bar\mu_{C(\mathcal{P}_{BC})})-g(\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal{P}_{BC})})
=d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})},
\] the marginal \(A\)-versus-\(C\) effect in the comparator population.
Step 4 (anchored subtraction in a single population). By (ii) the comparator estimate satisfies \(\hat d_{BC}^{\mathrm{AgD}}\xrightarrow{p}d_{BC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}\). Both surviving contrasts now live in the same population \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\), so the within-population additivity of relative effects (Lemma 14.1, evaluated in \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\)) gives \(d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}-d_{BC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}=d_{AB(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}\). Combining Steps 3 and 4 by Slutsky’s theorem yields \(\hat d_{AB}^{\mathrm{MAIC,anch}}=\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}-\hat d_{BC}^{\mathrm{AgD}}
\xrightarrow{p}d_{AB(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}\).
Non-collapsible scales. For collapsible measures (the identity and log scales, Definition 11.6) Step 4 is immediate. For non-collapsible measures (the log odds ratio, the log hazard ratio, Theorem 11.2) the marginal contrast is not the average of conditional contrasts, and the subtraction in Step 4 is licensed only under the scale-alignment conditions catalogued by the general anchored PAIC theorem (Theorem 17.1), which (ii) and (iii) supply; we invoke that theorem for the marginalization-then-subtraction step on such scales rather than reproving the collapsibility bookkeeping here. \(\square\)


Remark. What non-collapsibility demands, concretely. Because most health-technology submissions report odds ratios or hazard ratios, the last step of the proof deserves to be spelled out, not just cited. On a collapsible scale (identity, log-risk) the marginal effect is the covariate-average of the conditional effects, so once MAIC has matched the covariate distribution the marginal \(A\)-versus-\(C\) effect transports directly and the Bucher subtraction goes through. On a non-collapsible scale (log odds ratio, log hazard ratio) this is false: as Example 18.2 showed, the marginal contrast depends on the covariate spread and on the baseline risk, not only on what conditional effect the patients carry. Two concrete consequences follow. First, matching the mean covariate does not by itself make two marginal odds ratios comparable; you must match enough of the covariate distribution that the two populations marginalize the same way, which is why higher moments matter here (Section 18.4). Second, even after matching, the two marginal contrasts must be brought to a common baseline risk before they are subtracted; this is the “scale-alignment” content of Theorem 17.1, and in an anchored comparison it is the shared comparator \(C\) together with SEMA (ii) that supplies the common baseline. The systematic fix that never needs this bookkeeping is to integrate an individual-level model over the target covariate distribution, which is multilevel network meta-regression (Chapter 20); MAIC instead leans on the anchor and the shared-modifier structure to keep the two marginal effects on speaking terms. The practical warning for a reader is blunt: a MAIC that balances covariate means and then differences two published odds ratios has not automatically produced a valid comparison unless the scale-alignment conditions hold. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Where each hypothesis is spent, and what fails without it. Overlap (iv) is what makes the weights finite and the noise average out; without it MAIC is undefined or unstable (Theorem 18.8, Theorem 18.6). Balance of every imbalanced effect modifier (iii) is what makes the reweighted contrast equal the comparator contrast; omitting an imbalanced modifier leaves residual confounding-by- population and asymptotic bias, exactly the Bucher failure of Theorem 16.1 that MAIC was built to repair. Conditional constancy with shared modification (ii) is what licenses transporting \(\mu_A\) to \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\) and identifying \(\hat d_{BC}^{\mathrm{AgD}}\) with the \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\) contrast; it is the population-adjustment analogue of transitivity and the only assumption that is genuinely untestable from these two trials (Proposition 17.4). Sufficiency of the matched moments (v) is the linearity condition that makes first-moment matching enough; on nonlinear scales one matches more moments, and Theorem 17.3 records what is then identified. Randomization (i) supplies the within-trial unconfoundedness for free. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This result corresponds to F.6 in the proof catalogue.

title: 18  Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison
text:
18.10 Consistency of unanchored MAIC
When the index and comparator trials share no common comparator, there is no anchor to difference, and MAIC must compare the absolute outcomes of \(A\) and \(B\) across populations directly. The estimator becomes \[
\hat d_{AB}^{\mathrm{MAIC,unanch}}
:=g(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}})-g(\hat\mu_B^{\mathrm{MAIC}}),
\tag{18.19}\] where each weighted arm mean is transported to a common target population \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\). The price of discarding the anchor is a far stronger and largely untestable assumption set; this is the MAIC instance of Theorem 17.2.
Why this matters, and why it is dangerous. Without a shared comparator \(C\) there is no subtraction to cancel anything, so we must estimate the absolute outcome under \(A\) and under \(B\) separately and difference them. The single most important practical consequence is that we can no longer ignore purely prognostic variables: in the anchored case a covariate that shifts both arms equally cancels out of the contrast (Section 18.9), but here it shifts \(\mu_A\) and \(\mu_B\) and does not cancel, so every imbalanced prognostic variable, not only every effect modifier, must be measured and balanced. That is usually impossible to guarantee, which is why unanchored MAIC is a last resort.
Why the key assumption is untestable. Assumption (i) below says the conditional mean \(\mu_t(\mathbf{x})\) is the same in the source trial and in the target population \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\). We observe \(\mu_t\) only in the source trial; we never observe it in the target, because the whole reason we are doing an indirect comparison is that the target has no arm on treatment \(t\). There is therefore nothing in the data to check the assumption against: it is an act of faith about unmeasured differences between the two populations. Concretely, suppose \(A\) and \(B\) are two oncology drugs studied in separate single-arm or non-overlapping trials with no common comparator. If age is prognostic (older patients fare worse on either drug) and the \(A\) trial enrolled younger patients than the \(B\) trial, then the estimated absolute outcome under \(A\) is computed in a younger mix and under \(B\) in an older mix; unless age is fully measured and balanced, the head-to-head difference confounds “drug” with “age.” An anchored design would have let the shared comparator absorb the age effect by cancellation; the unanchored design has no such protection.









Anchored MAIC
Unanchored MAIC




Needs a common comparator \(C\)?
Yes
No


Estimand built from
the contrast \(\mu_A-\mu_C\)
the absolute means \(\mu_A\) and \(\mu_B\)


Must balance
imbalanced effect modifiers
imbalanced effect modifiers and prognostic variables


Key assumption
conditional constancy of relative effects, plus SEMA
conditional constancy of absolute effects


Checkable from the data?
partly (see the anchored table)
essentially not


Verdict
preferred whenever an anchor exists
last resort, with heavy sensitivity analysis




Theorem 18.5 (Consistency of unanchored MAIC) Fix a link scale \(g\) and a target population \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\). Assume:

(Conditional constancy of absolute effects, Definition 17.5.) For each treatment \(t\in\{A,B\}\) the conditional mean function \(\mu_t(\mathbf{x})\) is the same in its source population and in \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\).
(Complete, balanced effect modifiers and prognostic variables.) Every covariate that is an effect modifier on scale \(g\) or a prognostic variable (Definition 11.5) for either treatment, and is imbalanced between any of the source populations and \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\), is included in \(\mathbf{x}\) and balanced.
(Overlap.) The target moments lie in the relative interior of the supported features of each source, so finite positive weights exist and \(\mathrm{ESS}\to\infty\).
(Sufficiency of the matched moments.) Each \(\mu_t(\cdot)\) is affine in the matched features.

Then the unanchored MAIC estimator Equation 18.19 is consistent for the target contrast, \[
\hat d_{AB}^{\mathrm{MAIC,unanch}}\;\xrightarrow{\ p\ }\;d_{AB(\mathcal{P}^{*})}
=g(\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal{P}^{*})})-g(\bar\mu_{B(\mathcal{P}^{*})}).
\]


Proof. We give the argument in full, because its structure differs from the anchored case: there is no comparator subtraction to cancel a prognostic variable, so each absolute conditional mean must be identified outright.
Step 1 (identify the source conditional mean). The arm-\(A\) source IPD identifies the source-conditional mean \(\mu_A^{\mathrm{src}}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{src}}[Y\mid T=A,\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}]\). Under (i) this equals the target-conditional mean \(\mu_A(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}^{*}}[Y(A)\mid
\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}]\). Assumption (i) is strong: it requires that, conditional on \(\mathbf{x}\), no variable left out of \(\mathbf{x}\) shifts the absolute mean of \(Y(A)\) between source and target; by (ii) every imbalanced prognostic variable is in \(\mathbf{x}\), which is what reduces (i) to within-population unconfoundedness plus the absence of differentially distributed unmeasured prognostic variables.
Step 2 (identify the target marginal mean). By the g-formula (Theorem 10.4), \[
\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal{P}^{*})}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}\sim f_{*}}[\mu_A(\mathbf{X})]
=\int\mu_A(\mathbf{x})\,f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}.
\]
Step 3 (the weighted estimator hits it). MAIC reweights the source-\(A\) IPD to match the target moments, so by the affine-mean argument of Step 2 of Theorem 18.4, applied now to the absolute mean rather than a contrast, \[
\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}
=\frac{\sum_i w_i^{*}\,\mathbf{1}\{T_i=A\}\,Y_i}{\sum_i w_i^{*}\,\mathbf{1}\{T_i=A\}}
\xrightarrow{p}\int\mu_A(\mathbf{x})\,f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}=\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal{P}^{*})}.
\] Here is the decisive difference from the anchored case: the weighted mean must converge to the absolute target mean \(\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal{P}^{*})}\), not to a difference of conditional means against a shared comparator. There is no subtraction to cancel a prognostic variable, so the full conditional mean function \(\mu_A(\cdot)\), not merely the CATE \(\tau(\cdot)\), must be transported, which is why (ii) demands prognostic variables and not only effect modifiers.
Step 4 (the other arm and the contrast). The symmetric argument gives \(\hat\mu_B^{\mathrm{MAIC}}\xrightarrow{p}\bar\mu_{B(\mathcal{P}^{*})}\). By the continuous mapping theorem, \[
\hat d_{AB}^{\mathrm{MAIC,unanch}}=g(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}})-g(\hat\mu_B^{\mathrm{MAIC}})
\xrightarrow{p}g(\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal{P}^{*})})-g(\bar\mu_{B(\mathcal{P}^{*})})=d_{AB(\mathcal{P}^{*})}.
\qquad\square
\]


Remark. Why prognostic variables matter here but not in the anchored case. In the anchored estimator the quantity that enters is the CATE \(\tau(\mathbf{x})=\mu_A(\mathbf{x})-\mu_C(\mathbf{x})\). If \(w\) is a prognostic variable for both \(A\) and \(C\) that is not an effect modifier on the chosen scale, then it shifts \(\mu_A(\mathbf{x},w)\) and \(\mu_C(\mathbf{x},w)\) by the same amount, so it cancels in the difference: \(\mu_A(\mathbf{x},w)-\mu_C(\mathbf{x},w)=\mu_A(\mathbf{x})-\mu_C(\mathbf{x})\), and omitting \(w\) from \(\mathbf{x}\) does not bias the anchored estimate. In the unanchored estimator the quantity that enters is \(\mu_A(\mathbf{x})\) alone. If \(w\) is an omitted prognostic variable for \(A\), then \(\mu_A(\mathbf{x},w)\) depends on \(w\), and integrating it against the source’s \(f(w\mid\mathbf{x})\) rather than the target’s \(f^{*}(w\mid\mathbf{x})\) gives a different answer; the absolute mean is biased. This is the formal reason that unanchored population adjustment requires strictly more covariate coverage than anchored, and it is identical in form to the baseline-cancellation argument of Proposition 14.4 in Chapter 14: the anchor cancels the baseline; without it the baseline must be modeled. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Practical defensibility. Conditional constancy of absolute effects (i) is essentially untestable in the two-study setting (Proposition 17.4), and the adjustment set demanded by (ii), every imbalanced effect modifier and prognostic variable, is usually prohibitive. For these reasons Phillippo et al. (2016) treats unanchored comparisons as a last resort, to be accompanied by extensive sensitivity analysis over the adjustment set. On non-collapsible scales the target marginal contrast also depends on the target baseline risk, a further complication (Theorem 12.6); the systematic remedy is multilevel unanchored meta-regression (Chapter 26). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This result corresponds to F.7 in the proof catalogue.

title: 18  Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison
section: 18.11 The effective sample size and its bound
text:
18.11 The effective sample size and its bound
Reweighting is not free. A weighted estimator behaves, for the purpose of variance, like an unweighted estimator on a smaller sample, and the size of that smaller sample is the effective sample size.

Definition 18.3 (Effective sample size) For nonnegative weights \(w_1,\dots,w_n\), not all zero, the effective sample size is \[
\mathrm{ESS}\;:=\;\frac{\big(\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i\big)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i^2}.
\tag{18.20}\] It is invariant to rescaling all weights by a common positive constant. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Reader translation. Read the ESS as “how many equally weighted patients this weighted sample is worth.” If you threw away your weighted sample of \(n\) patients and replaced it with \(\mathrm{ESS}\) fresh patients, each counted once, you would get an estimate of the same precision. When the weights are equal the two are the same and \(\mathrm{ESS}=n\); when a few patients carry most of the weight the sample is effectively much smaller, because the estimate leans on those few. The following table makes the collapse concrete for the four-patient running example; notice how emphasis concentrating onto one patient drives the ESS toward \(1\).









Weights (\(n=4\))
Situation
\(\mathrm{ESS}\)
\(\mathrm{ESS}/n\)




\((1,1,1,1)\)
uniform (no adjustment)
\(4.00\)
\(1.00\)


\((1.5,1.5,0.5,0.5)\)
running Example 18.1 (one covariate matched)
\(3.20\)
\(0.80\)


\((2.25,0.75,0.75,0.25)\)
Section 18.16 (two covariates matched)
\(2.56\)

\((2.5,0.5,0.5,0.5)\)
one patient dominant

Theorem 18.6 (The effective-sample-size bound) For any nonnegative weights \(w_1,\dots,w_n\), not all zero, \[
\mathrm{ESS}=\frac{\big(\sum_i w_i\big)^2}{\sum_i w_i^2}\;\le\;n,
\] with equality if and only if all the weights are equal.
[machine-checked: theories/MAIC.v, Theorem ESS_upper_bound]


Proof. This is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (Chapter 2) applied to the vectors \(\mathbf{w}=(w_1,\dots,w_n)\) and \(\mathbf{1}_n=(1,\dots,1)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\): \[
\Big(\sum_i w_i\Big)^2=\langle\mathbf{w},\mathbf{1}_n\rangle^2
\le\|\mathbf{w}\|_2^2\,\|\mathbf{1}_n\|_2^2=\Big(\sum_i w_i^2\Big)\cdot n.
\] Dividing by \(\sum_i w_i^2>0\) gives \(\mathrm{ESS}\le n\). We exhibit the bound and its equality case self-containedly through Lagrange’s identity, which makes the slack explicit: \[
n\sum_i w_i^2-\Big(\sum_i w_i\Big)^2
=\sum_{i}\sum_{j}w_i^2-\sum_i\sum_j w_iw_j
=\tfrac12\sum_{i}\sum_{j}\big(w_i^2-2w_iw_j+w_j^2\big)
=\sum_{i<j}(w_i-w_j)^2\ge 0,
\] where the second equality writes \(n\sum_i w_i^2=\sum_j\sum_i w_i^2\) and uses the symmetry of the double sum under interchange of \(i\) and \(j\) to symmetrize. The right-hand side is a sum of squares, hence nonnegative, which gives \((\sum_i w_i)^2\le n\sum_i w_i^2\) and therefore \(\mathrm{ESS}\le n\); it vanishes if and only if \(w_i=w_j\) for all pairs \(i<j\), that is, if and only if all weights are equal. \(\square\)


Remark. The Coq proof. The companion development proves this bound without admissions. The elementary inequality \(2xy\le x^2+y^2\) is Lemma two_mul_le_sqr (a rearrangement of \(0\le(x-y)^2\)); an induction on \(n\) assembles it into the Cauchy-Schwarz statement \((\sum_i w_i)^2\le n\sum_i w_i^2\), named cauchy_schwarz_ones in its general form and cauchy_schwarz_n_weights specialized to the weight vector; dividing by the positive \(\sum_i w_i^2\) yields Theorem ESS_upper_bound. The inductive step is exactly the symmetrization used in Lagrange’s identity above. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The bound is what gives the ESS its meaning as a sample size: the most informative weighting, uniform weighting, retains all \(n\) observations, and any departure strictly reduces the effective count.
This result corresponds to F.8 in the proof catalogue.

title: 18  Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison
text:
18.12 Variance inflation
The effective sample size is not a metaphor; it is the literal denominator in the variance of a weighted mean.

Theorem 18.7 (Variance of a weighted mean and the inflation factor) Let \(Y_1,\dots,Y_n\) be uncorrelated with common mean \(\theta\) and common variance \(\sigma^2\), and let \(w_1,\dots,w_n\ge 0\) be fixed weights, not all zero. The weighted mean \(\hat\theta_w=\sum_i w_iY_i/\sum_i w_i\) is unbiased for \(\theta\) and has variance \[
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_w)=\sigma^2\,\frac{\sum_i w_i^2}{(\sum_i w_i)^2}
=\frac{\sigma^2}{\mathrm{ESS}}.
\tag{18.21}\] Consequently its variance is the unweighted variance \(\sigma^2/n\) inflated by the factor \[
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_w)}{\sigma^2/n}=\frac{n}{\mathrm{ESS}}\;\ge\;1,
\tag{18.22}\] with equality if and only if the weights are uniform (Theorem 18.6).


Proof. Unbiasedness is linearity of expectation: \(\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_w]=\sum_i w_i\theta/\sum_i w_i=\theta\). For the variance, the \(Y_i\) are uncorrelated with variance \(\sigma^2\), so \[
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_w)
=\frac{1}{(\sum_i w_i)^2}\sum_i w_i^2\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)
=\frac{\sigma^2\sum_i w_i^2}{(\sum_i w_i)^2}
=\frac{\sigma^2}{\mathrm{ESS}},
\] which is Equation 18.21. Dividing by \(\sigma^2/n\) gives the inflation factor \(n/\mathrm{ESS}\), and \(n/\mathrm{ESS}\ge 1\) is the bound Theorem 18.6, with the same equality condition. \(\square\)


Remark. The fundamental MAIC trade-off. Equation Equation 18.22 is the quantitative form of the central tension in population adjustment. Balancing more covariates, or balancing a fixed set more tightly against a distant target, reduces bias but spreads the weights and lowers the ESS, inflating the variance: \(\mathrm{ESS}=n/2\) doubles the variance, \(\mathrm{ESS}=n/10\) tenfolds it, equivalent to discarding ninety percent of the data. A common rule of thumb flags \(\mathrm{ESS}/n<0.5\) as substantial information loss and \(\mathrm{ESS}/n<0.1\) as an analysis dominated by a handful of patients. Because the weights are in fact estimated, Equation 18.21 is the leading term of the true variance; the honest variance that accounts for weight estimation is the sandwich of Theorem 18.9, and the bias-variance trade-off resurfaces in the simulation theory of Chapter 29. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This result corresponds to F.9 in the proof catalogue.

title: 18  Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison
text:
18.13 MAIC cannot extrapolate
The punchline first. Suppose the comparator \(BC\) trial enrolled patients aged \(75\) to \(85\), but your index \(AC\) trial enrolled no one over \(70\). Then MAIC cannot tell you what treatment \(A\) does at age \(80\), no matter how cleverly the weights are chosen, because you have no patients there to reweight. Reweighting can only shift emphasis among patients you already observed; it cannot conjure a treatment effect in a region of covariate space your trial never entered. This section proves that this is not a shortcoming of a particular estimator but a hard identification barrier: the target quantity is simply not determined by the data MAIC uses. The remedy is to model the effect across covariate space, which is what simulated treatment comparison (Chapter 19) and multilevel network meta-regression (Chapter 20) do, at the cost of a parametric assumption MAIC avoids.
Overlap is not merely a regularity condition for finite weights; it is a hard limit on what reweighting can ever learn. If the target population places mass where the IPD never looked, no choice of finite weights can recover the missing information, and the target estimand is not identified from the data MAIC uses.

Theorem 18.8 (Non-identification beyond the covariate support) Suppose there is a measurable region \(\mathcal{X}_0\subseteq\mathcal{X}\) with positive target probability but zero index support, \[
P_{\mathcal{P}_{BC}}(\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{X}_0)>0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
P_{\mathcal{P}_{AC}}(\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{X}_0)=0.
\] Then the comparator-population contrast \(d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}\) is not identified from the index IPD law of \((\mathbf{X},T,Y)\) together with the comparator density \(f_{BC}\): there exist two data-generating processes with identical index laws and identical \(f_{BC}\) but different \(d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}\). In particular, no estimator that is a functional of the index empirical distribution and the comparator moments, and so no finite-weight MAIC estimator Equation 18.18, can be consistent for \(d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}\) across all such processes.


Proof. The target contrast decomposes over the support gap. On the identity scale (the argument is identical on any scale after applying \(g\)), with CATE \(\tau(\mathbf{x})=\mu_A(\mathbf{x})-\mu_C(\mathbf{x})\), \[
d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}=\int_{\mathcal{X}\setminus\mathcal{X}_0}\tau(\mathbf{x})\,f_{BC}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}
+\int_{\mathcal{X}_0}\tau(\mathbf{x})\,f_{BC}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}.
\tag{18.23}\] The first integral is over the region the index trial observes and is a functional of the index law and \(f_{BC}\); the second integral is over \(\mathcal{X}_0\), where the index trial contributes no observations.
To prove non-identification, construct two processes that agree on everything observable yet differ in Equation 18.23. Let the index law of \((\mathbf{X},T,Y)\) and the comparator density \(f_{BC}\) be fixed. Choose two conditional-contrast functions \(\tau_1,\tau_2\) that coincide on the index support \(\operatorname{supp}(f_{AC})\subseteq\mathcal{X}\setminus\mathcal{X}_0\) but differ on \(\mathcal{X}_0\) in a way that changes the gap integral, that is \[
\int_{\mathcal{X}_0}\tau_1(\mathbf{x})\,f_{BC}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}
\neq\int_{\mathcal{X}_0}\tau_2(\mathbf{x})\,f_{BC}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x};
\] such functions exist because \(f_{BC}\) has positive mass on \(\mathcal{X}_0\), so the linear functional \(\tau\mapsto\int_{\mathcal{X}_0}\tau f_{BC}\) is not identically zero on functions supported in \(\mathcal{X}_0\). Because \(\tau_1\) and \(\tau_2\) agree on \(\operatorname{supp}(f_{AC})\) and the index trial never visits \(\mathcal{X}_0\), the two processes induce the same index law of \((\mathbf{X},T,Y)\) and the same \(f_{BC}\); yet by Equation 18.23 their values of \(d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}\) differ by the nonzero amount \(\int_{\mathcal{X}_0}(\tau_1-\tau_2)f_{BC}\). Hence the contrast is not a function of the observable law, which is non-identification. Any estimator built from the index empirical distribution and the comparator moments, MAIC included, takes the same value under the two processes and so is inconsistent for at least one of them. \(\square\)


Remark. Reweighting interpolates, it does not extrapolate. A finite-weight estimator outputs a weighted combination of the observed conditional contrasts \(\{\tau(\mathbf{x}_i)\}\), which can only land in their convex hull; it has no mechanism to report a value of \(\tau\) at an unobserved \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_0\). This is the population-level shadow of the convex-hull feasibility condition Equation 18.13: when \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC}\) escapes the hull, the weights diverge (Theorem 18.2), and the missing-mass integral in Equation 18.23 is exactly what the divergence is failing to capture. The remedy is not a better weighting but a model: an outcome model that interpolates \(\tau\) across covariate space, which is what simulated treatment comparison (Chapter 19) and multilevel network meta-regression (Chapter 20) provide, at the cost of a parametric assumption that MAIC avoids. Diagnostics should compare the index and comparator covariate ranges before any MAIC is attempted. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This result corresponds to F.10 in the proof catalogue.

title: 18  Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison
text:
18.14 Standard errors: the sandwich
The one-line rule for practice. Do not compute your standard errors as if the weights were known numbers. You chose the weights by fitting them to the very same patients whose outcomes you are now averaging, and pretending otherwise generally understates the uncertainty. The two honest options are the sandwich variance developed here and the bootstrap of Section 18.15; the naive fixed-weight standard error is not one of them.
The estimated weights make the naive variance Equation 18.21 wrong: it treats the weights as fixed when they were in fact fitted to the same data. The honest variance treats the entire procedure, weight fitting and outcome averaging, as a single system of estimating equations and applies the M-estimation sandwich of Chapter 5 (Definition 5.11).
Stack the parameters as \(\boldsymbol{\theta}=(\boldsymbol{\beta},\mu_A,\mu_C)\) and define the per-patient estimating function \(\boldsymbol{\psi}(\,\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\theta})\) with three blocks: the balance block, which fits \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\), and the two outcome blocks, which fit the weighted arm means, \[
\boldsymbol{\psi}(\mathbf{x}_i,T_i,Y_i;\boldsymbol{\theta})
=\begin{pmatrix}
e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i}\,\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i\\[2pt]
\mathbf{1}\{T_i=A\}\,e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i}\,(Y_i-\mu_A)\\[2pt]
\mathbf{1}\{T_i=C\}\,e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i}\,(Y_i-\mu_C)
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\boldsymbol{\psi}(\mathbf{x}_i,T_i,Y_i;\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})=\mathbf{0}.
\tag{18.24}\] The first block is the balance condition Equation 18.10; the second and third define \(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}\) and \(\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{MAIC}}\) of Equation 18.17. The normalization constant \(\alpha\) does not appear in the balance block because it multiplies the whole balance equation by the positive factor \(e^{\alpha}\), which cannot change whether that equation equals zero; only \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is a free parameter to be fit here, and \(\alpha\) is recovered afterward from the normalization (Equation 18.9).

Theorem 18.9 (Sandwich variance for MAIC) Suppose the M-estimator \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\) solving Equation 18.24 is consistent for \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0\) with the standard regularity conditions of Chapter 5 (the map \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mapsto\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\psi}]\) is differentiable with nonsingular Jacobian \(A=\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\boldsymbol{\psi}(\,\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)]\), and \(B=\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\psi}\boldsymbol{\psi}^\top]\) is finite). Then \[
\sqrt{n}\,(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)\xrightarrow{\ d\ }\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\,
\mathbb{V}),\qquad \mathbb{V}=A^{-1}B\,A^{-\top},
\tag{18.25}\] the sandwich variance of Definition 5.11, consistently estimated by \(\hat{\mathbb{V}}=\hat A^{-1}\hat B\,\hat A^{-\top}\) with \(\hat A=\tfrac1n\sum_i\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\boldsymbol{\psi}_i\) and \(\hat B=\tfrac1n\sum_i\boldsymbol{\psi}_i\boldsymbol{\psi}_i^\top\) evaluated at \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\). The asymptotic variance of the adjusted contrast \(\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=g(\hat\mu_C)-g(\hat\mu_A)\) follows by the delta method, and that of the anchored estimator Equation 18.18 by adding the independent variance of \(\hat d_{BC}^{\mathrm{AgD}}\).


Proof. Write \(M_n(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\tfrac1n\sum_i\boldsymbol{\psi}(\,\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\theta})\), so that \(M_n(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})=\mathbf{0}\) and \(M_n(\boldsymbol{\theta})\to M(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\psi}]\) with \(M(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)=\mathbf{0}\). By a first-order Taylor expansion of \(M_n\) about \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0\), with \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\) on the segment between \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0\), \[
\mathbf{0}=M_n(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
=M_n(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)+\nabla M_n(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\,(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_0).
\] By the law of large numbers \(\nabla M_n(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\xrightarrow{p}A\) (using consistency of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\) and continuity of the Jacobian), and \(A\) is nonsingular by hypothesis, so for large \(n\) it may be inverted: \[
\sqrt{n}\,(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)
=-\big(\nabla M_n(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\big)^{-1}\sqrt{n}\,M_n(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)
=-A^{-1}\sqrt{n}\,M_n(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)+o_p(1).
\] By the central limit theorem, \(\sqrt{n}\,M_n(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)=\tfrac1{\sqrt n}\sum_i
\boldsymbol{\psi}(\,\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},B)\) since the summands are independent and identically distributed with mean \(M(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)=\mathbf{0}\) and covariance \(B\). Slutsky’s theorem then gives \(\sqrt{n}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)\xrightarrow{d}-A^{-1}\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},B)
=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},A^{-1}BA^{-\top})\), which is Equation 18.25. Consistency of \(\hat{\mathbb{V}}=\hat A^{-1}\hat B\hat A^{-\top}\) is the law of large numbers applied to \(\hat A\) and \(\hat B\) together with continuity of matrix inversion. The delta method (the smooth-map asymptotics of Chapter 5, the same tool behind Theorem 5.6) propagates Equation 18.25 through \(g\) to the contrast, and the comparator term, being from a disjoint trial, contributes an additive independent variance as in the Bucher variance (Theorem 14.2). \(\square\)


Remark. Why naive standard errors are wrong, structurally. The Jacobian \(A\) of Equation 18.24 is block lower-triangular: the balance block depends only on \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\), but the outcome blocks depend on both \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) and the means, since the weights \(e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top
\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i}\) carry \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) into the outcome equations. Inverting a block-triangular \(A\) propagates the sampling uncertainty of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) into the variance of \((\hat\mu_A,\hat\mu_C)\) through the off-diagonal block. A naive analysis that treats the weights as fixed drops that off-diagonal block, that is, it pretends the balance block and the outcome blocks are uncoupled; it therefore generally misstates the variance. In typical MAIC applications the weight estimation adds positively correlated noise and the naive estimator is anticonservative; the sign is not universal, which is exactly why the full sandwich, not a fixed-weight shortcut, is needed. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This result corresponds to F.11 in the proof catalogue.

title: 18  Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison
text:
18.15 Standard errors: the bootstrap
The one-line rule for practice. To bootstrap a MAIC, resample the index patients with replacement and refit the weights from scratch on every resample, then recompute the adjusted contrast; the spread of those recomputed contrasts is your standard error. The common mistake is to freeze the fitted weights and resample only the outcomes, which quietly reproduces the wrong fixed-weight variance of Section 18.14. Refitting the weights each time is what lets the bootstrap feel the uncertainty in the weights themselves.
One technical term recurs below. A map \(\Psi\) of the data distribution is Hadamard-differentiable when it is smooth enough, in the functional sense used for the delta method in Chapter 5, that a small perturbation of the input distribution produces an approximately linear change in the output; it is the infinite-dimensional analogue of “differentiable,” and it is exactly the condition under which resampling the input (the bootstrap) correctly reproduces the sampling distribution of the output. (Fréchet differentiability, mentioned in the proof, is a slightly stronger version of the same idea.)
The sandwich variance requires differentiating the estimating equations; the nonparametric bootstrap sidesteps the algebra by resampling, and it is valid here because the whole MAIC map is smooth in the empirical distribution.

Theorem 18.10 (Validity of the nonparametric bootstrap for MAIC) Let \(\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=\Psi(\mathbb{P}_n)\), where \(\mathbb{P}_n\) is the empirical distribution of the index IPD and \(\Psi\) is the map that fits the entropy-balancing weights, forms the weighted arm means, and returns the contrast. Under the regularity conditions of Theorem 18.9 (in particular overlap, so that the balance Jacobian \(\partial_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mathbb{E}[e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Delta}}
\boldsymbol{\Delta}]\) is nonsingular at the solution), \(\Psi\) is Hadamard-differentiable at the index law, and therefore the nonparametric bootstrap is consistent: the bootstrap distribution of \(\sqrt{n}\big(\Psi(\mathbb{P}_n^{*})-\Psi(\mathbb{P}_n)\big)\) converges to the same limiting law as \(\sqrt{n}\big(\Psi(\mathbb{P}_n)-\Psi(\mathbb{P})\big)\), conditionally on the data and in probability. Bootstrap percentile and studentized intervals are thus asymptotically valid.


Proof. We verify the hypotheses of the functional delta method for the bootstrap (the named theorem we invoke is Theorem 23.9 of Vaart (1998)), namely that \(\Psi\) is a composition of Hadamard-differentiable maps of the empirical distribution.
First, the weight parameter is a smooth functional of the law. Define \(\mathbf{G}(\boldsymbol{\beta},F)=\int e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC})}
(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC})\,dF(\mathbf{x})\); the fitted \(\boldsymbol{\beta}(F)\) solves \(\mathbf{G}(\boldsymbol{\beta},F)=\mathbf{0}\), which is Equation 18.10 for \(F=\mathbb{P}_n\). The partial derivative \(\partial_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mathbf{G}=\int e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC})}
(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC})(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC})^\top\,dF\) is a positive multiple of a covariance-type matrix and is nonsingular at the solution under overlap (it is \(Z\cdot\nabla^2 Q\) in the notation of Equation 18.12, positive definite when the centered covariates span). The implicit function theorem then makes \(\boldsymbol{\beta}(F)\) Fréchet-, hence Hadamard-, differentiable in \(F\) along the directions generated by empirical processes.
Second, given \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\), the weighted arm means \(\mu_t(F,\boldsymbol{\beta})=\int\mathbf{1}\{T=t\}e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC})}
y\,dF\big/\int\mathbf{1}\{T=t\}e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC})}\,dF\) are ratios of integrals of bounded continuous transformations against \(F\), hence Hadamard-differentiable in \((F,\boldsymbol{\beta})\) wherever the denominator is bounded away from zero (guaranteed by positivity of the weights, Theorem 18.1). Third, the link \(g\) and the subtraction are smooth maps of the means. The composition \(\Psi\) of Hadamard-differentiable maps is Hadamard-differentiable by the chain rule for such maps (Vaart (1998), Theorem 20.9).
By the empirical-process central limit theorem \(\sqrt{n}(\mathbb{P}_n-\mathbb{P})\) converges to a tight Gaussian process, and that same process governs the bootstrap empirical measure. The functional delta method for the bootstrap (Vaart (1998), Theorem 23.9) then transfers the convergence through the Hadamard-differentiable \(\Psi\): the bootstrapped statistic and the original statistic share the limiting Gaussian law, which is precisely the sandwich law of Theorem 18.9. \(\square\)


Remark. Resample the whole procedure. Validity requires bootstrapping the entire map \(\Psi\), refitting the weights on each resample, not freezing the weights and resampling only the outcomes; freezing the weights reproduces the naive fixed-weight variance and inherits its bias (Theorem 18.9 remark). The bootstrap and the sandwich agree to first order and typically differ only by small-sample fluctuation; the bootstrap is often preferred in practice because it sidesteps assembling the Jacobian blocks of Equation 18.24 by hand, while the sandwich is cheaper when many bootstrap replicates would be costly. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This result corresponds to F.12 in the proof catalogue.

title: 18  Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison
text:
18.16 A fully worked two-covariate example
We carry a complete anchored MAIC from raw covariates to an adjusted indirect comparison, choosing the numbers so that every weight, the effective sample size, and the adjusted contrast are exact and checkable by hand. The example is genuinely two-dimensional, with one effect modifier and one purely prognostic covariate, so it also exhibits the dividing line between covariates that must be balanced and covariates whose balance is harmless but costly.

Example 18.3 (Anchored MAIC with one effect modifier and one prognostic covariate) The index trial \(AC\) has, in each arm, four patients sitting at the corners of a centered square in standardized covariate space, \[
\mathbf{x}\in\big\{(1,1),\,(1,-1),\,(-1,1),\,(-1,-1)\big\},
\] where \(x_1\) is an effect modifier of the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) benefit and \(x_2\) is purely prognostic. The index covariate mean is the center, \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{AC}=(0,0)\). The comparator trial \(BC\) reports the covariate mean \[
\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC}=(0.5,\,0.5),
\] so the index population is imbalanced against the comparator on both covariates. The outcome \(Y\) is a continuous severity score (lower is better) with conditional means, on the identity scale, given by \[
\mu_C(\mathbf{x})=20+2x_1+2x_2,
\qquad
\mu_A(\mathbf{x})=\mu_C(\mathbf{x})-\big(4+x_1\big)=16+x_1+2x_2.
\] Thus the conditional benefit of \(A\) over \(C\) is \(\mu_C(\mathbf{x})-\mu_A(\mathbf{x})=4+x_1\), which depends on the effect modifier \(x_1\) but not on \(x_2\); the prognostic covariate \(x_2\) shifts both arms equally and cancels in the contrast.
Step 1: set up the balance equation. The centered covariates are \(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i=\mathbf{x}_i-(0.5,0.5)\), which span \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and the target \((0.5,0.5)\) lies strictly inside the square \(\operatorname{conv}\{(\pm1,\pm1)\}=[-1,1]^2\), so by Theorem 18.2 a unique finite positive weight vector exists. The weights have the form \(w(\mathbf{x})=\exp(\alpha+\beta_1(x_1-0.5)+\beta_2(x_2-0.5))\), and we must solve the balance condition Equation 18.10.
Step 2: exploit symmetry. The point set and the target are both invariant under swapping the two coordinates, so the unique solution must satisfy \(\beta_1=\beta_2=:\beta\). Then, up to the constant \(\alpha\), \(w(\mathbf{x})\propto e^{\beta(x_1+x_2)}\), and the four corners take values \(x_1+x_2\in
\{2,0,0,-2\}\). The weighted mean of \(x_1\) is \[
\frac{\sum w\,x_1}{\sum w}
=\frac{e^{2\beta}(1)+1(1)+1(-1)+e^{-2\beta}(-1)}{e^{2\beta}+1+1+e^{-2\beta}}
=\frac{e^{2\beta}-e^{-2\beta}}{e^{2\beta}+e^{-2\beta}+2}
=\frac{2\sinh 2\beta}{2\cosh 2\beta+2}=\tanh\beta,
\] using \(\sinh 2\beta=2\sinh\beta\cosh\beta\) and \(\cosh 2\beta+1=2\cosh^2\beta\). Setting this equal to the target \(0.5\) gives \(\tanh\beta=\tfrac12\), that is \[
\beta=\operatorname{artanh}(0.5)=\tfrac12\ln\frac{1+0.5}{1-0.5}=\tfrac12\ln 3\approx 0.5493,
\qquad e^{2\beta}=3,\quad e^{-2\beta}=\tfrac13.
\] By symmetry the weighted mean of \(x_2\) is also \(\tanh\beta=0.5\), so both moments are matched.
Step 3: the explicit weights. Up to scale the corner weights are proportional to \(e^{\beta(x_1+x_2)}\in\{3,\,1,\,1,\,\tfrac13\}\), summing to \(3+1+1+\tfrac13=\tfrac{16}{3}\). Normalizing the four pattern weights to sum to \(4\) multiplies by \(4/(16/3)=\tfrac34\): \[
w_{(1,1)}=\tfrac94=2.25,\quad
w_{(1,-1)}=\tfrac34=0.75,\quad
w_{(-1,1)}=\tfrac34=0.75,\quad
w_{(-1,-1)}=\tfrac14=0.25.
\tag{18.26}\] These sum to \(4\), and one checks the balance directly: the weighted mean of \(x_1\) is \((2.25\cdot 1+0.75\cdot 1+0.75\cdot(-1)+0.25\cdot(-1))/4=2/4=0.5\), and likewise the weighted mean of \(x_2\) is \((2.25-0.75+0.75-0.25)/4=0.5\). The normalization multiplier follows from \(w_{(1,1)}=e^{\alpha}e^{\beta}=e^{\alpha}\sqrt3=2.25\), giving \(e^{\alpha}=2.25/\sqrt3=\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{4}\) and \(\alpha=\tfrac32\ln 3-\ln 4\approx 0.2616\).
Step 4: the effective sample size. With the four pattern weights Equation 18.26, \[
\sum_i w_i=4,\qquad
\sum_i w_i^2=2.25^2+0.75^2+0.75^2+0.25^2=5.0625+0.5625+0.5625+0.0625=6.25,
\] so \[
\mathrm{ESS}=\frac{4^2}{6.25}=\frac{16}{6.25}=2.56,\qquad \frac{\mathrm{ESS}}{n}=\frac{2.56}{4}=0.64.
\] Matching both covariate means cost \(36\%\) of the effective sample. The variance inflation factor is \(n/\mathrm{ESS}=4/2.56=1.5625\) (Theorem 18.7), so a weighted arm mean has standard error \(\sqrt{1.5625}=1.25\) times the unweighted standard error, a \(25\%\) increase. (The bound \(\mathrm{ESS}\le n\) of Theorem 18.6 is comfortably respected.)
Step 5: the weighted arm means. The arm-\(A\) outcomes at the four patterns are \(\mu_A(1,1)=19\), \(\mu_A(1,-1)=15\), \(\mu_A(-1,1)=17\), \(\mu_A(-1,-1)=13\); the arm-\(C\) outcomes are \(\mu_C(1,1)=24\), \(\mu_C(1,-1)=20\), \(\mu_C(-1,1)=20\), \(\mu_C(-1,-1)=16\) (we set \(Y\) equal to its conditional mean to keep the arithmetic exact; with noise the estimator is consistent rather than exact, Theorem 18.4). The weighted arm means are \[
\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=\frac{2.25(19)+0.75(15)+0.75(17)+0.25(13)}{4}=\frac{70}{4}=17.5,
\] \[
\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=\frac{2.25(24)+0.75(20)+0.75(20)+0.25(16)}{4}=\frac{88}{4}=22.
\] Both equal the comparator-population truth: \(\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}=16+0.5+2(0.5)=17.5\) and \(\bar\mu_{C(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}=20+2(0.5)+2(0.5)=22\), confirming Step 2 of Theorem 18.4.
Step 6: the adjusted index contrast. On the identity scale the benefit of \(A\) over \(C\) in the comparator population is \[
\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{MAIC}}-\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=22-17.5=4.5,
\] matching the true comparator-population benefit \(4+\bar x_{1,BC}=4+0.5=4.5\). The unadjusted index benefit, from the unweighted arm means \(\bar\mu_A^{\mathrm{unw}}=(19+15+17+13)/4=16\) and \(\bar\mu_C^{\mathrm{unw}}=(24+20+20+16)/4=20\), is \(20-16=4\), the benefit in the index population (\(4+\bar x_{1,AC}=4+0=4\)). MAIC has moved the estimate from \(4\) to \(4.5\), correcting for the higher value of the effect modifier \(x_1\) in the comparator population.
Step 7: the anchored indirect comparison. Suppose the comparator trial reports a \(B\)-versus-\(C\) benefit of \(\hat d_{BC}^{\mathrm{AgD}}=3.0\) in its own population. The anchored MAIC estimate of the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) benefit in \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\) is \[
\hat d_{AB}^{\mathrm{MAIC,anch}}=\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}-\hat d_{BC}^{\mathrm{AgD}}=4.5-3.0=1.5,
\] the target estimand \(d_{AB(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}=d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}-d_{BC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}=4.5-3.0=
1.5\). The unadjusted Bucher comparison would have used the index-population benefit \(4.0\) and produced \(4.0-3.0=1.0\), biased by \(-0.5\). The bias is exactly the effect-modification discrepancy \(d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}-d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{AC})}=4.5-4.0=0.5\), caused by the imbalance in the effect modifier \(x_1\) (\(\bar x_1=0.5\) in \(\mathcal{P}_{BC}\) versus \(0\) in \(\mathcal{P}_{AC}\)); this is precisely the transitivity failure of Theorem 16.1 that population adjustment removes. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. What the prognostic covariate cost. The effect modifier \(x_1\) had to be balanced: it drives the \(0.5\) bias correction. The prognostic covariate \(x_2\) did not need balancing for the contrast, because it cancels between the arms (\(\mu_A\) and \(\mu_C\) both carry \(+2x_2\)), yet we balanced it anyway, and doing so contributed to the drop in effective sample size from \(4\) to \(2.56\). Had we balanced only \(x_1\), the weights would have been less variable and the ESS higher, at no cost in bias on the identity scale. This is the anchored-case phenomenon of Theorem 18.4: only imbalanced effect modifiers are mandatory; balancing pure prognostic variables is harmless for bias but spends precision. In the unanchored case (Theorem 18.5) the prognostic \(x_2\) would not cancel, and balancing it would be mandatory, which is one more reason the unanchored estimator is so much more expensive. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 18  Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison
text:
18.17 Practitioner checklist
The theory of this chapter condenses into a short list of things to do, and to check in someone else’s analysis, when performing or reviewing a MAIC. Each item names the result it rests on.

Confirm overlap first. Compare the comparator’s reported covariate means (and ranges and standard deviations, when given) with the minimum and maximum in the index IPD. A comparator mean near or beyond an index extreme, or an optimizer that fails to converge or returns enormous weights, is an overlap failure, not a software glitch (Theorem 18.2, Theorem 18.8).
Balance every imbalanced effect modifier. These are mandatory in both anchored and unanchored MAIC. On a nonlinear link (log odds ratio, log hazard ratio) balance higher moments as well, because first-moment matching is insufficient there (Example 18.2, Section 18.4).
Prefer anchored whenever a common comparator exists. Anchored MAIC needs only effect modifiers; unanchored MAIC also needs every prognostic variable and rests on an untestable absolute-constancy assumption. Use unanchored only as a last resort, with sensitivity analysis over the adjustment set (Section 18.9, Section 18.10).
Report the effective sample size and flag low values. State \(\mathrm{ESS}\) and \(\mathrm{ESS}/n\); treat \(\mathrm{ESS}/n<0.5\) as substantial information loss and \(\mathrm{ESS}/n<0.1\) as an analysis driven by a handful of patients. Show standardized covariate differences before and after weighting to confirm balance was achieved (Theorem 18.6, Theorem 18.7).
Use honest standard errors. Compute uncertainty with the sandwich variance or a full bootstrap that refits the weights on each resample, never as if the weights were fixed; combine it with the published comparator effect’s own standard error, which is independent (Theorem 18.9, Theorem 18.10).
Mind the scale. On non-collapsible scales, matching covariate means does not by itself make two marginal odds ratios or hazard ratios comparable; confirm that the scale-alignment conditions hold or move to a model-based method (Theorem 11.2, Chapter 20).

title: 18  Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison
text:
18.18 Notes and references
Matching-adjusted indirect comparison was introduced by Signorovitch et al. (2010), who proposed reweighting the individual patient data of one trial so that its weighted baseline moments match those reported by a comparator trial, and recognized the weights as inverse-odds weights from a logistic model of trial membership. The entropy-balancing formulation, the derivation of the exponential weight form, the convex-duality analysis of existence, the effective-sample-size diagnostic, and the placement of MAIC within the anchored and unanchored population-adjustment framework follow the thesis of Phillippo (2019) and the NICE Decision Support Unit guidance Phillippo et al. (2016); the latter is the standard practical reference for which covariates to balance, the anchored-versus-unanchored decision, and the treatment of unanchored comparisons as a last resort. The maximum-entropy reading of covariate balancing, with its exponential-family solution and its convex dual, is the entropy-balancing method familiar from the causal-inference literature; the equivalence between entropy balancing and a calibrated logistic propensity model is a recurring theme there, and Theorem 18.3 is its MAIC instance, connected to the inverse-probability-weighting theory of Chapter 10 (Theorem 10.3, Definition 10.1) and the transportability theory of Chapter 12 (Definition 12.3, Theorem 12.2).
The convex-analytic facts underlying Theorem 18.2, that the gradient of a log-partition function maps onto the relative interior of the convex hull of the sufficient statistics and that the infimum is attained exactly when the origin lies in that relative interior, are standard in the theory of exponential families and convex duality; the coercivity argument given here is self-contained and avoids appealing to the general machinery of Rockafellar’s Convex Analysis. The effective-sample-size bound Theorem 18.6 is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, and the variance interpretation Equation 18.21 is the classical effective-sample-size formula for weighted means; both appear as Eq. (6.1) of Phillippo (2019). The non-extrapolation theorem Theorem 18.8 is the population-adjustment form of a positivity or overlap requirement, and its failure under poor covariate overlap is documented in the simulation studies of Phillippo (2019); the contrast with model-based methods that can interpolate motivates simulated treatment comparison (Chapter 19) and multilevel network meta-regression (Chapter 20). The sandwich variance Theorem 18.9 is M-estimation theory applied to the stacked weight-and-outcome equations (Definition 5.11), and the bootstrap validity Theorem 18.10 is the functional delta method for the bootstrap (Vaart (1998), Theorems 20.9, 23.9). The distinction between consistency and finite-sample unbiasedness, emphasized throughout Section 18.9 and Section 18.10, corrects a looseness in some of the early MAIC literature; it matters because the weights are estimated.
The companion Coq development formalizes the algebraic core of MAIC in theories/MAIC.v. The weight function \(w(\mathbf{x})=\exp(\text{linear predictor})\) is maic_weight_fn, proved positive in maic_weight_pos; the effective sample size is ESS, and the bound \(\mathrm{ESS}\le n\) is Theorem ESS_upper_bound, the machine-checked counterpart of Theorem 18.6. Its proof is built from the elementary two_mul_le_sqr (\(2xy\le x^2+y^2\)), assembled by induction into cauchy_schwarz_ones and its weight specialization cauchy_schwarz_n_weights, and the development records no admissions for these results. The anchored and unanchored estimators appear as effect_AC_MAIC and effect_AB_anchored, with the substantive consistency content (Theorem 18.4, Theorem 18.5) carried by named section hypotheses standing for conditional constancy, complete effect-modifier coverage, shared effect modification, and overlap, rather than as formalized probabilistic theorems; the optimization that fixes \((\alpha,\boldsymbol{\beta})\) in Theorem 18.1 is likewise pen-and-paper. Chapter 30 walks through MAIC.v in detail.
This chapter corresponds to results F.1 (method-of-moments balance), F.2 (the entropy objective), F.3 (the exponential weights), F.4 (existence and uniqueness), F.5 (the logistic-IPW equivalence), F.6 (anchored consistency), F.7 (unanchored consistency), F.8 (the ESS bound), F.9 (variance inflation), F.10 (the no-extrapolation theorem), F.11 (the sandwich variance), and F.12 (bootstrap validity) of the proof catalogue in proofs/F_maic.md. The general population-adjustment theory that MAIC specializes, conditional constancy in its relative and absolute forms (Definition 17.4, Definition 17.5), the shared-effect-modifier assumption (Definition 17.6), and the anchored and unanchored PAIC consistency theorems (Theorem 17.1, Theorem 17.2), is developed in Chapter 17. The regression-based alternative to reweighting, simulated treatment comparison, and its asymptotic equivalence to MAIC under a correctly specified linear outcome model (Theorem 19.7), is the subject of Chapter 19.

title: 18  Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison
text:
18.19 Exercises
Throughout, a starred exercise, marked \(\star\), has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first three exercises are warm-ups and interpretation checks that need only the ideas of this chapter; the later ones build toward the proofs, and the two starred ones are the most demanding.

Exercise 18.1 Reading the weights. (Warm-up.) In the running Example 18.1 the two severe patients received weight \(1.5\) each and the two mild patients weight \(0.5\) each. (a) In one sentence, say what a weight of \(1.5\) means for a severe patient, in terms of how many target-population patients they stand in for. (b) Why are the severe patients upweighted rather than the mild ones, given that the comparator trial was sicker? (c) Recompute the effective sample size from these weights and state, in plain words, how many equally weighted patients this reweighted sample is worth. (d) Without recomputing anything, would balancing a second imbalanced covariate raise or lower the ESS, and which result of this chapter guarantees the direction?


Exercise 18.2 Effect modifier or prognostic variable? (Interpretation.) For each covariate below, state whether it is most naturally an effect modifier, a prognostic variable, or both, and then say whether an anchored MAIC and an unanchored MAIC would each be obliged to balance it, assuming it is imbalanced between the trials. (a) A biomarker that predicts worse outcomes on every treatment but does not change the size of \(A\)’s benefit over \(C\). (b) Disease severity, which both worsens outcomes and enlarges the benefit of \(A\). (c) A covariate perfectly balanced between the two trials. Justify each answer in one sentence using the cancellation argument of Section 18.9.


Exercise 18.3 Judging a published MAIC. (Interpretation.) A submission reports an unanchored MAIC comparing drug \(A\) (from an IPD trial of \(n=400\) patients) against drug \(B\), balancing three covariates, with an effective sample size \(\mathrm{ESS}=28\) and a \(95\%\) confidence interval computed as though the weights were fixed. The comparator’s reported mean for one of the three covariates lies just above the largest value observed in the IPD. List, in order of severity, the credibility concerns you would raise, and name the result of this chapter behind each. (Consider at least: the anchored-versus-unanchored choice, the overlap of that one covariate, the \(\mathrm{ESS}/n\) ratio, and the variance method.)


Exercise 18.4 A one-covariate MAIC by hand. (Computation.) An index trial has four patients with a single covariate \(x\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}\) (one per value) and a comparator that reports mean \(\bar x_{BC}=0.5\). Write the balance equation \(\sum_i(x_i-0.5)e^{\beta(x_i-0.5)}=0\), solve for \(\beta\) numerically to three decimal places, report the normalized weights summing to \(4\), verify that the weighted mean is \(0.5\), and compute the effective sample size and the variance inflation factor. Comment on how the ESS would change if the target were \(\bar x_{BC}=1.5\) instead.


Exercise 18.5 Balancing a variance. (Computation.) Continue Example 18.3 but now require, in addition to matching both means at \(0.5\), that the weighted variance of \(x_1\) equal a reported comparator value \(s^2_{1,BC}=0.5\). Write the augmented feature map \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})=(x_1,x_2,x_1^2)\) and the corresponding three balance equations, explain why the solution generally has \(\beta_1\ne\beta_2\) once the squared term is added, and argue from Theorem 18.6 why adding the second-moment constraint can only decrease (never increase) the effective sample size.


Exercise 18.6 Recovering the logistic weights. (Computation.) Using Theorem 18.3, suppose a logistic trial-membership model has fitted coefficients \(\tilde\alpha=0.3\) and \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(0.8,-0.4)\). Write the inverse-odds weight as a function of \(\mathbf{x}\), identify the MAIC parameter \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\), and explain in one paragraph why the MAIC method of moments and logistic maximum likelihood give the same weight form but generally different fitted values when the comparator supplies only covariate means.


Exercise 18.7 The ESS and majorization. (Challenge.) Show that among all nonnegative weight vectors with a fixed sum, the effective sample size Equation 18.20 is maximized uniquely by the uniform vector, and more generally that if \(\mathbf{w}'\) majorizes \(\mathbf{w}\) (the sorted partial sums of \(\mathbf{w}'\) dominate those of \(\mathbf{w}\), with equal total, so \(\mathbf{w}'\) is the more concentrated or lopsided vector) then \(\mathrm{ESS}(\mathbf{w}')\le\mathrm{ESS}(\mathbf{w})\). Deduce Theorem 18.6 as the special case where \(\mathbf{w}'\) concentrates all weight on one coordinate. (Hint: \(\mathbf{w}\mapsto\sum_i w_i^2\) is Schur-convex, meaning it never decreases when weight is shifted from a smaller coordinate to a larger one; a Schur-convex function is therefore smallest at the most equal vector and largest at the most concentrated, which is exactly what the ESS bound records.)


Exercise 18.8 (\(\star\)) Decomposing the adjustment. (Proof.) In Example 18.3, replace the conditional benefit \(4+x_1\) by the general form \(b_0+b_1x_1+b_2x_2\) and the comparator mean by a general \((\bar x_{1},\bar x_{2})\) inside the square. Derive a closed-form expression for the MAIC-adjusted benefit \(\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}\) in terms of \(b_0,b_1,b_2\) and the target means, prove that it equals the true comparator-population benefit \(b_0+b_1\bar x_1+b_2\bar x_2\) for any weights achieving moment balance (not only the entropy weights), and conclude that on the identity scale with a linear benefit the choice of balancing objective affects the variance (through the ESS) but not the point estimate. Explain how this exact-on-the-mean property fails on the logit scale, connecting to the higher-moment discussion of Section 18.4 and Definition 7.7.


Exercise 18.9 (\(\star\)) Naive versus sandwich variance. (Challenge.) Consider the stacked estimating equations Equation 18.24 for a single-arm weighted mean (drop the \(C\) block). Write the \(2\times 2\) block-triangular Jacobian \(A\) in the scalar-covariate case, invert it explicitly, and show that the asymptotic variance of \(\hat\mu_A\) has the fixed-weight term \(\sigma^2/\mathrm{ESS}\) plus a correction attributable to estimating \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\). Identify the data configuration in which the correction vanishes (so that the naive and sandwich variances agree) and interpret it: it is the case where the outcome is uncorrelated, within the weighting, with the balancing covariate. Relate your finding to the remark following Theorem 18.9 on why fixed-weight standard errors are generally anticonservative.





Bucher, Heiner C., Gordon H. Guyatt, Lauren E. Griffith, and Stephen D. Walter. 1997. “The Results of Direct and Indirect Treatment Comparisons in Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.” Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 50 (6): 683–91.


Phillippo, David M., A. E. Ades, Sofia Dias, Stephen Palmer, Keith R. Abrams, and Nicky J. Welton. 2016. NICE DSU Technical Support Document 18: Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Submissions to NICE. Decision Support Unit, ScHARR, University of Sheffield.


Phillippo, David Mark. 2019. “Calibration of Treatment Effects in Network Meta-Analysis Using Individual Patient Data.” PhD thesis, University of Bristol.


Signorovitch, James E., Eric Q. Wu, Andrew P. Yu, et al. 2010. “Comparative Effectiveness Without Head-to-Head Trials: A Method for Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons.” PharmacoEconomics 28 (10): 935–45.


Vaart, A. W. van der. 1998. Asymptotic Statistics. Cambridge University Press.
