title: 19  Simulated Treatment Comparison
section: 19.9 STC consistency under the population-adjustment conditions
text:
19.9 STC consistency under the population-adjustment conditions
Theorem 19.3 established consistency for the marginal effect in the comparator population under correct specification and transportability of the outcome surface. The population-adjustment theory of Chapter 17 expresses transportability through the conditions on effect modifiers and prognostic variables that an indirect comparison actually needs, separately for the anchored and unanchored cases. We restate STC consistency in those terms (catalogue G.6), so that STC slots into the general framework alongside MAIC.

Remark. Two data scenarios, in the running example. Anchored is the situation we have carried throughout: the index trial randomizes \(A\) against \(C\) and the comparator trial randomizes \(B\) against the same \(C\), so \(C\) is a shared anchor and Bucher’s subtraction cancels the study baselines. Here STC need only get the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) contrast right in \(\mathcal P_{BC}\), so it must include every covariate that modifies that contrast (every effect modifier). Unanchored is the harder situation where the two trials share no common arm, for instance a single-arm study of \(A\) and a single-arm study of \(B\). Now there is no baseline to cancel, so STC must get each absolute arm outcome right in \(\mathcal P_{BC}\), which means including every covariate that is merely prognostic (that shifts the outcome level) in addition to every effect modifier. Concretely: if age is prognostic for the flare but does not change the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) effect, the anchored analysis may safely omit it, but the unanchored analysis may not, because age now moves arm levels that no longer cancel. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Theorem 19.6 (Anchored and unanchored STC consistency) Assume the outcome model Definition 19.1 is correctly specified on the chosen link scale, so \(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}\xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\xi_0\) by Theorem 19.1, and the integrals are computed as in Theorem 19.3.

Anchored. If conditional constancy of relative effects holds (Definition 17.4) and every effect modifier of the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) contrast that is distributed differently between the index and comparator populations is included in \(\mathbf x\) (the anchored sufficiency condition of Theorem 17.1), then the marginal STC estimator 1 is consistent for the target-population marginal relative effect \(d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\), and the anchored Bucher combination \(\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}-\hat d_{BC}\) is consistent for \(d_{AB(\mathcal P_{BC})}\).
Unanchored. If conditional constancy of absolute effects holds (Definition 17.5) and every prognostic variable and effect modifier distributed differently between the populations is included in \(\mathbf x\) (the unanchored condition of Theorem 17.2), then the unanchored marginal STC estimator, the single-arm predicted contrast \(g(\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{STC}})-g(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}})\) taken without a common anchor, is consistent for the target-population effect.

(Corresponds to G.6 in the proof catalogue.)


Proof. The argument is the regression-route counterpart of the MAIC consistency theorems Theorem 18.4 and Theorem 18.5, with the weighted mean replaced by the predicted marginal mean Equation 19.14.
Anchored. By Theorem 19.3, \(\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{STC}}\xrightarrow{p}\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}\) provided the source-fitted surface \(\mu_k(\cdot)\) is the correct conditional surface in the comparator population. Conditional constancy of relative effects (Definition 17.4) states that the conditional contrast Equation 19.3 is the same function of \(\mathbf x\) in both populations; including every differentially distributed effect modifier in \(\mathbf x\) (Theorem 17.1) makes the fitted conditional means transportable in the sense of Proposition 19.1, because any covariate that would otherwise carry an unmodeled interaction is now a modeled coordinate of \(\mathbf x\). Hence \(\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\xrightarrow{p}d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\). The comparator trial’s \(\hat d_{BC}\) already estimates \(d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}\) in its own population, so both contrasts now live in \(\mathcal P_{BC}\), transitivity holds across them by construction, and Theorem 14.1 gives consistency of the difference for \(d_{AB(\mathcal P_{BC})}\).
Unanchored. Without a common anchor the estimand is a contrast of absolute arm positions across populations, so the cancellation of study baselines that the anchor provides (the \(\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC}\) cancellation of Chapter 14) is unavailable, and the prognostic structure no longer drops out. Conditional constancy of absolute effects (Definition 17.5) is then required, and every differentially distributed prognostic variable as well as every effect modifier must be in \(\mathbf x\) (Theorem 17.2), so that both fitted arm surfaces \(\mu_A(\cdot)\) and \(\mu_C(\cdot)\), not merely their contrast, are transportable. Under these stronger hypotheses Proposition 19.1 applies to each arm separately, Theorem 19.3 gives \(\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{STC}}\xrightarrow{p}\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}\), and the continuous mapping theorem delivers consistency of the unanchored predicted contrast. \(\square\)

Why this matters. This is where STC stops being a stand-alone trick and becomes a citizen of the population-adjustment framework of Chapter 17: its consistency rests on exactly the same effect-modifier and prognostic-variable conditions that govern MAIC and ML-NMR, only discharged through a fitted regression instead of weights. The practical reading is a covariate-selection rule: for an anchored comparison, model every effect modifier that differs between the trials; for an unanchored one, model every prognostic variable too. Getting that list wrong is misspecification, and by the remark after Theorem 19.1 its price is bias, not merely variance.

Remark. STC against MAIC, assumption for assumption. STC and MAIC are dual routes through the same conditional-transportability framework, and Chapter 17 shows they target the same estimand when both are valid. Their hypotheses differ in two mirror-image ways. STC is stronger in demanding a correctly specified parametric outcome model, link and functional form and included covariates; if the model is wrong, STC inherits the pseudo-true bias of the misspecification remark after Theorem 19.1, whereas MAIC asks only that the matched moments balance and is robust to functional form beyond them. STC is weaker in demanding no overlap: a regression extrapolates where weights cannot exist (Theorem 18.8, Proposition 19.1), so STC’s variance is not inflated by poor overlap the way MAIC’s is by a small effective sample size (Theorem 18.6). The companion development records this trade-off as a comparison of method profiles in theories/Comparison.v; the two methods provably agree when both sets of assumptions hold, which we make precise next. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 19  Simulated Treatment Comparison
section: 19.10 Equivalence of MAIC and STC under a linear model
text:
19.10 Equivalence of MAIC and STC under a linear model
When the outcome model is linear and only first moments are matched, the weighting route and the regression route are not merely both valid; they are asymptotically the same estimator. This is catalogue result G.7. It explains the close agreement of MAIC and STC seen in practice when the outcome surface is near-linear and overlap is good, and it locates exactly where the two methods part company.
We first record the trivial but useful fact that the two methods agree whenever both are valid, the abstract statement that has a machine-checked counterpart.

Corollary 19.1 (Agreement under joint validity) Suppose the anchored MAIC assumptions and the anchored STC assumptions both hold, so that, by Theorem 18.4 and Theorem 19.6 respectively, each estimator is consistent for the same target estimand \(d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\). Then the two estimators have the same probability limit, \(\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{MAIC}}-\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\xrightarrow{p}0\).
[machine-checked: theories/Comparison.v, Theorem methods_agree_when_correct]


Proof. By hypothesis each estimator converges in probability to the common target \(d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\), so their difference converges in probability to \(0\) by the algebra of limits. The Coq theorem methods_agree_when_correct is this statement stripped to its logical core: from the two identification premises (MAIC’s assumptions imply its estimate equals the true effect, STC’s assumptions imply the same for its estimate) it derives equality of the two estimates. \(\square\)

The substantive theorem is sharper: under a linear model the agreement is exact in the limit even before invoking a shared target, because the two estimators are two consistent estimators of the same linear functional of the same parameters.

Theorem 19.7 (Asymptotic equivalence of MAIC and STC under a linear model) Suppose (i) the outcome model is linear with the identity link, \(\mathbb E[Y\mid k,X=\mathbf x]=\alpha_k+\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}\) for \(k\in\{A,C\}\); (ii) the MAIC weights are the entropy-balanced exponential weights of Theorem 18.1, with parameters chosen to satisfy the first-moment balance constraint (Definition 18.1, Definition 18.2); and (iii) only the first moments of the covariates are matched, the weighted index mean equalling \(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}\). Then the marginal STC estimator 1 and the MAIC weighted-difference estimator have the same probability limit, \[
\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\ \xrightarrow{p}\ (\alpha_C-\alpha_A)+\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_{(C)}-\boldsymbol\beta_{(A)})\ \xleftarrow{p}\ \hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{MAIC}},
\tag{19.20}\] and are therefore asymptotically equivalent. (Corresponds to G.7 in the proof catalogue.)


Proof. The common target. With the identity link, Proposition 19.2 gives the marginal arm position \(\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}=\alpha_k+\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}\), so the marginal relative effect Equation 19.9 in the comparator population is \[
d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}=\bar\mu_{C(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal P_{BC})}=(\alpha_C-\alpha_A)+\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_{(C)}-\boldsymbol\beta_{(A)}),
\] the right-hand quantity in Equation 19.20.
STC side. Under the linear model the predicted marginal means Equation 19.14 are, by linearity of expectation, \(\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{STC}}=\hat\alpha_k+\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(k)}\), so \(\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}=(\hat\alpha_C-\hat\alpha_A)+\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}^\top(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(C)}-\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(A)})\). By Theorem 19.1 the coefficient estimates are consistent, \((\hat\alpha_k,\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(k)})\xrightarrow{p}(\alpha_k,\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)})\), so \(\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\xrightarrow{p}d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\), the left convergence in Equation 19.20.
MAIC side. The MAIC estimator is the difference of weighted arm means \(\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=\sum_{i:T_i=k}w_i Y_i\big/\sum_{i:T_i=k}w_i\), with the entropy-balanced weights \(w_i=\exp(\hat\alpha_w+\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_w^\top(\mathbf x_i-\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}))\) of Theorem 18.1. Let \(P^\ast_k\) denote the limiting weighted law of the covariates in arm \(k\); under overlap and the law of large numbers for weighted averages, \(\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{MAIC}}\xrightarrow{p}\mathbb E_{P^\ast_k}[Y\mid T=k]=\mathbb E_{P^\ast_k}\bigl[\mathbb E[Y\mid k,X]\bigr]=\mathbb E_{P^\ast_k}[\alpha_k+X^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}]=\alpha_k+\mathbb E_{P^\ast_k}[X]^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}\), the middle step by the tower property and the linear model, the last by linearity of expectation. The first-moment balance constraint (iii) forces \(\mathbb E_{P^\ast_k}[X]=\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}\), so \(\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{MAIC}}\xrightarrow{p}\alpha_k+\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}=\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}\), the same arm limit as the STC side. Differencing the arms, \(\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{MAIC}}=\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{MAIC}}-\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}\xrightarrow{p}d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\), the right convergence in Equation 19.20.
Both estimators converge in probability to the same number, hence their difference converges to zero: they are asymptotically equivalent. \(\square\)


Remark. A one-line numeric check. Take the linear model of Exercise 19.10: \(\mathbb E[Y\mid C,x]=1+0.5x\) and \(\mathbb E[Y\mid A,x]=2+0.5x\), with target covariate mean \(\bar x_{BC}=1\). STC side: the predicted target means are \(\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{STC}}=1+0.5(1)=1.5\) and \(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}}=2+0.5(1)=2.5\), so the effect is \(1.5-2.5=-1\). MAIC side: entropy-balanced weights that pull the index covariate mean to \(\bar x_{BC}=1\) give weighted arm means \(\alpha_k+\beta_{(k)}\cdot 1\), again \(1.5\) and \(2.5\), so the effect is again \(-1\). The two routes land on the identical number because, under a linear model, the weighted mean of \(Y\) depends on the covariates only through their first moment, which is exactly what MAIC matches and what STC’s linear prediction uses. This is why the two methods so often agree in practice: near-linear outcome and good overlap make them two computations of the same first-moment functional. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Where the equivalence breaks. The proof used linearity twice and first-moment balance once, and the equivalence fails as soon as any of the three is removed.

Nonlinear link. If \(g\) is not the identity, \(\mu_k(\mathbf x)=g^{-1}(\eta_k(\mathbf x))\) is curved, STC’s response-scale integration carries the Jensen terms of Theorem 19.2, and MAIC’s first-moment balance no longer reproduces them; the two estimators target the same marginal effect but by different finite-sample routes and need not coincide except in the limit, and only then if both remain consistent.
Higher moments needed. If the conditional mean involves \(\mathbf x\) nonlinearly, for instance a quadratic term \(\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\gamma\mathbf x\), then \(\mathbb E_{P^\ast_k}[\mathbb E[Y\mid k,X]]\) depends on the second moment of \(P^\ast_k\), which first-moment balance does not pin to \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\); MAIC then estimates a different number from STC unless the higher moments are also matched.
Nonlinear interactions. Even with the identity link, an interaction structure richer than the additive \(\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_2\) makes the conditional contrast a nonlinear function of \(\mathbf x\), and first-moment balance is again insufficient.

In practice the two methods agree closely when overlap is good and the outcome surface is near-linear, and diverge under poor overlap, where MAIC’s variance inflates (Theorem 18.6) while STC extrapolates, or under misspecification, where STC is biased while MAIC remains robust to functional form beyond the matched moments. The choice between them is the choice between trusting a model and trusting an overlap. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 19  Simulated Treatment Comparison
text:
19.11 Notes and references
Simulated treatment comparison was introduced by Caro and Ishak (2010) under the title “No head-to-head trial? Simulate the missing arms,” as a regression-and-simulation alternative to matching; the original proposal is the conditional plug-in of Definition 19.2, evaluated at the comparator covariate means. The distinction between conditional and marginal STC, the diagnosis of the plug-in bias as non-collapsibility, and the recommendation to integrate on the response scale are due to the population-adjustment methods literature, principally the NICE technical support document Phillippo et al. (2016) and the thesis of Phillippo (2019) (Sections 2.2 to 2.4), which also frame STC and MAIC as the outcome-regression and weighting implementations of one conditional-transportability problem; the estimand-based reframing in terms of marginal versus conditional targets and the transportability of the outcome surface is developed by Chandler and Ishak (2026). The identification of marginal STC as g-computation standardized to a target population (Proposition 19.1) places it in the lineage of Hernán and Robins (2020) and Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983), and is the seed of the multilevel network meta-regression of Phillippo et al. (2020) (Chapter 20), which embeds the same response-scale integration inside a coherent Bayesian network model and removes STC’s reliance on a separate Bucher step. The comparison of MAIC and STC against the MLE asymptotics of Theorem 5.6 follows the GLM treatment of McCullagh and Nelder (1989) and the M-estimation theory of Vaart (1998), the latter also supplying the Bernstein-von Mises theorem behind Theorem 19.5.
This chapter corresponds to results G.1 through G.7 of the proof catalogue in proofs/G_stc.md: the outcome MLE asymptotics G.1 (Theorem 19.1), the conditional plug-in bias G.2 (Theorem 19.2), the marginal STC consistency G.3 (Theorem 19.3), the non-collapsibility counterexample G.4 (Theorem 19.4), Bayesian g-computation G.5 (Theorem 19.5), STC consistency under the Chapter 17 conditions G.6 (Theorem 19.6), and the MAIC-STC equivalence G.7 (Theorem 19.7).
Two results carry machine-checked tags confirmed in the companion Coq development. The marginal STC contrast identity Theorem 19.3 is Theorem STC_consistent in theories/STC.v, which proves the response-scale identity \(\texttt{effect\_AC\_STC}=\mathbb E_2[Y_A^{\mathrm{target}}]-\mathbb E_2[Y_C^{\mathrm{target}}]\) from the per-arm transported g-computation premises; the link transformation and uniform convergence are the analytic additions made here. The collapsibility boundary Proposition 19.2 is Lemma STC_collapse_linear in the same file, which proves that a linear outcome model makes the marginal STC estimate equal the treatment coefficient using only linearity of the abstract target expectation, the single property a nonlinear link destroys. The agreement-under-joint-validity corollary Corollary 19.1 is Theorem methods_agree_when_correct in theories/Comparison.v, the logical core of the equivalence. The non-collapsibility counterexample Theorem 19.4 is deliberately left as pen-and-paper arithmetic over the logit, as its content is a numerical witness rather than an algebraic identity; the companion file confirms only the collapsible boundary. As in Chapter 14, the Coq files treat the target-population expectation as an abstract linear operator, so the formalization captures the algebraic content while leaving the measure-theoretic construction of the integral Equation 19.14 to the caller. The files theories/OutcomeRegression.v (g-computation, the source-population analogue) and theories/Comparison.v (the MAIC-versus-STC method profiles) provide the surrounding structure.

title: 19  Simulated Treatment Comparison
text:
19.12 Exercises
An exercise marked with a star (\(\star\)) has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first two are warm-ups; do them before the proof-heavy exercises that follow.

Exercise 19.1 (Warm-up, computation) A full STC table by hand. An index trial fits the logistic model \(\operatorname{logit}\mu_C(x)=-0.5+0.7x\) and \(\operatorname{logit}\mu_A(x)=0.4+0.7x\) for a single binary covariate \(x\) (so there is no effect modification). The target comparator population has \(\Pr_{BC}(x=1)=0.6\). (a) Compute the four fitted event probabilities \(\mu_C(0),\mu_C(1),\mu_A(0),\mu_A(1)\) with \(\operatorname{expit}\). (b) Conditional plug-in: evaluate the linear predictors at \(\bar x_{BC}=0.6\) and report the plug-in log odds ratio of \(A\) versus \(C\). (c) Marginal STC: average the fitted probabilities over the target on the natural outcome scale, apply the logit, and report the marginal log odds ratio. (d) State which of (b) and (c) a health technology assessment should use, and by how much they differ. This is the five-step workflow of Section 19.2 with the Bucher step omitted.


Exercise 19.2 (Warm-up, interpretation) Which scale, which average? In one or two sentences each, explain to a colleague: (a) why “average then link” and “link then average” give different answers for an odds ratio but the same answer for a risk difference; (b) what “simulated” refers to in simulated treatment comparison; and (c) why STC can predict into a comparator population that MAIC cannot weight into, and what STC must assume to justify that prediction. No arithmetic required.


Exercise 19.3 Recompute with a new target. In the worked example Example 19.3, keep the fitted model (\(\hat\alpha=-1\), \(\hat\beta_1=1\), \(\hat\gamma=1.5\), \(\hat\beta_2=0\)) but change the target biomarker prevalence to \(\Pr_{BC}(X=1)=0.3\). Compute the conditional plug-in log odds ratio, the marginal STC log odds ratio in the new target, and the non-collapsibility gap between them. Confirm that the plug-in is unchanged at \(1.5\) while the marginal value moves, and explain why the plug-in ignores the covariate distribution entirely.


Exercise 19.4 With effect modification. Repeat Example 19.3 but with \(\hat\beta_2=0.8\) (the biomarker now modifies the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) effect), so \(\operatorname{logit}\mu_A(x)=0.5+1.8x\). With target prevalence \(\bar x_{BC}=0.8\) and source prevalence \(0.5\), compute the conditional plug-in, the target marginal STC, and the source marginal log odds ratios. Show that the source-to-target shift is now much larger than in the \(\hat\beta_2=0\) case, and identify how much of the conditional-versus-marginal gap is non-collapsibility and how much is effect modification interacting with the covariate shift.


Exercise 19.5 Identity link is exact. Prove directly from Definition 19.3 that for the identity link the conditional plug-in STC estimator Equation 19.7 and the marginal STC estimator 1 have the same probability limit for every covariate distribution, recovering Proposition 19.2 without the Taylor expansion. Then exhibit a continuous outcome with a log link for which they differ, and compute the gap using Example 19.1.


Exercise 19.6 No overlap required. Let the index trial observe the covariate only on \([0,1]\) but the target place mass on \([1,2]\). Explain why the marginal STC integral Equation 19.14 is still defined while the MAIC weights are not, and state precisely the assumption (correctness of \(\mu_k\) off the index support) that STC must add to justify the extrapolation. Relate this to Proposition 19.1 and Theorem 18.8.


Exercise 19.7 Direction of the gap. For the logit link with equal arm slopes (\(\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf 0\)) and a covariate symmetric about its mean, use Equation 19.12 and the sign of \((\operatorname{expit})''\), which is positive for \(\eta<0\) and negative for \(\eta>0\), to argue that the conditional-at-the-mean odds ratio is generically farther from the null than the marginal odds ratio. Confirm the direction against the counterexample Theorem 19.4, where the conditional \(1.5\) exceeds the marginal \(1.227\).


Exercise 19.8 (\(\star\)) The collapsible contrast. Using Example 19.1, prove that under the log link with Gaussian covariates the conditional plug-in STC is unbiased for the marginal effect if and only if \(\boldsymbol\beta_1^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_2+\tfrac12\boldsymbol\beta_2^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_2=0\), and in particular whenever there is no effect modification (\(\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf 0\)). Contrast this with the logit link, where Theorem 19.4 shows the plug-in is biased even with \(\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf 0\). Conclude that collapsibility of the contrast is a property of the link, and relate your finding to the collapsibility of the rate ratio in Chapter 11. (A solution appears in Appendix F.)


Exercise 19.9 (\(\star\)) Delta-method variance of marginal STC. Let \(\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi)\) be the STC functional Equation 19.19. Using Theorem 19.1 and the delta method (Theorem 5.3), show that \(\sqrt n(\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}-d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}})\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,\nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi_0)^\top\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\xi_0)^{-1}\nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi_0))\), and write the gradient \(\nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi_0)\) as an integral of \(g^{-1}{}'\) against \(f_{BC}\) for each coordinate of \(\boldsymbol\xi\). Explain why Theorem 19.5 reproduces this variance asymptotically, and why the Bayesian route avoids computing the gradient. Under misspecification, replace \(\mathcal I^{-1}\) by the sandwich of Definition 5.11 and state what \(\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi^\ast)\) then estimates. (A solution appears in Appendix F.)


Exercise 19.10 MAIC equals STC, numerically. Construct a linear-model dataset with one covariate: arm means \(\mathbb E[Y\mid C,x]=1+0.5x\) and \(\mathbb E[Y\mid A,x]=2+0.5x\) (so \(\boldsymbol\beta_2=0\)), source covariate mean \(0\), target covariate mean \(\bar x_{BC}=1\). Compute the marginal STC effect from Theorem 19.7, then verify that entropy-balanced MAIC weights matching the first moment give the same limit. Now add a quadratic term \(0.3x^2\) to the comparator arm only and show that first-moment MAIC and STC now disagree, matching the breakdown clause of the equivalence remark.

title: 20  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression I: The Aggregation Principle
text:
20.1 Introduction
Part IV gave two ways to repair the indirect comparison once one trial hands us individual patient data (IPD). Matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC, Chapter 18) reweights the IPD trial so that its weighted covariate moments equal the aggregate comparator’s, then reads off the relative effect in the reweighted pseudo-population; simulated treatment comparison (STC, Chapter 19) fits an outcome regression to the IPD and predicts what its arms would do in the comparator’s covariate distribution. Both are pairwise repairs of a single Bucher triangle, both target the comparator population and no other, and both buy their cure with assumptions that are exact only on a linear scale. On a nonlinear link such as the logit or the log, matching covariate means and plugging those means into the model is not the same as averaging the model over the population: the difference is the ecological bias of Definition 16.2, and it is the residue that Theorem 16.1 could not remove from aggregate data alone.
This chapter opens Part V with the method that resolves all three limitations at once: multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR), introduced by Phillippo et al. (2020) and Phillippo (2019). The idea is a single change of viewpoint. Instead of repairing one triangle at a time, write one individual-level outcome model for the whole network, with study baselines, prognostic main effects, and treatment-by-covariate effect modifiers (the individual model, Definition 20.1). Every study, whether it reports IPD or only summaries, is a sample from this one model restricted to its own covariate distribution. For a study that reports only aggregate data (AgD), the quantity we can predict is not an individual outcome but a study average, and the correct study average is obtained by integrating the individual model over that study’s covariate distribution (the aggregate model, Definition 20.2). The bridge between the two levels is the aggregation theorem (Theorem 20.1): the mean outcome of an AgD arm is the integral of the inverse link of the linear predictor against the covariate density, \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\int_{\mathcal X} g^{-1}\!\big(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)\big)\,f_j(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x .
\] This single identity is the whole of ML-NMR’s claim to coherence. IPD studies contribute their patients one by one, with no integration because each covariate vector is observed; AgD studies contribute through the integral, with the covariate distribution standing in for the individuals we cannot see. The two contributions enter one likelihood and estimate one set of parameters.
The aggregation theorem also explains, in one line, why everyone before us was biased. If you do the cheap thing and plug the mean covariate into the model, you compute \(g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf x}_j))\), the inverse link of the average; the correct quantity is the average of the inverse link. Because \(g^{-1}\) is nonlinear, Jensen’s inequality (Theorem 4.6) separates the two, and the gap is exactly the ecological bias (Theorem 20.2). ML-NMR removes that gap not by an approximation but by performing the integral. The remainder of the chapter studies the integral itself across the three links that organize the applied literature. On the identity link the inverse link is affine, the integral is the mean, and aggregation is exact: there is nothing to integrate and ML-NMR collapses to ordinary meta-regression on covariate means (Theorem 20.3). On the log link with normally distributed covariates the integral is the moment generating function of a normal (Definition 4.7), which we know in closed form, and the aggregate mean is an explicit exponential (Theorem 20.4). On the logit link the integral is the mean of a logit-normal, which has no elementary closed form (Theorem 20.5); this is the obstruction that forces the quasi-Monte Carlo machinery of Chapter 22. An optional unifying lemma (Lemma 20.2, developed in Section 20.8) shows that all three cases are one object viewed three ways: the aggregate mean is the inverse link smoothed by the heat semigroup, and the three links differ only in whether that smoothing has a closed form.
We close with a fully worked numerical example, computable by hand on a calculator, that contrasts the naive plug-in aggregate mean with the integrated one on the logit scale, exhibits the sign reversal of the bias between a low-risk and a high-risk arm, and reads off the resulting distortion of the marginal odds ratio. The chapter owns results H.1 to H.7 of the proof catalogue. Throughout, \(g\) is the link function of Definition 7.2, \(\eta_{jk}\) the study-\(j\), arm-\(k\) linear predictor, \(f_j\) the study-\(j\) covariate density, and \(\boldsymbol\xi\) the full parameter vector, all as in Notation. Later chapters of Part V build on this foundation: discrete outcomes and the approximation theory (Chapter 21), numerical integration by copulas and low-discrepancy sequences (Chapter 22), target-population estimands, identifiability, and the sense in which ML-NMR generalizes standard network meta-analysis (Chapter 23), Bayesian computation (Chapter 24), general likelihoods (Chapter 25), and the unanchored extension ML-UMR (Chapter 26).

title: 20  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression I: The Aggregation Principle
text:
20.2 A running clinical example
Before any formalism, fix a concrete picture to carry through the chapter. It is deliberately small, and every abstract object introduced below will be pointed back to it.

Remark. The plaque psoriasis network (running example). Suppose a health technology assessment (HTA) body must choose between two active drugs for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis: treatment \(B\), a new interleukin-17 (IL-17) inhibitor, and treatment \(C\), an established competitor. The outcome is PASI 75, a binary success indicator equal to \(1\) if a patient achieves a \(75\%\) reduction in the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index by week 12 and \(0\) otherwise. No trial compares \(B\) against \(C\) directly. Instead:

an IPD trial randomizes patients to placebo \(A\) and the new drug \(B\), and reports every patient’s covariates and outcome, including whether the patient is biologic-naive (has never taken a biologic drug) or biologic-experienced;
an AgD trial randomizes patients to placebo \(A\) and the competitor \(C\), but reports only arm-level summaries: how many patients in each arm achieved PASI 75, the arm sizes, and the mean and standard deviation of the covariates.

The analyst wants the relative effect of \(B\) versus \(C\) in a chosen target population. This is the anchored indirect comparison of Part III (both trials share the placebo anchor \(A\)), now with a mix of individual and aggregate evidence. Two features of the outcome drive everything. First, PASI 75 response depends on covariates: biologic-naive patients respond more often, and the IL-17 inhibitor \(B\) works especially well in them, so biologic-naive status is an effect modifier of the \(B\)-versus-placebo contrast. Second, because the outcome is binary, the natural model is logistic regression, whose link is nonlinear; and it is exactly on a nonlinear link that “average the patients, then predict” and “predict at the average patient” come apart. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Why insist on a population-averaged (marginal) answer rather than the effect at some typical patient? Because that is what the decision maker buys. An HTA body reimburses a drug for a whole target population and wants the average response it will produce there; it does not want the response of a hypothetical patient whose every covariate sits exactly at the population mean, a patient who may not exist. The estimand of interest is therefore the marginal effect in the target population, and the central technical question of this chapter is how to compute an arm’s marginal response from an individual-level model. (The choice of target population, and the precise estimand, are the subject of Chapter 23; here the target is simply each AgD study’s own population.)
What ML-NMR does with the two trials is asymmetric, and the asymmetry is the whole method. For the IPD trial it uses each patient one at a time: it reads that patient’s covariates, forms the predicted response, and compares it with the observed outcome. For the AgD trial it cannot do this, because it never sees an individual patient’s covariates; it sees only that (say) \(37\) of \(100\) patients on arm \(C\) responded, together with the arm’s covariate summaries. So it must predict the arm’s average response, and the correct average is obtained by running the individual model across the whole spread of covariates in that arm and averaging the predictions. That spread of covariates is the study’s case mix, written \(f_j\) below. For the AgD trial the case mix is not observed patient-by-patient; it is reconstructed from the reported means, standard deviations, and (where available) correlations. We treat that reconstruction as given for now and return to it in Chapter 22; the reader should simply hold the picture that \(f_j\) is “the distribution of patient types in study \(j\).”
By the end of the chapter we will compute, for a single AgD study of this kind, that plugging the mean covariate into the logistic model reports a \(B\)-versus-\(C\) odds ratio inflated by about \(8\%\) relative to the correct integrated value, a distortion produced entirely by predicting at the average patient instead of averaging over patients. Everything between here and there is the machinery that makes that statement precise and general.

title: 20  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression I: The Aggregation Principle
section: 20.3 The network and its covariate distributions
text:
20.3 The network and its covariate distributions
We fix the data structure for the whole of Part V.

Remark. The mixed network. A network comprises \(J\) studies indexed by \(j\) and \(K\) treatments indexed by \(k\). Study \(j\) randomizes patients to a subset of the treatments (its arms); we write \(k\) for an arm and reuse \(k\) for the treatment given on that arm, the network being connected in the sense of Chapter 15 so that every treatment is reachable. Each study is one of two kinds. An IPD study reports, for every patient \(i\) on arm \(k\), the baseline covariate vector \(\mathbf x_{ijk}\in\mathbb R^d\), the arm, and the outcome \(Y_{ijk}\). An AgD study reports only summaries: arm sizes \(n_{jk}\), an outcome summary per arm (an event count, a sample mean, a Kaplan-Meier curve), and enough covariate information to pin down a covariate distribution, typically the per-covariate means and standard deviations and, with luck, a correlation matrix. The covariate distribution of study \(j\) is a probability density \(f_j\) on the covariate space \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), with distribution function \(F_j\), mean \(\bar{\mathbf x}_j=\int_{\mathcal X}\mathbf x\,f_j(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x\), and covariance \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\). For an IPD study \(f_j\) is the empirical distribution of the observed covariates, known exactly; for an AgD study \(f_j\) must be reconstructed from the reported marginal summaries and a dependence assumption, the construction we postpone to Chapter 22. Discrete covariates replace the density \(f_j\) by a probability mass function and the integral by a sum throughout, with no change to any statement of this chapter. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The phrase “covariate distribution of a study” deserves a word, because it is where ML-NMR parts company with the per-patient potential-outcomes language of Part II. We treat the covariate vector of a randomly drawn patient in study \(j\) as a random variable \(X\) with law \(f_j\), and we treat the outcome model as fixed across the network. The randomness in an AgD summary then has two sources: the sampling of covariates from \(f_j\) and the conditional sampling of outcomes given covariates. Integrating out the first source is precisely the aggregation operation. We make this explicit now.

Remark. What is known about \(f_j\), and what is reconstructed. For an IPD study \(f_j\) is not modeled at all: it is the observed empirical distribution of the covariates, so any average against \(f_j\) is just a sample average over the actual patients. For an AgD study \(f_j\) is a genuine modeling assumption. A trial that reports only the mean and standard deviation of age and of body-mass index pins down each covariate’s marginal distribution (often taken normal, or a suitable bounded law), but says nothing about how the covariates co-vary. To get the joint case mix \(f_j\) one must supply the missing dependence, typically by assuming a Gaussian copula (Chapter 22) with a correlation borrowed from the IPD study or from external data, for instance a correlation of \(0.3\) between age and body-mass index. This is real modeling with real uncertainty, and it is the price an AgD study pays for not releasing its patients. We carry \(f_j\) as given throughout this chapter and treat its construction, and the sensitivity of the answer to it, in Chapter 22. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 20  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression I: The Aggregation Principle
text:
20.4 The individual-level model
The model is the IPD network meta-regression of Chapter 17 written for an arbitrary number of studies and treatments. Its only novelty relative to that chapter is the use to which we put it: it will be the common model from which both IPD and AgD likelihoods descend.

Definition 20.1 (The ML-NMR individual-level model) Fix a link function \(g\) (Definition 7.2) with inverse \(g^{-1}\). For individual \(i\) in study \(j\) on arm \(k\) with covariate vector \(\mathbf x\in\mathcal X\), the individual-level model specifies the conditional mean outcome \(\theta_{ijk}=\mathbb E[Y_{ijk}\mid X=\mathbf x,\,\text{arm }k]\) through the linear predictor \[
g(\theta_{ijk})=\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)
:=\mu_j+\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}+\gamma_k ,
\tag{20.1}\] where \[
\mu_j\ \text{is the study-}j\text{ baseline},\quad
\boldsymbol\beta_1\ \text{prognostic main effects},\quad
\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\ \text{effect-modifier interactions},\quad
\gamma_k\ \text{the treatment effect},
\] subject to the reference-treatment constraints \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,1}=\mathbf 0\) and \(\gamma_1=0\) for the network reference treatment \(k=1\). Conditional on the covariate and the arm, outcomes are drawn independently from an outcome family \(\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}\) (the conditional distribution of the outcome given its mean; for PASI 75 this is the Bernoulli or binomial law, for a count the Poisson, for a continuous measurement the normal) with mean \(\theta_{ijk}\) and possible dispersion parameter \(\boldsymbol\phi\), \[
Y_{ijk}\mid X=\mathbf x,\ \text{arm }k\ \sim\ \pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}\!\big(g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)),\,\boldsymbol\phi\big).
\] The full parameter vector is \(\boldsymbol\xi=\big(\{\mu_j\}_{j=1}^J,\ \boldsymbol\beta_1,\ \{\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\}_{k=2}^K,\ \{\gamma_k\}_{k=2}^K,\ \boldsymbol\phi\big)\). We write \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}:=\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\) for the total covariate slope on arm \(k\), so that \(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)=\mu_j+\gamma_k+\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\) is affine in \(\mathbf x\) (affine means linear plus a constant: a straight-line function of \(\mathbf x\), with no squared or self-interaction terms, so that its average equals its value at the average covariate). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reading the four terms. The decomposition Equation 20.1 is the GLM linear predictor of Definition 7.2 organized by causal role. The baseline \(\mu_j\) is a study-specific intercept; it absorbs the prognostic level of study \(j\) and is treated either as a free fixed effect or, in a random-effects version, as exchangeable across studies (Definition 8.3, Definition 8.1). The prognostic slope \(\boldsymbol\beta_1\) multiplies the covariate the same way on every arm: it shifts the outcome level but cancels from any within-study contrast, so it is not an effect modifier. The interaction \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\) multiplies the covariate differently across arms: it bends the conditional treatment contrast and is therefore the effect modification of Definition 11.3. The treatment effect \(\gamma_k\) is the arm-\(k\)-versus-reference contrast at \(\mathbf x=\mathbf 0\). The shared effect modifier assumption (Definition 17.6) is the structural hypothesis \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\) shared across the treatments being compared; it is what makes the network identifiable from a mix of IPD and AgD, a matter we take up in Chapter 23. The whole apparatus reduces to standard network meta-analysis when \(\boldsymbol\beta_1=\mathbf 0\) and every \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\mathbf 0\), and to IPD network meta-regression when every study reports IPD; both reductions are proved in Chapter 23. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Clinical translation of the model terms. For the running example, with the single covariate \(x=\) biologic-naive status, the four terms read as follows.








Symbol
Name
Plain meaning in the running example




\(\mu_j\)
study baseline
log-odds of PASI 75 in study \(j\) for a placebo patient at \(\mathbf x=\mathbf 0\)


\(\gamma_k\)
treatment effect
how much arm \(k\) shifts the log-odds versus placebo, at \(\mathbf x=\mathbf 0\)


\(\boldsymbol\beta_1\)
prognostic effect
how biologic-naive status shifts response the same way on every arm


\(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\)
effect modification
how biologic-naive status shifts the benefit of arm \(k\) specifically


\(f_j\)
case mix
the fraction of biologic-naive versus experienced patients in study \(j\)



The distinction between the two slopes is the whole reason effect modification matters. Suppose biologic-naive patients respond better whatever they take: that is a prognostic effect, carried by \(\boldsymbol\beta_1\), and it raises both arms equally, so it cancels from the \(B\)-minus-placebo contrast. Now suppose instead that being biologic-naive makes the IL-17 inhibitor \(B\) work even better than it makes placebo look: that is effect modification, carried by \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}\), and it does not cancel from the contrast. A study with more biologic-naive patients will then report a larger \(B\)-versus-placebo effect, purely through its case mix. That is why an indirect comparison across studies with different case mixes needs the covariate model at all.
The constraints \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,1}=\mathbf 0\) and \(\gamma_1=0\) are identifiability conventions, not clinical claims. They fix the reference treatment \(k=1\) as the origin against which the others are measured, exactly as a regression with a categorical predictor drops one level as its baseline. They do not assert that the reference treatment has no biological effect or no effect modification; they only say that the other treatments are measured relative to it. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This is result H.1 of the proof catalogue (corresponds to H.1; Phillippo et al. 2020, Eq. 2; Phillippo 2019, Eq. 4.1b).

Remark. Why a shared effect modifier assumption is needed (preview). The interaction \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\) is the one thing an AgD study cannot see directly: an AgD study reports one number per arm, so it cannot reveal how outcome varies with covariate within an arm. Only an IPD study exposes that within-study slope. ML-NMR can still use AgD studies to help estimate effect modification, but only under the shared effect modifier assumption (SEMA, Definition 17.6): the interaction coefficients \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\) are the same across studies, because they attach to the treatment, not to the study. Under SEMA the IPD trial estimates \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}\), and the AgD trial’s case mix \(f_j\) then tells us how much of its reported effect is explained by that same interaction, which is what links the two into one estimable model. If SEMA fails, say the IL-17 inhibitor’s effect modification by biologic-naive status differs between the IPD and AgD populations, then the AgD study’s single summary per arm cannot separate a genuine treatment effect from a case-mix artifact, and the indirect comparison is not identified from aggregate data alone. This is the same identification wall that Chapter 16 hit for standard NMA; ML-NMR does not repeal it, it makes the assumption explicit and testable wherever IPD overlaps. The full identifiability analysis is Chapter 23. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 20  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression I: The Aggregation Principle
text:
20.5 The aggregate-level model
An AgD study reports an arm average, not individual outcomes. The model for that average must be a function of the parameters \(\boldsymbol\xi\) and the study covariate distribution \(f_j\), and the right function is the one that respects the level at which the nonlinearity acts.

Definition 20.2 (The ML-NMR aggregate-level model) For an AgD study \(j\) on arm \(k\) with covariate density \(f_j\), the aggregate-level mean outcome is the average over the covariate distribution of the response-scale conditional mean, \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}:=\int_{\mathcal X} g^{-1}\!\big(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)\big)\,f_j(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x ,
\tag{20.2}\] the bullet subscript \(\bullet\) denoting the average over individuals. Read \(\theta_{\bullet jk}\) as “the dot-mean”: it is the model-predicted arm-level response (an event risk, a mean, or a rate) for study \(j\) and arm \(k\) after averaging over that study’s case mix, and the bullet marks the individual index that has been averaged away. The reported arm summary is modeled by an aggregate outcome family with this mean, \[
\text{summary}_{jk}\ \sim\ \pi_{\mathrm{Agg}}\!\big(\theta_{\bullet jk},\,n_{jk}\big),
\] for example \(\mathrm{Bin}(n_{jk},\theta_{\bullet jk})\) for a binary event count, the appropriate normal law for a continuous sample mean, or a count model for an event rate. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

One statistical point deserves to be said in the main text rather than buried, because most readers meet ML-NMR through binary outcomes. For a binary outcome the arm’s event count is a sum of \(n_{jk}\) patient-level Bernoulli draws whose success probabilities \(g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x_i))\) differ from patient to patient, since the covariates differ. A sum of non-identical Bernoulli variables is a Poisson-binomial random variable (Definition 4.11), not a binomial; the binomial law \(\mathrm{Bin}(n_{jk},\theta_{\bullet jk})\) used in Definition 20.2 therefore replaces those varying probabilities by their common average \(\theta_{\bullet jk}\) and is, strictly, an approximation. It is an excellent approximation when the probabilities do not vary wildly across the arm, and Chapter 21 quantifies exactly when it is safe; we flag it now so the reader knows from the outset that the “right” aggregate law for binary data is not quite the binomial they might expect.

Remark. Integrate the response scale, not the link scale. The single decision that defines ML-NMR is where the inverse link is applied. Equation Equation 20.2 applies \(g^{-1}\) to the linear predictor at each covariate value and then averages; it does not average the linear predictor and then apply \(g^{-1}\). The two operations agree only when \(g^{-1}\) is affine. For every other link they differ by the ecological bias of Definition 16.2, and the order in Equation 20.2 is the order that matches the data-generating process, because the data are generated patient by patient at the response scale and only then summed. The choice of \(\pi_{\mathrm{Agg}}\) is a separate modeling step; for binary outcomes the exact law of the event count is a Poisson binomial (Definition 4.11) rather than a binomial, and the discrepancy and its control are the subject of Chapter 21. In this chapter we study the mean Equation 20.2, which all choices of \(\pi_{\mathrm{Agg}}\) share. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. A first taste of the gap, in one line of arithmetic. Take a single arm of the running example whose patients split evenly into two covariate groups, and suppose the individual model gives a PASI 75 response probability of \(0.60\) for the biologic-naive half and \(0.10\) for the biologic-experienced half. The arm’s true average response is the average of the two risks, \[
\theta_\bullet=\tfrac12(0.60)+\tfrac12(0.10)=0.35 .
\] The naive alternative summarizes the arm by its average log-odds and converts back. The two log-odds are \(\mathrm{logit}(0.60)=0.405\) and \(\mathrm{logit}(0.10)=-2.197\), their average is \(-0.896\), and \[
\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}=\mathrm{expit}(-0.896)=0.290 .
\] The true arm response is \(35\%\); the plug-in reports \(29\%\). The six-percentage-point gap is pure Jensen inequality: averaging on the risk scale is not the same as averaging on the log-odds scale and converting back. This tiny sum is the whole chapter in miniature. The theorems below say when the gap is zero (identity link), when it has a closed form (log link), when it changes sign (logit), and how it distorts a treatment contrast. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Response scale versus link scale, by outcome type. The order-of-operations warning is easiest to hold onto through the three outcome types a reader will actually meet. The response scale is where the outcome lives (a risk, a rate, a mean); the link scale is where the model is linear (log-odds, log-rate, or the mean itself). Aggregation must average on the response scale.

This is result H.2 of the proof catalogue (corresponds to H.2; Phillippo 2019, Eq. 4.1d).

title: 20  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression I: The Aggregation Principle
text:
20.6 The aggregation theorem
We now prove that Equation 20.2 is forced, not chosen: it is the mean of the marginal outcome of an AgD patient, and the AgD likelihood is built from the same integral. The argument is elementary, resting only on the chain rule for densities, Fubini’s theorem (Theorem 4.8), and the tower property (Corollary 4.1), also called the law of iterated expectations, but it is the load-bearing identity of the whole method.
In words, before the symbols: imagine for a moment that we could see every patient in the AgD arm. We would evaluate each patient’s conditional response from the individual model, and their likelihood contributions would simply multiply, exactly as for an IPD study. We cannot see them; we see only the arm summary. The theorem says that averaging the individual model over the plausible covariate values, weighted by the case mix \(f_j\), reproduces precisely the marginal law of one such unseen patient, and hence the arm summary. Two consequences follow, and they are why the theorem is worth proving. The arm’s mean is the integral Equation 20.2 (part (b)), and the arm’s likelihood is built from that same integral (part (c)). Any other rule for turning the individual model into an arm prediction, in particular the plug-in rule of the next section, would be inconsistent with this data-generating process and would bias the estimated treatment effects. That is the sense in which the integral is forced, not chosen.

Theorem 20.1 (Aggregation theorem) Adopt the individual-level model Equation 20.1, and suppose that within study \(j\) the covariate vector \(X\) of a randomly drawn patient has law \(f_j\) and that, conditional on \(X=\mathbf x\) and arm \(k\), the outcome \(Y\) has the family \(\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)),\boldsymbol\phi)\) with conditional density or mass function \(L_{i\mid x}(\boldsymbol\xi;y,\mathbf x):=\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y\mid g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)),\boldsymbol\phi)\). Then:
(a) Marginal individual likelihood. The outcome of a patient whose covariate is not observed (the AgD case) has marginal density or mass function \[
L_i(\boldsymbol\xi;y)=\int_{\mathcal X} L_{i\mid x}(\boldsymbol\xi;y,\mathbf x)\,f_j(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x .
\tag{20.3}\]
(b) Aggregate mean. The marginal mean outcome of an AgD patient on arm \(k\) in study \(j\) is the integral Equation 20.2, \[
\mathbb E[Y_{ijk}]=\int_{\mathcal X} g^{-1}\!\big(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)\big)\,f_j(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x=\theta_{\bullet jk}.
\tag{20.4}\]
(c) Aggregate likelihood. If the \(n_{jk}\) patients of arm \(k\) in study \(j\) have independent covariate draws from \(f_j\) and conditionally independent outcomes \(\mathbf y_{jk}=(y_{1jk},\dots,y_{n_{jk}jk})\), their joint marginal likelihood factors, \[
\bar L_{jk}(\boldsymbol\xi;\mathbf y_{jk})=\prod_{i=1}^{n_{jk}} L_i(\boldsymbol\xi;y_{ijk}),
\tag{20.5}\] and when only a summary statistic of \(\mathbf y_{jk}\) is reported, the likelihood of that summary is its law under the aggregate family \(\pi_{\mathrm{Agg}}(\theta_{\bullet jk},n_{jk})\) of Definition 20.2.


Proof. (a). By the chain rule for densities the joint density of \((Y,X)\) for an AgD patient on arm \(k\) factors as the product of the conditional density of \(Y\) given \(X\) and the marginal density of \(X\), \[
p(y,\mathbf x\mid\boldsymbol\xi)=p(y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\xi)\,f_j(\mathbf x)
=L_{i\mid x}(\boldsymbol\xi;y,\mathbf x)\,f_j(\mathbf x).
\] The marginal density of \(Y\) is obtained by integrating out \(\mathbf x\), \[
L_i(\boldsymbol\xi;y)=\int_{\mathcal X} p(y,\mathbf x\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\,d\mathbf x
=\int_{\mathcal X} L_{i\mid x}(\boldsymbol\xi;y,\mathbf x)\,f_j(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x,
\] which is Equation 20.3. The integrand is nonnegative and jointly measurable, so by the Tonelli half of Theorem 4.8 the integral is well defined and \(L_i(\boldsymbol\xi;\cdot)\) is a genuine density: integrating it over \(y\) and exchanging the order of integration, \(\int_y\int_{\mathbf x} L_{i\mid x}f_j
=\int_{\mathbf x}\big(\int_y L_{i\mid x}\,dy\big)f_j=\int_{\mathbf x} 1\cdot f_j=1\), since each conditional law \(L_{i\mid x}(\boldsymbol\xi;\cdot,\mathbf x)\) integrates to one.
(b). By the model the conditional mean is \(\mathbb E[Y\mid X=\mathbf x]=g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x))\). The tower property (Corollary 4.1) gives \[
\mathbb E[Y_{ijk}]=\mathbb E\big[\,\mathbb E[Y\mid X]\,\big]
=\mathbb E\big[g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(X))\big]
=\int_{\mathcal X} g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x))\,f_j(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x=\theta_{\bullet jk},
\] the last equality being the definition of expectation under \(f_j\). Equivalently, multiply Equation 20.3 by \(y\) and integrate, exchanging the order of integration by the Fubini half of Theorem 4.8 (legitimate whenever \(\mathbb E|Y|<\infty\), which holds for every outcome family used in practice): \(\int_y y\,L_i(\boldsymbol\xi;y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbf x}\big(\int_y y\,L_{i\mid x}\,dy\big)f_j
=\int_{\mathbf x} g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x))\,f_j(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x\), the inner integral being the conditional mean. This is Equation 20.4.
(c). Conditional on \(\boldsymbol\xi\), distinct patients have independent covariate draws and conditionally independent outcomes, so the pairs \((Y_{ijk},X_{ijk})\) are mutually independent; independence is preserved under the marginalization of part (a), because a function (here the marginal density) of independent random variables computed coordinatewise yields independent marginals. Hence the joint marginal density of \(\mathbf y_{jk}\) is the product Equation 20.5. If the data reduce to a summary statistic \(T(\mathbf y_{jk})\), its likelihood is by definition the density or mass of \(T\) under the joint law; modeling that law by \(\pi_{\mathrm{Agg}}(\theta_{\bullet jk},n_{jk})\), whose mean is \(\theta_{\bullet jk}\) by part (b), is the aggregate-level model of Definition 20.2. \(\square\)


Remark. Why this is the defining identity. Part (b) is the sentence “the aggregate mean is the integral of the inverse link against the covariate density,” and it is the whole content of ML-NMR’s coherence claim. An IPD study evaluates Equation 20.1 at each observed \(\mathbf x_{ijk}\) and needs no integral; an AgD study evaluates the integral Equation 20.2 against \(f_j\). Both feed the same parameters \(\boldsymbol\xi\) into one likelihood, the product over studies of Equation 20.5 and the IPD analogue. The price of admission is the integral, and the rest of Part V is the study of how to compute it: in closed form when the link and covariate distribution permit (the next three sections), and by numerical integration when they do not (Chapter 22). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This is result H.3 of the proof catalogue (corresponds to H.3; Phillippo 2019, Eq. 4.1c; Phillippo et al. 2020, Section 3).

Remark. IPD and AgD contributions, side by side. Make the two likelihood contributions concrete on the running example. Suppose the AgD trial reports that \(37\) of the \(100\) patients on its competitor arm \(C\) achieved PASI 75. ML-NMR models that count with the aggregate law of Definition 20.2, \(\mathrm{Bin}(100,\theta_{\bullet
jC})\), where the single arm-level risk \(\theta_{\bullet jC}\) is itself the case-mix average Equation 20.2 of the individual risks \(\mathrm{expit}(\eta_{jC}(\mathbf x))\) over that arm’s covariate distribution \(f_j\). Contrast the IPD trial: there a patient with observed covariate \(\mathbf x_i\) on arm \(B\) contributes the conditional Bernoulli factor \(\mathrm{expit}(\eta_{jB}(\mathbf x_i))^{y_i}\big(1-\mathrm{expit}(\eta_{jB}(\mathbf x_i))\big)^{1-y_i}\), with no integral, because the covariate is known. The two study types thus differ only in whether the covariate is integrated out: IPD conditions on each observed \(\mathbf x_i\); AgD integrates over the unseen ones. Both feed the same coefficients \(\mu_j,\gamma_k,\boldsymbol\beta_1,\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\). One point of possible confusion: parts (a) and (c) wrote a per-patient marginal likelihood \(L_i\) for the AgD arm even though we never observe an individual AgD patient. That is a derivational device. Writing the per-patient marginal first makes the arm-summary likelihood, the thing we actually fit, drop out cleanly from the independence in part (c). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reduction to standard network meta-analysis (the bridge from Chapter 15). A reader arriving from Chapter 15 can see the old model sitting inside this one. Set \(\boldsymbol\beta_1=\mathbf 0\) and every \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\mathbf 0\), so there are no covariate terms. Then \(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)=\mu_j+\gamma_k\) does not depend on \(\mathbf x\), the integral Equation 20.2 has a constant integrand, and \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\int_{\mathcal X} g^{-1}(\mu_j+\gamma_k)\,f_j(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x=g^{-1}(\mu_j+\gamma_k),
\] with no dependence on \(f_j\) at all. The aggregate likelihood Equation 20.5 then reduces to the standard network meta-analysis likelihood with study baselines \(\mu_j\) and treatment effects \(\gamma_k\): aggregation does nothing, because there is nothing to average over. Consequently aggregation bias vanishes identically here for every link, consistent with Theorem 20.2 below (the linear predictor is degenerate, \(\mathrm{Var}(\eta_{jk}(X))=0\)). Standard NMA is thus the covariate-free corner of ML-NMR; the full statement, including the reduction to IPD network meta-regression, is Chapter 23. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 20  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression I: The Aggregation Principle
text:
20.7 The aggregation-bias theorem
The temptation, and the practice of pre-ML-NMR meta-regression, is to skip the integral and feed the model the study mean covariate. We now show exactly what that costs. Define the plug-in (naive) aggregate mean \[
\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}:=g^{-1}\!\big(\eta_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf x}_j)\big),
\qquad
\bar{\mathbf x}_j=\int_{\mathcal X}\mathbf x\,f_j(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x ,
\tag{20.6}\] the inverse link evaluated at the linear predictor of the mean covariate. Because \(\eta_{jk}\) is affine, linearity of expectation gives \(\eta_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf x}_j)=\mathbb E[\eta_{jk}(X)]\), so \(\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}=g^{-1}\big(\mathbb E[\eta_{jk}(X)]\big)\) is the inverse link of the average linear predictor, whereas the correct \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=\mathbb E\big[g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(X))\big]\) is the average of the inverse link. Jensen’s inequality is the precise statement of their difference. It is worth naming the two objects clearly, because the whole chapter turns on keeping them apart: the plug-in is a conditional prediction (the response at one covariate value, namely the mean) wearing the costume of an arm summary, whereas the integral is the genuinely marginal prediction (the response averaged over the arm’s case mix). “Marginal over \(f_j\)” and “conditional at a covariate value” are different quantities on any curved link, and ML-NMR’s target estimand is the marginal one while the model is written conditionally.

Theorem 20.2 (Aggregation bias) Let \(\eta_{jk}(X)\) be the linear predictor evaluated at the random covariate \(X\sim f_j\), with \(\bar{\mathbf x}_j=\mathbb E[X]\), and suppose \(g^{-1}\) is convex or concave on an interval containing the support of \(\eta_{jk}(X)\). Then the plug-in and integrated aggregate means Equation 20.6 and Equation 20.2 satisfy \[
\begin{aligned}
g^{-1}\ \text{convex on the support}&:\quad \theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\ \le\ \theta_{\bullet jk},\\
g^{-1}\ \text{concave on the support}&:\quad \theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\ \ge\ \theta_{\bullet jk},
\end{aligned}
\tag{20.7}\] and the inequality is an equality if and only if either \(g^{-1}\) is affine on the support of \(\eta_{jk}(X)\) or \(\eta_{jk}(X)\) is degenerate, the latter meaning \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}=0\). The signed discrepancy is exactly the ecological bias of Definition 16.2, \[
\mathrm{EB}_{jk}:=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}-\theta_{\bullet jk}
=g^{-1}\!\big(\eta_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf x}_j)\big)-\int_{\mathcal X} g^{-1}\!\big(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)\big)f_j(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x .
\tag{20.8}\]


Proof. Apply Jensen’s inequality (Theorem 4.6) with the convex function \(\varphi=g^{-1}\) and the integrable random variable \(W:=\eta_{jk}(X)\). The inequality reads \(\varphi(\mathbb E[W])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(W)]\), that is \(g^{-1}(\mathbb E[\eta_{jk}(X)])\le\mathbb E[g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(X))]\). By the affine identity \(\mathbb E[\eta_{jk}(X)]=\eta_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf x}_j)\) the left side is \(\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\) and by Equation 20.2 the right side is \(\theta_{\bullet jk}\), which is the convex case of Equation 20.7. If \(g^{-1}\) is concave then \(-g^{-1}\) is convex and the same argument applied to \(-g^{-1}\) reverses the inequality, giving the concave case.
For the equality case, the strict form of Theorem 4.6 states that for a strictly convex \(\varphi\) the inequality is strict unless \(W\) is almost surely constant. Decompose: if \(g^{-1}\) is affine on the support, then \(g^{-1}(w)=a+bw\) there and \(\mathbb E[g^{-1}(W)]=a+b\,\mathbb E[W]=g^{-1}(\mathbb E[W])\), an equality; this is the degenerate-curvature case. Otherwise \(g^{-1}\) is strictly convex (or strictly concave) on a subinterval that \(W\) charges with positive probability, and then equality forces \(W\) to be almost surely constant, that is \(\eta_{jk}(X)=\eta_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf x}_j)\) almost surely. Since \(\eta_{jk}\) is affine with slope \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\), this says \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top(X-\bar{\mathbf x}_j)=0\) almost surely, equivalently \(\mathrm{Var}(\eta_{jk}(X))=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}=0\), which is the stated degeneracy. The identity Equation 20.8 is Equation 20.6 minus Equation 20.2 and coincides termwise with the ecological-bias formula Equation 16.8 of Definition 16.2. \(\square\)


Remark. This is the resolution of Theorem 16.1. Chapter 16 diagnosed the bias of the unadjusted indirect comparison as a difference of population-averaged conditional contrasts that did not cancel (Theorem 16.1), and named the arm-level residue the ecological bias (Definition 16.2). Theorem Theorem 20.2 shows that the residue is exactly the gap between plugging in the mean and integrating, and Theorem 20.1 shows that ML-NMR closes the gap by doing the integral Equation 20.2 rather than approximating it. MAIC and STC attack the same gap by other means: MAIC’s first-moment matching (Theorem 18.1) makes \(\bar{\mathbf x}\) agree across populations but leaves the within-population curvature gap untouched unless higher moments are matched too, and STC’s mean-covariate prediction is precisely the plug-in Equation 20.6 unless the regression is centered and integrated (Theorem 19.3). ML-NMR is the systematic cure because it never plugs in. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why this matters for an indirect comparison. A reader might shrug at an arm-level bias of a percentage point or two. The point is that an indirect comparison is a contrast of arm means, and the biases need not cancel. Each arm has its own total slope \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\), sits at its own mean linear predictor \(m_k\), and therefore lives in its own curvature region of \(g^{-1}\); on the logit link one arm can be in the convex region and the other in the concave region, so the plug-in underestimates one arm and overestimates the other. When we subtract to form the treatment contrast, the two biases add rather than cancel. A small, innocuous-looking error in each arm becomes a systematic distortion of the exact quantity the HTA body is deciding on. The worked example Example 20.1 makes this concrete: two arm-level biases of about \(1\%\) combine into an \(8\%\) inflation of the odds ratio. This is the practical reason ML-NMR integrates rather than plugs in. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The qualitative sign in Equation 20.7 is sharpened to a quantity by a second-order expansion, which we will use to predict the bias in the worked example and to read off the closed-form cases that follow.

20.7.1 The leading-order bias
The next lemma is the workhorse of the chapter: it converts the qualitative sign of the bias into a number, proportional to the variance of the linear predictor, and it is exactly what the log and logit results below specialize. A reader in a hurry can take away one sentence: the aggregation bias is, to leading order, half the curvature of the inverse link times the variance of the linear predictor.

Lemma 20.1 (Leading-order aggregation bias) Suppose \(g^{-1}\) is three times continuously differentiable with bounded third derivative on a neighborhood of \(m:=\eta_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf x}_j)\), and write \(v:=\mathrm{Var}(\eta_{jk}(X))=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\) for the variance of the linear predictor. Then, as the covariate distribution concentrates so that \(v\to 0\) with the standardized linear predictor having bounded third absolute moment, \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}=g^{-1}(m)+\tfrac12\,(g^{-1})''(m)\,v+o(v),
\qquad
\theta_{\bullet jk}-\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}=\tfrac12\,(g^{-1})''(m)\,v+o(v).
\tag{20.9}\] In particular the integrated mean exceeds the plug-in mean to leading order exactly where \(g^{-1}\) is convex (\((g^{-1})''(m)>0\)), in agreement with Theorem 20.2, and the leading bias is proportional to the variance of the linear predictor, which is the quadratic form \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\) in the total slope.


Proof. Write \(\eta_{jk}(X)=m+\sqrt v\,U\), where \(U:=(\eta_{jk}(X)-m)/\sqrt v\) has mean \(0\) and variance \(1\); this is legitimate because \(\mathbb E[\eta_{jk}(X)]=m\) by the affine identity. Taylor’s theorem with Lagrange remainder gives, for some \(\zeta\) between \(m\) and \(\eta_{jk}(X)\), \[
g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(X))=g^{-1}(m)+(g^{-1})'(m)\,\sqrt v\,U+\tfrac12 (g^{-1})''(m)\,v\,U^2+\tfrac16 (g^{-1})'''(\zeta)\,v^{3/2}U^3 .
\] Take expectations. The linear term vanishes because \(\mathbb E[U]=0\); the quadratic term gives \(\tfrac12(g^{-1})''(m)\,v\) because \(\mathbb E[U^2]=1\); and the remainder is bounded in absolute value by \(\tfrac16\big(\sup|(g^{-1})'''|\big)\,v^{3/2}\,\mathbb E|U|^3\), which is \(O(v^{3/2})=o(v)\) under the bounded third-moment hypothesis. Hence \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=\mathbb E[g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(X))]=g^{-1}(m)+\tfrac12(g^{-1})''(m)v+o(v)\). Subtracting \(\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}=g^{-1}(m)\) gives the second display. \(\square\)

This refinement and Theorem 20.2 are result H.4 of the proof catalogue (corresponds to H.4; Phillippo 2019, Eq. 4.8).

title: 20  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression I: The Aggregation Principle
section: 20.8 A unifying view: aggregation is heat flow
text:
20.8 A unifying view: aggregation is heat flow

Remark. Optional section; read it for insight, skip it to keep moving. This section is structural insight, not machinery you need in order to fit or interpret an ML-NMR model. A reader who wants the method can jump straight to Section 20.9 and lose nothing operationally. The payoff for staying is a single organizing picture that answers a question the next three sections would otherwise raise one at a time: why do the identity, log, and probit links keep closed-form aggregate means while the logit does not? The answer is that averaging a function against a normal distribution is the same operation as letting heat diffuse for a moment, and only some functions stay simple under diffusion. The same picture tells you the sign of the aggregation bias at a glance and reproduces the leading-order expansion of the previous section as the first instant of the flow. None of this is required; it is the “one picture for three theorems,” offered for the reader who wants to see the unity. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Before specializing to the three links, we record the structural fact that ties their closed-form behavior together. When the linear predictor is normally distributed, which by the affine-image theorem (Theorem 4.14) happens exactly when the covariates are jointly normal, the integrated aggregate mean is the inverse link smoothed by Gaussian convolution (each value of the inverse link is replaced by a normal-weighted average of its nearby values), and Gaussian convolution is the heat semigroup (the operation that evolves a temperature profile forward in time under the heat equation). The three links then differ only in whether the heat flow of the inverse link is elementary.

Lemma 20.2 (The aggregate mean is a heat flow of the inverse link) Let \(\psi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be measurable with \(|\psi(z)|\le Ce^{a|z|}\) for some constants \(C,a\), and suppose \(\psi\) is twice continuously differentiable with \(|\psi'|,|\psi''|\le C e^{a|z|}\). For \(\eta\sim\mathcal N(m,\tau)\) with \(\tau\ge 0\) define \[
u(m,\tau):=\mathbb E[\psi(\eta)]=\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(z)\,\phi(z;m,\tau)\,dz,
\] where \(\phi(\cdot;m,\tau)\) is the \(\mathcal N(m,\tau)\) density. Then \(u\) solves the heat equation \[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial \tau}=\frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial m^2},
\qquad
\lim_{\tau\downarrow 0} u(m,\tau)=\psi(m),
\tag{20.10}\] so that \(u(\cdot,\tau)=e^{(\tau/2)\,\partial_m^2}\psi\) is the inverse link diffused for “time” \(\tau\) equal to the variance of the linear predictor. Consequently, if the covariates in study \(j\) are jointly normal, \(X\sim\mathcal N(\bar{\mathbf x}_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)\), then with \(\psi=g^{-1}\), \(m=\eta_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf x}_j)\), and \(\tau=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\), the aggregate mean is \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=u(m,\tau)\).


Proof. The \(\mathcal N(m,\tau)\) density is a translate of the heat kernel: writing \(G(\xi,\tau)=(2\pi\tau)^{-1/2}
\exp(-\xi^2/2\tau)\) we have \(\phi(z;m,\tau)=G(z-m,\tau)\), and a direct differentiation verifies that \(G\) solves \(\partial_\tau G=\tfrac12\partial_\xi^2 G\) on \(\tau>0\). Indeed \(\partial_\tau G=G\big(-\tfrac1{2\tau}+\tfrac{\xi^2}{2\tau^2}\big)\) and \(\partial_\xi G=-\tfrac{\xi}{\tau}G\), so \(\partial_\xi^2 G=\big(\tfrac{\xi^2}{\tau^2}-\tfrac1\tau\big)G
=2\partial_\tau G\). Because \(G(z-m,\tau)\) depends on \(m\) and \(z\) only through \(z-m\), we have \(\partial_m\phi=-\partial_z\phi\) and hence \(\partial_m^2\phi=\partial_z^2\phi\), while \(\partial_\tau\phi=\tfrac12\partial_z^2\phi=\tfrac12\partial_m^2\phi\). Therefore, differentiating under the integral sign, \[
\partial_\tau u=\int\psi(z)\,\partial_\tau\phi\,dz=\tfrac12\int\psi(z)\,\partial_m^2\phi\,dz=\tfrac12\,\partial_m^2 u,
\] which is Equation 20.10. The differentiations under the integral are justified by dominated convergence: the \(m\)- and \(\tau\)-derivatives of \(\phi(z;m,\tau)\) are \(\phi\) times polynomials in \((z-m)/\tau\), and the growth bound \(|\psi(z)|\le Ce^{a|z|}\) times such a Gaussian-with-polynomial factor is integrable and locally bounded uniformly in \((m,\tau)\) on compact subsets of \(\{\tau>0\}\), by completing the square in the exponent. For the initial condition, substitute \(z=m+\sqrt\tau\,s\) to write \(u(m,\tau)=\int\psi(m+\sqrt\tau\,s)\,\phi(s;0,1)\,ds\); as \(\tau\downarrow0\) the integrand converges pointwise to \(\psi(m)\phi(s;0,1)\) and is dominated by \(C e^{a|m|}e^{a\sqrt\tau|s|}\phi(s;0,1)\le C'e^{a|m|}(e^{as}+e^{-as})\phi(s;0,1)\) for \(\tau\le1\), an integrable bound, so dominated convergence gives \(u(m,\tau)\to\psi(m)\int\phi(s;0,1)ds=\psi(m)\). The final claim is the affine-image theorem (Theorem 4.14): for \(X\sim\mathcal N(\bar{\mathbf x}_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)\) the scalar \(\eta_{jk}(X)=\mu_j+\gamma_k+X^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\) is normal with mean \(\eta_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf x}_j)=m\) and variance \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}=\tau\), so \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=\mathbb E[g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(X))]=u(m,\tau)\). \(\square\)


Remark. One picture for three theorems. The heat-flow view organizes the rest of the chapter. The variance \(\tau\) plays the role of time: at \(\tau=0\) (a degenerate covariate distribution, all mass at \(\bar{\mathbf x}_j\)) there is no diffusion and \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=g^{-1}(m)=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\), no aggregation bias; as \(\tau\) grows the inverse link is smoothed and the bias accumulates. The leading-order expansion Equation 20.9 is the first step of the heat flow, \(u\approx\psi+\tfrac{\tau}{2}\psi''\). The identity link is the fixed point of the flow (\(\psi''=0\)); the log link is an eigen-type orbit on which the flow stays exponential; the probit link is carried by the flow to a rescaled probit; and the logit link is carried to a function with no elementary name. We take these in turn. \(\blacktriangleleft\)
