title: 20  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression I: The Aggregation Principle
text:
20.9 The identity link: exact aggregation
On the identity scale the inverse link is the identity map, which is affine, so the equality case of Theorem 20.2 holds for every covariate distribution, not only the normal one. This is the one link on which ML-NMR needs no integral.

Theorem 20.3 (Exactness of identity-link aggregation) Suppose \(g\) is the identity link, \(g^{-1}(z)=z\). Then for every study covariate distribution \(f_j\) with mean \(\bar{\mathbf x}_j\), the integrated and plug-in aggregate means coincide and equal the linear predictor at the mean covariate, \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\int_{\mathcal X}\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)\,f_j(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x
=\mu_j+\gamma_k+\bar{\mathbf x}_j^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}
=\eta_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf x}_j)=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk},
\tag{20.11}\] so the aggregation bias Equation 20.8 vanishes identically. Conversely, if a link makes \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\) for every covariate distribution supported on an open set, then \(g^{-1}\) is affine on that set.


Proof. For the identity link \(g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x))=\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)\), so Equation 20.2 reads \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=\int\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)f_j(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x=\mathbb E[\eta_{jk}(X)]\). Since \(\eta_{jk}\) is affine, linearity of expectation gives \(\mathbb E[\eta_{jk}(X)]=\mu_j+\gamma_k+\mathbb E[X]^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}=\eta_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf x}_j)\), which is Equation 20.11; the plug-in Equation 20.6 is the same quantity, so \(\mathrm{EB}_{jk}=0\).
For the converse, suppose \(g^{-1}(\mathbb E[W])=\mathbb E[g^{-1}(W)]\) for \(W=\eta_{jk}(X)\) under every covariate law on an open set, equivalently \(\psi(\mathbb E[W])=\mathbb E[\psi(W)]\) for \(\psi=g^{-1}\) and every law of \(W\) on the open interval \(I:=\eta_{jk}(\text{open set})\). Take \(W\) to put mass \(\tfrac12\) at each of two points \(w_1,w_2\in I\); then the identity reads \(\psi\big(\tfrac{w_1+w_2}{2}\big)=\tfrac12\psi(w_1)+\tfrac12\psi(w_2)\), which is Jensen’s functional equation (also called the midpoint-affine or Cauchy-Jensen equation): the value at a midpoint equals the average of the values at the two endpoints, for every pair of points. It is a standard fact that a function that is midpoint-affine on an interval and continuous there must be genuinely affine, a straight line \(\psi(w)=a+bw\); continuity is what upgrades the midpoint identity (which on its own only pins down values at dyadic averages) to affinity at every point. Here continuity is free, because \(g\), hence \(g^{-1}\), is \(C^2\) by Definition 7.2. Hence \(\psi=g^{-1}\) is affine on \(I\). \(\square\)


Remark. ML-NMR on the identity scale is meta-regression on means. When Equation 20.11 holds, the aggregate likelihood Equation 20.5 depends on the covariate distribution only through its mean \(\bar{\mathbf x}_j\), and ML-NMR reduces to the familiar network meta-regression that regresses study-level outcomes on study-level mean covariates. This is the precise sense in which the identity scale is benign: there is no within-study aggregation to do, only across-study regression, and the second moments of \(f_j\) are irrelevant. It is also why first-moment matching is exactly sufficient for MAIC on the identity scale, a point flagged in the moment-balance discussion of Chapter 18; the curvature that first-moment matching ignores is present on every other scale and absent on this one. Identity-scale exactness is the friendly exception, not the rule: continuous outcomes summarized by means are often modeled this way, but binary, count, and time-to-event outcomes live on the curved scales of the next two sections. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This is result H.5 of the proof catalogue (corresponds to H.5; Phillippo 2019, Section 4.3.2).

section: 20.10 The log link: a closed form through the moment generating function
text:
20.10 The log link: a closed form through the moment generating function
On the log scale the inverse link is the exponential, which is convex, so by Theorem 20.2 the plug-in mean underestimates the truth. When the covariates are jointly normal the integral Equation 20.2 is the moment generating function of a normal random variable evaluated at \(t=1\), and we computed that transform in closed form in Chapter 4. The result is one of the few exact aggregate means in ML-NMR and underlies the closed-form Poisson aggregate likelihood of Chapter 21.

Theorem 20.4 (Closed-form log-link aggregation under normal covariates) Suppose \(g\) is the log link, \(g^{-1}(z)=e^{z}\), and that the covariates in study \(j\) are jointly normal, \(X\sim\mathcal N(\bar{\mathbf x}_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)\). Then the aggregate mean Equation 20.2 is \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\exp\!\Big(\mu_j+\gamma_k+\bar{\mathbf x}_j^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}
+\tfrac12\,\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\,\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\Big),
\qquad \boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}=\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}.
\tag{20.12}\] Equivalently \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\cdot\exp\!\big(\tfrac12\,\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\big)\), so the plug-in mean is biased downward by the exact multiplicative factor \(e^{\,v/2}\ge 1\) with \(v=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\), with equality only when the total slope \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\) lies in the null space of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\).


Proof. Set \(W:=\eta_{jk}(X)=\mu_j+\gamma_k+X^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\), an affine function of the normal vector \(X\). By the affine-image theorem (Theorem 4.14), \(W\) is univariate normal with mean and variance \[
m:=\mathbb E[W]=\mu_j+\gamma_k+\bar{\mathbf x}_j^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k},
\qquad
v:=\mathrm{Var}(W)=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k},
\] so \(W\sim\mathcal N(m,v)\). By Equation 20.2 and the definition of the moment generating function (Definition 4.7), \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\mathbb E[e^{W}]=M_W(1),
\] the MGF of \(W\) at \(t=1\). The MGF of \(\mathcal N(m,v)\) is \(M_W(t)=\exp(mt+\tfrac12 v t^2)\), the scalar case \(p=1\) of the multivariate-normal MGF Equation 4.13. Evaluating at \(t=1\) gives \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=\exp(m+\tfrac12 v)\), which is Equation 20.12. The factorization \(\exp(m+\tfrac12 v)=e^{m}\cdot e^{v/2}=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\cdot e^{v/2}\) follows from \(\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}=g^{-1}(m)=e^{m}\), and \(v=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\ge 0\) because \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\succeq 0\) (Theorem 4.9), with \(v=0\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}=\mathbf 0\). \(\square\)


Remark. Consistency with the bias and heat-flow results. The multiplicative factor \(e^{v/2}\ge1\) is the exact form of the downward plug-in bias predicted qualitatively by Theorem 20.2 (convex \(g^{-1}=\exp\), hence \(\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}\le\theta_\bullet\)) and to leading order by Equation 20.9: there \((g^{-1})''(m)=e^{m}\), so the leading bias is \(\tfrac12 e^{m}v=\tfrac{v}{2}\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}\), matching the expansion \(e^{m}(e^{v/2}-1)=e^{m}(\tfrac{v}{2}+o(v))\). The closed form is also the heat flow of Lemma 20.2 with \(\psi=\exp\): the function \(u(m,\tau)=e^{m+\tau/2}\) solves \(\partial_\tau u=\tfrac12\partial_m^2 u\) with \(u(m,0)=e^m\), because both \(\partial_\tau u\) and \(\tfrac12\partial_m^2 u\) equal \(\tfrac12 e^{m+\tau/2}\); the exponential is carried by the heat semigroup to a shifted exponential, which is why the log link keeps a closed form. The two hypotheses are essential. Drop joint normality, and \(\mathbb E[e^{W}]\) is the MGF of a non-normal law, generally not elementary; drop the log link, and \(W\) is still normal but \(\mathbb E[g^{-1}(W)]\) is no longer an MGF. The first failure is repaired by numerical integration (Chapter 22); the second is the subject of the next section. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This is result H.6 of the proof catalogue (corresponds to H.6; Phillippo 2019, Section 4.3.2).

section: 20.11 The logit link: no elementary closed form
text:
20.11 The logit link: no elementary closed form
Binary outcomes are modeled on the logit scale, where \(g^{-1}(z)=\mathrm{expit}(z):=e^{z}/(1+e^{z})\) is the standard logistic function, the cumulative distribution function of the logistic law. It is bounded, smooth, convex for \(z<0\) and concave for \(z>0\), with the inflection at \(z=0\). The change of curvature across \(z=0\) is what makes the logit aggregation bias different in kind from the log: it has no fixed sign, it vanishes at a symmetric configuration, and the integral that defines \(\theta_{\bullet jk}\) has no elementary closed form even for normal covariates. We prove the structural facts in full and then explain the absence of a closed form by contrast with the probit link, whose superficially similar integral is elementary.
The practical bottom line comes first, because it is what a data analyst needs and it does not depend on the proofs: for a binary outcome with genuinely varying covariates, the aggregate risk usually cannot be written in closed form and must be computed by numerical integration (Chapter 22), and the plug-in error can point either way depending on the arm’s baseline risk. Here is the risk interpretation of that sign, stated before we prove it. Because \(\mathrm{expit}\) is convex below zero and concave above zero, and because the mean linear predictor \(m\) is below zero exactly when the arm’s average risk is below \(50\%\):

in a low-risk arm (mean risk below \(50\%\), so \(m<0\)), covariate heterogeneity pulls the true average risk upward relative to the plug-in value: the plug-in underestimates;
in a high-risk arm (mean risk above \(50\%\), so \(m>0\)), heterogeneity pulls the true average risk downward: the plug-in overestimates;
at exactly \(50\%\) (\(m=0\)), the two effects balance and the bias is zero, however spread out the covariates are.

The following table is that picture in numbers. It tabulates \(\mathrm{expit}\) and the sign of its curvature along the linear-predictor axis, and reads off the direction in which integrating moves the arm risk away from the naive plug-in value.

This is the qualitative content of Theorem 20.5(c) below; the worked example Example 20.1 realizes it with real numbers, one arm on each side of the inflection.

Proposition 20.1 (The probit aggregate mean is elementary) Suppose the inverse link is the standard normal distribution function, \(g^{-1}=\Phi\) (the probit link), and the linear predictor is normal, \(\eta_{jk}(X)\sim\mathcal N(m,\tau)\) with \(\tau\ge0\). Then the aggregate mean is the elementary closed form \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\mathbb E[\Phi(\eta_{jk}(X))]=\Phi\!\Big(\frac{m}{\sqrt{1+\tau}}\Big).
\tag{20.13}\]


Proof. This is the Gaussian probit integral established in Chapter 16 as Lemma 16.4, with \(a=0,\,b=1\) and the roles \((m,\sigma^2)\leftrightarrow(m,\tau)\): there it is shown that for \(Z\sim\mathcal N(m,\tau)\) one has \(\mathbb E[\Phi(a+bZ)]=\Phi\big((a+bm)/\sqrt{1+b^2\tau}\big)\), by writing \(\Phi(a+bZ)=P(U\le a+bZ\mid Z)\) for an independent standard normal \(U\) and standardizing the normal difference \(U-bZ\) through its moment generating function. Specializing \(a=0,b=1\) gives Equation 20.13. Equivalently, in the heat-flow language of Lemma 20.2, \(u(m,\tau)=\Phi(m/\sqrt{1+\tau})\) solves \(\partial_\tau u=\tfrac12\partial_m^2 u\) with \(u(m,0)=\Phi(m)\): writing \(u=\Phi(m\,(1+\tau)^{-1/2})\) and \(\varphi=\Phi'\), one computes \(\partial_m u=\varphi\,(1+\tau)^{-1/2}\), \(\partial_m^2 u=\varphi'\,(1+\tau)^{-1}=-\tfrac{m}{(1+\tau)^{2}}\varphi\) using \(\varphi'(x)=-x\varphi(x)\), and \(\partial_\tau u=-\tfrac{m}{2}(1+\tau)^{-3/2}\varphi=\tfrac12\partial_m^2 u\), with \(u(m,0)=\Phi(m)\). \(\square\)


Remark. Probit is easy, logit is not: the same integral, two fates. It is worth seeing the divide numerically before the theorem explains it. Take a normal linear predictor with mean \(m=1\) and variance \(\tau=1\). The probit aggregate mean is elementary by Equation 20.13, \[
\Phi\!\Big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+1}}\Big)=\Phi(0.7071)=0.7602 .
\] The logit aggregate mean is the same shape of integral, with \(\mathrm{expit}\) in place of \(\Phi\), but it has no such formula; evaluated numerically it is \[
J(1,1)=\int_{\mathbb R}\mathrm{expit}(z)\,\phi(z;1,1)\,dz=0.6967 .
\] Two nearby S-shaped links, fed identical \((m,\tau)\), give different aggregate risks (\(0.760\) versus \(0.697\)), and only one of the two can be written down. The next theorem isolates exactly why. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Theorem 20.5 (Logit-link aggregation: structure and the absence of a closed form) Let the inverse link be \(g^{-1}=\mathrm{expit}\) and let the linear predictor be normal, \(\eta_{jk}(X)\sim\mathcal N(m,\tau)\) with \(\tau>0\), where \(m=\eta_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf x}_j)\) and \(\tau=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\). Define the logit-normal integral \[
J(m,\tau):=\int_{\mathbb R}\mathrm{expit}(z)\,\phi(z;m,\tau)\,dz=\theta_{\bullet jk}\in(0,1).
\tag{20.14}\] Then:
(a) Reflection and the symmetric point. \(J(m,\tau)=1-J(-m,\tau)\) for all \(m\), and in particular \(J(0,\tau)=\tfrac12\) for every \(\tau\ge0\). Thus when the linear predictor at the mean covariate is zero the aggregation bias Equation 20.8 vanishes exactly, despite \(g^{-1}\) being nonlinear and \(\tau>0\).
(b) Monotonicity. \(J(\cdot,\tau)\) is strictly increasing, with \(\partial_m J(m,\tau)=\mathbb E[\mathrm{expit}'(\eta_{jk}(X))]=\mathbb E[\mathrm{expit}(\eta)(1-\mathrm{expit}(\eta))]>0\).
(c) Sign of the bias. To leading order in \(\tau\), \(\theta_{\bullet jk}-\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}
=\tfrac12\,\mathrm{expit}''(m)\,\tau+o(\tau)\) with \(\mathrm{expit}''(m)=\mathrm{expit}(m)(1-\mathrm{expit}(m))(1-2\,\mathrm{expit}(m))\), which is positive for \(m<0\) and negative for \(m>0\): the plug-in mean underestimates the integrated mean in the low-risk region (\(m<0\)) and overestimates it in the high-risk region (\(m>0\)).
(d) No elementary closed form. Unlike the probit aggregate mean Equation 20.13, the logit-normal integral \(J(m,\tau)\) admits no representation as a finite combination of elementary functions of \((m,\tau)\); the aggregate likelihood under the logit link must therefore be evaluated by numerical integration.


Proof. (a). The logistic function satisfies \(\mathrm{expit}(-z)=1-\mathrm{expit}(z)\), since \(\mathrm{expit}(z)+\mathrm{expit}(-z)=\frac{e^{z}}{1+e^{z}}+\frac{1}{1+e^{z}}=1\). Substitute \(z\mapsto -z\) in Equation 20.14 and use the Gaussian symmetry \(\phi(-z;m,\tau)=\phi(z;-m,\tau)\): \[
J(m,\tau)=\int \mathrm{expit}(z)\phi(z;m,\tau)\,dz
=\int \mathrm{expit}(-z)\phi(-z;m,\tau)\,dz
=\int\big(1-\mathrm{expit}(z)\big)\phi(z;-m,\tau)\,dz=1-J(-m,\tau).
\] Setting \(m=0\) gives \(J(0,\tau)=1-J(0,\tau)\), hence \(J(0,\tau)=\tfrac12\). Since \(\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}=\mathrm{expit}(0)=\tfrac12\) as well, the bias Equation 20.8 is zero at \(m=0\).
(b). Because \(\mathrm{expit}\) is smooth with all derivatives bounded, differentiation under the integral is justified by dominated convergence (the \(m\)-derivative of \(\phi\) is \(\phi\) times a linear factor, integrable against a bounded function). Hence \(\partial_m J(m,\tau)=\int\mathrm{expit}(z)\,\partial_m\phi(z;m,\tau)\,dz\); integrating by parts, or equivalently using \(\partial_m\phi=-\partial_z\phi\) and moving the derivative onto \(\mathrm{expit}\), gives \(\partial_m J=\int\mathrm{expit}'(z)\phi(z;m,\tau)\,dz=\mathbb E[\mathrm{expit}'(\eta)]\). Since \(\mathrm{expit}'(z)=\mathrm{expit}(z)(1-\mathrm{expit}(z))\in(0,\tfrac14]\) is strictly positive, the integral is strictly positive, so \(J(\cdot,\tau)\) is strictly increasing.
(c). Apply the leading-order expansion Lemma 20.1 with \(g^{-1}=\mathrm{expit}\), whose third derivative is bounded; then \(\theta_{\bullet jk}-\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}=\tfrac12\mathrm{expit}''(m)\tau+o(\tau)\). Writing \(\sigma:=\mathrm{expit}(m)\), we have \(\mathrm{expit}'=\sigma(1-\sigma)\) and, differentiating again, \(\mathrm{expit}''=\sigma'(1-2\sigma)=\sigma(1-\sigma)(1-2\sigma)\). The factor \(\sigma(1-\sigma)>0\) always, and \(1-2\sigma\) has the sign of \(-m\) because \(\sigma=\mathrm{expit}(m)>\tfrac12\iff m>0\). Hence \(\mathrm{expit}''(m)>0\) for \(m<0\) and \(<0\) for \(m>0\), giving the stated signs.
(d). We argue by contrast with the probit case and by the structure of the integral. First reduce: by the heat-flow lemma Lemma 20.2, \(J(m,\tau)=u(m,\tau)\) is the solution of the heat equation \(\partial_\tau u=\tfrac12\partial_m^2 u\) with initial data \(u(m,0)=\mathrm{expit}(m)\). For the probit initial data \(\Phi\) the solution is the elementary rescaled probit Equation 20.13, because \(\Phi\) is itself a Gaussian integral and Gaussian convolution of a Gaussian integral is again a Gaussian integral, only with an enlarged variance; this is the algebraic miracle exploited in Proposition 20.1. The logistic initial data \(\mathrm{expit}\) enjoys no such stability: it is not a Gaussian integral, and its Gaussian convolution is the mean of a logit-normal random variable, a transcendental function of \((m,\tau)\) for which no closed form in elementary functions, nor in the error function with elementary arguments, is known. The obstruction is specifically the Gaussian weight, not the logistic function alone: the indefinite integral \(\int\mathrm{expit}(z)\,dz=\log(1+e^{z})\) is elementary (the softplus function), so the difficulty in Equation 20.14 is introduced entirely by integrating against \(\phi\). We record the standard fact, used throughout the ML-NMR literature (Phillippo et al. (2020)), that \(J(m,\tau)\) is non-elementary and must be computed numerically; the structural facts (a) to (c) are exactly the qualitative information that survives the absence of a formula, and Chapter 22 supplies the numerical method that evaluates Equation 20.14 to controlled error. \(\square\)


Remark. The honest status of part (d). Parts (a) to (c) are theorems in the full sense: the reflection identity, the value \(\tfrac12\) at \(m=0\), strict monotonicity, and the sign of the leading bias are proved without appeal to authority. Part (d) is the assertion that no elementary antiderivative-style formula exists, and we have argued it rather than invoked a Liouville-type impossibility theorem, because the latter is outside the scope of this book. The argument is the right one for the purpose: it isolates the obstruction (the Gaussian weight, since \(\mathrm{expit}\) alone has the elementary antiderivative \(\log(1+e^{z})\)), and it exhibits the neighboring probit problem that does have a closed form (Proposition 20.1), so the reader sees precisely why logit and probit, so alike in shape, diverge under aggregation. The practical consequence is unambiguous and is what matters for the method: every binary-outcome ML-NMR model must integrate Equation 20.14 numerically, which is the computational problem that occupies Chapter 22. A popular approximation, the probit substitution \(\mathrm{expit}(z)\approx\Phi(\kappa z)\) with \(\kappa=\sqrt{\pi/8}\approx0.6267\) chosen to match the slopes at the origin (so that \(\kappa\,\phi(0)=\mathrm{expit}'(0)=\tfrac14\)), turns Equation 20.14 into the elementary Equation 20.13 and is sometimes used as a fast initializer; it is an approximation, not an identity, and ML-NMR uses exact numerical integration in the fitted model. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This is result H.7 of the proof catalogue (corresponds to H.7; Phillippo 2019, Section 4.3.2). The probit companion Proposition 20.1 is the aggregation counterpart of Lemma 16.4 of Chapter 16.

text:
20.12 A fully worked example
We compute the plug-in and integrated aggregate means in two settings: a binary outcome on the logit scale with a discrete covariate, where the integral is a finite sum and every number is verifiable on a calculator, and a count outcome on the log scale with a normal covariate, where the closed form Equation 20.12 applies. The logit example is the more instructive, because it exhibits the sign reversal of the bias between arms and its consequence for the marginal odds ratio.

20.12.1 Logit link with a binary effect modifier

Example 20.1 (Plug-in versus integrated aggregate risk on the logit scale) Continue the running plaque psoriasis example, now zooming into a single AgD study \(j\) that reports PASI 75 response (a binary outcome) on two arms: a reference arm \(C\), an established comparator, and an active arm \(B\), the new IL-17 inhibitor. The one binary effect modifier is \(x\in\{0,1\}\), with \(x=1\) for biologic-naive patients and \(x=0\) for biologic-experienced, and its study prevalence is \(q:=P(x=1)=0.5\) (the study is half biologic-naive). The covariate distribution \(f_j\) is the two-point law with \(f_j(0)=f_j(1)=\tfrac12\) and mean \(\bar x_j=q=0.5\). On the logit scale (\(g=\mathrm{logit}\), \(g^{-1}=\mathrm{expit}\)) take the individual model Equation 20.1 with \[
\mu_j=-1,\qquad \beta_1=0.5\ (\text{prognostic}),\qquad \beta_{2,B}=1.0\ (\text{effect modifier}),\qquad \gamma_B=0.8,
\] and reference-arm constraints \(\beta_{2,C}=0,\ \gamma_C=0\). The total slopes are \(\beta_{\mathrm{tot},C}=\beta_1=0.5\) and \(\beta_{\mathrm{tot},B}=\beta_1+\beta_{2,B}=1.5\), and the arm linear predictors are \(\eta_C(x)=-1+0.5x\) and \(\eta_B(x)=-1+1.5x+0.8=-0.2+1.5x\).
Conditional risks at the two covariate values. Evaluating \(\mathrm{expit}\) (rounding to five decimals):

Integrated aggregate risks (the correct ML-NMR quantities), by Equation 20.2 with the two-point \(f_j\): \[
\theta_{\bullet C}=\tfrac12(0.26894)+\tfrac12(0.37754)=0.32324,\qquad
\theta_{\bullet B}=\tfrac12(0.45017)+\tfrac12(0.78583)=0.61800.
\]
Plug-in aggregate risks (the naive quantities), by Equation 20.6 at \(\bar x_j=0.5\), where \(\eta_C(0.5)=-0.75\) and \(\eta_B(0.5)=0.55\): \[
\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet C}=\mathrm{expit}(-0.75)=0.32082,\qquad
\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet B}=\mathrm{expit}(0.55)=0.63414.
\]
Arm-level bias and the sign reversal. The ecological biases Equation 20.8 are \[
\mathrm{EB}_C=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet C}-\theta_{\bullet C}=0.32082-0.32324=-0.00242,\qquad
\mathrm{EB}_B=0.63414-0.61800=+0.01614.
\] The reference arm has \(m_C=\eta_C(0.5)=-0.75<0\), where \(\mathrm{expit}\) is convex, so the plug-in underestimates (\(\mathrm{EB}_C<0\)); the active arm has \(m_B=\eta_B(0.5)=0.55>0\), where \(\mathrm{expit}\) is concave, so the plug-in overestimates (\(\mathrm{EB}_B>0\)). This is the sign reversal of Theorem 20.5(c), and it is the crux: the bias does not cancel across arms but compounds in the contrast.
The marginal odds ratio. The reported estimand is the marginal \(B\)-versus-\(C\) log odds ratio in study \(j\), \(g(\theta_{\bullet B})-g(\theta_{\bullet C})\) on the logit scale. The integrated (ML-NMR) value is \[
\mathrm{logit}(0.61800)-\mathrm{logit}(0.32324)=0.48107-(-0.73893)=1.22000,
\] whereas the plug-in value telescopes, because \(\mathrm{logit}\circ\mathrm{expit}\) is the identity, to the conditional log odds ratio at the mean covariate: \[
\mathrm{logit}(\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet B})-\mathrm{logit}(\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet C})
=\eta_B(0.5)-\eta_C(0.5)=0.55-(-0.75)=1.30000=\gamma_B+\beta_{2,B}\,\bar x_j .
\] The naive aggregation thus reports the conditional-at-the-mean log odds ratio \(1.30000\), while the correct marginal log odds ratio is \(1.22000\). The ecological bias of the contrast is \[
1.30000-1.22000=0.08000\ \text{on the log-odds scale},
\] an odds-ratio inflation of \(e^{0.08000}=1.0833\), roughly an eight percent distortion produced entirely by plugging in the mean instead of integrating. ML-NMR reports \(1.22000\); pre-ML-NMR meta-regression on the mean covariate reports \(1.30000\). In HTA terms, the naive analysis would credit the IL-17 inhibitor with an odds ratio of \(e^{1.30000}=3.669\) against the comparator, when the correct population-average figure is \(e^{1.22000}=3.387\): a real difference in the number a reimbursement decision would rest on, and it came from nothing but the order of two operations. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

A remark on what made this hand-computable: the discrete covariate turned the integral Equation 20.2 into a two-term sum, so the logit-normal obstruction of Theorem 20.5 did not arise; with a continuous covariate the same contrast would require the numerical integration of Chapter 22. Note also the clean identity that the plug-in marginal log odds ratio equals exactly the conditional log odds ratio at the mean covariate, \(\gamma_B+\beta_{2,B}\bar x_j\), which is why naive meta-regression silently estimates a conditional, not a marginal, effect; the difference is the non-collapsibility gap of Definition 7.7, here realized as aggregation bias.


20.12.2 Log link with a normal covariate

Example 20.2 (Closed-form aggregate rate on the log scale) Consider an AgD study \(j\) reporting a count outcome on the log scale (\(g=\log\), \(g^{-1}=\exp\)) with a single continuous covariate \(X\sim\mathcal N(\bar x_j,\sigma_j^2)\), \(\bar x_j=2\), \(\sigma_j^2=1\). Take the active-arm parameters \(\mu_j=0\), \(\beta_1=0.3\), \(\beta_{2,k}=0.2\), \(\gamma_k=0.5\), so \(\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}=\beta_1+\beta_{2,k}=0.5\) and \(v=\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^2\sigma_j^2=0.25\cdot1=0.25\). The mean linear predictor is \(m=\mu_j+\gamma_k+\bar x_j\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}=0+0.5+2(0.5)=1.5\).
By the closed form Equation 20.12, \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\exp\!\big(m+\tfrac12 v\big)=\exp(1.5+0.125)=\exp(1.625)=5.0784,
\] while the plug-in rate is \[
\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}=\exp(m)=\exp(1.5)=4.4817 .
\] The plug-in underestimates by the exact multiplicative factor \(e^{v/2}=e^{0.125}=1.1331\), a thirteen percent correction; the leading-order prediction of Equation 20.9, \(\theta_\bullet-\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}
\approx\tfrac12 e^{m}v=\tfrac12(4.4817)(0.25)=0.5602\), is close to the exact difference \(5.0784-4.4817=0.5967\), the small discrepancy being the \(o(v)\) curvature beyond second order. Because \(\exp\) is convex everywhere, the bias here has a fixed sign (\(\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}\le\theta_\bullet\) always), in contrast to the logit case where the sign reversed between arms. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 20  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression I: The Aggregation Principle
text:
20.13 Aggregation bias and non-collapsibility
The worked example ended on a claim that deserves its own statement, because it links this chapter to a long-running debate in epidemiology. Recall the two odds ratios it produced. The plug-in log odds ratio was exactly \(1.30\), and it equaled the conditional log odds ratio at the mean covariate, \(\gamma_B+\beta_{2,B}\bar x_j\); the integrated log odds ratio was \(1.22\), the marginal log odds ratio in the study population. They differ not because of any estimation error but because the odds ratio is non-collapsible (Definition 7.7): the population-average of conditional odds ratios is not the odds ratio of the population-average risks, even with no confounding and no modeling mistake.
This is worth isolating, because it is a genuine source of confusion. Aggregation bias, as this chapter defines it, is a Jensen gap between “predict at the mean” and “average the predictions.” Non-collapsibility is the statement that the odds ratio, specifically, changes when you marginalize a conditional model over a covariate, even a covariate that is not a confounder. On the logit scale these are two names for one piece of arithmetic: marginalizing the conditional logistic model over the case mix is the integral Equation 20.2, and the gap it opens between the conditional-at-the-mean contrast and the marginal contrast is the non-collapsibility of the odds ratio. The worked example shows the marginal odds ratio \(e^{1.22}=3.39\) pulled toward the null relative to the conditional \(e^{1.30}=3.67\); this attenuation toward the null is the characteristic direction of odds-ratio non-collapsibility for a covariate that affects the outcome, and it is why a marginal odds ratio from an aggregate trial and a conditional odds ratio from a patient-level model are not directly comparable numbers.
Two practical consequences follow. First, an analyst must decide which estimand the decision maker wants; ML-NMR targets the marginal effect in a stated population and computes it honestly by integrating, whereas plug-in meta-regression silently reports a conditional-at-the-mean effect and mislabels it as a population effect. Second, the risk difference and the log risk ratio are collapsible in the no-confounding case, so on the identity and log links this particular gap does not arise. (Aggregation can still bias the log link through Jensen, as Theorem 20.4 shows, but that is variance-driven curvature, not non-collapsibility.) The odds ratio is the scale on which the two phenomena coincide, which is why binary outcomes are where the fights happen. Chapter 7 introduced non-collapsibility for a single logistic regression; this section has shown that it is the same phenomenon as logit aggregation bias, now playing out across a network.

title: 20  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression I: The Aggregation Principle
text:
20.14 Notes and references
Multilevel network meta-regression was introduced by Phillippo et al. (2020) and developed at length in the doctoral thesis Phillippo (2019), whose Chapter 4 is the source of the aggregation principle treated here. The individual model Equation 20.1 is their Equation (2) and thesis Equation (4.1b); the aggregate mean Equation 20.2 is thesis Equation (4.1d); the aggregation theorem Theorem 20.1 is the likelihood identity of thesis Equation (4.1c) and the manuscript’s Section 3; and the aggregation-bias identity Equation 20.8 is thesis Equation (4.8). The names “individual-level model” and “aggregate-level model” follow the multilevel-modeling reading in which patients are nested within studies, and the two levels are linked by integration rather than by the usual random intercept.
The aggregation-bias theorem Theorem 20.2 is Jensen’s inequality (Theorem 4.6) applied to the inverse link, and it is the same mathematical fact as the ecological bias of aggregate regression (Definition 16.2) diagnosed in Chapter 16 and as the non-collapsibility of marginal effects (Definition 7.7) discussed in Chapter 7. The leading-order expansion Lemma 20.1 is the delta-method or Laplace heuristic made into a theorem with a remainder bound; it is folklore in the ecological-inference literature. The heat-flow lemma Lemma 20.2 is the observation that Gaussian smoothing is the heat semigroup \(e^{(\tau/2)\partial^2}\); we have not seen it stated for ML-NMR, though it is implicit whenever a closed-form aggregate mean is derived under normal covariates, and it gives the cleanest account of why the log and probit links keep closed forms (their inverse links, \(\exp\) and \(\Phi\), are stable under Gaussian convolution) while the logit link does not. The probit closed form Proposition 20.1 reuses the Gaussian probit integral of Owen (1956), derived in this book as Lemma 16.4.
The log-link closed form Theorem 20.4 is the log-normal mean and is standard; it underlies the closed-form Poisson aggregate likelihood that Chapter 21 takes up. The logit-normal integral Equation 20.14 is the mean of a logit-normal distribution; its non-elementarity (Theorem 20.5) is well known and is the reason ML-NMR for binary outcomes is a numerical-integration method, treated in Chapter 22 via Sklar’s theorem (Sklar (1959)), Sobol’ sequences (Sobol’ (1967)), and the quasi-Monte Carlo error theory descending from the Koksma-Hlawka inequality. The probit substitution \(\mathrm{expit}(z)\approx\Phi(\kappa z)\) mentioned in the remark after Theorem 20.5 is the logistic-to-normal slope match; it is an approximation only and is not used in the fitted ML-NMR likelihood, which integrates numerically.
There is no machine-checked counterpart to this chapter. The Coq development accompanying the book (Phillippo (2019) notwithstanding) formalizes the potential-outcomes, propensity-score, MAIC, and STC material of Parts II to IV but stops short of ML-NMR, whose mathematical content is the numerical analysis of Chapters 21 and 22 rather than the algebra of the earlier parts; we note this gap in the work log. The aggregation identity Theorem 20.1 is, however, a single application of the chain rule, Fubini’s theorem (Theorem 4.8), and the tower property (Corollary 4.1), all of which are formalized in the probability libraries the development depends on, so a future formalization would be short.

title: 20  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression I: The Aggregation Principle
text:
20.15 Exercises
A starred exercise (\(\star\)) has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The exercises are graded: the first two are warm-ups and interpretation questions that need only arithmetic and the ideas of the chapter; the later ones build to the algebra and the proofs. Read the warm-ups even if you skip the proofs, since they carry the applied message.

Exercise 20.1 (Warm-up: same mean covariate, different aggregate risk) Two AgD studies enroll patients for the same binary outcome on the logit scale and report the same mean covariate \(\bar x\), but study 1’s patients are tightly clustered around \(\bar x\) while study 2’s are widely spread. Explain in one short paragraph, without any calculation, why the ML-NMR aggregate risk can differ between the two studies even though their plug-in risks \(\mathrm{expit}(\eta(\bar x))\) are identical. Which study’s true risk sits further from its plug-in value, and why? (You are re-deriving in words why matching only the mean covariate, as first-moment MAIC does, cannot by itself remove aggregation bias.)


Exercise 20.2 (Warm-up: the six-point gap by hand) An arm splits evenly into two covariate groups with individual PASI 75 response probabilities \(0.60\) and \(0.10\). (a) Compute the true aggregate response as the average of the two risks. (b) Compute the two log-odds, average them, and apply \(\mathrm{expit}\) to obtain the plug-in response. (c) Confirm the plug-in underestimates, and say which case of Theorem 20.2 (convex or concave \(g^{-1}\)) you are in by checking the sign of the mean log-odds. (This is the mini-example of Section 20.5 redone from scratch.)


Exercise 20.3 (Bias as a function of prevalence (\(\star\))) Repeat the logit worked example Example 20.1 with the effect-modifier prevalence changed to \(q=P(x=1)=0.3\), keeping all four parameters \(\mu_j=-1,\ \beta_1=0.5,\ \beta_{2,B}=1.0,\ \gamma_B=0.8\). (a) Recompute the integrated aggregate risks \(\theta_{\bullet C},\theta_{\bullet B}\) as the two-point averages \((1-q)\,\mathrm{expit}(\eta(0))+q\,\mathrm{expit}(\eta(1))\). (b) Recompute the plug-in risks at \(\bar x_j=q=0.3\). (c) Confirm that the plug-in marginal log odds ratio again equals \(\gamma_B+\beta_{2,B}\bar x_j\) exactly, and report the ecological bias of the contrast. (d) Explain, using Theorem 20.5(c), why decreasing \(q\) moves both arms’ mean linear predictors \(m_C,m_B\) downward and what that does to the sign of each arm’s bias.


Exercise 20.4 (The identity link is the only universally exact link (\(\star\))) Prove that a twice-differentiable link \(g\) satisfies \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\) for every nondegenerate covariate distribution and every choice of total slope \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\) if and only if \(g\) is the identity link up to an affine reparameterization, that is \(g^{-1}(z)=a+bz\) with \(b\ne0\). (Hint: by Theorem 20.3 the condition forces \(g^{-1}\) affine on every interval; deduce \(g^{-1}\) is globally affine, and translate this into a statement about \(g\).) Conclude that aggregation bias is unavoidable on any genuinely nonlinear scale, including the logit, log, probit, and complementary log-log.


Exercise 20.5 (Variance, not mean, drives the log-link bias) On the log scale with normal covariates, use Theorem 20.4 to show that the multiplicative plug-in bias \(\theta_{\bullet jk}/\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}=e^{v/2}\) depends on the covariate distribution only through the variance \(v=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\) of the linear predictor and not at all through its mean. Two studies with identical covariate means \(\bar{\mathbf x}_j\) but different covariance matrices therefore have identical plug-in rates but different true rates; compute the ratio of their true rates when \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\) is scaled by a factor \(c>0\).


Exercise 20.6 (Verifying the heat-flow lemma on the three links) Using Lemma 20.2, verify directly that each of the following is the solution \(u(m,\tau)\) of the heat equation \(\partial_\tau u=\tfrac12\partial_m^2 u\) with the stated initial data, and identify which link each corresponds to. (a) \(u(m,\tau)=m\) with \(u(m,0)=m\). (b) \(u(m,\tau)=e^{m+\tau/2}\) with \(u(m,0)=e^m\). (c) \(u(m,\tau)=\Phi(m/\sqrt{1+\tau})\) with \(u(m,0)=\Phi(m)\). (d) Explain why no elementary \(u\) exists for \(u(m,0)=\mathrm{expit}(m)\), relating your answer to Theorem 20.5(d).


Exercise 20.7 (When first-moment matching is not enough) Two AgD studies report the same covariate mean \(\bar x=0\) for a single continuous effect modifier, but study 1 has variance \(\sigma_1^2=0.25\) and study 2 has variance \(\sigma_2^2=4\). The outcome is binary on the logit scale with \(\eta(x)=\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}\,x\) and \(\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}=1\). (a) Using Theorem 20.5(a), show that both studies have aggregate risk exactly \(\tfrac12\), so that here the variance does not bias the arm mean. (b) Now shift the baseline to \(\eta(x)=0.8+x\) so that the mean linear predictor is \(m=0.8\); using Lemma 20.1, estimate the aggregation bias in each study to leading order and explain why first-moment matching (which equates \(\bar x\) but ignores \(\sigma^2\)) leaves a residual bias that differs between the two studies. Relate this to the second-moment-matching remark in Chapter 18.


Exercise 20.8 (Closed-form aggregation with two correlated covariates) Let \(\mathbf X\sim\mathcal N(\bar{\mathbf x}_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)\) in \(\mathbb R^2\) with \(\bar{\mathbf x}_j=(1,2)^\top\) and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_j=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.5\\0.5&2\end{pmatrix}\), log link, and total slope \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}=(0.4,-0.3)^\top\), with \(\mu_j=0\) and \(\gamma_k=0.2\). (a) Compute \(m=\mu_j+\gamma_k+\bar{\mathbf x}_j^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\) and \(v=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\). (b) Report the integrated aggregate rate \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=e^{m+v/2}\) and the plug-in rate \(e^m\). (c) Show that flipping the sign of the off-diagonal covariance to \(-0.5\) changes \(v\) and hence the bias, even though the marginal variances and means are unchanged, and interpret this as the dependence of aggregation bias on the joint, not merely marginal, covariate distribution.


Exercise 20.9 (Reduction to network meta-analysis) Show that when \(\boldsymbol\beta_1=\mathbf 0\) and \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\mathbf 0\) for every \(k\), the linear predictor Equation 20.1 reduces to \(\eta_{jk}=\mu_j+\gamma_k\), the integral Equation 20.2 reduces to \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=g^{-1}(\mu_j+\gamma_k)\) with no dependence on \(f_j\), and hence the aggregate likelihood Equation 20.5 is exactly the standard network meta-analysis likelihood with study baselines \(\mu_j\) and treatment effects \(\gamma_k\). (This is the NMA special case proved in full generality in Chapter 23.) Explain why aggregation bias is identically zero in this case for every link, and reconcile this with Theorem 20.2.


Exercise 20.10 (A two-sided bound on the logit aggregation bias) Let \(\eta_{jk}(X)\sim\mathcal N(m,\tau)\) on the logit scale. Using \(0\le\mathrm{expit}''(z)\le\) its maximum modulus and the exact second-moment identity \(\mathbb E[(\eta-m)^2]=\tau\), prove the nonasymptotic bound \[
\big|\,\theta_{\bullet jk}-\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\,\big|\ \le\ \tfrac12\Big(\sup_z|\mathrm{expit}''(z)|\Big)\,\tau
=\tfrac{1}{12\sqrt3}\,\tau,
\] where \(\sup_z|\mathrm{expit}''(z)|=1/(6\sqrt3)\) is attained at \(z=\pm\log(2+\sqrt3)\). (Hint: bound the Taylor remainder of Lemma 20.1 by the supremum of the second derivative rather than discarding it, using \(\mathrm{expit}(\eta)-\mathrm{expit}(m)-\mathrm{expit}'(m)(\eta-m)=\tfrac12\mathrm{expit}''(\zeta)(\eta-m)^2\).) Compare this guaranteed bound with the exact bias computed in Example 20.1.

Solutions to the starred exercises Exercise 20.3 and Exercise 20.4 appear in Appendix F.




Owen, Donald B. 1956. “Tables for Computing Bivariate Normal Probabilities.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 27 (4): 1075–90.


Phillippo, David Mark. 2019. “Calibration of Treatment Effects in Network Meta-Analysis Using Individual Patient Data.” PhD thesis, University of Bristol.


Phillippo, David M., Sofia Dias, A. E. Ades, et al. 2020. “Multilevel Network Meta-Regression for Population-Adjusted Treatment Comparisons.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series A 183 (3): 1189–210. https://doi.org/10.1111/rssa.12579.


Sklar, Abe. 1959. “Fonctions de répartition à \(n\) Dimensions Et Leurs Marges.” Publications de l’Institut de Statistique de l’Université de Paris 8: 229–31.


Sobol’, Ilya M. 1967. “On the Distribution of Points in a Cube and the Approximate Evaluation of Integrals.” USSR Computational Mathematics and Mathematical Physics 7 (4): 86–112.

title: 21  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression II: Discrete Outcomes and Approximation Theory
text:
21.1 Introduction
Chapter 20 built the engine of multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR) on a single idea, the aggregation principle: to honor an aggregate-data (AgD) study we write the individual-level model (Definition 20.1), push each individual’s linear predictor through the inverse link, and average on the response scale before comparing with the reported summary (Definition 20.2, Theorem 20.1). For a continuous outcome on the identity scale that average is itself the linear predictor evaluated at the covariate mean (Theorem 20.3), and the aggregate likelihood is an ordinary normal: the arithmetic was gentle because summation and the identity link commute. This chapter takes up the outcomes for which they do not, the counts and the binary events that dominate health-technology assessment, whose aggregate is not a smooth average of a single quantity but a sum of many small, non-identical random contributions, one per patient.
Two questions organize the chapter. First, what is the exact law of that sum? Second, since the exact law is in general intractable, what tractable distribution approximates it, and how large is the error? The answers split cleanly by outcome type, and the split is itself instructive.
For count outcomes the news is good and then subtle. A sum of independent Poisson variables is again Poisson, with rate equal to the sum of the rates, and this holds whether or not the rates are identical (Lemma 21.1); the Poisson family is closed under convolution with addition of parameters. So conditional on the patients’ covariates the aggregate count is exactly Poisson (Theorem 21.1), and no approximation is needed at that level. The subtlety is that the covariates are themselves random draws from the study population, so the rate of the conditional Poisson is random, and marginalizing over it yields not a Poisson but a mixed Poisson (a Poisson whose rate is itself random, drawn from a distribution and then averaged out), which carries the same mean and a strictly larger variance. The excess, the overdispersion, is the count-data fingerprint of the within-study covariate variation that ML-NMR exists to respect, and we compute it exactly under Gaussian covariates.
For binary outcomes the news is that the obvious guess is wrong. A sum of independent Bernoulli variables with a common success probability is binomial, but a sum of Bernoullis with different success probabilities, exactly the situation when each patient’s event risk \(p_i=\operatorname{expit}(\eta(x_i))\) depends on that patient’s covariates, is not binomial. It is the Poisson binomial distribution (Definition 4.11), whose exact probability mass function is a sum over all \(\binom{n}{y}\) subsets of size \(y\) and is hopeless to evaluate directly for the sample sizes of a real trial. We derive its structure cleanly through the probability generating function (Theorem 21.2), and then face the practical need for a tractable surrogate. Two classical surrogates answer that need, and they are genuinely different, a point the early ML-NMR literature was careful to separate and we are careful to keep separate here. Le Cam’s approximation replaces the Poisson binomial by a Poisson with matched mean and controls the total-variation error by the elegant bound \(\sum_i p_i^2\); we give the full coupling proof (Theorem 21.3), one of the few places in Part V where a sharp inequality, rather than a numerical recipe, carries the argument. The adjusted two-parameter binomial instead matches the first two moments exactly, producing a binomial whose count is automatically bounded above by its sample size and whose dispersion is correct (Theorem 21.4); it is the surrogate used in practice for binary ML-NMR. We close with a fully worked example that computes an aggregate binary likelihood three ways, by integration to a marginal binomial, by the exact Poisson binomial, and by the adjusted binomial, with the Le Cam Poisson alongside for contrast, and shows by hand which is faithful and which is not.
Throughout, the notation is that of Chapter 20 and of Notation: a study indexed \(j\), an arm or treatment indexed \(k\), individuals indexed \(i\), an outcome \(Y_{ijk}\) with conditional mean \(\theta_{ijk}=g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(x_{ijk}))\) for the link \(g\) (Definition 7.2) and linear predictor \(\eta_{jk}\) of Definition 20.1, and the aggregate mean \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=\int_{\mathcal X}g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(x))\,f_j(x)\,dx\) of Definition 20.2. We write \(Y_{\bullet jk}=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{jk}}Y_{ijk}\) for the aggregate count over the \(n_{jk}\) individuals of arm \(k\) in study \(j\), and we drop the study and arm subscripts to \(Y_\bullet\), \(n\), \(\theta_\bullet\), \(\eta\), \(\mathbf x\) wherever a single arm is under discussion. This chapter corresponds to results H.8 to H.11 of the proof catalogue.

title: 21  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression II: Discrete Outcomes and Approximation Theory
text:
Example 21.1 (A running example: an oncology responder arm) Throughout this chapter we return to one aggregate-data (AgD) arm from a hypothetical oncology network. Study \(AB\) compares drug \(A\) against drug \(B\); for the drug-\(A\) arm it reports only the number of responders out of the patients treated, a responder being a binary outcome (tumor shrinkage past a fixed threshold). We do not see individual records for this arm, only summary covariates (baseline severity, prior lines of therapy). The ML-NMR model of Chapter 20, fitted to the individual-patient-data (IPD) studies elsewhere in the network, assigns any covariate profile \(x\) a response probability \(p=\operatorname{expit}(\eta(x))\), where \(\operatorname{expit}(z)=e^{z}/(1+e^{z})\) is the inverse of the logit link (Definition 7.2).
Two facts make the aggregate awkward. First, patients differ: a frail, heavily pretreated patient may have response probability near \(0.1\), a fit, treatment-naive patient near \(0.7\). Second, we must turn those unequal per-patient probabilities into a single likelihood for the reported total. The naive move is to average the risks to a common \(\bar p\) and write \(\mathrm{Bin}(n,\bar p)\); much of this chapter is about what that shortcut gets wrong and how to repair it.
To keep every number checkable by hand, our concrete instance uses five equally weighted covariate profiles with model-predicted response probabilities \[
\mathbf p=(p_1,\dots,p_5)=(0.1,\ 0.3,\ 0.4,\ 0.5,\ 0.7),
\qquad \bar p=0.4,
\] the vector we carry all the way to the fully worked Example 21.5. These five are profiles that summarize the covariate distribution (the numerical integration nodes of Chapter 22), not necessarily five real patients. Whether we hold them fixed or regard the arm as a random sample from the distribution they summarize is exactly the conditional-versus-marginal choice that organizes everything below. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 21  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression II: Discrete Outcomes and Approximation Theory
section: 21.2 The aggregate count and its two laws
text:
21.2 The aggregate count and its two laws
Fix a single AgD arm with \(n\) individuals. The individual-level model gives, conditional on patient \(i\)’s covariate vector \(x_i\), a mean \(\theta_i=g^{-1}(\eta(x_i))\) on the outcome scale; the outcomes \(Y_i\) are conditionally independent given the covariates. The object the AgD study reports is some function of the aggregate count \(Y_\bullet=\sum_i Y_i\), typically the total number of events \(y_\bullet=\sum_i y_i\) out of \(n\), and the aggregate likelihood is the law of \(Y_\bullet\) evaluated at \(y_\bullet\). There are two distinct probability laws in play, and conflating them is the principal hazard of this subject, so we isolate them now.

Remark. Conditional versus marginal. The conditional law of \(Y_\bullet\) fixes the covariate values \(\mathbf x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\) of the \(n\) specific patients and treats only the outcomes as random; it is the law of a sum of independent variables with parameters \(\theta_i=g^{-1}(\eta(x_i))\) that differ from patient to patient. The marginal law additionally treats each \(x_i\) as an independent draw from the study covariate distribution \(f_j\) and integrates it out, so that the patients become exchangeable and each single outcome has the aggregate mean \(\theta_\bullet=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim f_j}[g^{-1}(\eta(X))]\) of Definition 20.2. The marginal law is the mixture of the conditional laws over random covariate configurations. The two have the same mean, \(n\theta_\bullet\), but in general different variances, because randomizing the covariates injects extra variability; the gap between them is the recurring theme of this chapter, appearing as overdispersion for counts (Theorem 21.1) and as the difference between the integrated and adjusted binomials for binary events (Example 21.5). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Before any machinery, here is the whole distinction in two patients and numbers a reader can check in a minute. It is the seed of the fully worked example at the end of the chapter.

Example 21.2 (Two patients, two laws, by hand) Take the two extreme profiles of the running example (Example 21.1): a frail patient with response probability \(0.1\) and a fit patient with response probability \(0.7\), and suppose the study population is exactly these two profiles in equal proportion (a single binary effect modifier, frail versus fit, prevalence one half). Consider an arm of \(n=2\).
Conditional law (profiles held fixed). Fix one patient at each profile. Then \(Y_\bullet=Y_1+Y_2\) with \(Y_1\sim\mathrm{Ber}(0.1)\) and \(Y_2\sim\mathrm{Ber}(0.7)\) independent, so \[
P(Y_\bullet=0)=0.9\cdot 0.3=0.27,\quad
P(Y_\bullet=1)=0.1\cdot 0.3+0.9\cdot 0.7=0.66,\quad
P(Y_\bullet=2)=0.1\cdot 0.7=0.07,
\] with mean \(0.1+0.7=0.8\) and variance \(0.1(0.9)+0.7(0.3)=0.30\).
Marginal law (patients drawn at random). Now let each of the two patients be an independent draw from the population, so marginally each is \(\mathrm{Ber}(0.4)\) (the average risk) and \(Y_\bullet\sim\mathrm{Bin}(2,0.4)\): \[
P(Y_\bullet=0)=0.36,\quad P(Y_\bullet=1)=0.48,\quad P(Y_\bullet=2)=0.16,
\] with mean \(0.8\) and variance \(2(0.4)(0.6)=0.48\).
The two laws share the mean \(0.8\) but differ in variance, \(0.30\) against \(0.48\). The extra \(0.18\) is the price of randomizing which profile each patient occupies; it equals \(n\,s_p^2\) with \(s_p^2=\tfrac12\big[(0.1-0.4)^2+(0.7-0.4)^2\big]=0.09\) the variance of the two risks. This single pair of numbers is the entire conditional-versus-marginal theme in miniature, and it returns, with five profiles instead of two, as Step 7 of Example 21.5. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

For binary outcomes the marginal law is immediate and is the likelihood ML-NMR uses by default, so we record it before turning to the finer conditional analysis.

Proposition 21.1 (The integrated binomial aggregate likelihood) Suppose the individual outcomes are Bernoulli, \(Y_i\mid X_i\sim\mathrm{Ber}(g^{-1}(\eta(X_i)))\), that the covariates \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are independent and identically distributed draws from \(f_j\), and that the outcomes are conditionally independent given the covariates. Then marginally the \(Y_i\) are independent and identically distributed \(\mathrm{Ber}(\theta_\bullet)\) with \(\theta_\bullet\) the aggregate mean of Definition 20.2, and the aggregate count is exactly binomial, \[
Y_\bullet=\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\ \sim\ \mathrm{Bin}(n,\theta_\bullet),
\qquad
\theta_\bullet=\int_{\mathcal X}g^{-1}(\eta(x))\,f_j(x)\,dx .
\tag{21.1}\]


Proof. By the tower property, that averaging a conditional probability over the conditioning variable returns the unconditional probability, for each \(i\), \(P(Y_i=1)=\mathbb{E}_{X_i}\!\big[P(Y_i=1\mid X_i)\big]=\mathbb{E}_{X_i}\!\big[g^{-1}(\eta(X_i))\big]
=\theta_\bullet\), the last equality being the definition of the aggregate mean (Definition 20.2), which exists by Theorem 20.1. The pairs \((X_i,Y_i)\) are independent across \(i\) and identically distributed, so the marginal outcomes \(Y_i\) are independent and identically distributed \(\mathrm{Ber}(\theta_\bullet)\); their sum is \(\mathrm{Bin}(n,\theta_\bullet)\) by the definition of the binomial as a sum of independent identical Bernoullis (Definition 4.9). \(\square\)


Remark. Reader translation. Integrating the covariate out first says: treat every future patient from this arm’s target population as carrying the same average response chance \(\theta_\bullet\), even though any one patient’s risk would differ if we saw their covariates. The aggregate count is then an ordinary binomial, exactly as if the arm had run \(n\) identical coin flips with success probability \(\theta_\bullet\). Nothing is approximated; the only assumption is that the \(n\) patients are an exchangeable sample from \(f_j\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why this is not the end of the story. Proposition Proposition 21.1 is exact, requires no approximation, and is the binary aggregate likelihood of the original ML-NMR (Phillippo et al. (2020)): compute \(\theta_\bullet\) by numerical integration (Chapter 22) and treat the reported events as \(\mathrm{Bin}(n,\theta_\bullet)\). Its one assumption is that the \(n\) patients are an exchangeable sample from \(f_j\), so that integrating the covariate out is legitimate before forming the count. The conditional view, which keeps the per-patient risks \(p_i\) distinct, is needed for three purposes that occupy the rest of the chapter: to understand the structure of an aggregate event count as a sum of unequal risks (Theorem 21.2); to quantify how a Poisson surrogate for that count behaves (Theorem 21.3); and to build the moment-matched binomial that is preferred when one works directly with the integration nodes that represent \(f_j\) as a fixed design rather than as a random sample (Theorem 21.4). The gap between the marginal law Equation 21.1 and the conditional law is exactly the overdispersion we now compute for counts. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 21  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression II: Discrete Outcomes and Approximation Theory
section: 21.3 A roadmap of the aggregate laws
text:
21.3 A roadmap of the aggregate laws
It is tempting to ask which single likelihood is the binary ML-NMR likelihood. The honest answer is that there are two, and they are not rivals: they are the correct laws for two different ways of representing an AgD study’s covariates. If the arm’s patients are regarded as an exchangeable random sample from the covariate distribution, one integrates the covariate out first and the exact aggregate is the integrated binomial \(\mathrm{Bin}(n,\theta_\bullet)\) of Proposition 21.1. If instead the covariate distribution is represented by a fixed set of integration nodes carrying distinct risks \(p_i\) (the numerical grid of Chapter 22), one conditions on those nodes and the aggregate is a Poisson binomial (Section 21.5), for which the adjusted binomial of Section 21.7 is the practical two-moment surrogate. The per-node risks \(p_i\) are themselves produced by the numerical integration of Chapter 22, which represents the covariate density \(f_j\) by nodes drawn through a Gaussian copula \(C_\Omega\); throughout this chapter we take the \(p_i\) as given inputs and study only what to do with them.
The count case splits the same way, and Table 21.1 collects all five situations. With covariates held fixed the aggregate is exact (Poisson or Poisson binomial); only when the covariates are treated as random does the story change, into overdispersion for counts and into a plain binomial for binary events. The right-hand column points to the section that fills in each row.

text:
21.4 Count outcomes: the Poisson aggregate
Count outcomes, modeled with the log link so that \(g^{-1}(\eta)=e^{\eta}\), are the easy case at the conditional level and the instructive case at the marginal level. The conditional ease rests on a closure property of the Poisson family that the binomial family lacks, so we prove it first and in full. The reason to dwell on so elementary a fact is the contrast it draws: the very same closure fails for the Bernoulli, and that single failure is what forces the approximation theory of the second half of the chapter (Section 21.6, Section 21.7).

Lemma 21.1 (A sum of independent Poissons is Poisson) Let \(Y_1,\dots,Y_n\) be independent with \(Y_i\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda_i)\), \(\lambda_i>0\), the rates not necessarily equal. Then \[
\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\ \sim\ \mathrm{Poi}\!\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\Big).
\tag{21.2}\]


Proof. It suffices to treat \(n=2\) and induct, since \(Y_1+\cdots+Y_{n}=(Y_1+\cdots+Y_{n-1})+Y_n\) is a sum of two independent Poissons once the inductive hypothesis identifies the first summand as \(\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{n-1})\). For \(X\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\) and \(Y\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\mu)\) independent, the convolution formula for the law of a sum of independent nonnegative integer variables gives, for \(k=0,1,2,\dots\), \[
P(X+Y=k)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}P(X=j)\,P(Y=k-j)
=\sum_{j=0}^{k}e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^{j}}{j!}\,e^{-\mu}\frac{\mu^{k-j}}{(k-j)!}.
\] Factor out \(e^{-(\lambda+\mu)}\) and multiply and divide by \(k!\): \[
P(X+Y=k)=\frac{e^{-(\lambda+\mu)}}{k!}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}\lambda^{j}\mu^{k-j}
=\frac{e^{-(\lambda+\mu)}}{k!}\,(\lambda+\mu)^{k},
\] the inner sum being \((\lambda+\mu)^k\) by the binomial theorem. This is the mass function of \(\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda+\mu)\) (Definition 4.10), proving the case \(n=2\) and, by induction, Equation 21.2.
A second proof records the structural reason, and it is this mechanism, not the conclusion, that we reuse: it shows in Section 21.5 precisely why the Bernoulli analogue breaks. By Definition 4.10 the moment generating function (MGF, Definition 4.7) of \(Y_i\) is \(M_{Y_i}(t)=\exp(\lambda_i(e^{t}-1))\), finite for all \(t\). By the product rule for MGFs of independent sums (Theorem 4.12), \[
M_{\sum_i Y_i}(t)=\prod_{i=1}^n\exp\!\big(\lambda_i(e^{t}-1)\big)
=\exp\!\Big(\Big(\textstyle\sum_i\lambda_i\Big)(e^{t}-1)\Big),
\] which is the MGF of \(\mathrm{Poi}(\sum_i\lambda_i)\); by the uniqueness theorem for moment generating functions (Theorem 4.11) the sum has that law. \(\square\)


Remark. The asymmetry with the binomial. In plain terms: pooling several Poisson counts just adds their rates, so there is nothing to approximate for counts, whereas pooling several Bernoulli events does not stay binomial unless the individual risks are equal. Closure under convolution with parameter addition is special. It holds for the Poisson regardless of whether the rates agree, which is why count outcomes give no trouble at the conditional level. It fails for the Bernoulli: a sum of Bernoullis is binomial only when the success probabilities are equal, and otherwise leaves the binomial family entirely for the Poisson binomial of Section 21.5. The whole approximation apparatus of this chapter, Le Cam and the adjusted binomial, exists to repair this single missing closure property in the binary case. The MGF proof makes the contrast precise: the Poisson MGF \(\exp(\lambda(e^t-1))\) multiplies into the same functional form with \(\lambda\) summed, whereas the Bernoulli MGF \(1-p+pe^t\) multiplies into \(\prod_i(1-p_i+p_ie^t)\), which is the form of a binomial MGF \(((1-p)+pe^t)^n\) only when every \(p_i\) is the same \(p\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

We can now state the law of the aggregate count, both conditionally and marginally. Write \(\eta(x)=\eta_{jk}(x)\) for the arm’s linear predictor and \(W=W(X)=e^{\eta(X)}\) for the random conditional rate of a single individual, so that \(\theta_\bullet=\mathbb{E}[W]\) is the aggregate mean of Definition 20.2 and \(\sigma_W^2:=\operatorname{Var}(W)\) measures how much that rate varies across the study population. (Here \(W\) is a scalar random rate, not the vector space \(W\) of Part I.) The theorem that follows has three layers, worth holding apart: conditional on the patients’ covariates the aggregate count is exactly Poisson; marginally, once the covariates are themselves random, it is an overdispersed mixed Poisson; and under Gaussian covariates the overdispersion collapses to a closed form.

Theorem 21.1 (The Poisson aggregate likelihood and its overdispersion) Let the individual count outcomes satisfy \(Y_i\mid X_i\sim\mathrm{Poi}(W_i)\) with \(W_i=e^{\eta(X_i)}\), conditionally independent given the covariates, and let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be independent and identically distributed draws from \(f_j\).

(Conditional law.) Conditional on the covariate configuration \(\mathbf X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)\), the aggregate count is exactly Poisson, \[
Y_\bullet=\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\ \Big|\ \mathbf X\ \sim\ \mathrm{Poi}\!\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n W_i\Big).
\tag{21.3}\]
(Marginal law.) Marginally over the covariates, \(Y_\bullet\) has the mixed Poisson law \[
P(Y_\bullet=y)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf X}\!\left[e^{-\Lambda}\frac{\Lambda^{y}}{y!}\right],
\qquad \Lambda=\sum_{i=1}^n W_i,
\tag{21.4}\] with mean and variance \[
\mathbb{E}[Y_\bullet]=n\theta_\bullet,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y_\bullet)=n\theta_\bullet+n\sigma_W^2 .
\tag{21.5}\] The marginal count is therefore overdispersed relative to a Poisson of the same mean, by exactly \(n\sigma_W^2\ge 0\), with equality (a genuine Poisson) if and only if \(W\) is degenerate, that is, if and only if the linear predictor \(\eta(X)\) is almost surely constant across the population.
(Gaussian covariates.) If in addition \(X\sim\mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)\) and \(\eta(x)=\mu+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}\) is affine in \(x\) (with \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}=\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\) the total covariate slope of Definition 20.1, the prognostic slopes \(\boldsymbol\beta_1\) plus this arm’s effect-modifier interactions \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\)), then the relative overdispersion has the closed form \[
\frac{\sigma_W^2}{\theta_\bullet^2}
=\exp\!\big(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}\big)-1 .
\tag{21.6}\]



Proof. Part 1. Conditional on \(\mathbf X\), the rates \(W_i=e^{\eta(X_i)}\) are fixed positive numbers and the \(Y_i\) are independent \(\mathrm{Poi}(W_i)\); Lemma 21.1 gives \(Y_\bullet\mid\mathbf X\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\sum_i W_i)\), which is Equation 21.3.
Part 2. The marginal mass function is the expectation of the conditional Poisson mass function over the law of \(\mathbf X\), which is Equation 21.4. For the moments, write \(\Lambda=\sum_i W_i\) and use the tower property and the conditional Poisson identities \(\mathbb{E}[Y_\bullet\mid\mathbf X]=\Lambda\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_\bullet\mid\mathbf X)=\Lambda\) (mean equals variance for a Poisson, Definition 4.10). For the mean, \[
\mathbb{E}[Y_\bullet]=\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[Y_\bullet\mid\mathbf X]\big]=\mathbb{E}[\Lambda]
=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{E}[W_i]=n\theta_\bullet,
\] since each \(W_i\) has mean \(\theta_\bullet=\mathbb{E}[e^{\eta(X)}]\). For the variance, the law of total variance, \[
\operatorname{Var}(Y_\bullet)
=\mathbb{E}\big[\operatorname{Var}(Y_\bullet\mid\mathbf X)\big]
+\operatorname{Var}\big(\mathbb{E}[Y_\bullet\mid\mathbf X]\big)
=\mathbb{E}[\Lambda]+\operatorname{Var}(\Lambda),
\] holds because \(\mathbb{E}[Y^2]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y^2\mid\mathbf X]]
=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid\mathbf X)+\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathbf X]^2]\) and subtracting \(\mathbb{E}[Y]^2=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathbf X]]^2\) leaves precisely the two displayed terms. Now \(\mathbb{E}[\Lambda]=n\theta_\bullet\) as above, and by independence of the \(W_i\), \(\operatorname{Var}(\Lambda)=\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(W_i)=n\sigma_W^2\). Hence \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_\bullet)=n\theta_\bullet+n\sigma_W^2\), which is Equation 21.5. The excess over the mean is \(n\sigma_W^2\ge 0\), zero exactly when \(\sigma_W^2=\operatorname{Var}(e^{\eta(X)})=0\), that is when \(e^{\eta(X)}\), equivalently \(\eta(X)\), is almost surely constant.
Part 3. Under the stated Gaussian assumption \(\eta(X)=\mu+X^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}\) is an affine function of a normal vector, hence univariate normal: for \(X\sim\mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu_j,
\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)\) the scalar \(a+\mathbf b^\top X\) has moment generating function \(\mathbb{E}[e^{t(a+\mathbf b^\top X)}]=\exp\!\big(t(a+\mathbf b^\top\boldsymbol\mu_j)
+\tfrac12 t^2\,\mathbf b^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\mathbf b\big)\), which is the MGF of a univariate normal (Definition 4.12), so \(\eta(X)\sim\mathcal N(m,s^2)\) with \(m=\mu+\boldsymbol\mu_j^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}\) and \(s^2=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}\). Then \(W=e^{\eta(X)}\) is log-normal (a variable whose logarithm is normal), and because \(\mathbb{E}[W^{r}]=\mathbb{E}[e^{r\eta(X)}]\) is the normal MGF of \(\eta(X)\) read off at \(t=r\), its moments are values of that MGF (Definition 4.12): with \(M(t)=e^{mt+s^2t^2/2}\), \[
\theta_\bullet=\mathbb{E}[W]=\mathbb{E}[e^{\eta(X)}]=M(1)=e^{m+s^2/2},
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[W^2]=\mathbb{E}[e^{2\eta(X)}]=M(2)=e^{2m+2s^2}.
\] The first identity is the closed form of the aggregate rate under the log link (Theorem 20.4). Therefore \[
\sigma_W^2=\mathbb{E}[W^2]-\mathbb{E}[W]^2=e^{2m+2s^2}-e^{2m+s^2}=e^{2m+s^2}\big(e^{s^2}-1\big)
=\theta_\bullet^2\big(e^{s^2}-1\big),
\] using \(\theta_\bullet^2=e^{2m+s^2}\). Dividing by \(\theta_\bullet^2\) gives Equation 21.6. \(\square\)


Example 21.3 (Overdispersion in a two-profile count arm) A hospitalization-count arm has \(n=40\) patients and a single binary effect modifier (say, prior hospitalization: yes or no) with prevalence one half. The log-link linear predictor gives conditional rate \(W=1\) event per patient at one profile and \(W=3\) at the other, so \[
\theta_\bullet=\mathbb{E}[W]=\tfrac12(1+3)=2,\qquad
\mathbb{E}[W^2]=\tfrac12(1+9)=5,\qquad
\sigma_W^2=5-2^2=1.
\] By Equation 21.5 the marginal count has mean \(n\theta_\bullet=40\cdot 2=80\) and variance \(n\theta_\bullet+n\sigma_W^2=80+40=120\), a dispersion index \(120/80=1.5\). A plain \(\mathrm{Poi}(n\theta_\bullet)=\mathrm{Poi}(80)\) would claim variance \(80\); ignoring the overdispersion understates the true variance by \(40/120\approx 33\%\), so it treats the reported count as far more informative than it is, and an AgD arm modeled that way would pull the network estimate too hard. This is the count-data face of the conditional-versus-marginal gap of Example 21.2. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reading the overdispersion. The factor \(e^{s^2}-1\) in Equation 21.6 is the squared coefficient of variation of the random rate \(W\), and \(s^2=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}^\top
\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}\) is the variance that the covariates induce in the linear predictor through the prognostic and effect-modifying slopes. When those slopes are small, or the covariate spread \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\) is small, \(s^2\) is near zero and \(e^{s^2}-1\approx s^2\) is negligible, so the Poisson approximation to the marginal count is excellent and one may safely use \(\mathrm{Poi}(n\theta_\bullet)\) as the aggregate likelihood. For a concrete feel, recall \(\theta_\bullet=e^{m+s^2/2}\) from the log-link identity (Theorem 20.4); if \(s^2=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j
\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}=0.25\), the relative overdispersion is \(e^{0.25}-1\approx 0.28\), so the rate’s coefficient of variation is \(\sqrt{0.28}\approx 0.53\) and each patient contributes excess count variance \(\sigma_W^2\approx 0.28\,\theta_\bullet^2\) beyond the Poisson baseline. When the effect modifiers are strong and dispersed, the overdispersion is real and ignoring it understates the uncertainty of the aggregate count, exactly the ecological-bias phenomenon of Definition 16.2 seen now in the second moment rather than the first. The naive claim that the marginalized count is itself Poisson is false in this regime; Equation 21.5 is the correct statement. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. The negative-binomial remedy. When the overdispersion \(n\sigma_W^2\) is not negligible, a Poisson aggregate likelihood is misspecified in its variance, and a two-parameter count law is wanted. The natural choice is the negative binomial, which arises precisely as a Gamma-mixed Poisson: if the random rate \(\Lambda\) were Gamma distributed, the mixture Equation 21.4 would be exactly negative binomial. The log-normal mixing implied by Gaussian covariates is not Gamma, so the match is by moments rather than in law, but a negative binomial calibrated to the mean \(n\theta_\bullet\) and variance \(n\theta_\bullet+n\sigma_W^2\) of Equation 21.5 restores correct dispersion; its extra dispersion parameter plays the role of a study-level random effect on the count scale (Definition 8.3). This is the count-data analogue of the adjusted binomial we build for binary outcomes in Section 21.7, and the two share the same logic: keep the correct first two moments, accept a parametric family that is convenient and respects the natural support. Concretely, in the two-profile arm of Example 21.3 this means calibrating a negative binomial to mean \(80\) and variance \(120\) (a dispersion index of \(1.5\)); in ML-NMR practice the same excess variance is more often absorbed by a study-level random effect on the log-rate (Definition 8.3), which keeps each covariate profile Poisson while letting the arm as a whole be overdispersed, than by switching count families outright. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This development corresponds to H.8 in the proof catalogue. The catalogue records the corrected statement, that the marginalized aggregate is a mixed Poisson with the overdispersion Equation 21.5, not a plain Poisson; Lemma 21.1 is the closure property that makes the conditional aggregate exact.
