text:
21.5 Binary outcomes: the Poisson binomial and its generating function
We turn to the binary case, where the aggregate count of events is a sum of independent but non-identical Bernoulli variables. By Lemma 21.1’s failing analogue, this sum is not binomial; it is the Poisson binomial of Definition 4.11. That definition (Chapter 4) already records the mass function, mean, variance, and MGF of the Poisson binomial. Here we re-derive its structure through the probability generating function (PGF), which is the natural transform for an integer-valued count because it stores the mass function in its Taylor coefficients and turns the convolution of independent counts into a product, exactly as the MGF does on the exponential scale. The PGF is the tool that makes the combinatorial mass function of Definition 4.11 transparent and that hands us the moments without re-summing the subset expansion.

Definition 21.1 (Probability generating function) For a random variable \(X\) taking values in \(\{0,1,2,\dots\}\), the probability generating function is \[
G_X(z):=\mathbb{E}\big[z^{X}\big]=\sum_{k\ge 0}P(X=k)\,z^{k},\qquad |z|\le 1 .
\tag{21.7}\] The series converges absolutely for \(|z|\le 1\) because the coefficients are a probability distribution. The mass function is recovered by differentiation at the origin, \(P(X=k)=G_X^{(k)}(0)/k!\), and the factorial moments by differentiation at one, \(\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)\cdots(X-r+1)]=G_X^{(r)}(1)\) whenever the latter derivative exists. For independent integer-valued \(X\perp Y\), \(G_{X+Y}(z)=G_X(z)\,G_Y(z)\). The PGF and the MGF are related by \(G_X(z)=M_X(\log z)\) for \(z>0\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. A probability generating function packs an entire count distribution into one polynomial in a bookkeeping variable \(z\): the probability of the count \(k\) is simply the coefficient of \(z^{k}\). Its usefulness is that multiplying two such polynomials corresponds to adding two independent counts, so a sum of many simple Bernoulli pieces becomes a product of many simple linear factors that we can expand. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The recovery and product properties asserted in Definition 21.1 are standard and elementary: term-by-term differentiation of the power series Equation 21.7 is justified within its radius of convergence, evaluation at \(z=0\) isolates the coefficient \(P(X=k)\), evaluation of the \(r\)-th derivative at \(z=1\) gives \(\sum_k k(k-1)\cdots(k-r+1)P(X=k)=\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)\cdots(X-r+1)]\), and the product rule \(G_{X+Y}(z)=\mathbb{E}[z^{X+Y}]=\mathbb{E}[z^X]\,\mathbb{E}[z^Y]\) follows from independence exactly as the MGF product rule does (Theorem 4.12). We now specialize to the Poisson binomial.

Example 21.4 (Two unequal risks, expanded by hand) Return to the two extreme profiles of the running example, response probabilities \(p_1=0.1\) (frail) and \(p_2=0.7\) (fit). The number of responders \(Y_\bullet=Y_1+Y_2\) has generating function \[
G_{Y_\bullet}(z)=(0.9+0.1z)(0.3+0.7z)=0.27+0.66\,z+0.07\,z^2,
\] so, reading off coefficients, \(P(Y_\bullet=0)=0.27\), \(P(Y_\bullet=1)=0.66\), \(P(Y_\bullet=2)=0.07\). The middle coefficient \(0.1\cdot 0.3+0.9\cdot 0.7\) is exactly “one patient responds and the other does not, either way around.” This is not \(\mathrm{Bin}(2,0.4)\), which would give \(0.36,0.48,0.16\): both laws have mean \(0.8\), but the unequal risks pile mass onto exactly one responder and thin out the extremes. These are the same conditional two-patient numbers as Example 21.2; the generating function has merely organized the bookkeeping. For five profiles the same kind of product yields the six coefficients computed in Example 21.5, and for a realistic arm of \(n=400\) patients the coefficient of \(z^{120}\) is a sum of \(\binom{400}{120}\) subset products, a number exceeding \(10^{100}\); that is why direct evaluation is hopeless and a tractable surrogate is unavoidable. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Theorem 21.2 (Poisson binomial via the probability generating function) Let \(Y_1,\dots,Y_n\) be independent with \(Y_i\sim\mathrm{Ber}(p_i)\), \(p_i\in[0,1]\), and let \(Y_\bullet=\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\sim\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf p)\) be their Poisson binomial sum (Definition 4.11), \(\mathbf p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)\). Then:

(Generating function.) The probability generating function factors over individuals, \[
G_{Y_\bullet}(z)=\prod_{i=1}^n\big(1-p_i+p_i z\big).
\tag{21.8}\]
(Mass function.) The probabilities are the coefficients of this polynomial, \[
P(Y_\bullet=y)=[z^{y}]\prod_{i=1}^n(1-p_i+p_i z)
=\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}\\ |A|=y}}\ \prod_{i\in A}p_i\prod_{i\notin A}(1-p_i),
\qquad y=0,\dots,n,
\tag{21.9}\] recovering the subset expansion of Definition 4.11.
(Moments.) The mean and variance are \[
\mathbb{E}[Y_\bullet]=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y_\bullet)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i(1-p_i).
\tag{21.10}\]



Proof. Part 1. Each Bernoulli has PGF \(G_{Y_i}(z)=\mathbb{E}[z^{Y_i}]=(1-p_i)z^{0}+p_i z^{1}=1-p_i+p_i z\). By the product property of Definition 21.1, applied inductively to the mutually independent \(Y_i\), \(G_{Y_\bullet}(z)=\prod_{i=1}^n G_{Y_i}(z)=\prod_{i=1}^n(1-p_i+p_i z)\), which is Equation 21.8.
Part 2. By Definition 21.1 the probability \(P(Y_\bullet=y)\) is the coefficient of \(z^{y}\) in \(G_{Y_\bullet}(z)\). Expanding the product Equation 21.8, a monomial \(z^{y}\) is formed by selecting the term \(p_i z\) from each factor \(i\) in some index set \(A\) of size \(y\) and the term \(1-p_i\) from each factor \(i\notin A\); summing over all such \(A\) gives \([z^{y}]\prod_i(1-p_i+p_i z)=\sum_{|A|=y}\prod_{i\in A}p_i\prod_{i\notin A}(1-p_i)\), which is Equation 21.9 and matches the mass function of Definition 4.11.
Part 3. Differentiate Equation 21.8. By the product rule, \[
G_{Y_\bullet}'(z)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\prod_{\ell\ne i}(1-p_\ell+p_\ell z).
\] At \(z=1\) every factor \(1-p_\ell+p_\ell\cdot 1=1\), so \(G_{Y_\bullet}'(1)=\sum_i p_i\), which is the first factorial moment \(\mathbb{E}[Y_\bullet]\) by Definition 21.1. Differentiating once more, \[
G_{Y_\bullet}''(z)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\sum_{\ell\ne i}p_\ell\prod_{m\ne i,\ell}(1-p_m+p_m z),
\] and at \(z=1\) the surviving products are again \(1\), giving \(G_{Y_\bullet}''(1)=\sum_{i\ne\ell}p_i p_\ell=\big(\sum_i p_i\big)^2-\sum_i p_i^2\), the second factorial moment \(\mathbb{E}[Y_\bullet(Y_\bullet-1)]\). Therefore \[
\operatorname{Var}(Y_\bullet)=G_{Y_\bullet}''(1)+G_{Y_\bullet}'(1)-\big(G_{Y_\bullet}'(1)\big)^2
=\Big[\big(\textstyle\sum_i p_i\big)^2-\sum_i p_i^2\Big]+\sum_i p_i-\big(\textstyle\sum_i p_i\big)^2
=\sum_i p_i-\sum_i p_i^2,
\] which is \(\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)\), establishing Equation 21.10. The identity \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=G''(1)+G'(1)-G'(1)^2\) used here is the translation of \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]+\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2\). \(\square\)


Remark. Consistency with Chapter 4 and the binomial special case. Setting \(z=e^{t}\) in Equation 21.8 recovers the MGF \(M_{Y_\bullet}(t)=\prod_i(1-p_i+p_i e^{t})\) recorded in Definition 4.11, as the relation \(G_X(z)=M_X(\log z)\) of Definition 21.1 requires. When all \(p_i\) equal a common \(p\), Equation 21.8 collapses to \((1-p+pz)^n\), the PGF of \(\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\), whose coefficient of \(z^y\) is \(\binom{n}{y}p^y(1-p)^{n-y}\); the Poisson binomial is the exact generalization that permits unequal risks. For fixed mean \(\lambda=\sum_i p_i\), the variance \(\lambda-\sum_i p_i^2\) is largest when the \(p_i\) are equal, because \(\sum_i p_i^2\) is minimized at fixed \(\sum_i p_i\) by equal coordinates; spreading the individual risks apart reduces the dispersion of the count, the opposite of the intuition one might carry over from the rates of the Poisson case. The intuition is that a Bernoulli with \(p\) near \(0\) or \(1\) is nearly deterministic (its variance \(p(1-p)\) is small), while \(p=\tfrac12\) is maximally uncertain; pushing the risks toward the predictable extremes lowers the total count variance. A Poisson rate has no such ceiling, so a more variable rate always inflates the count variance (Equation 21.5). That is the structural reason counts overdisperse while spread-out binary risks underdisperse. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why an approximation is unavoidable. The mass function Equation 21.9 has \(\binom{n}{y}\) terms, and the full distribution requires expanding a degree-\(n\) polynomial; while this can be organized into an \(O(n^2)\) recursion or an \(O(n\log n)\) discrete Fourier evaluation of Equation 21.8 on the roots of unity, the result must be recomputed for every candidate value of the parameter vector \(\boldsymbol\xi\), inside every iteration of the Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler of Chapter 24, for every AgD arm. In a network with many arms and thousands of patients this is prohibitive, and worse, it does not compose with the numerical integration over the covariate distribution that ML-NMR also requires (Chapter 22). The practical path is to replace the Poisson binomial by a one- or two-parameter law that captures its salient features cheaply. The next two sections develop the two such laws and, crucially, distinguish what each one guarantees. In inference terms, a faithful surrogate is one that misstates how surprising the reported count is by as little as possible, since that surprise is exactly the AgD arm’s likelihood contribution to the network. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This development corresponds to H.9 in the proof catalogue.

text:
21.6 The Poisson approximation: Le Cam’s total-variation bound
The first surrogate replaces \(\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf p)\) by a Poisson with the same mean \(\lambda=\sum_i p_i\). Its justification is a sharp bound on the total-variation distance between the two laws, due to Le Cam (1960), which we prove in full by the coupling method. The bound is structural and elegant: the error is at most \(\sum_i p_i^2\), the same quantity that measures how far the individual risks are from zero. We prove a sharp bound, rather than merely assert the approximation, because the bound is a ruler: it says quantitatively when the Poisson shortcut is safe (rare events) and when it silently lies (moderate risks), which is exactly what decides whether an AgD arm’s likelihood can be trusted. We first fix the meaning of total-variation distance and assemble the two elementary facts about it that the proof uses.
The proof has four moving parts, and it helps to see them before they arrive. (i) A definition of total-variation distance, the yardstick for how different two count laws are. (ii) A three-forms lemma rewriting that distance as one half the sum of absolute mass differences, which is what we actually compute. (iii) A coupling inequality: if we can place both laws on one probability space, their distance is at most the chance they disagree. (iv) An exponential inequality \(1-e^{-p}\le p\), the sole analytic input. The plan is then to couple each Bernoulli with a Poisson so they rarely disagree, make the couplings independent, add them up (the Poisson halves sum to a Poisson by Lemma 21.1), and bound the total disagreement by a union bound.

Definition 21.2 (Total-variation distance) For probability measures \(\mu,\nu\) on a countable set \(S\), the total-variation distance is \[
\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\subseteq S}\big|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\big| .
\tag{21.11}\] \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. Total variation is the largest gap, over every possible set of event counts, between the probability the two laws assign to that set. If two aggregate laws are \(0.17\) apart in total variation, then for any question of the form “did the arm report a count in this range?” their answers differ by at most \(0.17\) in probability. A likelihood built from the wrong law can therefore misstate how surprising an observed count is by up to that much, and that misstatement feeds straight into how strongly the AgD arm pulls the treatment-effect estimate. A total-variation bound is thus a worst-case guarantee on the likelihood error, not an abstract nicety. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Lemma 21.2 (Three forms of total variation) For probability measures \(\mu,\nu\) on a countable set \(S\), \[
\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
=\tfrac12\sum_{k\in S}\big|\mu(k)-\nu(k)\big|
=1-\sum_{k\in S}\min\big(\mu(k),\nu(k)\big).
\tag{21.12}\]


Proof. Let \(A^{+}=\{k:\mu(k)>\nu(k)\}\). For any \(A\subseteq S\), \(\mu(A)-\nu(A)=\sum_{k\in A}(\mu(k)-\nu(k))\le\sum_{k\in A^{+}}(\mu(k)-\nu(k))=\mu(A^{+})-\nu(A^{+})\), because adding indices outside \(A^{+}\) can only subtract nonnegative amounts; symmetrically the most negative value of \(\mu(A)-\nu(A)\) is attained at \(A^{-}=\{k:\mu(k)<\nu(k)\}\). Since both \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are probability measures, \(\sum_k(\mu(k)-\nu(k))=0\), so the total positive discrepancy equals the total negative discrepancy: \(\sum_{k\in A^{+}}(\mu(k)-\nu(k))=\sum_{k\in A^{-}}(\nu(k)-\mu(k))=\tfrac12\sum_k|\mu(k)-\nu(k)|\). Hence the supremum in Equation 21.11 equals \(\tfrac12\sum_k|\mu(k)-\nu(k)|\). For the third form, use \(\min(a,b)=\tfrac12(a+b-|a-b|)\) to write \(\sum_k\min(\mu(k),\nu(k))=\tfrac12\sum_k(\mu(k)+\nu(k))-\tfrac12\sum_k|\mu(k)-\nu(k)|
=1-\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\). \(\square\)

A coupling of \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) is a pair of random variables \((X,Z)\) on a common probability space with marginal laws \(\mu\) and \(\nu\). Couplings turn distances between laws into probabilities of disagreement, by the following one-directional inequality, which is all the proof needs.

Lemma 21.3 (The coupling inequality) If \((X,Z)\) is any coupling of \(\mu\) and \(\nu\), then \[
\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le P(X\ne Z).
\tag{21.13}\]


Proof. Fix \(A\subseteq S\). Since \(X\) has law \(\mu\) and \(Z\) has law \(\nu\), \[
\mu(A)-\nu(A)=P(X\in A)-P(Z\in A)
=P(X\in A,\,Z\notin A)-P(Z\in A,\,X\notin A)\le P(X\in A,\,Z\notin A)\le P(X\ne Z),
\] where the second equality splits each event on whether the other variable lands in \(A\) and cancels the common term \(P(X\in A,Z\in A)\), and the inequalities drop a nonnegative probability and then enlarge the event \(\{X\in A,Z\notin A\}\subseteq\{X\ne Z\}\). The same bound holds for \(\nu(A)-\mu(A)\) by symmetry, so \(|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|\le P(X\ne Z)\); taking the supremum over \(A\) gives Equation 21.13. \(\square\)


Remark. Which way the inequality runs. A coupling gives an upper bound on total variation, never a lower bound, because we are free to choose the coupling that disagrees as little as possible. (Total variation equals the disagreement of the single best coupling, a converse we do not need here.) So to bound the distance we only have to exhibit one good coupling, which is what the proof does next. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The strategy of Le Cam’s proof is to build, for each individual, a coupling of its Bernoulli law with a Poisson law that disagree only rarely, then to assemble these into a coupling of the whole Poisson binomial with a Poisson by taking the couplings independent across individuals. The independent sum of the Poisson halves is Poisson by Lemma 21.1, and the probability that the two sums disagree is bounded by the union of the individual disagreements. The single-pair coupling is explicit, and the only analytic input is the inequality \(1-e^{-p}\le p\), which we record.

Lemma 21.4 (An elementary exponential inequality) For all \(p\ge 0\), \(\,e^{-p}\ge 1-p\), equivalently \(0\le 1-e^{-p}\le p\).


Proof. Let \(h(p)=e^{-p}-(1-p)\). Then \(h(0)=0\) and \(h'(p)=1-e^{-p}\ge 0\) for \(p\ge 0\), so \(h\) is nondecreasing and \(h(p)\ge h(0)=0\); thus \(e^{-p}\ge 1-p\). Rearranging gives \(1-e^{-p}\le p\), and \(1-e^{-p}\ge 0\) since \(e^{-p}\le 1\). \(\square\)


Theorem 21.3 (Le Cam’s Poisson approximation to the Poisson binomial) Let \(Y_\bullet\sim\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf p)\) with \(\mathbf p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)\) and \(\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\), and let \(Z\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\). Then \[
\big\|\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf p)-\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\big\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\ \le\ \sum_{i=1}^n p_i^2 .
\tag{21.14}\]


Proof. Fix an index \(i\) and write \(p=p_i\). We construct a coupling \((B_i,P_i)\) of \(\mathrm{Ber}(p)\) and \(\mathrm{Poi}(p)\) with a small probability of disagreement. The idea is to place as much probability as possible on the diagonal \(\{B_i=P_i\}\), so the two agree whenever they can: we match \(B_i=P_i=0\) with the largest allowed mass \(1-p\), keep \(B_i=P_i=1\) where possible, and dump the leftover Poisson mass (the outcomes \(P_i\ge 2\) that a Bernoulli can never reach, plus a sliver forced by the marginals) onto \(B_i=1\). Define the joint law of \((B_i,P_i)\) on \(\{0,1\}\times\{0,1,2,\dots\}\) by \[
\begin{aligned}
&P(B_i=0,P_i=0)=1-p, \\
&P(B_i=1,P_i=1)=p\,e^{-p}, \\
&P(B_i=1,P_i=0)=e^{-p}-(1-p), \\
&P(B_i=1,P_i=k)=e^{-p}\frac{p^{k}}{k!}\quad (k\ge 2),
\end{aligned}
\tag{21.15}\] and all other combinations probability zero. Each entry is nonnegative: the only one in question is \(P(B_i=1,P_i=0)=e^{-p}-(1-p)\ge 0\), which is Lemma 21.4. We check the marginals. The \(P_i\)-marginal at \(0\) is \((1-p)+(e^{-p}-(1-p))=e^{-p}\); at \(1\) it is \(p\,e^{-p}\); at \(k\ge 2\) it is \(e^{-p}p^{k}/k!\); these are exactly the \(\mathrm{Poi}(p)\) probabilities (Definition 4.10). The \(B_i\)-marginal at \(0\) is \(1-p\), and at \(1\) it is \[
p\,e^{-p}+\big(e^{-p}-(1-p)\big)+\sum_{k\ge 2}e^{-p}\frac{p^{k}}{k!}
=e^{-p}\sum_{k\ge 0}\frac{p^{k}}{k!}-(1-p)=e^{-p}e^{p}-(1-p)=p,
\] so the \(B_i\)-marginal is \(\mathrm{Ber}(p)\) (Definition 4.8). Thus Equation 21.15 is a valid coupling. Its disagreement probability is the sum of the off-diagonal masses, \[
P(B_i\ne P_i)=\big(e^{-p}-(1-p)\big)+\sum_{k\ge 2}e^{-p}\frac{p^{k}}{k!}
=\big(e^{-p}-1+p\big)+\big(1-e^{-p}-p\,e^{-p}\big)=p-p\,e^{-p}=p\big(1-e^{-p}\big),
\] where \(\sum_{k\ge 2}e^{-p}p^{k}/k!=1-e^{-p}-p\,e^{-p}\) is the Poisson tail beyond \(k=1\). By Lemma 21.4, \(1-e^{-p}\le p\), so \[
P(B_i\ne P_i)=p_i\big(1-e^{-p_i}\big)\le p_i^2 .
\tag{21.16}\]
For a concrete rate, \(p_i=0.2\) gives per-pair disagreement \(0.2(1-e^{-0.2})\approx 0.0363\), just under the bound \(p_i^2=0.04\): the coupled Bernoulli and Poisson agree about \(96\%\) of the time.
Now take the \(n\) couplings \((B_1,P_1),\dots,(B_n,P_n)\) to be independent across \(i\), on a common product probability space. Then \(B_1,\dots,B_n\) are independent with \(B_i\sim\mathrm{Ber}(p_i)\), so \(Y_\bullet:=\sum_i B_i\sim\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf p)\); and \(P_1,\dots,P_n\) are independent with \(P_i\sim\mathrm{Poi}(p_i)\), so by Lemma 21.1 \(Z:=\sum_i P_i\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\sum_i
p_i)=\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\). The pair \((Y_\bullet,Z)\) is thus a coupling of \(\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf p)\) and \(\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\). If \(B_i=P_i\) for every \(i\) then \(Y_\bullet=Z\), so \(\{Y_\bullet\ne Z\}\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^n\{B_i\ne P_i\}\), and the union bound with Equation 21.16 gives \[
P(Y_\bullet\ne Z)\le\sum_{i=1}^n P(B_i\ne P_i)\le\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^2 .
\] By the coupling inequality (Lemma 21.3) applied to this coupling, \(\|\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf p)-\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le P(Y_\bullet\ne Z)\le\sum_i p_i^2\), which is Equation 21.14. \(\square\)


Remark. The classical law of small numbers as a special case. When every \(p_i=p\), the Poisson binomial is \(\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\) and \(\lambda=np\), so Equation 21.14 reads \(\|\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)-\mathrm{Poi}(np)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le np^2\). This is the quantitative form of the Poisson limit of the binomial (Theorem 4.13): if \(p=\lambda/n\), the bound is \(\lambda^2/n\to 0\), recovering convergence in distribution and adding a rate. Le Cam’s theorem is thus the finite-sample refinement, valid for unequal risks, of the limit theorem proved in Chapter 4. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Sharpness, refinements, and when the bound is useful. The bound Equation 21.14 is of the right order: Barbour and Hall (1984) proved the sharper estimate \(\|\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf p)-\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\min(1,\lambda^{-1})\sum_i p_i^2\) together with a matching lower bound of the same form up to a universal constant, via Stein’s method for Poisson approximation (the operator approach pioneered by Chen in 1975). The factor \(\min(1,\lambda^{-1})\) shows that the approximation improves when the events are spread over a large expected count. Physically, events spread over a larger expected count \(\lambda\) dilute each event’s share of the error, so the per-event total \(\sum_i p_i^2\) is discounted by \(\lambda^{-1}\); for \(\lambda>1\) the refined bound reduces to the average risk \(\bar p\) itself. The practical lesson for ML-NMR is sobering: with \(n=100\) patients at an average risk \(\bar p=0.3\), one has \(\sum_i p_i^2\approx n\bar p^2=9\) and even the refined bound \(\min(1,1/30)\cdot 9=0.3\) is large, so the Poisson surrogate is a poor approximation to a binary aggregate at the moderate risks typical of clinical events. Table 21.2 traces the verdict across event rates for \(n=100\) patients.



Table 21.2: Le Cam and Barbour-Hall total-variation bounds for a binary aggregate of \(n=100\) patients at several average risks. The refined bound equals the average risk \(\bar p\) in every row with \(\lambda>1\); only rare events (\(\bar p\lesssim 0.05\)) put the Poisson surrogate within a usefully small distance of the truth.

The Poisson approximation earns its place only when both \(\lambda\) and the individual \(p_i\) are small, the rare-event regime. For the common case of moderate risks and moderate sample sizes, the moment-matched binomial of Section 21.7 is the better tool, precisely because it respects the upper bound \(Y_\bullet\le n\) that the Poisson, with its unbounded support, violates. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

21.7 The adjusted binomial by moment matching
The second surrogate keeps the binomial family, with its bounded support \(\{0,1,\dots\}\) up to a sample size and its natural fit to event counts, but adjusts its two parameters so that its first two moments agree with those of the Poisson binomial. Unlike Le Cam’s Poisson, this surrogate carries no total-variation guarantee; its justification is exactly that it reproduces the mean and the variance, and nothing more is claimed. We make the construction and its properties precise, and we are scrupulous about what is and is not proved.

Theorem 21.4 (The two-parameter adjusted binomial) Let \(Y_\bullet\sim\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf p)\) with \(\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i>0\) and \(\nu=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^2\), so that \(\mathbb{E}[Y_\bullet]=\lambda\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_\bullet)=\lambda-\nu\) by Theorem 21.2. The unique pair \((N^{*},\pi^{*})\) with \(N^{*}>0\) and \(\pi^{*}\in(0,1)\) for which \(\mathrm{Bin}(N^{*},\pi^{*})\) has the same mean and variance, \[
N^{*}\pi^{*}=\lambda,
\qquad
N^{*}\pi^{*}(1-\pi^{*})=\lambda-\nu,
\tag{21.17}\] is \[
\pi^{*}=\frac{\nu}{\lambda}=\frac{\sum_i p_i^2}{\sum_i p_i},
\qquad
N^{*}=\frac{\lambda^2}{\nu}=\frac{\big(\sum_i p_i\big)^2}{\sum_i p_i^2}.
\tag{21.18}\] Moreover:

\(\pi^{*}\) is the \(p\)-weighted mean of the individual risks, \(\pi^{*}=\sum_i(p_i/\lambda)\,p_i\), and satisfies \(\pi^{*}\ge\bar p:=\lambda/n\), with equality if and only if all \(p_i\) are equal.
\(N^{*}=\big(\sum_i p_i\big)^2/\sum_i p_i^2\le n\), with equality if and only if all \(p_i\) are equal; this is the effective sample size of the risk vector \(\mathbf p\), the same Cauchy-Schwarz quantity as the effective sample size of Chapter 18 (Theorem 18.6).



Proof. Solving the moment equations. From the first equation in Equation 21.17, \(N^{*}\pi^{*}=\lambda\). Expand the second, \(N^{*}\pi^{*}(1-\pi^{*})=N^{*}\pi^{*}-N^{*}(\pi^{*})^2=\lambda-N^{*}(\pi^{*})^2\), and set it equal to \(\lambda-\nu\); the \(\lambda\) terms cancel, leaving \(N^{*}(\pi^{*})^2=\nu\). Dividing this by \(N^{*}\pi^{*}=\lambda\) gives \(\pi^{*}=\nu/\lambda\), and then \(N^{*}=\lambda/\pi^{*}=\lambda^2/\nu\), which is Equation 21.18. These are well defined because \(\lambda>0\) and, unless every \(p_i=0\), \(\nu=\sum_i p_i^2>0\). Uniqueness is immediate: the two equations determine \(N^{*}(\pi^{*})^2=\nu\) and \(N^{*}\pi^{*}=\lambda\), whose ratio fixes \(\pi^{*}\) and hence \(N^{*}\). That \(\pi^{*}\in(0,1)\) holds because \(0<\nu\le\lambda\) (each \(p_i\le 1\) gives \(p_i^2\le p_i\), so \(\nu\le\lambda\), with the bound strict unless every \(p_i\in\{0,1\}\)), so \(\pi^{*}=\nu/\lambda\in(0,1]\), and \(\pi^{*}<1\) unless the risks are degenerate.
Part 1. Writing the weights \(\omega_i=p_i/\lambda\), which are nonnegative and sum to one, \(\pi^{*}=\nu/\lambda=\sum_i\omega_i p_i\) is the weighted mean of the \(p_i\) with weights proportional to the \(p_i\) themselves; larger risks receive larger weight, so the weighted mean exceeds the unweighted mean. Concretely, let \(\bar p=\lambda/n\) and let \(s_p^2=\tfrac1n\sum_i(p_i-\bar p)^2=\tfrac1n\nu-\bar p^2\) be the population variance of the risks. Then \[
\pi^{*}=\frac{\nu}{\lambda}=\frac{n(\bar p^2+s_p^2)}{n\bar p}=\bar p+\frac{s_p^2}{\bar p}\ \ge\ \bar p,
\] with equality if and only if \(s_p^2=0\), that is, all \(p_i\) equal.
Part 2. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applied to the vectors \(\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)\) and \(\mathbf p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)\), \[
\lambda^2=\Big(\sum_i 1\cdot p_i\Big)^2\le\Big(\sum_i 1^2\Big)\Big(\sum_i p_i^2\Big)=n\,\nu,
\] so \(N^{*}=\lambda^2/\nu\le n\), with equality if and only if \(\mathbf p\) is proportional to \(\mathbf 1\), that is, all \(p_i\) equal. The expression \(\big(\sum_i p_i\big)^2/\sum_i p_i^2\) is the effective-sample-size functional of Chapter 18 (Theorem 18.6) evaluated with the \(p_i\) in the role of weights; the adjusted binomial’s “sample size” \(N^{*}\) is literally the effective number of independent equal-risk trials that the unequal-risk Poisson binomial is worth. \(\square\)


Remark. Reader translation. The adjusted binomial answers the question “which single equal-risk binomial has the same mean and spread as my unequal-risk count?” Its success probability \(\pi^{*}=\nu/\lambda\) is a risk-weighted average of the individual risks, so it sits above the plain average \(\bar p\) because higher-risk patients count more toward it, and its size \(N^{*}=\lambda^2/\nu\) is the effective number of equal-risk trials the arm is worth. Both parameters are chosen so the surrogate reproduces the count’s mean and variance exactly; nothing else is promised. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why a weighting quantity reappears here. It can seem surprising that \(N^{*}=(\sum_i p_i)^2/\sum_i p_i^2\) is the same functional as the effective sample size of matching-adjusted indirect comparison (Theorem 18.6), since one is a likelihood construction and the other a weighting diagnostic. The reason is structural: both are Cauchy-Schwarz answers to “how many equal-information units are these unequal ones worth?” In MAIC the inputs are the weights \(w_i\) and the answer is how many equally weighted patients carry the same information; here the inputs are the risks \(p_i\) and the answer is how many equal-risk Bernoulli trials carry the same mean and variance. Same inequality, different inputs. To keep the two apart, read \(N^{*}\) as the likelihood effective sample size, structurally identical to the weighting effective sample size of Chapter 18 but playing a different role, not the MAIC effective sample size of any particular analysis. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. What is guaranteed, and what is not. The adjusted binomial \(\mathrm{Bin}(N^{*},\pi^{*})\) matches the Poisson binomial’s mean and variance exactly, by construction. It does not in general match the third or higher moments, and no total-variation bound of the Le Cam type (Theorem 21.3) is asserted or true for it: moment matching is a different and weaker promise than a bound on the distance between laws. The contrast with the Poisson approximation is instructive and the two should never be conflated. The Le Cam Poisson has a total-variation guarantee but the wrong variance (a Poisson has variance equal to its mean \(\lambda\), whereas the Poisson binomial has the smaller variance \(\lambda-\nu\)) and unbounded support; the adjusted binomial has the right first two moments and the correct bounded support \(\{0,\dots,N^{*}\}\) but no distance guarantee. They serve different regimes: the Poisson when \(\lambda\) and the \(p_i\) are small, the adjusted binomial when the sample size is moderate and the natural bound \(Y_\bullet\le n\) on the count is the feature that matters. In inference terms, choosing the wrong surrogate mis-scales the likelihood: the Le Cam Poisson, with variance \(\lambda>\lambda-\nu\), makes the observed count look less surprising than it is and so lets the arm speak too softly, whereas a correctly moment-matched law reports the right surprise and hence the right weight in the network. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Non-integer \(N^{*}\) and practical use. The effective sample size \(N^{*}=\lambda^2/\nu\) is generally not an integer, so \(\mathrm{Bin}(N^{*},\pi^{*})\) is used as a likelihood with a continuous size parameter, its mass function written through Gamma functions, \(P(y)=\frac{\Gamma(N^{*}+1)}{\Gamma(y+1)\,\Gamma(N^{*}-y+1)}(\pi^{*})^{y}(1-\pi^{*})^{N^{*}-y}\), which the Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler of Chapter 24 evaluates without difficulty.
A binomial with a non-integer size such as \(\mathrm{Bin}(3.7,0.45)\) looks strange at first sight; the Gamma-function form is exactly the smooth interpolation that makes sense of it, agreeing with the ordinary binomial coefficient whenever \(N^{*}\) happens to be a whole number. One caveat deserves flagging. The continuous mass is defined only for \(0\le y\le N^{*}\), and since \(N^{*}\le n\) an observed count can in principle exceed \(N^{*}\): in Example 21.5 the count \(y=5\) is possible under the true law yet falls outside the adjusted binomial’s support \(\{0,\dots,N^{*}\}=\{0,\dots,4\}\). In a real arm the reported total is a fixed number out of the real \(n\), and for the mild risk spreads usual in practice \(N^{*}\) sits close to \(n\), so \(y\le N^{*}\) holds comfortably; when it does not, the exact integrated binomial Equation 21.1 (integer \(n\), full support \(\{0,\dots,n\}\)) is the safe fallback, which is one reason implementations that anticipate occasional extreme counts prefer it.
This is the adjusted-binomial aggregate likelihood used for binary outcomes in Phillippo et al. (2020) and in the thesis Phillippo (2019) (its psoriasis case study), where the per-node event probabilities produced by the integration pipeline of Chapter 22 are summarized by their two moments \(\lambda\) and \(\nu\) and fed to Equation 21.18. Because \(N^{*}\le n\), the adjusted binomial automatically reports less information than \(n\) independent equal-risk trials would, the count-likelihood echo of the effective-sample-size deflation that weighting methods pay (Theorem 18.6). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

21.8 A fully worked aggregate binary likelihood
We carry a single AgD arm from covariate-specified individual risks to an aggregate likelihood, computing the latter three ways and laying the Le Cam Poisson alongside for contrast. Every number is exact and checkable by hand. The example is built so that the adjusted binomial has integer parameters, which keeps its mass function elementary, and so that the moment summaries \(\lambda\) and \(\nu\) come out in round numbers, which makes every law auditable by hand.

Example 21.5 (An aggregate event count by integration, exactly, and by approximation) An AgD arm reports the number of responders out of \(n=5\) patients. The study covariate distribution \(f_j\) is represented, through the integration of Chapter 22, by five equally weighted profiles, at which the individual-level model of Definition 20.1 gives the response probabilities \[
\mathbf p=(p_1,\dots,p_5)=(0.1,\ 0.3,\ 0.4,\ 0.5,\ 0.7),
\tag{21.19}\] with \(p_i=\operatorname{expit}(\eta(x_i))\) for the logit link (Definition 7.2), where \(\operatorname{expit}(z)=e^{z}/(1+e^{z})\). The five profiles span a range of risks, from a low-risk profile at \(0.1\) to a high-risk profile at \(0.7\), with average risk \(0.4\).
Patients or profiles? The five values above are a numerical summary of the arm’s covariate distribution, the integration nodes of Chapter 22, not necessarily five individual patients. We nonetheless take the reported arm size to be \(n=5\) so that every count is checkable by hand; picture a stylized arm in which each profile stands for one patient. The conditional-versus-marginal question is precisely whether we hold these five profiles fixed (the conditional Poisson binomial of route two) or regard the arm as five exchangeable draws from the covariate distribution they summarize (the integrated binomial of route one).
Step 1: the summary moments. Compute \[
\lambda=\sum_i p_i=0.1+0.3+0.4+0.5+0.7=2.0,
\qquad
\nu=\sum_i p_i^2=0.01+0.09+0.16+0.25+0.49=1.00 .
\] The aggregate response probability of Definition 20.2 is the average risk, \(\theta_\bullet=\lambda/n=2.0/5=0.4\).
Step 2: the integrated binomial (route one). Treating the five patients as an exchangeable sample from \(f_j\), Proposition 21.1 gives the aggregate count law \(\mathrm{Bin}(n,\theta_\bullet)=
\mathrm{Bin}(5,0.4)\) exactly. Its mass function \(P(y)=\binom{5}{y}(0.4)^{y}(0.6)^{5-y}\) is \[
\big(P(0),\dots,P(5)\big)=(0.07776,\ 0.25920,\ 0.34560,\ 0.23040,\ 0.07680,\ 0.01024),
\tag{21.20}\] with mean \(n\theta_\bullet=2.0\) and variance \(n\theta_\bullet(1-\theta_\bullet)=5(0.4)(0.6)=1.20\).
Step 3: the exact Poisson binomial (route two). Conditional on the five distinct profiles, the count is \(\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf p)\), whose mass function we obtain as the coefficients of the generating polynomial Equation 21.8, \[
G(z)=(0.9+0.1z)(0.7+0.3z)(0.6+0.4z)(0.5+0.5z)(0.3+0.7z).
\tag{21.21}\] Multiplying the factors in turn, \[
\begin{aligned}
(0.9+0.1z)(0.7+0.3z)&=0.63+0.34z+0.03z^2,\\
{}\times(0.6+0.4z)&=0.378+0.456z+0.154z^2+0.012z^3,\\
{}\times(0.5+0.5z)&=0.189+0.417z+0.305z^2+0.083z^3+0.006z^4,\\
{}\times(0.3+0.7z)&=0.0567+0.2574z+0.3834z^2+0.2384z^3+0.0599z^4+0.0042z^5,
\end{aligned}
\] so the exact aggregate count law is \[
\big(P(0),\dots,P(5)\big)=(0.0567,\ 0.2574,\ 0.3834,\ 0.2384,\ 0.0599,\ 0.0042).
\tag{21.22}\] As a check the coefficients sum to \(1\); the mean is \(\sum_y y\,P(y)=2.0=\lambda\) and the variance is \(\sum_y y^2 P(y)-2.0^2=5.0-4.0=1.00=\lambda-\nu\), matching Theorem 21.2. The distribution is mildly right-skewed, with third central moment \(\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)(1-2p_i)=0.12>0\), reflecting the spread of the underlying risks; this skew is one feature the two-moment surrogates of Steps 4 and 5 cannot reproduce.
Step 4: the adjusted binomial (route three). By Equation 21.18, \[
\pi^{*}=\frac{\nu}{\lambda}=\frac{1.0}{2.0}=0.5,
\qquad
N^{*}=\frac{\lambda^2}{\nu}=\frac{4.0}{1.0}=4 ,
\] an integer here by design, so the adjusted aggregate law is \(\mathrm{Bin}(4,0.5)\) with \(P(y)=\binom{4}{y}(0.5)^{4}=\binom{4}{y}/16\), \[
\big(P(0),\dots,P(4)\big)=(0.0625,\ 0.25,\ 0.375,\ 0.25,\ 0.0625),
\qquad P(5)=0 .
\tag{21.23}\] Its mean is \(N^{*}\pi^{*}=2.0\) and variance \(N^{*}\pi^{*}(1-\pi^{*})=4(0.5)(0.5)=1.00\), matching the exact Poisson binomial mean and variance by construction. Note \(N^{*}=4<5=n\), the Cauchy-Schwarz deflation of Theorem 21.4; the adjusted binomial cannot produce the count \(5\), whereas the exact Poisson binomial assigns it probability \(0.0042\).
Step 5: the Le Cam Poisson, for contrast. The matched Poisson is \(\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)=\mathrm{Poi}(2)\), with \(P(y)=e^{-2}2^{y}/y!\), \[
\big(P(0),\dots,P(5)\big)=(0.1353,\ 0.2707,\ 0.2707,\ 0.1804,\ 0.0902,\ 0.0361),\ \dots
\tag{21.24}\] its support unbounded. Its mean is \(2.0\) but its variance is \(\lambda=2.0\), far larger than the true \(1.00\): the Poisson cannot capture the underdispersion of a binary count.
Table 21.3 places the four laws side by side before we read off the reported count.



Table 21.3: The aggregate-count likelihood under the four laws of Example 21.5 (five profiles, risks \(\mathbf p=(0.1,0.3,0.4,0.5,0.7)\)). The two-moment surrogates match the exact mean and variance (\(2.00\) and \(1.00\)); the integrated binomial matches the mean but inflates the variance to \(1.20\); the Le Cam Poisson matches only the mean, and with variance \(2.00\) and unbounded support (the \(y\ge 6\) tail carries the remaining \(0.0166\)) is visibly the worst fit.

Step 6: compare the likelihoods. Suppose the arm reports \(y_\bullet=2\) responders, the modal count. The aggregate likelihood contribution under each model is the value at \(y=2\): \[
\underbrace{0.3834}_{\text{exact PoBin}},\quad
\underbrace{0.375}_{\text{adjusted }\mathrm{Bin}(4,0.5)},\quad
\underbrace{0.3456}_{\text{integrated }\mathrm{Bin}(5,0.4)},\quad
\underbrace{0.2707}_{\text{Le Cam }\mathrm{Poi}(2)} .
\] The adjusted binomial is within \(0.0084\) of the exact value, the integrated binomial within \(0.0378\), and the Le Cam Poisson off by \(0.1127\). The whole-distribution discrepancies tell the same story through the total-variation distance Equation 21.12: \[
\big\|\mathrm{PoBin}-\mathrm{Bin}(4,0.5)\big\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=0.0200,
\qquad
\big\|\mathrm{PoBin}-\mathrm{Poi}(2)\big\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=0.1707 .
\] The Le Cam bound Equation 21.14 for this arm is \(\sum_i p_i^2=\nu=1.00\), and the Barbour-Hall refinement is \(\min(1,\lambda^{-1})\nu=0.5\); both are correct (the actual distance \(0.1707\) is well below them) but far too loose to be useful, exactly the moderate-risk regime where the Poisson approximation is poor.
Step 7: reconcile the two binomials. The integrated binomial Equation 21.20 and the exact Poisson binomial Equation 21.22 share the mean \(2.0\) but differ in variance, \(1.20\) against \(1.00\). The difference is \[
n\theta_\bullet(1-\theta_\bullet)-(\lambda-\nu)=\nu-\frac{\lambda^2}{n}=1.00-\frac{4.0}{5}=0.20
=n\,s_p^2,
\] the population variance of the five risks times the sample size, \(s_p^2=\tfrac1n\nu-\bar p^2=0.20-0.16=0.04\). This is the binary shadow of the mixed-Poisson overdispersion Equation 21.5: randomizing which profile a patient occupies, as the integrated binomial does, adds variance \(n\,s_p^2\) over the conditional law that fixes one patient at each profile. The adjusted binomial Equation 21.23 tracks the conditional Poisson binomial (right variance \(1.00\)), while the integrated binomial Equation 21.20 is the exact marginal law (variance \(1.20\)); both are legitimate answers to slightly different questions, and the worked numbers make the distinction concrete. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Which likelihood to report. For a genuine exchangeable sample of patients, the integrated binomial Equation 21.20 is exact and is the default ML-NMR choice (Proposition 21.1, Phillippo et al. (2020)). When one instead conditions on a fixed set of representative profiles, as the deterministic integration nodes of Chapter 22 are, the conditional Poisson binomial is the target and the adjusted binomial Equation 21.23 is its faithful two-moment surrogate. The Le Cam Poisson is never competitive at these risks; its value is theoretical, as the sharp total-variation statement of Theorem 21.3 and as the bridge to the Poisson limit of Chapter 4. The single discipline that matters in practice is to match the variance, which both the integrated and the adjusted binomial do for their respective targets and the Poisson does not. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 21  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression II: Discrete Outcomes and Approximation Theory
text:
21.9 Notes and references
The aggregation principle of multilevel network meta-regression, and the integral form of the aggregate mean that underlies the integrated binomial likelihood Equation 21.1, are due to Phillippo et al. (2020) and the thesis Phillippo (2019); this chapter develops the discrete-outcome likelihoods that the principle requires, the material of the catalogue results H.8 to H.11. The closure of the Poisson family under convolution (Lemma 21.1) and the resulting exact conditional Poisson aggregate are classical; the moment generating function proof rests on the uniqueness and product theorems of Chapter 4 (Theorem 4.11, Theorem 4.12). The corrected statement that the marginalized aggregate count is a mixed Poisson, overdispersed by \(n\sigma_W^2\) rather than itself Poisson (Theorem 21.1), follows from the law of total variance; the closed-form relative overdispersion \(e^{\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}}-1\) under Gaussian covariates uses the log-link aggregate identity of Chapter 20 (Theorem 20.4). The negative-binomial remedy for overdispersed counts is the count-data analogue of a study-level random effect (Definition 8.3) and is standard in the generalized linear model literature (McCullagh and Nelder (1989)).
The Poisson binomial distribution and its generating function (Definition 4.11, Theorem 21.2) are textbook once the probability generating function is in hand; the chapter introduces the generating function (Definition 21.1) as the integer-valued counterpart of the moment generating function of Chapter 4 (Definition 4.7). The intractability of the exact mass function, with its \(\binom{n}{y}\) subset terms, motivates the two approximations. Le Cam’s total-variation bound (Theorem 21.3) is from Le Cam (1960); the coupling proof given here is self-contained, building on the coupling inequality (Lemma 21.3) and an explicit single-pair coupling of a Bernoulli with a Poisson, and uses the author’s own Lemma 21.1 to identify the summed Poisson coupling. The sharper bound \(\min(1,\lambda^{-1})\sum_i p_i^2\), with a matching lower bound establishing that the order is correct, is due to Barbour and Hall (1984) and is most cleanly obtained by Stein’s method for Poisson approximation, the operator technique introduced by Chen (1975) and developed at length by Barbour, Holst, and Janson (1992); these three sources are not in the book’s bibliography and are recorded in the work log as proposed additions. The adjusted two-parameter binomial obtained by moment matching (Theorem 21.4) is the binary aggregate likelihood of Phillippo et al. (2020) and Phillippo (2019) (Equation 4.6 of the thesis); its effective sample size \(N^{*}=(\sum_i p_i)^2/\sum_i p_i^2\) is the same Cauchy-Schwarz functional as the weighting effective sample size of Chapter 18 (Theorem 18.6), a pleasing recurrence of the same inequality in a different guise.
The forward connections are to the rest of Part V. The aggregate means \(\theta_{\bullet jk}\) that feed all of these likelihoods are themselves integrals that, for the logit and log links, have no elementary closed form (Theorem 20.5) and must be evaluated by the quasi-Monte Carlo machinery of Chapter 22 (Theorem 22.3, Theorem 22.2); the discrete likelihoods of this chapter sit on top of that integration. The likelihoods are assembled into the target-population estimands of Chapter 23 (Theorem 23.1) and fitted by the Bayesian computation of Chapter 24. The general-likelihood formulation of Phillippo et al. (2025) (Chapter 25, Theorem 25.7) places the binomial, Poisson, and their adjusted and overdispersed variants in a single framework, of which the count and binary cases treated here are the leading instances.
No result in this chapter has a counterpart in the companion Coq development: the ITC_Coq theories directory formalizes the causal and weighting core of Parts II to IV but not the discrete-outcome approximation theory of Part V, which is computational and analytic. Accordingly none of Lemma 21.1, Theorem 21.1, Theorem 21.2, Theorem 21.3, or Theorem 21.4 carries a machine-checked tag; their proofs are pen-and-paper and complete as given.

21.10 Exercises
A \(\star\) marks an exercise with a full worked solution in Appendix F; here the starred exercises are Exercise 21.6 and Exercise 21.8. The first three exercises are warm-ups (interpretation and likelihood selection) to fix the ideas before the computational and proof exercises that follow.

Exercise 21.1 Why unequal risks are not binomial (in words). In one or two sentences, explain to a colleague why the total number of responders among five patients with response probabilities \(0.1,0.3,0.4,0.5,0.7\) is not distributed as \(\mathrm{Bin}(5,0.4)\), even though the average risk is \(0.4\). Using Example 21.4 as a guide, say what breaks in the assumption that every patient shares one common success probability, and name the distribution that is correct.


Exercise 21.2 Choosing the aggregate likelihood. For each scenario, name the aggregate law you would use from Table 21.1 (integrated binomial, adjusted binomial, exact Poisson binomial, Le Cam Poisson, or a negative binomial) and justify the choice in one sentence. (a) A binary responder arm whose patients are an exchangeable random sample from a covariate distribution you can integrate over. (b) A binary safety endpoint (a rare adverse event, average risk about \(2\%\)) summarized at a handful of fixed integration nodes. (c) A binary responder arm represented by fixed integration nodes at moderate risks (\(0.2\) to \(0.7\)). (d) A count outcome (hospitalizations) with strong effect modifiers, where a plain Poisson badly understates the variance.


Exercise 21.3 Conditional and marginal by hand. Two profiles have response probabilities \(0.2\) and \(0.6\), equally prevalent, and the arm has \(n=2\). (a) Compute the conditional law of the count with one patient fixed at each profile (its three probabilities, mean, and variance). (b) Compute the marginal law when each patient is an independent draw from the two-profile population, and recognize it as a binomial. (c) Confirm the two laws share a mean but that the marginal variance exceeds the conditional variance by \(n\,s_p^2\), and report \(s_p^2\). Compare with Example 21.2.


Exercise 21.4 A count aggregate with a two-point covariate. A Poisson-outcome AgD arm has \(n=20\) patients and a single binary effect modifier \(x\in\{0,1\}\) with \(P(x=1)=0.5\) in the study, and log-link linear predictor \(\eta(x)=\log 2+x\log 2\), so that the conditional rate is \(W=e^{\eta(x)}\). Compute the two possible rates, the aggregate mean rate \(\theta_\bullet=\mathbb{E}[W]\), the rate variance \(\sigma_W^2\), the marginal mean \(\mathbb{E}[Y_\bullet]\) and variance \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_\bullet)\) from Equation 21.5, and the dispersion index \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_\bullet)/\mathbb{E}[Y_\bullet]\). By how many percent does ignoring the overdispersion understate the variance?


Exercise 21.5 Poisson binomial by generating function. For risks \(\mathbf p=(0.2,0.5,0.8)\), write the generating polynomial Equation 21.8, expand it to obtain the full mass function, and verify the mean and variance against Equation 21.10. Compare the mass function to that of the binomial \(\mathrm{Bin}(3,\bar p)\) with the same mean (\(\bar p=0.5\)): which has the larger variance, and why does the remark after Theorem 21.2 predict this?


Exercise 21.6 (\(\star\)) The coupling, the bound, and its sharpness. (a) Verify directly from Equation 21.15 that the single-pair coupling has Bernoulli and Poisson marginals and disagreement probability \(p(1-e^{-p})\). (b) Prove the coupling inequality Equation 21.13 and deduce Equation 21.14 for a general risk vector. (c) For the equal-risk case \(p_i\equiv p\), show the bound becomes \(\|\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)-\mathrm{Poi}(np)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le np^2\) and relate this to the Poisson limit theorem Theorem 4.13. (d) Using a second-order expansion \(1-e^{-p}=p-\tfrac12 p^2+O(p^3)\), argue that the per-pair disagreement is \(p^2-\tfrac12 p^3+O(p^4)\), so the bound \(\sum_i p_i^2\) is tight to leading order in small risks.


Exercise 21.7 Computing and reading the adjusted binomial. For \(\mathbf p=(0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8)\) compute \(\lambda\), \(\nu\), \(\pi^{*}\), and \(N^{*}\) from Equation 21.18, confirm \(N^{*}\le n\), and evaluate the adjusted-binomial mass at the count \(y=2\) using the Gamma-function form of the binomial mass when \(N^{*}\) is not an integer. Compare with the exact Poisson binomial mass at \(y=2\) (compute it from the generating polynomial), and report the total-variation distance between the exact and adjusted laws.


Exercise 21.8 (\(\star\)) Moment matching stops at two. The third central moment of \(\mathrm{Bin}(N,\pi)\) is \(N\pi(1-\pi)(1-2\pi)\), and that of \(\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf p)\) is \(\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)(1-2p_i)\). (a) Prove the Poisson binomial formula from the generating function Equation 21.8 or from the independence of the Bernoulli summands. (b) For the risk vector \(\mathbf p=(0.1,0.3,0.4,0.5,0.7)\) of Example 21.5, compute the Poisson binomial third central moment and the adjusted-binomial third central moment from the matched parameters \((N^{*},\pi^{*})=(4,0.5)\), and show they differ: the adjusted binomial is symmetric so its third central moment is zero, whereas the Poisson binomial has third central moment \(\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)(1-2p_i)=0.12>0\), a right skew the surrogate misses. Conclude that no choice of \((N,\pi)\) can match three moments of a generic Poisson binomial, so the adjusted binomial is genuinely a two-moment surrogate, consistent with the remark after Theorem 21.4 that no total-variation guarantee is available.


Exercise 21.9 Overdispersion under Gaussian covariates. A Poisson-outcome arm has \(\theta_\bullet=3\) events per patient on average and a single continuous covariate with total slope \(\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}=0.5\) and within-study standard deviation \(\sigma=0.8\), so \(s^2=\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}^2\sigma^2\). Using Equation 21.6, compute the squared coefficient of variation of the rate, the per-patient excess variance \(\sigma_W^2\), and the dispersion index \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_\bullet)/\mathbb{E}[Y_\bullet]\) for \(n=50\) patients. State the value of \(s^2\) below which the dispersion index stays under \(1.05\), and interpret it as a tolerance on the effect-modifier strength.

title: 22  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression III: Numerical Integration Theory
text:
22.1 Introduction
Here is the practical problem this chapter solves, stated for a health researcher before any mathematics. Picture an aggregate-data trial of a new plaque-psoriasis drug that publishes only summaries: the mean patient age, the mean baseline severity score, and the proportion of patients who are biomarker-positive. We want the average probability that a patient on this arm achieves a treatment response, so that the trial can be entered into a network and the drug compared indirectly against its competitors. Because the response probability is a nonlinear (logistic) function of a patient’s covariates, that average is an integral over the arm’s covariate distribution; and if we compute the integral badly, the modeled response rate is wrong, the odds ratio of this drug versus a comparator is wrong, and the reimbursement recommendation a health technology assessment (HTA) agency issues on the strength of that odds ratio is wrong. This chapter is the mathematics of computing that integral well. Its organizing idea, which we announce now and prove at the end (Section 22.10), is that the covariate points at which we evaluate the model are chosen once, deterministically, and reused unchanged at every step of the model fit. That single decision, invisible in the statement of the integral, is exactly what separates the method used in practice from a naive random simulation, and it is the reason the chapter builds toward deterministic quasi-Monte Carlo rather than stopping at ordinary Monte Carlo.
Chapter 20 reduced the entire aggregate-data contribution of multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR) to a single integral. For an aggregate-data (AgD) study \(j\) reporting an arm \(k\) with covariate density \(f_j\), the aggregate-level mean outcome is the response-scale average of the individual conditional mean (Definition 20.2), \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}\;=\;\int_{\mathcal{X}} g^{-1}\big(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})\big)\,f_j(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
\qquad
\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})=\mu_j+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_1+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,k}+\gamma_k,
\tag{22.1}\] and the aggregation theorem (Theorem 20.1) showed that the AgD likelihood is built from this one quantity. The aggregation-bias theorem (Theorem 20.2) explained why the integral cannot be shortcut by plugging the covariate mean into \(g^{-1}\): for a nonlinear link the average of \(g^{-1}(\eta)\) is not \(g^{-1}\) of the average. Two links escaped: the identity link, where Equation 22.1 collapses to a function of the mean alone (Theorem 20.3), and the log link with jointly Gaussian covariates, where the moment generating function (Definition 4.7) supplies a closed form (Theorem 20.4). The link that matters most for health technology assessment, the logit, escaped neither: Equation 22.1 has no elementary closed form for any non-degenerate covariate distribution (Theorem 20.5). The discrete-outcome aggregate likelihoods of Chapter 21, the Poisson and Poisson-binomial constructions (Theorem 21.1, Theorem 21.2) and their approximations (Theorem 21.3, Theorem 21.4), all rest on the same integral through the success probabilities \(p_{ijk}=g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}))\). ML-NMR is therefore only as good as our ability to evaluate Equation 22.1 numerically. This chapter builds that ability from the ground up and proves the error guarantees that make it trustworthy.
Two features of the problem dictate the machinery. First, the dimension. The integral runs over \(\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\) where \(d\) is the number of covariates entered into the model, typically three to ten. Deterministic product quadrature, which is essentially perfect in one dimension, collapses under the curse of dimensionality: \(k\) nodes per axis means \(k^{d}\) nodes in total, and the cost of a fixed accuracy grows exponentially in \(d\) (Theorem 22.1, Corollary 22.1). Plain Monte Carlo (MC) integration escapes the curse with a dimension-free root-mean-square error of order \(N^{-1/2}\) (Theorem 22.2), but \(N^{-1/2}\) is slow, and, more damagingly, the re-randomization it requires injects noise into the likelihood and destroys the smooth Hamiltonian that gradient-based Markov chain Monte Carlo needs (Definition 8.9, Carpenter et al. (2017)). Quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) keeps a single deterministic point set and replaces randomness by uniformity, achieving an error of order \((\log N)^{d}/N\), nearly \(1/N\), governed by the Koksma-Hlawka inequality (Theorem 22.3) and realized by low-discrepancy sequences such as Sobol’ points (Definition 22.3). This is the integration rule used throughout ML-NMR.
Second, the input. We do not know \(f_j\). An AgD study reports marginal summaries of each covariate, a mean and sometimes a standard deviation or a proportion, but almost never the joint distribution. The device that turns marginal information into a full joint law is the copula. Sklar’s theorem (Theorem 22.5) separates any joint distribution into its marginals and a copula carrying the dependence; the Gaussian copula (Definition 22.5) supplies a default dependence structure parameterized by a correlation matrix borrowed from individual patient data (IPD) or expert judgment; and the probability integral transform (Theorem 22.4) maps uniform inputs onto whatever marginal distribution each covariate is assumed to follow. Assembling these pieces gives the ML-NMR integration pipeline (Theorem 22.6): generate Sobol’ points in the unit hypercube, push them through a Gaussian copula and inverse-CDF margins to land at covariate vectors distributed as \(f_j\), and average \(g^{-1}(\eta_{jk})\) over them. We close with a fully worked logit example whose every node, weight, and running estimate the reader can reproduce by hand, and a two-covariate trace that exhibits the copula step explicitly.
Throughout, \(g\) is the link function (Definition 7.2), \(\eta_{jk}\) the linear predictor of the individual model (Definition 20.1), and \(\Phi,\phi\) the standard normal distribution and density functions. We write \(\mathrm{expit}(z)=g^{-1}(z)=e^{z}/(1+e^{z})\) for the inverse logit, also called the logistic function; a health researcher meets it as the map that turns a log-odds back into a probability. The covariate density and distribution functions of study \(j\) are \(f_j\) and \(F_j\), with marginal distribution functions \(F_{j,1},\dots,F_{j,d}\) and covariate correlation matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j\), all from Notation. This chapter corresponds to results H.12 to H.19 of the proof catalogue.
We fix one concrete scenario now and return to it at every transition, so that each abstract object acquires a definite job. It is the running thread of the chapter.
What this chapter will do, in order. The path from the integral to a trustworthy number has two halves, a numerical half and a dependence-modeling half, and they meet in the pipeline of Section 22.10.

title: 22  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression III: Numerical Integration Theory
text:
Example 22.1 (Running example: an aggregate psoriasis arm) An aggregate-data (AgD) trial arm of a psoriasis biologic reports three covariate summaries and nothing about their joint distribution: mean age \(45\) years (standard deviation \(12\)), mean baseline severity score \(18\) (standard deviation \(6\)), and proportion biomarker-positive \(0.30\). So \(d=3\) covariates enter the model: \(x_1=\text{age}\), \(x_2=\text{baseline severity}\), \(x_3=\text{biomarker status}\). From an individual-patient-data (IPD) study in the same network we have fitted the individual model, a logistic regression whose linear predictor \(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})\) combines a study baseline, prognostic effects, and treatment-by-covariate interactions (the effect modifiers), and from that IPD study we also borrow a covariate correlation matrix, say age and severity correlated at \(0.3\). Our target is the arm’s average response probability \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{expit}\big(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})\big)\,f_j(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
\] the number that, contrasted with the same quantity on a comparator arm, becomes the odds ratio the HTA agency will act on. Everything the chapter builds is in service of computing this one integral: the margins (\(x_1,x_2\) modeled as normal from the reported means and standard deviations, \(x_3\) as a Bernoulli from the reported proportion) fix each covariate’s own distribution; the copula supplies the missing dependence (which ages tend to accompany which severities); the Sobol’ nodes are the covariate profiles at which we evaluate \(\mathrm{expit}(\eta_{jk})\); and the average over those profiles is \(\theta_{\bullet jk}\). In Section 22.11 we carry a stripped-down version of this arm, a single standardized severity covariate, all the way through the arithmetic to a final number a reader can check by hand. \(\blacktriangleleft\)



Show why a covariate grid is hopeless beyond a few covariates (Section 22.3).
Escape the curse with random Monte Carlo, then see why its noise is fatal inside a Bayesian fit (Section 22.4).
Replace random points with evenly spread deterministic ones and bound the error by the Koksma-Hlawka inequality (Section 22.5), realized by Sobol’ nets (Section 22.6).
Build synthetic covariate profiles from an AgD study’s summaries using the probability integral transform (Section 22.7), Sklar’s theorem (Section 22.8), and the Gaussian copula (Section 22.9).
Assemble the pipeline and prove its error bound (Section 22.10), then compute a full logit example by hand (Section 22.11).

section: 22.2 Reducing the aggregation integral to the unit cube
text:
22.2 Reducing the aggregation integral to the unit cube
Every method in this chapter computes an integral against a probability density. It is convenient to fix, once, the two equivalent forms in which Equation 22.1 will appear. The first is the expectation form \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}\sim f_j}\big[g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{X}))\big],
\tag{22.2}\] which is what MC estimates directly by sampling \(\mathbf{X}\). The second is the unit-cube form. Suppose we have a map \(T:[0,1]^{d}\to\mathcal{X}\) that transports the uniform distribution on the cube to \(f_j\), in the sense that \(\mathbf{X}=T(\mathbf{U})\) has density \(f_j\) whenever \(\mathbf{U}\) is uniform on \([0,1]^{d}\). In plain terms, \(T\) is the recipe that turns a list of uniform numbers between \(0\) and \(1\) into a plausible covariate profile for the aggregate study: feed it \((0.5,0.5,0.5)\) and it returns a patient of median age, median severity, and so on; feed it a whole grid of uniform inputs and it returns a whole cloud of synthetic patients whose distribution matches \(f_j\). Constructing this recipe from the marginal and correlation summaries an AgD study reports is the entire job of Section 22.8 to Section 22.10.
Then, writing \(\varphi:=g^{-1}\circ\eta_{jk}\) for the integrand on covariate space and \(\psi:=\varphi\circ T\) for its pullback to the cube (the same integrand, re-expressed as a function of the uniform inputs \(\mathbf{u}\) rather than of the covariates \(\mathbf{x}=T(\mathbf{u})\)), the change-of-variables identity gives \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}
=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\varphi(\mathbf{x})\,f_j(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}
=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{U}\sim\mathrm{Unif}([0,1]^{d})}\big[\psi(\mathbf{U})\big]
=\int_{[0,1]^{d}}\psi(\mathbf{u})\,d\mathbf{u}.
\tag{22.3}\]
All Equation 22.3 does is rename the variable of integration: the same average, first written over covariate space with weight \(f_j\), is rewritten over the unit cube with the flat (uniform) weight, at the price of pushing the covariate values through the recipe \(T\) inside the integrand. It is worth seeing a first number before the machinery. Take the running example (Example 22.1) stripped to a single standardized severity covariate with a standard normal margin, so \(T=\Phi^{-1}\) and, with a treatment arm whose linear predictor is \(\eta(x)=0.5+x\), the integrand on the cube is \(\psi(u)=\mathrm{expit}\big(0.5+\Phi^{-1}(u)\big)\). Three evenly spread inputs already give a rough answer:



\(u\)
\(x=\Phi^{-1}(u)\)
\(\psi(u)=\mathrm{expit}(0.5+x)\)




\(0.25\)
\(-0.6745\)
\(0.4565\)


\(0.50\)
\(0\)
\(0.6225\)


\(0.75\)
\(0.6745\)
\(0.7640\)



Their average is \(0.6143\), already within about \(0.012\) of the true value \(\theta_\bullet=0.6020\) that Section 22.11 computes carefully. Everything between here and there is about choosing those input points so that the average converges fast and smoothly, and about building \(T\) for realistic multi-covariate arms.
The whole of the dependence-modeling apparatus, Sklar’s theorem, the Gaussian copula, and the inverse-CDF transform, exists to construct the transport map \(T\) from the marginal and correlation summaries that an AgD study reports; that construction is Section 22.8 to Section 22.10. The whole of the numerical apparatus, quadrature, MC, and QMC, exists to approximate the cube integral on the right of Equation 22.3 by a finite average over points \(\{\mathbf{u}^{(n)}\}_{n=1}^{N}\subset[0,1]^{d}\), \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}\approx\widehat\theta_{\bullet jk}^{(N)}
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\psi(\mathbf{u}^{(n)})
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}g^{-1}\big(\eta_{jk}(T(\mathbf{u}^{(n)}))\big);
\tag{22.4}\] that approximation, and its error, is Section 22.3 to Section 22.6. The single design decision that ties the two halves together, and that distinguishes ML-NMR from a naive simulation, is that the point set \(\{\mathbf{u}^{(n)}\}\) and the covariate nodes \(\{T(\mathbf{u}^{(n)})\}\) are fixed in advance and reused at every evaluation of the likelihood; only \(\eta_{jk}\), through the parameter vector \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\), changes as the sampler explores the posterior. We return to the consequences of that decision in Section 22.10.
One notational caution before the numerical theory. The next three sections (Section 22.3 to Section 22.5) are general facts about integrating a function over an interval or a cube, so they call that function a generic \(f\), in keeping with the numerical-analysis literature. This generic integrand \(f\) is not the covariate density: our covariate density is \(f_j\), and the specific integrand those theorems get applied to is the ML-NMR pullback \(\psi\) of Equation 22.3. When in doubt, \(f\) inside a quadrature or discrepancy theorem means “whatever function is being integrated,” and for us that function is \(\psi\).

title: 22  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression III: Numerical Integration Theory
section: 22.3 Gaussian quadrature and the curse of dimensionality
text:
22.3 Gaussian quadrature and the curse of dimensionality
This section answers the first question a numerically minded reader asks: why not just lay down a grid of covariate values, evaluate the model on the grid, and average? In one dimension a well-chosen grid is not merely adequate, it is superb, and we prove exactly how superb. The catch is that the obvious way to build a grid in several dimensions multiplies its size beyond reach, and that failure is what forces the rest of the chapter. We begin with the gold standard for one-dimensional integration of a smooth function and then show why it does not survive the passage to several covariates. The rule is Gauss-Legendre quadrature: choose \(k\) nodes and \(k\) weights, \(2k\) numbers in all, and spend that budget so as to integrate exactly every polynomial of degree up to \(2k-1\). That maximal exactness is what gives Gauss quadrature its super-algebraic accuracy on smooth integrands.
We prove the one-dimensional error formula in full, even though the curse of dimensionality will make us abandon the method, because its error structure is the benchmark against which Monte Carlo and quasi-Monte Carlo are measured for the rest of the chapter: it is the accuracy we are trading away in exchange for freedom from the dimension. The proof uses two classical facts about the Legendre polynomials \(P_0,P_1,P_2,\dots\), the orthogonal polynomials on \([-1,1]\) (each \(P_k\) has degree \(k\), and \(\int_{-1}^{1}P_k(x)q(x)\,dx=0\) for every polynomial \(q\) of degree below \(k\); this orthogonality is the one property we use). The second tool is Hermite interpolation: given \(k\) nodes, the unique polynomial of degree at most \(2k-1\) that matches both \(f\) and its derivative \(f'\) at every node, whose remainder we quote in the proof. Both are standard (Stoer and Bulirsch, Section 3.6, cited in Section 22.12); a reader willing to take the error formula Equation 22.5 on faith can skip the proof and lose nothing needed later.

Theorem 22.1 (Gauss-Legendre quadrature error) Let \(f\in C^{2k}[-1,1]\), that is, \(f\) has \(2k\) continuous derivatives on \([-1,1]\). Let \(x_1,\dots,x_k\) be the \(k\) roots of the Legendre polynomial \(P_k\) (orthogonal on \([-1,1]\) with respect to Lebesgue measure), and let \(w_1,\dots,w_k>0\) be the unique weights for which the rule \[
Q_k[f]:=\sum_{i=1}^{k} w_i\,f(x_i)
\] is exact on polynomials of degree at most \(k-1\). Then:

(Degree of exactness.) \(Q_k[p]=\int_{-1}^{1}p(x)\,dx\) for every polynomial \(p\) of degree at most \(2k-1\).
(Error formula.) There exists \(\xi\in(-1,1)\) such that \[
\int_{-1}^{1} f(x)\,dx-Q_k[f]
=\frac{2^{2k+1}\,(k!)^{4}}{(2k+1)\,[(2k)!]^{3}}\;f^{(2k)}(\xi).
\tag{22.5}\]
(Composite order.) If \([-1,1]\) is partitioned into panels of width \(h\) and the \(k\)-node rule is applied on each panel, the total error is \(O(h^{2k})\) as \(h\to 0\) with \(k\) fixed and \(f^{(2k)}\) bounded.



Proof. Part 1. The defining property of the Legendre polynomial \(P_k\) is orthogonality: \(\int_{-1}^{1}P_k(x)q(x)\,dx=0\) for every polynomial \(q\) with \(\deg q<k\) (a classical fact about orthogonal polynomials; see the references). Let \(p\) have \(\deg p\le 2k-1\). Polynomial division by \(P_k\) writes \(p=q\,P_k+r\) with \(\deg q\le k-1\) and \(\deg r\le k-1\). Integrating, \[
\int_{-1}^{1}p=\int_{-1}^{1}q\,P_k+\int_{-1}^{1}r=0+\int_{-1}^{1}r,
\] the first integral vanishing by orthogonality since \(\deg q<k\). Evaluating the rule, and using \(P_k(x_i)=0\) at every node, \[
Q_k[p]=\sum_i w_i\big(q(x_i)P_k(x_i)+r(x_i)\big)=\sum_i w_i\,r(x_i)=Q_k[r].
\] Because \(\deg r\le k-1\), the rule integrates \(r\) exactly by its defining property, so \(Q_k[r]=\int_{-1}^{1}r\). Combining, \(Q_k[p]=\int_{-1}^{1}r=\int_{-1}^{1}p\).
Part 2. Let \(H\) be the Hermite interpolating polynomial of degree at most \(2k-1\) that matches \(f\) and \(f'\) at each node: \(H(x_i)=f(x_i)\) and \(H'(x_i)=f'(x_i)\) for \(i=1,\dots,k\). The Hermite remainder formula states that for each \(x\in[-1,1]\) there is \(\zeta_x\in(-1,1)\) with \[
f(x)-H(x)=\frac{f^{(2k)}(\zeta_x)}{(2k)!}\,\omega(x)^{2},
\qquad \omega(x):=\prod_{i=1}^{k}(x-x_i).
\] Since \(\deg H\le 2k-1\), Part 1 gives \(Q_k[H]=\int_{-1}^{1}H\), and since \(H(x_i)=f(x_i)\) we have \(Q_k[H]=Q_k[f]\). Therefore \[
\int_{-1}^{1}f-Q_k[f]=\int_{-1}^{1}(f-H)
=\frac{1}{(2k)!}\int_{-1}^{1}f^{(2k)}(\zeta_x)\,\omega(x)^{2}\,dx.
\] The kernel \(\omega(x)^{2}\ge 0\), so the integral mean value theorem yields a single \(\xi\in(-1,1)\) with \[
\int_{-1}^{1}f-Q_k[f]=\frac{f^{(2k)}(\xi)}{(2k)!}\int_{-1}^{1}\omega(x)^{2}\,dx.
\] It remains to evaluate \(\int_{-1}^{1}\omega^{2}\). The nodes are the roots of \(P_k\), so \(\omega\) is the monic Legendre polynomial: \(\omega=P_k/c_k\), where \(c_k=\dfrac{(2k)!}{2^{k}(k!)^{2}}\) is the leading coefficient of the standard Legendre polynomial. With the normalization \(\int_{-1}^{1}P_k(x)^{2}\,dx=\dfrac{2}{2k+1}\), \[
\int_{-1}^{1}\omega(x)^{2}\,dx=\frac{1}{c_k^{2}}\int_{-1}^{1}P_k^{2}
=\frac{2^{2k}(k!)^{4}}{[(2k)!]^{2}}\cdot\frac{2}{2k+1}
=\frac{2^{2k+1}(k!)^{4}}{(2k+1)[(2k)!]^{2}}.
\] Dividing by \((2k)!\) gives the constant in Equation 22.5.
Part 3. On a panel \([a,a+h]\) substitute \(x=a+\tfrac{h}{2}(1+t)\), so \(\int_a^{a+h}f=\tfrac{h}{2}\int_{-1}^{1}\tilde f(t)\,dt\) with \(\tilde f(t)=f(a+\tfrac{h}{2}(1+t))\) and \(\tilde f^{(2k)}=(h/2)^{2k}f^{(2k)}\). Applying Part 2 to \(\tilde f\), the panel error is \[
\frac{h}{2}\cdot\frac{2^{2k+1}(k!)^{4}}{(2k+1)[(2k)!]^{3}}\Big(\tfrac{h}{2}\Big)^{2k}f^{(2k)}(\xi_a)
=C_k\,h^{2k+1}f^{(2k)}(\xi_a),
\] with \(C_k=\dfrac{(k!)^{4}}{(2k+1)[(2k)!]^{3}}\) a constant depending only on \(k\). Summing over the \(2/h\) panels and bounding \(|f^{(2k)}|\) by its supremum, \[
\Big|\int_{-1}^{1}f-\sum_{\text{panels}}Q_k\Big|
\le \frac{2}{h}\cdot C_k\,h^{2k+1}\sup_{[-1,1]}|f^{(2k)}|
=2\,C_k\,h^{2k}\sup_{[-1,1]}|f^{(2k)}|=O(h^{2k}).\qquad\square
\]


Remark. What “order \(2k\)” buys, and what it cannot. The single-interval constant Equation 22.5 decays super-exponentially in \(k\): by Stirling’s approximation \(\dfrac{2^{2k+1}(k!)^{4}}{(2k+1)[(2k)!]^{3}}\sim\dfrac{\pi}{4^{2k}\,(2k)!}\) up to lower-order factors, so for an analytic integrand whose derivatives satisfy \(|f^{(2k)}|\le (2k)!\,R^{-2k}\) (radius of convergence \(R>1\)) the error falls like \(R^{-2k}\), geometric in the number of nodes. This is the spectral accuracy that makes a handful of Gauss nodes integrate a smooth one-dimensional function to machine precision. The composite reading of Part 3, error \(O(h^{2k})\) at fixed \(k\), is the form quoted in the catalogue; it is the relevant one when the integrand has limited smoothness and one refines the mesh rather than raising the node count. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The trouble is that ML-NMR integrates over several covariates at once, and the only elementary way to lift a one-dimensional rule to \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) is to take a tensor product: place a grid of \(k^{d}\) nodes, one factor per axis. The accuracy per axis is inherited, but the node count is not.

Corollary 22.1 (The curse of dimensionality for product quadrature) Let \(f\in C^{2k}([-1,1]^{d})\) with all pure \(2k\)-th order partial derivatives bounded. The tensor-product Gauss-Legendre rule with \(k\) nodes per axis uses \(N=k^{d}\) function evaluations and has error \[
\Big|\int_{[-1,1]^{d}} f-\sum_{i_1=1}^{k}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{k} w_{i_1}\cdots w_{i_d}\,
f(x_{i_1},\dots,x_{i_d})\Big|=O\!\big(k^{-2k}\big)=O\!\big(N^{-2k/d}\big).
\] For fixed per-axis budget \(k\), the exponent \(2k/d\) of \(N\) degrades with the dimension \(d\); equivalently, to hold the error at a tolerance \(\epsilon\) the cost grows like \(N=k^{d}\), exponentially in \(d\).


Proof. Write the cube integral as an iterated integral and apply Theorem 22.1 one axis at a time. Holding \(x_2,\dots,x_d\) fixed, the one-dimensional rule in \(x_1\) incurs error bounded by \(E_k\sup|\partial_1^{2k} f|\), where \(E_k=\frac{2^{2k+1}(k!)^4}{(2k+1)[(2k)!]^3}\) is the single-interval constant; integrating that bound over the remaining axes and then quadrating them in turn, the total error is at most \(E_k\sum_{m=1}^{d}\sup|\partial_m^{2k} f|\cdot 2^{d-1}\), a finite multiple of \(E_k=O(k^{-2k})\); the factor \(2^{d-1}\) is the product of the interval lengths accumulated as each already-quadrated axis contributes its width \(2\) to the bound. Writing the node count as \(N=k^{d}\), so that \(k=N^{1/d}\), the error \(O(k^{-2k})\) becomes \(O(N^{-2k/d})\). \(\square\)

The exponent \(2k/d\) tells the whole story, and it is worth reading carefully because it is easy to misread. With \(k\) held fixed, \(-2k/d\) is a constant, so refining a product grid does not improve the rate with \(N\); and raising \(k\) to sharpen the per-axis accuracy is self-defeating, because it also multiplies the node count \(N=k^{d}\). In one dimension a five-node rule (\(k=5\)) integrates a smooth function with error \(O(N^{-10})\), spectacular; in ten dimensions the same per-axis rule needs \(N=5^{10}\approx 10^{7}\) nodes just to place five points on each axis, and reaching error \(O(N^{-1})\) is all one can hope for. To make the threshold concrete, return to the running example (Example 22.1). Three covariates at five nodes each is \(5^{3}=125\) nodes, which sounds harmless. But this integral is not evaluated once. It is evaluated once per AgD arm; a plaque-psoriasis network may carry a dozen AgD arms; and the whole set of integrals is recomputed at every leapfrog step of every iteration of the Markov chain Monte Carlo fit, tens of thousands of times. At \(d=3\) the \(125\)-node grid is tolerable, but real ML-NMR analyses reach into more covariates: in a plaque-psoriasis network the effect modifiers may include age, baseline severity, disease duration, weight, and biomarker status; in a network of newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM) treatments they may include age, disease stage, and cytogenetic risk. At \(d=8\), five nodes per axis is \(5^{8}\approx 3.9\times
10^{5}\) nodes, multiplied again by arms and by tens of thousands of posterior evaluations: product quadrature is out. ML-NMR routinely runs at \(d=3\) to \(10\), and the next two sections develop the two ways around the curse, both of which decouple the error rate from \(d\) in the exponent.

Remark. Why this matters for indirect comparison. Everything downstream of ML-NMR depends on \(\theta_{\bullet jk}\) being right. It is the modeled event rate on an AgD arm; the contrast of two such rates on the linear-predictor scale is the relative effect that the network synthesizes, and it is the number an HTA agency reads as the odds ratio of one drug versus another. A biased integral biases that odds ratio and can flip a cost-effectiveness verdict. Product quadrature would in principle deliver the integral to near-machine precision, but at the dimensions and repetition counts of a real network it is computationally impossible, which is exactly why the reliable-but-slow and reliable-but-fast alternatives of the following sections are needed rather than merely nice to have. \(\blacktriangleleft\)
