title: 23  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression IV: Estimands, Identifiability, and Generality
text:
23.9 A worked target-population estimate
We carry a complete target-population calculation from a fitted ML-NMR model to relative effects in two different target populations, choosing a single binary effect modifier so that every integral is a two-term sum and every number can be checked with a calculator. The example exhibits, concretely, the three phenomena of Theorem 23.1: integration over a target covariate distribution (part a), the conditional contrast depending only on the covariate mean (part b), and the marginal contrast on a non-collapsible scale being genuinely population-specific (part c).

Example 23.3 (Population-adjusted estimates in two target populations) A connected network with an IPD trial on \(\{A,C\}\) and an AgD trial on \(\{B,C\}\) has been fitted under SEMA on the logit scale, with a single binary effect modifier \(X\in\{0,1\}\). This is the anticoagulant network of Example 23.1: \(A\) the new oral anticoagulant, \(B\) warfarin, \(C\) the shared comparator, the event a major bleed, and \(X=1\) an older patient. Throughout, \(\operatorname{expit}(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\) is the inverse-logit, so \(\operatorname{expit}(\eta)\) is the modeled bleeding probability at linear predictor \(\eta\). The fitted network-level coefficients (treated as exact for transparency, as in the worked examples of Chapters 18 and 19) are \[
\boldsymbol\beta_1=0.4,\quad \boldsymbol\beta_2=0.5,\quad \gamma_A=0.8,\quad \gamma_B=0.3,\quad \gamma_C=0,
\] so the arm linear predictors in a population with reference baseline \(\mu_{*}\) are, by Equation 23.4, \[
\eta_C(x)=\mu_{*}+0.4x,\quad
\eta_A(x)=\mu_{*}+0.4x+0.8+0.5x,\quad
\eta_B(x)=\mu_{*}+0.4x+0.3+0.5x.
\] The outcome is unfavorable (the event is bad), so on the logit scale a larger value of an active-versus-\(C\) contrast means the active treatment raises the odds of the bad event relative to \(C\).
Target \(\mathcal P^{*}\): \(\Pr(X=1)=0.6\), baseline \(\mu_{*}=-0.5\). The linear predictors and their inverse-logits at the two covariate values are \[
\begin{array}{llll}
\eta_C(0)=-0.5, & \operatorname{expit}=0.377541; & \eta_C(1)=-0.1, & \operatorname{expit}=0.475021;\\
\eta_A(0)=\ \ 0.3, & \operatorname{expit}=0.574443; & \eta_A(1)=\ \ 1.2, & \operatorname{expit}=0.768525;\\
\eta_B(0)=-0.2, & \operatorname{expit}=0.450166; & \eta_B(1)=\ \ 0.7, & \operatorname{expit}=0.668188.
\end{array}
\] The target arm means Equation 23.4 are the \(0.4/0.6\) weighted averages over \(X\): \[
\bar\theta_C=0.4(0.377541)+0.6(0.475021)=0.436029,
\] \[
\bar\theta_A=0.4(0.574443)+0.6(0.768525)=0.690892,\qquad
\bar\theta_B=0.4(0.450166)+0.6(0.668188)=0.580979.
\] Their logits are \(g(\bar\theta_C)=-0.257295\), \(g(\bar\theta_A)=0.804292\), \(g(\bar\theta_B)=0.326794\), so the target marginal contrasts Equation 23.5 are \[
\Delta_{CA}(\mathcal P^{*})=0.804292-(-0.257295)=1.061587\quad(A\text{ versus }C),
\] \[
\Delta_{CB}(\mathcal P^{*})=0.326794-(-0.257295)=0.584089\quad(B\text{ versus }C),
\] \[
\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})=0.804292-0.326794=0.477498\quad(A\text{ versus }B).
\] The anchored identity holds exactly: \(\Delta_{CA}-\Delta_{CB}=1.061587-0.584089=0.477498=\Delta_{BA}\), confirming that the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) marginal effect is the difference of the two active-versus-\(C\) marginal effects in the same population, the network-consistency relation that licenses the indirect comparison. In words, in this older target (60 percent of patients in the older band) the model says the new drug \(A\) raises the odds of a major bleed relative to \(C\) by a marginal log odds ratio of \(1.06\) (an odds ratio near \(2.9\)), warfarin \(B\) raises them by \(0.58\) (odds ratio near \(1.8\)), and \(A\) versus \(B\) is a marginal log odds ratio of \(0.48\) (odds ratio near \(1.6\)): the new drug bleeds more than warfarin in this population.
The conditional contrasts. By Equation 23.7 the population-average conditional contrasts on the logit scale depend only on the covariate mean \(\bar x_{*}=0.6\): \[
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{CA}=\gamma_A+\boldsymbol\beta_2\bar x_{*}=0.8+0.5(0.6)=1.1,\quad
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{CB}=0.3+0.5(0.6)=0.6,\quad
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{BA}=\gamma_A-\gamma_B=0.5.
\] The \(A\)-versus-\(B\) conditional contrast is the SEMA constant \(0.5\) of Equation 23.8, with the interaction terms canceling. The marginal \(A\)-versus-\(B\) effect \(0.477498\) is smaller in magnitude than the conditional \(0.5\): a non-collapsibility gap of \(0.022502\), the attenuation toward the null that marginalizing a logistic model over a covariate produces (Definition 7.7, Theorem 20.2). For the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) contrast the gap is \(1.1-1.061587=0.038413\).
Target \(\mathcal P^{**}\): \(\Pr(X=1)=0.2\), same baseline \(\mu_{*}=-0.5\). The inverse-logits are unchanged (the linear predictors do not depend on the population’s covariate distribution); only the averaging weights change, to \(0.8/0.2\): \[
\bar\theta_C=0.397037,\qquad \bar\theta_A=0.613259,\qquad \bar\theta_B=0.493770,
\] with logits \(-0.417828\), \(0.461032\), \(-0.024920\), giving marginal contrasts \[
\Delta_{CA}(\mathcal P^{**})=0.878860,\qquad
\Delta_{CB}(\mathcal P^{**})=0.392908,\qquad
\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{**})=0.485952.
\] The conditional contrasts move with the new mean \(\bar x_{*}=0.2\): \(\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{CA}=0.8+0.5(0.2)=0.9\) and \(\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{CB}=0.3+0.5(0.2)=0.4\), while \(\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{BA}=\gamma_A-\gamma_B=0.5\) as before.
What the two targets show. The \(A\)-versus-\(C\) estimate is genuinely population-specific: its conditional value moves from \(1.1\) in \(\mathcal P^{*}\) to \(0.9\) in \(\mathcal P^{**}\), and its marginal value from \(1.061587\) to \(0.878860\), simply because the effect modifier \(X\) has a different mean in the two populations and \(\boldsymbol\beta_2\neq 0\). This is effect modification transported: the same fitted model gives different relative effects in different target populations, which is exactly the flexibility of Theorem 23.1(a) that MAIC and STC, locked to the comparator population, do not offer. The \(A\)-versus-\(B\) conditional contrast, by contrast, is pinned at \(\gamma_A-\gamma_B=0.5\) in both populations by SEMA (Equation 23.8); yet its marginal value still drifts, from \(0.477498\) to \(0.485952\), a residual population dependence that is pure non-collapsibility (Theorem 23.1(c)): even with the conditional effect fixed, the marginal odds ratio depends on the covariate spread and baseline risk of the target. A practitioner reporting a marginal odds ratio must therefore name the target population; a practitioner reporting the conditional log odds ratio under SEMA may quote the single number \(0.5\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Baseline risk also matters, on a non-collapsible scale. Repeating the \(\mathcal P^{*}\) calculation (\(\Pr(X=1)=0.6\)) but with a high-risk baseline \(\mu_{*}=1.0\) instead of \(-0.5\) gives arm means \(\bar\theta_C=0.773734\), \(\bar\theta_A=0.905476\), \(\bar\theta_B=0.854484\), hence a marginal \(A\)-versus-\(C\) contrast \(\Delta_{CA}=1.030086\) and an \(A\)-versus-\(C\) non-collapsibility gap of \(1.1-1.030086=0.069914\), nearly double the gap \(0.038413\) at the low-risk baseline. The conditional contrast is \(1.1\) in both, unchanged by the baseline. This is the second half of Theorem 23.1(c): on a non-collapsible scale the marginal estimand depends on the target baseline \(\mu_{*}\), not only on the covariate distribution, which is why producing a marginal target-population estimate requires the target baseline risk as an input. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. The same example on the identity scale (collapsibility in one line). Rerun target \(\mathcal P^{*}\) (\(\Pr(X=1)=0.6\), \(\mu_{*}=-0.5\)) on the identity link, so \(\theta_t(x)=\eta_t(x)\) and the contrast is a plain difference of means. The arm means are the weighted linear predictors \(\bar\theta_C=0.4(-0.5)+0.6(-0.1)=-0.26\), \(\bar\theta_A=0.4(0.3)+0.6(1.2)=0.84\), and \(\bar\theta_B=0.4(-0.2)+0.6(0.7)=0.34\), so the marginal contrasts are \(\Delta_{CA}=1.10\), \(\Delta_{CB}=0.60\), \(\Delta_{BA}=0.50\). These equal the conditional contrasts \(\gamma_A+\boldsymbol\beta_2\bar x_{*}=1.10\), \(0.60\), and \(\gamma_A-\gamma_B=0.50\) exactly: on a collapsible scale marginal and conditional coincide (Theorem 23.1(c)). The baseline \(\mu_{*}\) has vanished from every contrast, because on the identity scale it is an additive shift common to both arms; changing it to \(\mu_{*}=1.0\) leaves all three differences unchanged. Contrast this with the logit scale above, where the baseline did not cancel and the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) marginal effect drifted with the population. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 23  Multilevel Network Meta-Regression IV: Estimands, Identifiability, and Generality
text:
23.10 Notes and references
Multilevel network meta-regression and all four results of this chapter are due to Phillippo et al. (2020) and the thesis Phillippo (2019) (Chapter 4 for the model, estimands, and identifiability; the target-population estimand is §4.4, the two-study and large-network identifiability §4.5 and §4.6, and the generality discussion §4.1 and §4.7). The chapter corresponds to results H.20 (the target-population estimand integral, Theorem 23.1), H.21 (two-study identifiability under SEMA, Theorem 23.2), H.22 (large-network identifiability, Theorem 23.3), and H.23 (the generality theorem, Theorem 23.4) of the proof catalogue in proofs/H_ml_nmr.md.
The target-population estimand Theorem 23.1 is the ML-NMR realization of the transport g-formula estimands of Chapter 17 (Theorem 17.4, catalogue E.12), which in turn rest on the conditional-transportability theory of Chapter 12; the collapsibility dichotomy in part (c) is the non-collapsibility of Chapter 7 (Definition 7.7) made operational, the same phenomenon that forces the marginal-versus-conditional choice in STC (Chapter 19) and that the worked example exhibits numerically. The expansion beyond the base draft of Phillippo (2019) is in three places. First, the catalogue’s one-line claim that “the AgD trial identifies \(\gamma_B\) via the aggregate likelihood” is here given a complete proof through the monotonicity lemma Lemma 23.2, which isolates the elementary fact (an aggregate mean is strictly increasing in any additive shift of the linear predictor) that makes a single aggregate mean identify a single scalar; the same lemma then powers the large-network argument. Second, the no-SEMA non-identification is upgraded from a remark to the proposition Proposition 23.1, with an explicit binary-covariate two-point construction showing the comparison survives in the comparator population and is lost at every other target, the regression mirror of the testability analysis Proposition 17.4 of Chapter 17. Third, the large-network theorem Theorem 23.3 is given a full block rank argument for the shared and treatment-class cases (IPD identifies the interaction; monotonicity identifies the per-arm intercepts; connectivity, in the incidence-rank sense of Theorem 15.3, separates baselines from treatment effects), with the exchangeable case treated honestly as Bayesian identifiability via the normal-normal partial pooling of Theorem 8.3; the absence of a frequentist rank statement for AgD-only interactions in the exchangeable case is recorded as a limitation, following Phillippo (2019) §4.6.
The generality theorem Theorem 23.4 collects reductions to the fixed-effects NMA of Chapter 15 (Theorem 15.3) and Bucher of Chapter 14 (Theorem 14.1), to the IPD-NMR of Chapter 15 (Theorem 15.5), and to the population-adjustment methods of Part IV: MAIC (Theorem 18.4) and STC (Theorem 19.6, Theorem 19.3). The STC reduction is the exact functional identity that the ML-NMR aggregation integral equals the marginal STC predicted mean, so STC is ML-NMR with the outcome model fitted on the IPD alone and the target fixed to the comparator; the MAIC reduction is the coincidence of probability limits under a linear surface, already proved in another guise as the MAIC-STC equivalence Theorem 19.7. The complementary fact that ML-NMR, like STC and unlike MAIC, does not require covariate overlap but does require correct specification on the target support is the regression-versus-weighting trade-off of Chapter 19, and it is why ML-NMR can report estimates in target populations that no single trial sampled. Ecological bias (Definition 16.2, Chapter 16), the bias of naive meta-regression on study-level means, is exactly what the response-scale integration of Equation 23.4 avoids, by Theorem 20.2.
ML-NMR has no counterpart in the companion Coq development: there is no ML_NMR.v (or aggregation or network-meta-regression file) in theories/, and the manuscript records this deliberately, because the substantive content of ML-NMR is numerical (quasi-Monte Carlo integration, Sobol’ sequences, copulae) rather than algebraic, and the algebraic core, the aggregation identity, is a single application of Fubini and conditional independence that would add little once a measure-theoretic probability layer were in place. Accordingly none of the results in this chapter carries a machine-checked tag; the identifiability building blocks they invoke, the NMA and IPD-NMR rank theorems of Chapter 15, are likewise pen-and-paper in this development. Chapter 30 discusses what is and is not in the Coq tree.

23.11 Exercises
Throughout, a \(\star\) marks an exercise whose full solution appears in Appendix F. The exercises are labeled by type and roughly ordered from warm-up and interpretation through computation to proof and challenge; a beginner should manage the two warm-ups and Exercise 23.3 after one reading, while Exercise 23.5 and the starred exercises are proof-building challenges.

Exercise 23.1 Warm-up (interpretation). Which population, in words. For the anticoagulant decision of Example 23.1, a NICE submission wants the effect of \(A\) versus \(B\) in the UK NHS population, which is older than the IPD trial and differs from the AgD trial too. State which population’s covariate distribution ML-NMR should average the fitted surface over, and explain in one or two sentences why MAIC and STC, as defined in Part IV, cannot target that population directly. Which single extra input does a marginal odds ratio in that population require that a conditional log odds ratio does not?


Exercise 23.2 Warm-up (reading the tables). What must you supply? Using Table 23.3 and Table 23.4, list the target-population inputs needed to report each of: (i) a conditional log odds ratio; (ii) a marginal odds ratio; (iii) a risk difference on the identity scale. In each case say whether the target baseline risk \(\mu_{*}\) is needed, and give the one-sentence reason (collapsible or not).


Exercise 23.3 Computation. A third target by hand. Continue Example 23.3 with a third target population having \(\Pr(X=1)=0.5\) and baseline \(\mu_{*}=0\). Compute the six inverse-logit values, the three target arm means \(\bar\theta_A,\bar\theta_B,\bar\theta_C\), the three marginal contrasts \(\Delta_{CA},\Delta_{CB},\Delta_{BA}\), and verify the anchored identity \(\Delta_{CA}-\Delta_{CB}=\Delta_{BA}\) to six decimals. Report the conditional contrasts from Equation 23.7 and the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) non-collapsibility gap.


Exercise 23.4 Interpretation and computation. Collapsibility kills the population dependence. Redo Example 23.3 on the identity link (replace \(\operatorname{expit}\) by the identity, so \(\theta_t(x)=\eta_t(x)\)), using the same coefficients and the two targets \(\mathcal P^{*}\) (\(\Pr(X=1)=0.6\)) and \(\mathcal P^{**}\) (\(\Pr(X=1)=0.2\)). Show that the marginal and conditional contrasts coincide, that the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) contrast equals \(\gamma_A-\gamma_B=0.5\) in both targets, and that the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) contrast depends on the target only through \(\bar x_{*}\). Explain, by reference to Theorem 20.3 and Theorem 23.1(c), why the baseline \(\mu_{*}\) has now disappeared from every contrast.


Exercise 23.5 Challenge (proof). Monotonicity with a tilt instead of a shift. Replace the additive shift in Lemma 23.2 by a one-parameter family \(c\mapsto\Theta_{\mathbf v}(c):=\int g^{-1}(c\,\mathbf v^\top x+h(x))f(x)\,dx\) that tilts the linear predictor along a fixed direction \(\mathbf v\). Show that \(\Theta_{\mathbf v}\) need not be monotone in \(c\), and exhibit a density \(f\) on \(\{0,1\}\) (or on a two-point support) and a direction for which two values of \(c\) give the same \(\Theta_{\mathbf v}\). Explain how this non-monotonicity is exactly the obstruction that defeats identification of a free interaction vector from one aggregate mean, connecting to the manifold in Proposition 23.1.


Exercise 23.6 Computation. Counting in a three-study network. Consider \(J=3\) studies on \(K=3\) treatments \(\{1,2,3\}\) (reference \(1\)): study \(1\) is IPD on \(\{1,2\}\), study \(2\) is AgD on \(\{1,3\}\), study \(3\) is AgD on \(\{2,3\}\), with a single covariate (\(p=1\)) and shared EM. List the free parameters and their count, draw the treatment graph and verify connectivity, and walk through blocks (i) to (iii) of Theorem 23.3 to confirm that every parameter is identified. Which single arm supplies the shared interaction \(\boldsymbol\beta_2\), and why must it be the IPD arm?


Exercise 23.7 (\(\star\)) Challenge (derivation). A closed form for the non-collapsibility gap. For a single binary effect modifier \(X\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\Pr(X=1)=q\), the logit link, and SEMA, derive a closed-form expression for the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) non-collapsibility gap \(\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{BA}-\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})=(\gamma_A-\gamma_B)-\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})\) in terms of \(\mu_{*},\boldsymbol\beta_1,\boldsymbol\beta_2,\gamma_A,\gamma_B,q\). Prove that the gap is zero when \(q\in\{0,1\}\) (a degenerate covariate) and when \(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2=0\) (no spread in the active-arm linear predictors), in agreement with Theorem 20.2, and confirm your formula reproduces the value \(0.022502\) at the inputs of Example 23.3. Discuss why the gap, unlike the conditional contrast, cannot be eliminated by SEMA.


Exercise 23.8 (\(\star\)) Proof. The STC reduction in detail. Fix a logistic outcome family. Write the marginal STC predicted arm means (Chapter 19) for an IPD trial on \(\{A,C\}\) standardized to a comparator covariate distribution \(f_{BC}\), and the ML-NMR aggregate arm means Equation 23.2 over the same \(f_{BC}\) using the same fitted linear predictor. Prove the two are identical as functionals, and identify precisely the two ways in which a full ML-NMR fit differs from this restriction: namely, that ML-NMR’s likelihood incorporates the AgD outcomes through Theorem 20.1, and that ML-NMR’s estimand Theorem 23.1 admits any target population. Conclude that STC is the special case of ML-NMR obtained by fitting the outcome surface on the IPD alone and fixing the target to the comparator, and state, with reference to Theorem 19.6 and the no-extrapolation theorem of Chapter 18, one situation in which the extra information ML-NMR uses changes the answer and one in which it does not.

title: 24  Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics
text:
24.1 Introduction
The three preceding chapters built the multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR) model and showed how its aggregate-data likelihood is an integral of an individual-level integrand against a covariate distribution (the aggregation theorem, Theorem 20.1), how that integral is computed by quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) on the unit hypercube (Theorem 22.6), and how the resulting model is identified and estimated (Theorem 23.1, Theorem 23.4). Nothing in that development told us how to actually fit the model, nor how to know whether the fit can be trusted. That is the business of this chapter.
ML-NMR and its unanchored extension are estimated by Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), specifically by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) and its adaptive form the No-U-Turn Sampler, the engine of the Stan probabilistic programming language (Carpenter et al. (2017)) on which the reference software is built. We proved in Chapter 8 that HMC (Definition 8.9) leaves the target posterior invariant, by way of the Metropolis-Hastings detailed-balance argument (Theorem 8.9). Invariance is a statement about the limiting behavior of an idealized chain. A real analysis runs a finite number of finite chains, and faces two distinct and additive sources of error that a responsible report must certify are small.
The first is the Monte Carlo error of the sampler itself: the chains may not have reached the stationary distribution (lack of convergence), and even at stationarity their draws are autocorrelated, so a run of length \(N\) carries less information than \(N\) independent draws. The hierarchical structure of ML-NMR makes this acute. Random effects on study baselines and on treatment contrasts (Definition 8.3, Definition 8.1) introduce a variance parameter \(\tau\) whose joint posterior with the effects it governs has a pathological “funnel” geometry that defeats a naive sampler. Section Section 24.4 shows how to remove the funnel by reparameterization, and proves precisely why it works in terms of the leapfrog geometry of Definition 8.9. Sections Section 24.5 and Section 24.6 give the two workhorse convergence diagnostics, the Gelman-Rubin potential scale reduction statistic \(\hat R\) and the effective sample size, and derive both from first principles.
The second source is unique to ML-NMR among the methods in this book: a numerical-integration error nested inside the likelihood. Every evaluation of the aggregate likelihood approximates an integral by a finite QMC sum, so the model the sampler actually targets is a perturbation of the intended one. Section 2 turns the Koksma-Hlawka bound of Chapter 22 (Theorem 22.3) into an operational diagnostic and proves the doubling rule that certifies the integration grid is fine enough.
The chapter closes with model comparison. Sections Section 24.8 and 1 develop the deviance information criterion (DIC), the widely applicable information criterion (WAIC), and leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV), prove the relationships among them as estimates of the same expected predictive density, and give the Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS) algorithm that makes LOO-CV computable without refitting the model. A fully worked diagnostic example, every number checkable by hand, ties the pieces together in Section 24.11. The chapter corresponds to results I.1 to I.6 of the proof catalogue.
Throughout, \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) denotes the full parameter vector, \(\mathbf y\) the observed data, \(\pi(\boldsymbol{\xi})\) the prior, \(p(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol{\xi})\) the likelihood, and \(\pi(\boldsymbol{\xi}\mid\mathbf y)\propto p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol{\xi})\pi(\boldsymbol{\xi})\) the posterior, as in Notation and Chapter 8. We write a generic scalar quantity of interest as \(\theta=h(\boldsymbol{\xi})\), for instance a treatment contrast \(d_{ab}\) or a marginal probability \(\theta_{\bullet jk}\).

title: 24  Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics
text: Remark. A note on two effective sample sizes. The symbol \(\mathrm{ESS}\) of Notation is the effective sample size of a weighted sample, \(\mathrm{ESS}=(\sum_i w_i)^2/\sum_i w_i^2\), which governed the variance inflation of MAIC in Chapter 18. The effective sample size of an autocorrelated MCMC chain, developed in Section 24.6, is a different quantity with a different formula, and to keep them apart we write it \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\). Both answer the same kind of question, “how many independent draws is this sample worth,” but one loses efficiency to unequal weights and the other to serial correlation. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 24  Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics
section: 24.2 The sampler in one page: HMC, NUTS, warmup, and divergences
text:
24.2 The sampler in one page: HMC, NUTS, warmup, and divergences
Before the diagnostics, a page on the machine they diagnose, for the reader who has fit a model in Stan but never looked under the hood. None of this is proved here; it recaps Chapter 8 and fixes the vocabulary the practical remarks below depend on.
What a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler does. We cannot write the posterior \(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\) down in closed form for an ML-NMR model, but we can draw a long sequence of parameter vectors \(\boldsymbol\xi^{(1)},\boldsymbol\xi^{(2)},\dots\) whose histogram reproduces it. Each draw is proposed from the current one and then accepted or rejected; the accepted draws are our sample, and any posterior summary, a mean or a credible interval for the contrast \(d_{AC}\), is just an average over them. That is Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC).
Why Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. A random-walk proposal (as in random-walk Metropolis or Gibbs sampling) staggers blindly, and in the tens of correlated dimensions of an ML-NMR fit almost every proposed step is rejected, so the sampler barely moves. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) instead treats the negative log posterior \(U(\boldsymbol\xi)=-\log\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\) as a landscape and rolls a frictionless puck across it, using the gradient \(\nabla U\) to steer. A single HMC move can travel a long way across the posterior while rarely being rejected, which is why HMC, not random-walk Metropolis, is the sampler that makes ML-NMR feasible: random-walk methods die in high dimensions, and HMC uses gradient information to take long, directed steps.
How the puck moves: the leapfrog integrator. The puck’s path obeys Newtonian mechanics, which the computer solves in small time steps of size \(\epsilon\), the step size, using the leapfrog integrator of Definition 8.9. Each leapfrog step gives the puck’s momentum a half-kick from the gradient, drifts its position, then completes the kick; we write \(r\) for that momentum. The single number \(\epsilon\) controls how large each step is, and getting it wrong is the source of the trouble in Section 24.4.
What the No-U-Turn Sampler adds. Plain HMC needs the user to choose how many leapfrog steps to take per move. The No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) chooses automatically: it keeps stepping until the trajectory starts to double back on itself (a “U-turn”), so no trajectory-length tuning is required. NUTS is the algorithm Stan actually runs.
Warmup versus sampling. A run has two phases. During warmup the sampler is both moving from its arbitrary starting point toward the region where the posterior mass actually lives (the typical set, which for a high-dimensional posterior is a thin shell away from the mode, so finding the mode and sampling the posterior are different tasks) and tuning two knobs: the step size \(\epsilon\) and a mass matrix, a linear rescaling of the parameters that makes the landscape rounder. Warmup draws are tuned-away and discarded; only the post-warmup draws, taken with the knobs frozen, are kept. Everything called “\(N\) draws” below means post-warmup draws.
Divergent transitions. When the landscape has a region of very sharp curvature, a fixed step size \(\epsilon\) is too coarse to follow it: the leapfrog puck flies off, the simulated energy jumps by more than a set threshold, and Stan records a divergent transition. A divergence is not a rounding nuisance; it flags a part of the posterior the sampler could not enter, so that region is under-sampled and any summary that depends on it, often the heterogeneity \(\tau\) and the effects tied to it, can be biased. Even a handful of divergences after warmup must be explained, not ignored. The rest of Section 24.4 is, at bottom, the story of where these divergences come from and how a change of coordinates removes them.
The vocabulary in one place:







Term
One-line meaning




MCMC
draw a dependent sequence whose histogram is the posterior


HMC
gradient-guided proposals that move far with few rejections


NUTS
HMC that picks its own trajectory length; the Stan default


step size \(\epsilon\)
how large each leapfrog step is; too large diverges, too small crawls


mass matrix
a rescaling of parameters learned in warmup to round out the geometry


warmup
the discarded tuning phase; the rest are post-warmup draws


typical set
the region carrying the posterior mass, where the sampler should live


divergent transition
a step the integrator could not follow; a flag of unexplored geometry

title: 24  Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics
section: 24.3 A running example: a two-study evidence network
text:
24.3 A running example: a two-study evidence network
Every diagnostic below is illustrated on one small network, carried from section to section so that the abstractions attach to something concrete. It is the smallest network that still has all the features that make ML-NMR computation delicate.
The data. Two randomized trials inform a plaque psoriasis indirect comparison with a binary outcome, achieving a \(75\%\) reduction in the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (a “PASI 75 response”).

Study \(AB\) compares treatment \(A\) (control) with treatment \(B\) and reports individual patient data (IPD): for each of its patients we have the treatment arm, the outcome, and two baseline covariates, age and disease severity, each centered and scaled.
Study \(BC\) compares \(B\) with \(C\) and reports only aggregate data (AgD): per arm, the number of responders out of the arm total, plus the arm’s mean age and mean severity.

The network is the chain from \(A\) to \(B\) to \(C\): \(B\) is the common comparator, so the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) contrast \(d_{AC}\) is estimated only indirectly, by combining the within-study contrasts. This is exactly the ITC problem of Parts III and IV, now fit as one ML-NMR model.
The model. On the log-odds (logit) scale the linear predictor for a patient with covariates \(\mathbf
x\) on arm \(k\) in study \(j\) is, as in Notation, \[
\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)=\mu_j+\boldsymbol\beta_1^\top\mathbf x+\gamma_k+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}^\top\mathbf x,
\] with the convention \(\gamma_k=0\) and \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\mathbf 0\) on the reference arm, study baselines \(\mu_{AB},\mu_{BC}\), prognostic effects \(\boldsymbol\beta_1\), a treatment main effect \(\gamma_k\), and age-and-severity effect modifiers \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\). Because \(B\) appears in both studies, its relative effect is treated as exchangeable across studies with a random-effects heterogeneity scale \(\tau\) (the NMA layer of Definition 13.4).
Why this network stresses every diagnostic. It has exactly one study per contrast. That single fact drives the whole chapter:

\(\tau\) is estimated from a single pair of contrasts, so it is weakly identified; its posterior reaches toward \(0\), which is the funnel of Section 24.4, so the fit needs the non-centered parameterization.
The aggregate study \(BC\) contributes to the likelihood only through an integral of the individual-level response over its covariate distribution, a two-dimensional integral over age and severity that must be done by QMC (2).
With so few studies, one of them can dominate: the \(\widehat k\) diagnostic of PSIS-LOO

will tell us whether \(d_{AC}\) rests on a single study.

And we will want to compare models, for instance with and without the age effect modifier \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2}\), which is the job of WAIC and LOO (Section 24.8).

Keep this network in mind: at each transition we return to it and read the diagnostic in its terms.

title: 24  Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics
text:
24.4 Centered and non-centered parameterizations
The random-effects layer of an ML-NMR model is, at its core, the normal hierarchy of Chapter 8: a vector of study- or contrast-level effects drawn from a common population distribution whose scale \(\tau\) is itself estimated. We isolate that layer and study how the algebraic form in which it is written to the sampler changes the geometry HMC must traverse, even though it cannot change the posterior distribution. This is the content of catalogue result I.1.
Here is the problem in one picture, before any algebra. In our running network \(\tau\) is the scale of the random treatment contrast, estimated from a single pair of studies, so the posterior lets \(\tau\) wander close to \(0\). Plot the draws of a study effect \(\theta_j\) against \(\log\tau\). The cloud is shaped like a trumpet bell, or a funnel: wide at the top, where \(\tau\) is large and the effects \(\theta_j\) range freely, and pinched to a needle at the bottom, where \(\tau\) is small and every \(\theta_j\) is forced close to the common mean \(\mu\). A sampler exploring this shape must take large steps in the wide mouth and minute steps in the narrow neck. A single step size cannot do both: tuned for the mouth it flies out of the neck and diverges; tuned for the neck it crawls hopelessly in the mouth. That mismatch is the whole pathology, and the fix is to change coordinates so the funnel becomes a cylinder. The two coordinate systems are the centered and non-centered parameterizations.

Definition 24.1 (Centered and non-centered parameterization) Consider the normal hierarchy for effects \(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_J\) with population mean \(\mu\) and scale \(\tau>0\), \[
\theta_j \mid \mu,\tau \sim \mathcal N(\mu,\tau^2), \qquad j=1,\dots,J,
\tag{24.1}\] embedded in a model whose remaining likelihood depends on the \(\theta_j\) through data terms.

The centered parameterization (CP) takes the unknowns to be \((\mu,\tau,\theta_1,\dots,\theta_J)\) themselves, so that Equation 24.1 enters the prior directly.
The non-centered parameterization (NCP) takes the unknowns to be \((\mu,\tau,\tilde\theta_1,\dots,
\tilde\theta_J)\) with standardized effects \[
\tilde\theta_j \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\ \text{ a priori}, \qquad
\theta_j := \mu + \tau\,\tilde\theta_j,
\tag{24.2}\] and the data terms are written as functions of the deterministic transform \(\mu+\tau\tilde\theta_j\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)



Remark. Reader translation. Both parameterizations describe the identical statistical model and give the identical answer; they differ only in what the sampler is asked to move around in. The centered form (CP) samples the effects \(\theta_j\) directly. The non-centered form (NCP) samples standardized shocks \(\tilde\theta_j\) of fixed unit scale and reconstructs \(\theta_j=\mu+\tau\tilde\theta_j\) afterward, so the width of the effect is carried by \(\tau\) rather than baked into the coordinate. The point of the section is that this cosmetic-looking choice decides whether HMC sees a funnel or a cylinder. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The two are the same model: Equation 24.2 is an invertible change of variables that carries the standard normal prior on \(\tilde\theta_j\) to the \(\mathcal N(\mu,\tau^2)\) prior on \(\theta_j\). We record this precisely, because the equivalence is what licenses choosing between them on purely computational grounds.

Lemma 24.1 (The two parameterizations define one posterior) Fix \((\mu,\tau)\) with \(\tau>0\). The map \(T_{\mu,\tau}:\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}\mapsto\boldsymbol\theta\) defined by \(\theta_j=\mu+\tau\tilde\theta_j\) is a diffeomorphism of \(\mathbb R^J\) with constant Jacobian determinant \(\tau^{J}\). The CP joint density in \((\mu,\tau,\boldsymbol\theta)\) and the NCP joint density in \((\mu,\tau,\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta})\) are related by this change of variables, and the two analyses return identical posteriors for every quantity \(h(\mu,\tau,\boldsymbol\theta)\).


Proof. For fixed \((\mu,\tau)\) the map is affine with linear part \(\tau I_J\), hence a bijection of \(\mathbb R^J\) with Jacobian matrix \(\tau I_J\) and determinant \(\tau^J\neq 0\); it is its own smooth inverse \(\tilde\theta_j=(\theta_j-\mu)/\tau\), so it is a diffeomorphism. Writing \(\varphi\) for the standard normal density, the NCP prior on \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}\) is \(\prod_j\varphi(\tilde\theta_j)\). Pushing it forward through \(T_{\mu,\tau}\) by the change-of-variables formula gives, at \(\boldsymbol\theta=
T_{\mu,\tau}(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta})\), \[
\prod_{j}\varphi(\tilde\theta_j)\cdot\left|\det \tfrac{\partial\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}}{\partial
\boldsymbol\theta}\right|
=\prod_{j}\varphi\!\Big(\tfrac{\theta_j-\mu}{\tau}\Big)\cdot\tau^{-J}
=\prod_{j}\mathcal N(\theta_j;\mu,\tau^2),
\] which is exactly the CP prior. Because the likelihood is written in both as a function of the same numbers \(\theta_j=\mu+\tau\tilde\theta_j\), and the priors on \((\mu,\tau)\) are shared, the joint densities agree under the transform. A diffeomorphic reparameterization leaves all integrals, hence all posterior expectations and quantiles of any \(h\), invariant. \(\square\)


Remark. What the proof is saying, in words. A diffeomorphism is just a change of variables that is smooth and smoothly invertible, so no information is lost or created by switching between \(\boldsymbol\theta\) and \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}\). The change-of-variables formula is the multivariable version of the \(u\)-substitution from calculus: when you rewrite a density in new coordinates you must multiply by the Jacobian factor (here the constant \(\tau^{-J}\)) to keep total probability equal to one. Because that bookkeeping is exact, every probability, mean, and credible interval is identical in the two coordinates. This is the license we need: we may pick the parameterization purely for how well the sampler moves, with no effect on the reported treatment contrast. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

If the posteriors are identical, why does the choice matter? Because HMC does not sample the posterior directly; it simulates Hamiltonian trajectories whose stability and step size are dictated by the local curvature of the negative log density, and curvature is not invariant under reparameterization. We make this quantitative. Recall from Definition 8.9 that HMC sets \(U(\boldsymbol\xi)=-\log\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf
y)\) (the “potential energy”) and advances the state by the leapfrog integrator with a single global step size \(\epsilon\). The behavior of the leapfrog integrator on a quadratic potential is the whole story, and it is governed by one number.
To keep the section self-contained, recall the leapfrog integrator explicitly. It advances a position \(x\) and its momentum \(r\) by a step of size \(\epsilon\) in three substeps: a half-kick of the momentum by the gradient, \(r^{+}=r-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}U'(x)\); a full drift of the position, \(x'=x+\epsilon r^{+}\); and a second half-kick, \(r'=r^{+}-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}U'(x')\). The momentum \(r\) is the auxiliary “velocity” HMC gives the puck, and \(\epsilon\) is the same step size the sampler tunes in warmup. The next lemma analyzes this map on the simplest possible landscape, a parabola, because near any smooth mode the landscape is a parabola to second order; the one inequality it produces, the largest step the integrator can survive, is what governs both the funnel pathology and its non-centered cure. That is why a page on a harmonic oscillator earns its place: it is the single fact the entire section turns on.

Lemma 24.2 (Linear stability of the leapfrog integrator) Let \(U(x)=\tfrac12\omega^2 x^2\) be a one-dimensional harmonic potential with frequency \(\omega>0\) and unit mass. One leapfrog step of size \(\epsilon\) (as in Definition 8.9) acts on the state \((x,r)\) as the linear map \((x',r')^\top=A(x,r)^\top\) with \[
A=\begin{pmatrix} 1-\tfrac12\epsilon^2\omega^2 & \epsilon \\[2pt]
-\epsilon\omega^2\big(1-\tfrac14\epsilon^2\omega^2\big) & 1-\tfrac12\epsilon^2\omega^2 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad \det A=1 .
\tag{24.3}\] The iterates \(A^n\) remain bounded (the integrator is stable) if and only if \(\epsilon\omega\le 2\); for \(\epsilon\omega>2\) they grow geometrically, and the simulated trajectory diverges.


Proof. With \(U'(x)=\omega^2 x\), the three leapfrog substeps of Definition 8.9 read \(r^{+}=r-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\omega^2 x\), then \(x'=x+\epsilon r^{+}=(1-\tfrac12\epsilon^2\omega^2)x+
\epsilon r\), then \(r'=r^{+}-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\omega^2 x'\). Substituting \(x'\) into the last line, \[
r'=r-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\omega^2 x-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\omega^2\big[(1-\tfrac12\epsilon^2\omega^2)x+\epsilon
r\big]
=\big(1-\tfrac12\epsilon^2\omega^2\big)r-\epsilon\omega^2\big(1-\tfrac14\epsilon^2\omega^2\big)x,
\] which is Equation 24.3. Its determinant is \((1-\tfrac12\epsilon^2\omega^2)^2+\epsilon\cdot\epsilon\omega^2(1-\tfrac14\epsilon^2\omega^2)
=1-\epsilon^2\omega^2+\tfrac14\epsilon^4\omega^4+\epsilon^2\omega^2-\tfrac14\epsilon^4\omega^4=1\), confirming the volume preservation of Definition 8.9. Writing \(s=\epsilon\omega\), the trace is \(2-s^2\), so the eigenvalues of \(A\) solve \(\lambda^2-(2-s^2)\lambda+1=0\) with discriminant \((2-s^2)^2-4=s^2(s^2-4)\). If \(s<2\) the discriminant is negative, the eigenvalues are complex conjugates, and since their product is \(\det A=1\) they have modulus \(1\); the powers \(A^n\) are then conjugate to a rotation and stay bounded. If \(s>2\) the discriminant is positive, the eigenvalues are real with product \(1\), so one exceeds \(1\) in modulus and \(A^n\) grows like that eigenvalue to the \(n\); the trajectory diverges. At \(s=2\) the matrix has a defective double eigenvalue \(-1\) and \(\|A^n\|\) grows linearly. Hence stability holds exactly for \(\epsilon\omega\le 2\). \(\square\)

The frequency \(\omega\) in Lemma 24.2 is \(\sqrt{U''(x)}\), the square root of the local curvature of the potential. The lemma therefore says: the largest usable leapfrog step at a point is \(\epsilon\lesssim 2/\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}}\), where \(\lambda_{\max}\) is the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian \(\nabla^2 U\) there. A single global \(\epsilon\) can be efficient only if this curvature is roughly constant across the region the chain must visit. The next lemma computes the curvature in the two parameterizations and exposes the funnel.

Lemma 24.3 (Funnel curvature of the centered hierarchy) Consider Equation 24.1 with a single weakly-informed effect \(\theta_j\) whose data term contributes curvature \(c_j\ge 0\) in \(\theta_j\) (so \(c_j\) is the negative second derivative of the data log-likelihood in \(\theta_j\), a measure of how firmly the data pin down \(\theta_j\); when the data are weakly informative the likelihood is nearly flat in \(\theta_j\), its second derivative is near zero, and \(c_j\to 0\), the prior-dominated limit). Holding \((\mu,\tau)\) fixed:

In the centered parameterization the curvature of \(U\) in the \(\theta_j\) direction is \[
\frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial\theta_j^2}=\frac{1}{\tau^2}+c_j .
\tag{24.4}\]
In the non-centered parameterization the curvature of \(U\) in the \(\tilde\theta_j\) direction is \[
\frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial\tilde\theta_j^2}=1+\tau^2 c_j .
\tag{24.5}\]



Proof. The potential is \(U=-\log\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)=-\log(\text{prior})-\log(\text{likelihood})+
\text{const}\). In CP the prior term involving \(\theta_j\) is \(-\log\mathcal N(\theta_j;\mu,\tau^2)=
\frac{(\theta_j-\mu)^2}{2\tau^2}+\text{const}\), whose second derivative in \(\theta_j\) is \(1/\tau^2\); the data term adds \(c_j\) by definition, giving Equation 24.4. In NCP the prior term involving \(\tilde\theta_j\) is \(-\log\mathcal N(\tilde\theta_j;0,1)=\tfrac12\tilde\theta_j^2+\text{const}\), second derivative \(1\); the data term is the same function of \(\theta_j=\mu+\tau\tilde\theta_j\), and by the chain rule its second derivative in \(\tilde\theta_j\) is \((\partial\theta_j/\partial\tilde\theta_j)^2\) times its second derivative in \(\theta_j\), that is \(\tau^2 c_j\). Summing gives Equation 24.5. \(\square\)


Theorem 24.1 (Why the parameterization changes HMC geometry) In the prior-dominated regime \(c_j\to 0\) (a study or contrast about which the data are weakly informative):

(Centered funnels.) The CP curvature Equation 24.4 is \(1/\tau^2\), so by Lemma 24.2 the largest stable leapfrog step in the \(\theta_j\) direction is \(\epsilon_{\max}(\tau)=2\tau\), which tends to \(0\) as \(\tau\to 0\). The posterior of \((\theta_j,\log\tau)\) is a “funnel,” narrowing without bound as \(\tau\downarrow 0\); no single global \(\epsilon\) is both stable in the neck of the funnel and efficient in its mouth.
(Non-centered uniformizes.) The NCP curvature Equation 24.5 is \(1\), independent of \(\tau\), so the largest stable step is \(\epsilon_{\max}=2\) for every \(\tau\). The funnel is removed and a single step size suffices.

In the data-dominated regime \(\tau^2 c_j\gg 1\) (many informative studies, well-identified \(\tau\)) the roles reverse: NCP couples \(\tilde\theta_j\) to \(\tau\) through the data term Equation 24.5 and can mix worse than CP, whose curvature Equation 24.4 is then the well-conditioned \(c_j\). The practical rule is to use NCP when \(\tau\) is weakly identified (few studies) and CP when it is strongly identified.


Proof. Both claims are immediate from substituting the limiting curvatures of Lemma 24.3 into the stability threshold \(\epsilon_{\max}=2/\omega=2/\sqrt{\text{curvature}}\) of Lemma 24.2. For (1), curvature \(1/\tau^2\) gives \(\omega=1/\tau\) and \(\epsilon_{\max}=2\tau\to 0\); because \(\tau\) itself ranges over an interval reaching toward \(0\) under the posterior, the step size that is stable at the smallest visited \(\tau\) is far smaller than the step size that is efficient at typical \(\tau\), and HMC with one \(\epsilon\) must compromise. The Metropolis correction of Theorem 8.9 guards correctness by rejecting the divergent proposals that an over-large step produces in the neck, but at the cost of a collapse in acceptance and in distance traveled, which is observed in practice as “divergent transitions.” For (2), curvature \(1\) gives \(\epsilon_{\max}=2\) for all \(\tau\), so stability is uniform over the funnel. The reversal in the data-dominated regime is the same computation read in the other direction: when \(\tau^2 c_j\gg 1\) the NCP curvature Equation 24.5 grows with \(\tau\) while the CP curvature Equation 24.4 approaches the constant \(c_j\), so CP is the better-conditioned coordinate. \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters, and a map of the two regimes. The theorem is the rigorous version of “change coordinates so the funnel becomes a cylinder,” and it also warns that the cure can become the disease when the data are strong. The table records both regimes; “curvature” is the second derivative of \(U\) that Lemma 24.2 turns into a maximum stable step \(\epsilon_{\max}=2/\sqrt{\text{curv}}\).

For an indirect comparison this reads directly off the evidence network. Our running network has one study per contrast, so \(\tau\) is weakly identified and its posterior reaches into the neck: it is a non-centered problem, and fitting it centered would produce divergences clustered at small \(\tau\) and an untrustworthy heterogeneity estimate. A dense network with many studies per contrast identifies \(\tau\) strongly and belongs in the bottom row, where the centered form mixes better. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. The funnel in ML-NMR. In ML-NMR the effects \(\theta_j\) are study baselines \(\mu_j\) and random treatment contrasts \(\delta_{j,1k}\) (the random-effects NMA layer, Definition 13.4). Networks with few studies per contrast, the norm in health-technology-assessment submissions, sit squarely in the prior-dominated regime, where Theorem 24.1 prescribes the non-centered form. The reference software implements the non-centered parameterization by default for exactly this reason; the diagnostic signature of a residual funnel is a cluster of divergent transitions concentrated at small \(\tau\), visible in a scatter plot of any \(\theta_j\) against \(\log\tau\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This development corresponds to I.1 in the proof catalogue.

title: 24  Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics
section: 24.5 The Gelman-Rubin potential scale reduction statistic
text:
24.5 The Gelman-Rubin potential scale reduction statistic
Reparameterization makes the chains mix; diagnostics tell us whether they have. The first question is convergence: have the chains forgotten their starting points and settled to a common stationary distribution? The standard answer compares the spread of several independently started chains to the spread within each. If the chains agree, the between-chain spread is no larger than the within; if they have not converged, the between-chain spread is inflated. The Gelman-Rubin statistic makes this a number. This is catalogue result I.2, which we derive in full.
The bottom line first. The statistic is \(\widehat R=\sqrt{\widehat V/W}\), the ratio of a pooled, all-chains-together estimate of the posterior spread \(\widehat V\) to the average within-chain spread \(W\). Read it as a single question: are the separate chains telling the same posterior story? If they are, the two spreads agree and \(\widehat R\) sits at \(1\); if the chains have settled in different places or are still drifting, the pooled spread is inflated and \(\widehat R\) rises above \(1\). The working rule is to require \(\widehat R\le 1.01\) for every reported quantity. In the running example that means checking it not only on the headline contrast \(d_{AC}\) but on \(\tau\), the study baselines \(\mu_{AB},\mu_{BC}\), the effect modifier \(\boldsymbol\beta_2\), and the transformed marginal probabilities you report; the heterogeneity \(\tau\) is usually the last to converge and the one to watch. The rest of this section proves why this ratio has exactly that behavior; a reader who trusts the rule can skim to Section 24.6 on a first pass.
Throughout this section we have \(M\ge 2\) chains, each of post-warmup length \(N\), with draws \(\theta^{(m,t)}\) for chain \(m=1,\dots,M\) and iteration \(t=1,\dots,N\), of a scalar quantity \(\theta=h(\boldsymbol\xi)\).

Definition 24.2 (Within-chain, between-chain, and pooled variance estimators) With chain means \(\bar\theta^{(m)}=\frac1N\sum_t\theta^{(m,t)}\) and grand mean \(\bar{\bar\theta}=\frac1M\sum_m\bar\theta^{(m)}\), define \[
W=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^{M}s_m^2,\quad s_m^2=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\big(\theta^{(m,t)}-\bar\theta^{(m)}
\big)^2;\qquad
B=\frac{N}{M-1}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\big(\bar\theta^{(m)}-\bar{\bar\theta}\big)^2 ;
\tag{24.6}\] the within-chain variance \(W\) (the average of the per-chain sample variances) and the between-chain variance \(B\) (the sample variance of the chain means, scaled by \(N\)). The pooled marginal-variance estimator is \[
\widehat V=\Big(1-\tfrac1N\Big)W+\tfrac1N B .
\tag{24.7}\] \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. \(W\) asks how much a single chain wiggles around its own average; \(B\) asks how far the chain averages sit from one another. If the chains have converged to the same distribution these measure the same spread, so their combination \(\widehat V\) neither over- nor under-states the posterior variance. If the chains disagree, \(B\) is inflated by the disagreement while \(W\) is not, and the ratio \(\widehat V/W\) climbs above \(1\). The scaling by \(N\) in \(B\) is what puts the between-chain and within-chain pieces on the same footing. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The rationale for these particular combinations is not obvious from the formulas. We supply it with two exact expectation identities, valid under an explicit idealization of what “converged” means, and then read off the behavior of the statistic.

Lemma 24.4 (Expectation of the within-chain variance) Suppose each chain is second-order stationary, meaning its mean is constant along the chain and the covariance between two draws depends only on how many iterations separate them, not on where in the chain they sit, with marginal variance \(\sigma^2=\mathrm{Var}(\theta)\), and let \(v_N=\mathrm{Var}(\bar\theta^{(m)})\) be the variance of a single chain mean. Then \(\mathbb E[s_m^2]=
\frac{N}{N-1}(\sigma^2-v_N)\), and hence \[
\mathbb E[W]=\frac{N}{N-1}\big(\sigma^2-v_N\big).
\tag{24.8}\]


Proof. Let \(m_0=\mathbb E[\theta^{(m,t)}]\), constant in \(t\) by stationarity. Using \(\sum_t(\theta^{(m,t)}-\bar\theta^{(m)})^2=\sum_t\theta^{(m,t)2}-N\bar\theta^{(m)2}\) and taking expectations, \[
\mathbb E\!\Big[\textstyle\sum_t(\theta^{(m,t)}-\bar\theta^{(m)})^2\Big]
=\sum_t\big(\sigma^2+m_0^2\big)-N\big(v_N+m_0^2\big)
=N\sigma^2-Nv_N ,
\] because \(\mathbb E[\theta^{(m,t)2}]=\mathrm{Var}(\theta^{(m,t)})+m_0^2=\sigma^2+m_0^2\) and \(\mathbb E[\bar\theta^{(m)2}]=v_N+m_0^2\). Dividing by \(N-1\) gives \(\mathbb E[s_m^2]=\frac{N}{N-1}
(\sigma^2-v_N)\), and averaging over the \(M\) chains gives Equation 24.8. \(\square\)


Lemma 24.5 (Expectation of the between-chain variance) Suppose in addition that the \(M\) chains are mutually independent and share the common stationary distribution (in particular a common mean). Then \[
\mathbb E[B]=N v_N .
\tag{24.9}\]


Proof. Under the stated assumptions the chain means \(\bar\theta^{(1)},\dots,\bar\theta^{(M)}\) are independent and identically distributed with common variance \(v_N\). The quantity \(\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_m(\bar\theta^{(m)}-
\bar{\bar\theta})^2\) is the ordinary sample variance of these \(M\) numbers, which is an unbiased estimator of their common variance \(v_N\). Multiplying by \(N\), as in the definition Equation 24.6 of \(B\), gives \(\mathbb E[B]=Nv_N\). \(\square\)


Theorem 24.2 (Gelman-Rubin potential scale reduction) Define the potential scale reduction factor \[
\widehat R=\sqrt{\widehat V/W}.
\tag{24.10}\]

(Unbiasedness of \(\widehat V\) at stationarity.) Under the idealization of Lemma 24.4 and Lemma 24.5 (independent chains sharing one stationary law of finite variance \(\sigma^2\)), the pooled estimator is exactly unbiased for the marginal posterior variance, \[
\mathbb E[\widehat V]=\sigma^2 ,
\] for every \(N\) and every within-chain autocorrelation structure.
(One-sided bias and the limit.) For chains with non-negative autocorrelations, \(\mathbb E[\widehat V]\ge\mathbb E[W]\), with \[
\mathbb E[\widehat V]-\mathbb E[W]=\frac{N v_N-\sigma^2}{N-1}\ge 0 ,
\tag{24.11}\] so \(\widehat R\) is centered at or above \(1\); and if the chains are ergodic, so that \(v_N\to 0\) and \(Nv_N\to\sigma^2\big(1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_k\big)\) as \(N\to\infty\), then \(\mathbb E[W]\to\sigma^2\) and \(\widehat R\xrightarrow{p}1\).
(Detection of non-convergence.) If the chains are stationary but with different means \(m_1,\dots,m_M\) (over-dispersed starting points not yet forgotten, or distinct posterior modes), then \[
\mathbb E[\widehat V]=\sigma^2+\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{m}\big(m_m-\bar m\big)^2,
\qquad \bar m=\tfrac1M\textstyle\sum_m m_m ,
\] while \(\mathbb E[W]\) is unchanged at \(\frac{N}{N-1}(\sigma^2-v_N)\); the extra between-mean dispersion inflates \(\widehat V/W\) above \(1\) and does not vanish as \(N\to\infty\) unless the means coincide.



Proof. Part 1. By Equation 24.7 and linearity of expectation, \[
\mathbb E[\widehat V]=\Big(1-\tfrac1N\Big)\mathbb E[W]+\tfrac1N\mathbb E[B]
=\frac{N-1}{N}\cdot\frac{N}{N-1}\big(\sigma^2-v_N\big)+\frac1N\cdot N v_N
=\big(\sigma^2-v_N\big)+v_N=\sigma^2,
\] using Equation 24.8 and Equation 24.9. The cancellation is exact and uses no assumption on the autocorrelations beyond second-order stationarity.
Part 2. Subtracting Equation 24.8 from \(\mathbb E[\widehat V]=\sigma^2\), \[
\mathbb E[\widehat V]-\mathbb E[W]=\sigma^2-\frac{N}{N-1}\big(\sigma^2-v_N\big)
=\frac{(N-1)\sigma^2-N\sigma^2+Nv_N}{N-1}=\frac{Nv_N-\sigma^2}{N-1}.
\] Now \(v_N=\mathrm{Var}(\bar\theta^{(m)})=\frac{\sigma^2}{N}\big(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(1-\tfrac kN)\rho_k\big)\) by the variance-of-the-mean identity Proposition 24.1 (proved independently in Section 24.6, using nothing from this section, so there is no circular dependence), so \(Nv_N=\sigma^2\big(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(1-\tfrac kN)\rho_k\big)\ge
\sigma^2\) whenever every \(\rho_k\ge 0\); the gap Equation 24.11 is therefore non-negative, and since \(\widehat V\) and \(W\) are non-negative this gives \(\mathbb E[\widehat V]\ge\mathbb E[W]\), so \(\widehat R\) is centered at or above \(1\). For the limit, ergodicity makes \(v_N\to 0\), so \(\mathbb E[\widehat V]=\sigma^2\) forces \(\mathbb E[W]=\sigma^2-\frac{N-1}{N}^{-1}\!\cdots\to\sigma^2\) as well (equivalently, the gap Equation 24.11 is \(\frac{\sigma^2\cdot 2\sum_k(1-k/N)\rho_k}{N-1}\to 0\) because the bracket converges to the finite constant \(\sum_k\rho_k\)); both \(\widehat V\) and \(W\) converge to \(\sigma^2\) and their ratio to \(1\).
Part 3. When the chains have different means, the chain means \(\bar\theta^{(m)}\) are independent with \(\mathbb E[\bar\theta^{(m)}]=m_m\) and variance \(v_N\). The sample variance of independent variables with unequal means decomposes into the average variance plus the sample variance of the means: taking expectations in \(\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_m(\bar\theta^{(m)}-\bar{\bar\theta})^2\) gives \(v_N+\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_m
(m_m-\bar m)^2\). Hence \(\mathbb E[B]=Nv_N+\frac{N}{M-1}\sum_m(m_m-\bar m)^2\), and \[
\mathbb E[\widehat V]=\frac{N-1}{N}\mathbb E[W]+\frac1N\mathbb E[B]
=\sigma^2+\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_m\big(m_m-\bar m\big)^2 .
\] The within-chain expectation Equation 24.8 is untouched because it never references the cross-chain means. The extra term is a fixed positive constant independent of \(N\), so \(\widehat V/W\) stays bounded away from \(1\) as \(N\) grows, which is the diagnostic firing. \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters, and the three ways \(\widehat R\) fails. For an indirect comparison, a large \(\widehat R\) on the contrast \(d_{AC}\) means the estimate is not yet stable: rerun the analysis with a different seed and you could get a materially different number, which is indefensible in a reimbursement submission. Part 3 of the theorem is the precise reason, and it fires in three recognizable patterns. (i) Different modes: the chains settle in genuinely different places, for example a bimodal posterior for an effect modifier, so the chain means \(m_m\) differ and the extra term in Part 3 never vanishes. (ii) Slow drift: a chain has not reached the typical set and is still trending, which split-\(\widehat
R\) (below) is designed to catch by comparing each chain’s two halves. (iii) One rogue chain: a single chain stuck in the funnel neck while the others mix, dragging one \(m_m\) away from the rest. In all three the action is the same: do not read the posterior yet. Diagnose which parameter is bad and treat the cause, usually more warmup, the non-centered parameterization of Section 24.4, or a tighter prior on \(\tau\), rather than simply running longer. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reading \(\widehat R\), and modern refinements. Part 1 is the classical fact that \(\widehat V\) overestimates the posterior variance when the chains start over-dispersed (Part 3) and is unbiased once they have mixed (Part 1), while \(W\) underestimates it until each chain has explored the whole support (Part 2); \(\widehat R\) compresses both failures into a single number that descends to \(1\). The widely used threshold is \(\widehat R\le 1.01\) for every reported quantity. Two refinements are now standard: split- \(\widehat R\) divides each chain into two halves and treats them as separate chains, so that within-chain non-stationarity (a slow trend) inflates the between-chain term and is detected; and rank-normalized \(\widehat R\) applies the statistic to the normal scores of the pooled ranks, which makes it well defined for heavy-tailed or infinite-variance targets where \(\sigma^2\) in Theorem 24.2 would not exist. Both are due to a modern reassessment of the diagnostic and are the defaults in current software. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This development corresponds to I.2 in the proof catalogue.

title: 24  Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics
section: 24.6 Effective sample size for autocorrelated chains
text:
24.6 Effective sample size for autocorrelated chains
A chain can be perfectly converged (\(\widehat R=1\)) and still nearly useless if its draws are highly correlated, because correlated draws carry redundant information. The effective sample size quantifies exactly how many independent draws the chain is worth for estimating a posterior expectation. This is catalogue result I.3. The development rests on one exact variance identity for the mean of a stationary sequence, which we also used in Theorem 24.2.

Proposition 24.1 (Variance of the mean of a stationary chain) Let \(\theta^{(1)},\dots,\theta^{(N)}\) be second-order stationary with variance \(\sigma^2\) and lag-\(k\) autocorrelation \(\rho_k=\mathrm{Corr}(\theta^{(t)},\theta^{(t+k)})\). Then \[
\mathrm{Var}\big(\bar\theta_N\big)=\frac{\sigma^2}{N}\Big(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\Big(1-\frac kN\Big)\rho_k
\Big),\qquad \bar\theta_N=\frac1N\sum_{t=1}^N\theta^{(t)} .
\tag{24.12}\] If moreover \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\rho_k|<\infty\), then \(N\,\mathrm{Var}(\bar\theta_N)\to\sigma^2\,
\tau_{\mathrm{int}}\) as \(N\to\infty\), where \(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=1+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty\rho_k\) is the integrated autocorrelation time.


Proof. Expanding the variance of the sum and using stationarity, \(\mathrm{Cov}(\theta^{(s)},\theta^{(t)})=
\sigma^2\rho_{|s-t|}\), so \[
\mathrm{Var}(\bar\theta_N)=\frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{s=1}^N\sum_{t=1}^N\sigma^2\rho_{|s-t|}
=\frac{\sigma^2}{N^2}\Big(N+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(N-k)\rho_k\Big),
\] because the lag \(|s-t|=0\) occurs for the \(N\) diagonal pairs and each lag \(k\in\{1,\dots,N-1\}\) occurs for \(2(N-k)\) ordered pairs. Factoring \(N\) out of the bracket gives Equation 24.12. For the limit, each summand \((1-\tfrac kN)\rho_k\to\rho_k\) pointwise as \(N\to\infty\) and is dominated by \(|\rho_k|\), which is summable by hypothesis; dominated convergence gives \(\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(1-\tfrac kN)\rho_k\to\sum_{k\ge1}
\rho_k\), hence \(N\,\mathrm{Var}(\bar\theta_N)=\sigma^2(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(1-\tfrac kN)\rho_k)\to\sigma^2
\tau_{\mathrm{int}}\). \(\square\)


Definition 24.3 (Effective sample size of an MCMC chain) For a second-order stationary chain with integrated autocorrelation time \(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=1+2\sum_{k
\ge1}\rho_k\), the effective sample size for the posterior mean is \[
N_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{N}{\tau_{\mathrm{int}}}=\frac{N}{1+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\rho_k}.
\tag{24.13}\] With \(M\) chains of length \(N\) the total is \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}=MN/\tau_{\mathrm{int}}\). The ratio \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}/N\in(0,1]\) is the chain’s efficiency. In practice the infinite sum is truncated at the first lag where the estimated autocorrelations cease to be reliably positive (for example by Geyer’s initial-monotone-sequence rule), because sample autocorrelations at large lags are dominated by noise. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) answers “how many truly independent draws is this correlated chain worth?” A run of \(4000\) draws with \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}=4000\) is as good as \(4000\) coin flips; one with \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}=200\) carries the information of only \(200\). The integrated autocorrelation time \(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}\) is the exchange rate: each draw is worth \(1/\tau_{\mathrm{int}}\) of an independent draw. A low \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) does not bias the estimate; it makes it noisy, which for an ITC shows up as jittery credible-interval endpoints on the contrast. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The definition is justified by the property that gives it its name: \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) is the number of independent draws that would estimate the posterior mean with the same Monte Carlo variance.

Corollary 24.1 (\(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) equalizes Monte Carlo variance) Under the summability hypothesis of Proposition 24.1, the asymptotic Monte Carlo variance of the chain mean is \[
\mathrm{Var}(\bar\theta_N)\sim\frac{\sigma^2}{N_{\mathrm{eff}}}\qquad(N\to\infty),
\] the same as the variance \(\sigma^2/n\) of a mean of \(n=N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) independent draws. The Monte Carlo standard error of \(\bar\theta_N\) is therefore \(\sigma/\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff}}}\).


Proof. By Proposition 24.1, \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar\theta_N)\sim\sigma^2\tau_{\mathrm{int}}/N=\sigma^2/(N/
\tau_{\mathrm{int}})=\sigma^2/N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) from the definition Equation 24.13. Equating to the iid variance \(\sigma^2/n\) gives \(n=N_{\mathrm{eff}}\), and the standard error is the square root. \(\square\)


Example 24.1 (Effective sample size of an AR(1) chain) The first-order autoregressive process \(\theta^{(t)}=\phi\,\theta^{(t-1)}+\varepsilon_t\) with \(|\phi|<1\) and white-noise \(\varepsilon_t\) is the canonical model for a sticky MCMC chain; its lag-\(k\) autocorrelation is \(\rho_k=\phi^{k}\). Summing the geometric series, \[
\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=1+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty\phi^k=1+\frac{2\phi}{1-\phi}=\frac{1+\phi}{1-\phi},
\qquad N_{\mathrm{eff}}=N\,\frac{1-\phi}{1+\phi}.
\] A mildly autocorrelated chain with \(\phi=\tfrac13\) has \(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=2\) and efficiency \(\tfrac12\): \(N=4000\) draws are worth \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}=2000\). A sticky chain with \(\phi=0.9\) has \(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=19\) and efficiency \(1/19\): the same \(4000\) draws are worth only \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}
\approx 210\), a twentyfold loss. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The same formula, tabulated across stickiness, shows how fast efficiency collapses:
