The message for an indirect comparison: a chain can pass \(\widehat R\le 1.01\) and still be nearly useless if it is sticky, so \(\widehat R\) and \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) must be read together. In the running example a small \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) on \(d_{AC}\) warns that its posterior mean is imprecisely pinned down by Monte Carlo, and a small tail \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) (defined next) warns specifically that the \(95\%\) credible-interval endpoints reported to the payer are noisy.

Remark. Bulk and tail effective sample size. The estimate Equation 24.13 targets the posterior mean. Posterior quantiles, which determine credible intervals, are governed by the autocorrelation of indicator functions \(\mathbf 1\{\theta^{(t)}\le q\}\) rather than of \(\theta^{(t)}\) itself, and can mix far worse, especially deep in the tails. Current software therefore reports a bulk \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) (from the rank-normalized draws, for the center of the distribution) and a tail \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) (the minimum of the effective sizes for the \(5\%\) and \(95\%\) quantile indicators). A common standard is bulk and tail \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\ge 400\) across chains for inference, with larger tail \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) demanded when extreme quantiles are reported. A small tail \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) beside a healthy bulk \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) is the signature of a chain that estimates the posterior mean well but its interval endpoints poorly. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This development corresponds to I.3 in the proof catalogue.

title: 24  Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics
text:
24.7 Monitoring the numerical-integration error
We turn to the error peculiar to ML-NMR. Each aggregate-data study contributes to the likelihood through an integral of the individual-level integrand \(g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x))\) over the study’s covariate distribution (the aggregation theorem, Theorem 20.1), and that integral is replaced in computation by a QMC average over \(N\) points on the unit hypercube (Theorem 22.6). The sampler therefore targets not the exact posterior but its QMC approximation, and we must certify that the substitution is harmless. This is catalogue result I.4.
Write the exact aggregate-cell quantity as \(\theta=\int_{[0,1]^d}f(\mathbf u)\,d\mathbf u\), where the integrand \(f=g^{-1}\!\circ\eta_{jk}\circ\Psi\) folds the inverse link, the linear predictor, and the copula-plus-inverse-CDF transform \(\Psi\) of Chapter 22 (Theorem 22.4, Definition 22.5) into a function on the cube; write \(\widehat\theta^{(N)}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N f(\mathbf u_i)\) for its QMC estimate on the first \(N\) points of a Sobol’ sequence (Definition 22.3). The error is deterministic given the point set, and is controlled by the Koksma-Hlawka inequality of Chapter 22.
In words, and tied to the running network: the aggregate study \(BC\) never shows us its patients, only arm summaries, so to evaluate its likelihood we must average the individual response over the covariate mix in that arm. The transform \(\Psi\) is the recipe that turns a uniform grid point \(\mathbf
u\in[0,1]^d\) into a plausible patient’s covariate vector (age, severity) drawn from the arm’s fitted distribution; \(\eta_{jk}\) then gives that synthetic patient’s linear predictor, \(g^{-1}\) converts it to an event probability, and the QMC sum averages over a grid of such patients. So \(\theta\) is the arm’s expected event probability and \(\widehat\theta^{(N)}\) is our \(N\)-patient numerical approximation to it. Two glosses for the symbols carried over from Chapter 22: the Hardy-Krause variation \(V_{\mathrm{HK}}
(f)\) is a multivariable generalization of total variation, a measure of how much the integrand wiggles (its room to be mis-sampled by a finite grid), and the star discrepancy \(D_N^{*}\) measures how unevenly the \(N\) points fill the cube (small discrepancy means they cover it evenly). The Koksma-Hlawka bound below simply multiplies the two.

Remark. The error is bounded, not random. By Theorem 22.3, for \(f\) of finite Hardy-Krause variation, \[
\big|\widehat\theta^{(N)}-\theta\big|\le V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)\,D_N^{*}(P_N),
\tag{24.14}\] the product of the integrand’s variation and the star discrepancy \(D_N^{*}\) of the point set \(P_N\), which for a Sobol’ net is \(O\big((\log N)^d/N\big)\). Unlike the \(O(N^{-1/2})\) root-mean-square error of plain Monte Carlo (Theorem 22.2), Equation 24.14 is a worst-case bound with no probability attached. The difficulty is that \(V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)\) is unknown and usually uncomputable, so Equation 24.14 certifies a rate but not a usable constant. The operational diagnostic below sidesteps it by measuring convergence empirically. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Definition 24.4 (Doubling diagnostic for integration error) Let \(\widehat\theta^{(N)}\) and \(\widehat\theta^{(N/2)}\) be the QMC estimates of an aggregate-cell quantity using the first \(N\) and the first \(N/2\) points of the same Sobol’ sequence. The estimate is declared converged at tolerance \(\epsilon\) when the relative doubling increment satisfies \[
\frac{\big|\widehat\theta^{(N)}-\widehat\theta^{(N/2)}\big|}{\big|\widehat\theta^{(N)}\big|}<\epsilon
\tag{24.15}\] for every aggregate cell, for a small tolerance such as \(\epsilon=0.005\). If the criterion fails for any cell, \(N\) is doubled and the test repeated. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation, and a caution on the denominator. The rule is the numerical analyst’s oldest trick: if halving the grid barely changes the answer, the answer has stopped moving, so you can stop refining. The relative form divides by \(|\widehat\theta^{(N)}|\) so that “small” means small compared to the quantity itself. That is exactly wrong when the quantity is near zero (a rare-event probability) or naturally lives on a transformed scale that passes through zero (a log-odds or log-hazard): there the relative increment blows up for no real reason, and one should switch to an absolute tolerance on the quantity, or run the test on the probability scale where the target is bounded in \([0,1]\). In the running example the \(BC\) arm’s event probability sits comfortably away from \(0\) and \(1\), so the relative test is safe; a sparse-outcome cell would call for the absolute version. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The diagnostic measures the observable increment \(\widehat\theta^{(N)}-\widehat\theta^{(N/2)}\), whereas what we care about is the unobservable error \(\widehat\theta^{(N)}-\theta\). The following proposition shows that, whenever the error decays at a definite rate, the observable increment controls the unobservable error up to a known constant, which is what makes Equation 24.15 a valid stopping rule.

Proposition 24.2 (The increment bounds the error under geometric decay) Write \(e_N=\widehat\theta^{(N)}-\theta\) for the error and \(\Delta_N=\widehat\theta^{(N)}-
\widehat\theta^{(N/2)}=e_N-e_{N/2}\) for the observable increment. Suppose there is a contraction factor \(\rho\in[0,1)\) with \(|e_N|\le\rho\,|e_{N/2}|\) along the doubling sequence (a definite convergence rate). Then \[
|e_{N/2}|\le\frac{|\Delta_N|}{1-\rho}\qquad\text{and}\qquad |e_N|\le\frac{\rho\,|\Delta_N|}{1-\rho}.
\tag{24.16}\] Consequently, passing the relative test Equation 24.15 certifies a relative integration error of at most \(\tfrac{\rho}{1-\rho}\,\epsilon\) in \(\widehat\theta^{(N)}\), to leading order.


Proof. From \(\Delta_N=e_N-e_{N/2}\) and the triangle inequality, \(|e_{N/2}|=|e_N-\Delta_N|\le|e_N|+|\Delta_N|\le
\rho|e_{N/2}|+|\Delta_N|\). Rearranging, \((1-\rho)|e_{N/2}|\le|\Delta_N|\), which is the first bound in Equation 24.16 since \(\rho<1\); the second follows from \(|e_N|\le\rho|e_{N/2}|\). Dividing by \(|\theta|\approx|\widehat\theta^{(N)}|\) and using Equation 24.15, the relative error is at most \(\tfrac{\rho}{1-\rho}\,\epsilon\) to leading order in the small quantities. \(\square\)


Remark. What \(\rho\) is for QMC and for Monte Carlo. For a QMC rule with error envelope \(a_N=(\log N)^d/N\), the ratio of successive errors is \(a_N/a_{N/2}=\tfrac12\cdot\big(\tfrac{\log N}{\log N-\log 2}\big)^{d}\to
\tfrac12\) as \(N\to\infty\), so \(\rho\approx\tfrac12\) in the regime where the logarithmic factor is slowly varying, and Equation 24.16 gives \(|e_N|\lesssim|\Delta_N|\): the increment is itself a good error estimate. For plain Monte Carlo, \(a_N=N^{-1/2}\) gives \(a_N/a_{N/2}=1/\sqrt2\approx0.707\), so \(\rho\approx
0.707\) and the true error can be roughly \(2.4\) times the observed increment, a reminder that the doubling rule is sharper for QMC than for Monte Carlo. The logarithmic factor means \(\rho\) is only asymptotically \(\tfrac12\); in the pre-asymptotic regime one should keep \(\epsilon\) conservative, which is why the recommended tolerances are small. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Practical grid sizes and the combined budget. Empirically, \(N\in\{64,128,256\}\) Sobol’ points suffice for ML-NMR with two to four covariates, and the reference software defaults to \(N=64\); high-dimensional covariate sets (\(d>6\)) call for \(N=256\) or for an Owen-scrambled Sobol’ rule, a randomized QMC variant whose error has better behavior on non-smooth integrands. The total error in a posterior summary is the sum of the two contributions of this chapter, \[
\text{total error}\ \approx\ \underbrace{O\big(1/\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff}}}\big)}_{\text{MCMC error}}
\ +\ \underbrace{O\big((\log N)^d/N\big)}_{\text{QMC error}},
\] and a credible analysis drives both below the precision required of the reported contrast. The two are controlled by different levers: longer or better-mixed chains for the first, more integration points for the second. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why not just use a huge grid? Because the QMC sum sits inside the likelihood. Every one of the millions of likelihood evaluations that HMC performs, at every leapfrog step of every draw, re-runs the \(N\)-point sum for every aggregate cell, so the wall-clock cost of the entire fit scales linearly in \(N\): doubling the grid doubles the run time. The doubling diagnostic exists precisely to find the smallest \(N\) that is accurate enough, rather than paying for a large grid everywhere out of caution. For the running network, with \(d=2\) covariates in the \(BC\) arm, \(N=64\) Sobol’ points typically pass the test at \(\epsilon=0.005\); a submission with six or more effect modifiers is where one must check the doubling rule seriously and may need \(N=256\) or an Owen-scrambled rule. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This development corresponds to I.4 in the proof catalogue.

title: 24  Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics
section: 24.8 Information criteria: DIC, WAIC, and leave-one-out cross-validation
text:
24.8 Information criteria: DIC, WAIC, and leave-one-out cross-validation
We now turn from certifying a single fit to comparing fits. The right currency for Bayesian model comparison is out-of-sample predictive accuracy: how well would the fitted model predict a fresh observation? All three criteria of this section estimate the same target, the expected log pointwise predictive density, and the point of the section is to derive how they are related, why two of them (WAIC and LOO-CV) are nearly identical, and where the third (DIC) sits. This is catalogue result I.5.
Fix the data \(\mathbf y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)\) with a likelihood that factors across observations, \(p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\xi)=\prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\).

Remark. What is an observation in ML-NMR? The index \(i\) ranges over whatever units the likelihood factorizes into, and in a mixed IPD-plus-AgD model these are of two kinds. For the IPD study \(AB\) each individual patient is one factor, with \(p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\) a Bernoulli response probability. For the aggregate study \(BC\) the factor is one arm’s summary, with \(p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\) the binomial probability of that arm’s responder count given its integrated (QMC-averaged) event probability. So \(n\) counts individual patients from \(AB\) plus arm-cells from \(BC\), not studies and not contrasts. This choice of unit is not cosmetic: WAIC’s penalty, LOO’s held-out density, PSIS’s \(\widehat k\), and the standard error of a model-comparison difference are all computed per factor, so leaving out unit \(i\) means leaving out one patient (fine-grained, low influence) or one whole aggregate arm (coarse, high influence). When you read a large \(\widehat k\) in this model, first ask whether the flagged unit is a single patient or an entire aggregate arm. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Write the per-observation log likelihood as \(\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)=\log p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\) and its posterior mean and variance as \[
m_i=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)],
\qquad
v_i=\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)].
\] The posterior predictive density of a held-out replicate is \(p(\,\cdot\mid\mathbf y)=\mathbb
E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[p(\,\cdot\mid\boldsymbol\xi)]\) (the posterior predictive distribution of Chapter 8). The expected log pointwise predictive density (elpd) is the target, \[
\mathrm{elpd}=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E_{\tilde y_i}\big[\log p(\tilde y_i\mid\mathbf y)\big],
\] where \(\tilde y_i\) is a new observation from the true data-generating process at the \(i\)-th design point; larger elpd means better prediction. Its naive in-sample estimate, evaluating the predictive density at the observed data, is the log pointwise predictive density \[
\mathrm{lppd}=\sum_{i=1}^n\log p(y_i\mid\mathbf y)
=\sum_{i=1}^n\log\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}\big[p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\big].
\tag{24.17}\] The lppd is optimistic, because each \(y_i\) was used both to form the posterior and to test it. The criteria differ in how they correct that optimism.
The engine of the section is one exact identity that re-expresses the leave-one-out predictive density as a posterior expectation under the full posterior, so that it can be computed from a single fit.

Lemma 24.6 (Leave-one-out importance-sampling identity) Let \(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i})\) denote the posterior with the \(i\)-th observation removed. Then the leave-one-out predictive density is the posterior harmonic mean of the \(i\)-th likelihood, \[
p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=\frac{1}{\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}\big[\,1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)
\,\big]},
\tag{24.18}\] and more generally, for any integrable \(\psi\), \[
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i}}[\psi(\boldsymbol\xi)]
=\frac{\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}\big[\psi(\boldsymbol\xi)\,r_i(\boldsymbol\xi)\big]}
{\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}\big[r_i(\boldsymbol\xi)\big]},
\qquad r_i(\boldsymbol\xi)=\frac{1}{p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)} .
\tag{24.19}\]


Proof. Strategy. We relate the leave-one-out posterior to the full posterior by a single importance ratio, then read off the harmonic-mean form by choosing the test function \(\psi\) cleverly. Every step is one line of Bayes’ theorem; there is no hidden machinery.
Because the likelihood factors, removing \(y_i\) divides the full likelihood by the \(i\)-th factor, so \[
\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i})
=\frac{p(\mathbf y_{-i}\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\,\pi(\boldsymbol\xi)}{p(\mathbf y_{-i})}
=\frac{p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\,\pi(\boldsymbol\xi)}{p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\,p(\mathbf y_{-i})}
=\frac{p(\mathbf y)}{p(\mathbf y_{-i})}\cdot\frac{\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)}{p(y_i\mid
\boldsymbol\xi)},
\] using Bayes’ theorem (Theorem 8.3 is the conjugate special case; here we use only the proportionality \(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\propto p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\pi(\boldsymbol
\xi)\)). Thus the importance ratio of the leave-one-out posterior to the full posterior is \(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i})/\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)=\frac{p(\mathbf y)}{p(\mathbf
y_{-i})}\,r_i(\boldsymbol\xi)\), proportional to \(r_i(\boldsymbol\xi)=1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\). For any \(\psi\), \[
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i}}[\psi]
=\int\psi(\boldsymbol\xi)\,\frac{\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i})}{\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)}\,
\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\,d\boldsymbol\xi
=\frac{p(\mathbf y)}{p(\mathbf y_{-i})}\,\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[\psi\,r_i] .
\] Taking \(\psi\equiv 1\) gives \(1=\frac{p(\mathbf y)}{p(\mathbf y_{-i})}\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf
y}[r_i]\), which both pins the unknown constant and, on dividing, yields the self-normalized form Equation 24.19 (self-normalized because the denominator is estimated from the same draws, so the unknown constant \(p(\mathbf y)/p(\mathbf y_{-i})\) cancels and never has to be computed). Finally take \(\psi=p(y_i\mid\cdot)\): the numerator is \(\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf
y}[p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\,r_i]=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[1]=1\), so \[
p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i}}[p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)]
=\frac{1}{\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[r_i]}
=\frac{1}{\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)]},
\] which is Equation 24.18. \(\square\)

With the identity in hand we define the three criteria and prove how they relate. All are written so that lower is better, on the deviance scale (a factor of \(-2\) times a log predictive density), to match historical convention.

Definition 24.5 (DIC, WAIC, and LOO-CV) With \(D(\boldsymbol\xi)=-2\log p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\) the deviance and \(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}=
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[\boldsymbol\xi]\) the posterior mean:

the deviance information criterion is \(\mathrm{DIC}=D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})+2p_{D}\) with effective parameter count \(p_{D}=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[D(\boldsymbol\xi)]-D(\bar{\boldsymbol
\xi})\);
the widely applicable information criterion is \(\mathrm{WAIC}=-2\big(\mathrm{lppd}-p_{\mathrm
{WAIC}}\big)\) with \(p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid
\mathbf y}[\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)]\);
leave-one-out cross-validation is \(\mathrm{LOO}=-2\,\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_{\mathrm{loo}}\) with \(\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_{\mathrm{loo}}=\sum_{i=1}^n\log p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)



Remark. Reader translation. All three are “fit minus a complexity penalty,” on the deviance scale where lower is better. The first term rewards fitting the data you have; the penalty (\(2p_D\), \(2p_{\mathrm
{WAIC}}\), or the built-in leave-one-out of LOO) docks you for the optimism of having used each observation both to fit and to score the model. They differ only in how honestly they estimate that optimism, which the next theorem quantifies. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Theorem 24.3 (Relationships among the predictive criteria) Assume the posterior concentrates as \(n\to\infty\) in the standard regular way, so that for each \(i\) the posterior fluctuation of \(\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)\) has variance \(v_i=O(1/n)\) and third cumulant \(\kappa_{3,i}=o(v_i)\). Then:

(WAIC equals LOO to second order.) For each observation, \[
\log p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=\mathrm{lppd}_i-v_i+o(v_i),
\tag{24.20}\] where \(\mathrm{lppd}_i=\log\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)]\). Summing, \(\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_{\mathrm{loo}}=\mathrm{lppd}-p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}+o(1)\), so \(\mathrm{WAIC}=\mathrm{LOO}+o(1)\).
(DIC’s effective parameters.) For an approximately quadratic log likelihood with observed information \(\mathcal J=-\nabla^2\log p(\mathbf y\mid\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})\) (the curvature of the log likelihood at the posterior mean, the sample analogue of the Fisher information of Chapter 5), \[
p_{D}=\operatorname{tr}\!\big(\mathcal J\,\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\big)+o(1),
\tag{24.21}\] which under a flat prior, where the Bernstein-von Mises approximation gives \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\approx\mathcal J^{-1}\), equals the parameter dimension \(p\) to leading order. The WAIC penalty satisfies the same trace formula, \(p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=\operatorname{tr}
(\mathcal J\,\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y))+o(1)\), so \(p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=p_{D}+o(1)\) and all three criteria agree to leading order.
(Parameterization.) WAIC and LOO depend on \(\boldsymbol\xi\) only through the pointwise densities \(p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\) and are invariant under reparameterization of \(\boldsymbol\xi\); DIC depends on the posterior mean \(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}\) through \(D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})\) and is not.



Proof. Strategy and vocabulary. The whole of Part 1 is one Taylor expansion of a cumulant generating function: for a random quantity \(Z\), this is the function \(K(t)=\log\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]\) whose derivatives at \(t=0\) are the cumulants of \(Z\) (the first cumulant is the mean, the second the variance, the third \(\kappa_3\) a measure of skewness). The one trick is that the two predictive densities we must compare turn out to be exactly \(K\) evaluated at \(t=+1\) and at \(t=-1\), so subtracting two Taylor series does the work.
Part 1. Fix \(i\) and let \(K_i(t)=\log\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[e^{t\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)}]\) be the cumulant generating function of \(\ell_i\) under the posterior, with \(K_i(0)=0\), \(K_i'(0)=m_i\), \(K_i''(0)=v_i\), and third derivative the third cumulant \(\kappa_{3,i}\). By Taylor expansion, \[
K_i(t)=m_i t+\tfrac12 v_i t^2+\tfrac16\kappa_{3,i}t^3+\cdots .
\] Two evaluations give the two predictive densities. First, \(\mathrm{lppd}_i=\log\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi
\mid\mathbf y}[p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)]=\log\mathbb E[e^{\ell_i}]=K_i(1)=m_i+\tfrac12 v_i+O(\kappa_{3,i})\). Second, by the leave-one-out identity Equation 24.18, \[
\log p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=-\log\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}\big[e^{-\ell_i}\big]
=-K_i(-1)=-\big(-m_i+\tfrac12 v_i-\tfrac16\kappa_{3,i}+\cdots\big)=m_i-\tfrac12 v_i+O(\kappa_{3,i}).
\] Subtracting, \(\mathrm{lppd}_i-\log p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=v_i+O(\kappa_{3,i})=v_i+o(v_i)\) under the hypothesis \(\kappa_{3,i}=o(v_i)\), which rearranges to Equation 24.20. Summing over \(i\) and recognizing \(\sum_i v_i=p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}\) gives \(\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_{\mathrm{loo}}=\mathrm{lppd}-
p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}+o(1)\); multiplying by \(-2\), \(\mathrm{LOO}=\mathrm{WAIC}+o(1)\).
Part 2. Write \(\ell(\boldsymbol\xi)=\log p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\) and expand to second order about the posterior mean \(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}\), \[
\ell(\boldsymbol\xi)=\ell(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})+\nabla\ell(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})^\top(\boldsymbol\xi-
\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})-\tfrac12(\boldsymbol\xi-\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})^\top\mathcal J\,(\boldsymbol\xi-
\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})+\cdots,
\] with \(\mathcal J=-\nabla^2\ell(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})\). Taking the posterior expectation and using \(\mathbb E[\boldsymbol\xi-\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}]=\mathbf 0\) and \(\mathbb E[(\boldsymbol\xi-\bar{\boldsymbol
\xi})(\boldsymbol\xi-\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})^\top]=\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\), \[
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[\ell(\boldsymbol\xi)]=\ell(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})-\tfrac12
\operatorname{tr}\!\big(\mathcal J\,\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\big)+o(1).
\] Since \(p_D=\mathbb E[D(\boldsymbol\xi)]-D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})=-2\big(\mathbb E[\ell(\boldsymbol\xi)]-
\ell(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})\big)\), substituting gives Equation 24.21. Under a flat prior the posterior is approximately \(\mathcal N(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi},\mathcal J^{-1})\) (Bernstein-von Mises), so \(\mathrm{Var}
(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\approx\mathcal J^{-1}\) and \(p_D\approx\operatorname{tr}(I_p)=p\). For the WAIC penalty, linearize each \(\ell_i\) about \(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}\): \(\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)\approx\ell_i
(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})+\nabla\ell_i(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})^\top(\boldsymbol\xi-\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})\), so \(v_i=\mathrm{Var}[\ell_i]\approx\nabla\ell_i^\top\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\nabla\ell_i\) and \[
p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=\sum_i v_i\approx\operatorname{tr}\!\Big(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)
\sum_i\nabla\ell_i\nabla\ell_i^\top\Big)=\operatorname{tr}\!\big(\mathcal J\,\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi
\mid\mathbf y)\big)+o(1),
\] because the outer-product (empirical Fisher) information \(\sum_i\nabla\ell_i\nabla\ell_i^\top\) agrees with the observed information \(\mathcal J\) to leading order near the mode, where the score \(\sum_i\nabla\ell_i\) vanishes. Hence \(p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=p_D+o(1)\) and, combined with Part 1, \(\mathrm{DIC}=\mathrm{WAIC}+o(1)=
\mathrm{LOO}+o(1)\).
Part 3. \(\mathrm{WAIC}\) and \(\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_{\mathrm{loo}}\) are built only from the numbers \(\{p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\}\), which are densities of the data and are unchanged by any smooth invertible reparameterization \(\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto\boldsymbol\eta(\boldsymbol\xi)\) (the likelihood value at a parameter point does not depend on the coordinates used to name that point). DIC contains \(D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})\), and the posterior mean \(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}\) is not equivariant under nonlinear reparameterization (\(\overline{\boldsymbol\eta(\boldsymbol\xi)}\neq\boldsymbol\eta(\bar
{\boldsymbol\xi})\) in general), so \(D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})\), \(p_D\), and DIC change under reparameterization. \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters, and a scorecard. The theorem says the three criteria estimate one thing, out-of-sample predictive accuracy, and agree to leading order, so the choice among them is about robustness and honesty, not about targeting different quantities. For an indirect comparison you will be asked to justify a modeling choice, say whether to include the age effect modifier \(\boldsymbol\beta_2\) or which outcome model to use, and predictive criteria are the Bayesian answer. The scorecard:









Property
DIC
WAIC
LOO (PSIS)




Estimates out-of-sample elpd
yes
yes
yes


Uses the whole posterior, not just its mean
no
yes
yes


Pointwise (per-observation, gives a standard error)
no
yes
yes


Invariant to reparameterization
no
yes
yes


Per-observation reliability diagnostic
no
no
yes (\(\widehat k\))


Can misbehave (negative penalty on skew posteriors)
yes
rarely
flagged by \(\widehat k\)



The ranking is LOO, then WAIC, then DIC. Report WAIC or PSIS-LOO by default; report DIC only when an older NMA analysis you must compare against reported it, and then with these caveats stated. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Comparison is not checking. A subtle trap for the indirect-comparison analyst: a model can have the best WAIC or LOO in a candidate set and still answer the wrong question. Predictive criteria score fit to the observed evidence; they say nothing about whether the target population is right, whether the shared-effect-modifier assumption holds, or whether the networks overlap enough to transport an effect (Chapters 11, 12, and 17). Model checking, posterior predictive checks, prior-sensitivity analysis, and covariate-overlap diagnostics, is a separate obligation that must be met before model comparison is meaningful. Good LOO on a model that violates transportability is a precise answer to the wrong question. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Computation and recommendation. Every quantity here is computed from the posterior draws \(\{\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)}\}_{s=1}^S\) by replacing posterior expectations with sample averages: \(\mathrm{lppd}_i\approx\log\big(\tfrac1S\sum_s p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\big)\) and \(v_i\approx\) the sample variance of \(\{\log p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\}_s\). WAIC and LOO are pointwise (a contribution per observation), which yields a standard error for the criterion and for differences between models, and flags individual influential observations; DIC offers neither. Because DIC further depends on the non-equivariant posterior mean and can return a negative \(p_D\) for skewed posteriors, current practice prefers WAIC or, better, the LOO-CV of the next section, which estimates the same elpd while leaving each observation genuinely out. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This development corresponds to I.5 in the proof catalogue, and to result D.14 (the DIC decomposition) of Chapter 15.

title: 24  Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics
text:
24.9 Pareto-smoothed importance sampling LOO
The leave-one-out identity Equation 24.18 expresses \(p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})\) as a posterior expectation, hence as a single Monte Carlo average over the draws we already have, with no refitting. The catch is that the importance ratios \(r_i(\boldsymbol\xi)=1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\) are heavy-tailed: they are largest exactly where the \(i\)-th likelihood is smallest, in regions the full posterior visits rarely, so a few draws can dominate the sum and inflate its variance, sometimes to infinity. Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS) repairs the tail and, as a by-product, returns a diagnostic that says when the repair can be trusted. This is catalogue result I.6.

Definition 24.6 (Pareto-smoothed importance sampling LOO) Given posterior draws \(\{\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)}\}_{s=1}^S\) from the full posterior, form for each observation \(i\) the raw importance ratios \(r_i^{(s)}=1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\). PSIS proceeds:

Fit a generalized Pareto distribution (GPD) to the largest ratios (the upper tail, in practice the top \(20\%\) or the top \(\min\{0.2S,\,3\sqrt S\}\) ratios), obtaining a shape estimate \(\widehat k\) and scale estimate.
Replace those largest ratios by the expected GPD order statistics implied by the fit, and cap all ratios at the largest fitted value (smoothing and truncation), giving stabilized weights \(\bar
r_i^{(s)}\).
Estimate the leave-one-out predictive density by the self-normalized importance average of Equation 24.19, \[
\widehat p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=\frac{\sum_{s}\bar r_i^{(s)}\,p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})}
{\sum_{s}\bar r_i^{(s)}},
\tag{24.22}\] and report \(\mathrm{PSIS\text{-}LOO}=-2\sum_i\log\widehat p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})\).

The fitted shape \(\widehat k_i\) is retained as a per-observation reliability diagnostic. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation: what is being smoothed, and what \(\widehat k\) measures. To reuse one posterior fit as if we had refit it without observation \(i\), we reweight the draws by \(r_i=1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol
\xi)\): draws where the model fit \(y_i\) badly (small \(p\)) get large weight, because those are the draws the without-\(i\) posterior would favor. The danger is a handful of draws with tiny \(p(y_i\mid\cdot)\) and therefore enormous weights that swamp the sum, the way a single lottery winner swamps the mean income of a room. The generalized Pareto distribution (GPD) is the standard model for the extreme upper tail of such weights; its shape parameter \(k\) measures how heavy that tail is (larger \(k\) means a heavier tail, more prone to one dominating weight). PSIS fits a GPD to the largest weights, replaces them with the tamer values the fit predicts, and returns \(\widehat k\) as a thermometer for how dangerous the tail was. A large \(\widehat k\) says the reweighting is untrustworthy and, substantively, that unit \(i\) is influential. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

That the raw ratios are the correct importance weights is exactly Lemma 24.6: \(r_i\propto
\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i})/\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\), so Equation 24.19 targets the leave-one-out posterior. The reason smoothing is needed, and the meaning of the thresholds on \(\widehat
k\), both follow from a single fact about the moments of a Pareto tail.

Lemma 24.7 (Moments of a generalized Pareto tail) Let \(X\) have a generalized Pareto upper tail with shape \(k>0\) and scale \(\sigma>0\), that is survival function \(\bar F(x)=(1+k x/\sigma)^{-1/k}\) for \(x\ge 0\). Then \(\mathbb E[X^{m}]<\infty\) if and only if \(m<1/k\). In particular the mean is finite iff \(k<1\) and the variance is finite iff \(k<1/2\).


Proof. The density is \(f(x)=\tfrac1\sigma(1+kx/\sigma)^{-1/k-1}\), so as \(x\to\infty\), \(f(x)\sim C\,x^{-1/k-1}\) for a positive constant \(C\) (since \((1+kx/\sigma)^{-1/k-1}\sim(kx/\sigma)^{-1/k-1}\)). The \(m\)-th moment is \(\int_0^\infty x^m f(x)\,dx\); its convergence is determined by the integrand’s decay at infinity, where \(x^m f(x)\sim C\,x^{m-1/k-1}\). The integral \(\int^{\infty}x^{m-1/k-1}\,dx\) converges if and only if the exponent is below \(-1\), that is \(m-1/k-1<-1\), equivalently \(m<1/k\). Setting \(m=1\) gives finiteness of the mean iff \(k<1\), and \(m=2\) gives finiteness of the variance iff \(k<1/2\). \(\square\)


Theorem 24.4 (The shape parameter governs reliability) Let the importance ratios \(r_i\) have a generalized Pareto upper tail with shape \(\widehat k_i\). Then:

if \(\widehat k_i<\tfrac12\), the ratios have finite variance, the central limit theorem applies to the importance estimator, and the PSIS-LOO estimate Equation 24.22 is reliable;
if \(\tfrac12\le\widehat k_i<1\), the ratios have finite mean but infinite variance, so the raw estimator has no \(\sqrt S\) central-limit guarantee, although PSIS smoothing keeps the bias and variance moderate in practice up to about \(\widehat k_i\approx 0.7\);
if \(\widehat k_i\ge 1\), even the mean is infinite and the importance estimate is unusable; that observation must be evaluated by actually refitting the model without it.



Proof. By Lemma 24.7 the second moment of \(r_i\) is finite iff \(\widehat k_i<\tfrac12\), which is the classical condition for a \(\sqrt S\) central limit theorem for the self-normalized importance estimator Equation 24.19; this gives (1). For \(\tfrac12\le\widehat k_i<1\) the same lemma gives a finite mean but an infinite variance, so the importance average still converges to the right value by the law of large numbers but without a Gaussian error rate; the residual usefulness up to \(\widehat k_i\approx 0.7\) is the empirical finding that PSIS truncation and smoothing reduce the finite-sample error enough to be tolerable in that range, which is why \(0.7\) rather than \(0.5\) is the operational alarm. For \(\widehat k_i\ge 1\) the mean is infinite, the importance estimator does not even converge to a finite limit, and refitting is the only recourse; this is (3). \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters: an influential study in the running network. Suppose the fitted model reports \(\widehat k=0.8\) for the aggregate \(BC\) arm and \(\widehat k<0.5\) everywhere else. Read it twice, exactly as Theorem 24.4 licenses. As a computational warning, \(0.8\) exceeds the \(0.7\) alarm, so the PSIS-LOO contribution of that arm is unreliable and should be recomputed by actually refitting without it. As a substantive signal, it says the \(d_{BC}\) contrast, and therefore the indirect \(d_{AC}\) that depends on it, rests heavily on this one study: the estimate is one study away from changing. The correct response is a robustness analysis, refit without \(BC\) and report how far \(d_{AC}\) moves, which is precisely the kind of sensitivity check an HTA reviewer demands of a two-study network. A high \(\widehat
k\) is thus not only a caution about a number; it is the diagnostic pointing at the study your conclusion leans on. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why the harmonic-mean estimator fails, and PSIS as the fix. Setting all weights equal in Equation 24.18 recovers the notorious harmonic-mean estimator \(\widehat p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=
S/\sum_s 1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\), whose ratios \(r_i\) typically have \(\widehat k_i>\tfrac12\) and sometimes \(\widehat k_i\ge 1\); it is unstable precisely for the reason Theorem 24.4 isolates. PSIS replaces the offending upper tail of the \(r_i\) by the smooth GPD fit, which both stabilizes the estimate and yields \(\widehat k_i\) as a calibrated warning light. For ML-NMR and its unanchored extension, \(\widehat k_i\) flags aggregate cells or studies whose removal would most change the fit, so a large \(\widehat k_i\) is read twice: as a caution about the LOO number and as a substantive indication of an influential or poorly-fit data point. PSIS-LOO is the default method of the standard cross-validation software and the recommended criterion for these models. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. No machine-checked counterpart. None of the results of this chapter has a counterpart in the companion Coq development; the formalized tree ends with the algebraic content of population adjustment, and the computational and diagnostic material here is established by the proofs above and validated empirically rather than by mechanized proof. No theorem in this chapter carries a machine-checked tag. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This development corresponds to I.6 in the proof catalogue.

title: 24  Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics
section: 24.10 How to use this chapter in practice: a diagnostic workflow
text:
24.10 How to use this chapter in practice: a diagnostic workflow
The results above prove that each diagnostic does what it claims. This section assembles them into the order a health researcher should actually run, and into a single table to consult when one fires. The ordering principle is that model comparison is meaningless until the fit is computationally trustworthy, which is meaningless until the model has passed checking. So the sequence runs computation, then checking, then comparison, and never the reverse.
The order of operations.

Divergences and tree depth first. Before reading any estimate, check the count of divergent transitions after warmup and whether trajectories are hitting the maximum tree depth. A nonzero divergence count is a red flag that the sampler could not enter part of the posterior; treat it as a geometry problem (Section 24.4), not a “run longer” problem.
\(\widehat R\) next. Require \(\widehat R\le 1.01\) for every reported quantity: contrasts, \(\tau\), baselines, effect modifiers, and the transformed marginal probabilities. A failure here means the chains disagree (Section 24.5); do not read the posterior.
Bulk and tail \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\). With convergence established, check that both exceed about \(400\) per quantity (Section 24.6). Low bulk \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) makes the posterior mean noisy; low tail \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) makes the credible-interval endpoints noisy.
Inspect the culprits. For any parameter that failed, look at its trace and at pairs plots against \(\log\tau\); a funnel signature (divergences bunched at small \(\tau\)) points to the non-centered fix.
QMC doubling for aggregate cells. Confirm the integration grid is fine enough

so that the likelihood the sampler targeted is the one you meant.

Posterior predictive and assumption checks. Only a model that fits and that respects its transportability and effect-modification assumptions (Chapters 11, 12, 17) is worth comparing.
Then, and only then, PSIS-LOO or WAIC, reading \(\widehat k\) per unit before trusting the numbers (1).

The diagnostic table. Each row is a check; consult it when the check fires.

Divergences in depth, because they are the check most often mishandled. A divergence is the leapfrog integrator’s report that it lost the trajectory: the simulated energy jumped by more than a threshold, so the proposed move was discarded and, more importantly, a region of the posterior was left unexplored. Two consequences follow. First, divergences usually signal geometry, not too few iterations: running four times as long reproduces them in the same place. The remedies are the ones this chapter derived or named, the non-centered parameterization when \(\tau\) is weakly identified (Theorem 24.1), a higher adapt_delta so warmup chooses a smaller step size, a tighter prior on \(\tau\) to keep the chain out of the extreme neck, and rescaling covariates so the mass matrix can round the geometry. Second, a few divergences are not negligible: because they concentrate exactly where the geometry is worst, often at small \(\tau\), the parameters most affected are the heterogeneity and the study effects tied to it, which for a sparse network are the very quantities the indirect comparison is most sensitive to. The correct reaction to “12 divergences” is to find where they sit and remove their cause, not to report the fit with a footnote.

The contrasts and the effect modifier are healthy: \(\widehat R=1.00\), several thousand effective draws, so the reported \(d_{AC}=-0.42\) (an odds ratio of about \(0.66\) for \(A\) versus \(C\)) is stable and precise. The last row is the failure the whole chapter anticipates: \(\tau\) has \(\widehat R=1.08\gg 1.01\) and only \(90\) bulk effective draws, the signature of a residual funnel in a one-study-per-contrast network. Reported alongside, say, “14 divergent transitions, all at \(\tau<0.1\),” the diagnosis is unambiguous. The fix is not to publish \(d_{AC}\) with a caveat; it is to refit under the non-centered parameterization (already the default here, so one would instead tighten the prior on \(\tau\) and raise adapt_delta), confirm the divergences vanish and \(\tau\)’s \(\widehat R\) falls below \(1.01\), and only then read the contrast. That is what “checking whether an indirect comparison fit can be trusted” concretely means.

title: 24  Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics
text:
24.11 A worked diagnostic example
We run the full diagnostic battery on a small, hand-checkable instance, mimicking the report one would produce for a fitted ML-NMR model: convergence (\(\widehat R\)), efficiency (\(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\)), integration error (the doubling rule), and model comparison (WAIC and PSIS-LOO). Every number can be reproduced with a calculator.

Example 24.2 (A complete diagnostic report) The numbers here are deliberately tiny so every step is checkable by hand: read each block as the hand-computation behind one row of the summary table of Section 24.10, applied to the running network. Here \(\theta=d_{AB}\) is the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) log-odds contrast, and the two fitted observations stand for one IPD patient and one aggregate arm.
Convergence: \(\widehat R\). Two chains of length \(N=4\) are run for a treatment contrast \(\theta=d_{AB}\), giving the post-warmup draws \[
\text{chain 1: }(2,4,6,8),\qquad \text{chain 2: }(4,6,8,10).
\] The chain means are \(\bar\theta^{(1)}=5\) and \(\bar\theta^{(2)}=7\), grand mean \(\bar{\bar\theta}=6\). Each chain has the same sample variance, \(s_m^2=\frac{1}{3}\big[(\pm3)^2+(\pm1)^2\big]=\frac{1}{3}(9+1+1+9)=
\frac{20}{3}\), so \(W=\frac{20}{3}\approx 6.667\). The between-chain variance is \(B=\frac{N}{M-1}\big[(5-6)^2
+(7-6)^2\big]=\frac{4}{1}(1+1)=8\). The pooled estimator is \[
\widehat V=\Big(1-\tfrac14\Big)\tfrac{20}{3}+\tfrac14\cdot 8=5+2=7,
\qquad
\widehat R=\sqrt{\widehat V/W}=\sqrt{\tfrac{7}{20/3}}=\sqrt{\tfrac{21}{20}}=\sqrt{1.05}\approx 1.025 .
\] With \(\widehat R\approx 1.025>1.01\) the chains have not converged: the systematic offset between the chain means (5 versus 7) inflates \(\widehat V\) above \(W\), exactly the mechanism of part 3 of Theorem 24.2. The remedy is more warmup or a better parameterization (Section 24.4), after which \(\widehat R\) should fall below \(1.01\).
Efficiency: \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\). Suppose the converged chains behave like an AR(1) process. With lag-1 autocorrelation \(\phi=\tfrac13\), Example 24.1 gives \(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=\frac{1+1/3}{1-1/3}=2\) and efficiency \(\tfrac12\), so \(4000\) total draws are worth \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}=2000\) independent draws; the Monte Carlo standard error of the posterior mean is \(\sigma/\sqrt{2000}\). A stickier chain with \(\phi=0.9\) gives \(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=19\) and \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx 210\), below the working threshold of \(400\) and a signal to run longer or improve mixing.
Integration error: the doubling rule. A logit-link aggregate cell requires \(\theta=\int_0^1\operatorname{expit}\!\big(0.4+0.8\,\Phi^{-1}(u)\big)\,du\), the marginal event probability when the linear predictor is normal with mean \(0.4\) and standard deviation \(0.8\). We integrate with the one-dimensional Sobol’ sequence (the van der Corput sequence in base \(2\), Definition 22.3), whose first points are \(u_1=\tfrac12,\,u_2=\tfrac14,\,u_3=\tfrac34,\,u_4=\tfrac18,\dots\); the first eight integrand values are \[
0.599,\ 0.465,\ 0.719,\ 0.373,\ 0.658,\ 0.536,\ 0.789,\ 0.304,
\] averaging to \(\widehat\theta^{(8)}=0.5554\). Doubling the grid gives the sequence \[
\widehat\theta^{(16)}=0.5683,\quad \widehat\theta^{(32)}=0.5765,\quad \widehat\theta^{(64)}=0.5812,
\quad \widehat\theta^{(128)}=0.5838,\quad \widehat\theta^{(256)}=0.5853,
\] converging to the exact value \(\theta=0.5868\) (computable independently by high-order Gauss-Hermite quadrature). The relative doubling increments Equation 24.15 are \[
\frac{|0.5812-0.5765|}{0.5812}=0.0082,\quad
\frac{|0.5838-0.5812|}{0.5838}=0.0045,\quad
\frac{|0.5853-0.5838|}{0.5853}=0.0024 .
\] At tolerance \(\epsilon=0.005\) the criterion first passes at \(N=128\) (increment \(0.0045<0.005\)), and the next doubling confirms it (\(0.0024\)). The true relative error at \(N=128\) is \(|0.5838-0.5868|/0.5868=
0.0051\), consistent with the bound of Proposition 24.2 at \(\rho\approx\tfrac12\), which predicts a true relative error near the observed increment. So \(N=128\) points suffice for this cell at this tolerance.
Model comparison: WAIC and PSIS-LOO. Two observations are fit, and the pointwise likelihoods at \(S=4\) posterior draws are \[
p(y_1\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\in\{0.4,0.5,0.5,0.6\},\qquad
p(y_2\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\in\{0.2,0.3,0.3,0.4\}.
\] The pointwise predictive densities are the within-row means, \(\bar p_1=0.5\) and \(\bar p_2=0.3\), so \[
\mathrm{lppd}=\log 0.5+\log 0.3=-0.6931-1.2040=-1.8971 .
\] The WAIC penalties are the within-row sample variances of the log likelihoods. For \(y_1\), the logs are \((-0.9163,-0.6931,-0.6931,-0.5108)\) with mean \(-0.7033\) and sample variance \(v_1=0.02754\); for \(y_2\), the logs are \((-1.6094,-1.2040,-1.2040,-0.9163)\) with mean \(-1.2334\) and sample variance \(v_2=0.08123\). Hence \(p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=v_1+v_2=0.1088\) and \[
\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=\mathrm{lppd}-p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=-2.0059,\qquad
\mathrm{WAIC}=-2\,(-2.0059)=4.012 .
\] For LOO, the raw importance ratios are \(r_i^{(s)}=1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\), and because \(p\cdot r=1\) the self-normalized estimate Equation 24.22 with raw weights reduces to the harmonic mean \(\widehat p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=S/\sum_s r_i^{(s)}\). For \(y_1\), \(\sum_s r_1^{(s)}=2.5+2+2+1.667=8.167\), so \(\widehat p_1=4/8.167=0.4898\); for \(y_2\), \(\sum_s r_2^{(s)}=5+3.333+3.333+2.5=14.167\), so \(\widehat
p_2=4/14.167=0.2824\). Then \[
\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_{\mathrm{loo}}=\log 0.4898+\log 0.2824=-0.7137-1.2645=-1.9782,\qquad
\mathrm{LOO}=3.956 .
\] The two criteria agree to within \(4.012-3.956=0.056\) on the deviance scale, illustrating the asymptotic equivalence of part 1 of Theorem 24.3 even at this tiny sample size; the small gap is the higher-order \(o(v_i)\) term. With only \(S=4\) draws a generalized Pareto tail cannot be fit, so \(\widehat k\) is not reported here; in a real fit with thousands of draws one would read \(\widehat k_i\) for each observation against the \(0.7\) alarm of Theorem 24.4 before trusting the LOO numbers. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 24  Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics
text:
24.12 Notes and references
The chapter expands results I.1 to I.6 of the proof catalogue (proofs/I_computation.md) and the companion manuscript chapter on Bayesian computation, supplying complete proofs and the worked example. The underlying Bayesian-foundations results it draws on, Bayes’ theorem, conjugacy, the posterior predictive, and the detailed-balance correctness of HMC, are catalogue results L.1 to L.4, proved in Chapter 8 (Theorem 8.9, Definition 8.9, Theorem 8.3); the numerical-integration machinery it monitors, the Koksma-Hlawka inequality and the Sobol’ construction, are catalogue results H.12 to H.19 of Chapter 22 (Theorem 22.3, Theorem 22.2, Definition 22.3, Theorem 22.6); and the aggregation integral whose evaluation is at stake is the subject of Chapter 20 (Theorem 20.1, Theorem 20.4, Theorem 20.5). The DIC decomposition \(\mathrm{DIC}=D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})+2p_D\) is catalogue result D.14, introduced for network meta-analysis in Chapter 15.
The centered-versus-non-centered analysis and the funnel pathology it addresses are standard in the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo literature; the leapfrog stability threshold \(\epsilon\omega\le 2\) (Lemma 24.2) is the linear-stability analysis of the Stormer-Verlet integrator, and the funnel as the canonical hierarchical-model trap is due to Neal. The implementation of HMC and the No-U-Turn Sampler used by the reference ML-NMR software, including the automatic step-size and mass-matrix adaptation, is Stan (Carpenter et al. (2017)). The Gelman-Rubin statistic is the original convergence diagnostic of Gelman and Rubin; the exact expectation identities \(\mathbb E[\widehat V]=\sigma^2\) and \(\mathbb E[W]=\frac{N}{N-1}(\sigma^2-v_N)\) derived here (Theorem 24.2) make precise the “\(\widehat V\) overestimates, \(W\) underestimates” intuition, and the split and rank-normalized refinements are the modern reassessment of Vehtari and coauthors, who also introduced the bulk/tail effective sample sizes of Section 24.6. The variance-of-the-mean identity Equation 24.12 and the integrated autocorrelation time are classical time-series facts (see, for example, the MCMC standard-error literature of Geyer). The predictive-criterion framework, elpd as the target and lppd as its optimistic in-sample estimate, is due to Watanabe (WAIC) and to the cross-validation synthesis of Vehtari, Gelman, and Gabra; the exact leave-one-out importance identity Equation 24.18 and the Pareto-smoothing algorithm with its \(\widehat k\) diagnostic (Definition 24.6, Theorem 24.4) are from the PSIS-LOO papers of that group, and the generalized-Pareto moment characterization Lemma 24.7 is elementary extreme-value theory.
The proofs given here are pen-and-paper throughout. As recorded in the remark closing 1, none of this material has a machine-checked counterpart in the ITC_Coq development, whose formalized content ends with population-adjustment algebra; accordingly no theorem in this chapter carries a machine-checked tag.

title: 24  Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics
text:
24.13 Exercises
An exercise marked \(\star\) has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first two are warm-ups: read a diagnostic report and decide what to do, before any algebra.

Exercise 24.1 (Reading a Stan summary (warm-up, interpretation)) A fitted ML-NMR model reports, for the contrast \(d_{AC}\): \(\widehat R=1.00\), bulk \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}=2200\), tail \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}=1900\); and for the heterogeneity \(\tau\): \(\widehat R=1.06\), bulk \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}
=110\), tail \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}=160\), with \(9\) divergent transitions reported, all at small \(\tau\). In words, and without any calculation: which quantity do you trust, which do you not, what single mechanism from Section 24.4 most likely explains the pattern, and what would you change before reporting \(d_{AC}\)? Explain why “just run the chains four times longer” is the wrong first move.


Exercise 24.2 (Classify the diagnostics (warm-up, interpretation)) For each finding, state whether it is a hard failure that blocks reporting, a warning that needs investigation, or acceptable, and name the action, using the table of Section 24.10: (a) \(\widehat
R=1.004\) on every parameter; (b) bulk \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}=95\) on a treatment contrast; (c) Pareto \(\widehat k=0.9\) on one aggregate arm; (d) a QMC doubling increment of \(0.012\) at tolerance \(\epsilon=0.005\); (e) a WAIC difference between two models that is half the size of its standard error.


Exercise 24.3 (Computing \(\widehat R\)) Three chains of length \(N=5\) give the draws \((1,2,3,4,5)\), \((2,3,4,5,6)\), and \((3,4,5,6,7)\). Compute \(W\), \(B\), \(\widehat V\), and \(\widehat R\). Does the run pass the \(\widehat R\le 1.01\) threshold? Explain, using Theorem 24.2, why the answer is driven entirely by the spacing of the chain means.


Exercise 24.4 (A deterministic lower bound for \(\widehat R\) \((\star)\)) Show from the definitions Equation 24.6 and Equation 24.7 that \(\widehat V/W=\frac{N-1}{N}+\frac{B}{NW}\), and deduce that \(\widehat R\ge\sqrt{(N-1)/N}\) always, with \(\widehat R\ge 1\) if and only if \(B\ge W\). Using the stationarity expectations of Lemma 24.4 and Lemma 24.5, show that at convergence \(\mathbb E[B]=\mathbb E[W]\) in the iid-within-chain idealization, so that \(\widehat R\) is centered at \(1\), and identify the term that pushes it above \(1\) when the chains are positively autocorrelated but share a common stationary law. (Solution in Appendix F.)


Exercise 24.5 (Effective sample size from an autocorrelation sequence) A chain has estimated autocorrelations \(\rho_1=0.6\), \(\rho_2=0.36\), \(\rho_3=0.216\), and \(\rho_k=0.6^k\) thereafter. Using Definition 24.3, compute the integrated autocorrelation time and the efficiency \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}/N\). Compare with the AR(1) formula of Example 24.1 and explain why they coincide.


Exercise 24.6 (Leapfrog stability and the funnel) A centered hierarchical effect has prior-dominated curvature \(1/\tau^2\) (Lemma 24.3). Using Lemma 24.2, find the largest stable leapfrog step \(\epsilon_{\max}(\tau)\). If the posterior of \(\tau\) ranges over \([0.05,2]\) and a single global \(\epsilon\) must be stable everywhere, what is the largest admissible \(\epsilon\), and by what factor is it smaller than the step that would be efficient at the typical value \(\tau=1\)? Repeat for the non-centered parameterization and comment.


Exercise 24.7 (The doubling rule on a known integral) For \(\theta=\int_0^1 u^2\,du=\tfrac13\), compute the one-dimensional Sobol’ (van der Corput) estimates \(\widehat\theta^{(N)}\) for \(N\in\{2,4,8,16\}\), evaluate the relative doubling increments Equation 24.15, and report the smallest \(N\) at which the criterion passes at \(\epsilon=0.01\). Compare the observed errors \(|\widehat\theta^{(N)}-\tfrac13|\) with the increments and comment in the light of Proposition 24.2.


Exercise 24.8 (The leave-one-out identity) Prove the special case \(\psi=p(y_i\mid\cdot)\) of Equation 24.19 directly: starting from \(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i})\propto\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\), show that \(p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=1/\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)]\). Then explain in one sentence why estimating this by the sample harmonic mean of the draw-wise likelihoods can have infinite variance.


Exercise 24.9 (WAIC and LOO on a small posterior) Three posterior draws give pointwise likelihoods \(p(y_1\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7\}\) and \(p(y_2\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\in\{0.4,0.4,0.4\}\). Compute \(\mathrm{lppd}\), \(p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}\), and \(\mathrm{WAIC}\), and the raw-importance-sampling \(\mathrm{LOO}\). Why is the second observation’s contribution to \(p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}\) exactly zero, and what does that say about its influence?


Exercise 24.10 (Pareto tails and importance-sampling reliability \((\star)\)) Let \(X\) have the generalized Pareto upper tail \(\bar F(x)=(1+kx/\sigma)^{-1/k}\) with \(k>0\). Prove that \(\mathbb E[X^m]<\infty\) if and only if \(m<1/k\) (Lemma 24.7). Deduce the variance-finiteness threshold \(k<\tfrac12\) and the mean-finiteness threshold \(k<1\), and relate them to the PSIS-LOO diagnostic thresholds of Theorem 24.4. Explain why the operational alarm is set at \(\widehat k=0.7\) rather than at the theoretical variance threshold \(0.5\). (Solution in Appendix F.)





Carpenter, Bob, Andrew Gelman, Matthew D. Hoffman, et al. 2017. “Stan: A Probabilistic Programming Language.” Journal of Statistical Software 76 (1).

title: 25  General Likelihoods: Survival and Ordered Categorical Outcomes
text:
25.1 Introduction
The four preceding chapters built multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR) on a single integral. An individual in an aggregate-data (AgD) study is invisible: we never see the patient’s covariate vector \(\mathbf{x}\), only the study’s reported covariate distribution \(f_j\). To place an individual-level outcome model in the same network as that study, we average the individual model over \(f_j\). For a generalized linear model (GLM) the object that gets averaged is the conditional mean \(g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}))\), and the aggregate-level mean is \(\bar\theta_{jk}=\int g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}))\,f_j(\mathbf{x})\,
d\mathbf{x}\) (Theorem 20.1). Chapter 20 showed this average is exact on the identity link (Theorem 20.3), is the moment generating function on the log link (Theorem 20.4), and has no closed form on the logit link (Theorem 20.5); Chapter 22 then computed the intractable cases by quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) on a Sobol’ net (Definition 22.3, Theorem 22.6) with a Gaussian copula (Definition 22.5, Theorem 22.5) to encode covariate dependence. Chapters 23 and 24 established the estimands and the Bayesian computation. All of this was carried out for outcomes that fit a one-parameter GLM: continuous, binary, and count.
Health-technology-assessment (HTA) practice is dominated by outcomes that do not fit a one-parameter GLM. The single most common primary endpoint in oncology submissions is time to an event, recorded as a possibly right-censored survival time; cardiovascular and respiratory submissions add composite time-to-event endpoints; dermatology, oncology, and psychiatry report ordered categorical severity scales (the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index response bands, the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status, ordinal pain scales). A survival outcome is not summarized by a single mean: it is a whole curve, and its natural model lives on the hazard, an object indexed by time as well as by covariates. An ordered categorical outcome is a vector of cell probabilities tied together by a monotonicity constraint. Neither is a member of the exponential-dispersion family on which Chapters 20 to 23 were built. The question this chapter answers is whether ML-NMR is confined to that family, or whether the aggregation principle is deeper than the GLM that first carried it.
It is deeper. The aggregation in Theorem 20.1 never used the GLM structure of the integrand for anything except naming it a mean. What the method actually requires is one ingredient: an individual-level conditional likelihood, a function \(\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y\mid\boldsymbol\theta(
\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi))\) giving the probability (or density) of the outcome \(y\) for a patient with covariates \(\mathbf{x}\) under parameters \(\boldsymbol\xi\). Given that one object, the marginal likelihood of an AgD individual whose covariates are unobserved is the average of the conditional likelihood over the study’s covariate distribution, and the arm likelihood is the product of these marginal contributions over the (possibly reconstructed) individuals on the arm. This is the general-likelihood ML-NMR framework of Phillippo et al. (2025), and it makes ML-NMR the only population-adjustment method that extends verbatim to any outcome with a parametric individual model. By contrast, matching-adjusted indirect comparison (Chapter 18) balances reported moments and so needs the aggregate data in a moment form, and simulated treatment comparison (Chapter 19) needs an outcome regression on the IPD scale; neither absorbs a censored survival time or an ordinal band without bespoke surgery.
This chapter develops the framework with survival as the leading and hardest case. We define the survival function (Definition 25.1) and hazard (Definition 25.2) and prove the identity \(S=\exp(-\int h)\) that lets the hazard parameterize the entire distribution (Theorem 25.1). We then expose the feature that makes survival genuinely different from a GLM: under a proportional-hazards model the conditional log hazard ratio is a clean time-invariant linear function of the covariates (Theorem 25.2), yet the marginal hazard ratio one would estimate from a population is time-varying even when the conditional model is proportional (Theorem 25.3), a survival-scale instance of the non-collapsibility of Chapter 7 (Definition 7.7). The restricted mean survival time (Definition 25.3) repairs the collapsibility defect (Theorem 25.4) at the price of a transportability subtlety we flag for Chapter 26. We derive the right-censored individual likelihood (Definition 25.4) from first principles under independent censoring (Proposition 25.1), then build the two aggregation theorems that are the heart of the chapter: the marginal individual likelihood (Theorem 25.5) and the aggregate arm likelihood (Theorem 25.6), both resting on Theorem 20.1. The proportional-odds model (Definition 25.5) supplies the ordered-categorical case, and the general-likelihood theorem (Theorem 25.7) unifies everything: one integral, any outcome. A fully worked exponential-hazard example, in which every survival probability, every marginal hazard, the restricted mean, and the aggregate likelihood can be checked by hand, closes the development. This chapter corresponds to results J.1 to J.8 of the proof catalogue.
Throughout, \(T\ge 0\) denotes a time-to-event random variable, \(S\), \(h\), and \(H\) its survival, hazard, and cumulative-hazard functions, and \(g\) the link function (Definition 7.2) on whose scale the linear predictor \(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})\) of Notation is built. A population \(\mathcal{P}\) is a distribution over the covariate space \(\mathcal{X}\) with density \(f_{\mathcal{P}}\); \(f_j\) is the covariate density of study \(j\); \(\boldsymbol\xi\) is the full parameter vector. We write \(L_i(\boldsymbol\xi;y_i)\) for an individual likelihood contribution and \(\bar L_{jk}(\boldsymbol\xi)\) for the contribution of arm \(k\) of an AgD study \(j\).

section: 25.2 The core idea and a running example
text:
25.2 The core idea and a running example
Before any measure theory, here is the entire method in four sentences, together with one small trial to hold onto. Every abstract object in this chapter has a concrete counterpart in that trial, and every theorem below is an elaboration of one of these four steps. A reader who remembers only this section still has the essential idea.

Remark. The general-likelihood recipe, in four steps.

One patient, covariates known. Write the likelihood of the outcome for a single patient as if their covariates \(\mathbf{x}\) were observed: choose a conditional individual likelihood \(\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y\mid\text{parameters at }\mathbf{x})\). For a binary outcome this is the Bernoulli mass; for survival it is the censored kernel \(h^{\delta}S\); for an ordinal scale it is a category probability.
One patient, covariates unknown. In an aggregate-data (AgD) study the patient’s \(\mathbf{x}\) was never recorded, so average the conditional likelihood over the study’s reported covariate distribution \(f_j\). This single integral is the whole population adjustment.
Whole arm. Multiply those averaged contributions across the patients (or reconstructed pseudo-patients) on the arm.
Whole network. Share the treatment-effect parameters across studies, so every study estimates the same relative effects on one linear-predictor scale.

Steps 1 and 3 are ordinary likelihood bookkeeping; step 2 is the population adjustment that makes the AgD study comparable to the individual-level ones; step 4 is what makes it a network rather than a collection of separate models. Chapters 20 to 23 carried out these four steps for continuous, binary, and count outcomes. This chapter proves they go through unchanged for survival and ordered categorical outcomes, and states the theorem (Theorem 25.7) that makes “unchanged” precise. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Example 25.1 (A running two-arm myeloma trial) Throughout the chapter we follow one small oncology example, a stylized version of the multiple-myeloma progression-free-survival network of Phillippo et al. (2025). A single binary baseline covariate \(X\in\{0,1\}\) marks a high-risk cytogenetic subgroup, present in half the comparator population, \(P(X=1)=q=\tfrac12\). The endpoint is time to progression \(T\), in years, modeled with a constant (exponential) conditional hazard. On the control arm \(C\), \[
h_C(s\mid x)=\lambda_x,\qquad \lambda_0=1,\quad \lambda_1=3\ \ \text{events per year},
\] so a high-risk patient has triple the event rate of a standard-risk patient. Treatment \(A\) acts by proportional hazards with a covariate-independent hazard ratio \(\psi=\tfrac12\): it halves every patient’s hazard, \(h_A(s\mid x)=\tfrac12\lambda_x\), with no effect modification. This conditional model is as clean as a generalized linear model. The lesson of the chapter is that its marginal summaries nonetheless misbehave (the marginal hazard ratio drifts with time, Theorem 25.3) while its aggregate-data likelihood requires a genuine integral (Theorem 25.7). We revisit this trial after every definition and complete the full computation in Example 25.3. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 25  General Likelihoods: Survival and Ordered Categorical Outcomes
section: 25.3 The survival function and the hazard
text:
25.3 The survival function and the hazard
A time-to-event outcome is described equivalently by its distribution function, its survival function, its density, or its hazard. The hazard is the modeling target because it is the scale on which the standard proportional-hazards and accelerated-failure-time models are linear, and on which the network’s relative effects are reported.
In plain terms, the plan of this section is: define these four equivalent descriptions of a time-to-event outcome, prove that the hazard alone determines all the others (so a model placed on the hazard is automatically a complete model of the outcome), and read off the censored likelihood the network will consume. Keep the running trial in view throughout: the control hazard there is the single number \(\lambda_x\), and we will watch every survival probability, density, and cumulative risk flow from it.

Definition 25.1 (Survival function) Let \(T\ge 0\) be a time-to-event random variable with cumulative distribution function \(F_T\). The survival function of \(T\) is \[
S(t):=P(T>t)=1-F_T(t),\qquad t\ge 0,
\tag{25.1}\] and, given a covariate vector \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}\), the conditional survival function is \(S(t\mid\mathbf{x}):=P(T>t\mid \mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})\). The survival function is non-increasing and right-continuous, with \(\lim_{t\to-\infty}\) replaced by \(S(0^-)=1\); for a continuous \(T\) it is continuous with \(S(0)=1\), and for a proper distribution (one with \(P(T<\infty)=1\)) it satisfies \(\lim_{t\to\infty}S(t)=0\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Reader translation. \(S(t)\) is just the probability that a patient has not yet had the event by time \(t\). It starts at \(S(0)=1\), everyone event-free at enrollment, and decays toward \(0\). The three properties it inherits from the cumulative distribution function of Chapter 4, stated inline so that no back-reference is needed, are: \(S\) is non-increasing (the chance of surviving longer can only fall as the horizon grows), right-continuous, and runs from \(S(0)=1\) down to \(\lim_{t\to\infty}S(t)=0\) for a proper distribution (everyone eventually has the event). We take these as given rather than reprove them. In the running trial \(S_C(t\mid x)=e^{-\lambda_x t}\), so the one-year survival is \(e^{-1}=0.37\) for a standard-risk control patient (\(\lambda_0=1\)) and \(e^{-3}=0.05\) for a high-risk one (\(\lambda_1=3\)): the high-risk stratum is depleted far faster. The companion object is the instantaneous event rate among survivors.

Definition 25.2 (Hazard function and cumulative hazard) Let \(T\) be a continuous time-to-event variable with density \(f\) and survival \(S\), and fix \(t\) with \(S(t)>0\). The hazard function is \[
h(t):=\lim_{\Delta t\downarrow 0}\frac{P(t\le T<t+\Delta t\mid T\ge t)}{\Delta t}
=\frac{f(t)}{S(t)},
\tag{25.2}\] The second equality \(h=f/S\), the working form used throughout, is derived in the proof immediately below. Conditionally on covariates \(h(t\mid\mathbf{x}):=f(t\mid\mathbf{x})/S(t\mid\mathbf{x})\). The cumulative hazard is \[
H(t):=\int_0^t h(s)\,ds,\qquad H(t\mid\mathbf{x}):=\int_0^t h(s\mid\mathbf{x})\,ds .
\tag{25.3}\] The quantity \(h(t\mid\mathbf{x})\,\Delta t\) is, to first order in \(\Delta t\), the conditional probability of an event in the next short interval \([t,t+\Delta t)\) given survival to \(t\); the hazard is the local intensity of failure, a rate, not a probability, and it can exceed \(1\). A hazard of \(0.2\) per year does not mean a \(20\%\) chance over all follow-up; it means that among patients still event-free at time \(t\), a fraction of about \(0.2\,\Delta t\) have the event in the next interval of length \(\Delta t\) years, so roughly \(2\%\) in the next month. In the running trial the constant control hazard is \(\lambda_0=1\) per year for a standard-risk patient and \(\lambda_1=3\) per year for a high-risk one; the latter exceeds \(1\) and is still a perfectly valid rate. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Proof. We verify the second equality in Equation 25.2, which is the working form. By the definition of conditional probability and continuity of \(T\), \[
\frac{P(t\le T<t+\Delta t\mid T\ge t)}{\Delta t}
=\frac{P(t\le T<t+\Delta t)}{\Delta t\,P(T\ge t)}
=\frac{F_T(t+\Delta t)-F_T(t)}{\Delta t}\cdot\frac{1}{S(t)} ,
\] using \(P(T\ge t)=P(T>t)=S(t)\) for continuous \(T\). As \(\Delta t\downarrow 0\) the first factor tends to \(F_T'(t)=f(t)\) at every point of differentiability of \(F_T\), so the limit is \(f(t)/S(t)\). \(\square\)

The hazard is not merely one summary among several; it determines the distribution completely. This is the identity on which every parametric and semiparametric survival model rests, and it is the reason a model specified on the hazard scale yields a coherent likelihood.
Before the formal statement, the idea in one line: the hazard accumulates over time into the cumulative hazard \(H(t)=\int_0^t h\), and survival is the exponential of the negative accumulated risk, \(S=e^{-H}\). A patient survives past \(t\) exactly to the extent that the risk piled up over \([0,t]\) is small. The theorem makes this precise and, crucially, invertible: knowing the hazard at every time is the same as knowing the whole distribution, so a model that specifies the hazard has specified everything.

Theorem 25.1 (The survival function is the exponential of minus the cumulative hazard) Let \(T\) be a continuous time-to-event variable whose survival function \(S\) is absolutely continuous with \(S(0)=1\), and let \(h=f/S\) and \(H(t)=\int_0^t h(s)\,ds\) be its hazard and cumulative hazard. Then for every \(t\ge 0\) with \(S(t)>0\), \[
S(t)=\exp\!\Big(-\!\int_0^t h(s)\,ds\Big)=e^{-H(t)},
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
H(t)=-\log S(t).
\tag{25.4}\] The same identity holds conditionally on covariates, \(S(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\exp(-H(t\mid\mathbf{x}))\). Conversely, any measurable \(h\ge 0\) that is locally integrable with \(\int_0^\infty h=\infty\) defines, through Equation 25.4, a survival function of a proper continuous distribution with density \(f=h\,S\); thus the hazard and the distribution are in one-to-one correspondence.


Proof. Forward direction. Fix \(t_0\ge 0\) with \(S(t_0)>0\). Because \(S\) is non-increasing, \(S(s)\ge S(t_0)>0\) for all \(s\in[0,t_0]\), so \(S\) is bounded away from zero on \([0,t_0]\). Since \(S\) is absolutely continuous, so is \(\log S\) on \([0,t_0]\): the logarithm is continuously differentiable on the compact interval \([S(t_0),1]\), which contains the range of \(S\) over \([0,t_0]\), hence Lipschitz there, and a Lipschitz function composed with an absolutely continuous function is absolutely continuous. (Reminder for the reader meeting these words: a function is absolutely continuous when it is the integral of its own derivative, which is exactly the property that makes the fundamental theorem of calculus apply to it; it is Lipschitz on a set when the ratio of output change to input change stays bounded there. The logarithm has derivative \(1/u\), which is bounded on \([S(t_0),1]\) because \(u\) never drops below \(S(t_0)>0\), so it is Lipschitz there, and feeding an absolutely continuous input into a Lipschitz function preserves absolute continuity.) An absolutely continuous function is the integral of its almost-everywhere derivative (the fundamental theorem of calculus for the Lebesgue integral). At every point \(s\) where \(S\) is differentiable, differentiate the relation \(S=1-F_T\) term by term: since the density is the derivative of the cumulative distribution function, \(F_T'=f\) almost everywhere (Chapter 4), the constant \(1\) differentiates to \(0\), and \(S'(s)=-F_T'(s)=-f(s)\) almost everywhere. Hence \[
\frac{d}{ds}\log S(s)=\frac{S'(s)}{S(s)}=-\frac{f(s)}{S(s)}=-h(s)
\qquad\text{for almost every }s\in[0,t_0].
\] Integrating from \(0\) to \(t_0\) and using \(\log S(0)=\log 1=0\), \[
\log S(t_0)=\log S(0)-\int_0^{t_0}h(s)\,ds=-H(t_0),
\] and exponentiating gives \(S(t_0)=e^{-H(t_0)}\). As \(t_0\) was arbitrary subject to \(S(t_0)>0\), this is Equation 25.4. The conditional statement is identical with \(\mathbf{x}\) carried throughout, since for each fixed \(\mathbf{x}\) the function \(s\mapsto S(s\mid\mathbf{x})\) is an absolutely continuous survival function.
Converse. Let \(h\ge 0\) be locally integrable. Then \(H(t)=\int_0^t h\) is non-decreasing, absolutely continuous, with \(H(0)=0\), so \(S:=e^{-H}\) is non-increasing, absolutely continuous, \(S(0)=1\), and \(\lim_{t\to\infty}S(t)=e^{-\lim H(t)}=e^{-\infty}=0\) under the stated divergence \(\int_0^\infty h=\infty\). Hence \(S\) is the survival function of a proper continuous distribution. Its density is \(f=-S'=H'\,e^{-H}=h\,e^{-H}=h\,S\) almost everywhere, and \(f/S=h\) recovers the prescribed hazard. The map \(h\mapsto S\) and its inverse \(S\mapsto h=-(\log S)'\) are mutually inverse, giving the one-to-one correspondence. \(\square\)


Remark. Why the hazard scale. Identity Equation 25.4 is what lets a model place its structure on the hazard and still deliver a likelihood. Specify \(h(t\mid\mathbf{x})\), integrate to \(H(t\mid\mathbf{x})\), exponentiate to \(S(t\mid\mathbf{x})\), and the density \(f=h\,S\) and the censored likelihood of Definition 25.4 follow. A constant hazard \(h(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\lambda(\mathbf{x})\) gives the exponential model \(S(t\mid\mathbf{x})=e^{-\lambda(\mathbf{x})t}\); a power-law hazard \(h(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\lambda(\mathbf{x})\nu t^{\nu-1}\) gives the Weibull model \(S=e^{-\lambda(\mathbf{x})t^{\nu}}\); a flexible spline on \(\log h_0\) gives the M-spline baseline used by the multinma survival models of Phillippo et al. (2025). In the running trial the control hazard is the constant \(\lambda_x\), so \(H_C(t\mid x)=\lambda_x t\) and \(S_C(t\mid x)=e^{-\lambda_x t}\): the entire time-to-progression distribution of each stratum is pinned down by the single number \(\lambda_x\), which is exactly what a one-parameter exponential model asserts. All share the relation Equation 25.4. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This pair of definitions and the identity correspond to J.1, J.2, and J.3 in the proof catalogue.
