Remark. The two families in closed and not-closed form. For a continuous outcome with the identity link and the linear model \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathbf{x}]=\alpha_k+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\), aggregation is exact (Theorem 20.3): \(\theta_{\bullet B}=\alpha_B+\bar{\mathbf{x}}_B^\top
\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\), so Equation 26.9 solves in closed form, \[
\alpha_B=\bar y_B-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_B^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}},
\] needing only the comparator covariate mean. For a binary outcome with the logit link, Bernoulli individual model and binomial aggregate model, \(\Theta_B(\alpha_B)=\int\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B+
\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}\) has no closed form (Theorem 20.5), and Equation 26.9 is solved numerically after the integral is evaluated by the QMC rule of Theorem 26.3; here the comparator covariate distribution, not just its mean, enters. This is the binary “Type 1” model of Chandler and Ishak (2026a); the reference software mlumr fits it as one joint Stan model rather than by the two-step solve, but the two-step solve is what the identifiability argument exhibits and what the worked example of Section 26.15 carries out by hand. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Bayesian inference. In practice one does not separate the two steps. Place priors on \((\alpha_A,\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})\), for example weakly informative normals, and sample the posterior of the joint likelihood Theorem 26.6 by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Definition 8.9, Carpenter et al. (2017)); the QMC integral makes the comparator likelihood a smooth function of the parameters (Equation 22.20), so the gradient HMC needs is available. (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is, for present purposes, a black-box sampler that draws from the posterior using its gradient; Definition 8.9 has the mechanics, and nothing below depends on them.) The reason to fit both blocks jointly, rather than run the two-step solve of the proof, is uncertainty propagation: the joint posterior carries the estimation error in \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\) from the index arm through into the uncertainty in \(\alpha_B\), and hence into every target-population contrast, whereas plugging a single point estimate of \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\) into a separate solve for \(\alpha_B\) would understate that uncertainty. The two-step identification argument is the guarantee that the posterior concentrates: the index data pin \((\alpha_A,\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})\) and the comparator mean then pins \(\alpha_B\), so the likelihood has a unique maximizer in the limit. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This theorem corresponds to M.3 in the proof catalogue.

title: 26  Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression
text:
26.6 Relaxing SPFA with comparator subgroups
SPFA fails whenever the covariate genuinely modifies the treatment effect, that is when \(\boldsymbol\beta_A\ne\boldsymbol\beta_B\). A single aggregate outcome mean cannot then identify the model, because it supplies one equation for the \((d+1)\) unknowns \((\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)\). The remedy of Chandler and Ishak (2026a) is to demand more aggregate equations, by partitioning the comparator population into subgroups and using a reported outcome in each. Concretely, this means the comparator report must give, say, response rates separately for biomarker-positive and biomarker-negative patients, or Kaplan-Meier curves per risk stratum, each with its own covariate summary. The intuition is a counting argument any reader can hold onto: each subgroup outcome is one equation, the unknowns are the \(d+1\) numbers \((\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)\), and you need at least as many genuinely different equations as unknowns. “Genuinely different” is the catch, and the theorem makes it precise. Such stratified reporting is the exception rather than the rule, which is why the Type 1 model of Theorem 26.1 remains the workhorse.

Theorem 26.2 (Identifiability of the relaxed model from comparator subgroups) Drop SPFA and allow a treatment-specific comparator slope: the arm predictors are \(\eta_A(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_A+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_A\) and \(\eta_B(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_B\) with possibly distinct \(\boldsymbol\beta_A,\boldsymbol\beta_B\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\). Suppose the comparator source reports outcomes for \(Z\) non-overlapping subgroups \(z=1,\dots,Z\), with known within-subgroup covariate densities \(f_B^{z}\) and observed aggregate means \(\theta_{\bullet B}^{z,\mathrm{obs}}\), modeled by \[
\theta_{\bullet B}^{z}(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}g^{-1}\!\big(\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_B\big)\,f_B^{z}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
\qquad z=1,\dots,Z.
\tag{26.10}\] Let \(\boldsymbol\psi=(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\) and write \(w_z(\mathbf{x}):=(g^{-1})'(\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_B)>0\). If

(counting) \(Z\ge d+1\), and
(non-degeneracy) the \(Z\times(d+1)\) matrix \(M\) with rows \(\mathbf{m}_z^\top=\int w_z(\mathbf{x})\,(1,\mathbf{x}^\top)\,f_B^{z}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}\) has rank \(d+1\) at \(\boldsymbol\psi\),

then \(\boldsymbol\psi=(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)\) is locally identified by the \(Z\) subgroup equations Equation 26.10, given \(\alpha_A,\boldsymbol\beta_A\) from the index IPD. In particular two binary effect modifiers crossed into \(Z=4\) subgroups identify \(\boldsymbol\beta_B\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\). If instead \(Z<d+1\), the solution set of Equation 26.10 is a manifold of dimension at least \(d+1-Z\ge 1\), and \(\boldsymbol\psi\) is not identified.


Proof. Local identification when \(Z\ge d+1\) and \(M\) has full column rank. Define the map \(F:\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\to\mathbb{R}^{Z}\) by \(F(\boldsymbol\psi)=(\theta_{\bullet B}^{1}(\boldsymbol\psi),\dots,
\theta_{\bullet B}^{Z}(\boldsymbol\psi))\). Each component is differentiable, and by differentiating under the integral sign (the integrand and its \(\boldsymbol\psi\)-gradient are bounded for the standard links, so dominated convergence applies), \[
\frac{\partial\theta_{\bullet B}^{z}}{\partial\alpha_B}=\int w_z(\mathbf{x})\,f_B^{z}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
\qquad
\frac{\partial\theta_{\bullet B}^{z}}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta_B}=\int w_z(\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{x}\,f_B^{z}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
\] so the Jacobian \(DF(\boldsymbol\psi)\) is exactly the matrix \(M\) with rows \(\mathbf{m}_z^\top=\int w_z
(1,\mathbf{x}^\top)f_B^{z}\). By hypothesis (2) \(M\) has rank \(d+1\), its full column rank; since \(Z\ge d+1\) by hypothesis (1), \(DF(\boldsymbol\psi)\) has a left inverse, and the constant-rank form of the inverse function theorem gives a neighborhood of \(\boldsymbol\psi\) on which \(F\) is injective. Hence \(\boldsymbol\psi\) is the unique parameter in that neighborhood reproducing the observed subgroup means \((\theta_{\bullet B}^{z,\mathrm{obs}})_z\): it is locally identified. (The index parameters \(\alpha_A,\boldsymbol\beta_A\) are identified from the IPD as in Theorem 26.1, separately from the comparator block.)
Non-identification when \(Z<d+1\). The Jacobian \(DF(\boldsymbol\psi)=M\) is then a \(Z\times(d+1)\) matrix with \(Z<d+1\), so its rank is at most \(Z<d+1\) and its kernel has dimension at least \(d+1-Z\ge 1\). By the constant-rank theorem (or directly, by the implicit function theorem applied to the rank-\(Z\) system) the level set \(\{\boldsymbol\psi':F(\boldsymbol\psi')=F(\boldsymbol\psi)\}\) contains, near \(\boldsymbol\psi\), a smooth submanifold of dimension \(\ge d+1-Z\ge 1\); every point of it reproduces the same \(Z\) subgroup means. Distinct parameter values therefore give identical observable aggregate data, so \(\boldsymbol\psi\) is not identified. \(\square\)


Remark. What the subgroups must deliver. The non-degeneracy condition (2) is the requirement that the \(Z\) subgroups differ enough in their covariate distributions: the rows \(\mathbf{m}_z\) are the hazard-weighted subgroup moments of \((1,\mathbf{x})\), and they must span \(\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\). Two subgroups with identical covariate means contribute near-parallel rows and add little identifying power, exactly as two collinear regressors do in least squares. Crossing two binary effect modifiers gives four subgroups whose means sit at the four corners of a square in covariate space, which generically span \(\mathbb{R}^{3}\) and identify \((\alpha_B,\beta_{B,1},\beta_{B,2})\). This is the simulation design of Chandler and Ishak (2026a). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why Type 1 is the default. Subgroup-specific aggregate outcomes, an event rate or a Kaplan-Meier curve reported separately within each effect-modifier stratum, are rarely published. When they are not, only the single overall comparator mean is available, \(Z=1<d+1\), and by the theorem the relaxed model is not identified; one must invoke SPFA and fit the Type 1 model of Theorem 26.1. Even when a few subgroups are reported, the mlumr documentation warns that the comparator slope \(\boldsymbol\beta_B\) is “weakly identified by aggregate data,” meaning that \(M\), while of full rank, is ill-conditioned, so informative priors or many subgroups are needed for stable estimation. The relaxed model is the principled way to accommodate effect modification, but its data demands are stringent. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Example 26.2 (Two subgroups identify a slope, but only if they differ) Take one binary covariate (\(d=1\)), the logit link, and the index parameters already fixed. The comparator now reports its response rate in two subgroups. In the favorable case the subgroups are the two covariate strata themselves: subgroup \(z=0\) is the biomarker-negative patients (covariate mean \(0\)) with observed response \(0.30\), and subgroup \(z=1\) is the biomarker-positive patients (covariate mean \(1\)) with observed response \(0.55\). Each subgroup integral Equation 26.10 is then a single point, so the two equations read \[
\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B)=0.30,\qquad \operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B+\beta_B)=0.55,
\] which solve exactly: \(\alpha_B=\operatorname{logit}(0.30)=-0.85\) and \(\alpha_B+\beta_B=\operatorname{logit}(0.55)=0.20\), so \(\beta_B=1.05\). Two aggregate numbers have identified both the comparator intercept and its slope, with no SPFA invoked. This is the Type 2 model, and the count \(Z=2=d+1\) meets the counting condition with room to spare on non-degeneracy, because the two subgroup means, \(0\) and \(1\), are as far apart as they can be.
Now spoil it. Suppose instead the two reported subgroups are “younger” and “older” patients, and the biomarker prevalence is almost the same in both, say covariate means \(0.48\) and \(0.52\). Each equation is now \(\theta_{\bullet B}^{z}\approx(1-\bar x_z)\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B)+\bar x_z\operatorname{expit}
(\alpha_B+\beta_B)\) with \(\bar x_z\) near \(0.5\) in both, so the two equations are nearly the same equation: together they pin the average level well, but say almost nothing about the slope \(\beta_B\), because shifting a little covariate mass between two nearly identical strata barely changes either subgroup’s outcome. The matrix \(M\) of Theorem 26.2 is then ill-conditioned; a small error in either reported rate swings the estimated \(\beta_B\) wildly. Counting (\(Z=d+1\)) is satisfied, yet non-degeneracy nearly fails, and only strong priors or a genuinely different third subgroup rescue the estimate. This is the arithmetic behind the mlumr warning that the relaxed comparator slope is “weakly identified by aggregate data.” \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This theorem corresponds to M.4 in the proof catalogue.

title: 26  Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression
text:
26.7 Aggregate marginalization by quasi-Monte Carlo
The aggregate integrals Equation 26.8 and Equation 26.10 are, except on the identity link, intractable in closed form. ML-UMR evaluates them with the exact pipeline ML-NMR uses, reconstructing the comparator covariate distribution from its reported margins and a correlation matrix and integrating on the unit hypercube. The result is a corollary of the hypercube-integration theorem of Chapter 22, recorded here in the unanchored notation.
Why an integral, and why the mean is not enough. Here is the practical reason for the machinery, in one paragraph. Arm \(B\)’s average outcome is \(\int g^{-1}(\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})
f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}\). On the identity link \(g^{-1}\) is linear, so the integral equals \(g^{-1}\) evaluated at the mean covariate \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_B\): the comparator’s reported means are all you need. On the logit link (and the hazard scale, and every nonlinear link) \(g^{-1}\) is curved, so the average of the outcome is not the outcome at the average covariate; the whole distribution of covariates matters, not just its mean. But the comparator paper reports margins, not patient rows. So the model fabricates a cloud of synthetic covariate points whose margins and correlations match what the paper reported, and averages the outcome over that cloud. The theorem below is the recipe for building the cloud, an inverse-CDF transform for each margin glued by a Gaussian copula for the correlations, together with a guarantee that a modest number of well-chosen points (a Sobol’ quasi-Monte Carlo net) makes the average accurate. A reader content with this picture may skim the theorem and rejoin at the discrete remark, where a single binary covariate collapses the integral to an exact two-point sum.

Theorem 26.3 (QMC marginalization of the comparator integral) Let the comparator covariate distribution \(f_B\) have continuous marginal distribution functions \(F_{B,1},\dots,F_{B,d}\) (Normal for a continuous covariate of reported mean and standard deviation, Bernoulli for a binary covariate of reported prevalence, and so on) and Gaussian-copula correlation matrix \(\boldsymbol\Omega_B=LL^\top\) (Definition 22.5). Let \(T:[0,1]^{d}\to\mathcal{X}\) be the transport map of Equation 22.17 built from these margins and \(L\). Then for any integrand \(\varphi:\mathcal{X}\to
\mathbb{R}\), in particular the response-scale arm mean \(\varphi=g^{-1}\circ\eta_B\), \[
\int_{\mathcal{X}}\varphi(\mathbf{x})\,f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}=\int_{[0,1]^{d}}\varphi\big(T(\mathbf{u})\big)\,d\mathbf{u},
\tag{26.11}\] and the Sobol’ QMC estimate over a net \(P_N=\{\mathbf{u}^{(n)}\}_{n=1}^{N}\) (Definition 22.3), \[
\widehat\theta_{\bullet B}^{(N)}(\boldsymbol\xi)=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^{N}g^{-1}\!\big(\alpha_B+T(\mathbf{u}^{(n)})^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\big),
\tag{26.12}\] satisfies, whenever the pullback \(\psi=g^{-1}\circ\eta_B\circ T\) has bounded Hardy-Krause variation (Definition 22.2; intuitively, \(\psi\) is not too wiggly on the cube, the multivariate analogue of a one-dimensional function of bounded total variation), \[
\big|\widehat\theta_{\bullet B}^{(N)}-\theta_{\bullet B}\big|\le V_{\mathrm{HK}}(\psi)\,D_N^{*}(P_N)=O\!\Big(V_{\mathrm{HK}}(\psi)\,\frac{(\log N)^{d}}{N}\Big).
\tag{26.13}\] The same pipeline, with \(f_B\) replaced by the target density \(f_{*}\), evaluates the target arm means \(\bar\theta_k(\mathcal{P}^{*})\) of Equation 26.1.


Proof. The change-of-variables identity Equation 26.11 is part 1 of Theorem 22.6: the map \(T\) pushes the uniform law on \([0,1]^{d}\) forward to \(f_B\), by the inverse-CDF transform (Theorem 22.4) on each margin and Sklar’s theorem (Theorem 22.5) for the Gaussian copula, so the expectation of \(\varphi(\mathbf{X})\) under \(\mathbf{X}\sim f_B\) equals the cube integral of \(\varphi\circ T\). Substituting \(\varphi=g^{-1}\circ\eta_B\) and the Sobol’ net gives Equation 26.12. The error bound Equation 26.13 is the Koksma-Hlawka inequality (Theorem 22.3) applied to \(\psi\) on the cube with the point set \(P_N\), exactly as in part 2 of Theorem 22.6; for continuous margins each \(F_{B,i}^{-1}\) is continuous and, for a bounded smooth link such as the logit, \(\psi\) is smooth and bounded, hence of bounded Hardy-Krause variation, so the Sobol’ discrepancy rate \(D_N^{*}=O((\log N)^{d}/N)\) yields the stated rate. Replacing \(f_B\) by \(f_{*}\) changes only the margins and correlation fed into \(T\), leaving the argument verbatim. \(\square\)


Remark. Discrete margins and the exact finite sum. When a covariate is discrete, its inverse distribution function is a step function, and the pullback \(\psi\) is piecewise constant in that coordinate, so its Hardy-Krause variation can be large and the smooth-integrand rate Equation 26.13 need not hold. This is not a defect in low dimension: a single binary covariate makes the integral an exact two-point sum, \(\theta_{\bullet B}=(1-\bar x_B)\,g^{-1}(\alpha_B)+\bar x_B\,g^{-1}(\alpha_B+\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})\), with no QMC error at all, and the worked example of Section 26.15 uses this exact form. For several discrete covariates, or mixed discrete and continuous sets, one enumerates the discrete cells and applies QMC within each continuous slice, or uses a randomized (Owen-scrambled, Owen (1956)) Sobol’ net whose error behaves better on non-smooth integrands. The reference software defaults to \(N=64\) Sobol’ points and provides a doubling diagnostic, check_integration(), the empirical convergence check of Definition 24.4, to verify that the integration error is negligible against the Markov chain Monte Carlo error before the results are interpreted. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Fixed nodes, smooth likelihood. As in ML-NMR, the integration nodes \(\mathbf{x}^{(n)}=T(\mathbf{u}^{(n)})\) depend only on the comparator’s reported margins and correlation, not on the parameters \(\boldsymbol\xi\); they are computed once. The aggregate mean Equation 26.12 is then a deterministic smooth function of \(\boldsymbol\xi\) with an exact gradient, which is what makes the joint posterior amenable to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Equation 22.20). Resampling the nodes at each step, as plain Monte Carlo would, would make the likelihood noisy and destroy the gradient; this is the same reason QMC, not Monte Carlo, is the integration rule throughout Part V. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This corresponds to M.5 in the proof catalogue.

title: 26  Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression
text:
26.8 Time-to-event outcomes
Survival is the outcome that motivates ML-UMR in oncology HTA, where the comparator is a single-arm trial reporting a Kaplan-Meier curve. The general-likelihood ML-NMR framework of Chapter 25 already extended aggregation from means to arbitrary individual likelihoods (Theorem 25.7); ML-UMR uses that framework in the unanchored setting, with SPFA acting on the log-hazard scale. We state the model and its consequences, building directly on the survival results of Chapter 25.
The survival workflow, before the formalism. Picture the archetypal case from Example 26.1: a single-arm trial of a new agent in advanced melanoma provides IPD (each patient’s covariates and survival time, some censored), while the comparator is a published chemotherapy trial showing only a Kaplan-Meier curve and a numbers-at-risk table. The analysis is a five-stage pipeline, and it helps to see the whole pipeline before the theorems dissect it.

Reconstruct pseudo-individual event and censoring times from the comparator’s published Kaplan-Meier curve and at-risk table (Theorem 26.5). These pseudo-patients carry times but no covariates.
Attach a covariate cloud. Pair the reconstructed comparator times with the comparator’s reported covariate distribution \(f_B\), the same Gaussian-copula reconstruction used for binary outcomes (Theorem 26.3); the covariates are integrated out, not matched one-to-one to pseudo-patients.
Integrate the censored likelihood over that covariate cloud, arm by arm, to form each source’s contribution to one joint likelihood (Equation 26.15, Theorem 26.6).
Fit the posterior by HMC, borrowing the index prognostic slope for the comparator through SPFA on the log-hazard scale.
Read off target estimands. For any chosen population, push the posterior through the covariate integral to get marginal survival, marginal hazard, RMST, and median survival (Theorem 26.7).

A word on direction, because survival flips the sign convention of the binary example. There a higher response probability was better, so a positive \(\Delta_{AB}\) favored \(A\). With survival a lower hazard is better and a longer survival is better: a hazard ratio of \(A\) versus \(B\) below \(1\), or an RMST difference (\(A\) minus \(B\)) above \(0\), favors the index treatment. We keep each estimand’s numerator explicit and restate the direction at each use.

Theorem 26.4 (ML-UMR for time-to-event outcomes) Let the index and comparator hazards follow a parametric survival model with shared baseline shape and SPFA on the log-hazard scale.
Proportional hazards (PH). With a baseline hazard \(h_0(t)>0\) and SPFA prognostic slope \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\), \[
h_k(t\mid\mathbf{x})=h_0(t)\,\exp\!\big(\eta_k(\mathbf{x})\big),
\qquad \eta_k(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_k+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}},\quad k\in\{A,B\},
\tag{26.14}\] which is the PH model Equation 25.5 with the single unanchored contrast \(\alpha_A-\alpha_B\) in place of the treatment effect and no effect-modification term.
Accelerated failure time (AFT). With an error distribution \(F_\epsilon\) and scale \(\sigma\), \(\log T=\eta_k(\mathbf{x})+\sigma\epsilon\), \(\epsilon\sim F_\epsilon\).
Then:
(a) Likelihood. The index contributes the right-censored individual likelihood Equation 25.12 at observed covariates; the comparator contributes, for each (possibly reconstructed) observation \((t_i,\delta_i)\) with unobserved covariates distributed as \(f_B\), the integrated censored likelihood \[
L_i^{(B)}(\boldsymbol\xi)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}h_B(t_i\mid\mathbf{x})^{\delta_i}\,S_B(t_i\mid\mathbf{x})\,f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
\tag{26.15}\] well defined and finite by Theorem 25.5 and evaluated by the QMC rule Theorem 26.3.
(b) Conditional log hazard ratio. Under PH and SPFA the conditional log hazard ratio of \(A\) versus \(B\) is the time-invariant, covariate-free, population-free scalar \[
\log\frac{h_A(t\mid\mathbf{x})}{h_B(t\mid\mathbf{x})}=\eta_A(\mathbf{x})-\eta_B(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_A-\alpha_B
\qquad\text{for all }t,\mathbf{x},
\tag{26.16}\] by Theorem 25.2 and Equation 26.5.
(c) Target-population marginal survival, hazard, RMST. For any target \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\), the marginal survival is the covariate average \(S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\int S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x})f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,
d\mathbf{x}\); the marginal hazard is the survivor-weighted average Equation 25.7; and the restricted mean survival time is the collapsible average \(\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=
\int\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}\) of Theorem 25.4.
(d) The marginal hazard ratio is time-varying. Even under the conditional PH and SPFA of Equation 26.14, the marginal hazard ratio \(h_A(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})/h_B(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})\) is in general not constant in \(t\), and is population-dependent, by Theorem 25.3.
(e) Scale misalignment: RMST is collapsible but not freely transportable. Although the RMST contrast is collapsible within any population, it is not transportable across populations from the log-hazard model. Precisely, under Equation 26.14 with \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\ne\mathbf{0}\), the conditional RMST contrast \(\mathbf{x}\mapsto\operatorname{RMST}_A(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})-\operatorname{RMST}_B(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})\) is a non-constant function of \(\mathbf{x}\), so its population average \[
\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AB}(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\big[\operatorname{RMST}_A(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})-\operatorname{RMST}_B(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})\big]\,f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}
\tag{26.17}\] depends on the whole target distribution \(f_{*}\) and differs across target populations even though the conditional log-hazard contrast Equation 26.16 is the single population-free scalar \(\alpha_A-\alpha_B\).


Proof. (a). The index term is Definition 25.4, derived from independent censoring in Proposition 25.1. For the comparator, the conditional kernel \(h_B(t\mid\mathbf{x})^{\delta}
S_B(t\mid\mathbf{x})\) is a nonnegative function of \(\mathbf{x}\) that is a density (in \(t\)) when \(\delta=1\) and a probability (the survival) when \(\delta=0\); in either case it is integrable against \(f_B\) by Theorem 25.5, giving the well-defined Equation 26.15, and the QMC evaluation is Theorem 26.3 applied to this integrand. (This integrated censored likelihood is the \(\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}=h^{\delta}S\) instance of the general-likelihood theorem Theorem 25.7.)
(b). By Theorem 25.2 the conditional log hazard ratio under PH is \(\eta_A(\mathbf{x})-
\eta_B(\mathbf{x})\), free of \(t\) and of the baseline; under SPFA this equals \(\alpha_A-\alpha_B\) by Equation 26.5, free also of \(\mathbf{x}\).
(c). Marginal survival is by definition the covariate average of conditional survival, and RMST collapsibility is Theorem 25.4 (a Tonelli exchange of the time and covariate integrals); the survivor-weighted marginal hazard is Lemma 25.1. All three carry over verbatim with \(f_{\mathcal{P}}=f_{*}\).
(d). Apply Theorem 25.3: writing \(h_B(t\mid\mathbf{x})=h_0(t)e^{\eta_B(\mathbf{x})}\) as a frailty model (one in which each individual’s hazard is scaled by a fixed positive multiplier, the frailty) with frailty \(\rho(\mathbf{x})=e^{\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}}\) (non-degenerate when \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\ne\mathbf{0}\) and the covariate varies under \(f_{*}\)), the constant conditional ratio is \(\psi=e^{\alpha_A-\alpha_B}\), and the theorem gives a marginal hazard ratio that equals \(\psi\) only at \(t=0\) and is strictly attenuated toward the null for \(t>0\), hence time-varying; the attenuation depends on \(f_{*}\) through the survivor distribution Equation 25.8, hence is population-dependent.
(e). Fix two covariate values \(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}'\) with \(\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}
\ne\mathbf{x}'^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\) (possible since \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\ne
\mathbf{0}\)). The conditional survival under arm \(k\) is, by Theorem 25.1, \(S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\exp(-e^{\eta_k(\mathbf{x})}H_0(t))\) with \(H_0(t)=\int_0^t h_0\), so the conditional RMST is \(\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})=\int_0^{\tau}\exp(-e^{\alpha_k+\mathbf{x}^\top
\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}}H_0(s))\,ds\), a strictly decreasing function of the scalar \(e^{\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}}\) (larger frailty, smaller survival, smaller area). The contrast \[
\Delta(\mathbf{x}):=\operatorname{RMST}_A(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})-\operatorname{RMST}_B(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})
=\int_0^{\tau}\Big[e^{-e^{\alpha_A}r(\mathbf{x})H_0(s)}-e^{-e^{\alpha_B}r(\mathbf{x})H_0(s)}\Big]ds,
\quad r(\mathbf{x}):=e^{\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}},
\] is a non-constant function of \(r(\mathbf{x})\) whenever \(\alpha_A\ne\alpha_B\): as \(r(\mathbf{x})\downarrow0\) both exponentials tend to \(1\) and \(\Delta\to0\), while at a finite \(r(\mathbf{x})\) the two areas differ, so \(\Delta(\mathbf{x})\) is not constant in \(\mathbf{x}\). Therefore its average Equation 26.17 against \(f_{*}\) is a genuine functional of the distribution of \(r(\mathbf{X})\) under \(f_{*}\), not a function of a single moment, and two targets with different covariate distributions give different \(\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AB}(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})\), even though the conditional log-hazard contrast Equation 26.16 is the same scalar \(\alpha_A-\alpha_B\) in every population. \(\square\)


Remark. Part (e) in two numbers. The scale-misalignment proof is the densest block in the chapter, so here is a concrete check with the exponential model of the survival coda (Section 26.15): \(h_k(t\mid x)=
\lambda_k e^{\beta x}\), \(\beta=\log 2\), \(\lambda_A=0.10\), \(\lambda_B=0.15\), horizon \(\tau=10\). The conditional RMST contrast \(\Delta(x)=\operatorname{RMST}_A(\tau\mid x)-\operatorname{RMST}_B(\tau\mid x)\) with \(\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid x)=(1-e^{-\lambda_k e^{\beta x}\tau})/(\lambda_k e^{\beta x})\) evaluates to \(\Delta(0)=6.321-5.179=1.142\) at \(x=0\) and \(\Delta(1)=4.323-3.167=1.156\) at \(x=1\): not the same number. Because \(\Delta(x)\) varies with \(x\), its population average shifts with the covariate mix, giving a target-population RMST contrast of \(0.5(1.142)+0.5(1.156)=1.149\) under \(P(X=1)=0.5\) but \(0.7(1.142)+0.3(1.156)=1.146\) under \(P(X=1)=0.3\). The gap is small in this benign example, but it is genuine, and it grows with the strength of the covariate effect \(\beta\) and the horizon \(\tau\). The conditional log hazard ratio, by contrast, is the single number \(\log(\lambda_B/\lambda_A)\) in every population: that is the transportable object, and the RMST contrast is not. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Which estimand to report. Part (b) gives the clean transportable object: the conditional log hazard ratio, a single number under SPFA, valid in every population. Part (d) warns that the marginal hazard ratio, the quantity a single Cox fit reports, is time-varying and population-dependent, hence not a transportable parameter; the mlumr default reports the scalar marginal hazard ratio as its value at the start of follow-up, \(t=0\), and exposes the full curve through predict(type = "loghr"). Part (e) is the subtle one, and is the unanchored instance of the scale-misalignment caveat flagged after Theorem 25.4 in Chapter 25: the RMST contrast is collapsible and clinically interpretable, but because the model is fitted on the log-hazard scale while RMST lives on the time scale, transporting the RMST contrast to a population with a different covariate distribution requires that target distribution and is not licensed by SPFA on the log-hazard scale alone. The practical recommendation, following Chandler and Ishak (2026c), is to report the conditional log hazard ratio as the primary transportable summary and the target-population RMST as a collapsible read-out in each named population. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Baselines and distributions. The reference implementation supports exponential, Weibull, and Gompertz PH models and their AFT counterparts (exponential-AFT, Weibull-AFT, log-normal, log-logistic, gamma, generalized gamma), plus flexible M-spline and piecewise-exponential baselines with a random-walk smoothing prior, following the multinma survival models of Phillippo et al. (2025). The choice of baseline shape is orthogonal to the SPFA structure: SPFA constrains the covariate slope, the baseline \(h_0(t)\) is shared across arms by the PH assumption, and the unanchored contrast is carried entirely by \(\alpha_A-\alpha_B\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This theorem corresponds to M.6 in the proof catalogue.

title: 26  Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression
section: 26.9 Reconstructing pseudo-individual data from a Kaplan-Meier curve
text:
26.9 Reconstructing pseudo-individual data from a Kaplan-Meier curve
The comparator likelihood Equation 26.15 is a product over individual observations \((t_i,\delta_i)\), but a published survival study reports a Kaplan-Meier curve and a numbers-at-risk table, not individual times. We reconstruct pseudo-individual data that reproduce the published curve, and prove that the reconstruction is exact in the idealized noiseless case.
Recall the Kaplan-Meier (product-limit) estimator. With distinct observed event times \(t_1<t_2<\cdots<t_m\), \(n_j\) patients at risk just before \(t_j\), and \(d_j\) events at \(t_j\), the estimator is \[
\widehat S(t)=\prod_{j:\,t_j\le t}\Big(1-\frac{d_j}{n_j}\Big),
\qquad \widehat S(t)=1\text{ for }t<t_1 .
\tag{26.18}\] Between consecutive event times the number at risk decreases by the events at \(t_j\) and by the patients censored in \([t_j,t_{j+1})\), say \(c_j\) of them: \(n_{j+1}=n_j-d_j-c_j\).

Theorem 26.5 (Exact reconstruction of pseudo-IPD from a Kaplan-Meier curve) Suppose the published report provides, without digitization error, the step survival curve Equation 26.18 (equivalently the event times \(t_1<\cdots<t_m\) and the survival values \(\widehat S(t_j)\)) together with the numbers at risk \(n_1,\dots,n_m\) at the event times and the initial sample size \(n_B=n_1+(\text{any
pre-}t_1\text{ censoring})\). Then:

The event counts are uniquely determined by the curve and the risk set, \[
d_j=n_j\Big(1-\frac{\widehat S(t_j)}{\widehat S(t_{j-1})}\Big),\qquad j=1,\dots,m,\ \ \widehat S(t_0):=1,
\tag{26.19}\] and the censoring counts are determined by the risk-set recursion \(c_j=n_j-d_j-n_{j+1}\) (with \(n_{m+1}\) the final reported at-risk number).
Any pseudo-sample \(\{(t_i,\delta_i)\}_{i=1}^{n_B}\) that realizes these per-interval event counts \(d_j\) and censoring counts \(c_j\) (placing \(d_j\) events exactly at \(t_j\) and \(c_j\) censorings anywhere in \([t_j,t_{j+1})\)) has Kaplan-Meier estimator identical to the published Equation 26.18 at every \(t\).
The reconstruction preserves the marginal survival distribution exactly but discards individual-level covariate information: the pseudo-sample carries no covariate values, so it informs only the marginal \((t,\delta)\) law and not any covariate-stratified survival.



Proof. (1). From the product form Equation 26.18, consecutive values satisfy \(\widehat S(t_j)/\widehat S(t_{j-1})=1-d_j/n_j\), because the product for \(\widehat S(t_j)\) is the product for \(\widehat S(t_{j-1})\) times the single extra factor \((1-d_j/n_j)\). Solving for \(d_j\) gives Equation 26.19; the value is uniquely determined because \(n_j>0\) and the ratio \(\widehat S(t_j)/\widehat S(t_{j-1})\in(0,1]\) are both given. With \(d_j\) known and the at-risk numbers \(n_j,n_{j+1}\) given, the risk-set conservation \(n_{j+1}=n_j-d_j-c_j\) solves uniquely for \(c_j=n_j-d_j-
n_{j+1}\). (These are nonnegative integers up to the rounding inherent in reading \(\widehat S\); the Guyot algorithm rounds and redistributes to keep the counts integer and the at-risk numbers matched.)
(2). Construct a pseudo-sample with exactly \(d_j\) events at time \(t_j\) and \(c_j\) censorings at arbitrary times in \([t_j,t_{j+1})\). Its Kaplan-Meier estimator is computed from Equation 26.18 using its own event times and risk sets. At time \(t_1\) the pseudo-sample has \(n_B\) at risk and \(d_1\) events, matching \(n_1,d_1\). Inductively, if the pseudo-sample has \(n_j\) at risk just before \(t_j\) (matching the published \(n_j\)), then it has \(d_j\) events at \(t_j\) and \(c_j\) censorings in \([t_j,t_{j+1})\) by construction, so just before \(t_{j+1}\) it has \(n_j-d_j-c_j=n_{j+1}\) at risk, matching the published \(n_{j+1}\); the censorings in the open interval contribute no event factor and only reduce the risk set. Hence at every event time the pseudo-sample has the same \((n_j,d_j)\) as the published data, so its product-limit estimator equals Equation 26.18 factor by factor, at every \(t\). (The placement of censorings within an interval is irrelevant to the estimator, which only counts how many remain at risk at the next event time, so the reconstruction is unique as a curve even though the exact censoring times are not.)
(3). The pseudo-sample is a list of times and event indicators with no covariates attached, so any statistic that depends only on the marginal \((t,\delta)\) distribution (the survival curve, the marginal hazard, the RMST) is reproduced, while any covariate-conditional statistic is not recoverable from it. This is the standard limitation: the reconstruction is faithful at the margin and silent about within-strata structure. \(\square\)


Example 26.3 (A three-event Kaplan-Meier inversion by hand) Suppose the comparator report gives \(n_B=20\) patients, event times \(t_1<t_2<t_3\), at-risk numbers \(n_1=20\), \(n_2=14\), \(n_3=10\) (and \(n_4=8\) after \(t_3\)), and the published step-curve values \(\widehat S(t_1)=0.800\), \(\widehat S(t_2)=0.629\), \(\widehat S(t_3)=0.503\). Apply Equation 26.19 with \(\widehat S(t_0):=1\): \[
d_1=20\Big(1-\tfrac{0.800}{1}\Big)=4,\quad
d_2=14\Big(1-\tfrac{0.629}{0.800}\Big)=3,\quad
d_3=10\Big(1-\tfrac{0.503}{0.629}\Big)=2,
\] and the risk-set recursion \(c_j=n_j-d_j-n_{j+1}\) gives the censoring counts \(c_1=20-4-14=2\), \(c_2=14-3-10=1\), \(c_3=10-2-8=0\). So the published curve and at-risk table pin down exactly \(4\) events then \(2\) censorings, \(3\) events then \(1\) censoring, then \(2\) events with \(8\) still at risk. Any pseudo-sample placing events and censorings this way reproduces the curve factor by factor (part 2 of the theorem). But note what the pseudo-sample does not have: a covariate for any of these \(20\) patients. The reconstruction recovers the marginal survival times and nothing about who was biomarker-positive or how old anyone was. That is why the survival likelihood Equation 26.15 still integrates over the reported covariate distribution \(f_B\): the pseudo-times supply the \((t,\delta)\) margin, \(f_B\) supplies the covariate cloud, and the two are combined but never matched patient by patient. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. From idealized inversion to the Guyot algorithm. Theorem Theorem 26.5 is the exact case in which the at-risk number is known at every event time. In practice the numbers at risk are reported only at a coarse grid of follow-up times, and the survival values are read off a figure with digitization error. The algorithm of Guyot and colleagues (Guyot et al. 2012) solves the same inversion under these realistic constraints: it allocates censorings between reported at-risk times so that the implied risk sets match the table, then applies Equation 26.19 event by event, iterating to reconcile the curve drops with the at-risk evolution. The output is pseudo-IPD whose Kaplan-Meier curve matches the published one to within digitization noise; Chandler and Ishak (2026c) and the mlumr function set_agd_surv() implement it for the comparator arm. Sensitivity analyses over several independent digitizations quantify the reconstruction uncertainty, which is the price the unanchored survival comparison pays for having only a published figure. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This theorem corresponds to M.7 in the proof catalogue, and supplies the reconstruction whose existence Chapter 25 invoked in the remark following Theorem 25.6.

title: 26  Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression
text:
26.10 The joint individual-plus-aggregate likelihood
The two data sources are combined into one likelihood, and one posterior. The factorization is the unanchored instance of the aggregate arm likelihood of Chapter 25.

Theorem 26.6 (The joint ML-UMR likelihood) Assume the index observations are conditionally independent given their covariates and \(\boldsymbol\xi\), and the comparator observations are conditionally independent given their (unobserved) covariates and \(\boldsymbol\xi\), with comparator covariates drawn independently from \(f_B\). Then the joint likelihood of the index IPD \(\mathbf{Y}^{(A)}\) and the comparator data \(\mathbf{Y}^{(B)}\) factorizes as \[
L_{\mathrm{joint}}(\boldsymbol\xi)=\underbrace{\prod_{i=1}^{n_A}\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}\!\big(y_i^{(A)}\mid g^{-1}(\eta_A(\mathbf{x}_i)),\boldsymbol\phi\big)}_{\text{index IPD, covariates observed}}\;\cdot\;\underbrace{\prod_{i=1}^{n_B}\int_{\mathcal{X}}\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}\!\big(y_i^{(B)}\mid g^{-1}(\eta_B(\mathbf{x})),\boldsymbol\phi\big)\,f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}}_{\text{comparator AgD, covariates integrated}},
\tag{26.20}\] where for survival the kernel is the censored likelihood \(h^{\delta}S\) and the comparator factors use the reconstructed pseudo-IPD of Theorem 26.5. With a prior \(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi)\) the posterior is \(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathcal{D})\propto L_{\mathrm{joint}}(\boldsymbol\xi)\,
\pi(\boldsymbol\xi)\), and the two sources are weighted automatically by their information content.


Proof. Index factor. In the index source the covariates \(\mathbf{x}_i\) are observed, so each individual contributes its conditional likelihood \(\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y_i^{(A)}\mid g^{-1}(\eta_A(\mathbf{x}_i)),
\boldsymbol\phi)\) evaluated at the known covariate; conditional independence makes the index likelihood the product of these, the first factor of Equation 26.20.
Comparator factor. In the comparator source the covariates are unobserved. By Theorem 25.5, the marginal likelihood of one comparator observation \(y_i^{(B)}\), integrating out its covariate distributed as \(f_B\), is \(\int_{\mathcal{X}}\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y_i^{(B)}\mid
g^{-1}(\eta_B(\mathbf{x})),\boldsymbol\phi)f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}\); by Theorem 25.6, conditional independence of the comparator outcomes given covariates together with independent covariate draws makes the comparator likelihood the product of these marginal contributions, the second factor of Equation 26.20. (For a sufficient summary, a binomial event count or a normal sample mean, the product collapses to the corresponding aggregate one-line likelihood with mean \(\theta_{\bullet B}\), as in Definition 20.2; for survival no single summary is sufficient and the product runs over the reconstructed pseudo-IPD.)
Joint factorization and posterior. The index and comparator sources are independent given \(\boldsymbol\xi\) (different patients in different studies), so their joint likelihood is the product of the two factors, which is Equation 26.20. Multiplying by the prior and normalizing gives the posterior. \(\square\)

Why this matters. This single likelihood is what makes ML-UMR a model rather than a two-step recipe: the index IPD and the comparator AgD enter one posterior, so uncertainty flows automatically from each source into the final contrast, and the same fitted object yields the estimand in every target population. It is the unanchored counterpart of the ML-NMR likelihood of Chapter 20, with the comparator arm’s covariates integrated out instead of observed. The next remark is a caution against over-reading this: more comparator data sharpen \(\alpha_B\) but never test the borrowed slope.

Remark. Automatic information weighting, and what it is not. The posterior weights each source by its likelihood curvature: a large index sample sharpens \((\alpha_A,\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})\), and a large comparator sample (more events, more at-risk follow-up) sharpens \(\alpha_B\) through the aggregate factor. This is unlike MAIC and STC, which condition on the index IPD and use the comparator data only for reweighting or for the comparator-arm value; ML-UMR puts both data types into one likelihood and lets the posterior balance them. What the weighting is not is a substitute for the identifying assumption: the comparator factor informs only the one scalar \(\alpha_B\) (Type 1) or the \((d+1)\)-vector \((\alpha_B,
\boldsymbol\beta_B)\) when subgroups are reported (Type 2, Theorem 26.2); the slope \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\) that projects the index surface onto the comparator arm comes from the IPD under SPFA, and no amount of comparator data tests that projection in the Type 1 model. The reference model also has no random-effects term for between-study heterogeneity: the comparator rows are treated as one population, a limitation recorded in the mlumr documentation. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This theorem corresponds to M.8 in the proof catalogue.

title: 26  Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression
section: 26.11 Marginal survival, hazard, and RMST in target populations
text:
26.11 Marginal survival, hazard, and RMST in target populations
From the joint posterior we read off any target-population estimand by pushing the posterior through the integration pipeline. We state the construction and its convergence.

Theorem 26.7 (Target-population survival estimands from the posterior) Let \(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathcal{D})\) be the ML-UMR posterior Theorem 26.6, and fix a target population \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\) with covariate density \(f_{*}\) and a horizon \(\tau\). For each arm \(k\in\{A,B\}\) define the functionals \[
S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*};\boldsymbol\xi)=\!\int S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)f_{*}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x},
\quad
\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*};\boldsymbol\xi)=\!\int_0^{\tau}\! S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*};\boldsymbol\xi)\,dt,
\tag{26.21}\] and the marginal hazard \(h_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*};\boldsymbol\xi)\) by the survivor-weighted formula Equation 25.7. Then:

Each functional is a continuous (indeed smooth) function of \(\boldsymbol\xi\), so its posterior is the well-defined pushforward of \(\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathcal{D})\), summarized by posterior draws.
The estimands of the table below are obtained from these functionals; the survival, RMST, and median are collapsible read-outs (averages of conditional quantities), while the marginal hazard ratio and its log are non-collapsible and time-varying by Theorem 26.4(d).








Estimand
Formula




Marginal survival
\(S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\int S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x})f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}\)


Marginal hazard
\(h_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\dfrac{\int h_k(t\mid\mathbf{x})S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x})f_{*}}{\int S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x})f_{*}}\)


RMST
\(\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\int_0^{\tau}S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})\,dt\)


RMST contrast
\(\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AB}(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\operatorname{RMST}_A-\operatorname{RMST}_B\)


Marginal log HR at \(t\)
\(\log\!\big[h_A(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})/h_B(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})\big]\)


Median survival
the \(t\) solving \(S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\tfrac12\)




Computed by QMC over \(N\) Sobol’ nodes for the inner covariate integral and \(S\) posterior draws for the outer parameter integral, the posterior mean of any of these estimands converges, as \(N\to\infty\) and \(S\to\infty\), to the true posterior mean, with QMC error \(O((\log N)^{d}/N)\) (Theorem 26.3) and Monte Carlo error \(O(S^{-1/2})\).



Proof. (1). For fixed \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(t\), \(S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)=\exp(-e^{\eta_k(\mathbf{x};
\boldsymbol\xi)}H_0(t;\boldsymbol\xi))\) is a smooth function of \(\boldsymbol\xi\) (composition of the smooth exponential with the affine \(\eta_k\) and the parametric cumulative baseline \(H_0\)), bounded in \([0,1]\). Integrating against the probability measure \(f_{*}\) preserves smoothness and boundedness by differentiation under the integral sign (dominated convergence, the derivative bounded by an integrable envelope), so \(S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*};\boldsymbol\xi)\) is smooth in \(\boldsymbol\xi\); integrating over \(t\in[0,\tau]\) gives the smooth RMST functional by Tonelli (Theorem 4.8, Theorem 25.4). A smooth function of \(\boldsymbol\xi\) has a well-defined pushforward law under the posterior, estimated by applying the functional to each posterior draw.
(2). The marginal survival, RMST, RMST contrast, and median are averages or monotone read-outs of conditional survival, hence collapsible by Theorem 25.4; the marginal hazard is the survivor-weighted average Lemma 25.1, and its ratio across arms is non-collapsible and time-varying by Theorem 26.4(d). The table simply records these formulas.
(3). For each posterior draw \(\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)}\), the inner integral \(S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*};
\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\) is approximated by the QMC average \(\frac1N\sum_n S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x}^{(n)};
\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\) over Sobol’ nodes \(\mathbf{x}^{(n)}=T(\mathbf{u}^{(n)})\) for \(f_{*}\), with error \(O((\log N)^{d}/N)\) by Theorem 26.3 (the survival integrand is smooth and bounded). The posterior mean is then the average over draws, \(\frac1S\sum_s(\cdot)\), with Monte Carlo error \(O(S^{-1/2})\) by the central limit theorem for the (stationary) posterior sample, exactly as in Bayesian g-computation (Definition 19.5). The two errors add, and both vanish as \(N,S\to\infty\). \(\square\)

Which of the six estimands should a health researcher actually report? Table 26.4 pairs each with the clinical question it answers and flags whether it travels across populations. The rule of thumb, defended in the remark below, is to report the conditional log hazard ratio as the transportable summary and the RMST (or median) as the clinically interpretable read-out in each named target population, and to treat the marginal hazard ratio with care, because it is neither constant in time nor portable across populations.



Table 26.4: Which survival estimand to report. Everything except the conditional log hazard ratio is population-specific and must be recomputed for each target \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\); the RMST and median are at least collapsible (clean averages of conditional quantities), while the marginal hazard ratio is neither collapsible nor time-constant.










Estimand
Clinical question it answers
Transportable?




Marginal survival \(S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})\)
what fraction of this population is alive at \(t\) under arm \(k\)
population-specific


Median survival
the time by which half this population has had the event
population-specific


RMST \(\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})\)
average event-free time up to horizon \(\tau\), per arm
collapsible, but population-specific


RMST contrast
average event-free time gained on \(A\) versus \(B\) up to \(\tau\)
collapsible; differs across populations (Theorem 26.4)


Marginal hazard ratio at \(t\)

not transportable; time-varying


Conditional log HR \(\alpha_A-\alpha_B\)

the single transportable scalar







Remark. The whole point of the marginalization. Parts (1) and (3) are what let ML-UMR report a survival contrast in a population represented by neither trial: choose any \(f_{*}\), push the posterior through Equation 26.21, and summarize. The honest cost is part (2) together with Theorem 26.4(e): the marginal hazard ratio is not a single transportable number, and the RMST contrast, though collapsible, must be recomputed for each target distribution. The transportable scalar is the conditional log hazard ratio \(\alpha_A-\alpha_B\) of Equation 26.16, valid in every population under SPFA. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This theorem corresponds to M.9 in the proof catalogue.

title: 26  Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression
text:
26.12 ML-UMR and unanchored STC
ML-UMR has a pairwise ancestor. We show that, in the comparator population, the SPFA model reduces exactly to unanchored STC, and that its extension to other targets is what the multilevel formulation buys, at the cost of the stronger assumption.
Put plainly, and this is the motivation worth holding before the formalism: we want to know exactly what ML-UMR buys over the simpler method a health researcher may already know. So we prove the two agree where STC is valid, the comparator population, and pinpoint where they part company, every other target. The agreement is reassuring (ML-UMR is not doing anything exotic at the comparator); the extension to other populations is the entire value added; and SPFA is the price of that extension. A reader who trusts this paragraph can read the theorem as its proof.

Theorem 26.8 (Equivalence with unanchored STC at the comparator, extension elsewhere) Adopt SPFA and suppose the comparator AgD provide a sufficient outcome summary (an event count, a sample mean) so that the comparator likelihood factor of Theorem 26.6 is the aggregate model with mean \(\theta_{\bullet B}\), and let \(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}\) be the (limiting) maximizer of the joint likelihood. Then:

(Calibration identity.) At \(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}\) the fitted comparator aggregate mean equals the observed comparator outcome, \(\theta_{\bullet B}(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})=\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}\); equivalently \(\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}_B)=\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}\).
(Equivalence at the comparator population.) With target \(\mathcal{P}^{*}=\mathcal{P}_B\), the ML-UMR estimand Equation 26.1 equals the unanchored marginal STC estimator of Definition 19.4, namely \[
\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}_B)=g\!\big(\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}_B)\big)-g\!\big(\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}\big),
\qquad
\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}_B)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}g^{-1}\!\big(\eta_A(\mathbf{x})\big)f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
\tag{26.22}\] the index surface integrated over the comparator covariate distribution, contrasted on the link scale with the observed comparator outcome. Under the conditions of Theorem 19.3 and the unanchored condition of Theorem 19.6(2), both are consistent for \(\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}_B)\).
(Strict extension elsewhere.) For a target \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\ne\mathcal{P}_B\), ML-UMR produces \(\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}^{*})\) by integrating both arms against \(f_{*}\) using the fitted \(\alpha_B\) and \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\), whereas unanchored STC, lacking a model for arm \(B\) beyond the observed comparator outcome, cannot move arm \(B\) off \(\mathcal{P}_B\). The extension uses SPFA, which is strictly stronger than the assumption STC needs for its native comparator-population estimand (Proposition 26.1).



Proof. (1). Write the comparator factor as the aggregate model \(\pi_{\mathrm{Agg}}(\text{summary}_B\mid
\theta_{\bullet B}(\boldsymbol\xi),n_B)\), a one-parameter exponential-family likelihood in the mean \(\theta_{\bullet B}\) (binomial in the event proportion, normal in the sample mean). Its score in \(\theta_{\bullet B}\) vanishes exactly when the fitted mean equals the observed sufficient statistic, the standard mean-matching property of the exponential family; since \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\) is fixed by the index factor and \(\theta_{\bullet B}\) is a strictly monotone function of the free parameter \(\alpha_B\) (Lemma 23.2), the joint maximizer sets \(\theta_{\bullet B}(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})
=\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}\). By Equation 26.8, \(\theta_{\bullet B}=\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}_B)\), giving the identity.
(2). At target \(\mathcal{P}_B\) the ML-UMR arm means are \(\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}_B)=\int g^{-1}(\eta_A)
f_B\) and \(\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}_B)=\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) by part (1), so the estimand Equation 26.1 is \(g(\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}_B))-g(\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}})\), which is Equation 26.22. The unanchored marginal STC estimator of Definition 19.4 fits the outcome surface on the index IPD, predicts arm \(A\) in the comparator population as \(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}}=\int g^{-1}
(\eta_A)f_B=\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}_B)\), and contrasts it on the link scale with the comparator’s own observed outcome \(g(\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}})\); this is exactly Equation 26.22. Hence the two coincide. Consistency of the arm-\(A\) prediction is Theorem 19.3 under correct specification and transportability of the index surface to \(\mathcal{P}_B\); the unanchored validity of using the comparator’s observed outcome as the arm-\(B\) value is Theorem 19.6(2) under constancy of absolute effects, which SPFA supplies. The Bayesian version of Equation 26.22 is the pushforward of the posterior through the same functional, the Bayesian g-computation of Definition 19.5.
(3). For \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\ne\mathcal{P}_B\), ML-UMR evaluates \(\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}^{*})=\int g^{-1}
(\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}\) with the fitted \(\alpha_B\) and the SPFA slope; this requires the arm-\(B\) conditional surface at covariate values typical of \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\), which Lemma 26.2 supplies only because SPFA fixes the comparator slope equal to the index slope. Unanchored STC, having fit no outcome model for treatment \(B\) (no comparator IPD), has no value for arm \(B\) away from the observed comparator outcome, so it cannot evaluate \(\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}^{*})\); its estimand is defined only at \(\mathcal{P}_B\). Thus ML-UMR strictly extends the set of admissible targets, and the extension is powered by SPFA, which Proposition 26.1 shows is strictly stronger than the shared-effect-modifier assumption. \(\square\)


Remark. The honest summary. Chandler and Ishak (2026a) state in their conclusions that ML-UMR “simplifies to unanchored STC in the comparator population”; part (2) is that statement, proved. The value added by ML-UMR is not at the comparator, where it agrees with the older and assumption-lighter STC, but at other target populations, where STC is silent. That added scope is bought entirely with SPFA. Whether the extra targets are worth the stronger, untestable assumption is an application-specific judgment, and the safe default, when SPFA is doubtful, is to report only the comparator-population contrast, where ML-UMR and unanchored STC coincide. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This theorem corresponds to M.10 in the proof catalogue.

title: 26  Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression
text:
26.13 SPFA versus SEMA
We now prove precisely the sense in which the unanchored assumption is stronger than the anchored one.

Proposition 26.1 (SPFA is strictly stronger than SEMA) Consider the linear-predictor model of Definition 20.1 with treatments carrying interaction vectors \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\), and the two assumptions, stated for the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) contrast: \[
\text{SEMA: }\ \boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B},
\qquad
\text{SPFA: }\ \boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}=\mathbf{0}.
\] Then:

(SPFA \(\Rightarrow\) SEMA.) SPFA implies SEMA.
(Anchored cancellation under SEMA.) In the anchored triangle with common comparator \(C\) (\(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,C}=\mathbf{0}\)), SEMA makes the conditional \(A\)-versus-\(B\) contrast free of the covariate, \(\eta_A(\mathbf{x})-\eta_B(\mathbf{x})=\gamma_A-\gamma_B\), even when the shared interaction \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}\) is nonzero, because the modification cancels against the anchor.
(Unanchored necessity of SPFA.) In the unanchored two-treatment network, the conditional \(A\)-versus-\(B\) contrast \(\eta_A(\mathbf{x})-\eta_B(\mathbf{x})=(\gamma_A-\gamma_B)+\mathbf{x}^\top
(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})\) is free of \(\mathbf{x}\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}\); and the arm-\(B\) absolute surface is determined by the index IPD (which identifies only \(\boldsymbol\beta_A=\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}\), with one arm taken as reference so \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\mathbf{0}\)) if and only if \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}=\mathbf{0}\), that is SPFA.
(Strictness.) The implication in (1) is strict: there exist data-generating processes satisfying SEMA but not SPFA, namely any with a shared nonzero interaction \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}
\ne\mathbf{0}\).



Proof. (1). If \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}=\mathbf{0}\) then in particular \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}\), so SPFA implies SEMA.
(2). In the anchored model the active-versus-comparator predictors are \(\eta_A(\mathbf{x})=\mu+
\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_A+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}\) and \(\eta_B(\mathbf{x})=
\mu+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}\) (sharing the study baseline and prognostic term as contrasts against \(C\)). Subtracting, \(\eta_A(\mathbf{x})-\eta_B(\mathbf{x})=(\gamma_A-\gamma_B)+\mathbf{x}^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}-
\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})\); under SEMA the bracket \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}=\mathbf{0}\) vanishes, leaving \(\gamma_A-\gamma_B\), free of \(\mathbf{x}\), regardless of the common value \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}\), which may be any nonzero vector. The anchor (the common \(C\), against which both contrasts are formed) is what allows the nonzero modification to cancel.
(3). The contrast expression is the same algebra as in (2). It is constant in \(\mathbf{x}\) iff the linear term \(\mathbf{x}^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})\) is identically zero, iff \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}\) (taking \(\mathbf{x}\) to range over a set spanning \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\)). Now the unanchored index IPD is single-arm and identifies only the total slope \(\boldsymbol\beta_A=\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}\) (by Lemma 26.1 there is no within-network contrast to separate \(\boldsymbol\beta_1\) from \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}\)); fixing the index arm as reference sets \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\mathbf{0}\), so \(\boldsymbol\beta_A=\boldsymbol\beta_1\). The comparator slope is \(\boldsymbol\beta_B=\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}\). The arm-\(B\) surface is determined by the index-identified \(\boldsymbol\beta_1\) alone (so that knowing one scalar \(\alpha_B\) pins \(\eta_B\) everywhere, Lemma 26.2) iff \(\boldsymbol\beta_B=\boldsymbol\beta_1\), iff \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}=\mathbf{0}\), which is SPFA. Without it, \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}\) is unidentified from the single comparator mean (Theorem 26.9(3) below), and the projection fails.
(4). Take any model with \(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}=\mathbf{c}\ne\mathbf{0}\). It satisfies SEMA (\(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}\)) but violates SPFA (\(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}
\ne\mathbf{0}\)). Hence the set of SPFA-compliant processes is a proper subset of the SEMA-compliant ones: SPFA is strictly stronger. \(\square\)


Remark. One picture. SEMA says the two active treatments modify the outcome identically, so their contrast is flat; SPFA says they do not modify it at all. The anchored design exploits a common comparator to cancel shared modification, so it can live with SEMA; the unanchored design has nothing to cancel against and must assume there is nothing to cancel, which is SPFA. The same gap is the difference between conditional constancy of relative effects (Definition 17.4), which anchored adjustment needs, and conditional constancy of absolute effects (Definition 17.5), which unanchored adjustment needs; SPFA is the parametric face of the latter, as established in Lemma 26.2. The Chandler-Ishak posters describe SPFA as “a limitation inherent to unanchored comparisons,” and this proposition is the precise statement of that remark. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This proposition corresponds to M.11 in the proof catalogue.

title: 26  Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression
section: 26.14 Identifiability and the limits of unanchored comparison
text:
26.14 Identifiability and the limits of unanchored comparison
We collect the identifiability frontier into one theorem and then survey the limits that no estimator can overcome.

Theorem 26.9 (Identifiability frontier of ML-UMR) In the unanchored two-treatment network, with the index parameters \((\alpha_A,\boldsymbol\beta_A)\) identified from the IPD, the comparator block has the following identifiability:

SPFA, overall AgD (one aggregate mean). \((\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})\) identified (\(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\) from IPD, \(\alpha_B\) from the single mean): the model is just identified (Theorem 26.1).
SPFA, subgroup AgD (\(Z\ge2\) means). Over-identified: \(\alpha_B\) solves any one subgroup equation, and the remaining \(Z-1\) equations are testable constraints (a goodness-of-fit check on SPFA).
No SPFA, overall AgD. \((\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\) is not identified from a single aggregate mean: the solution set of \(\Theta_B(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)=\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) is a \(d\)-dimensional manifold.
No SPFA, subgroup AgD with \(Z\ge d+1\). \((\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)\) identified under the non-degeneracy of Theorem 26.2.



Proof. (1) is Theorem 26.1: \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\) from the full-rank IPD design and \(\alpha_B\) as the unique root of the strictly monotone \(\Theta_B\) (Lemma 23.2), one unknown matched by one equation.
(2). Under SPFA, \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\) is known from the IPD and only \(\alpha_B\) is free, so each subgroup equation \(\Theta_B^{z}(\alpha_B)=\theta_{\bullet B}^{z,\mathrm{obs}}\) determines \(\alpha_B\) by monotonicity; with \(Z\ge2\) subgroups the system is over-determined in the single unknown \(\alpha_B\), and the \(Z-1\) residual equations are constraints that hold only if SPFA is correct, hence a test of SPFA. In practice the test is operationalized as a posterior predictive check: fit the SPFA model, then compare each observed subgroup outcome against its posterior predictive distribution under the fitted single \(\alpha_B\); a systematic discrepancy (some subgroups over-predicted, others under-predicted, in a pattern aligned with a covariate) is evidence against SPFA. The parametric counterpart is a likelihood-ratio or score test of the Type 1 model nested in the relaxed Type 2 model of Theorem 26.2.
(3). With \(\boldsymbol\beta_B\) free, the map \((\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)\mapsto\Theta_B(\alpha_B,
\boldsymbol\beta_B)\) goes from \(\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\) to \(\mathbb{R}\); its gradient \(\int(g^{-1})'(\alpha_B+
\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_B)(1,\mathbf{x}^\top)f_B\) is a nonzero row vector (the integrand is positive), so by the implicit function theorem the level set \(\{\Theta_B=\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}\}\) is a smooth manifold of dimension \((d+1)-1=d\ge1\) near any solution. Every point of it reproduces the same observed mean, so distinct parameters give identical data: not identified. (This is the \(Z=1<d+1\) case of Theorem 26.2.)
(4) is Theorem 26.2 with \(Z\ge d+1\) and the full-rank weighted-moment matrix \(M\). \(\square\)

Three structural limits are shared by every unanchored method, ML-UMR included, and follow from the theory already developed.

Remark. Inherent limits. First, the identifying assumption is untestable in the overall-AgD case: by Theorem 26.9(3) a single comparator mean cannot distinguish SPFA from any effect-modifying alternative, so SPFA must be defended externally; it becomes testable only with subgroup AgD (Theorem 26.9(2)). Second, no unanchored method can remove confounding by unmeasured prognostic factors: the projection Equation 26.6 transports the index surface in the measured covariates only, and an imbalanced prognostic variable omitted from \(\mathbf{x}\) biases the absolute arm positions exactly as in the necessity direction of Theorem 17.2. Third, the comparator covariate distribution \(f_B\) is reconstructed from reported margins and an assumed correlation (Theorem 26.3); misspecifying it biases the aggregate integral and hence \(\alpha_B\). For survival, the Kaplan-Meier reconstruction (Theorem 26.5) adds digitization noise on top. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Empirical behavior under SPFA violation (simulation evidence, not theorems). The Chandler-Ishak studies report simulation results under specific data-generating mechanisms; we record them as evidence, not as proved statements, and the worked example of Section 26.15 derives the qualitative pattern by hand. For binary outcomes (Chandler and Ishak 2026a), with about 1000 patients per arm and two correlated binary prognostic factors, the SPFA model estimating the comparator-population log odds ratio shows absolute bias below about \(0.009\) and 95% interval coverage near nominal across no-, weak-, and strong-modification scenarios; the index-population (transported) estimate degrades as modification strengthens, with bias around \(-0.06\) (about \(-11\%\)) under weak modification and around \(-0.29\) (about \(-67\%\)) under strong modification, and coverage falling accordingly. The relaxed model (Theorem 26.2) restores small bias and near-nominal coverage when subgroup AgD are available. For survival outcomes (Chandler and Ishak 2026c), RMST estimands are near-unbiased with near-nominal coverage when SPFA holds, degrade modestly under weak modification, and show substantial bias (often exceeding 25% to 30%) and undercoverage in the index population under strong modification. The robust pattern, derived analytically in Section 26.15, is that the comparator- population estimand is anchored by the observed comparator outcome and so resists SPFA violation, while non-comparator targets are fragile because the wrong slope is extrapolated to a different covariate distribution. Different mechanisms can give different profiles; these numbers are illustrative, not universal. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. When to use ML-UMR. First, a triage against ML-NMR. If even one study connects the index and comparator treatments through a common comparator, use the anchored machinery: Bucher (Chapter 14), network meta-analysis (Chapter 15), or connected ML-NMR (Chapters 20 to 25), all of which need only SEMA and let the IPD check for effect modification rather than assuming it away. Reach for ML-UMR only when the network is genuinely disconnected, so that no anchor exists and SPFA becomes unavoidable. The one-line rule: prefer ML-NMR whenever a connecting study exists; use ML-UMR when it does not (see Table 26.1). That settled, the method is appropriate when individual data exist for the index treatment, only aggregate data exist for the comparator, no connected (anchored) network is available, SPFA is defensible from clinical knowledge, and the comparator’s covariate summaries are reported. Where SPFA is doubtful, the defensible report is the comparator-population contrast (where ML-UMR coincides with unanchored STC, Theorem 26.8), interpreted as population-specific rather than transportable, in line with the NICE guidance of Phillippo et al. (2016). The mlumr cautions, no between-study heterogeneity term, weak identification of the relaxed comparator slope, non-collapsibility of the hazard ratio, and the need to verify integration convergence, are the practical face of these limits. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This theorem corresponds to M.12 in the proof catalogue.

title: 26  Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression
text:
26.15 A worked unanchored example
We carry a complete binary ML-UMR analysis through by hand, choosing one binary covariate so that every integral is an exact two-point sum (Theorem 26.3, discrete remark) and every number can be checked with a calculator. This is the running example of Example 26.1 made numerical. The covariate \(X\in\{0,1\}\) is a binary biomarker (say PD-L1 positivity, with \(X=1\) for biomarker-positive); the outcome is a binary response (a good outcome, so a higher probability is better, and biomarker-positive patients respond better under the fitted index model); the link is the logit, \(g=
\operatorname{logit}\), \(g^{-1}=\operatorname{expit}\).
Inputs. Fitting the index IPD on treatment \(A\) returns the prognostic model \[
\eta_A(x)=\alpha_A+\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\,x,\qquad \hat\alpha_A=-0.5,\ \ \hat\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}=1.0,
\] so the index conditional response probabilities are \(p_A(0)=\operatorname{expit}(-0.5)=0.3775\) and \(p_A(1)=\operatorname{expit}(0.5)=0.6225\). The comparator AgD on treatment \(B\) report \(n_B=200\) patients, \(r_B=77\) responders (crude proportion \(\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}=0.385\)), and biomarker prevalence \(\bar x_B=P(X=1\mid\mathcal{P}_B)=0.50\). The index population has biomarker prevalence \(\bar x_A=P(X=1\mid\mathcal{P}_A)=0.30\). We use the constants \(\operatorname{expit}(-1)=0.2689\), \(\operatorname{expit}(-0.5)=0.3775\), \(\operatorname{expit}(0)=0.5\), \(\operatorname{expit}(0.5)=0.6225\).
The whole analysis lives in the two rows \(x=0\) and \(x=1\); Table 26.5 collects every conditional probability the steps below use, including the SPFA-violation column of Step 6. Reading it now makes each step a lookup rather than a fresh computation.



Table 26.5: Every number in the worked example, by covariate stratum. The fitted and true arm-\(B\) columns both average to the observed comparator response \(0.385\) under the comparator weights \((0.5,0.5)\), which is why the comparator-population contrast is unbiased; they diverge pointwise, so under the index weights \((0.7,0.3)\) they average to different values (\(0.3383\) versus \(0.2989\)), which is the index-population bias of Step 6.













Covariate \(x\)
weight in \(\mathcal{P}_B\)
weight in \(\mathcal{P}_A\)
\(p_A(x)\)
fitted \(p_B(x)\) under SPFA
true \(p_B(x)\), slope \(2\)




\(x=0\) (biomarker-negative)
\(0.5\)

\(0.2689\)
\(0.1694\)


\(x=1\) (biomarker-positive)
\(0.5\)
