\(0.6225\)
\(0.5000\)
\(0.6011\)






Step 1: identify \(\alpha_B\) (Theorem 26.1, Equation 26.9). Under SPFA the comparator shares the slope \(\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}=1.0\). With the binary covariate the aggregate mean is the exact two-point sum \[
\Theta_B(\alpha_B)=(1-\bar x_B)\,\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B)+\bar x_B\,\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B+1)
=0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B)+0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B+1).
\] This is strictly increasing in \(\alpha_B\) (Lemma 23.2), so the equation \(\Theta_B(\alpha_B)=0.385\) has a unique root. Bracketing: \(\Theta_B(-1.0)=0.5(0.2689)+0.5(0.5)=0.3845\) and \(\Theta_B(-0.9)=0.5(0.2891)+0.5(0.5250)=0.4070\), so the root lies just above \(-1.0\); to the precision of the reported proportion, \(\hat\alpha_B=-1.00\). (The fitted aggregate mean \(\Theta_B(-1.00)=0.3845\) matches the observed \(0.385\) to within rounding, the exact-calibration identity of Theorem 26.8(1).)
Step 2: the conditional contrast. Under SPFA the conditional log odds ratio of \(A\) versus \(B\) is the single number, free of \(x\) and of population, \[
\eta_A(x)-\eta_B(x)=\hat\alpha_A-\hat\alpha_B=-0.5-(-1.0)=0.5
\qquad(\text{@eq-spfa-constant-contrast}).
\]
Step 3: the estimand in the comparator population \(\mathcal{P}_B\) (\(\bar x_B=0.5\)). The arm means are exact two-point sums: \[
\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}_B)=0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(-0.5)+0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(0.5)=0.5(0.3775)+0.5(0.6225)=0.5000,
\] \[
\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}_B)=0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(-1.0)+0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(0)=0.5(0.2689)+0.5(0.5)=0.3845,
\] the latter equal to the observed comparator proportion, as it must be. The marginal log odds ratio is \[
\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}_B)=\operatorname{logit}(0.5000)-\operatorname{logit}(0.3845)=0-(-0.4706)=0.4706 .
\]
Step 4: the estimand in the index population \(\mathcal{P}_A\) (\(\bar x_A=0.3\)). Now integrate against the index covariate distribution: \[
\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}_A)=0.7(0.3775)+0.3(0.6225)=0.4510,
\qquad
\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}_A)=0.7(0.2689)+0.3(0.5)=0.3383,
\] \[
\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}_A)=\operatorname{logit}(0.4510)-\operatorname{logit}(0.3383)=(-0.1966)-(-0.6711)=0.4745 .
\]
Step 5: read the non-collapsibility. The conditional log odds ratio is \(0.5\) in every population (Step 2), but the marginal log odds ratio is \(0.4706\) in \(\mathcal{P}_B\) and \(0.4745\) in \(\mathcal{P}_A\), both attenuated toward the null \(0\) and differing slightly between populations. This is exactly the collapsibility dichotomy of Theorem 23.1(c): on the non-collapsible logit scale the marginal estimand depends on the whole target distribution, while the conditional contrast does not. The attenuation and its population dependence are the Definition 7.7 phenomenon, here visible in two hand-computed numbers.
Step 6: robustness at the comparator, fragility at the index, under SPFA violation. Suppose the true comparator model has a steeper slope, \(\beta_B^{\mathrm{true}}=2.0\ne\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}=1.0\) (strong effect modification), with a true intercept calibrated so that the comparator-population proportion is still \(0.385\) at \(\bar x_B=0.5\): solving \(0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(\alpha)+0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(\alpha+2)=
0.385\) gives \(\alpha_B^{\mathrm{true}}=-1.59\). Then:

Comparator population. The true arm-\(B\) mean in \(\mathcal{P}_B\) is \(0.385\) by construction, identical to the SPFA fit of Step 3; the true arm-\(A\) mean is \(0.5\) (arm \(A\) is correctly specified). So the true \(\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}_B)=0.4706\) equals the SPFA estimate: no bias at the comparator, because the observed comparator outcome anchors the arm-\(B\) mean there regardless of the slope.
Index population. The true arm-\(B\) mean in \(\mathcal{P}_A\) (\(\bar x_A=0.3\)) is \(0.7\,\operatorname{expit}(-1.59)+0.3\,\operatorname{expit}(0.41)=0.7(0.1694)+0.3(0.6011)=0.2989\), whereas the SPFA model (slope \(1.0\), \(\hat\alpha_B=-1.0\)) gives \(\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}_A)=0.3383\) from Step 4. The true index-population log odds ratio is \(\operatorname{logit}(0.4510)-\operatorname{logit}(0.2989)=
(-0.1966)-(-0.8525)=0.6559\), while the SPFA estimate is \(0.4745\). The bias is \(0.4745-0.6559=-0.1814\), about \(-28\%\): substantial bias at the index population, because the wrong slope is extrapolated from the comparator’s covariate distribution (mean \(0.5\)) to the index’s (mean \(0.3\)).

This is the central empirical pattern of Theorem 26.9 derived by hand: SPFA-invoking ML-UMR is robust where it is anchored by data (the comparator population) and fragile where it must extrapolate (any other target), and the fragility grows with the strength of the violated effect modification and with the distance between the covariate distributions. When SPFA is doubtful, report only \(\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}_B)\).

Remark. A survival coda. The same phenomena appear on the time scale. Take an exponential PH model with one binary covariate, \(h_k(t\mid x)=\lambda_k\,e^{\beta x}\), \(\beta=\log2\) (here \(X=1\) marks a poor-prognosis stratum, for example elevated LDH, that doubles the hazard; lower hazard is better, so on this time-to-event scale \(X=1\) is unfavorable, unlike the favorable response biomarker of the binary example), index rate \(\lambda_A=0.10\) and comparator rate \(\lambda_B=0.15\), so the conditional hazard ratio of \(B\) versus \(A\) is the constant \(\lambda_B/\lambda_A=1.5\) at every \(t\) and \(x\) (SPFA on the log-hazard scale, Equation 26.16). In a population with \(P(X=1)=0.5\), the marginal survival is \(\bar S_k(t)=0.5\,e^{-\lambda_k t}+0.5\,e^{-2\lambda_k t}\), and the marginal hazard ratio \(\bar h_B(t)/\bar h_A(t)\) equals \(1.500\) at \(t=0\), dips to \(1.438\) at \(t=5\) and \(1.398\) at \(t=10\), then drifts back to \(1.491\) by \(t=50\): time-varying, attenuated toward \(1\), exactly Theorem 26.4(d) and Theorem 25.3. The restricted mean survival times to \(\tau=10\) are \(\operatorname{RMST}_A=5.32\) and \(\operatorname{RMST}_B=4.17\) (each the exact integral \(0.5\frac{1-e^{-\lambda\tau}}{\lambda}+0.5\frac{1-e^{-2\lambda\tau}}{2\lambda}\)), a collapsible difference of \(1.15\) time units favoring the index treatment, the collapsible read-out of Theorem 26.7. Recomputing the RMST difference in a population with \(P(X=1)=0.3\) gives a different value, the scale- misalignment of Theorem 26.4(e): collapsible within each population, but not the same number across them. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 26  Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression
text:
26.16 Notes and references
Multilevel unanchored meta-regression is the contribution of Chandler and Ishak (2026a), who introduced the binary and continuous SPFA and relaxed-SPFA models and the simulation evidence summarized in Section 26.14, and of Chandler and Ishak (2026c), who extended the method to time-to-event outcomes with parametric and flexible baselines and the Kaplan-Meier reconstruction of the comparator arm. The method is an extension beyond the 2019 thesis of Phillippo (2019): it inherits the multilevel network meta-regression framework of Phillippo et al. (2020) and its general-likelihood extension of Phillippo et al. (2025) (Chapters 20 to 25), specifically the Sobol’ quasi-Monte Carlo integration (Definition 22.3, Sobol’ (1967); Owen (1956)) with a Gaussian copula (Definition 22.5, Theorem 22.5, Sklar (1959)) developed in Chapter 22, and reuses that machinery in the disconnected setting. The reference implementation is the mlumr R package of Sofi-Mahmudi and Chandler, which fits the SPFA and relaxed models by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo in Stan (Carpenter et al. (2017)), alongside frequentist STC and a naive benchmark, and whose documentation supplies the practical cautions recorded in Section 26.14; it is an adaptation of the GPL-3 multinma package of Phillippo. The transportability framing of population-adjusted indirect comparison that situates the unanchored estimand, conditional constancy of absolute effects (Definition 17.5) versus relative effects (Definition 17.4), is developed by Chandler and Ishak (2026b) and in Chapter 17; the NICE Technical Support Document guidance is Phillippo et al. (2016).
The structural results of this chapter are new statements of the catalogue items M.1 to M.12, proved in the book’s notation. The single-arm conflation (Lemma 26.1) and the SPFA-as- absolute-constancy lemma (Lemma 26.2) make explicit why the unanchored design needs the stronger assumption; the identifiability theorems (Theorem 26.1, Theorem 26.2, Theorem 26.9) rest on the aggregate-monotonicity lemma Lemma 23.2 of Chapter 23 and an inverse-function-theorem argument for the relaxed model; the equivalence with unanchored STC (Theorem 26.8) specializes the marginal STC consistency of Chapter 19 (Theorem 19.3, Theorem 19.6) and the generality theorem of Chapter 23 (Theorem 23.4), and the strict-strengthening proposition (Proposition 26.1) makes precise the relationship to the shared-effect-modifier assumption (Definition 17.6). The survival development (Theorem 26.4, Theorem 26.7) builds entirely on the general-likelihood survival results of Chapter 25, the survival-hazard identity (Theorem 25.1), the conditional and marginal hazard ratios (Theorem 25.2, Theorem 25.3), the censored likelihood (Definition 25.4, Proposition 25.1), the integrated likelihoods (Theorem 25.5, Theorem 25.6), and the collapsible restricted mean survival time (Theorem 25.4); the scale-misalignment result Theorem 26.4(e) is the unanchored counterpart of the caveat flagged after Theorem 25.4. The Kaplan-Meier reconstruction (Theorem 26.5) is the exact-inversion form of the algorithm of Guyot and colleagues (Guyot et al. 2012), whose realistic version handles coarse at-risk tables and digitization error.
There is no machine-checked counterpart for this chapter. The companion Coq development (~/Documents/GitHub/ITC_Coq/theories/) does not formalize ML-UMR: there is no ML_UMR.v, and ML-NMR itself is unformalized for the reasons given in Chapter 25’s notes (the integration and survival content exceed the development’s analysis machinery). The algebraic core closest to formalization is the contrast-cancellation phenomenon of Proposition 26.1, which parallels the anchored cancellation in theories/EffectModifiers.v, and the STC reduction of Theorem 26.8, whose comparator- population identity is the unanchored reading of theories/STC.v’s STC_consistent and methods_agree_when_correct; but the unanchored setting requires absolute-effect transport rather than contrast transport, a different algebraic structure that is not currently mechanized. The proofs above are therefore pen-and-paper and self-contained. This chapter corresponds to results M.1 (the unanchored setting), M.2 (SPFA), M.3 (the SPFA model and identifiability), M.4 (the relaxed model), M.5 (QMC marginalization), M.6 (time-to-event), M.7 (pseudo-IPD reconstruction), M.8 (the joint likelihood), M.9 (target-population survival), M.10 (equivalence with unanchored STC), M.11 (SPFA versus SEMA), and M.12 (the identifiability frontier and limits) of the proof catalogue in proofs/M_ml_umr.md.

title: 26  Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression
text:
26.17 Exercises
Throughout, an exercise marked \(\star\) has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first three exercises are conceptual warm-ups that use the tables of this chapter and need no derivation; the remainder build the computations and proofs.

Exercise 26.1 (Warm-up: read the data picture.) A mock HTA dossier reports an index single-arm trial of drug \(A\) with patient-level age, biomarker status, and response; and for the comparator \(B\), only the overall response rate, the sample size, and the mean age and biomarker prevalence (no subgroup outcomes, no covariate correlation). Using Table 26.3, state for each of \(\alpha_A\), \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\), \(\alpha_B\), \(\boldsymbol\beta_B\), \(f_B\), and \(f_{*}\) whether this evidence identifies it, reconstructs it, or leaves it to assumption, and say whether a Type 1 or a Type 2 model is possible (Definition 26.3). What single additional item would the report need to make the relaxed model identifiable?


Exercise 26.2 (Interpretation: why SPFA cannot be tested.) In one short paragraph, explain to a clinical colleague why the Type 1 ML-UMR model cannot check SPFA from the two studies (cite Theorem 26.9), and why an anchored comparison can tolerate effect modification that an unanchored one cannot (cite Table 26.2). Then give one clinical scenario where SPFA is plausible and one where it is clearly false, and say which target-population estimate would be most, and which least, trustworthy in the false case (cite Step 6 of Section 26.15).


Exercise 26.3 (Interpretation: choose the method.) For each evidence set, decide whether to use anchored NMA or ML-NMR, Type 1 ML-UMR, Type 2 relaxed ML-UMR, or only unanchored STC, and justify in one sentence using Table 26.1: (a) two single-arm trials sharing no comparator, the comparator reporting only an overall response rate; (b) the same, but the comparator reports response rates in four biomarker-by-age cells; (c) an index and a comparator trial that each contain a common placebo arm; (d) an unanchored pair in which SPFA is clinically indefensible and only the comparator population matters for the decision.


Exercise 26.4 The conflation, concretely. In a single-arm index study with the logit link and no covariates, the model is \(\operatorname{logit}P(Y=1)=\mu+\gamma_A\). Show that the likelihood depends on \((\mu,\gamma_A)\) only through \(\alpha=\mu+\gamma_A\), that the maximum likelihood estimate of \(\alpha\) is \(\operatorname{logit}(\bar y)\) with \(\bar y\) the observed response proportion, and that \(\mu\) and \(\gamma_A\) are individually unidentified (Lemma 26.1). Explain in one sentence why an anchored two-arm study does not have this problem.


Exercise 26.5 (\(\star\)) Identifying the comparator intercept. With the logit link, SPFA slope \(\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}=0.8\), a single binary covariate with comparator prevalence \(\bar x_B=0.4\), and an observed comparator response proportion \(\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}=0.30\), write the two-point aggregation equation \(\Theta_B(\alpha_B)=0.30\) explicitly and solve it for \(\alpha_B\) to two decimal places by bracketing and linear interpolation (Theorem 26.1, Lemma 23.2). Then compute the comparator- population marginal response under arm \(B\) and verify it equals \(0.30\). Using an index fit \(\alpha_A=-0.2\), compute the conditional and the comparator-population marginal log odds ratios of \(A\) versus \(B\), and comment on the gap.


Exercise 26.6 Continuous outcomes need only the mean. For a continuous outcome with the identity link and the linear model \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid x]=\alpha_k+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\), prove that \(\alpha_B=\bar y_B-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_B^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\) exactly (using Theorem 20.3), so that ML-UMR for a continuous outcome under SPFA needs only the comparator covariate mean, not its full distribution. Deduce that for the identity link the target estimand \(\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}^{*})=\alpha_A-\alpha_B\) is the same in every target population, and explain why this collapsibility fails for the logit link.


Exercise 26.7 Counting subgroups. In the relaxed model with \(d=2\) continuous covariates, you have \(Z=3\) comparator subgroups. State whether \((\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\) is identified, citing the counting condition of Theorem 26.2, and describe a configuration of subgroup covariate means for which the non-degeneracy condition (full rank of the weighted-moment matrix \(M\)) holds and one for which it fails. What changes if a fourth subgroup is added?


Exercise 26.8 ML-UMR equals unanchored STC at the comparator. Using the calibration identity Theorem 26.8(1) and the marginal STC definition Definition 19.4, show by direct substitution that at \(\mathcal{P}^{*}=\mathcal{P}_B\) the SPFA ML-UMR estimand and the unanchored marginal STC estimator are the same expression Equation 26.22. Then exhibit, in one or two sentences, why STC cannot produce the estimand at a target \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\ne\mathcal{P}_B\) while ML-UMR can, and name the assumption that powers the difference.


Exercise 26.9 Time-varying marginal hazard ratio. In the exponential PH survival coda of Section 26.15 (\(h_k(t\mid x)=\lambda_k e^{\beta x}\), \(\beta=\log2\), \(\lambda_A=0.10\), \(\lambda_B=0.15\), \(P(X=1)=0.5\)), derive the closed form \(\bar h_k(t)=\lambda_k\frac{(1-\pi)+2\pi e^{-\lambda_k t}}{(1-\pi)+\pi e^{-\lambda_k t}}\) with \(\pi=0.5\) (using Lemma 25.1), and confirm by direct computation the marginal hazard ratios \(1.500\) at \(t=0\), \(1.398\) at \(t=10\), and the limit \(\lambda_B/\lambda_A\) as \(t\to\infty\). Explain in terms of survivor selection (Theorem 25.3) why the ratio dips below the conditional value for intermediate \(t\) and returns toward it as \(t\to\infty\).


Exercise 26.10 (\(\star\)) Collapsible but not transportable, unanchored. For the exponential PH model of the survival coda, write \(\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid x)=\frac{1-\exp(-\lambda_k e^{\beta x}\tau)}{\lambda_k e^{\beta x}}\) and hence the population RMST contrast \(\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AB}(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})\) as a two-point average over \(P(X=1)=\pi^{*}\). Prove that this contrast is collapsible within each population (Theorem 25.4) but differs between two populations with \(\pi^{*}=0.5\) and \(\pi^{*}=0.3\), and give the numerical difference at \(\tau=10\). Relate your finding to Theorem 26.4(e) and contrast it with the conditional log hazard ratio, which is the single number \(\log(\lambda_B/\lambda_A)\) in every population.


Exercise 26.11 Where the bias goes. Reproduce the SPFA-violation calculation of Step 6 of Section 26.15 with a weaker true comparator slope \(\beta_B^{\mathrm{true}}=1.5\) (instead of \(2.0\)): find the calibrated true intercept \(\alpha_B^{\mathrm{true}}\) from \(\Theta_B^{\mathrm{true}}(\alpha)=0.385\) at \(\bar x_B=0.5\), then compute the true and SPFA-estimated index-population (\(\bar x_A=0.3\)) marginal log odds ratios and the bias. Confirm that the comparator-population bias is zero and that the index-population bias is smaller in magnitude than the \(-0.18\) of the strong-violation case, illustrating Theorem 26.9 and the empirical pattern that bias grows with the strength of the violated modification.

Solutions to the starred exercises Exercise 26.5 and Exercise 26.10 appear in Appendix F.

title: 27  Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching
text:
27.1 Introduction
Consider a situation that arises constantly in oncology health technology assessment (HTA). A novel therapy, say a CAR-T cell product for relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma, is licensed on the strength of a single-arm Phase II trial: every enrolled patient received the new agent, so the trial carries no internal control against which a treatment effect could be measured. To report how the new agent compares with standard chemoimmunotherapy, the analyst must borrow a control arm from outside the trial, from one of several external Phase III trials or disease registries of the standard regimens. Those external studies do not contain the new agent, so there is no shared treatment to anchor the comparison, and they rarely release patient-level data; each publishes only a short table of baseline covariate means, mean age, proportion male, a mean severity marker, and little else. Which external study should supply the borrowed control arm? Choosing wrongly can reverse the sign of the reported effect and drive a reimbursement decision the wrong way, so the stakes are the whole submission. This chapter answers the prior question that every method of Parts IV and V silently assumed away: before adjusting for population differences, how do we choose the comparator study to adjust toward, using only the aggregate covariate summaries the external studies report? The workable answer, together with a sharp statement of what it can and cannot guarantee, is the subject of the chapter, and we will follow one running trial example (Example 27.1) from the first definition to the final caveat.
Every method in Parts IV and V began once a comparator had already been chosen. Matching-adjusted indirect comparison (Chapter 18), simulated treatment comparison (Chapter 19), multilevel network meta-regression (Chapter 20), and multilevel unanchored meta-regression (Chapter 26) all take as given a pair of studies, an index trial with individual patient data (IPD) and a designated comparator trial with aggregate data (AgD), and then do the work of bridging their populations. In a connected anchored network the comparator is not a choice at all: the common control treatment forces it, and the only question is how to adjust. But two situations strip away that luxury. A disconnected network offers several AgD studies, none sharing a common comparator with the index trial, any of which could in principle serve as the external arm for an unanchored comparison; the analyst must select one. A single-arm study, having no internal control, must borrow its entire comparator arm from an external population, and the choice of which external study to borrow is the whole analysis. This chapter is about that prior choice: how to pick a comparator study before the population-adjustment machinery is switched on.
The practical rule, described in the Bristol Compass blog on disconnected ML-NMR and implemented in the uitc diagnostic package (a full citation for both is forthcoming; see Section 27.12), is disarmingly simple. Each candidate comparator study reports a vector of covariate summaries, typically baseline means; the index population reports its own; choose the candidate whose summaries lie closest to the index population on some distance between summary vectors. The content of the rule is entirely in the word “closest,” because there is no single distance on \(\mathbb{R}^p\) and the candidates can be ranked differently by different choices. We develop the natural candidates: the Euclidean and standardized Euclidean distances (Definition 27.2), the Mahalanobis distance and its identification with a whitened Euclidean distance (Theorem 27.1), and the Manhattan, Minkowski, Gower, and mean-absolute standardized-mean-difference distances (Definition 27.4). We prove which of these are invariant to a change in the units of a covariate and which are not (Theorem 27.2, Proposition 27.2), because a distance whose ranking flips when age is recorded in months rather than years is a poor basis for a decision.
We then ask the only question that matters for validity: does a small covariate-summary distance bound the bias of the eventual adjusted estimate? The answer is a sharp dichotomy that this chapter proves in full. When the conditional contrast is affine in the covariates, the transport bias is exactly a linear functional of the covariate-mean gap, and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality turns any of the quadratic-form distances into a rigorous bias bound (Theorem 27.3), connecting comparator selection directly to the unanchored consistency theorem of Chapter 17 (Theorem 17.2). When the contrast is merely Lipschitz, a bias bound survives, but only against the Wasserstein distance between full distributions (Theorem 27.4), and a distance between means is provably not a Wasserstein distance: it is a lower bound on it, never an upper bound. The consequence, made precise in Proposition 27.4, is the central honest caveat of the chapter. Two populations can have identical covariate means, hence zero distance under every metric we define, and yet different target effects, because a nonlinear contrast sees the spread and not only the center, and because an unmeasured prognostic variable can differ while every observed summary agrees. Aggregate-level distance matching is therefore a diagnostic and design tool, not a transportability theorem: a small distance makes a population bridge more plausible and, under linearity, controls the residual bias, but it certifies neither the shared prognostic factor assumption (Definition 26.2) nor conditional constancy of absolute effects (Definition 17.5) nor the absence of unmeasured imbalance. A fully worked example ranking four candidate comparators under five criteria, in which the three principal distances each select a different winner and the actual bias is computed exactly, closes the development. This material is an extension beyond the population-adjustment theory of Phillippo (2019), prompted by the disconnected-network setting of Chandler and Ishak (2026a), and corresponds to results O.1 to O.7 of the proof catalogue.
Throughout, \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0\in\mathbb{R}^p\) denotes the covariate-summary vector of the index population (the population in which we hold IPD, or whose effect we wish to report), and \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_1,\dots,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_J\in\mathbb{R}^p\) the summary vectors of the \(J\) candidate comparator studies, following the study-mean notation \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j\) of Notation. We write \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_j=\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0\) for the covariate gap of candidate \(j\), \(\ell\in\{1,\dots,p\}\) for the covariate index, and \(\|\mathbf{v}\|_A=\sqrt{\mathbf{v}^\top
A\,\mathbf{v}}\) for the quadratic-form norm of a positive-definite \(A\). The bold vector \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\), a gap between covariate means, is a different object from the plain scalar \(\delta_{j,\,t_1 t_k}\) of Notation, which is a within-study treatment contrast; the boldface marks the vector throughout, following the vector-versus-scalar convention of the book, and the two never appear together. Read \(\|\mathbf{v}\|_A\) simply as “the length of \(\mathbf{v}\) measured with the ruler \(A\)”: when \(A=I\) it is the ordinary length, and a general \(A\succ0\) (read \(A\succ0\) as “\(A\) is symmetric positive definite,” so that \(\mathbf{v}^\top A\mathbf{v}>0\) for every \(\mathbf{v}\ne\mathbf 0\) and the square root is real) stretches some directions and shrinks others.
A reader who wants the destination before the journey can consult the map in Table 27.1. The single practical recommendation, defended in the sections that follow, is compressed into it: if you compute only one distance, compute the standardized Euclidean distance, and if the index study supplies a covariance matrix, add the Mahalanobis distance and treat any disagreement between the two as a signal that the ranking depends on covariate correlations rather than on the data.

title: 27  Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching
text:
27.2 The comparator-selection problem
We fix the decision the chapter addresses.

Definition 27.1 (Aggregate-level comparator selection) Let the index population have covariate-summary vector \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0\in\mathbb{R}^p\), and let candidate comparator studies \(j=1,\dots,J\) report covariate-summary vectors \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j\in\mathbb{R}^p\) on the same \(p\) covariates. Given a distance \(d:\mathbb{R}^p\times\mathbb{R}^p\to[0,\infty)\) on summary vectors, the aggregate-level matching rule selects \[
j^{*}\;\in\;\arg\min_{1\le j\le J}\; d\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j\big).
\tag{27.1}\] The selected study \(j^{*}\) is the observed comparator whose reported population summaries are closest to the index population on the chosen scale. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. Each candidate study is reduced to one number, its distance from the index population, and the rule picks the smallest. The only content is what “distance” means, because a candidate that looks closest under one sensible distance can look farthest under another. The rest of the chapter is a tour of the reasonable choices and a proof of exactly how much a small distance does, and does not, buy you. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

We anchor every definition to one small scenario, carried from here to the end of the chapter.

Example 27.1 (A running example: two candidate comparator trials) Return to the single-arm lymphoma trial of the introduction. The index study reports two baseline covariate means, mean age in years and a mean severity biomarker in its natural units, and two external Phase III trials, \(P\) and \(Q\), are candidate sources of the borrowed control arm. Their reported means are

The reference scales \(s=(10,4)\) are the index-study standard deviations of the two covariates. The index covariance, also from the index study, is \[
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}100 & 20\\ 20 & 16\end{pmatrix},
\] so age and biomarker are positively correlated, \(\operatorname{corr}=20/(10\cdot4)=0.5\). The covariate gaps and their standardized versions \(\mathbf{z}_j=(\delta_{j1}/s_1,\ \delta_{j2}/s_2)\) are \[
\boldsymbol{\delta}_P=(10,\ 4),\quad \mathbf{z}_P=(1.0,\ 1.0);
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\delta}_Q=(6,\ -4),\quad \mathbf{z}_Q=(0.6,\ -1.0).
\] In words: Study \(P\)’s patients are older and have a higher biomarker, both covariates up together, the direction in which age and biomarker naturally co-vary in the index trial. Study \(Q\)’s patients are somewhat older but have a lower biomarker, the two covariates moving in opposite directions, against the correlation. The central surprise of the chapter, foreshadowed here and computed in Section 27.4 and Section 27.5, is that raw and standardized Euclidean distance will both judge \(Q\) the closer match, while the Mahalanobis distance will judge \(P\) the closer match, purely because \(P\) respects the age-biomarker correlation and \(Q\) fights it. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The rule Equation 27.1 is a design rule: it ranks the candidates and names a winner, to be fed into an unanchored MAIC, STC, or ML-UMR. It is not yet a claim about validity. To see both what it can do and what it cannot, recall the two regimes that make it necessary.

Remark. Why selection is forced in disconnected and single-arm evidence. In the anchored triangle of Chapter 14 the index trial \(AC\) and the comparator trial \(BC\) share the control \(C\), and the Bucher contrast \(\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}\) differences the shared anchor away. A disconnected network has no such shared treatment between the index trial and the studies reporting the comparator of interest, so there is no anchor to difference and the comparison must be unanchored: the absolute outcome of the index treatment is compared to the absolute outcome of a comparator drawn from a different population (Chapter 17, Theorem 17.2; Chapter 26). When several AgD studies report that comparator, each defines a different bridging population, and the analyst must choose. A single-arm index study is the limiting case: lacking any internal control, its entire counterfactual arm is an external population, and selecting the most similar external study is the only lever available. In both regimes the choice precedes, and conditions the credibility of, the adjustment that follows. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. What a good choice buys, and what it does not. Unanchored population adjustment is consistent only when every imbalanced prognostic variable and effect modifier is measured and balanced and the target covariate values lie inside the index covariate support (Theorem 17.2, hypotheses (iii) and (iv)). Choosing a comparator with smaller covariate gaps makes both conditions easier to meet: a smaller gap means less reweighting, a higher effective sample size (Theorem 18.6), and a target nearer the interior of the support, so finite stable weights are more likely to exist. The distance is a proxy for “how hard the bridge will be.” It is not a proxy for “whether the bridge is valid,” because the unmeasured and the nonlinear escape it entirely; that gap is the subject of Section 27.9. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This setup corresponds to O.1 in the proof catalogue.

title: 27  Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching
section: 27.3 A practical workflow, and what selection is for
text:
27.3 A practical workflow, and what selection is for
Before any algebra, it helps to see where comparator selection sits in a real submission. Distance matching is one step of a longer pipeline, and it is neither the first step nor the last.

Fix the target. State the population in which the effect must be reported (here, the index single-arm trial’s population) and the estimand (for instance, a marginal log odds ratio versus standard of care). Everything downstream is measured against this target.
Assemble candidates. From a systematic review, list every external study that reports the comparator treatment and the baseline covariates you will need. These are the candidate comparators \(j=1,\dots,J\).
Screen for clinical and design comparability first. Before computing a single distance, discard candidates that differ in line of therapy, outcome definition, follow-up length, standard of care, eligibility, or measurement practice. Distance matching operates only among studies that already pass this clinical screen; a small covariate distance cannot rescue an incomparable trial.
Choose the covariate set. Include the effect modifiers and prognostic variables that are both clinically justified and reported across the surviving candidates, and record which important covariates are missing from which studies.
Harmonize and scale. Put every covariate on a common definition, choose reference scales, and compute several distances. Inspect which covariates drive each distance and estimate the effective sample size (ESS) the eventual reweighting would leave (Section 27.8, Theorem 18.6).
Carry uncertainty forward. Feed the chosen comparator into an unanchored MAIC, STC, or ML-UMR, and carry any disagreement between distances, any missing covariate, and any residual imbalance into a quantitative bias analysis (Chapter 28).

What could still go wrong?
quantitative bias analysis (Chapter 28)







Remark. Why a cheap pre-analysis screen, rather than adjusting on every candidate. A natural objection is: if there are four candidate comparators, why not simply run four unanchored MAICs and keep the one with the best effective sample size? Three reasons. First, an unanchored adjustment against a badly matched comparator can produce extreme weights, a tiny ESS, or an optimization that fails to converge at all, so the “try them all” strategy often has no clean output to compare. Second, choosing the comparator after seeing four different treatment estimates is selection on the outcome: it inflates the apparent effect and destroys any pre-registration guarantee. Third, distance matching is computed from published covariate tables alone, before the outcome is touched, so it is cheap, reproducible, and blind to the answer. It is a screen, run once, up front, on data an HTA reviewer can check. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Where entropy balancing and individual-level reweighting live. The word “matching” in this chapter’s title is aggregate-level: it matches summary vectors, not patients. The individual-level reweighting tools, the method-of-moments weights of MAIC (Chapter 18), and entropy balancing (Hainmueller’s minimum relative-entropy weights, derived in the individual-level setting), operate after a comparator has been chosen and require the index individual patient data; they solve a different problem, how to reweight patients so that a chosen comparator’s moments are met. This chapter is strictly the upstream, aggregate step that decides which comparator to reweight toward, using only the means each study publishes. If you were expecting entropy balancing here, it belongs to the individual-level material of Chapter 18; distance matching is the design step before it. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Choosing the covariates and the reference scales. Two applied choices decide what the distance measures.

Which covariates. Include a covariate only if it is a plausible effect modifier (Definition 11.3) or prognostic variable (Definition 11.5) and is reported by every surviving candidate. A covariate reported by some candidates but not others cannot enter a common distance; dropping a genuine effect modifier to keep a candidate in the running is a substantive decision to be recorded, not hidden. Do not pad the distance with many weakly prognostic covariates: each one dilutes the gaps that actually drive bias.
Which reference scale. When the index individual patient data are available, the index standard deviations are the natural reference scales, because the eventual reweighting is toward the index population. When no IPD are available, a pooled or comparator-reported standard deviation is used instead; for a binary covariate with prevalence \(\pi\), the Bernoulli standard deviation \(\sqrt{\pi(1-\pi)}\) is standard; a missing standard deviation is usually borrowed from a comparable covariate or a pooled value. Note the asymmetry proved later: re-expressing a covariate in different units does not change the standardized ranking (Theorem 27.2), but changing the reference scale while holding units fixed can change the winner (Exercise 27.3), so the reference-scale choice is a modeling decision that belongs in the write-up, not a harmless re-expression. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 27  Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching
text:
27.4 Euclidean and standardized Euclidean distances
The first candidate is the ordinary straight-line distance, and its first defect is that it depends on the units in which the covariates happen to be recorded.

Definition 27.2 (Euclidean and standardized Euclidean distance) The Euclidean distance between the index summary \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0\) and a candidate summary \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j\) is the \(\ell_2\) norm of their gap, \[
d_E\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j\big)\;=\;\big\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big\|_2
\;=\;\sqrt{\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\big(\bar{x}_{j\ell}-\bar{x}_{0\ell}\big)^2}.
\tag{27.2}\] Let \(s_1,\dots,s_p>0\) be reference scales, one per covariate, typically an IPD standard deviation, a reported comparator standard deviation, or, for a binary covariate with prevalence \(\pi\), the Bernoulli standard deviation \(\sqrt{\pi(1-\pi)}\). Writing \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\dots,s_p)\) and the standardized gap \(\mathbf{z}_j=S^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\), with components \(z_{j\ell}=(\bar{x}_{j\ell}-\bar{x}_{0\ell})/s_\ell\), the standardized Euclidean distance is \[
d_{SE}\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big)\;=\;\big\|\mathbf{z}_j\big\|_2
\;=\;\big\|S^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big\|_2
\;=\;\sqrt{\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\left(\frac{\bar{x}_{j\ell}-\bar{x}_{0\ell}}{s_\ell}\right)^2}.
\tag{27.3}\] \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why standardize. The raw distance Equation 27.2 adds squared gaps measured in incompatible units, so it is dominated by whichever covariate carries the largest numerical magnitude. A gap of one year in mean age and a gap of \(0.5\) in a proportion contribute \(1\) and \(0.25\) to the raw squared distance, yet the proportion gap is a far larger fraction of that covariate’s natural spread. Dividing each gap by a reference scale renders the contributions commensurate: each standardized component \(z_{j\ell}\) is the familiar standardized mean difference of that covariate, a dimensionless number measured in standard deviations. The uitc package defaults to \(d_{SE}\) for exactly this reason, reserving the raw \(d_E\) for covariates that are already on a common scale. The formal statement that standardization removes the unit dependence is Theorem 27.2 below. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. The running example, raw and standardized. Take the two candidate trials of Example 27.1. The raw Euclidean distances are \[
d_E(P)=\sqrt{10^2+4^2}=\sqrt{116}=10.77,
\qquad
d_E(Q)=\sqrt{6^2+(-4)^2}=\sqrt{52}=7.21,
\] and the standardized Euclidean distances, using the standardized gaps \(\mathbf{z}_P=(1.0,1.0)\) and \(\mathbf{z}_Q=(0.6,-1.0)\), are \[
d_{SE}(P)=\sqrt{1.0^2+1.0^2}=\sqrt2=1.414,
\qquad
d_{SE}(Q)=\sqrt{0.6^2+1.0^2}=\sqrt{1.36}=1.166 .
\] The standardized numbers read directly as “how many standard deviations apart”: Study \(P\) is exactly one standard deviation older and one higher on the biomarker; Study \(Q\) is \(0.6\) standard deviations older and one lower. Both the raw and the standardized distance rank \(Q\) ahead of \(P\). Hold on to that ranking: Section 27.5 overturns it once the age-biomarker correlation is taken into account. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 27  Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching
text:
27.5 The Mahalanobis distance and whitening
Standardization rescales each covariate but ignores their correlations. When the index IPD supplies a full covariance matrix, the Mahalanobis distance uses it, and the use turns out to be exactly a change of coordinates that decorrelates and standardizes the covariates simultaneously, an operation called whitening (the name borrows from signal processing: it turns a correlated covariate cloud into an uncorrelated, unit-variance cloud, like the flat spectrum of white noise). Before any formula, here is the picture to carry: the Mahalanobis distance asks whether the whole pattern of covariate differences looks unusual relative to the index trial’s covariate cloud. A gap that points along a direction in which the index patients naturally vary, or in which two covariates move together as they usually do, is unremarkable and counts for little; the same-sized gap in a direction the index patients rarely move, or against a correlation they usually respect, is surprising and counts for a lot.

Definition 27.3 (Mahalanobis distance) Let \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}\) be a positive-definite covariance matrix for the covariates, typically the index-IPD sample covariance. The Mahalanobis distance is the \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\)-quadratic-form norm of the gap, \[
d_M\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\big)
\;=\;\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\delta}_j^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j}
\;=\;\big\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}}.
\tag{27.4}\] \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. The Mahalanobis distance is the quadratic-form norm \(\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}}\) from the chapter opening: the length of the gap measured with the ruler \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\) in place of the identity (recall \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
\succ0\) means \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is symmetric positive definite, so \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\) exists and the square root is real). The ruler \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\) is large in directions where the index patients are tightly clustered and small in directions where they are widely spread, so it charges a heavy price for a gap along a low-variance direction and a light price for a gap along a high-variance one. When the covariates are uncorrelated and on equal footing, \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=I\), the ruler is the identity and \(d_M\) is the ordinary Euclidean distance. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The defining identity is that this distance is an ordinary Euclidean distance after a linear transform that “whitens” the covariates, that is, makes their covariance the identity. We prove it for any matrix square root, then specialize to the two used in practice.

Theorem 27.1 (Whitening equivalence of the Mahalanobis distance) Let \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ 0\) and let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}\) be any invertible matrix with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=BB^\top\) (such a \(B\) exists by Theorem 4.9). Then the Mahalanobis distance is the Euclidean norm of the whitened gap \(B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\): \[
d_M\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\big)
\;=\;\big\|B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big\|_2 .
\tag{27.5}\] In particular this holds for the lower-triangular Cholesky factor \(B=L\) with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=LL^\top\), and for the symmetric positive-definite square root \(B=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\) of Theorem 4.9. Moreover:

If \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\operatorname{diag}(s_1^2,\dots,s_p^2)\) is diagonal, then \(d_M\) reduces to the standardized Euclidean distance \(d_{SE}\) with reference scales \(s_\ell\).
The whitened covariates \(\mathbf{u}_j=B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\) have, under the model in which \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is the true covariance, identity covariance: \(\operatorname{Cov}(B^{-1}\mathbf{X})=
B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{-\top}=I_p\).



Proof. That a factorization \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=BB^\top\) with invertible \(B\) exists is part of Theorem 4.9: since \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ0\) is symmetric, the spectral theorem writes \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=Q\Lambda
Q^\top\) with \(Q\) orthogonal (\(Q^\top Q=I\)) and \(\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_p)\), and positive-definiteness forces every eigenvalue \(\lambda_i>0\); the spectral construction there produces the symmetric square root \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}=Q\operatorname{diag}
(\sqrt{\lambda_1},\dots,\sqrt{\lambda_p})Q^\top\), which is invertible because every \(\lambda_i>0\) and satisfies \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\); taking \(B=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\) (symmetric, so \(B=B^\top\) and \(BB^\top=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\)) gives one such \(B\), and the Cholesky factor gives another.
For any invertible \(B\) with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=BB^\top\), taking inverses and using \((BB^\top)^{-1}=B^{-\top}B^{-1}\), \[
\boldsymbol{\delta}_j^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j
=\boldsymbol{\delta}_j^\top B^{-\top}B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j
=\big(B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big)^\top\big(B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big)
=\big\|B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big\|_2^2 .
\] Taking nonnegative square roots gives Equation 27.5. For part 1, if \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\operatorname{diag}(s_1^2,\dots,s_p^2)\) then \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(s_1^{-2},\dots,s_p^{-2})\) and \[
\boldsymbol{\delta}_j^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j
=\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\frac{\delta_{j\ell}^2}{s_\ell^2}
=\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\left(\frac{\bar{x}_{j\ell}-\bar{x}_{0\ell}}{s_\ell}\right)^2
=d_{SE}\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big)^2 ,
\] which is Equation 27.3. For part 2, the covariance of a linear map is \(\operatorname{Cov}(B^{-1}\mathbf{X})=B^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{X})B^{-\top}
=B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{-\top}=B^{-1}(BB^\top)B^{-\top}=I_p\). \(\square\)


Remark. The running example, and the promised reversal. Return to Example 27.1, with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}100&20\\20&16\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]\). Its inverse is \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}=\tfrac{1}{1200}\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}16&-20\\-20&100\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]\), so the Mahalanobis quadratic form is \(d_M^2=\tfrac{1}{75}\delta_1^2+\tfrac{1}{12}\delta_2^2
-\tfrac{1}{30}\delta_1\delta_2\). Evaluating on the two gaps \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_P=(10,4)\) and \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_Q=(6,-4)\), \[
d_M(P)=\sqrt{\tfrac{100}{75}+\tfrac{16}{12}-\tfrac{40}{30}}=\sqrt{1.333}=1.155,
\qquad
d_M(Q)=\sqrt{\tfrac{36}{75}+\tfrac{16}{12}+\tfrac{24}{30}}=\sqrt{2.613}=1.617 .
\] Now the Mahalanobis distance ranks \(P\) ahead of \(Q\), the exact reverse of the raw and standardized verdict. The reason is visible in the cross term. Study \(P\) moved age and biomarker up together, the direction the index correlation \(\operatorname{corr}=0.5\) expects, so its cross term is negative (\(-\tfrac{40}{30}\)) and cancels much of the distance: a concordant move is cheap. Study \(Q\) moved them in opposite directions, against the correlation, so its cross term is positive (\(+\tfrac{24}{30}\)) and adds to the distance: a discordant move is expensive. The standardized distance, blind to the correlation, saw only that \(Q\)’s total standardized magnitude (\(\sqrt{1.36}\)) is smaller than \(P\)’s (\(\sqrt2\)) and called \(Q\) closer; the Mahalanobis distance sees that \(Q\)’s direction is the improbable one and calls \(P\) closer. Which verdict should drive the decision is exactly the question Section 27.8 settles, and the answer is “it depends on the unknown contrast.” \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Mahalanobis is Euclidean in the right coordinates. Equation Equation 27.5 says the Mahalanobis distance measures the gap in coordinates where the covariate cloud has been sphered to an isotropic unit ball. A direction in which the covariates are highly variable, or two covariates that move together, are “cheap” to differ in, because such differences are expected under \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\); a direction of low variance, or a discordant move against a strong correlation, is “expensive.” Part 1 shows that standardized Euclidean distance is the special case that keeps the variances but discards the correlations, that is, it whitens with the diagonal of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). The worked example of Section 27.10 exhibits a candidate that standardized Euclidean distance and Mahalanobis distance rank oppositely for exactly this reason. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. The Mahalanobis distance is a genuine metric. By Equation 27.5, \(d_M(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=
\|B^{-1}(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\|_2\) is the Euclidean metric composed with the invertible linear map \(B^{-1}\); the symmetry, triangle inequality, and positive-definiteness of \(d_M\) are inherited from those of \(\|\cdot\|_2\) because \(B^{-1}\) is injective. The same argument makes \(d_{SE}\) a metric. This is recorded as part of Proposition 27.1. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 27  Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching
text:
27.6 Further distances
The uitc toolkit offers several alternatives to the \(\ell_2\) family, each answering a slightly different question about the covariate gap. A reader in a hurry can treat this section as reference material: the standardized Euclidean and Mahalanobis distances of the previous two sections are the workhorses, and the variants here earn their place only when a specific question makes one of them apt (the single worst-matched covariate, or mixed continuous and binary covariate types). Skip to Section 27.7 on a first reading and return when a variant is needed.

Definition 27.4 (Manhattan, Minkowski, mean-SMD, and Gower distances) With standardized gap components \(z_{j\ell}=(\bar{x}_{j\ell}-\bar{x}_{0\ell})/s_\ell\) as in Definition 27.2, define:
The Manhattan (or \(\ell_1\)) distance, the sum of absolute standardized gaps, \[
d_1\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\big|z_{j\ell}\big|.
\tag{27.6}\]
The Minkowski distance of order \(q\ge 1\), which interpolates between them, \[
d_q\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big)
=\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\big|z_{j\ell}\big|^{q}\right)^{1/q},
\qquad
d_\infty=\max_{1\le\ell\le p}\big|z_{j\ell}\big| ,
\tag{27.7}\] with \(q=1\) the Manhattan distance, \(q=2\) the standardized Euclidean distance, and the limit \(q\to\infty\) the Chebyshev distance, the largest single standardized gap.
The mean absolute standardized mean difference (mean-SMD), the Manhattan distance averaged over covariates, \[
d_{\mathrm{SMD}}\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big)
=\frac1p\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\big|z_{j\ell}\big|
=\frac1p\,d_1\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big).
\tag{27.8}\]
The Gower distance, for mixed continuous and binary covariates, with a positive range \(r_\ell\) for each continuous covariate and binary covariates coded in \([0,1]\), \[
d_G\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j\big)=\frac1p\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}g_{j\ell},
\qquad
g_{j\ell}=\begin{cases}
\min\!\big\{\,|\bar{x}_{j\ell}-\bar{x}_{0\ell}|/r_\ell,\ 1\,\big\}, & \ell\text{ continuous},\\[2pt]
|\bar{x}_{j\ell}-\bar{x}_{0\ell}|, & \ell\text{ binary}.
\end{cases}
\tag{27.9}\] \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. What each variant emphasizes, and what is excluded. Raising the order \(q\) concentrates attention on the single worst-matched covariate: \(d_\infty\) ignores all but the maximal standardized gap, so a candidate with one badly mismatched covariate is penalized regardless of how well the rest agree, whereas \(d_1\) trades off freely across covariates. The mean-SMD rescales \(d_1\) to the per-covariate average, which makes it directly comparable across analyses with different numbers of covariates and ties the diagnostic to the standardized-mean-difference balance tables of the propensity-score literature, where a common rule of thumb flags any \(|z_{j\ell}|>0.1\) as imbalance. The Gower distance handles continuous and binary covariates on one footing by range-scaling and truncating the continuous gaps. The uitc toolkit deliberately omits cosine, Hamming, Jaccard, Sorensen-Dice, and Haversine distances for this task: those measure angular similarity, binary-set overlap, or geographic separation, none of which is the right notion for a gap between continuous covariate means. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. A tiny Gower calculation. Suppose a candidate is summarized by one continuous covariate, mean age, and one binary covariate, proportion male. Let the pooled ages run from \(40\) to \(80\), so the age range is \(r_{\text{age}}=40\), and let the index means be age \(60\) and proportion male \(0.5\). A candidate reporting mean age \(68\) and proportion male \(0.7\) has \[
g_{\text{age}}=\min\!\Big\{\tfrac{|68-60|}{40},\,1\Big\}=\min\{0.2,\,1\}=0.2,
\qquad
g_{\text{male}}=|0.7-0.5|=0.2,
\] and Gower distance \(d_G=\tfrac12(0.2+0.2)=0.2\). The range division puts the \(8\)-year age gap on the same \([0,1]\) footing as the \(0.2\) difference in a proportion, and the truncation at \(1\) means that even a wildly out-of-range age gap (say a candidate with mean age \(120\), giving \(|120-60|/40=1.5\), capped to \(1\)) counts no more than a complete binary disagreement. This is why Gower is the natural choice when continuous and binary covariates must be compared together. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

For these to support a coherent “closest” in Definition 27.1, they should at least be genuine distances. We record which are, and where the metric axioms can fail.

Proposition 27.1 (Metric properties of the covariate-summary distances) Fix the reference scales \(s_\ell>0\), the covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ0\), and the Gower ranges \(r_\ell>0\). Then:

The standardized Euclidean distance \(d_{SE}\) and the Mahalanobis distance \(d_M\) are metrics on \(\mathbb{R}^p\).
For every \(q\in[1,\infty]\) the Minkowski distance \(d_q\) is a metric on \(\mathbb{R}^p\); the mean-SMD \(d_{\mathrm{SMD}}=d_1/p\) is a metric. For \(0<q<1\) the function in Equation 27.7 is not a metric: it violates the triangle inequality.
The Gower distance \(d_G\) is a metric on the product covariate space.



Proof. Part 1. By Definition 27.2 and Theorem 27.1, \(d_{SE}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=
\|S^{-1}(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\|_2\) and \(d_M(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=\|B^{-1}(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\|_2\) with \(S^{-1}\) and \(B^{-1}\) invertible. For any invertible linear map \(T\), the function \(N(\mathbf{v})=\|T\mathbf{v}\|_2\) is a norm: it is absolutely homogeneous and satisfies the triangle inequality because \(\|\cdot\|_2\) does and \(T\) is linear, and \(N(\mathbf{v})=0\) forces \(T\mathbf{v}=0\), hence \(\mathbf{v}=0\) by injectivity of \(T\). A norm of a difference is a metric, giving part 1.
Part 2. For \(q\in[1,\infty]\) the map \(\mathbf{v}\mapsto\|\mathbf{v}\|_q\) is the \(\ell_q\) norm, and \(d_q(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=\|S^{-1}(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\|_q\) is the corresponding metric; the only nontrivial axiom is the triangle inequality, which is Minkowski’s inequality \(\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}\|_q\le\|\mathbf{u}\|_q+\|\mathbf{w}\|_q\). We verify the three orders this book uses directly. For \(q=1\) it is the triangle inequality for \(|\cdot|\) summed over coordinates; for \(q=\infty\) it is \(\max_\ell|u_\ell+w_\ell|\le\max_\ell(|u_\ell|+|w_\ell|)\le\max_\ell|u_\ell|+
\max_\ell|w_\ell|\); for \(q=2\) it follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, since \(\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}\|_2^2=\|\mathbf{u}\|_2^2+2\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{w}+\|\mathbf{w}\|_2^2
\le\|\mathbf{u}\|_2^2+2\|\mathbf{u}\|_2\|\mathbf{w}\|_2+\|\mathbf{w}\|_2^2
=(\|\mathbf{u}\|_2+\|\mathbf{w}\|_2)^2\). For general \(q\in[1,\infty)\) the inequality is the named Minkowski inequality, which we cite here; its derivation from Hölder’s inequality is exactly the content of Exercise 27.5, so the single case not verified in the display above is signposted to a worked exercise rather than left as a gap. Since \(d_{\mathrm{SMD}}=d_1/p\) is a positive scalar multiple of a metric, it is a metric.
For \(0<q<1\) the triangle inequality fails. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) take \(\mathbf{a}=(0,0)\), \(\mathbf{b}=(1,0)\), \(\mathbf{c}=(1,1)\) with unit reference scales. Then \(d_q(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c})=(1+1)^{1/q}=2^{1/q}\) while \(d_q(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})+d_q(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c})=1+1=2\); since \(1/q>1\) we have \(2^{1/q}>2\), so the direct distance exceeds the detour and the triangle inequality is violated.
Part 3. For a continuous coordinate, \(\rho_\ell(a,b)=|a-b|/r_\ell\) is a metric on \(\mathbb{R}\), and we claim its truncation \(\min\{\rho_\ell,1\}\) is again a metric. Symmetry and positive-definiteness are immediate; for the triangle inequality, given points \(a,b,c\), if either of \(\min\{\rho_\ell(a,b),1\}\) or \(\min\{\rho_\ell(b,c),1\}\) equals \(1\) then the right-hand side is at least \(1\ge\min\{\rho_\ell(a,c),1\}\), and otherwise both are below \(1\), so \(\rho_\ell(a,b),\rho_\ell(b,c)<1\) and \(\min\{\rho_\ell(a,c),1\}\le\rho_\ell(a,c)\le\rho_\ell(a,b)+\rho_\ell(b,c)
=\min\{\rho_\ell(a,b),1\}+\min\{\rho_\ell(b,c),1\}\). Thus each \(g_\ell\) is a per-coordinate metric (the binary case \(|a-b|\) on \([0,1]\) being a metric outright). A nonnegative weighted sum of metrics composed with coordinate projections is a pseudometric on the product, and it separates points here because each \(g_\ell(a_\ell,b_\ell)=0\) forces \(a_\ell=b_\ell\); therefore \(d_G=\frac1p\sum_\ell g_\ell\) is a metric. \(\square\)

title: 27  Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching
text:
27.7 Scale dependence and scale invariance
A change in the unit of a covariate, age in months rather than years, weight in pounds rather than kilograms, is a coordinate map \(\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}\) with \(A=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_p)\) and \(a_\ell>0\). A distance fit to drive a decision should not let such a relabeling change the decision. The standardized and Mahalanobis families pass this test; the raw Euclidean distance fails it, and fails it badly enough to reverse the ranking of candidates.
Here is the concrete picture behind the formal statement. Record age in months instead of years and you multiply every age by \(12\); but the standard deviation of age is also multiplied by \(12\), so the standardized age gap, the gap divided by that standard deviation, is unchanged, because the factor of \(12\) cancels in the ratio. Re-expressing the same data in different units therefore cannot move a standardized distance. That is all “coherent rescaling” means in the theorem below: the covariate and every auxiliary input tied to its units (its reference scale, its Gower range, its row and column of the covariance matrix) are re-expressed together, exactly as they would be in any honest re-recording of the data. The practical stake is a regulatory one. A reviewer who asks “would your comparator choice have changed if the sponsor had reported age in months rather than years?” is asking precisely whether the chosen distance is scale-invariant, and the next theorem lets you answer “no, it could not have” for the standardized and Mahalanobis families, while Proposition 27.2 shows you would have to answer “yes, possibly” for the raw Euclidean distance.

Theorem 27.2 (Scale invariance of standardized and Mahalanobis distances) Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_p)\) with every \(a_\ell>0\), and apply the coherent rescaling that maps every summary vector \(\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}\) and rescales the auxiliary inputs in step: the reference scales \(s_\ell\mapsto a_\ell s_\ell\) (so \(S\mapsto AS\)), the Gower ranges \(r_\ell\mapsto
a_\ell r_\ell\), and the Mahalanobis covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mapsto A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A\). Then the standardized Euclidean distance \(d_{SE}\), the Manhattan, Minkowski, and Chebyshev distances \(d_q\) (\(q\in[1,\infty]\)), the mean-SMD \(d_{\mathrm{SMD}}\), the Gower distance \(d_G\), and the Mahalanobis distance \(d_M\) are all unchanged. Moreover the Mahalanobis distance is invariant under any invertible affine reparameterization \(\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{c}\) with \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}\) invertible, not only diagonal \(A\), provided \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mapsto A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A^\top\).


Proof. Under the coherent rescaling the standardized components are unchanged coordinatewise: the rescaled gap is \(A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0=A\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\) with \(\ell\)-th entry \(a_\ell\delta_{j\ell}\), and dividing by the rescaled reference scale \(a_\ell s_\ell\) gives \[
\frac{a_\ell\,\delta_{j\ell}}{a_\ell s_\ell}=\frac{\delta_{j\ell}}{s_\ell}=z_{j\ell}.
\] Every distance built from the standardized vector \(\mathbf{z}_j\) alone, namely \(d_{SE}=\|\mathbf{z}_j\|_2\), \(d_q=\|\mathbf{z}_j\|_q\) for \(q\in[1,\infty]\), and \(d_{\mathrm{SMD}}=\|\mathbf{z}_j\|_1/p\), is therefore a function of unchanged quantities and is unchanged. For the Gower distance the continuous terms are \(\min\{a_\ell|\delta_{j\ell}|/(a_\ell r_\ell),1\}=\min\{|\delta_{j\ell}|/r_\ell,1\}\), unchanged, and the binary terms involve no continuous unit, so \(d_G\) is unchanged.
For the Mahalanobis distance, take the general invertible affine map \(\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}+
\mathbf{c}\); the constant \(\mathbf{c}\) cancels in the gap, which becomes \(A\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\), and the covariance becomes \(A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A^\top\). Using \((A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A^\top)^{-1}=
A^{-\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}A^{-1}\), \[
\big(A\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big)^\top\big(A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A^\top\big)^{-1}\big(A\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big)
=\boldsymbol{\delta}_j^\top A^\top A^{-\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}A^{-1}A\,\boldsymbol{\delta}_j
=\boldsymbol{\delta}_j^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j ,
\] so \(d_M\) is unchanged. The diagonal coherent rescaling is the special case \(A=\operatorname{diag}(a_\ell)\), for which \(A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A=A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A^\top\). \(\square\)

The raw Euclidean distance enjoys none of this. It is not merely rescaled by a unit change; the rescaling reweights the covariates unequally and can overturn which candidate is judged closest.

Proposition 27.2 (Raw Euclidean distance is scale-dependent and can reverse rankings) Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_p)\) with \(a_\ell>0\). In general \(d_E(A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j)\ne d_E(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j)\), because \[
d_E\big(A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j\big)^2=\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}a_\ell^2\,\delta_{j\ell}^2 ,
\tag{27.10}\] a reweighting of the squared gaps by \(a_\ell^2\). There exist two candidates whose raw-Euclidean ranking is reversed by a change of units in a single covariate.


Proof. Equation Equation 27.10 is immediate from \(A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0=
A\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\) and the diagonal form of \(A\). For the reversal, take \(p=2\) and two candidates with gaps \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_1=(1,2)\) and \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_2=(2,1)\). With unit scaling both have squared distance \(1^2+2^2=2^2+1^2=5\), so they tie. Rescale the first coordinate by \(a_1=10\) and keep \(a_2=1\). Then \[
d_E(A\boldsymbol{\delta}_1)^2=10^2\cdot1+1\cdot4=104,
\qquad
d_E(A\boldsymbol{\delta}_2)^2=10^2\cdot4+1\cdot1=401 ,
\] so candidate \(1\) is now strictly closer than candidate \(2\), whereas before they were equidistant; a unit change has manufactured a strict preference. Perturbing \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_1\) to \((1,2+\varepsilon)\) for small \(\varepsilon>0\) makes candidate \(2\) strictly closer under unit scaling (\(5<5+4\varepsilon+
\varepsilon^2\)) while candidate \(1\) remains strictly closer after the rescaling, an outright reversal of the strict ranking. \(\square\)


Remark. The decision-theoretic moral. Because the comparator-selection rule Equation 27.1 returns an \(\arg\min\), only the ranking of candidates matters, and Proposition 27.2 shows the raw Euclidean ranking is an artifact of the recording units. Standardized Euclidean and Mahalanobis distances are immune (Theorem 27.2), which is why uitc recommends them whenever covariates carry mixed units. The worked example of Section 27.10 exhibits a concrete reversal: raw Euclidean distance there selects the candidate with the largest eventual bias, precisely because it is dominated by a large-unit covariate. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 27  Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching
text:
27.8 Bias bounds from covariate-summary distance
A distance is worth minimizing only if minimizing it reduces the bias of the eventual estimate. We now prove exactly when it does. Throughout this section we work under conditional constancy, so that the conditional contrast (or, in the unanchored case, each conditional mean) is the same function of the covariates in the index and comparator populations; the only cross-population difference is the covariate distribution. The quantity of interest is the transport bias \[
B_j\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}\big[\tau(\mathbf{X})\big]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}\big[\tau(\mathbf{X})\big],
\tag{27.11}\] the difference between the marginal effect over the comparator population \(\mathcal{P}_j\) and the marginal effect over the index population \(\mathcal{P}_0\), where \(\tau\) is the shared conditional contrast. Under conditional constancy this \(B_j\) is the residual bias incurred by treating comparator \(j\)’s population as a stand-in for the index population, or equivalently the bias that remains if the covariate gap \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\) is left unadjusted; it is the population-level quantity that the unanchored consistency theorem (Theorem 17.2) requires to vanish.

Remark. Reader translation of the two working assumptions. Two phrases carry this whole section. Conditional constancy (Definition 17.5) means the conditional contrast \(\tau(\mathbf{x})\), the treatment effect among patients whose covariates equal \(\mathbf{x}\), is the same function of \(\mathbf{x}\) in the index and comparator populations; what differs between the populations is only how many patients sit at each value of \(\mathbf{x}\). If that holds, the sole thing a comparator’s population changes is the covariate mix, so any transport bias is due entirely to the covariate gap. Transport bias \(B_j\) is then just the difference between the average effect you would report over the comparator’s patient mix and the average effect over the index patient mix: it is what you get wrong by handing an estimand defined for the index population to a population with a different covariate distribution. A small covariate distance is our attempt to keep that difference small; the rest of the section is about when it succeeds. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


27.8.1 The linear case: an exact Cauchy-Schwarz bound
When the contrast is affine, the bias is a linear functional of the covariate-mean gap, and the quadratic-form distances bound it sharply.
What does “affine contrast” mean for a real outcome, and when is it plausible? Fit an outcome model on the link scale, the logit (log-odds) scale for a binary response, the log scale for a hazard, with a linear predictor of the Chapter 20 form \(\eta=\mu+\boldsymbol{\beta}_1^\top\mathbf{x}+(\gamma+\boldsymbol{\beta}_2
^\top\mathbf{x})\,T\), where \(T\) is the treatment indicator. The conditional contrast on that scale, the treatment effect at covariate value \(\mathbf{x}\), is \[
\tau(\mathbf{x})=\eta\big|_{T=1}-\eta\big|_{T=0}=\gamma+\boldsymbol{\beta}_2^\top\mathbf{x},
\] which is affine in \(\mathbf{x}\) with intercept \(\alpha=\gamma\) and slope vector \(\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{\beta}_2\). So in the theorem below \(\alpha\) is the treatment effect at \(\mathbf{x}=\mathbf 0\) and \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is the vector of effect-modifier slopes: each \(\beta_\ell\) says how much the treatment’s effect on the link scale changes per unit of covariate \(\ell\). The affine case is therefore exactly “a linear outcome model on the link scale whose treatment effect is modified linearly by the covariates, with no covariate-by-covariate or higher-order terms.” It is a reasonable working hypothesis when effect modification is mild and roughly linear, and it is the sensitivity input under which comparator distance provably bounds bias. Two poles are worth noting: if \(\boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf 0\) there is no effect modification and the transport bias is zero for any covariate gap; the entire difficulty lives in the direction of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\ne\mathbf 0\), which is why the theorem’s bound pairs the gap with \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\).

Theorem 27.3 (Linear bias bound) Suppose the shared conditional contrast is affine in the covariates, \(\tau(\mathbf{x})=\alpha+\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\mathbf{x}\). Then the transport bias Equation 27.11 is the linear functional of the covariate-mean gap \[
B_j=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}_j
=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0\big),
\tag{27.12}\] and it is bounded by either quadratic-form distance:

with \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\dots,s_p)\), \[
|B_j|\;\le\;\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2\;\cdot\;d_{SE}\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big),
\tag{27.13}\] with equality if and only if the standardized gap \(\mathbf{z}_j=S^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\) is parallel to \(S\boldsymbol{\beta}\);
with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ0\), \[
|B_j|\;\le\;\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}}\;\cdot\;
d_M\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\big)
=\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\cdot\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}},
\tag{27.14}\] with equality if and only if \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\) is parallel to \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}\).



Proof. The intercept \(\alpha\) cancels in the difference Equation 27.11, leaving \(B_j=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[\mathbf{X}]-\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}[\mathbf{X}]=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0)
=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\), which is Equation 27.12.
Bound 1. Insert \(S^{-1}S=I\): \(B_j=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top S S^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j=
(S\boldsymbol{\beta})^\top\mathbf{z}_j\). By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in \(\mathbb{R}^p\), \[
|B_j|=\big|(S\boldsymbol{\beta})^\top\mathbf{z}_j\big|
\le\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2\,\|\mathbf{z}_j\|_2
=\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2\,d_{SE}\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big),
\] which is Equation 27.13. Cauchy-Schwarz holds with equality if and only if the two vectors are linearly dependent, that is, \(\mathbf{z}_j\parallel S\boldsymbol{\beta}\).
Bound 2. Write \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\) with the symmetric square root of Theorem 4.9 and insert \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}=I\): \[
B_j=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}_j
=\big(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\beta}\big)^\top
\big(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big).
\] By Cauchy-Schwarz, \[
|B_j|\le\big\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\beta}\big\|_2
\big\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big\|_2
=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}}\,
\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\delta}_j^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j}
=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}}\;
d_M\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\big),
\] which is Equation 27.14, using Equation 27.4 for the last factor. Equality holds if and only if \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\parallel\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}
\boldsymbol{\beta}\); applying the invertible map \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\) to both sides, this is \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\parallel\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}\). \(\square\)


Remark. Reading the bounds. Both bounds factor the bias into a fixed coefficient magnitude, \(\|S
\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2\) or \(\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\), which does not depend on the candidate, times a distance, which does. Because the coefficient factor is common to all candidates, each distance ranks the candidates exactly by its own bound on \(|B_j|\): selecting the \(d_{SE}\)-minimizer minimizes the standardized bound, and selecting the \(d_M\)-minimizer minimizes the Mahalanobis bound. The two bounds need not agree on the winner, because \(\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2\,d_{SE}\) and \(\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\,d_M\) are different upper bounds on the same \(|B_j|\); the equality conditions say each bound is tight for the candidate whose gap aligns with the coefficient vector in the relevant geometry. This is not a defect but the precise sense in which the right distance is the one matched to the unknown contrast direction \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\), a point the worked example makes concrete and the caveat of Section 27.9 makes unavoidable. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Connection to unanchored consistency. The transport bias Equation 27.11 is the population-level obstacle in the unanchored PAIC theorem Theorem 17.2. That theorem recovers the target estimand only when every imbalanced effect modifier and prognostic variable is balanced, so that no residual covariate gap survives; its necessity clause exhibits the bias as an integral that is nonzero exactly when an imbalanced covariate is omitted. Under the affine specialization \(\tau(\mathbf{x})=\alpha+\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\mathbf{x}\), which is hypothesis (v) “sufficiency of the matched moments” of Theorem 18.4 and the affine-\(\mu_t\) hypothesis of Theorem 17.2, that integral collapses to the inner product Equation 27.12, and Theorem 27.3 bounds it by the covariate-summary distance. Comparator selection therefore bounds the very bias the consistency theorem assumes away: a smaller distance means a smaller worst-case residual bias, under linearity. The qualifier “under linearity” is essential, and Section 27.8.2 and Section 27.9 show what happens without it. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. The running example: exact bias and the two bounds. Suppose, as a sensitivity input, the effect-modifier slopes are \(\boldsymbol{\beta}=(0.1,\,0.5)\), that is, the treatment’s effect on the link scale rises by \(0.1\) per year of age and by \(0.5\) per biomarker unit. Then the exact transport biases of Example 27.1 are \[
B_P=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}_P=0.1(10)+0.5(4)=3.0,
\qquad
B_Q=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}_Q=0.1(6)+0.5(-4)=-1.4 .
\] The standardized Cauchy-Schwarz bound uses \(S\boldsymbol{\beta}=(1,2)\), so \(\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2=\sqrt5=2.236\), giving \(|B_P|\le 2.236(1.414)=3.16\) and \(|B_Q|\le2.236(1.166)=2.61\); the Mahalanobis bound uses \(\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\sqrt7=2.646\), giving \(|B_P|\le2.646(1.155)=3.06\) and \(|B_Q|\le2.646(1.617)=4.28\). Both bounds dominate the exact biases, as they must. Now the honest lesson: the standardized winner \(Q\) has the smaller true bias (\(1.4\) against \(3.0\)), while the Mahalanobis winner \(P\) has the larger true bias, so for this particular \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) the standardized distance was the faithful ranker and Mahalanobis was misled. Had \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) pointed along the high-variance, positively-correlated axis of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), the verdict would flip and Mahalanobis would be faithful. Since \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is unknown when the comparator is chosen, no distance is guaranteed to rank by bias; this is exactly Proposition 27.4, previewed here in arithmetic. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Bias against variance: the effective-sample-size tradeoff. A closer comparator is not automatically the better analysis, because comparator selection trades bias against variance, and the mean distance governs both. Under the linear bound, the mean distance caps the bias; and the same distance also controls the variance, because the subsequent unanchored MAIC reweights the index sample (size \(n\)) to match the comparator’s means, and a larger standardized gap forces more extreme weights and hence a smaller effective sample size \(\mathrm{ESS}=(\sum_i w_i)^2/\sum_i w_i^2\) (Theorem 18.6), inflating the variance by the factor \(n/\mathrm{ESS}\). The schematic pattern, for an index study of \(n=200\), is



Table 27.3: How the mean distance drives the effective sample size after reweighting. The \(\mathrm{ESS}\) column is illustrative: the true value depends on the index individual patient data, not on the means alone.
