Two consequences. First, in the linear case there is usually no dramatic conflict: the minimum-distance candidate tends to minimize both the bias bound and the reweighting variance at once. The genuine tension appears among candidates of comparable distance, where one breaks the tie by projected \(\mathrm{ESS}\), and in the fact that a far comparator’s variance can explode (bottom row) faster than a nearer comparator’s bias bound grows, so a mean-squared-error view, \(\mathrm{MSE}\approx \text{bias}^2+\text{variance}\), can prefer a slightly closer, higher-\(\mathrm{ESS}\) candidate even when its bias bound is not the smallest. Second, and more important, the distance bounds bias only under linearity; a close, high-\(\mathrm{ESS}\) comparator can still be badly biased through nonlinearity or unmeasured imbalance (Section 27.9). The defensible practice is to report distance and projected \(\mathrm{ESS}\) together and to choose on the mean-squared-error picture, not on distance alone. This trade-off is developed as Exercise 27.9 and connects to the simulation estimands of Chapter 29. \(\blacktriangleleft\)



27.8.2 The nonlinear case: a Lipschitz-Wasserstein bound
The punchline of this subsection first, because it is easy to lose in the machinery: the clean linear bound of Theorem 27.3 has no analogue at the level of covariate means once the contrast is nonlinear. A bias bound still exists, but it needs a distance between whole distributions, not between their centers, and no distance between means can supply it. This is the deepest reason aggregate distance matching is a diagnostic and not a transportability theorem, and the rest of the section makes it precise.
When the contrast is not affine, the mean gap no longer determines the bias, because a nonlinear \(\tau\) responds to the whole distribution and not only its center. A bias bound survives, but the distance it requires is between full distributions.
Before the formal statement, here is the object in plain terms. A coupling of the index and comparator covariate distributions is a way of pairing each comparator patient with an index patient, that is, a joint distribution whose two margins are the two populations. Picture the comparator patients as piles of sand sitting at their covariate values and the index patients as holes to be filled at theirs; a coupling is a transport plan saying how much sand moves from each pile to each hole. The Wasserstein-1 distance \(W_\rho(\mathcal{P}_j,\mathcal{P}_0)\) is the cost of the cheapest such plan, where moving one unit of mass a covariate-distance \(\rho\) costs \(\rho\): it is the minimum average distance patients must be shifted in covariate space to turn one population’s covariate distribution into the other’s. Unlike a gap between means, it sees the whole shape of each distribution, its spread and its tails, not only its center. For instance, to turn a population with everyone at \(x=0\) into one split evenly between \(x=-1\) and \(x=+1\), half the mass moves one unit left and half moves one unit right, an average move of \(1\), so \(W_\rho=1\), even though the two means agree at \(0\); this is the example of Proposition 27.4. The next theorem says a Lipschitz contrast, one that cannot change faster than a fixed rate \(L\) as the covariates change, can differ across two populations by at most \(L\) times this transport cost.

Theorem 27.4 (Lipschitz bias bound via the Wasserstein distance) Let \((\mathcal{X},\rho)\) be a metric space and let \(\mathcal{P}_0,\mathcal{P}_j\) be probability measures on \(\mathcal{X}\) with finite first moment. Suppose the conditional contrast \(\tau:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz with respect to \(\rho\), that is \(|\tau(\mathbf{x})-\tau(\mathbf{x}')|\le L\,\rho(\mathbf{x},
\mathbf{x}')\) for all \(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}'\). Then the transport bias is bounded by the Wasserstein-1 distance, \[
\big|B_j\big|
=\Big|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[\tau]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}[\tau]\Big|
\;\le\;L\;W_\rho\big(\mathcal{P}_j,\mathcal{P}_0\big),
\qquad
W_\rho(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q})=\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q})}\int\rho(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})
\,d\gamma(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}),
\tag{27.15}\] where \(\Pi(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q})\) is the set of couplings of \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{Q}\).


Proof. Let \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mathcal{P}_j,\mathcal{P}_0)\) be any coupling, that is, a joint law of a pair \((\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})\) whose first marginal is \(\mathcal{P}_j\) and whose second marginal is \(\mathcal{P}_0\). Because the marginals reproduce the two expectations, \[
B_j=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[\tau]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}[\tau]
=\mathbb{E}_\gamma\big[\tau(\mathbf{X})-\tau(\mathbf{Y})\big].
\] Taking absolute values, then using Jensen’s inequality for the convex function \(|\cdot|\) (Theorem 4.6) and the Lipschitz hypothesis, \[
|B_j|=\big|\mathbb{E}_\gamma[\tau(\mathbf{X})-\tau(\mathbf{Y})]\big|
\le\mathbb{E}_\gamma\big|\tau(\mathbf{X})-\tau(\mathbf{Y})\big|
\le L\,\mathbb{E}_\gamma\big[\rho(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})\big].
\] This holds for every coupling \(\gamma\), so taking the infimum over \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mathcal{P}_j,
\mathcal{P}_0)\) of the right-hand side gives \(|B_j|\le L\,W_\rho(\mathcal{P}_j,\mathcal{P}_0)\), which is Equation 27.15. \(\square\)


Remark. Why the Wasserstein distance is the right yardstick (Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality). The bound Equation 27.15 used a single coupling; remarkably, the best possible bound of this shape is again a Wasserstein distance. The Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality states \[
W_\rho(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q})=\sup_{\|f\|_{\mathrm{Lip}_\rho}\le1}
\big|\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{P}f-\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{Q}f\big|,
\] where the supremum runs over all functions \(f\) that are \(1\)-Lipschitz with respect to \(\rho\), meaning \(f\) changes by at most the distance between its inputs (\(\|f\|_{\mathrm{Lip}_\rho}\) is the smallest such rate). Read from right to left, it says the Wasserstein distance is the worst-case transport bias over every \(1\)-Lipschitz contrast: no unit-Lipschitz contrast can separate the two populations by more than \(W_\rho\), and some contrast comes arbitrarily close. That is exactly why \(W_\rho\), and not some cruder distributional distance, is the natural yardstick for Lipschitz transport bias, and why the bound in terms of it cannot be improved. Applying the identity to \(f=\tau/L\) recovers Equation 27.15. We gave the elementary coupling proof above because it is self-contained and needs only Theorem 4.6; the duality is recorded here for the reader who wants to know the bound is tight, not merely valid. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The decisive point is that a distance between means is not a Wasserstein distance between distributions. It is only a lower bound on it, so a small mean distance does not imply a small Wasserstein distance, hence does not bound the nonlinear bias.

Proposition 27.3 (Mean distance lower-bounds the Wasserstein distance) With \(\rho\) the Euclidean metric on \(\mathbb{R}^p\), the Euclidean distance between covariate means is dominated by the Wasserstein-1 distance between the covariate distributions: \[
d_E\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j\big)
=\big\|\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0\big\|_2
\;\le\;W_\rho\big(\mathcal{P}_j,\mathcal{P}_0\big).
\tag{27.16}\] Consequently a small Wasserstein distance forces a small mean distance, but a small (or zero) mean distance places no upper bound on the Wasserstein distance, and hence none on the nonlinear bias of Equation 27.15.


Proof. For any coupling \(\gamma\) of \((\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})\) with marginals \(\mathcal{P}_j,\mathcal{P}_0\), the vector Jensen inequality (Theorem 4.6 applied to the convex norm \(\|\cdot\|_2\)) gives \[
\big\|\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0\big\|_2
=\big\|\mathbb{E}_\gamma[\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{Y}]\big\|_2
\le\mathbb{E}_\gamma\big\|\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{Y}\big\|_2
=\mathbb{E}_\gamma\big[\rho(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})\big].
\] Taking the infimum over couplings gives Equation 27.16. The implication is one-directional: the example in Proposition 27.4 has \(d_E=0\) yet \(W_\rho>0\) and nonzero bias, so no reverse inequality can hold. \(\square\)

title: 27  Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching
section: 27.9 Distance is a diagnostic, not a validity guarantee
text:
27.9 Distance is a diagnostic, not a validity guarantee
We now state and prove the chapter’s central caveat. Every distance of this chapter is a function of the reported covariate summaries; the means are the universally available summary, and all of the distances reduce to zero when the means coincide. The next proposition shows that zero distance carries no guarantee about the target effect, in two independent ways: through nonlinearity, which the means cannot see, and through unmeasured variables, which no observed summary can see.

Proposition 27.4 (Zero covariate-summary distance does not bound transport bias) Let \(d\) be any covariate-summary distance of this chapter that is computed from the covariate means alone: Euclidean, standardized Euclidean, Mahalanobis, Manhattan, Minkowski, mean-SMD, or Gower with the means as inputs.

(Nonlinearity.) There exist populations \(\mathcal{P}_0,\mathcal{P}_j\) with identical covariate means, hence \(d(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j)=0\) for every such \(d\), and a conditional contrast \(\tau\) for which the target effects differ, \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[\tau]\ne\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}
[\tau]\). Consequently no inequality of the form \(|B_j|\le C\,d(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j)\) can hold for a finite constant \(C\) uniformly over contrasts; the transport bias is not a function of any mean-based distance.
(Unmeasured imbalance.) There exist populations whose observed covariate \(\mathbf{X}\) has identical distributions, hence zero distance under every summary of \(\mathbf{X}\), that nonetheless differ in an unobserved prognostic variable \(W\) in a way that makes the unanchored target means \(\mathbb{E}[\mu_t(\mathbf{X},W)]\) differ across populations.



Proof. Part 1. Let the covariate be scalar. Let \(\mathcal{P}_0\) place all mass at \(X=0\), and let \(\mathcal{P}_j\) place mass \(\tfrac12\) at \(X=-1\) and mass \(\tfrac12\) at \(X=+1\). Both have mean \(\bar{x}_0=\bar{x}_j=0\), so every mean-based distance is zero. Take the nonlinear contrast \(\tau(x)=x^2\). Then \[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}[\tau]=0^2=0,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[\tau]=\tfrac12(-1)^2+\tfrac12(1)^2=1,
\] so \(B_j=1\ne0\) while \(d=0\). Since \(|B_j|=1>C\cdot0\) for every finite \(C\), no bound of the stated form can hold. It is worth seeing this against Theorem 27.4 in full. On the support \(\{-1,0,1\}\) the contrast \(\tau(x)=x^2\) is Lipschitz: for any two points \(|x^2-y^2|=|x+y|\,|x-y|\le 2|x-y|\), so we may take \(L=2\). The Wasserstein distance is \(W_\rho(\mathcal{P}_j,\mathcal{P}_0)=1\), by the following explicit transport plan: move the mass \(\tfrac12\) sitting at \(x=-1\) to \(x=0\) (a shift of distance \(1\)) and the mass \(\tfrac12\) sitting at \(x=+1\) to \(x=0\) (a shift of distance \(1\)), for an average move of \(\tfrac12\cdot1+\tfrac12\cdot1=1\); no plan does better, since all the mass of \(\mathcal{P}_j\) must arrive at the single point \(0\) where \(\mathcal{P}_0\) lives, each unit travelling at least distance \(1\). The Lipschitz bound then reads \[
|B_j|=1\;\le\;L\,W_\rho=2\cdot1=2 ,
\] which holds with room to spare, while the mean distance \(d_E=0\) vanishes. The bias is real, it is controlled by the full-distribution distance, and it is wholly invisible to the means: it hides in the spread, which no mean-based distance records.
Part 2. Let the observed covariate \(\mathbf{X}\) have the same law in \(\mathcal{P}_0\) and \(\mathcal{P}_j\), and let an unobserved prognostic variable \(W\), which one should picture concretely as ECOG performance status, a strong prognostic factor in oncology that the single-arm Phase II might record but that the external Phase III reports only partially or on an incompatible scale, so it never enters the shared covariate table, have mean \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}[W]=0\) in the index population and \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[W]=1\) in the comparator population, with \(W\) independent of \(\mathbf{X}\) in each. Let the conditional mean depend on \(W\), for instance \(\mu_t(\mathbf{x},w)=w\) for the relevant arm. Every distance computed from \(\mathbf{X}\) is zero because the laws of \(\mathbf{X}\) agree, yet the unanchored target means differ: \[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}[\mu_t(\mathbf{X},W)]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}[W]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[\mu_t(\mathbf{X},W)]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[W]=1.
\] This is exactly the omitted-prognostic-variable bias of Theorem 17.2: with \(W\) absent from the adjustment set, the inner difference of its necessity integral Equation 17.17 does not vanish, and no comparator term cancels it in the unanchored contrast. \(\square\)


Remark. What aggregate-level matching is, and is not, good for. Parts 1 and 2 of Proposition 27.4 delimit the method precisely. Aggregate-level distance matching is a sound basis for: a comparator-selection rule when several bridging studies are available (Definition 27.1); an overlap diagnostic to be inspected before any unanchored MAIC, STC, or ML-UMR, since a large distance forewarns of heavy reweighting and low effective sample size (Theorem 18.6); and a sensitivity-analysis input that names which covariates drive the bridge. It is not a substitute for adjusting every imbalanced effect modifier (Definition 11.3) and prognostic variable (Definition 11.5); it is not a proof of the shared prognostic factor assumption (Definition 26.2); it is not a proof of conditional constancy of absolute effects (Definition 17.5); and it is no guard whatever against unmeasured imbalance. It presupposes, and does not establish, the clinical and design comparability of the trials, which must be judged separately and before any distance is computed (step 3 of Section 27.3): two studies can match on age, sex, and biomarker means and still differ in line of therapy, outcome definition, follow-up, or standard of care, and no small distance repairs that. The quantitative bias analysis of Chapter 28 is the tool for the residual and unmeasured part that distance matching leaves untouched. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Second-moment distances narrow, but do not close, the gap. Part 1 exploits that the means agree while the variances differ. One can blunt this particular counterexample by augmenting the summary with second moments and using a distance that also compares the covariances, \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0\) against \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\); this is the diagnostic analogue of MAIC second-moment balancing (Chapter 18) and of the joint-distribution modeling that ML-NMR achieves through a copula (Definition 22.5, Chapter 22). But no finite collection of moments closes the gap for every contrast: Exercise 27.7 constructs two populations matching in mean and variance whose target effects differ under a quartic contrast, and Part 2 shows that unmeasured variables defeat any summary of the observed covariates regardless of how many moments it includes. Distance matching on richer summaries is a better diagnostic, never a validity proof. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

This material corresponds to O.7 in the proof catalogue.

title: 27  Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching
section: 27.10 A fully worked example: ranking four comparators
text:
27.10 A fully worked example: ranking four comparators
We rank four candidate comparator studies for a single-arm index study, computing every distance and the exact bias by hand, and exhibit the chapter’s three lessons at once: the raw Euclidean ranking is an artifact of units, the standardized and Mahalanobis distances disagree because of covariate correlation, and the distance that tracks the actual bias is the one matched to the contrast direction.

Example 27.2 (Selecting among four comparator studies) The index single-arm study reports covariate means on three baseline covariates, mean age (years), proportion male, and mean biomarker level (units), \[
\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0=(60,\;0.5,\;10),
\] with reference scales \(s=(10,\;0.5,\;4)\) (the biomarker and age standard deviations from the index IPD, and the Bernoulli standard deviation \(\sqrt{0.5\cdot0.5}=0.5\) for sex), and index covariance \[
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}100&0&20\\[1pt]0&0.25&0\\[1pt]20&0&16\end{pmatrix},
\] in which age and biomarker are positively correlated, \(\operatorname{corr}=20/(10\cdot4)=0.5\), and sex is uncorrelated with both. (This \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ0\): its leading minors are \(100>0\), \(100\cdot0.25=25>0\), and \(\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=0.25\,(100\cdot16-20^2)=300>0\).) Four candidate comparator studies report means \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_A,\dots,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_D\), with covariate gaps \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_j=\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0\) and standardized gaps \(\mathbf{z}_j=S^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\): \[
\begin{array}{llll}
\text{Study } A: & \boldsymbol{\delta}_A=(12,\;0.05,\;1), & \mathbf{z}_A=(1.2,\;0.1,\;0.25),\\
\text{Study } B: & \boldsymbol{\delta}_B=(6,\;0.30,\;4.8), & \mathbf{z}_B=(0.6,\;0.6,\;1.2),\\
\text{Study } C: & \boldsymbol{\delta}_C=(1,\;0.45,\;6), & \mathbf{z}_C=(0.1,\;0.9,\;1.5),\\
\text{Study } D: & \boldsymbol{\delta}_D=(8,\;0.20,\;4), & \mathbf{z}_D=(0.8,\;0.4,\;1.0).
\end{array}
\]
Raw Euclidean (Equation 27.2). Squaring and summing the raw gaps, \[
d_E(A)=\sqrt{12^2+0.05^2+1^2}=\sqrt{145.00}=12.04,
\quad
d_E(B)=\sqrt{6^2+0.3^2+4.8^2}=\sqrt{59.13}=7.69,
\] \[
d_E(C)=\sqrt{1^2+0.45^2+6^2}=\sqrt{37.20}=6.10,
\quad
d_E(D)=\sqrt{8^2+0.2^2+4^2}=\sqrt{80.04}=8.95.
\] The raw ranking is \(C\prec B\prec D\prec A\), so raw Euclidean distance selects Study \(C\).
Standardized Euclidean (Equation 27.3). Using the standardized gaps, \[
d_{SE}(A)=\sqrt{1.2^2+0.1^2+0.25^2}=\sqrt{1.5125}=1.230,
\quad
d_{SE}(B)=\sqrt{0.6^2+0.6^2+1.2^2}=\sqrt{2.16}=1.470,
\] \[
d_{SE}(C)=\sqrt{0.1^2+0.9^2+1.5^2}=\sqrt{3.07}=1.752,
\quad
d_{SE}(D)=\sqrt{0.8^2+0.4^2+1.0^2}=\sqrt{1.80}=1.342.
\] The standardized ranking is \(A\prec D\prec B\prec C\), so standardized Euclidean distance selects Study \(A\): the opposite winner from the raw distance. The reversal is intuitive. Study \(A\)’s \(12\)-year age gap dominates the raw distance, but in standard-deviation units it is only \(1.2\) SD; Study \(C\)’s gaps are tiny in raw units (a \(1\)-year age gap, a \(6\)-unit biomarker gap) yet large when standardized (\(0.9\) SD in sex, \(1.5\) SD in biomarker), and the raw distance, blind to scale, mistakes \(C\) for the closest.
Mahalanobis (Equation 27.4). With \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\) having entries \((\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1})_{11}=\tfrac{1}{75}\), \((\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1})_{22}=4\), \((\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1})_{33}=\tfrac{1}{12}\), and \((\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1})_{13}=-\tfrac{1}{60}\) (from inverting the age-biomarker block \(\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}100&20\\20&16\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]\), of determinant \(1200\), and the scalar sex block), the quadratic form is \(d_M^2=\tfrac{1}{75}\delta_1^2+4\delta_2^2+\tfrac{1}{12}\delta_3^2
-\tfrac{1}{30}\delta_1\delta_3\). Evaluating, \[
d_M(A)=\sqrt{1.613}=1.270,
\quad
d_M(B)=\sqrt{1.800}=1.342,
\quad
d_M(C)=\sqrt{3.623}=1.904,
\quad
d_M(D)=\sqrt{1.280}=1.131.
\] The Mahalanobis ranking is \(D\prec A\prec B\prec C\), so Mahalanobis distance selects Study \(D\): a third, distinct winner. The reason is the age-biomarker correlation. Study \(D\)’s gap \((8,0.2,4)\) moves age and biomarker up together, exactly the direction the index covariance expects, so it is “cheap” in Mahalanobis geometry; standardized Euclidean distance, ignoring the correlation, charges \(D\) for both moves separately and ranks it behind \(A\).
Mean-SMD (Equation 27.8). Averaging the absolute standardized gaps, \(d_{\mathrm{SMD}}(A)=1.55/3=0.517\), \(d_{\mathrm{SMD}}(B)=2.40/3=0.800\), \(d_{\mathrm{SMD}}(C)=2.50/3=0.833\), \(d_{\mathrm{SMD}}(D)=2.20/3=0.733\), giving the ranking \(A\prec D\prec B\prec C\), the same as standardized Euclidean, as the \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) norms of a common standardized vector must often agree.
The four criteria are collected below; each column’s minimum is the selected study.

Which winner is right? The bias bound decides. Suppose, as a sensitivity input, the unanchored conditional contrast is taken to be affine, \(\tau(\mathbf{x})=\alpha+\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\mathbf{x}\), with \(\boldsymbol{\beta}=(0.1,\;2,\;0.5)\), so that \(S\boldsymbol{\beta}=(1,1,2)\) and \(\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2=\sqrt6\). By Theorem 27.3 the exact transport bias is \(B_j=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}_j=(S\boldsymbol{\beta})^\top\mathbf{z}_j=z_{j1}+z_{j2}+
2z_{j3}\): \[
B_A=1.8,\qquad B_D=3.2,\qquad B_B=3.6,\qquad B_C=4.0 .
\] The exact-bias ranking \(A\prec D\prec B\prec C\) coincides with the standardized Euclidean and mean-SMD rankings, and the standardized winner \(A\) is indeed the minimum-bias comparator. The raw Euclidean winner \(C\) has the largest bias of the four, \(4.0\); selecting by raw distance would have chosen the worst comparator, the concrete reversal promised by Proposition 27.2. The Mahalanobis winner \(D\) has bias \(3.2\), larger than \(A\)’s, because the contrast direction \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is not aligned with the covariance geometry that Mahalanobis distance rewards.
The Cauchy-Schwarz bounds and their equality cases are worth seeing. The standardized bound \(\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2\,d_{SE}=\sqrt6\,d_{SE}\) gives, for Study \(B\), \[
\sqrt6\cdot\sqrt{2.16}=\sqrt{12.96}=3.600=|B_B|,
\] an exact equality, because \(\mathbf{z}_B=(0.6,0.6,1.2)=0.6\,(1,1,2)=0.6\,S\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is parallel to \(S\boldsymbol{\beta}\), meeting the equality condition of Equation 27.13. The Mahalanobis bound \(\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\,d_M=\sqrt{8}\,d_M\) gives, for Study \(D\), \[
\sqrt8\cdot\sqrt{1.28}=\sqrt{10.24}=3.200=|B_D|,
\] again exact, because \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_D=(8,0.2,4)=0.4\,(20,0.5,10)=0.4\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is parallel to \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}\), meeting the equality condition of Equation 27.14 (one verifies \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}=(20,0.5,10)\) and \(\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}=8\)). For every study both bounds dominate the exact bias, as they must. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reading the four rankings, and where \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) comes from. The calculation compresses into one interpretation table.



Table 27.4: Why each criterion selects a different comparator, and how to report the disagreement.

The vector \(\boldsymbol{\beta}=(0.1,2,0.5)\) is a sensitivity input, not a quantity available when the comparator is chosen. In practice it would be borrowed from a published regression of the outcome on the covariates, elicited from clinical experts, or, most honestly, varied across a plausible range with the ranking recomputed at each setting; here it is a teaching device that lets us see, after the fact, which distance happened to align with the truth. Because it is unknown up front, the practical recommendation is the one the table’s last two columns dramatize: report the ranking under several distances, flag any disagreement as a signal that the choice is geometry-dependent, and carry the ambiguity into the sensitivity analysis rather than trusting a single number. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. The lesson of the example. Three reputable distances selected three different comparators. Standardized Euclidean distance happened to rank by the true bias here because its implicit geometry, equal weight per standardized covariate, was closer to the contrast direction \(S\boldsymbol{\beta}=(1,1,2)\) than the Mahalanobis geometry was. Had \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) pointed along the high-variance axis of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), the Mahalanobis ranking would have been the faithful one. Since \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is unknown at selection time, no distance is guaranteed to rank by bias; this is Proposition 27.4 made arithmetic. The defensible practice is to report the ranking under several distances, flag disagreement as a signal that the choice is geometry-dependent, and carry the ambiguity into the sensitivity analysis rather than trusting a single number. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 27  Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching
text:
27.11 Connection to the Coq formalization
Aggregate-level distance matching is a design heuristic, a rule for choosing which comparator to adjust toward, and unlike the estimators of Parts IV and V it makes no claim of unbiasedness that a proof assistant could certify. Its absence from the companion Coq development is therefore deliberate, not an item left on a backlog: there is no theories/DistanceMatching.v because there is no correctness theorem about the selection rule itself to mechanize. What the chapter does prove is elementary linear algebra and analysis, and every piece already lives in the development in another guise. The whitening identity Equation 27.5 is a one-line consequence of \((BB^\top)^{-1}=B^{-\top}B^{-1}\) and the existence of a matrix square root, the latter being the symmetric-square-root construction underlying Theorem 4.9. The linear bias bounds Equation 27.13 and Equation 27.14 are the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, the same inequality the development formalizes for the effective-sample-size bound: the machine-checked Theorem ESS_upper_bound of theories/MAIC.v (tagged on Theorem 18.6) is built from the elementary \(2xy\le x^2+y^2\) assembled by induction into a Cauchy-Schwarz statement, and a future DistanceMatching.v could reuse that lemma verbatim to certify Theorem 27.3. Schematically, the single statement such a file would prove is one Cauchy-Schwarz application,
(* Linear bias bound, schematic form of Theorem distance-linear-bias-bound. *)
(* |beta . delta| <= ||beta||_Sigma * ||delta||_{inverse Sigma}. *)
Theorem distance_linear_bias_bound :
  forall (Sigma : SPDMatrix) (beta delta : Vector),
    Rabs (dot beta delta)
      <= sqrt (quad_form Sigma beta) * sqrt (quad_form (inverse Sigma) delta).
which is exactly Equation 27.14, the Mahalanobis factor \(\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}}\) written out. The non-identification proposition Proposition 27.4 is a pair of finite arithmetic counterexamples and would formalize directly. None of these results is currently mechanized, so this chapter carries no [machine-checked] tags; Chapter 30 documents the boundary of the formal development, of which distance matching lies outside.

title: 27  Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching
text:
27.12 Notes and references
Aggregate-level covariate-distance matching is an extension beyond the population-adjustment theory of Phillippo (2019), motivated by the disconnected-network and single-arm settings that the multilevel unanchored meta-regression of Chandler and Ishak (2026a) addresses and that the transportability reframing of Chandler and Ishak (2026b) places in estimand terms. The practical rule of selecting the candidate study minimizing a covariate-summary distance is described in the Bristol Compass blog on extending ML-NMR to disconnected networks, and the suite of distances studied here, standardized Euclidean (the default), Euclidean, Mahalanobis, Manhattan, Minkowski, Gower, and mean-absolute standardized-mean-difference, is the diagnostic toolkit implemented in the uitc R package; bibliographic entries for both the blog and the package are proposed in the chapter work log.
The distances themselves are classical. The Mahalanobis distance and its whitening interpretation (Theorem 27.1) originate with Mahalanobis; its reduction to standardized Euclidean distance for diagonal covariance and its full affine invariance (Theorem 27.2) are standard facts of multivariate analysis, here proved from Theorem 4.9. The Gower distance for mixed continuous and binary data is due to Gower. Minkowski’s inequality, invoked in Proposition 27.1 for the general \(\ell_q\) triangle inequality, is the standard named result; the orders \(q\in\{1,2,\infty\}\) used in this book are proved directly there from the coordinatewise triangle inequality and Cauchy-Schwarz. The mean-SMD diagnostic and the \(|z|>0.1\) rule of thumb are the covariate-balance conventions of the propensity-score literature, transposed from the individual level to study summaries.
The bias theory is the chapter’s own contribution to the catalogue. The linear bound Theorem 27.3 is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applied to the affine specialization of the unanchored transport bias of Theorem 17.2, and it makes precise the sense in which comparator selection bounds the residual bias that the consistency theorem assumes away. The Lipschitz bound Theorem 27.4 is the elementary coupling side of Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality; a reference for the duality and for the Wasserstein distance is the optimal-transport literature (Villani), proposed in the work log. The lower bound Proposition 27.3, that the mean gap never exceeds the Wasserstein distance, uses the vector Jensen inequality Theorem 4.6 and is what makes the non-identification of Proposition 27.4 unavoidable rather than accidental: mean distance is a floor on distributional distance, never a ceiling. The reader who wants the residual and unmeasured-confounding part of the problem, which distance matching cannot touch, should continue to the quantitative bias analysis of Chapter 28, where the E-value and tipping-point methods quantify exactly the bias that a zero distance fails to rule out.
This chapter corresponds to results O.1 (the comparator-selection problem), O.2 (Euclidean and standardized Euclidean distance), O.3 (the Mahalanobis whitening equivalence), O.4 (the Manhattan, Minkowski, Gower, and mean-SMD distances), O.5 (scale dependence and invariance), O.6 (the linear and Lipschitz bias bounds), and O.7 (the non-identification caveat) of the proof catalogue in proofs/O_distance_matching.md, expanding each catalogue sketch into a complete proof and adding the metric-property proposition Proposition 27.1 and the Wasserstein lower bound Proposition 27.3.

title: 27  Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching
text:
27.13 Exercises
An exercise marked \(\star\) has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The exercises are tagged by type; start with the warm-ups, which need only arithmetic, before the computation, proof, and challenge problems.

Exercise 27.1 (Warm-up, computation) Two distances by hand. The index study reports covariate means \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0=(50,\,20)\) on (age in years, biomarker in units) with reference scales \(s=(10,\,5)\). Two candidate comparators report \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_1=(58,\,24)\) and \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_2=(46,\,30)\). (a) Compute the raw Euclidean and the standardized Euclidean distance of each candidate to the index, and state which candidate each distance selects. (b) Using the index covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}100&30\\30&25\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]\), compute the two Mahalanobis distances and say whether they agree with the standardized ranking. You can check your method against the fully worked Example 27.1.


Exercise 27.2 (Warm-up, interpretation) A comparator-selection memo. Using Example 27.2, write a short decision memo, one paragraph, for an HTA submission that (a) names the comparator you would carry forward and why, (b) reports the disagreement among the raw, standardized, and Mahalanobis rankings and explains it in one sentence a non-mathematician could follow, and (c) states what you would do if the Mahalanobis winner (Study \(D\)) had poor clinical comparability, say a different line of therapy, while the standardized winner (Study \(A\)) had better trial-design similarity. Which would you choose, and what does Section 27.3 say about the order in which comparability and distance are assessed?


Exercise 27.3 (Computation) Reference scale changes the winner. Recompute the standardized Euclidean ranking in Example 27.2 using comparator-reported standard deviations \(s'=(8,\,0.5,\,6)\) in place of the index scales \(s=(10,\,0.5,\,4)\). Report the new \(d_{SE}\) for all four studies and the new winner, and explain why Theorem 27.2 does not apply (the change is not a coherent rescaling of a single coordinate system but a change of reference scales alone). Comment on which reference scale is preferable when index IPD is available.


Exercise 27.4 (Computation) Worst-covariate selection. For the four studies of Example 27.2 compute the Chebyshev distance \(d_\infty=\max_\ell|z_{j\ell}|\) and the Minkowski distances \(d_3\) and \(d_4\). Show that the ranking under \(d_q\) moves toward the Chebyshev ranking as \(q\) grows, and identify the study whose selection is most sensitive to the choice of \(q\). Interpret the result for a decision-maker who regards a single badly mismatched covariate as disqualifying.


Exercise 27.5 (Proof) The triangle inequality at the boundary. Prove that \(d_q\) in Equation 27.7 is a metric for every \(q\in[1,\infty]\) by establishing Minkowski’s inequality \(\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}\|_q\le
\|\mathbf{u}\|_q+\|\mathbf{w}\|_q\) from Hölder’s inequality, and show by the explicit three-point configuration of Proposition 27.1 that the triangle inequality fails for every \(q\in(0,1)\). Conclude that the uitc restriction \(q\ge1\) is exactly the range in which the Minkowski “distance” deserves the name.


Exercise 27.6 (\(\star\), proof) Full affine invariance of the Mahalanobis distance. Prove that if the covariates are reparameterized by any invertible affine map \(\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{c}\) and the covariance is transformed accordingly to \(A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A^\top\), then the Mahalanobis distance is unchanged, whereas the standardized Euclidean distance is invariant only for diagonal \(A\). Exhibit a nondiagonal \(2\times2\) invertible \(A\) and a pair of candidates whose standardized Euclidean ranking is reversed by the reparameterization while their Mahalanobis ranking is preserved. Explain what this says about the sense in which Mahalanobis distance is the “coordinate-free” member of the family.


Exercise 27.7 (\(\star\), challenge) Matching means and variances is still not enough. Strengthen Proposition 27.4 by constructing two scalar covariate distributions with identical mean and identical variance, hence zero distance under any diagnostic built from the first two moments, whose target effects differ under a nonlinear contrast. (Hint: let \(\mathcal{P}_0\) put mass \(\tfrac12\) at each of \(\pm1\), and let \(\mathcal{P}_1\) put mass \(\tfrac34\) at \(0\) and mass \(\tfrac18\) at each of \(\pm2\); verify both have mean \(0\) and variance \(1\), then evaluate the quartic contrast \(\tau(x)=x^4\).) Report the two target effects, the resulting bias, and the implication for MAIC second-moment balancing: balancing through any fixed finite set of moments leaves a residual bias for sufficiently nonlinear contrasts.


Exercise 27.8 (Computation) Verifying the Lipschitz bound. For the two distributions of Proposition 27.4 Part 1, \(\mathcal{P}_0=\delta_0\) and \(\mathcal{P}_1=\tfrac12\delta_{-1}+\tfrac12\delta_{+1}\), compute the Wasserstein-1 distance \(W_\rho(\mathcal{P}_1,\mathcal{P}_0)\) under the Euclidean ground metric by exhibiting the optimal coupling, confirm the mean-distance lower bound \(d_E=0\le W_\rho\) of Proposition 27.3, and verify the Lipschitz bias bound Equation 27.15 for the contrast \(\tau(x)=x^2\) on the support \(\{-1,0,1\}\) with its Lipschitz constant \(L=2\). State why the bound is not tight here and which feature of \(\tau\) would make it tight.


Exercise 27.9 (Interpretation) Distance against effective sample size. Argue that, all else equal, a comparator with a larger standardized Euclidean distance from the index population requires more aggressive reweighting in a subsequent unanchored MAIC and hence a lower effective sample size. Using Theorem 18.6 and the variance-inflation factor \(n/\mathrm{ESS}\), explain why comparator selection trades bias (bounded by the distance under Theorem 27.3) against variance (governed by the ESS), and sketch how this trade-off would enter a mean-squared-error criterion for choosing among candidates of comparable distance. Relate the trade-off to the simulation-study estimands of Chapter 29.





Chandler, Conor, and K. Jack Ishak. 2026a. “Anchors Away: Navigating Unanchored Indirect Comparisons with Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2606.20341.


Chandler, Conor, and K. Jack Ishak. 2026b. “Reframing Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons as a Transportability Problem: An Estimand-Based Perspective and Implications for Health Technology Assessment.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2602.17041.


Phillippo, David Mark. 2019. “Calibration of Treatment Effects in Network Meta-Analysis Using Individual Patient Data.” PhD thesis, University of Bristol.

title: 28  Quantitative Bias Analysis for Indirect Comparisons
text:
28.1 Introduction
When a health technology assessment (HTA) committee, for example a NICE appraisal panel or an FDA advisory committee, must decide whether to reimburse a new treatment against an established comparator, the pivotal evidence is frequently an indirect comparison rather than a head-to-head trial. The committee’s sharpest question is seldom “what is the point estimate?” but “how confident are you that the estimate survives a covariate you were never able to adjust for?” This chapter develops the mathematics of answering that question honestly, so that a reimbursement dossier can report not merely an effect but a defensible statement about how fragile that effect is.
Every method in this book up to now has removed bias by measuring the variable that causes it. The anchored Bucher comparison (Theorem 14.1) is exact when every effect modifier is shared and common; matching-adjusted indirect comparison (Chapter 18) reweights the individual patient data (IPD) until the imbalanced effect modifiers are balanced; simulated treatment comparison (Chapter 19) and multilevel network meta-regression (Chapter 20) model the same covariates inside an outcome regression. All of them adjust for a covariate by using it. What none of them can do is adjust for a covariate that was never measured, or, in the most common and most dangerous case for an unanchored indirect comparison, one that the comparator publication never reported.
The distinction is worth a table, because it says precisely where this chapter begins. Each earlier method neutralizes a covariate only by having access to it in some form; QBA is what remains when even that access is gone.
The threat is sharpest in the unanchored setting. Chapter 17 showed that an unanchored population-adjusted indirect comparison (PAIC) is consistent only under conditional constancy of absolute effects and balance of every imbalanced prognostic variable, not merely the effect modifiers (Theorem 17.2, Definition 17.5), and Chapter 12 showed that the shared-effect-modifier assumption is by itself insufficient to identify the target-population contrast (Theorem 12.6). The single covariate that escapes the analysis, an unmeasured effect modifier (Definition 11.3) whose distribution differs between the two trial populations, is residual bias that no reweighting and no outcome model can touch, because the quantity it depends on, the covariate’s distribution in the comparator population, is simply unknown. The honest response is not to pretend the bias is zero but to quantify it: to ask how large the unmeasured mechanism would have to be to matter, and to report the answer alongside the point estimate. This is quantitative bias analysis (QBA), the subject of this chapter.
QBA originates in epidemiology, where the same three threats to validity recur in every observational study: uncontrolled confounding, selection of the study sample on exposure and outcome, and mismeasurement of variables. The canonical reference is the monograph of Lash et al. (2021), whose deterministic and probabilistic machinery we adapt. We develop four instruments, in increasing sophistication. First, the E-value of VanderWeele and Ding (2017): a single number, derived from the point estimate alone, giving the minimum strength of unmeasured confounding or effect modification, on the risk-ratio scale, that could explain the observed effect away. We give its full derivation, resting on a sharp bound for the confounding bias factor that we prove from scratch. Second, an indirect-comparison-specific E-value that exploits a structural feature unique to the unanchored ITC: the unmeasured covariate is observed in the analyst’s own IPD, so half of the sensitivity problem is estimable rather than assumed, and the resulting E-value is sharper and can certify a result as provably robust. Third, the NORTA (normal-to-anything) construction, which imputes the unreported joint distribution of the comparator’s covariates by gluing the reported margins to a dependence structure borrowed from the IPD through a Gaussian copula (Definition 22.5, Theorem 22.4); we prove that the construction reproduces the margins exactly and induces precisely the intended copula. Fourth, the tipping-point analysis and its probabilistic upgrade, which locate the assumed value of the unreported covariate at which the conclusion reverses and place a prior distribution over that value to propagate the uncertainty honestly.
This material is new to the formal theory of indirect comparison; it is not in the proof catalogue, and it has no machine-checked counterpart in the companion Coq development. We therefore build it from first principles, proving every bound in full and grounding each tool in a fully worked, hand-checkable example at the end of the chapter.
Throughout, \(g\) is the link function on whose scale effects are reported and modeled, and \(g^{-1}\) its inverse; for binary and count outcomes the analysis scale is the log odds ratio or log rate ratio, so the effects of interest live on the risk-ratio scale where the E-value is defined. We write \(\mathrm{RR}\), \(\mathrm{OR}\), \(\mathrm{HR}\) for risk, odds, and hazard ratios as in Notation. The symbol \(U\) denotes the unmeasured (in the confounding sense) or unreported (in the ITC sense) covariate, distinguished from the measured covariate vector \(\mathbf{x}\); \(\mathbf{b}\) denotes a vector of bias parameters; and we reserve the plain italic \(E\) for the E-value, distinct from the expectation operator \(\mathbb{E}[\cdot]\).
This chapter builds five instruments. They are not competitors but a toolkit: some answer how robust is the estimate?, one answers what value would overturn it?, one answers how do I propagate my uncertainty about that value?, and one is the machinery that builds the comparator population the others need. Keep the following map in view.
We anchor all five to one concrete comparison, introduced now and computed in full in Section 28.8.

Remark. Prognostic variable versus effect modifier, in one line. Two kinds of covariate recur throughout the book, and the difference decides which comparisons they threaten. A prognostic variable shifts a patient’s outcome risk regardless of which treatment they take; an effect modifier changes the size of the treatment effect itself, so the benefit of \(B\) over \(A\) differs across its levels (Definition 11.3). An anchored comparison, which subtracts a within-trial contrast, is undisturbed by a purely prognostic variable and needs only its effect modifiers balanced; an unanchored comparison has no such protection and needs balance of every imbalanced prognostic variable as well (Theorem 17.2). That is why the unreported covariate is the sharpest threat exactly in the unanchored setting, and why the running example below places its unreported covariate there. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Example 28.1 (A running example: an unanchored COPD comparison) A manufacturer seeks reimbursement for a new inhaled therapy \(B\) for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Only a single-arm trial of \(B\) is available, with full individual patient data (IPD); the established comparator \(A\) has only a published summary. The outcome is a severe exacerbation within 12 months, a bad event, so a risk ratio below \(1\) favors \(B\). Two baseline covariates matter. The first, \(x_R\), is age (standardized), which the \(A\) publication reports as a mean and standard deviation. The second, \(u\), is baseline lung function \(\mathrm{FEV}_1\) (forced expiratory volume in one second, in liters; higher is healthier, so it lowers exacerbation risk): the \(A\) publication does not report it at all. An unanchored analysis that plugs the IPD value of \(\mathrm{FEV}_1\) into the comparator population returns an adjusted risk ratio of about \(\mathrm{RR}=0.50\) (\(95\%\) confidence interval \(0.30\) to \(0.81\)), so \(B\) appears to roughly halve the exacerbation risk. The committee’s question is the subject of this chapter: how much of that apparent benefit could be an artifact of the unreported \(\mathrm{FEV}_1\)?
We carry this trial through every instrument below, previewing each result where the instrument is defined and computing all of it by hand in Section 28.8. The model fitted to the IPD, with a log link on the risk, is \(\log P(Y=1\mid x_R,u)=\beta_0+\beta_R x_R+\beta_U u\) with \(\beta_0=-1.0\), \(\beta_R=0.4\) (older age raises risk), and \(\beta_U=-0.5\) (higher \(\mathrm{FEV}_1\) lowers risk); the comparator reports age mean \(m_R=1.0\), standard deviation \(\sigma_R=0.5\), and its own event risk \(\mu_0=0.47\), and in the IPD the covariate \(\mathrm{FEV}_1\) has mean \(\bar{x}_U=2.0\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_U=1.0\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 28  Quantitative Bias Analysis for Indirect Comparisons
text:
28.2 The framework of bias analysis
Bias analysis begins by writing down, explicitly, the mechanism that links what we observe to what is true. An estimate is valid when the estimator converges to the estimand; it is biased by a systematic error when a structural feature of the data, distinct from sampling variability, drives a wedge between the two. Quantitative bias analysis makes that wedge a function of named, interpretable parameters and then explores it.
A natural first reaction to a worrying covariate is to fit a richer model that includes it. The reason that does not work here is worth stating plainly: in an unanchored indirect comparison the covariate is unreported by the comparator, so there is no column for it in the comparator data and no likelihood can condition on it. Bayesian model expansion is the right tool when you hold the data and merely distrust a functional form; quantitative bias analysis is the right tool when the data themselves are missing and the best you can do is ask how bad the omission could be. QBA does not recover the missing information; it bounds the damage.

Definition 28.1 (Quantitative bias analysis) Let \(\theta\) be a target estimand and \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{obs}}\) an estimator that is consistent for a biased surrogate \(\theta_{\mathrm{obs}}=\theta\cdot B(\mathbf{b})\) (multiplicative scale) or \(\theta_{\mathrm{obs}}=\theta + B(\mathbf{b})\) (additive scale), where the bias function \(B\) depends on a vector of bias parameters \(\mathbf{b}\in\mathcal{B}\) that index the unverified structural assumptions (the strength and imbalance of an unmeasured confounder, the selection probabilities of each cell, the sensitivity and specificity of a mismeasured variable, or the comparator distribution of an unreported covariate). A quantitative bias analysis is the map \[
\mathbf{b}\;\longmapsto\;\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\mathbf{b})
\;=\;h\big(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{obs}},\mathbf{b}\big),
\tag{28.1}\] where the correction \(h\) inverts the bias model, returning the value of the target consistent with the observed estimate under the assumed \(\mathbf{b}\). The analysis is deterministic when \(\mathbf{b}\) ranges over a fixed grid or a single value, and probabilistic when \(\mathbf{b}\) carries a prior distribution \(\pi\) that is propagated to a distribution over \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}\). The three classical threats, uncontrolled confounding, selection bias, and misclassification, are the corners of the bias triangle and each supplies its own \(B\) and \(h\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader’s translation. Read Definition 28.1 as a recipe with three moves: (i) name the unverified quantities as a parameter vector \(\mathbf{b}\) (how imbalanced the missing covariate is, how strongly it acts, and so on); (ii) write the bias as an explicit function \(B(\mathbf{b})\) of them; (iii) invert it to see what the honest estimate would have been. On the multiplicative scale the correction divides: \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}=\hat\theta_{\mathrm{obs}}/B(\mathbf{b})\), as in the risk-ratio confounding factor below. On the additive scale it subtracts: for a risk difference distorted by a selection or misclassification shift \(B(\mathbf{b})\), the corrected estimate is \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{obs}}-B(\mathbf{b})\). The three corners of the bias triangle just supply three different shapes of \(B\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


28.2.1 A practical workflow
Before the derivations, here is the applied procedure the rest of the chapter makes precise, written as a health researcher would run it for an unanchored indirect comparison.

Identify the threat. Name the covariate that is imbalanced and unreported by the comparator, and decide whether it is prognostic, an effect modifier, or both.
Estimate what you can. From the IPD, read off the covariate’s association with the outcome, \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=\exp(|\beta_U|)\) on a ratio scale, and its own IPD distribution.
Screen with an E-value. Compute the E-value and, using \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\), the sharper indirect-comparison E-value (Section 28.4). If the latter is \(+\infty\), stop: the result is certified robust to this covariate.
Choose plausible comparator values. Fix a range or a prior for the covariate’s comparator marginal from external evidence (registries, related trials, elicitation); this is a sensitivity assumption, not new data.
Build the comparator population. If dependence with the reported covariates matters, use NORTA


to glue your assumed marginal to a dependence structure borrowed from the IPD; otherwise the marginal alone suffices.


Compute the sensitivity curve and its tipping point. Marginalize the IPD outcome model over each assumed value to get \(\Delta(m)\), and locate the value \(m^{\dagger}\) at which the conclusion reverses (Section 28.6).
Propagate the uncertainty. Place a prior on the comparator marginal and report the systematic and total intervals and the probability of benefit (Section 28.7).
Report honestly. State the E-value, the tipping point in the covariate’s own units, and whether a believable comparator value would overturn the conclusion.

The sections below justify each step; the running example runs all eight. A handful of risk-ratio labels recur across those steps, so the following dictionary fixes them once.







Symbol
How to read it




\(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{crude}}\), \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}\)
the confounded thing the data show, before removing bias (used interchangeably)


\(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{adj}}\), \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{true}}\)
the de-biased target you would see with the confounder controlled (likewise interchangeable)


\(B(\mathbf{b})\)
the general bias function of Definition 28.1


\(B\) (no argument)
the specific confounding bias factor of Lemma 28.1, one instance of \(B(\mathbf{b})\)


\(\mathrm{RR}_{XY}\)
the risk ratio of \(Y\) across levels of \(X\) (so \(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\), \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\) read off the roles \(E\) = exposure, \(U\) = unmeasured covariate, \(D\) = disease)


\(E\) (italic), \(\mathbb{E}\)
the E-value Equation 28.9 and the expectation operator: never the exposure, which we write \(A\)



The simplest instance, and the one that motivates the E-value, is a single binary unmeasured confounder acting on a risk ratio. We derive its correction now, both because it is the prototype of Equation 28.1 and because the E-value is exactly the question “how large must \(\mathbf{b}\) be?” asked of this model.

Lemma 28.1 (Confounding bias factor for a binary confounder) Consider a binary exposure (treatment) \(A\in\{0,1\}\), a binary outcome \(D\), and a binary unmeasured confounder \(U\in\{0,1\}\) with prevalence \(p_1=P(U=1\mid A=1)\) among the exposed and \(p_0=P(U=1\mid A=0)\) among the unexposed. Suppose \(U\) is the only confounder, so that within strata of \(U\) the exposure is unconfounded, and suppose \(U\) acts on the outcome with a constant risk ratio \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=P(D=1\mid U=1,A=a)/P(D=1\mid U=0,A=a)\) that does not depend on \(a\). Then the crude (confounded) risk ratio and the \(U\)-adjusted risk ratio differ by the multiplicative bias factor \[
B \;=\; \frac{p_1\,(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)+1}{p_0\,(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)+1},
\qquad
\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{adj}}=\frac{\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{crude}}}{B}.
\tag{28.2}\] In particular \(B=1\) when \(p_1=p_0\) (the confounder is balanced) or \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=1\) (the confounder is inert).


Proof. Write \(r_a=P(D=1\mid A=a)\) for the marginal risk in arm \(a\) and \(q_a(u)=P(D=1\mid A=a,U=u)\) for the stratum risks. The lemma’s constant-risk-ratio hypothesis says exactly that the within-arm outcome risk ratio across \(U\) is \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\), that is \(q_a(1)/q_a(0)=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\), so \(q_a(1)=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\,q_a(0)\). By the law of total probability, \(r_a=q_a(0)\,(1-p_a)+q_a(1)\,p_a=q_a(0)\big[(1-p_a)+p_a\,\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\big]=q_a(0)\big[1+p_a(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)\big]\). The crude risk ratio is therefore \[
\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{crude}}=\frac{r_1}{r_0}
=\frac{q_1(0)}{q_0(0)}\cdot\frac{1+p_1(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)}{1+p_0(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)}.
\] Because \(U\) is the only confounder, the ratio \(q_1(0)/q_0(0)\) of the stratum-\(U{=}0\) risks is the unconfounded, \(U\)-adjusted risk ratio \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{adj}}\) (the within-stratum exposure effect, assumed constant across \(U\)). The remaining factor is exactly \(B\) in Equation 28.2, so \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{crude}}=\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{adj}}\cdot B\), which rearranges to the stated correction. Setting \(p_1=p_0\) makes numerator and denominator equal, \(B=1\); setting \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=1\) makes both equal \(1\), again \(B=1\). \(\square\)


Remark. What the bias factor says. In words, the crude estimate you see equals the true effect times a factor that measures how differently the confounder is spread across the two arms. That factor is a product of two intuitions the formula makes exact: a confounder equally common in both arms (\(p_1=p_0\)) cannot bias anything, and a confounder unrelated to the outcome (\(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=1\)) cannot either. Bias needs both an imbalance and an outcome link, which is exactly why an unreported covariate is dangerous only when it is both differently distributed across the trials and prognostic. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. The deterministic correction needs three numbers you rarely have. Formula Equation 28.2 is the correction \(h\) of Definition 28.1 with bias parameters \(\mathbf{b}=(p_1,p_0,\mathrm{RR}_{UD})\). It is honest but demanding: it presumes the analyst can name the prevalence of the unmeasured confounder in each arm and its outcome association. Selection bias and misclassification have analogous corrections (the selection odds ratio divides out of the crude odds ratio; the classification correction inverts the sensitivity-specificity map cell by cell), each with its own \(\mathbf{b}\); see Lash et al. (2021). The E-value of the next section sidesteps the need to specify \(\mathbf{b}\) by turning the question around. \(\blacktriangleleft\)



28.2.2 The other two corners: selection and misclassification
The bias triangle has three vertices, and the rest of this chapter develops only the confounding vertex, because it is the one that maps directly onto the unreported effect modifier of an unanchored comparison. For completeness we record the other two corrections, both standard and both taken from Lash et al. (2021) rather than re-derived here, so the reader can see the common shape: each names bias parameters, writes a \(B\), and inverts it.
Selection bias. When inclusion in the analysis depends on both exposure and outcome, let \(s_{ad}\) be the probability that a subject with exposure \(a\in\{0,1\}\) and outcome \(d\in\{0,1\}\) enters the sample. The observed (selected-sample) odds ratio and the target-population odds ratio differ by the multiplicative selection bias factor \[
B_{\mathrm{sel}}=\frac{s_{11}\,s_{00}}{s_{10}\,s_{01}},
\qquad
\mathrm{OR}_{\mathrm{adj}}=\frac{\mathrm{OR}_{\mathrm{obs}}}{B_{\mathrm{sel}}},
\tag{28.3}\] so selection is harmless exactly when the four selection probabilities factor into an exposure term times an outcome term (no exposure-by-outcome interaction in who gets in).
Misclassification. When a binary exposure is measured with sensitivity \(\mathrm{Se}=P(A^{*}=1\mid A=1)\) and specificity \(\mathrm{Sp}=P(A^{*}=0\mid A=0)\), where \(A^{*}\) is the recorded and \(A\) the true exposure, the true exposed count \(N_1\) in a stratum of size \(n\) with observed exposed count \(N_1^{*}\) is recovered by inverting the classification map, \[
N_1=\frac{N_1^{*}-(1-\mathrm{Sp})\,n}{\mathrm{Se}+\mathrm{Sp}-1},
\tag{28.4}\] valid whenever \(\mathrm{Se}+\mathrm{Sp}>1\) (the measurement is better than a coin flip); one applies it within outcome strata and recomputes the effect from the corrected counts. Both corrections have probabilistic upgrades, priors on \((s_{ad})\) or on \((\mathrm{Se},\mathrm{Sp})\), exactly as in Section 28.7. In an indirect comparison the confounding corner dominates, so from here on bias means residual imbalance in an unreported covariate unless stated otherwise.

title: 28  Quantitative Bias Analysis for Indirect Comparisons
text:
28.3 The E-value
The E-value asks not “what is the bias, given \(\mathbf{b}\)?” but “how strong must \(\mathbf{b}\) be to overturn the conclusion?” To answer it we need a bound that holds for any unmeasured confounder, not just a binary one with a constant association, in terms of two scalar sensitivity parameters. The bound of VanderWeele and Ding (2017), building on the bias-factor analysis of Ding and VanderWeele, is sharp, and we prove it in full.
Fix a binary exposure \(A\) and binary outcome \(D\), with an unmeasured confounder \(U\) taking values in a finite set \(\mathcal{U}\). Write \(f_a(u)=P(U=u\mid A=a)\) for the confounder distribution in arm \(a\) and \(p_a(u)=P(D=1\mid A=a,U=u)\) for the stratum risks. Define the two sensitivity parameters \[
\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\;=\;\max_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\frac{f_1(u)}{f_0(u)},
\qquad
\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\;=\;\frac{\max_{u}p_0(u)}{\min_{u}p_0(u)},
\tag{28.5}\] both at least \(1\). A word on the subscripts, which follow the E-value literature and are unrelated to the italic E-value \(E\) of Equation 28.9 or to the expectation \(\mathbb{E}\): in \(\mathrm{RR}_{XY}\) the pair \(XY\) reads “the risk ratio of \(Y\) across levels of \(X\)”, with \(E\) naming the exposure role (the treatment variable we write \(A\)), \(U\) the unmeasured covariate, and \(D\) the disease outcome. So \(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\) measures how exposure shifts the confounder distribution and \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\) how the confounder shifts outcome risk. In words, \(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\) is the largest factor by which any confounder level is over-represented in the exposed relative to the unexposed arm, and \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\) is the widest spread of outcome risk across confounder levels within the unexposed arm.

Remark. A number to hold onto. Suppose a biomarker is twice as common in the exposed arm as in the unexposed arm, \(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}=2\), and carries a threefold spread in outcome risk, \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=3\). The bound below says the most these two facts can bias a risk ratio is \(\mathrm{BF}_U=\dfrac{2\times 3}{2+3-1}=\dfrac{6}{4}=1.5\): no configuration of that confounder can inflate an observed risk ratio by more than a factor of \(1.5\). The next lemma proves this formula and, crucially, that \(1.5\) is attained, not merely an over-cautious ceiling. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Lemma 28.2 (Sharp bound on the confounding bias factor) With the notation above, suppose \(U\) carries all the confounding, so that within strata of \(U\) the exposure is unconfounded. Then the confounding bias factor \(B\) relating the observed risk ratio to the \(U\)-adjusted (causal) risk ratio standardized to the exposed (that is, averaging the stratum risks over the exposed arm’s confounder distribution) satisfies \[
B\;\le\;\mathrm{BF}_U\;:=\;\frac{\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\,\mathrm{RR}_{UD}}{\mathrm{RR}_{EU}+\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1},
\tag{28.6}\] and the bound is sharp: for every pair \((\mathrm{RR}_{EU},\mathrm{RR}_{UD})\) with both values at least \(1\) there is a confounder configuration attaining equality.


Proof. The bias factor as a ratio of weighted averages. Because \(U\) carries all the confounding, the counterfactual risk had the exposed arm been left unexposed is, by standardization over the exposed confounder distribution, \(\sum_u p_0(u)f_1(u)\). Hence the causal risk ratio for the effect on the exposed is \(\big(\sum_u p_1(u)f_1(u)\big)\big/\big(\sum_u p_0(u)f_1(u)\big)\), while the observed risk ratio is \(\big(\sum_u p_1(u)f_1(u)\big)\big/\big(\sum_u p_0(u)f_0(u)\big)\). Dividing, the common numerator cancels and \[
B=\frac{\sum_{u}p_0(u)f_1(u)}{\sum_{u}p_0(u)f_0(u)}
=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{f_1}[\,p_0(U)\,]}{\mathbb{E}_{f_0}[\,p_0(U)\,]}.
\tag{28.7}\] The bias factor is the ratio of the unexposed-risk function averaged over the two confounder distributions.
Reduction to a box. Both \(B\) and the constraints are invariant to multiplying \(p_0(\cdot)\) by a positive constant, so normalize \(\min_u p_0(u)=1\); then \(p_0(u)\in[1,R]\) for all \(u\), where \(R:=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\). Write \(S:=\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\), so the constraint \(\max_u f_1(u)/f_0(u)\le S\) reads \(f_1(u)\le S f_0(u)\) for every \(u\). We maximize Equation 28.7 over \(p_0\in[1,R]^{\mathcal{U}}\) and over probability vectors \(f_1,f_0\) obeying this pointwise constraint.
Maximizing over \(p_0\): the optimum is at a vertex. Fix \(f_1,f_0\) and vary a single coordinate \(t=p_0(u)\in[1,R]\), holding the others fixed. Writing \(a,b>0\) for the partial sums over the other coordinates, \(B(t)=\big(a+f_1(u)\,t\big)\big/\big(b+f_0(u)\,t\big)\), whose derivative \(B'(t)=\big(f_1(u)\,b-f_0(u)\,a\big)\big/\big(b+f_0(u)\,t\big)^2\) has a sign independent of \(t\): a ratio of two affine functions of \(t\) is monotone across the whole interval, since the numerator of \(B'(t)\) never changes sign. A function monotone in each coordinate separately attains its maximum over the box \([1,R]^{\mathcal{U}}\) at a vertex, because moving any single coordinate toward its better endpoint never lowers \(B\), so no interior point can be optimal; hence the optimum has every \(p_0(u)\in\{1,R\}\), and coordinate ascent reaches it.
The two-cell reduction. At such a vertex, partition \(\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}_R\sqcup\mathcal{U}_1\) with \(p_0=R\) on \(\mathcal{U}_R\) and \(p_0=1\) on \(\mathcal{U}_1\). Put \(a=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}_R}f_1(u)\) and \(b=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}_R}f_0(u)\), the masses the two confounder distributions place on the high-risk set. Then \(\sum_u p_0(u)f_1(u)=R\,a+(1-a)=1+(R-1)a\) and likewise the denominator is \(1+(R-1)b\), so \[
B=\frac{1+(R-1)a}{1+(R-1)b}.
\tag{28.8}\] This is increasing in \(a\) and decreasing in \(b\). The pointwise constraint gives \(a=\sum_{\mathcal{U}_R}f_1\le S\sum_{\mathcal{U}_R}f_0=S\,b\), and of course \(a\le 1\); so for fixed \(b\) the largest feasible \(a\) is \(\min(1,S b)\).
Optimizing the two cells. If \(Sb\le 1\), set \(a=Sb\); then \(B=\big(1+(R-1)Sb\big)\big/\big(1+(R-1)b\big)=:g(b)\), and the numerator of \(g'(b)\) is \[
(R-1)S\big(1+(R-1)b\big)-\big(1+(R-1)Sb\big)(R-1)
=(R-1)\big[S+S(R-1)b-1-(R-1)Sb\big]=(R-1)(S-1)\ge 0,
\] where the two middle terms \(S(R-1)b\) and \((R-1)Sb\) cancel; so \(g\) increases and we push \(b\) up to the regime boundary \(Sb=1\), that is \(b=1/S\) with \(a=1\). If instead \(Sb>1\), then \(a=1\) and \(B=R\big/\big(1+(R-1)b\big)\) decreases in \(b\), so we push \(b\) down to the same boundary \(b=1/S\). Either way the maximum is at \(a=1\), \(b=1/S\), giving \[
B^{\star}=\frac{1+(R-1)}{1+(R-1)/S}=\frac{R}{(S+R-1)/S}=\frac{RS}{R+S-1}
=\frac{\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\,\mathrm{RR}_{UD}}{\mathrm{RR}_{EU}+\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1}=\mathrm{BF}_U,
\] which is Equation 28.6.
Sharpness. The optimizing configuration is realizable with a two-point confounder \(\mathcal{U}=\{0,1\}\): take \(p_0(0)=1\), \(p_0(1)=R\), put all of the exposed mass on the high-risk level, \(f_1(1)=1\), and split the unexposed mass as \(f_0(1)=1/S\), \(f_0(0)=1-1/S\), which satisfies \(f_1(1)/f_0(1)=S\) and \(f_1(0)/f_0(0)=0\le S\). Substituting into Equation 28.7 returns \(B=\mathrm{BF}_U\) exactly, so no smaller bound is possible. \(\square\)


Remark. Why sharpness, not just validity, matters. Many sensitivity bounds are merely valid: the true bias is no larger than the bound. Sharpness says more, that the bound is attained by an actual confounder configuration, so it cannot be improved. This is what lets the E-value be an exact threshold rather than a conservative guess. A valid but loose bound would overstate how much confounding is needed and so overstate robustness; a bound that is attained means “an association of exactly the stated size on both legs is enough, and nothing weaker is”, which is the precise claim a reader can act on. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The bound depends on the data only through the two sensitivity parameters, and it is symmetric in them: \(\mathrm{BF}_U\) is unchanged under \(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\leftrightarrow\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\). The E-value is the point on the curve \(\mathrm{BF}_U=\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) where the two parameters are equal.

Theorem 28.1 (The E-value and its minimality) Let \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}>1\) be an observed risk ratio (for a protective effect \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}<1\), replace it by \(1/\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) throughout). Define the E-value \[
E\;=\;\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}+\sqrt{\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}\,(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}-1)}.
\tag{28.9}\] Then:

Unmeasured confounding can fully explain the observed association away (reduce the true risk ratio to the null) only if the two sensitivity parameters satisfy \(\mathrm{BF}_U=\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\mathrm{RR}_{UD}/(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}+\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)\ge\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}\).
Setting \(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=E\) achieves equality \(\mathrm{BF}_U=\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}\), and \(E\) is the smallest common value with this property.
\(E\) is minimal in the strong sense that if both sensitivity parameters are strictly below \(E\) then \(\mathrm{BF}_U<\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}\), so the result cannot be explained away: at least one of \(\mathrm{RR}_{EU},\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\) must be at least \(E\).

Moreover \(E\ge 1\), with \(E=1\) iff \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}=1\), and \(E\) is strictly increasing in \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}\), so a larger observed effect is harder to explain away.


Proof. Part 1. Write \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{true}}\cdot B\) with \(B\) the confounding bias factor. “Explaining away” means \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{true}}\le 1\), i.e. \(B\ge\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}\). By Lemma 28.2 the largest bias factor attainable with sensitivity parameters \((\mathrm{RR}_{EU},\mathrm{RR}_{UD})\) is \(\mathrm{BF}_U\), so such a \(B\) exists only if \(\mathrm{BF}_U\ge\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}\).
Part 2. On the diagonal \(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=v\ge 1\), \(\mathrm{BF}_U(v,v)=v^2/(2v-1)\). Setting this equal to \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}=:\rho\) gives \(v^2=\rho(2v-1)\), i.e. the quadratic \(v^2-2\rho v+\rho=0\), whose roots are \(v=\rho\pm\sqrt{\rho^2-\rho}=\rho\pm\sqrt{\rho(\rho-1)}\). The smaller root is below \(1\) for \(\rho>1\) (at \(\rho=2\) it equals \(2-\sqrt2\approx0.586\)), hence infeasible: \(v\) is a common value of the two sensitivity parameters, which are risk ratios of associations and so are at least \(1\) by construction (Equation 28.5), forcing \(v\ge1\); the admissible root is the larger one, \(E=\rho+\sqrt{\rho(\rho-1)}\), which is Equation 28.9. To see \(E\) is the smallest common value giving \(\mathrm{BF}_U\ge\rho\), note \(\psi(v):=v^2/(2v-1)\) has derivative \(\psi'(v)=\big(2v(2v-1)-2v^2\big)/(2v-1)^2=2v(v-1)/(2v-1)^2\ge 0\) for \(v\ge1\), so \(\psi\) is increasing; thus \(\mathrm{BF}_U(v,v)=\psi(v)\ge\rho\) holds exactly for \(v\ge E\).
Part 3. The bias factor is increasing in each argument: with \(x=\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\), \(y=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\), \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{xy}{x+y-1}=\frac{y(x+y-1)-xy}{(x+y-1)^2}=\frac{y(y-1)}{(x+y-1)^2}\ge0,
\] and symmetrically in \(y\). Hence if \(x<E\) and \(y<E\) then \(\mathrm{BF}_U(x,y)<\mathrm{BF}_U(E,E)=\rho=\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}\), contradicting Part 1; so at least one parameter is \(\ge E\). Finally \(E(\rho)=\rho+\sqrt{\rho(\rho-1)}\) has \(E(1)=1\) and \(E'(\rho)=1+\frac{2\rho-1}{2\sqrt{\rho(\rho-1)}}>0\) for \(\rho>1\), so \(E\ge1\) with equality iff \(\rho=1\), and \(E\) strictly increases in \(\rho\). \(\square\)


Remark. Why this matters, and a feel for the formula. The E-value converts an estimate into a robustness score on the same scale a clinician already uses for risk ratios, which is why it travels well into an HTA report and why it now appears routinely alongside NMA and ITC estimates. A quick numerical anchor: for an observed \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}=2\), \(E=2+\sqrt{2\cdot 1}=2+\sqrt2\approx 3.41\), so confounding would need a risk-ratio strength above \(3.4\) on both legs to erase a doubling of risk. The shape \(E=\rho+\sqrt{\rho(\rho-1)}\) repays reading: near the null (\(\rho\to 1^{+}\)) it behaves like \(1+\sqrt{\rho-1}\), rising as the square root of the excess, so a barely significant estimate has an E-value only a little above \(1\) and is easy to explain away; for large \(\rho\) it grows like \(2\rho\), so strong estimates demand proportionally strong confounding. For our COPD running example the plug-in effect is \(\mathrm{RR}=0.50\), giving \(E\approx 3.44\) (computed in Section 28.8); an unreported prognostic difference weaker than a \(3.4\)-fold association on each leg cannot overturn it. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reading and reporting the E-value. The E-value translates a point estimate into a single interpretable number: an unmeasured confounder (or, in the ITC setting below, an unmeasured effect modifier) would have to be associated with both the treatment assignment and the outcome by a risk ratio of at least \(E\), beyond the measured covariates, to explain the observed effect away; anything weaker cannot. A large \(E\) signals a robust finding, a small one a fragile finding. One also reports the E-value of the confidence-interval limit nearest the null, computed by Equation 28.9 with \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) replaced by that limit (and equal to \(1\) when the interval already includes the null): it is the strength of confounding needed to shift the interval to touch the null. The E-value is a property of the estimate alone, requiring no specification of the bias parameters; that economy is its appeal and also its limitation, since it is silent on whether confounding of strength \(E\) is plausible. The general bound was established by Ding and VanderWeele and popularized as the E-value by VanderWeele and Ding (2017); the same \(\mathrm{BF}_U\) bounds the bias for total-population standardization, not only the effect-on-treated standardization we proved. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Mind the scale: the E-value lives on the risk-ratio scale. Formula Equation 28.9 takes a risk ratio. Feeding it a log odds ratio, or an odds ratio for a common outcome, is a common and consequential misuse. Convert first. The practical rules, with the approximate conversions of VanderWeele and Ding (2017), are collected here.

title: 28  Quantitative Bias Analysis for Indirect Comparisons
text:
28.4 The indirect-comparison E-value
In a classical observational study both sensitivity parameters in Equation 28.5 are unknown, and the symmetric E-value is the natural summary. An unanchored indirect comparison is different in a way that can be exploited. The covariate that threatens the comparison, an effect modifier (Definition 11.3) that is imbalanced between the IPD and comparator populations and is unreported by the comparator, is nonetheless observed in the analyst’s own IPD. Its association with the outcome is therefore estimable from the IPD outcome model, even though its distribution in the comparator population is not. One of the two arms of the bias factor becomes known data rather than an assumed sensitivity parameter, and the E-value sharpens accordingly.
The map from the classical confounding picture to the indirect-comparison picture is worth pinning down, because every symbol in the E-value derivation keeps its algebra but changes its clinical referent.







Classical confounding (Section 28.3)
Unanchored ITC (this section)




exposure \(A\in\{0,1\}\)
trial-population membership: IPD population versus comparator population

the IPD (index-treatment) population
