The last row is the whole point: half of the sensitivity problem is estimated rather than guessed.
We set the stage with the unanchored estimand of Chapter 17. The IPD study fits an outcome model \(g\big(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid \mathbf{x},u]\big)=\beta_0+\boldsymbol{\beta}_R^{\top}\mathbf{x}+\beta_U u\) on the reported covariates \(\mathbf{x}\) and the unreported covariate \(U\). The comparator-population effect of the index treatment against the comparator, on the analysis scale, is the g-computation contrast \[
\Delta=g\!\left(\int g^{-1}\!\big(\beta_0+\boldsymbol{\beta}_R^{\top}\mathbf{x}+\beta_U u\big)\,
dF_0(\mathbf{x},u)\right)-g(\mu_0),
\tag{28.10}\] where \(F_0\) is the comparator covariate distribution and \(\mu_0\) its reported outcome under the comparator treatment. In words, reading Equation 28.10 from the inside out: take the IPD outcome model, predict each comparator patient’s risk as if they had received the index treatment from their covariates \((\mathbf{x},u)\), average those predicted risks over the comparator population \(F_0\), transform that average back to the analysis scale with \(g\), and subtract the comparator’s own reported outcome \(g(\mu_0)\). The result is what the index-versus-comparator contrast would be in the comparator population. The bias from omitting \(U\) is the gap between \(\Delta\) computed with \(U\) held at the analyst’s best guess (its IPD value) and \(\Delta\) computed at \(U\)’s true, unknown comparator value. On the risk-ratio scale this bias is a bias factor, and the question of the E-value is how large the across-arm imbalance of \(U\) must be to produce it, given that \(U\)’s outcome association is pinned down by the IPD.
Two things need saying before the definition. First, what “\(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\)” means: it is not the treatment effect but the amount of bias that would have to be present to nullify it, read on the ratio scale. If the adjusted risk ratio is \(0.50\), explaining it away means multiplying it back up to \(1\), a factor of \(2\); so \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=1/0.50=2.0\), and in general \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\exp(|\Delta_{\mathrm{IPD}}|)\), where \(\Delta_{\mathrm{IPD}}\) is the log-scale adjusted effect with the unreported covariate held at its IPD value. “Held at its IPD value” means the comparator population is given the covariate’s IPD distribution as a best guess, so \(\Delta_{\mathrm{IPD}}\) is the plug-in adjusted effect, not the covariate’s raw mean. Second, why the formula has three cases: with the outcome association fixed at \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\), the bias factor can never exceed \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\) no matter how extreme the imbalance (proved as Proposition 28.1 below), so the equation \(\mathrm{BF}_U=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) has a finite solution only when \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}<\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\); that ceiling is what splits the definition into its three branches.

Definition 28.2 (The indirect-comparison E-value) Consider an unanchored indirect comparison on a ratio scale (binary or count outcome). Let \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\ge 1\) be the observed bias factor, the ratio-scale magnitude \(\exp(|\Delta_{\mathrm{IPD}}|)\) of the adjusted effect Equation 28.10 evaluated with the unreported covariate held at its IPD value, and let \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=\exp(|\beta_U|)\ge 1\) be the IPD-estimated association of the unreported covariate \(U\) with the outcome, conditional on the reported covariates. The indirect-comparison E-value is the minimum across-arm association \(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\) that the unreported covariate must have, given \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\), to produce a bias factor as large as \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\): \[
E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=
\begin{cases}
1, & \mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\le 1,\\[2pt]
\dfrac{\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\,(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)}{\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}},
& 1<\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}<\mathrm{RR}_{UD},\\[8pt]
+\infty, & \mathrm{RR}_{UD}\le\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}.
\end{cases}
\tag{28.11}\] \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reading the three cases. The indirect-comparison E-value answers one question, “how imbalanced would the unreported covariate have to be, across the two trial populations, to overturn the result, given how strongly the IPD says it acts on the outcome?”, and its three cases are three honest answers. If \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\le 1\) the estimate already sits at or past the null and no bias is needed, so \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=1\). If \(1<\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}<\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\) a finite imbalance suffices, and the formula returns exactly how much. If \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\le\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) the covariate is too weakly prognostic to matter: no imbalance, however extreme, can manufacture enough bias, and \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=+\infty\) certifies the result robust to this covariate. The word “infinite” here does not mean “no bias exists”; it means “no across-arm imbalance in this one covariate can explain the result away, under the single-covariate bias-factor model, with \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\) treated as fixed.” That narrower claim is exactly what a dossier can defend. For the running example the IPD gives \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=1.65\), below the needed \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=2.01\), so we land in the third case and \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=+\infty\) (computed in Section 28.8). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The three cases, and in particular the infinite case that the symmetric E-value can never deliver, follow from the same sharp bound.

Proposition 28.1 (Derivation and the robustness certificate) With \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) and \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\) as in Definition 28.2:

If \(1<\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}<\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\), the value Equation 28.11 is the unique \(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\) solving \(\mathrm{BF}_U(\mathrm{RR}_{EU},\mathrm{RR}_{UD})=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\), and it exceeds \(1\).
The maximum bias factor achievable by any finite across-arm imbalance, with the outcome association fixed at \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\), is \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\) itself: \(\lim_{\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\to\infty}\mathrm{BF}_U(\mathrm{RR}_{EU},\mathrm{RR}_{UD})=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\), the limit being approached from below and monotonically. Consequently, if \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\le\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\), no across-arm imbalance can overturn the result under the single-covariate bias model, and \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=+\infty\) is a provable robustness certificate.
When the IPD-estimated outcome association happens to equal the symmetric E-value, \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=E\) with \(E\) from Equation 28.9 applied to \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\), the indirect-comparison E-value coincides with it, \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=E\).



Proof. Part 1. Solve \(\mathrm{BF}_U(x,y)=\dfrac{xy}{x+y-1}=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) for \(x=\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\) with \(y=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\) fixed. Cross-multiplying, \(xy=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}(x+y-1)\), hence \(x\,(y-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}})=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}(y-1)\) and \(x=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}(y-1)/(y-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}})\), which is Equation 28.11. When \(1<\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}<y\) the denominator is positive and \(x>0\); moreover \(x-1=\big(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}(y-1)-(y-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}})\big)/(y-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}})
=(y-1)(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}-1)/(y-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}})>0\), so \(x>1\). Uniqueness is immediate since \(\mathrm{BF}_U(\cdot,y)\) is strictly increasing in its first argument (Part 3 of 2).
Part 2. For fixed \(y>1\), \(\mathrm{BF}_U(x,y)=\dfrac{xy}{x+y-1}=\dfrac{y}{1+(y-1)/x}\uparrow y\) as \(x\to\infty\), monotonically since \((y-1)/x\) decreases. Thus the achievable bias factor is bounded above by \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\). If \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\le\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) the target is unreachable for every finite imbalance, so the minimal sufficient \(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\) is \(+\infty\) by convention, and the result cannot be explained away by imbalance in \(U\) alone no matter how extreme; this is the certificate. (Algebraically, the formula Equation 28.11 has a nonpositive denominator here, confirming no finite solution.)
Part 3. If \(y=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=E\) then, by Part 2 of 2, \(\mathrm{BF}_U(E,E)=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\), so \(x=E\) already solves the equation; by uniqueness \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=E\). \(\square\)


Corollary 28.1 (The indirect-comparison E-value against the symmetric one) Fix an observed bias factor \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\rho>1\) and regard \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}\) as a function of the IPD-estimated outcome association \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=y\). On the finite range \(y>\rho\) the map \(y\mapsto E_{\mathrm{ITC}}(y)=\rho(y-1)/(y-\rho)\) is strictly decreasing, with \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}(y)\to+\infty\) as \(y\downarrow\rho\) and \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}(y)\to\rho\) as \(y\to\infty\). It crosses the symmetric E-value \(E=\rho+\sqrt{\rho(\rho-1)}\) exactly at \(y=E\): for \(\rho<y<E\) it exceeds \(E\), and for \(y>E\) it is smaller than \(E\).


Proof. Differentiating, \[
\frac{d}{dy}\,\frac{\rho(y-1)}{y-\rho}
=\rho\,\frac{(y-\rho)-(y-1)}{(y-\rho)^2}
=\frac{\rho(1-\rho)}{(y-\rho)^2}<0
\quad\text{for }\rho>1,
\] so \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}\) strictly decreases on \(y>\rho\). The two limits are immediate from the rational form: as \(y\downarrow\rho\) the denominator \(\to 0^{+}\) with positive numerator, and as \(y\to\infty\) the ratio \(\rho(y-1)/(y-\rho)\to\rho\). By Proposition 28.1(3), \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}(E)=E\); strict monotonicity then forces \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}(y)>E\) for \(\rho<y<E\) and \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}(y)<E\) for \(y>E\). \(\square\)


Remark. What “sharper” does and does not mean. It is tempting to say the indirect-comparison E-value is “always larger because it uses more information”; Corollary 28.1 shows that is false. The ITC E-value is better calibrated, not uniformly larger: by plugging in the known \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\) it can land above or below the symmetric E-value. A weakly prognostic unreported covariate (\(y<E\), and especially \(y\le\rho\)) is harder or impossible to weaponize, so more imbalance would be required and \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}>E\); a strongly prognostic one (\(y>E\)) needs less imbalance to do damage, so \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}<E\). Using the data can cut either way, and that honest calibration, not a guaranteed increase, is the gain. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why this is the honest summary for an unmeasured effect modifier. The infinite case has no analogue in the classical E-value, where both arms are unknown and the bias factor can be pushed arbitrarily high by sending both to infinity. Here one arm is data. If the IPD says \(U\) is only weakly prognostic (\(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\) small), then even a wildly imbalanced \(U\) cannot manufacture a large bias, and the unanchored comparison is robust to it whatever the comparator distribution turns out to be. This is exactly the residual-bias question raised by Theorem 12.6, now answered quantitatively for one covariate at a time. Three caveats must travel with the number, all visible in the derivation: it treats the IPD-estimated \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=\exp(|\beta_U|)\) as fixed, propagating none of that estimate’s sampling uncertainty; it is a single-covariate bias-factor argument, so several jointly imbalanced covariates require the multivariate analysis of 1; and it is a ratio-scale quantity, defined for binary and count outcomes, not for continuous or time-to-event effects, for which the tipping-point analysis of Section 28.6 is the appropriate instrument. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

section: 28.5 NORTA: imputing the unreported covariate distribution
text:
28.5 NORTA: imputing the unreported covariate distribution
Before any formulas, the practical problem NORTA solves. The comparator publication gives you a few margins: the distribution of each covariate on its own, usually just a mean and a standard deviation (age is \(62\pm 9\) years, say) or a prevalence (\(30\%\) are current smokers). A margin says nothing about how two covariates move together in that population, their dependence (do older patients tend to have worse lung function?). To recompute the adjusted effect you need the full joint distribution of all covariates in the comparator population, and you are missing two things: the margin of the unreported covariate, which you must assume, and all of the dependence, which the comparator never reports. NORTA fills both gaps in a disciplined way. You supply the assumed margins, and you borrow the dependence from the one place it is observed, your own IPD. The name is literal, normal to anything: start from correlated normal draws, which carry the borrowed dependence, then reshape each coordinate into the margin you want. The rest of this section makes “reshape” and “borrow the dependence” precise and flags that borrowing as the method’s key assumption.
The E-value summarizes the threat of a single unmeasured covariate without ever simulating it. To go further, to actually recompute the adjusted effect Equation 28.10 under an assumption about the unreported covariate, we must construct a comparator-population covariate distribution that (i) honors every reported marginal summary, (ii) places a chosen marginal on the unreported covariate, and (iii) carries a credible dependence structure linking them. Aggregate comparator data fix the margins but say nothing about the dependence (Sklar’s theorem, Theorem 22.5, makes this precise: the margins and the copula are separately specifiable). The only place the dependence is observed is the IPD. The NORTA (normal-to-anything) construction supplies exactly this: it glues the target margins to a Gaussian copula (Definition 22.5) whose correlation is borrowed from the IPD.

Theorem 28.2 (The NORTA construction) Let \(F_1,\dots,F_d\) be target univariate distribution functions, with generalized inverses \(F_j^{-1}\), and let \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\succeq 0\) be a correlation matrix (symmetric, unit diagonal). Draw \(\mathbf{Z}=(Z_1,\dots,Z_d)\sim\mathcal{N}_d(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega})\) and set \[
X_j\;=\;F_j^{-1}\!\big(\Phi(Z_j)\big),\qquad j=1,\dots,d,
\tag{28.12}\] where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function. Then:

(Exact margins.) For every target \(F_j\), discrete or continuous, \(X_j\sim F_j\).
(Induced copula.) If in addition every \(F_j\) is continuous, the joint distribution function of \(\mathbf{X}=(X_1,\dots,X_d)\) is \[
F_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x})=C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\big(F_1(x_1),\dots,F_d(x_d)\big),
\tag{28.13}\] so \(\mathbf{X}\) has margins \(F_1,\dots,F_d\) and Gaussian copula \(C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\); by uniqueness in Sklar’s theorem \(C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\) is the unique copula of \(\mathbf{X}\).



Proof. Part 1. Since \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) has unit diagonal, each \(Z_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), and \(\Phi\) is continuous, so by the probability integral transform (Theorem 22.4, part 2) the variable \(U_j:=\Phi(Z_j)\) is uniform on \((0,1)\). By the inverse-transform property (Theorem 22.4, part 1), \(F_j^{-1}(U_j)\sim F_j\) for any distribution function \(F_j\). Hence \(X_j=F_j^{-1}(\Phi(Z_j))\sim F_j\), with no continuity required.
Part 2. Let \(U_j=\Phi(Z_j)\) as above; by Proposition 22.1 the vector \((U_1,\dots,U_d)\) has joint distribution function exactly the Gaussian copula \(C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\). The defining equivalence of a generalized inverse, \(\{F_j^{-1}(u)\le x\}=\{u\le
F_j(x)\}\) (the Galois inequality Equation 22.12, used in Theorem 22.4), gives for each coordinate \(\{X_j\le x_j\}=\{F_j^{-1}(U_j)\le x_j\}=\{U_j\le F_j(x_j)\}\). Intersecting over \(j\), \[
F_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x})=P\Big(\bigcap_{j=1}^{d}\{X_j\le x_j\}\Big)
=P\Big(\bigcap_{j=1}^{d}\{U_j\le F_j(x_j)\}\Big)
=C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\big(F_1(x_1),\dots,F_d(x_d)\big),
\] which is Equation 28.13. With continuous margins, Sklar’s theorem (Theorem 22.5) says the copula in the factorization \(F_{\mathbf{X}}=C(F_1,\dots,F_d)\) is unique, and we have exhibited it as \(C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\). \(\square\)


Remark. Reader’s translation. Theorem 28.2 is the guarantee that the recipe does what the introduction promised. Part 1 says the simulated covariates land on exactly the margins you asked for (the assumed prevalence or mean is honored, discrete or continuous). Part 2 says the dependence you wired in through \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) comes out as exactly a Gaussian copula, with nothing sneaking in from the marginal reshaping. So you may choose margins and dependence separately and trust that both emerge as specified, which is what makes NORTA a reliable comparator-population generator. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The construction is exact for the margins but leaves one question open: how to choose \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) so that the simulated population reproduces the dependence seen in the IPD. The natural target is the rank correlation, because it is what survives the marginal transforms and because it is invariant to the choice of margins.

Lemma 28.3 (Spearman matching for the Gaussian copula) Let \((X_j,X_k)\) be constructed by Equation 28.12 with continuous margins and Gaussian-copula correlation \(\Omega_{jk}=\rho^{N}\). Then:

Spearman’s rank correlation \(\rho^{S}(X_j,X_k)\) depends only on the copula \(C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\), not on the margins \(F_j,F_k\); it equals \(\rho^{S}(Z_j,Z_k)\).
For the bivariate Gaussian copula, \(\rho^{S}=\frac{6}{\pi}\arcsin(\rho^{N}/2)\). Hence choosing \[
\rho^{N}=2\sin\!\big(\pi\,\rho^{S}_{\mathrm{IPD}}/6\big)
\tag{28.14}\] makes the simulated Spearman correlation equal the IPD Spearman correlation \(\rho^{S}_{\mathrm{IPD}}\) exactly.



Proof. Part 1. Spearman’s rho is the Pearson correlation of the probability-integral transforms, \(\rho^{S}(X_j,X_k)=\operatorname{corr}\!\big(F_j(X_j),F_k(X_k)\big)\). For continuous margins, \(F_j(X_j)=F_j\big(F_j^{-1}(\Phi(Z_j))\big)=\Phi(Z_j)\), since \(F_j\circ F_j^{-1}\) is the identity on the range of a continuous \(F_j\). The map \(\Phi\) is strictly increasing, so \(\operatorname{corr}(\Phi(Z_j),\Phi(Z_k))\) is a functional of the joint law of \((Z_j,Z_k)\) alone, hence of the copula; it does not involve \(F_j,F_k\). This proves the invariance and the identity \(\rho^{S}(X_j,X_k)=\rho^{S}(Z_j,Z_k)\).
Part 2. The identity \(\rho^{S}=\frac{6}{\pi}\arcsin(\rho^{N}/2)\) for a bivariate normal with correlation \(\rho^{N}\) is the classical “arcsine law” for the grade correlation of the Gaussian copula; we take it as a known property of the bivariate normal (see the Notes). Inverting, \(\rho^{N}=2\sin(\pi\rho^{S}/6)\), which is Equation 28.14; feeding the IPD value \(\rho^{S}_{\mathrm{IPD}}\) on the right reproduces it as the simulated Spearman correlation by Part 1. \(\square\)


Remark. Why rank correlation, and the discrete and definiteness caveats. The Pearson correlation of \((X_j,X_k)\) produced by Equation 28.12 is in general not \(\Omega_{jk}\): the nonlinear marginal transforms \(F_j^{-1}\circ\Phi\) distort linear correlation, and the distortion depends on the margins. Rank correlation is the right invariant precisely because, by Lemma 28.3, it passes through the transforms untouched, which is why the implementation borrows the IPD’s Spearman matrix and maps it by Equation 28.14. Two practical points. First, for a binary covariate (the unreported \(U\) is often binary) the margin is discrete, so Lemma 28.3 is approximate: the transform \(F_j(X_j)\) is no longer exactly uniform (Theorem 22.4, part 2 fails for discrete \(F\)), and the induced copula in Theorem 28.2 is one of the many copulas Sklar’s theorem allows rather than a unique one. The marginal-recovery guarantee (part 1) still holds exactly. Second, the element-wise transform Equation 28.14 applied to an empirical Spearman matrix need not return a positive semidefinite matrix, so before constructing the copula one projects it onto the nearest correlation matrix (symmetrize, floor the eigenvalues at a small positive value, and rescale to unit diagonal). Both adjustments are benign and standard. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. What actually changes when \(U\) is binary, and how much to trust the borrowed correlation. Two applied points, since the unreported covariate is often a binary flag (a biomarker-positive indicator, a smoking status). First, the discrete caveat above is narrow in its consequences. Marginal recovery stays exact: if you assume a comparator prevalence of \(30\%\), the simulated population has prevalence \(30\%\), full stop. What becomes approximate is only the dependence: the Spearman match Equation 28.14 no longer lands the simulated rank correlation exactly on the IPD value, and the copula is no longer unique. In practice this perturbs the induced covariate correlations slightly, and hence the adjusted effect slightly, but it never distorts the assumed prevalence, which is usually the very quantity the sensitivity analysis is sweeping. Second, borrowing the IPD dependence is a substantive assumption, not a technical convenience: it asserts that age and lung function (say) hang together in the comparator population the way they do in your trial. When that is doubtful, the honest move is to redo the analysis under a few alternative correlation matrices (including independence and a strong correlation of each sign) and report the range. If the conclusion is stable across them the borrowing did no harm; if it is not, the dependence itself has become a bias parameter deserving its own sensitivity sweep. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

With the comparator covariate population in hand, the deterministic ITC bias analysis is a sweep: choose a grid of assumed marginals for the unreported covariate, and for each one simulate the comparator population by Equation 28.12, marginalize the IPD outcome model over it, and record the adjusted effect Equation 28.10. The resulting curve is the input to the tipping-point and probabilistic analyses.

Example 28.2 (NORTA with a borrowed dependence, in closed form) The worked example of Section 28.8 takes the comparator covariates independent, which makes NORTA invisible; here we let NORTA do its job so the dependence is seen to bite. Keep the running COPD model \(\log P(Y=1\mid x_R,u)=\beta_0+\beta_R x_R+\beta_U u\) with \(\beta_R=0.4\), \(\beta_U=-0.5\), normal margins \(x_R\sim\mathcal{N}(1.0,0.5^2)\) (age) and \(u\sim\mathcal{N}(2.0,1.0^2)\) (\(\mathrm{FEV}_1\)), and comparator risk \(\mu_0=0.47\). Suppose the IPD reports a Spearman rank correlation between age and \(\mathrm{FEV}_1\) of \(\rho^{S}_{\mathrm{IPD}}=-0.3\) (older patients tend to have worse lung function). NORTA borrows it through Equation 28.14: the Gaussian-copula correlation is \[
\rho^{N}=2\sin\!\big(\pi\,(-0.3)/6\big)=2\sin(-0.1571)=-0.313.
\] For normal margins the copula correlation is the Pearson correlation, so \(\operatorname{Cov}(x_R,u)=\rho^{N}\sigma_R\sigma_U=-0.313\times 0.5\times 1.0=-0.1564\). The linear predictor \(W=\beta_0+\beta_R x_R+\beta_U u\) is then normal with variance \[
\operatorname{Var}(W)=\beta_R^2\sigma_R^2+\beta_U^2\sigma_U^2+2\beta_R\beta_U\operatorname{Cov}(x_R,u)
=0.04+0.25+2(0.4)(-0.5)(-0.1564)=0.29+0.0626=0.3526,
\] against \(\operatorname{Var}(W)=0.29\) under independence. By the log-normal mean \(\mathbb{E}[e^{W}]=\exp\!\big(\mathbb{E}[W]+\tfrac12\operatorname{Var}(W)\big)\), the dependence adds \(\tfrac12(0.3526-0.29)=0.0313\) to the log risk, so the adjusted log-risk-ratio moves from \(-0.700\) (the independence value of Section 28.8) to \(-0.700+0.0313=-0.669\), a risk ratio of \(e^{-0.669}=0.512\) instead of \(0.497\). Borrowing a realistic negative age-lung-function dependence nudges the estimate about \(3\%\) toward the null; a positive borrowed correlation would push it the other way. That shift, invisible to the margins alone, is exactly the information NORTA imports from the IPD. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 28  Quantitative Bias Analysis for Indirect Comparisons
text:
28.6 Tipping-point analysis
A sensitivity curve answers “what if the unreported mean were such-and-such?” The tipping point distills the curve to its single decision-relevant value: the assumed marginal of the unreported covariate at which the conclusion changes.

Definition 28.3 (Tipping point) Let \(m\mapsto\Delta(m)\) be the sensitivity curve that maps an assumed comparator marginal \(m\) of the unreported covariate \(U\) (its mean for a continuous covariate, its prevalence for a binary one) to the adjusted effect Equation 28.10 on the analysis scale, all other inputs held fixed. Fix a decision threshold \(c\) (the null value, \(c=0\) on a log-ratio or difference scale, by default). A tipping point is a value \(m^{\dagger}\) with \[
\Delta(m^{\dagger})=c.
\tag{28.15}\] The tipping gap is \(m^{\dagger}-\bar{x}_{U}\), the signed distance from the value \(\bar{x}_U\) the covariate takes in the IPD. Given a plausible range \([m_{\mathrm{lo}},m_{\mathrm{hi}}]\) for the comparator marginal, the conclusion is flagged fragile if \(m^{\dagger}\in[m_{\mathrm{lo}},m_{\mathrm{hi}}]\), since a believable comparator value would reverse it, and robust if \(m^{\dagger}\) lies outside the range. One may report the tipping point of the confidence limit nearest the threshold in place of the point estimate. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader’s translation. The tipping point is the sensitivity analysis a clinician can argue about directly, because it speaks in the covariate’s own units. It says: the conclusion holds unless the comparator’s true mean \(\mathrm{FEV}_1\) (or prevalence, for a binary covariate) is as extreme as \(m^{\dagger}\). You then ask a subject-matter question, not a statistical one: is \(m^{\dagger}\) inside the range of values the comparator population could plausibly have? If yes, the result is fragile; if no, it is robust. The tipping gap \(m^{\dagger}-\bar{x}_U\) measures how far the comparator would have to differ from your IPD before the story changes. For the running example this comes out at \(m^{\dagger}=0.6\) liters, against an IPD mean of \(2.0\) (see Section 28.8). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

For the tipping point to be a well-defined single number we need the sensitivity curve to be monotone, so that it crosses the threshold at most once. The next proposition shows monotonicity holds under the natural structural assumptions, via a coupling argument that fixes the copula draws and moves only the unreported margin.

Proposition 28.2 (Monotonicity and existence of the tipping point) Suppose the unreported covariate enters the IPD outcome model through a single term \(\beta_U u\) with \(\beta_U\neq 0\), the link \(g\) is continuous and strictly monotone (so \(g^{-1}\) is monotone), and the assumed marginal family \(\{F_{U,m}\}\) is ordered by first-order stochastic dominance in \(m\) through a quantile function \(F_{U,m}^{-1}(t)\) that is nondecreasing in \(m\) for each \(t\in(0,1)\) (as for a location family, where \(F_{U,m}^{-1}(t)=m+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(t)\), or a Bernoulli family, where \(F_{U,m}^{-1}(t)=\mathbf{1}\{t>1-m\}\)). Construct the comparator population by NORTA Equation 28.12 with a fixed correlation matrix and fixed reported margins. Then:

The sensitivity curve \(\Delta(m)\) is monotone in \(m\), strictly so where \(g^{-1}\) is strictly monotone; its direction is the sign of \(\beta_U\) (composed with the monotonicity of \(g\)).
If the threshold \(c\) lies between \(\Delta(m_{\mathrm{lo}})\) and \(\Delta(m_{\mathrm{hi}})\), a tipping point \(m^{\dagger}\in[m_{\mathrm{lo}},m_{\mathrm{hi}}]\) exists and is unique. If \(c\) lies outside the interval spanned by \(\Delta\) over the plausible range, there is no tipping point inside the range and the conclusion is robust on that range.


The idea behind the proof is simpler than its machinery. If pushing the unreported covariate up always moves the predicted outcome the same way, because it enters the model through a single term \(\beta_U u\) with a fixed sign, then the sensitivity curve can only go one direction and so crosses any threshold at most once. The one technical device is a coupling: use the same normal draws \(\mathbf{Z}\) for every assumed value \(m\), changing only the quantile function applied to the last coordinate, so that raising \(m\) raises that covariate for every simulated patient at once and never touches the others. Monotonicity then survives the averaging over patients.

Proof. Part 1. Realize the comparator covariates by the common-\(\mathbf{Z}\) coupling of Equation 28.12: draw \(\mathbf{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}_d(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega})\) once, set the reported coordinates \(X_{R,j}=F_{R,j}^{-1}(\Phi(Z_j))\) (independent of \(m\)) and the unreported coordinate \(U(m)=F_{U,m}^{-1}(\Phi(Z_d))\). By hypothesis \(F_{U,m}^{-1}(t)\) is nondecreasing in \(m\) for each fixed \(t=\Phi(Z_d)\), so for \(m\le m'\) we have \(U(m)\le U(m')\) pointwise in \(\mathbf{Z}\), while \(\mathbf{X}_R\) is unchanged. The linear predictor \(\eta(m)=\beta_0+\boldsymbol{\beta}_R^{\top}\mathbf{X}_R+\beta_U U(m)\) is therefore monotone in \(m\) with the sign of \(\beta_U\), pointwise in \(\mathbf{Z}\), and since \(g^{-1}\) is monotone, the per-subject prediction \(g^{-1}(\eta(m))\) is monotone in \(m\) pointwise. Taking expectation over \(\mathbf{Z}\) preserves the inequality, so the marginal mean \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Z}}[g^{-1}(\eta(m))]\) is monotone in \(m\); applying the monotone \(g\) and subtracting the constant \(g(\mu_0)\) leaves \(\Delta(m)\) monotone, with strictness inherited wherever \(g^{-1}\) is strictly monotone and \(\beta_U\neq0\).
Part 2. The curve \(\Delta\) is continuous in \(m\) (the integrand is continuous in \(m\) and bounded by an integrable envelope, so dominated convergence makes the marginal mean continuous; \(g\) is continuous). A continuous monotone function on \([m_{\mathrm{lo}},m_{\mathrm{hi}}]\) attains the value \(c\) exactly once when \(c\) lies between its endpoint values (intermediate value theorem plus injectivity from strict monotonicity), giving a unique \(m^{\dagger}\) in the range; if \(c\) is outside the endpoint interval, \(\Delta-c\) keeps a constant sign on the range, so no crossing occurs and the sign of the conclusion is constant, i.e. robust. \(\square\)


Remark. Computation and the link to the E-value. In practice the curve is evaluated on a grid by the NORTA marginalization of 1, and the crossing is located by one-dimensional root-finding (interpolation plus a bracketed solver) on the grid. The tipping point and the indirect-comparison E-value are two windows onto the same residual bias: the tipping point speaks in the natural units of the covariate’s comparator marginal, which is the most transparent scale for a clinician to judge plausibility, while \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}\) recasts the same threat as a ratio-scale association. They can give qualitatively different impressions, since a small tipping gap and a large \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}\) both occur, and reporting both is the cautious practice. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: 28  Quantitative Bias Analysis for Indirect Comparisons
text:
28.7 Probabilistic bias analysis
Deterministic analysis commits to a single bias parameter or sweeps a bare grid. Probabilistic bias analysis instead places a prior distribution over the bias parameters and propagates it, separating two kinds of uncertainty that a single confidence interval conflates: the systematic uncertainty from not knowing the bias parameter, and the ordinary random sampling uncertainty.

Definition 28.4 (Probabilistic bias analysis) Let \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\mathbf{b})\) be the QBA correction Equation 28.1 and let \(\pi\) be a prior on the bias parameter \(\mathbf{b}\in\mathcal{B}\), encoding external evidence about it. The probabilistic bias analysis draws \(\mathbf{b}^{(s)}\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}\pi\) for \(s=1,\dots,S\), computes the adjusted effects \(\theta^{(s)}=\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\mathbf{b}^{(s)})\), and reports two intervals:

the systematic interval, the central \(1-\alpha\) empirical quantiles of \(\{\theta^{(s)}\}_{s=1}^{S}\), which captures bias-parameter uncertainty alone;
the total interval, the same quantiles of the error-perturbed draws \(\theta_{\mathrm{tot}}^{(s)}=\theta^{(s)}+\varepsilon^{(s)}\) with \(\varepsilon^{(s)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathrm{SE}^2)\) independent draws of the sampling error, which folds ordinary statistical uncertainty on top.

Draws that violate a structural constraint (a negative reconstructed cell count, an out-of-range prevalence) are discarded, and the retained fraction is reported. The probability of benefit is the share of draws on the favorable side of the threshold, \(\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{ben}}=S^{-1}\sum_s\mathbf{1}\{\theta^{(s)}\text{ favorable}\}\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Where the prior comes from, and which draws to throw away. The prior \(\pi\) is a sensitivity assumption, external evidence about the bias parameter, never new data from the trial, and it must be defensible in a report. Practical defaults: for a continuous comparator mean, center a normal or truncated normal prior at the IPD value and set its standard deviation to a fraction of the IPD standard deviation (a half or a third), widening it when the comparator population is known to differ; for a binary comparator prevalence, elicit a plausible interval from a clinician and fit a Beta prior whose central range matches it (for instance \(\mathrm{Beta}(2,8)\) has mean \(0.2\) and most of its mass in \([0.03,0.45]\)). Registries, baseline tables of related trials, and epidemiologic cohorts are the usual sources; when nothing is known, a deliberately wide prior is the conservative choice. Invalid draws are those a prior can produce but the world cannot: a normal prior on a prevalence can wander below \(0\) or above \(1\), a drawn covariance can be incompatible with the fixed margins, a reconstructed cell count can go negative. These are discarded and the retained fraction reported; a large discard rate is itself a warning that the prior is misspecified. In the running example the prior is \(\mathcal{N}(2.0,0.3^2)\), an IPD-centered normal whose standard deviation is about a third of the IPD’s (see Section 28.8). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The two intervals estimate well-defined population quantities, and the Monte Carlo estimates converge to them; we record this so the procedure is not merely a heuristic.

Theorem 28.3 (Consistency of the probabilistic-bias-analysis intervals) Let \(\theta=\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\mathbf{b})\) with \(\mathbf{b}\sim\pi\) have distribution function \(G_{\mathrm{sys}}\) (the law of the correction under the prior, the systematic distribution), and let \(G_{\mathrm{tot}}\) be the law of \(\theta+\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathrm{SE}^2)\) independent of \(\theta\), that is the convolution \(G_{\mathrm{tot}}(t)=\int\Phi\!\big((t-\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\mathbf{b}))/\mathrm{SE}\big)\,d\pi(\mathbf{b})\). As the number of draws \(S\to\infty\):

The empirical quantiles of \(\{\theta^{(s)}\}\) converge almost surely to the quantiles of \(G_{\mathrm{sys}}\) at every continuity point of \(G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{-1}\); likewise the error-perturbed quantiles converge to those of \(G_{\mathrm{tot}}\).
\(\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{ben}}\to P(\theta\text{ favorable})\) almost surely.
\(G_{\mathrm{tot}}\) is continuous and strictly increasing wherever \(\mathrm{SE}>0\), so its quantiles are unique and the total interval is well defined for every \(\alpha\).



Proof. Part 1. The draws \(\theta^{(s)}=\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\mathbf{b}^{(s)})\) are independent and identically distributed with distribution function \(G_{\mathrm{sys}}\), so by the Glivenko-Cantelli theorem the empirical distribution function \(\widehat{G}_{S}\) converges to \(G_{\mathrm{sys}}\) uniformly, almost surely. Uniform convergence of distribution functions implies convergence of the corresponding quantile (generalized inverse) functions at every point where \(G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{-1}\) is continuous, which is the standard quantile-convergence consequence of Glivenko-Cantelli. For the total interval, note \(\theta_{\mathrm{tot}}^{(s)}=\theta^{(s)}+\varepsilon^{(s)}\) are iid with distribution function \(G_{\mathrm{tot}}\) (the independent sum has the stated convolution law), and apply Glivenko-Cantelli again.
Part 2. The indicators \(\mathbf{1}\{\theta^{(s)}\text{ favorable}\}\) are iid Bernoulli with mean \(P(\theta\text{ favorable})\) and finite variance, so the strong law of large numbers gives \(\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{ben}}\to P(\theta\text{ favorable})\) almost surely.
Part 3. For \(\mathrm{SE}>0\) the inner map \(t\mapsto\Phi((t-\theta_0)/\mathrm{SE})\) is continuous and strictly increasing for each \(\theta_0\), and these properties are preserved under the mixture \(\int(\cdot)\,d\pi\): continuity by dominated convergence (the integrand is bounded by \(1\)), strict monotonicity because for \(t<t'\) the integrand strictly increases for every \(\theta_0\) and the prior integrates a strictly positive gap to a positive number. Hence \(G_{\mathrm{tot}}\) is a continuous, strictly increasing distribution function, with unique quantiles. \(\square\)


Remark. Interpretation. The systematic interval answers “how much does my conclusion move as the unknown bias parameter ranges over its prior?”; the total interval answers “and what does ordinary sampling error add on top?” Their difference is the price of the missing information, isolated from statistical noise; that separation is the entire point of probabilistic bias analysis (Lash et al. (2021)). In the unanchored ITC the bias parameter is the comparator marginal of the unreported covariate, the correction \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}\) is the NORTA marginalization, and a normal or beta prior on that marginal yields the two intervals directly. When the sensitivity curve is monotone (Proposition 28.2) the favorable fraction \(\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{ben}}\) is a clean Monte Carlo estimate of the prior probability that the comparator marginal lies on the favorable side of the tipping point. In the language of the rest of the book this is the same random-effects logic as a Bayesian NMA (Chapter 15), except the “random” quantity is not a study effect drawn from a hierarchical prior but the unreported covariate value drawn from an external prior, and the total interval is its predictive spread folded together with sampling error. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

section: 28.8 A worked E-value and tipping-point example
text:
28.8 A worked E-value and tipping-point example
We now carry the running COPD comparison of Example 28.1 through every instrument of the chapter, choosing the numbers so that each quantity is exactly reproducible by hand. Recall the setup: the new inhaled therapy \(B\) is compared, unanchored, against comparator \(A\) on the binary outcome severe exacerbation within 12 months, analyzed on the log-risk-ratio scale. The IPD outcome model, fitted with a log link, is \[
\log P(Y=1\mid x_R,u)=\beta_0+\beta_R\,x_R+\beta_U\,u,
\qquad
\beta_0=-1.0,\ \beta_R=0.4,\ \beta_U=-0.5,
\] where \(x_R\) is the one reported covariate (standardized age) and \(u\) the one unreported covariate (baseline \(\mathrm{FEV}_1\), a prognostic factor the comparator did not report). The comparator publication reports the marginal of \(x_R\) as mean \(m_R=1.0\), standard deviation \(\sigma_R=0.5\), and its own event risk \(\mu_0=0.47\); it does not report \(u\). In the IPD, \(u\) has mean \(\bar{x}_U=2.0\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_U=1.0\). For a hand-checkable marginalization we take \(x_R\) and \(u\) independent in the comparator population (Gaussian copula equal to the independence copula) and both normal.
The sensitivity curve in closed form. Under independence and normality, the comparator-population risk of the index treatment is a product of normal moment generating functions. With \(\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]=e^{t\mu+t^2\sigma^2/2}\) for \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \[
r_B(m)=\mathbb{E}\!\big[e^{\beta_0+\beta_R X_R+\beta_U U}\big]
=\exp\!\Big(\beta_0+\beta_R m_R+\tfrac12\beta_R^2\sigma_R^2+\beta_U m+\tfrac12\beta_U^2\sigma_U^2\Big),
\] where \(m\) is the assumed comparator mean of \(U\). The unanchored log-risk-ratio against the comparator is \(\Delta(m)=\log r_B(m)-\log\mu_0=K+\beta_U m\) with \[
K=\beta_0+\beta_R m_R+\tfrac12\beta_R^2\sigma_R^2+\tfrac12\beta_U^2\sigma_U^2-\log\mu_0.
\] Plugging in: \(\beta_R m_R=0.4\), \(\tfrac12\beta_R^2\sigma_R^2=\tfrac12(0.16)(0.25)=0.02\), \(\tfrac12\beta_U^2\sigma_U^2=\tfrac12(0.25)(1)=0.125\), and \(-\log(0.47)=0.755\), so \(K=-1.0+0.4+0.02+0.125+0.755=0.300\). The sensitivity curve is the line \[
\Delta(m)=0.300-0.5\,m,
\] monotone decreasing in \(m\) exactly as Proposition 28.2 predicts (sign of \(\beta_U=-0.5\)).
(a) The standard E-value. The natural plug-in for the unknown comparator mean of \(U\) is the IPD value \(\bar{x}_U=2.0\), giving the adjusted effect \(\Delta(2.0)=0.300-1.0=-0.700\), that is a risk ratio \(\mathrm{RR}=e^{-0.700}=0.497\): treatment \(B\) roughly halves the risk. The corresponding bias factor to explain this away is \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=e^{0.700}=2.014\). The symmetric E-value Equation 28.9 is \[
E=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}+\sqrt{\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}-1)}
=2.014+\sqrt{2.014\times1.014}=2.014+\sqrt{2.042}=2.014+1.429=3.443.
\] An unmeasured effect modifier would need a risk-ratio association of at least \(3.44\) with both the treatment-population membership and the outcome to nullify the result; an association of, say, \(1.5\) on each arm could not. Had the analysis instead reported a confidence limit nearest the null of, for example, \(\mathrm{RR}=1/1.3\) (i.e. bias factor \(1.3\)), its E-value would be \(1.3+\sqrt{1.3\times0.3}=1.3+0.625=1.925\).
(b) The tipping point. Solving \(\Delta(m^{\dagger})=0\) gives \(m^{\dagger}=0.300/0.5=0.600\). The tipping gap is \(m^{\dagger}-\bar{x}_U=0.600-2.000=-1.400\): the comparator’s true mean of \(U\) would have to fall to \(0.6\), far below the IPD value of \(2.0\), before the conclusion reverses. If the plausible range for the comparator mean is, say, \([1.4,2.6]\) (the IPD value plus or minus \(0.6\)), then \(m^{\dagger}=0.6\) lies outside it, and the conclusion is robust to the unreported covariate over the plausible range.
The whole sensitivity analysis fits in one small table. Sweeping the assumed comparator mean \(m\) of \(\mathrm{FEV}_1\) through the affine curve \(\Delta(m)=0.300-0.5\,m\) gives:

The tipping point \(m^{\dagger}=0.6\) sits well below the plausible range \([1.4,2.6]\), so every plausible comparator value leaves \(B\) favored: a table restatement of the robustness verdict.
(c) The indirect-comparison E-value. The IPD-estimated outcome association of \(U\) is \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=e^{|\beta_U|}=e^{0.5}=1.649\). Compare it to the observed bias factor \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=2.014\). Since \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=1.649<2.014=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\), we are in the third case of Definition 28.2: by Proposition 28.1 the maximal bias factor any imbalance in \(U\) can produce, with its outcome association fixed at \(1.649\), is \(1.649\) itself, which is smaller than the \(2.014\) needed. Hence \[
E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=+\infty:
\] no across-arm imbalance in \(U\) can overturn the result, a robustness certificate the symmetric E-value of part (a) cannot provide. This is the sentence such a certificate puts in a dossier: the unreported \(\mathrm{FEV}_1\), estimated from the IPD to carry an outcome association of \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=1.65\), is too weakly prognostic to matter; since no across-arm imbalance can produce a bias factor exceeding \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\), while a factor of \(2.01\) would be needed to nullify the result, the comparison is robust to \(\mathrm{FEV}_1\) regardless of its comparator distribution. To exhibit the finite formula, suppose instead the IPD had estimated a stronger prognostic covariate, \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=3.0\). Then \[
E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=\frac{\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)}{\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}}
=\frac{2.014\times(3.0-1)}{3.0-2.014}=\frac{4.028}{0.986}=4.085,
\] so the across-arm association would need to reach \(4.09\) to explain the result away. As a consistency check on Proposition 28.1(3), set \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=E=3.443\) from part (a); the formula returns \(2.014\times2.443/(3.443-2.014)=4.920/1.429=3.443=E\), recovering the symmetric E-value exactly, as it must when both arms are equal.
(d) Probabilistic bias analysis. Suppose external evidence supports a normal prior on the comparator mean of \(U\), \(m\sim\mathcal{N}(2.0,\,0.3^2)\), centered at the IPD value with a standard deviation of \(0.3\). Because the sensitivity curve is affine, \(\Delta(m)=0.300-0.5\,m\), the adjusted effect is itself normal: \[
\Delta\sim\mathcal{N}\!\big(0.300-0.5\times2.0,\ 0.5^2\times0.3^2\big)
=\mathcal{N}(-0.700,\ 0.0225),\qquad \mathrm{sd}=0.150.
\] The systematic \(95\%\) interval is \(-0.700\pm1.96\times0.150=(-0.994,\,-0.406)\), i.e. a risk ratio in \((0.370,\,0.666)\), entirely below \(1\). Folding in a trial sampling standard error of, say, \(\mathrm{SE}=0.25\), the total standard deviation is \(\sqrt{0.150^2+0.25^2}=\sqrt{0.085}=0.292\), and the total \(95\%\) interval is \(-0.700\pm1.96\times0.292=(-1.271,\,-0.129)\), a risk ratio in \((0.281,\,0.879)\), still below \(1\). The probability of benefit is \(\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{ben}}=P(\Delta<0)\): systematically \(\Phi(0.700/0.150)=\Phi(4.67)\approx1.000\), and in total \(\Phi(0.700/0.292)=\Phi(2.40)=0.992\). Every instrument agrees: the unreported effect modifier is a real but, here, a manageable threat, and the conclusion that \(B\) lowers risk survives it. The systematic interval, narrow because the prior is informative about the comparator mean, is exactly the “how much we do not know about \(U\)” component, cleanly separated from the wider total interval that adds sampling error.

28.9 Notes and references
The deterministic and probabilistic framework of Definition 28.1 and Definition 28.4 follows the monograph of Lash et al. (2021) (Fox, MacLehose, and Lash), which is the standard reference for the bias triangle, the confounding bias factor of Lemma 28.1, the selection and misclassification corrections mentioned in passing, and the systematic-versus-total interval decomposition. The bias factor Equation 28.2 for a binary confounder goes back to Schlesselman; we have reproduced only the confounding corner in full because it is the one the E-value rests on.
The E-value (2) and the sharp bias-factor bound (Lemma 28.2) are due to VanderWeele and Ding; we cite VanderWeele and Ding (2017), the article that introduced the E-value and its interpretation. The vertex argument and the two-cell optimization in our proof of Lemma 28.2 follow the structure of the Ding-VanderWeele “sensitivity analysis without assumptions” result; the derivation here standardizes to the exposed (the effect-on-treated bias factor), and the same bound is known to hold for total-population standardization. The indirect-comparison E-value of Definition 28.2 and the robustness certificate of Proposition 28.1 specialize the bound to the unanchored ITC by treating the \(U\)-outcome association as estimable from the IPD; this exploitation of the IPD is, to our knowledge, due to the recent ITC bias-analysis literature (Ren and colleagues, 2025) and is implemented in the uitc and mlumr packages, whose lessons informed the worked example. The connection to the insufficiency of the shared-effect-modifier assumption is Theorem 12.6, and the object being stress-tested is the effect modifier of Definition 11.3.
The NORTA construction (Theorem 28.2) is the normal-to-anything method of Cario and Nelson; it is the copula sampler of Proposition 22.1 composed with the inverse-CDF transform (Theorem 22.4), assembled into the Gaussian-copula joint law guaranteed by Sklar’s theorem (Theorem 22.5, Sklar (1959)). The same machinery underlies the ML-NMR integration of Chapter 22 and the ML-UMR pseudo-population of Chapter 26; here it is repurposed to impute an unreported comparator distribution rather than to integrate a reported one. The Spearman-matching transform Equation 28.14 rests on the arcsine law \(\rho^{S}=\frac{6}{\pi}\arcsin(\rho^{N}/2)\) for the grade correlation of the bivariate normal, a classical identity (Kruskal; see Nelsen’s copula text); we used it rather than reproved it, since a full derivation of the arcsine law is a self-contained exercise in bivariate-normal geometry. The positive-definite projection noted after Lemma 28.3 is the standard nearest-correlation-matrix repair.
This chapter has no counterpart in the proof catalogue and no machine-checked counterpart in the ITC_Coq development: quantitative bias analysis for indirect comparison is new material, built here from the cited primary sources. The tipping-point monotonicity proposition (Proposition 28.2) and the probabilistic-bias-analysis convergence theorem (Theorem 28.3) are, as far as we know, folklore made precise; their proofs use only the coupling of Equation 28.12 and the Glivenko-Cantelli theorem.
For the reader who wants to go deeper, the essential sources sort cleanly by instrument.

Quantitative bias analysis in general: Lash et al. (2021) (Fox, MacLehose, and Lash), the standard monograph, including the selection and misclassification corners of Section 28.2.2 that this chapter only sketches.
The E-value: VanderWeele and Ding (2017), for the definition, the interpretation, and the approximate scale conversions for odds and hazard ratios collected in Section 28.3.
NORTA and copulas: Cario and Nelson for the normal-to-anything construction, and Nelsen’s copula text for Sklar’s theorem and the arcsine law used in Lemma 28.3.
The ITC specialization: the recent indirect-comparison bias-analysis literature, implemented in the uitc and mlumr packages, for the exploitation of the IPD that gives Definition 28.2 its edge.

28.10 Exercises
A star (\(\star\)) marks an exercise with a full solution in Appendix F. The first three are warm-ups on reading and interpretation; the later ones build to the proofs.

Exercise 28.1 (Reading an E-value (warm-up)) A published unanchored comparison reports an adjusted hazard ratio of \(\mathrm{HR}=0.62\) (\(95\%\) confidence interval \(0.45\) to \(0.85\)) for a rare event, and states an E-value of \(2.6\) for the point estimate and \(1.7\) for the confidence limit nearest the null.

In one sentence, say what the number \(2.6\) means to a committee, using the phrase “risk-ratio association on both legs”.
A discussant claims an unmeasured prognostic difference between the trial populations could plausibly reach a risk-ratio association of \(1.5\) on each leg. Does that threaten the result? What association would?
Why is the confidence-limit E-value (\(1.7\)) the more conservative number to report?



Exercise 28.2 (Judging a tipping point (interpretation)) In the running COPD example the tipping point for the comparator mean of \(\mathrm{FEV}_1\) is \(m^{\dagger}=0.6\) liters, while the IPD mean is \(2.0\) liters and the plausible comparator range is \([1.4,2.6]\).

State, in clinical language, what would have to be true of the comparator population for the conclusion to reverse.
Is the conclusion fragile or robust on this range, and why? What single piece of external evidence would most change your verdict?



Exercise 28.3 (A dossier paragraph (interpretation)) Using the running example’s results (adjusted \(\mathrm{RR}=0.50\), symmetric E-value \(3.44\), indirect-comparison E-value \(+\infty\) because \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=1.65<2.01=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\), and tipping point \(m^{\dagger}=0.6\) outside the plausible range), write a single honest paragraph for an HTA committee stating the estimate, the robustness verdict, and the one caveat that still travels with it (the single-covariate, fixed-\(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\) assumption).


Exercise 28.4 (Computing E-values) An unanchored comparison reports an adjusted risk ratio of \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}=1.8\) with \(95\%\) confidence interval \((1.2,\,2.7)\).

Compute the E-value of the point estimate using Equation 28.9.
Compute the E-value of the confidence limit nearest the null.
A reviewer notes that the measured covariates leave at most a residual association of risk ratio \(1.4\) on each arm. Can unmeasured confounding of that strength explain the result away? Justify using






Exercise 28.5 (Protective effects) Show that for a protective observed effect \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}<1\), applying Equation 28.9 to \(1/\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) gives the same E-value as the following symmetric construction: the smallest \(E\ge 1\) such that confounding with \(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=E\) can raise the true risk ratio back up to the null. Compute the E-value for \(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}=0.5\).


Exercise 28.6 (The indirect-comparison E-value and its certificate (\(\star\))) Use the worked example’s model (same \(\beta_0,\beta_R,m_R,\sigma_R,\sigma_U\), comparator risk \(\mu_0=0.47\), IPD value \(\bar{x}_U=2.0\)), but now suppose the IPD estimates a stronger unreported covariate, \(\beta_U=-0.8\).

Recompute the constant \(K=\beta_0+\beta_R m_R+\tfrac12\beta_R^2\sigma_R^2+\tfrac12\beta_U^2\sigma_U^2
-\log\mu_0\), the sensitivity curve \(\Delta(m)=K+\beta_U m\), the adjusted effect \(\Delta(2.0)\), the observed bias factor \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\exp(|\Delta(2.0)|)\), and the outcome association \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=e^{|\beta_U|}\). (Both \(K\) and the slope change, since each depends on \(\beta_U\).)
Decide whether \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}\) is finite or infinite using Proposition 28.1, and compute it if finite. Then verify the finite formula on the artificial pair \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=1.5\), \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=2.5\).
Prove the general statement behind the certificate: for fixed \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}>1\), the bias factor \(\mathrm{BF}_U(\mathrm{RR}_{EU},\mathrm{RR}_{UD})\) is strictly increasing in \(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\) and bounded above by \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\), with the bound approached but never attained.



Exercise 28.7 (The sharp bound for a binary confounder) Specialize Lemma 28.2 to a binary confounder \(U\in\{0,1\}\) with unexposed-arm risks \(p_0(0),p_0(1)\) and confounder distributions \(f_1,f_0\). Starting from the exact bias factor Equation 28.7, verify directly (without the vertex argument) that \(B\le \mathrm{RR}_{EU}\mathrm{RR}_{UD}/(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}+\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)\), and identify the configuration of \((f_1,f_0,p_0)\) that attains equality. Confirm it matches the configuration in the proof of Lemma 28.2.


Exercise 28.8 (NORTA recovers any margin (\(\star\))) Let \(F\) be the Bernoulli\((\pi)\) distribution function and let \(Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\).

Write down \(F^{-1}\) (the generalized inverse) explicitly and show that \(X=F^{-1}(\Phi(Z))\) is Bernoulli\((\pi)\), confirming Theorem 28.2(1) for a discrete margin.
Show by counterexample that Theorem 28.2(2) can fail for this discrete margin: exhibit two distinct correlation parameters \(\rho^{N}\) that induce the same bivariate distribution of two such Bernoulli variables, so the copula is not unique. Explain why marginal recovery nonetheless still holds.
For a continuous margin, prove that the Pearson correlation of \((X_1,X_2)=\big(F_1^{-1}(\Phi(Z_1)),
F_2^{-1}(\Phi(Z_2))\big)\) need not equal \(\rho^{N}=\operatorname{corr}(Z_1,Z_2)\), by taking \(F_1=F_2\) a lognormal margin and computing both correlations for \(\rho^{N}=1\).



Exercise 28.9 (Tipping points for a nonmonotone curve) Suppose an analyst balances two unreported covariates \(U_1,U_2\) jointly, with the adjusted effect a function \(\Delta(m_1,m_2)\) of both assumed means.

Give an example of an outcome model and margins for which the single-covariate sensitivity curve \(m_1\mapsto\Delta(m_1,m_2^{0})\) (with \(m_2\) fixed) is not monotone, so that Proposition 28.2 does not apply. (Hint: let \(U_1\) enter the outcome model nonlinearly, for example through \(u_1^2\).)
Explain what “the tipping point” should mean when the sensitivity surface crosses the threshold on a curve rather than at a point, and how a plausible region (rather than a range) for \((m_1,m_2)\) enters the robust-versus-fragile verdict.



Exercise 28.10 (Probabilistic analysis with a beta prior) The unreported covariate is binary with comparator prevalence \(m\in(0,1)\), and the sensitivity curve is \(\Delta(m)=0.2-1.5\,m\) on the log-odds-ratio scale (threshold \(c=0\)). Place a Beta\((2,8)\) prior on \(m\) (mean \(0.2\)).

Find the tipping prevalence \(m^{\dagger}\) and decide robust-versus-fragile against the plausible range \([0.05,0.40]\).
Using that \(\Delta\) is a decreasing affine function of \(m\), express the probability of benefit \(P(\Delta<0)=P(m>m^{\dagger})\) in terms of the Beta\((2,8)\) distribution function, and state whether the systematic interval for \(\Delta\) excludes the null. (You may leave the Beta integral in closed form via its polynomial density.)






Lash, Timothy L., Matthew P. Fox, and Richard F. MacLehose. 2021. Applying Quantitative Bias Analysis to Epidemiologic Data. 2nd ed. Springer.


Sklar, Abe. 1959. “Fonctions de répartition à \(n\) Dimensions Et Leurs Marges.” Publications de l’Institut de Statistique de l’Université de Paris 8: 229–31.


VanderWeele, Tyler J., and Peng Ding. 2017. “Sensitivity Analysis in Observational Research: Introducing the e-Value.” Annals of Internal Medicine 167 (4): 268–74.

title: 29  Simulation Study Theory
text:
29.1 Introduction
The theorems of Parts II to V are limit statements. They certify that an estimator is consistent: that matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) recovers the target contrast as the index sample grows (Theorem 18.4), that the unanchored estimators do so only under the far stronger absolute-constancy hypothesis (Theorem 17.2), that multilevel network meta-regression removes the aggregation bias a standard network meta-analysis cannot (Theorem 20.2, Theorem 16.1). What these theorems do not say is how an estimator behaves at the sample sizes a health-technology-assessment dossier actually carries: a single index trial of a few hundred patients, a comparator known only through a published mean. Consistency is a statement about the horizon; the analyst stands at a finite distance from it. Four questions remain open at that distance, and none of them is answerable by a limit theorem alone.
How large is the finite-sample bias, and is the residual bias of an “asymptotically unbiased” method negligible at the sample size in hand? How does one method’s variance compare with another’s, so that a slightly biased but stable estimator can be preferred to an unbiased but volatile one? Do the nominal ninety-five percent confidence intervals actually contain the truth ninety-five percent of the time, or does the variance approximation that produced them quietly fail? And how do all of these degrade when the method’s assumptions are violated, when an effect modifier is omitted, when the populations barely overlap, when the outcome model is wrong? These are empirical questions about the sampling distribution of an estimator at finite \(n\), and the instrument that answers them is the simulation study: fix a data-generating mechanism whose truth you control, draw many datasets from it, apply each candidate method to each dataset, and summarize how the resulting estimates scatter around the known target. The decisive advantage of this instrument is that in a simulation we build the world ourselves, so the truth is known by construction: unlike a real analysis, where the target effect can never be observed and an estimator’s error can only be guessed at, a simulation lets us measure that error directly, by comparing every estimate against the number we put in.
This chapter is the mathematics of that instrument. The central conceptual move, which organizes everything that follows, is to recognize that a simulation study has two sample sizes, governing two asymptotics. The first is \(n\), the size of each simulated dataset; it controls the statistical behavior of the estimator and is the variable in every consistency theorem of the preceding chapters. The second is \(R\), the number of simulated datasets, the replications; it controls how precisely the simulation measures that behavior, and it is a budget the analyst sets, not a feature of the data. A performance measure such as bias or coverage is a functional of the estimator’s sampling distribution at a fixed \(n\), hence a fixed but unknown number; here a functional is simply a rule that takes an entire distribution as its input and returns a single number, the way a mean or a variance summarizes a distribution, and the sampling distribution in question, written \(F_n\) and defined precisely in Definition 29.2 below, is what the average estimates; the simulation estimates it by a Monte Carlo average over the \(R\) replications, an estimate that carries its own sampling error. Confusing the two asymptotics is the cardinal sin of simulation practice: reporting a bias to four decimal places from \(R=100\) replications, or declaring two methods’ coverages different when the difference is within Monte Carlo noise. We will be scrupulous about keeping them apart, and the recurring discipline is to attach to every reported performance number a Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) that quantifies the \(R\)-driven uncertainty.
The two sample sizes of a simulation, and the two limits they govern, can be laid side by side. The columns are independent: a large \(R\) cannot cure a small-\(n\) deficiency, and a large \(n\) cannot excuse too few replications.
The plan is as follows. Section 29.2 sets out the ADEMP framework of Morris et al. (2019), the now-standard checklist (aims, data-generating mechanism, estimands, methods, performance measures) that disciplines the design and reporting of a simulation study, and formalizes a simulation study as a triple of a sampling distribution, a family of performance functionals, and their Monte Carlo estimators (Definition 29.1, catalogue K.1). Section 29.3 treats bias and its Monte Carlo standard error, proving that the Monte Carlo bias estimator is exactly unbiased for the true bias with a variance that shrinks as \(1/R\) (Definition 29.3, K.2). Section 29.4 develops the empirical and model-based standard errors and interval coverage, proving the unbiasedness of the empirical variance and the binomial law of the coverage estimator (Definition 29.4, K.3). Section 29.5 proves the mean-squared-error decomposition into squared bias plus variance, both as a population identity and as an exact finite-sample identity for the Monte Carlo estimators (Theorem 29.1, K.4). Section 29.6 is the analytic heart of the chapter: it derives the limiting coverage of a Wald interval as an explicit function of a single standardized asymptotic bias parameter, showing that coverage is nominal exactly when the method is asymptotically unbiased and that under a fixed specification bias coverage collapses to zero as \(n\to\infty\), so that more data makes a biased method’s intervals worse (Theorem 29.2, K.5). Section 29.7 treats Type I error and power, which turn out to be the coverage theorem read through the duality of tests and intervals (Definition 29.5, K.6). Section 29.8 anchors the variance comparisons of a simulation in the Cramér-Rao bound (Theorem 5.7), the theoretical floor below which no regular method’s empirical standard error can fall. Section 29.9 states, as precisely as an empirical finding can be stated, the main robustness conclusion of the Phillippo (2019) simulation study and its unanchored extension (Proposition 29.2, K.7), tying each ranked claim either to a theorem proved earlier or to the cited simulation evidence. Section 29.10 carries a complete miniature simulation from its ADEMP specification through every performance computation by hand. This chapter owns catalogue results K.1 to K.7.
Throughout, \(\theta\) denotes the scalar estimand (a relative effect \(d_{ab(\mathcal{P})}\) on a stated scale, in the applications of interest), \(\hat\theta_n\) a method’s estimator computed from a dataset of size \(n\), \(\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n\) the standard error that method reports for it, and \(I_n\) the associated nominal \((1-\alpha)\) interval. A simulation produces \(R\) independent replicate values \(\hat\theta^{(1)}_n,\dots,\hat\theta^{(R)}_n\), with \(\bar{\hat\theta}=R^{-1}\sum_{r}\hat\theta^{(r)}_n\) their average. We write \(z_{\alpha/2}\) for the upper \(\alpha/2\) standard-normal quantile, so that \(\Phi(z_{\alpha/2})=1-\alpha/2\) and \(P(|Z|\le z_{\alpha/2})=1-\alpha\) for \(Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\); for the usual \(\alpha=0.05\), \(z_{\alpha/2}=1.96\). The asymptotic toolkit is the one assembled in Chapter 5: the weak law of large numbers, the central limit theorem, Slutsky’s theorem (Theorem 5.2), the continuous mapping theorem (Theorem 5.1), and the delta method (Theorem 5.3).
The chapter uses a compact vocabulary of performance quantities. The following glossary collects them; the single most important distinction, stressed throughout, is between the two kinds of standard error, the one a method reports for a single analysis and the one the simulation reports for its own summary.
The last row is not a property of any single analysis: it is the simulation’s own sampling error, and it is the quantity that shrinks when the analyst runs more replications. Confusing \(\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n\), the uncertainty in one estimate, with \(\mathrm{MCSE}\), the uncertainty in the reported bias, coverage, or mean squared error, is a frequent novice error; the two answer different questions and have different remedies.

A health-technology-assessment team must compare a new interleukin-23 inhibitor \(A\) against an established interleukin-17 inhibitor \(B\) for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. title: 29  Simulation Study Theory
text:
29.2 The ADEMP framework
A simulation study can be run badly in many ways: by simulating from a mechanism that no one can reconstruct, by reporting an estimand the methods were never trying to estimate, by summarizing with a statistic that hides the behavior of interest. Morris et al. (2019) distilled good practice into a five-part specification whose initials spell ADEMP. We adopt it as the definitional backbone of the chapter and then attach to it the probabilistic objects that the performance measures will be functionals of. The value of the checklist is that each letter forces one decision into the open where it can be criticized: the aims stop a study from being a fishing expedition, the data-generating mechanism makes the simulated world reproducible, the estimand fixes what “the truth” even is before any method is judged against it, the methods list what is being compared, and the performance measures decide what “good” means. A simulation that skips any one of these can silently answer the wrong question.

Definition 29.1 (The ADEMP framework for a simulation study) A simulation study is specified by five components.

Aims (A). The scientific questions to be answered, stated before any data are simulated: for example, “quantify the bias of MAIC for the marginal \(A\)-versus-\(B\) log-odds-ratio when a binary effect modifier is omitted, as a function of its imbalance between trials.”
Data-generating mechanism (DGM, D). A fully specified probability model \(\mathbb{P}=\mathbb{P}_n\) from which datasets of size \(n\) are drawn: the covariate distribution, the treatment assignment, the outcome model with all its parameters, and any features (overlap, effect-modification strength) that the aims require to be varied across scenarios. A study comprises a finite set of DGMs, one per scenario.
Estimands (E). The target quantities, defined as functionals \(\theta=\theta(\mathbb{P})\) of the DGM. In the population-adjustment setting \(\theta\) is a marginal relative effect \(d_{ab(\mathcal{P})}\) in a named target population \(\mathcal{P}\) on a named scale \(g\); because the DGM is known, \(\theta\) is known exactly, by analytic calculation or by a large auxiliary simulation.
Methods (M). The estimation procedures under comparison, each a measurable map from a dataset to a triple \((\hat\theta_n,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n,I_n)\) of a point estimate, a standard error, and a nominal \((1-\alpha)\) interval. In this book the methods are the naive Bucher comparison (Theorem 14.1), MAIC (Chapter 18), simulated treatment comparison (Chapter 19), and multilevel network meta-regression (Chapter 20), with their unanchored counterparts (Chapters 17, 26).
Performance measures (P). The summaries of a method’s behavior across replications: bias, empirical and model-based standard error, mean squared error, interval coverage, and, where the aim is testing, Type I error and power. Each is a functional \(\mu(F_n)\) of the sampling distribution \(F_n\) of \((\hat\theta_n,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n,I_n)\) under the DGM at fixed \(n\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)


The following table instantiates the five components for the running psoriasis comparison, so the abstract checklist has a concrete referent before we turn it into probability.







ADEMP component
The running psoriasis comparison




Aims
Quantify the bias and \(95\%\) interval coverage of MAIC and of the naive Bucher comparison for the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) PASI mean difference, as baseline-severity imbalance between the trials varies.


Data-generating mechanism
Draw \(n\) patients per arm; baseline severity \(x_1\) and age \(x_2\) from chosen distributions with a set between-trial imbalance; PASI reduction from a linear model with an \(x_1\)-by-treatment interaction; independent outcome noise. The \(BC\) trial is then reduced to arm means, mimicking the published aggregate data.


Estimands
\(\theta=d_{AB(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}\), the marginal \(A\)-versus-\(B\) mean difference in the \(BC\) population, computed exactly from the known model (Section 29.10).


Methods
MAIC (Chapter 18) and the naive Bucher comparison (Theorem 14.1), each returning an estimate \(\hat\theta_n\), a standard error \(\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n\), and a \(95\%\) interval \(I_n\).


Performance measures
Bias, empirical and model-based standard error, mean squared error, and coverage, each with its Monte Carlo standard error.



Which pieces are which is worth stressing, because a novice designing a simulation must know what to fix and what to vary. The covariate distributions and the outcome model are chosen by the analyst to resemble the real trials; the between-trial imbalance and the effect-modification strength are varied across scenarios, where each scenario is one cell of the design grid, that is, one combination of overlap, effect-modifier imbalance, effect-modification strength, and sample size; the trial sizes are set to mimic the real dossier; and the estimand is derived from the chosen model, not observed. Only the performance measures are outputs. A method, stripped of the formal language of measurable maps, is in plain terms a computer program that takes one simulated trial dataset and returns three things: a point estimate, a standard error, and a confidence interval.

Remark. How the truth is known, and how it is computed. In a real analysis the target effect \(\theta\) is unknown, which is the entire difficulty; in a simulation the analyst chose the data-generating mechanism, so \(\theta=\theta(\mathbb{P})\) is determined and can be computed to any desired accuracy. Computing it is a marginalization, not a guess. On the identity (mean-difference) scale of the running example, the marginal estimand is the average of the conditional treatment effect over the target population’s covariate distribution, \[
\theta=\int \tau(x)\,f_{\mathcal{P}}(x)\,dx,\qquad \tau(x)=\mu_1(x)-\mu_0(x),
\] which for a linear outcome model reduces to evaluating the conditional effect at the covariate mean. On a non-collapsible scale (Definition 7.7), such as a marginal log-odds-ratio, one cannot average the conditional log-odds-ratios: the truth must be obtained by marginal standardization, integrating the conditional outcome probabilities over \(f_{\mathcal{P}}(x)\) first, forming the marginal event probabilities under each treatment, and only then taking the contrast. When the integral has no closed form (a survival estimand, a probit-normal average), the analyst computes \(\theta\) by a large auxiliary simulation, drawing an enormous sample from the known mechanism and reading off the marginal effect; this auxiliary draw has nothing to do with the \(R\) replications and is made once, as accurately as compute allows. The lesson is that even with the model fully known, “the truth” for a marginal, non-collapsible estimand is an integral, which is exactly why population adjustment is subtle. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The fourth and fifth components hide the structure that makes the chapter mathematical. Fix a scenario (a DGM) and a method. Applying the method to a dataset of size \(n\) yields a random triple whose law, written \(F_n\), is the sampling distribution. Every performance measure is a deterministic functional of \(F_n\), hence a fixed number once \(n\) is fixed; what the simulation reports is a Monte Carlo estimate of that number.

Definition 29.2 (Performance measures as functionals; the two sample sizes) Let \(F_n\) be the sampling distribution of \((\hat\theta_n,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n,I_n)\) under a fixed DGM, and let \(\theta\) be the estimand. The performance measures are the functionals \[
\mathrm{Bias}_n=\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_n]-\theta,\quad
\mathrm{Var}_n=\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_n),\quad
\mathrm{MSE}_n=\mathbb{E}[(\hat\theta_n-\theta)^2],\quad
\mathrm{Cov}_n=P(\theta\in I_n),
\tag{29.1}\] all expectations and probabilities taken under \(F_n\). A Monte Carlo experiment draws \(R\) independent datasets from the DGM, producing independent and identically distributed (iid) replicate triples \((\hat\theta^{(r)}_n,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}^{(r)}_n,I^{(r)}_n)\), \(r=1,\dots,R\), each with law \(F_n\); the performance measures are estimated by their sample analogues over these \(R\) replicates. Two asymptotic regimes act on the experiment: the statistical limit \(n\to\infty\), which governs the functionals Equation 29.1 themselves and is the subject of the consistency theorems of earlier chapters; and the Monte Carlo limit \(R\to\infty\), which governs the precision with which the sample analogues estimate Equation 29.1. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Reader translation. Read \(F_n\) as the joint distribution of everything one run of a method produces on a dataset of size \(n\): the estimate, the standard error it reports, and the interval it forms. It is a distribution over a triple, not a single number, though most performance measures use only one margin of it, such as the spread of \(\hat\theta_n\). At a fixed \(n\) this artificial world has a definite true bias and a definite true coverage; we simply do not know them, because we cannot evaluate the distribution in closed form. So we do the next best thing: we rebuild the artificial world \(R\) times and average. Every performance number in this chapter is such an average, and every one therefore comes with a Monte Carlo standard error measuring how much the average would wobble if we reran the \(R\) replications. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why the two-sample-size view matters. A consistency theorem controls \(\mathrm{Bias}_n\to 0\) as \(n\to\infty\); it says nothing about how well \(R\) replications measure \(\mathrm{Bias}_n\) at a fixed, practically relevant \(n\). Conversely, no number of replications can reveal small-sample bias that the chosen \(n\) does not exhibit: pushing \(R\to\infty\) at fixed \(n\) converges the sample analogues to the exact functionals Equation 29.1 at that \(n\), not to their \(n\to\infty\) limits. The analyst chooses the grid of \(n\) values to span the regime of interest and chooses \(R\) large enough that Monte Carlo error does not swamp the differences between methods. The performance measures below are designed so that each comes with an MCSE quantifying exactly the second source of error. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The remaining sections instantiate the fifth ADEMP component, one performance measure at a time, proving in each case (i) what functional of \(F_n\) the measure targets, (ii) that the Monte Carlo estimator is unbiased or consistent for it, and (iii) the size of its Monte Carlo standard error. This corresponds to K.1 in the proof catalogue.

Remark. Numbers to hang the symbols on. It helps to carry one arithmetic instance through the definitions that follow. In the running example the true effect is \(\theta=1.5\) PASI points. Imagine five simulated trials of the adjusted method returning estimates \(0.9,0.9,1.4,1.9,1.9\) points. Their average is \(1.4\), so the estimated bias is \(1.4-1.5=-0.1\) point; their spread gives an empirical standard error of \(0.5\); and if three of the five \(95\%\) intervals contain \(1.5\), the estimated coverage is \(3/5=0.6\). Every definition below turns one of these back-of-envelope numbers into a general formula, and Section 29.10 works the same instance in full, including why five replications are far too few to trust any of these numbers. \(\blacktriangleleft\)
