title: Appendix A — Notation Glossary
text:
A.1 How to use this appendix
This appendix is the reference index for the book’s notation. It has two parts. The first repeats every symbol introduced in Notation, grouped by the same topics, and adds for each symbol a one-line gloss together with the chapter that introduces it, naming the defining environment by its slug where one exists. The second is an alphabetical glossary of every formally defined term in the book; each entry gives a one-sentence statement of the term and a pointer to the chapter and the definition slug that fixes it. The conventions themselves, that bold lowercase letters denote vectors and bold uppercase letters denote matrices, that random variables are capitalized when the distinction from a realized value matters, that an unsubscripted probability refers to the population under discussion, and that \(\square\) closes a proof while \(\blacktriangleleft\) closes a definition, example, or remark, are stated in Notation and are not repeated here. Nothing in this appendix is proved; it is a single place to look up a symbol or a definition and to follow the slug to the statement that establishes it.
Throughout, “Ch.” abbreviates chapter, and a slug such as @def-effect-modifier names the cross-referenceable definition environment in the chapter where the term is established; that slug is the exact cross-reference an author would use to cite the result.
There are two ways in. If you have seen a symbol and want to know what it is, use the symbol tables of Section A.6, grouped by role from linear algebra through population adjustment. If you have heard a term and want its meaning, use the alphabetical glossary of Section A.8; the clusters in Section A.7 gather related terms so a whole family can be read at once. In either place the final column names the chapter and, where a formal definition fixes the item, the slug of that definition. That slug is the cross-reference key that takes you to the formal definition in the chapter that establishes it. The chapter legend in Table A.1 turns each “Ch.” number into its subject and part, so that “Ch. 14” reads as “Bucher indirect comparison,” not a bare number.
Four short aids come before the tables: a compact key to the conventions (Section A.2), a worked notation key that maps the symbols onto a single anchored comparison (Section A.3), a table of symbols that carry more than one meaning (Section A.4), and a plain-language note on effect scales (Section A.5).

title: Appendix A — Notation Glossary
section: A.2 A compact key to the conventions
text:
A.2 A compact key to the conventions
The full conventions live in Notation; the few a reader most often needs are repeated here, since a reader who reaches for a glossary is usually already unsure. Bold lowercase letters (\(\mathbf{x}\), \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\)) are vectors; bold uppercase letters (\(\mathbf{X}\), \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\)) are matrices; plain letters are scalars. A capital letter is a random variable and the matching lowercase letter is a value it takes: \(X\) is the random covariate, \(x\) a realized covariate value, \(\mathbf{x}\) the covariate vector for one patient, and \(\mathcal{X}\) the set of all possible covariate values. A probability \(P(\cdot)\) with no subscript refers to the population under discussion. The index letters are fixed: \(i\) is a patient, \(j\) a study, \(k\) an arm, and \(a,b,c\) name treatments, so \(\eta_{ijk}\) reads “patient \(i\), study \(j\), arm \(k\).” The symbol \(\square\) closes a proof and \(\blacktriangleleft\) closes a definition, example, or remark.

title: Appendix A — Notation Glossary
section: A.3 A worked notation key: one anchored comparison

A.3 A worked notation key: one anchored comparison
To pin the symbols to a familiar picture, read them off a single indirect comparison. Treatments \(A\) and \(B\) were never studied head to head. An \(AC\) trial compares \(A\) against a common comparator \(C\); a separate \(BC\) trial compares \(B\) against the same \(C\). A health technology assessment wants the \(A\) versus \(B\) effect in a target population \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\). The symbols then read as follows.



Table A.2: One anchored comparison, symbol by symbol.









Symbol
In this anchored comparison




\(j\)
the study: here \(j=AC\) or \(j=BC\)


\(i\)
a patient inside one of the two trials


\(\mathbf{x}_i\)
patient \(i\)’s baseline covariate vector (age, disease severity, and so on)


\(\mathcal{P}^{*}\)
the target population in which the answer is wanted


\(\hat d_{AC},\ \hat d_{BC}\)
the within-trial estimates, each a \(\hat d_{ab(j)}\), of \(A\) versus \(C\) and of \(B\) versus \(C\)


\(d_{AB(\mathcal{P}^{*})}\)
the wanted marginal \(A\) versus \(B\) contrast in \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\), on a stated scale


the Bucher step
\(\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}\), valid when relative effects are constant across the populations (@def-anchored-comparison)






Had the two trials shared no comparator, the comparison would be unanchored and would rest on the stronger prognostic assumptions of Chapters 17 and 26; the same \(i\), \(j\), \(\mathbf{x}_i\), and \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\) still apply.

title: Appendix A — Notation Glossary
section: A.5 A note on effect scales
text:
A.5 A note on effect scales
Many entries below turn on two distinctions that run through the whole book, so they are worth stating plainly once. The first is marginal versus conditional. A conditional effect \(\tau^g_{ab}(x)\) compares treatments within a fixed covariate value \(x\); a marginal effect compares treatments after averaging outcomes over a whole population. On a non-collapsible scale, such as the odds ratio, these two differ even when nothing is confounded, which is exactly why the book keeps them apart. The second is outcome scale versus link scale. The outcome scale is the natural scale of the response, a probability, a rate, or a survival time; the link scale, also called the linear-predictor scale, is the scale on which the model is linear, reached by applying the link \(g\) (for a probability, the log-odds). Relative effects such as \(d_{ab(\mathcal{P})}\) live on a stated scale, and odds ratios, risk ratios, risk differences, and hazard ratios are not interchangeable: an assumption true on one scale can fail on another. The book names the scale whenever it matters; the defined terms @def-scale-alignment, @def-collapsibility, and @def-marginal-effect make the point precisely.

A.8 Alphabetical glossary of defined terms
Every formally stated definition in the book appears below, sorted alphabetically by its leading term (ignoring case, punctuation, and parentheticals). The “Defined in” column gives the chapter and the slug of the definition; that slug is the cross-reference that links to the statement in the rendered book. Terms whose meaning is scale-dependent, notably effect modification and collapsibility, are stated for a fixed link \(g\), as in the chapter that defines them.



Table A.15: Alphabetical glossary of the book’s defined terms.










Term
One-sentence meaning
Defined in




Active classical axioms
The classical logical axioms, such as functional extensionality and the law of the excluded middle, that the Coq development assumes.
Ch. 30, @def-active-axioms


ADEMP framework
A protocol that specifies a simulation study by its Aims, Data-generating mechanisms, Estimands, Methods, and Performance measures.
Ch. 29, @def-ademp

The individual-level model integrated over a study’s covariate distribution so that aggregate study arms can enter the likelihood.
Ch. 20, @def-aggregate-model

The two evidence configurations in which the index and comparator studies either share a common treatment arm (anchored) or do not (unanchored).
Ch. 17, @def-pat-setups

The Bucher estimator \(\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}\) that differences two within-study contrasts to a shared comparator.
Ch. 14, @def-anchored-comparison

A network meta-analysis written at the level of arm means, each one a study baseline plus a treatment effect on the link scale.
Ch. 15, @def-nma-arm-model

The population-mean potential-outcome contrast \(\tau=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)]\).
Ch. 9, @def-ate

The mean potential-outcome contrast among the units that actually received treatment.

A linearly independent set that spans a vector space.

A model whose unit-level parameters are themselves drawn from shared population-level priors.

Two equivalent ways to write a hierarchical model that induce different posterior geometries for sampling.

Characteristic polynomial
The polynomial \(\det(A-\lambda I)\) whose roots are the eigenvalues of \(A\).
Ch. 3, @def-characteristic-polynomial


Cochran’s \(Q\) statistic
The inverse-variance-weighted sum of squared deviations of study estimates from their pooled value, the basis of heterogeneity tests.
Ch. 13, @def-cochran-q-stat


Coefficient of determination
\(R^2\), the fraction of total response variation explained by the regression.
Ch. 6, @def-r-squared


Collapsibility and direct collapsibility
Whether the marginal effect equals the common conditional effect (collapsible) or always equals a covariate-weighted average of conditional effects (directly collapsible).
Ch. 11, @def-collapsibility


Collapsibility and non-collapsibility of an effect measure
Whether a measure’s marginal value coincides with its conditional value when that conditional value is constant across strata.
Ch. 7, @def-non-collapsibility


Comparator selection (aggregate-level)
Choosing, among candidate aggregate studies, the one whose covariate profile is closest to the target population.
Ch. 27, @def-comparator-selection


Conditional average treatment effect
The covariate-conditional contrast \(\tau(x)=\mu_1(x)-\mu_0(x)\).
Ch. 9, @def-cate


Conditional constancy of absolute effects (unanchored)
The condition that each arm’s conditional mean outcome is the same function of covariates across the populations being linked.
Ch. 17, @def-conditional-constancy-absolute


Conditional constancy of relative effects (anchored)
The condition that the conditional treatment effect \(\tau^g_{ab}(x)\) is the same function of covariates across populations.
Ch. 17, @def-conditional-constancy-relative


Conditional effect
The stratum-specific link-scale contrast \(\tau^g_{ab}(x)=g(\mu_b(x))-g(\mu_a(x))\).
Ch. 11, @def-conditional-effect


Conditional expectation
The mean-square-optimal predictor \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Z]\) of \(X\) given \(Z\).
Ch. 4, @def-conditional-expectation


Conditional independence
\(X\perp Y\mid Z\): the conditional joint law of \(X\) and \(Y\) given \(Z\) factorizes.
Ch. 4, @def-conditional-independence


Conditional (plug-in) STC
The relative effect produced by evaluating the fitted outcome model at the comparator covariate mean.
Ch. 19, @def-stc-conditional


Consistency
The property that an estimator converges in probability to its target as the sample size grows.
Ch. 5, @def-consistent-estimator


Constancy of relative effects
The assumption that the marginal relative effect \(d_{ab}\) takes the same value in every study population.
Ch. 14, @def-constancy-relative-effects


Copula
A distribution on the unit cube with uniform margins that couples given marginals into a joint law (Sklar’s theorem).
Ch. 22, @def-copula


Coverage
With the empirical and model-based standard errors, the probability that a stated confidence interval contains the estimand.
Ch. 29, @def-coverage


Credible set
A region carrying a stated posterior probability, in equal-tailed or highest-posterior-density form.
Ch. 8, @def-credible-interval


Definiteness
The sign pattern of a symmetric matrix’s quadratic form: positive or negative (semi)definite, or indefinite.
Ch. 3, @def-definiteness


Detailed balance (reversibility)
The pairwise probability-flux symmetry that guarantees a target stationary distribution for a Markov chain.
Ch. 8, @def-detailed-balance


Deviance and residual deviance
Twice the log-likelihood gap between the saturated model and the fitted model.
Ch. 7, @def-deviance


Deviance information criterion
A Bayesian model-comparison score combining posterior fit with the effective number of parameters.
Ch. 15, @def-dic


DIC, WAIC, and LOO-CV
The three predictive criteria used to compare fitted hierarchical models.
Ch. 24, @def-comp-criteria


Diagonalizable and similar matrices
A matrix similar to a diagonal one, and the relation \(B=S^{-1}AS\) between matrices.
Ch. 3, @def-diagonalizable


Digital \((t,m,s)\)-nets and the Sobol’ sequence
Low-discrepancy point sets with guaranteed equidistribution across dyadic boxes.
Ch. 22, @def-sobol-net


Dimension
The common cardinality shared by every basis of a vector space.
Ch. 1, @def-dimension


Distance variants
The Manhattan, Minkowski, mean standardized-mean-difference, and Gower covariate distances.
Ch. 27, @def-distance-variants


Doubling diagnostic for integration error
A check that bounds numerical integration error by comparing estimates computed at \(N\) and at \(2N\) nodes.
Ch. 24, @def-integration-error-monitoring


Ecological (aggregation) bias
The gap between the plug-in arm mean \(g^{-1}(\eta(\bar x))\) and the covariate-averaged mean \(\int g^{-1}(\eta(x))\,f(x)\,dx\).
Ch. 16, @def-ecological-bias


Effect modifier
A covariate on which the conditional treatment effect depends, a property defined relative to a chosen scale.
Ch. 11, @def-effect-modifier


Effective sample size
\(\mathrm{ESS}=\left(\sum_i w_i\right)^2/\sum_i w_i^2\), the equivalent unweighted size of a weighted sample.
Ch. 18, @def-maic-ess


Effective sample size of an MCMC chain
The autocorrelation-deflated equivalent number of independent posterior draws.
Ch. 24, @def-mcmc-ess


Efficiency and asymptotic efficiency
The property of attaining the Cramér-Rao lower bound exactly or in the large-sample limit.
Ch. 5, @def-efficient-estimator


Eigenvalue and eigenvector
A scalar \(\lambda\) and nonzero vector \(v\) with \(Av=\lambda v\).
Ch. 3, @def-eigenvalue


Entropy-balancing problem
The convex program minimizing weight divergence from uniformity subject to covariate-balance constraints, whose solution is an exponential tilt.
Ch. 18, @def-entropy-balancing


Estimator, bias, variance, mean squared error
A statistic used to target a parameter, together with its bias, variance, and mean squared error.
Ch. 5, @def-estimator


Euclidean and standardized Euclidean distance
The ordinary and variance-scaled \(\ell_2\) distances between covariate-mean vectors.
Ch. 27, @def-euclidean-distance


E-value (indirect-comparison)
The smallest unreported-covariate association that could reduce an unanchored estimate to the null.
Ch. 28, @def-itc-evalue


Exchangeability
The property that a sequence’s joint law is invariant under permutation of its indices.
Ch. 8, @def-exchangeability


Exponential dispersion family
Densities of the form \(\exp\{(y\theta-b(\theta))/a(\phi)+c(y,\phi)\}\), the common template for the normal, binomial, and Poisson laws; \(\theta\) is the natural parameter and \(\phi\) the dispersion that scales the variance.
Ch. 7, @def-exponential-family


Fisher information
The variance of the score, equivalently minus the expected Hessian of the log-likelihood.
Ch. 5, @def-fisher-information


Fixed-effect meta-analysis model
A pooling model in which all studies estimate one common effect, combined by inverse-variance weighting.
Ch. 13, @def-fixed-effect-ma


Fixed effects and random effects
Parameters treated as fixed unknowns versus parameters modeled as draws from a population distribution.
Ch. 8, @def-random-effects


Four fundamental subspaces
The column space, null space, row space, and left null space of a matrix.
Ch. 1, @def-column-space


Gaussian copula
The copula \(C_\Omega(\mathbf{u})=\Phi_\Omega\big(\Phi^{-1}(u_1),\dots,\Phi^{-1}(u_d)\big)\) induced by a correlated normal vector.
Ch. 22, @def-gaussian-copula


Generalizability
A within-population property: a sample’s estimand equals the estimand of its own source population.
Ch. 12, @def-generalizability


Generalized linear model
A regression with an exponential-family response and a link-transformed linear mean.
Ch. 7, @def-glm


Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
An MCMC method that proposes distant, high-acceptance moves by simulating gradient-driven Hamiltonian dynamics.
Ch. 8, @def-hmc


Hardy-Krause variation
A multidimensional measure of a function’s variation that bounds quasi-Monte Carlo error.
Ch. 22, @def-hardy-krause-variation


Hat matrix and residual maker
The projection \(H\) onto \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})\) and its complement \(M=I-H\).
Ch. 6, @def-hat-matrix


Hazard function and cumulative hazard
The instantaneous event rate \(h(t)\) and its integral \(H(t)\).
Ch. 25, @def-hazard


\(I^2\) and \(H^2\) heterogeneity statistics
The share of total variability attributable to between-study heterogeneity, and its ratio form.
Ch. 13, @def-i-squared


Ignorability
Conditional independence of treatment and potential outcomes given covariates, in strong, weak, or mean form.
Ch. 9, @def-ignorability


Independence
The property that a joint law factorizes into the product of its marginals.
Ch. 4, @def-independence


Individual-level model (ML-NMR)
The link-scale model \(g(\theta_{ijk})=\mu_j+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_1+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,k}+\gamma_k\) for each individual.
Ch. 20, @def-individual-model


Individual patient data and aggregate data
Per-patient covariates and outcomes (IPD) versus published summary statistics (AgD).
Ch. 17, @def-pat-data-structures


Individual treatment effect
The unit-level, generally unobservable contrast \(Y(1)-Y(0)\).
Ch. 9, @def-individual-effect


Inner product space
A vector space carrying a symmetric, bilinear, positive-definite form.
Ch. 2, @def-inner-product


Invertible matrix
A square matrix possessing a two-sided inverse, equivalently one of full rank.
Ch. 1, @def-invertible


Kernel and image
The set of inputs a linear map sends to zero and the set of outputs it attains.
Ch. 1, @def-kernel-image


Likelihood and log-likelihood
The data density read as a function of the parameter, and its logarithm.
Ch. 5, @def-likelihood


Linear independence
The property that the only vanishing linear combination of a set of vectors is the trivial one.
Ch. 1, @def-linear-independence


Linear map
A function between vector spaces that preserves addition and scalar multiplication.
Ch. 1, @def-linear-map


Linear model
The model \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) with mean-zero, constant-variance, uncorrelated errors.
Ch. 6, @def-linear-model


Link function
A monotone smooth map \(g\) with \(g(\mu)=\eta\) relating the mean to the linear predictor.
Ch. 7, @def-link-function


M-estimator and estimating equation
A parameter value solving an estimating equation \(\sum_i\psi(X_i;\theta)=\mathbf{0}\).
Ch. 5, @def-m-estimator


Mahalanobis distance
The covariance-whitened distance \(\sqrt{(x-y)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-y)}\).
Ch. 27, @def-mahalanobis-distance


Marginal and average-conditional relative effects
The two population-level contrasts that diverge whenever the effect measure is non-collapsible.
Ch. 16, @def-conditional-marginal-contrast


Marginal effect
The contrast of link-transformed population-mean outcomes, \(g(\mathbb{E}[\mu_b(X)])-g(\mathbb{E}[\mu_a(X)])\).
Ch. 11, @def-marginal-effect


Marginal likelihood and Bayes factor
The prior-averaged data density, and the ratio of two models’ marginal likelihoods.
Ch. 8, @def-marginal-likelihood


Marginal link-scale position
The link-transformed population-mean outcome of a single arm.
Ch. 14, @def-marginal-link-position


Marginal STC
The estimator that averages predicted individual outcomes over the comparator population before contrasting on the link scale.
Ch. 19, @def-stc-marginal


Maximum likelihood estimator
The parameter value that maximizes the likelihood.
Ch. 5, @def-mle


Method-of-moments covariate balance
Choosing weights so that the weighted individual covariate moments match the comparator’s published moments.
Ch. 18, @def-moment-balance


Moment generating function
\(M_X(\mathbf{t})=\mathbb{E}[e^{\mathbf{t}^\top X}]\), which fixes the law when finite near the origin.
Ch. 4, @def-mgf


Monte Carlo bias estimator, relative bias, and Monte Carlo standard error
The empirical bias of an estimator over simulation repetitions, and the Monte Carlo uncertainty in that estimate.
Ch. 29, @def-bias-mcse


Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse
The unique matrix \(A^{+}\) satisfying the four Penrose conditions, giving the minimum-norm least-squares solution.
Ch. 3, @def-pseudoinverse


Multivariate normal
The \(p\)-variate Gaussian \(\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) fixed by its mean vector and covariance matrix.
Ch. 4, @def-mvn


Node-splitting
An inconsistency check that compares direct and indirect evidence on a single network contrast.
Ch. 15, @def-node-splitting


Norm and induced norm
A nonnegative, homogeneous, triangle-inequality length function, here induced by an inner product.
Ch. 2, @def-norm


Normal distribution
The Gaussian law \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), with distribution function \(\Phi\) and density \(\phi\).
Ch. 4, @def-normal


Orthogonal complement
The subspace of all vectors orthogonal to every vector of a given subspace.
Ch. 2, @def-orthogonal-complement


Orthogonal projection matrix
A symmetric matrix with \(P=P^\top=P^2\) (idempotent: applying it twice does no more than applying it once) sending each vector to its nearest point in a subspace.
Ch. 2, @def-projection-matrix


Orthogonality
The relation between two vectors whose inner product is zero.
Ch. 2, @def-orthogonality


Parametric statistical model
A family of distributions indexed by a finite-dimensional parameter \(\theta\in\Theta\).
Ch. 5, @def-statistical-model


Pareto-smoothed importance sampling LOO
A stabilized leave-one-out cross-validation estimate carrying a tail-index diagnostic \(\hat k\).
Ch. 24, @def-psis-loo


Performance measures as functionals
Simulation performance written as functionals of the sampling distribution, distinguishing the data and repetition sample sizes.
Ch. 29, @def-sim-performance-functional


Poisson binomial distribution
The law of a sum of independent, non-identical Bernoulli trials with probability vector \(\mathbf{p}\).
Ch. 4, @def-poisson-binomial


Poisson distribution
The count law with mean equal to variance \(\lambda\), the rare-event limit of the binomial.
Ch. 4, @def-poisson


Positivity (overlap)
The requirement that each treatment has positive probability in every covariate stratum, \(0<e(x)<1\).
Ch. 9, @def-positivity


Posterior predictive distribution
The law of new data averaged over the parameter posterior.
Ch. 8, @def-posterior-predictive


Potential outcomes
The outcomes \(Y(0)\) and \(Y(1)\) a unit would exhibit under each treatment level.
Ch. 9, @def-potential-outcome


Probabilistic bias analysis
Assigning bias parameters prior distributions and propagating them into a bias-adjusted interval.
Ch. 28, @def-probabilistic-bias-analysis


Probability generating function
\(\mathbb{E}[s^N]\) for a nonnegative-integer variable, which encodes its mass function.
Ch. 21, @def-pgf


Probability space
The triple \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)\) of sample space, event \(\sigma\)-algebra (the collection of events that can be assigned a probability), and probability measure.
Ch. 4, @def-probability-space


Prognostic variable
A covariate on which the conditional mean outcome depends, whether or not it modifies the treatment effect.
Ch. 11, @def-prognostic-variable


Proof-status tiers
The classification of the book’s results by their degree of machine verification in the Coq development.
Ch. 30, @def-coq-proof-status


Propensity score
The conditional treatment probability \(e(x)=P(T=1\mid X=x)\), the coarsest balancing score.
Ch. 10, @def-propensity-score


Proportional-odds model
An ordinal regression in which treatment shifts every cumulative logit by a common amount.
Ch. 25, @def-proportional-odds


Quadratic form
The map \(x\mapsto x^\top A x\) associated with a symmetric matrix \(A\).
Ch. 3, @def-quadratic-form


Quantitative bias analysis
The practice of quantifying how strong an unmeasured bias would have to be to overturn a study’s conclusion.
Ch. 28, @def-quantitative-bias-analysis


Random-effects meta-analysis model
A model with exchangeable study effects drawn from a distribution of heterogeneity variance \(\tau^2\).
Ch. 13, @def-random-effects-ma


Random variable and its law
A function on the sample space, measurable so that probabilities can attach to its values, together with the distribution it induces.
Ch. 4, @def-random-variable


Rank and nullity
The dimension of the image and the dimension of the kernel of a map or matrix.
Ch. 1, @def-rank


Rayleigh quotient
The ratio \(x^\top A x/x^\top x\), whose extrema over \(x\neq\mathbf{0}\) are the extreme eigenvalues of symmetric \(A\).
Ch. 3, @def-rayleigh-quotient


Real vector space
A set closed under addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the eight vector-space axioms over \(\mathbb{R}\).
Ch. 1, @def-vector-space


Reference-treatment parameterization
Expressing every treatment effect relative to one designated network reference treatment.
Ch. 15, @def-reference-treatment-param


Regularity conditions
Smoothness and identifiability assumptions under which the score and information behave classically.
Ch. 5, @def-regular-model


Residual deviance
The deviance of a fitted network model relative to the saturated model, used as a goodness-of-fit summary.
Ch. 15, @def-residual-deviance


Residual, total, and explained sums of squares
The orthogonal decomposition \(\mathrm{TSS}=\mathrm{RSS}+\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}\) of response variation.
Ch. 6, @def-sums-of-squares


Restricted maximum likelihood
Variance-component estimation from the likelihood of error contrasts, removing the downward bias of full maximum likelihood.
Ch. 8, @def-reml


Restricted mean survival time
The area under the survival curve to a horizon \(\tau\), \(\int_0^\tau S(t)\,dt\).
Ch. 25, @def-rmst


Right-censored individual likelihood
The contribution \(f(t)^\delta S(t)^{1-\delta}\) combining observed events and right-censored observations.
Ch. 25, @def-censored-likelihood


Sandwich (robust) variance estimator
The \(A^{-1}BA^{-\top}\) variance for M-estimators, valid under model misspecification.
Ch. 5, @def-sandwich-variance


Saturated model
The GLM with one parameter per observation, reproducing the data exactly.
Ch. 7, @def-saturated-model


Scale alignment
Choosing the effect scale on which a transportability or invariance assumption actually holds.
Ch. 12, @def-scale-alignment


Score function
The gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameter.
Ch. 5, @def-score


Shared effect modifier assumption (SEMA)
The assumption that the compared active treatments carry identical effect-modifier interactions, \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,A}=\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,B}\).
Ch. 17, @def-sema


Shared prognostic factor assumption (SPFA)
The assumption that covariate-outcome slopes coincide across treatments, which forces the absence of effect modification.
Ch. 26, @def-spfa


Span
The set of all finite linear combinations of a collection of vectors.
Ch. 1, @def-span


Stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA)
No interference between units and a single version of each treatment, giving consistency \(Y=Y(T)\).
Ch. 9, @def-sutva


Star discrepancy
The worst-case gap between the empirical and uniform measures over anchored boxes, the quasi-Monte Carlo accuracy criterion.
Ch. 22, @def-star-discrepancy


Statistical interaction
A nonzero product term in the linear predictor, equivalently a covariate-dependent treatment coefficient.
Ch. 11, @def-statistical-interaction


STC estimands
The marginal and the conditional-at-the-mean targets a simulated treatment comparison may estimate.
Ch. 19, @def-stc-estimands


STC outcome model
The individual patient outcome regression, carrying treatment-covariate interactions, used for cross-study prediction.
Ch. 19, @def-stc-outcome-model


Structural invariance of the conditional model
The condition that the conditional mean potential outcome \(\mu_t(x)\) does not depend on population membership.
Ch. 12, @def-transport-invariance


Subspace
A nonempty subset of a vector space that is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
Ch. 1, @def-subspace


Survival function
\(S(t)=P(T>t)\), the probability of surviving beyond time \(t\).
Ch. 25, @def-survival-function


Target-population marginal and conditional contrasts
The ML-NMR estimands obtained by integrating the fitted model over a chosen target population.
Ch. 23, @def-mlnmr-target-contrast


Tipping point
The magnitude of bias at which an adjusted estimate crosses a decision threshold such as the null.
Ch. 28, @def-tipping-point


Total-variation distance
The largest probability discrepancy two laws can assign any event, \(\sup_A\lvert\mu(A)-\nu(A)\rvert\).
Ch. 21, @def-total-variation


Transition kernel and stationary distribution
The one-step transition law of a Markov chain and the measure it leaves invariant.
Ch. 8, @def-markov-kernel


Transitivity (anchored triangle)
The assumption that each of the three triangle relative effects takes a common value across the three trial populations.
Ch. 14, @def-transitivity


Transportability
A between-population property: a target estimand is identified from source outcomes together with target covariates.
Ch. 12, @def-transportability


Unanchored (naive single-arm) comparison
A comparison of active arms across studies that discards the shared comparator.
Ch. 14, @def-unanchored-comparison


Unanchored disconnected two-study network
Two studies without a common comparator, linkable only under prognostic-factor assumptions.
Ch. 26, @def-unanchored-network


Variance, covariance, and the covariance matrix
The second central moments of a single variable, of a pair, and of a random vector.
Ch. 4, @def-variance-covariance


Wald, score, and likelihood-ratio statistics
The three asymptotically equivalent classical statistics for testing a parametric hypothesis.
Ch. 5, @def-test-statistics


Wald test, Type I error rate, and power
The Wald rejection rule together with its rejection probabilities under the null and under an alternative.
Ch. 29, @def-power-type1


Within-chain, between-chain, and pooled variance estimators
The variance components from which the \(\hat R\) convergence diagnostic is built.
Ch. 24, @def-comp-rhat-pieces

title: Appendix A — Notation Glossary
text:
A.9 Notes and sources
The source for this appendix is the book itself: the symbol tables reproduce Notation, which is the single source of truth for the symbols and conventions, extended by one table (Bayesian computation and model comparison, Table A.8) that gathers symbols from Chapters 8, 15, and 24 not yet listed there; the term glossary is assembled from the definition environments of Chapters 1 through 30. Where a symbol carries a formal definition, the slug in the “Introduced” column is that definition; where a term is glossed, the slug in the “Defined in” column links to its statement. The companion catalogues that the notation extends are the proof catalogue and the ITC_Coq development described in Chapter 30 and in Appendix G. Related reference appendices collect the objects that recur across chapters: the probability families of Appendix C, the matrix calculus identities of Appendix B, and the special functions of Appendix D.

title: Appendix B — Matrix Calculus
text:
B.1 A scalar warm-up: derivatives as first-order approximations
Several of the central derivations of this book are exercises in differentiating a function whose argument is a vector or a matrix. The normal equations of least squares come from setting the gradient of a quadratic form to zero (Definition 3.6 and the least-squares chapter); the score and Fisher information of a likelihood are a gradient and a negative expected Hessian (Definition 5.5); the restricted likelihood used for variance components in hierarchical models and meta-analysis is built from a log-determinant and an inverse-quadratic form (Chapters 8 and 13); and the calibration of matching weights and the variance propagation of population-adjusted estimators rest on Jacobians (Chapters 18 and 19). This appendix collects the matrix-calculus identities those chapters use and proves each one. It is reference material, but reference material with proofs: every formula below is derived from the definition of the derivative, so the reader can trust it and reconstruct it.
How to read this appendix. The identities here are tools, and different readers need different tools. If your goal is least squares and the normal equations, read the gradient and quadratic-form identities (Section B.4) and stop. If your goal is the delta method and variance propagation for MAIC and STC (Chapters 18 and 19), read the Jacobian convention (Definition B.2) and the chain rule (Theorem B.8). If your goal is restricted maximum likelihood and random-effects meta-analysis (Chapters 8 and 13), read the trace, inverse, and log-determinant identities (Section B.5) together with the worked covariance example (Section B.8). If your goal is efficient computation of a marginal likelihood in ML-NMR (Chapters 20 to 25), read the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity (Section B.6). A one-line map from each identity to the chapter that consumes it is the closing table of the appendix (Section B.10); a reader who wants that map first may jump there now and use it as a roadmap.
Two reading aids appear throughout. A short reader translation in italics follows each identity, saying in plain words what it computes and where the book uses it. A shape check in parentheses records the size of each factor: the single most common error in matrix calculus is a stray transpose or a nonconformable product, and a shape check catches it on sight.
The treatment is deliberately self-contained. We fix one set of layout conventions, compatible with the gradient and Jacobian already used in the foundations chapters, and we adopt the differential as the working tool. Differentials turn matrix differentiation into ordinary algebra: one expands a perturbation to first order, reads off a linear term, and identifies the derivative from it. This avoids the index gymnastics that make componentwise differentiation error-prone, while remaining completely rigorous. The prerequisites are the determinant, the adjugate and Cramer’s rule, and the characterization of invertibility, all developed in Strang (2016) and in Theorem 1.6.
Throughout, \(\|\cdot\|\) denotes any fixed norm on the relevant finite-dimensional space; because all norms on a finite-dimensional space are equivalent, the Landau symbols \(O(\cdot)\) and \(o(\cdot)\) do not depend on the choice. For matrices we will most often use the Frobenius norm \(\|A\|_F=\sqrt{\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}^2}\). We write \(E_{ij}=\mathbf{e}_i\mathbf{e}_j^\top\) for the standard basis matrix with a single \(1\) in position \((i,j)\) and zeros elsewhere. The symbol \(X^{-\top}\) abbreviates \((X^{-1})^\top=(X^\top)^{-1}\). See Notation for the standing conventions on bold vectors and matrices.
A note on symbols used only here. Two small conventions differ from the rest of the book, and we flag them so the reader is not tripped up. First, matrix calculus is traditionally written with plain capital letters for generic matrices; accordingly, in this appendix \(A\), \(X\), \(U\), \(V\), \(C\) denote generic matrices, not random variables, not the design matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) of the regression chapters, and not a covariance matrix, while bold letters such as \(\mathbf{x}\), \(\mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{1}_n\) are reserved for vectors. This is why the matrices here are unbolded even though the book’s standing convention (see Notation) bolds matrices; where a plain capital could be confused with a book-wide symbol we say so explicitly. Second, two pieces of asymptotic shorthand recur. The symbol \(o(\|\mathbf{h}\|)\) denotes a remainder that, divided by \(\|\mathbf{h}\|\), tends to \(0\) as \(\mathbf{h}\to\mathbf{0}\): it is strictly smaller than linear in the perturbation, so it disappears when we identify a derivative. The symbol \(O(\|\mathbf{h}\|^2)\) denotes a remainder bounded in absolute value by a constant times \(\|\mathbf{h}\|^2\), that is, at most quadratic; a quadratic remainder is in particular \(o(\|\mathbf{h}\|)\). The phrase “\(U\) is open” may be read as “\(U\) contains a small ball around each of its points,” so that a small perturbation in any direction stays inside \(U\) and the function is defined there; a reader who has not met open sets may replace “open \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)” by “a neighborhood of the point in question” without losing anything. Finally, \(f\) is called \(C^2\) if it has continuous second-order partial derivatives; this is the standard condition under which the mixed partials are equal, so the Hessian is symmetric.
Before any matrices, we recall the one idea that all of matrix calculus generalizes. For a differentiable scalar function of one real variable, the derivative \(f'(x)\) is the number for which \[
f(x+h)=f(x)+f'(x)\,h+o(h)\qquad(h\to 0).
\tag{B.1}\] Read this as: near \(x\), the function changes by approximately \(f'(x)\,h\), a quantity linear in the small step \(h\), plus an error \(o(h)\) too small to matter as \(h\to 0\). Every definition in this appendix is this one sentence with \(h\) replaced by a vector or a matrix perturbation and the ordinary product \(f'(x)\,h\) replaced by an inner product. Nothing more abstract is going on; matrix calculus is single-variable calculus with the slope promoted to a vector or a matrix.
The differential is simply a name for the linear part \(f'(x)\,h\). To see it in the smallest possible case, take \(f(x)=x^2\). Then \[
f(x+h)=(x+h)^2=x^2+2xh+h^2,
\] so the change \(f(x+h)-f(x)=2xh+h^2\) splits into a linear part \(2xh\) and a quadratic remainder \(h^2=o(h)\). We write \(df=2x\,dx\), meaning: the first-order change in \(f\) caused by a small change \(dx\) in \(x\) is \(2x\,dx\), and we read the derivative \(f'(x)=2x\) off the coefficient of \(dx\). The whole method of this appendix is exactly this three-step move, expand, discard everything smaller than linear, read off the coefficient, carried out for functions whose argument is a vector or a matrix. The single new feature is that matrices do not commute, so the coefficient may sit to the left or to the right of the perturbation \(dX\), and that order must be respected; getting it wrong is what produces a spurious transpose.
Geometrically, the derivative is the best linear approximation to the function at a point: a slope in one dimension, a direction of steepest ascent (the gradient) for a scalar field, a local linear map (the Jacobian) for a vector field, and a curvature (the Hessian) for the second order. Keeping those pictures in mind makes the algebra below easier to remember.

title: Appendix B — Matrix Calculus
section: B.2 Conventions: gradient, Jacobian, and the matrix derivative
text:
B.2 Conventions: gradient, Jacobian, and the matrix derivative
We first pin down what “the derivative” means for the three cases we need: a scalar function of a vector, a vector function of a vector, and a scalar function of a matrix. The conventions chosen here are exactly those already in force in the inference and regression chapters, so the formulas of this appendix can be dropped into those chapters without relabeling.
One choice deserves to be named, because it is the source of most apparent contradictions between textbooks. There are two competing traditions, called numerator layout and denominator layout, for arranging the partial derivatives of a function into an array. They differ by a transpose. We use denominator layout, meaning the derivative is given the same shape as the variable: the gradient of a scalar function of the vector \(\mathbf{x}\) is a column vector shaped like \(\mathbf{x}\), and the derivative of a scalar function of the matrix \(X\) is a matrix shaped like \(X\). This is the natural choice because it puts the gradient in the same space as the argument, so that a step \(\mathbf{x}\mapsto
\mathbf{x}-\eta\,\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\) makes sense without a transpose. The practical warning is this: if you meet a formula in a paper that disagrees with ours by a single transpose, it is almost certainly a layout difference and not an error. Numerator layout would report the gradient as a row; we never do.

Definition B.1 (Gradient of a scalar function of a vector) Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be open and \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\). We say \(f\) is differentiable at \(\mathbf{x}\in U\) if there is a vector \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), the gradient, with \[
f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h})=f(\mathbf{x})+\nabla f(\mathbf{x})^\top\mathbf{h}+o(\|\mathbf{h}\|)
\qquad\text{as }\mathbf{h}\to\mathbf{0}.
\tag{B.2}\] The gradient is a column vector of the same shape as \(\mathbf{x}\), with entries \([\nabla f(\mathbf{x})]_i=\partial f/\partial x_i\).

Reader translation. The gradient is the vector version of a slope: it collects the \(n\) partial derivatives into one column so that \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x})^\top\mathbf{h}\) gives the first-order change in \(f\) when we step from \(\mathbf{x}\) to \(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h}\). It is a column, not a row, precisely so that it lives in the same space as \(\mathbf{x}\); that is what lets a step \(\mathbf{x}-\eta\,\nabla
f(\mathbf{x})\) (gradient descent, and Fisher scoring in later chapters) even be written down. Its direction is the direction of steepest ascent of \(f\). In this book the gradient is the score \(\mathbf{s}(\boldsymbol\theta)=\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\ell(\boldsymbol\theta)\) of a log-likelihood (Definition 5.5) and the gradient of the least-squares objective that yields the normal equations.
This is the convention under which the least-squares objective \(S(\mathbf{b})\) has gradient \(\nabla S(\mathbf{b})=-2\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}+2\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}\), a column vector, and under which the score \(\mathbf{s}(\boldsymbol\theta)=\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\ell(\boldsymbol\theta)\) of Definition 5.5 is a column vector in the parameter space.

Definition B.2 (Jacobian of a vector function of a vector) Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be open and \(\mathbf{g}:U\to\mathbb{R}^{m}\). We say \(\mathbf{g}\) is differentiable at \(\mathbf{x}\in U\) if there is a matrix \(J_{\mathbf{g}}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), the Jacobian, with \[
\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h})=\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})+J_{\mathbf{g}}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{h}
+o(\|\mathbf{h}\|).
\tag{B.3}\] Its entries are \([J_{\mathbf{g}}(\mathbf{x})]_{ab}=\partial g_a/\partial x_b\): row \(a\) collects the partials of output \(g_a\), column \(b\) the partials with respect to input \(x_b\).

Reader translation. The Jacobian is the local linear map that best approximates \(\mathbf{g}\) near \(\mathbf{x}\): it is the matrix by which you multiply a small input change \(\mathbf{h}\) to get the resulting output change, \(\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h})-\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})\approx
J_{\mathbf{g}}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{h}\). This is the object the delta method uses to push the variance of an estimator through a smooth transformation, which is exactly how the variance of a population-adjusted effect is propagated in the MAIC and STC chapters (Chapters 18 and 19). A concrete \(2\times 2\) Jacobian is computed in Example B.2 below.
This is the \(q\times p\) Jacobian \(\mathbf{D}=[\partial g_a/\partial\theta_b]\) of the delta method (Theorem 5.3). The two conventions are consistent: a scalar function \(f\) is the special case \(m=1\), where the Jacobian is the \(1\times n\) row vector \(J_f(\mathbf{x})\), and comparing Equation B.2 with Equation B.3 gives the relationship \[
\nabla f(\mathbf{x})=J_f(\mathbf{x})^\top.
\tag{B.4}\] This equation looks like a paradox on first reading, so it is worth stating carefully: the gradient and the Jacobian of a scalar function are not the same object. The gradient \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\) is a column vector (denominator layout), while the Jacobian \(J_f(\mathbf{x})\) of the same scalar \(f\) is a \(1\times n\) row vector; one is literally the transpose of the other. There is no contradiction because they are two different arrangements of the same \(n\) partial derivatives. Throughout the book we use the gradient (the column). Say it once and the confusion never returns.
The Hessian of a twice differentiable \(f\) is the Jacobian of the gradient map \(\mathbf{x}\mapsto\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\), \[
\nabla^2 f(\mathbf{x})=J_{\nabla f}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},
\qquad
[\nabla^2 f(\mathbf{x})]_{ij}=\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i\,\partial x_j},
\] which is symmetric whenever \(f\) is \(C^2\), by the equality of mixed partials.
Reader translation. The Hessian is curvature: it is the matrix of second derivatives, and it records how fast the gradient itself is changing. Its sign pattern classifies a stationary point (positive definite Hessian means a strict local minimum, negative definite a maximum, indefinite a saddle), which is exactly how the least-squares and maximum-likelihood objectives of this book are shown to have genuine optima. Its role in inference is central: the observed information is the negative Hessian of the log-likelihood, and the Fisher information \(\mathcal{I}(\boldsymbol\theta)\) is its negative expectation (Definition 5.5), so the Hessian is what turns a fitted model into a standard error. It is also the matrix inverted at each step of Newton and Fisher scoring.
For functions of a matrix we use the natural extension: the derivative has the same shape as the matrix argument.

Definition B.3 (Derivative of a scalar function of a matrix) Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be open and \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) differentiable at \(X\in U\), meaning that there is a matrix \(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial X}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) with \[
f(X+H)=f(X)+\Big\langle \tfrac{\partial f}{\partial X},\,H\Big\rangle_F+o(\|H\|),
\qquad
\langle A,B\rangle_F:=\operatorname{tr}(A^\top B)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}.
\tag{B.5}\] The matrix \(\partial f/\partial X\) has entries \([\partial f/\partial X]_{ij}=\partial f/\partial X_{ij}\), and \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_F\) is the Frobenius inner product.

Reader translation. The Frobenius inner product \(\langle A,B\rangle_F=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}\) is not an arbitrary ceremony involving a trace: it is exactly the ordinary dot product of \(A\) and \(B\) after you flatten each matrix into a long vector of its entries. So Equation B.5 says the same thing as the gradient definition, only with the \(mn\) entries of \(X\) laid out as a rectangle instead of a column. That is also why the derivative with respect to a matrix is itself a matrix and not a giant unwieldy array: we keep the \(mn\) partial derivatives arranged in the same rectangle as \(X\) (denominator layout), so that \([\partial f/\partial X]_{ij}=\partial f/\partial X_{ij}\) sits in the slot of the entry it differentiates. The simplest instance is \(f(X)=\operatorname{tr}(X)\), whose derivative is the identity \(I\); it is worked in Example B.1 once we have the differential rules.
The bridge between the differential of a matrix function and its derivative is the following identification, the single most useful tool in this appendix.

Lemma B.1 (Identification of the derivative from the differential) Let \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable at \(X\in U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\). If a matrix \(G\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) satisfies \[
f(X+H)=f(X)+\operatorname{tr}(G^\top H)+o(\|H\|)\qquad\text{for all }H,
\] then \(\partial f/\partial X=G\). Such a \(G\) is unique.


Proof. Setting \(H=tE_{ij}\) for a scalar \(t\to 0\) in the hypothesis gives, after dividing by \(t\), \[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial X_{ij}}
=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(X+tE_{ij})-f(X)}{t}
=\operatorname{tr}(G^\top E_{ij})=G_{ij},
\] because \(\operatorname{tr}(G^\top E_{ij})=\sum_{k}(G^\top)_{ik}(E_{ij})_{ki}=G_{ij}\). Hence \(G=\partial f/\partial X\) entrywise, which is Equation B.5. Uniqueness is the same computation: if \(\operatorname{tr}(G^\top H)=\operatorname{tr}(\tilde G^\top H)\) for all \(H\), take \(H=E_{ij}\) to get \(G_{ij}=\tilde G_{ij}\) for every \(i,j\). \(\square\)

In words: expand \(f(X+H)\), keep only the part linear in \(H\), write it as \(\operatorname{tr}(G^\top H)\), and read off \(\partial f/\partial X=G\). Everything quadratic or smaller in \(H\) is absorbed into \(o(\|H\|)\). The same principle, with \(\operatorname{tr}(G^\top H)\) replaced by \(\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{h}\) or \(J\mathbf{h}\), identifies gradients and Jacobians in the vector case.
Why is this the most useful tool here? Because it splits a hard problem into an easy one. Computing a derivative entry by entry means differentiating \(mn\) scalar functions and keeping the bookkeeping straight, which is where sign and transpose errors creep in. Computing a differential, by contrast, is pure algebra: it obeys a product rule, a transpose rule, and a trace rule (developed next), so one manipulates whole matrices at once. The identification lemma is the hinge that connects the two. Once we have massaged the linear part of \(f(X+H)\) into the canonical form \(\operatorname{tr}(G^\top\,dX)\), the derivative is \(G\) for free, with no indices. Essentially every identity below is proved this way.

title: Appendix B — Matrix Calculus
section: B.3 The differential and its algebra
text:
B.3 The differential and its algebra
It is convenient to manipulate the linear term abstractly. For a map \(F\) between matrix spaces (a scalar, vector, or matrix being special cases), the differential at \(X\) is the linear map \(H\mapsto dF(X)[H]\) defined by \[
F(X+H)=F(X)+dF(X)[H]+o(\|H\|).
\] When the base point is understood we write \(dF\) for \(dF(X)[H]\) and treat \(dX:=H\) as a free increment. The derivative is recovered from the differential by Lemma B.1 in the scalar case and by reading off the coefficient matrix in the vector case. The following rules let us compute differentials of composite expressions without ever returning to indices.
What \(dX\) and \(dF\) mean, in plain words. Think of \(dX\) as a bookkeeping symbol standing for a small, arbitrary change applied to every entry of \(X\) at once (it is the perturbation \(H\), renamed). Then \(dF\) is the resulting first-order change in \(F\), the part of \(F(X+dX)-F(X)\) that is linear in \(dX\), with the smaller-than-linear remainder thrown away. This is precisely the scalar picture \(df=f'(x)\,dx\) from Section B.1, promoted to matrices. The one caution: \(dX\) is not a number, so when a rule produces a factor on each side of \(dX\), as in \(A\,(dX)\,B\), the order cannot be rearranged; the whole art of the method is to shuffle those factors, legally, until \(dX\) stands alone at the end inside a trace.

Lemma B.2 (Rules of differentials) Let \(F,G\) be differentiable matrix-valued maps and \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\) constants. Wherever the shapes are conformable, \[
\begin{aligned}
d(\alpha F+\beta G)&=\alpha\,dF+\beta\,dG, &&\text{(linearity)}\\
d(FG)&=(dF)\,G+F\,(dG), &&\text{(product rule)}\\
d(F^\top)&=(dF)^\top, &&\text{(transpose)}\\
d\operatorname{tr}(F)&=\operatorname{tr}(dF). &&\text{(trace)}
\end{aligned}
\] A constant matrix \(C\) has \(dC=0\).


Proof. Linearity is immediate from the definition, since the first-order term of a sum is the sum of the first-order terms, and \(d C=0\) holds because a constant satisfies \(C(X+H)=C(X)\) exactly.
Product rule. With \(F=F(X)\), \(G=G(X)\) and increments \(dF,dG\) of order \(\|H\|\), \[
F(X+H)\,G(X+H)
=\bigl(F+dF+o\bigr)\bigl(G+dG+o\bigr)
=FG+(dF)G+F(dG)+\underbrace{(dF)(dG)}_{O(\|H\|^2)}+o(\|H\|).
\] The cross term \((dF)(dG)\) is \(O(\|H\|^2)=o(\|H\|)\) because each factor is \(O(\|H\|)\) and the Frobenius norm is submultiplicative, meaning \(\|AB\|_F\le\|A\|_F\,\|B\|_F\) (the size of a product is at most the product of the sizes; this standard inequality is proved from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applied to the rows of \(A\) and columns of \(B\)). So the product of two first-order changes is a second-order quantity, the matrix analogue of the discarded \(h^2\) in \(f(x)=x^2\): two small things multiplied give something an order of magnitude smaller still, negligible at first order. Collecting the linear part gives \(d(FG)=(dF)G+F(dG)\).
Transpose and trace are linear operations with constant coefficients, so they commute with taking the first-order term: \((F+dF)^\top=F^\top+(dF)^\top\) and \(\operatorname{tr}(F+dF)=\operatorname{tr}F
+\operatorname{tr}(dF)\). \(\square\)

We will also use, repeatedly, the three elementary properties of the trace that turn a differential into the canonical form \(\operatorname{tr}(G^\top\,dX)\).

Lemma B.3 (Properties of the trace) For matrices of conformable shape and \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\): \[
\operatorname{tr}(\alpha A+\beta B)=\alpha\operatorname{tr}A+\beta\operatorname{tr}B,\qquad
\operatorname{tr}(A^\top)=\operatorname{tr}(A),\qquad
\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).
\] Consequently \(\operatorname{tr}(A^\top B)=\operatorname{tr}(B^\top A)=\langle A,B\rangle_F\), and the Frobenius inner product is symmetric.


Proof. Linearity is entrywise. For the transpose, \(\operatorname{tr}(A^\top)=\sum_i (A^\top)_{ii}=\sum_i
A_{ii}=\operatorname{tr}(A)\). For the cyclic property, with \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}\) and \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times p}\), \[
\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{k=1}^{q}A_{ik}B_{ki}
=\sum_{k=1}^{q}\sum_{i=1}^{p}B_{ki}A_{ik}=\operatorname{tr}(BA).
\] The last claim follows since \(\operatorname{tr}(A^\top B)=\operatorname{tr}((A^\top B)^\top)
=\operatorname{tr}(B^\top A)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}\). \(\square\)

The canonical-form recipe. These trace rules exist to serve one workflow, the recipe that recovers a matrix derivative from a differential. It has four steps.

Differentiate. Apply the differential rules of Lemma B.2 to \(f(X)\), treating \(dX\) as a small perturbation. Discard at once every term containing two factors of \(dX\) (those are \(o(\|dX\|)\)).
Trace it. Since \(f\) is scalar, \(df\) already equals its own trace; write \(df=\operatorname{tr}(df)\) if it is not yet a trace.
Isolate \(dX\). Use the cyclic property to rotate the factors until \(dX\) sits alone at the right end, producing the form \(\operatorname{tr}(M\,dX)\) for some matrix \(M\).
Read off. Rewrite \(M=G^\top\); then Lemma B.1 gives \(\partial f/\partial X=G\).

One warning is essential here, because the whole recipe leans on step 3. The cyclic property \(\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)\) extends to longer products as a rotation: \[
\operatorname{tr}(ABC)=\operatorname{tr}(BCA)=\operatorname{tr}(CAB).
\] You may rotate the factors around the circle, keeping their circular order. You may not permute them freely: in general \(\operatorname{tr}(ABC)\ne\operatorname{tr}(ACB)\), because swapping two factors breaks the circular order. Rotate, never reshuffle. Confusing the two is the commonest mistake in this style of calculation.
As a mini example of step 3, suppose a differentiation has produced the term \(\operatorname{tr}(A\,dX\,B)\) with \(A,B\) constant. Rotate \(dX\) to the end: \[
\operatorname{tr}(A\,dX\,B)=\operatorname{tr}(B A\,dX)
=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((A^\top B^\top)^\top dX\bigr),
\] so the coefficient is \(G=A^\top B^\top\) and the derivative of that piece is \(A^\top B^\top\). Notice we rotated \(B\) to the front, we did not swap it past \(A\).

Example B.1 (The two simplest matrix derivatives, from scratch) Take \(f(X)=\operatorname{tr}(X)\). By the trace rule \(d\operatorname{tr}(X)=\operatorname{tr}(dX)
=\operatorname{tr}(I^\top\,dX)\), so Lemma B.1 reads off \(\partial f/\partial X=I\): the derivative of the trace is the identity matrix. Now take \(f(X)=\operatorname{tr}(AX)\) with \(A\) constant. The product and trace rules give \(d\operatorname{tr}(AX)=\operatorname{tr}(A\,dX)
=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((A^\top)^\top dX\bigr)\), so \(\partial f/\partial X=A^\top\). These are the two identities of Theorem B.4, obtained here in one line each purely by the recipe, with no indices.

Reader translation. This is the payoff promised in the introduction: differentiating whole matrices by the recipe is quick and mechanical, whereas doing the same entry by entry (as in Theorem B.4’s alternative) is where errors hide. We reuse exactly this recipe for every identity in the next two sections.

title: Appendix B — Matrix Calculus
section: B.4 Linear, quadratic, and bilinear forms
text:
B.4 Linear, quadratic, and bilinear forms
These are the derivatives that appear in least squares and in the quadratic-form arithmetic of the normal theory of regression.

Theorem B.1 (Derivative of a linear form and of a linear map) Let \(\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\) and \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be constant.

The linear form \(f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{a}\) has gradient \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{a}\) for every \(\mathbf{x}\).
The linear map \(\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})=A\mathbf{x}\) has Jacobian \(J_{\mathbf{g}}(\mathbf{x})=A\) for every \(\mathbf{x}\).



Proof. For (1), \(f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h})=\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{h}
=f(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{h}\), with no remainder; comparison with Equation B.2 gives \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{a}\). Equivalently \(\partial(\sum_k a_k x_k)/\partial x_i=a_i\). For (2), \(\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h})=A\mathbf{x}+A\mathbf{h}=\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})+A\mathbf{h}\), again with no remainder, so Equation B.3 gives \(J_{\mathbf{g}}=A\). Entrywise, \(g_a=\sum_b A_{ab}x_b\) has \(\partial g_a/\partial x_b=A_{ab}\). \(\square\)

Reader translation. A linear form \(\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x}\) has a constant gradient, namely its own coefficient vector \(\mathbf{a}\) (shape check: \(\mathbf{a}\) is \(n\times 1\), matching \(\mathbf{x}\)); a linear map \(A\mathbf{x}\) has constant Jacobian \(A\) (shape check: \(A\) is \(m\times n\), mapping an \(n\)-vector step to an \(m\)-vector step). These are the “slope equals the coefficient” facts that make the linear predictor \(\boldsymbol\eta=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\) differentiate to the design matrix, which is the first step of every score computation in the regression and GLM chapters.

Example B.2 (A concrete \(2\times 2\) Jacobian) Let \(\mathbf{g}:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2\) be the nonlinear map \(\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})=(x_1^2 x_2,\; x_1+x_2^2)\). Its Jacobian collects the four partials, output by input: \[
J_{\mathbf{g}}(\mathbf{x})=
\begin{pmatrix}
\partial g_1/\partial x_1 & \partial g_1/\partial x_2\\[2pt]
\partial g_2/\partial x_1 & \partial g_2/\partial x_2
\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix} 2x_1 x_2 & x_1^2\\ 1 & 2x_2 \end{pmatrix}.
\] At the point \(\mathbf{x}=(1,2)\) this is the numerical matrix \(J_{\mathbf{g}}(1,2)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}4&1\\1&4\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Reading it as a local linear approximation: a small input step \(\mathbf{h}=(h_1,h_2)\) produces the output step \(J_{\mathbf{g}}(1,2)\,\mathbf{h}=(4h_1+h_2,\;h_1+4h_2)\) to first order. This is the picture behind the delta method (Theorem 5.3): to move a variance through \(\mathbf{g}\), sandwich the input covariance with this matrix.


Theorem B.2 (Derivative of a quadratic form) Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be constant, not necessarily symmetric, and let \(q(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}\). Then \[
\nabla q(\mathbf{x})=(A+A^\top)\mathbf{x},
\qquad
\nabla^2 q(\mathbf{x})=A+A^\top .
\tag{B.6}\] If \(A\) is symmetric, \(\nabla q(\mathbf{x})=2A\mathbf{x}\) and \(\nabla^2 q(\mathbf{x})=2A\).


Proof. Expand about \(\mathbf{x}\): \[
q(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h})
=(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h})^\top A(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h})
=\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}
+\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{h}+\mathbf{h}^\top A\mathbf{x}
+\mathbf{h}^\top A\mathbf{h}.
\] The term \(\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{h}\) is a scalar, hence equal to its transpose \(\mathbf{h}^\top A^\top\mathbf{x}\), so the two middle terms combine to \(\mathbf{h}^\top(A^\top+A)\mathbf{x}=\bigl((A+A^\top)\mathbf{x}\bigr)^\top\mathbf{h}\). The final term satisfies \(|\mathbf{h}^\top A\mathbf{h}|\le\|A\|\,\|\mathbf{h}\|^2=o(\|\mathbf{h}\|)\). Therefore \[
q(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h})=q(\mathbf{x})+\bigl((A+A^\top)\mathbf{x}\bigr)^\top\mathbf{h}+o(\|\mathbf{h}\|),
\] and Equation B.2 identifies \(\nabla q(\mathbf{x})=(A+A^\top)\mathbf{x}\). The gradient is the linear map \(\mathbf{x}\mapsto(A+A^\top)\mathbf{x}\), whose Jacobian is \(A+A^\top\) by Theorem B.1; that Jacobian is the Hessian. When \(A=A^\top\) these reduce to \(2A\mathbf{x}\) and \(2A\). \(\square\)

This is the identity behind the normal equations: the least-squares objective expands as \(S(\mathbf{b})=\mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{y}-2\mathbf{b}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}
+\mathbf{b}^\top(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})\mathbf{b}\), a quadratic form with symmetric matrix \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\), so Theorem B.2 and Theorem B.1 give \(\nabla S(\mathbf{b})=-2\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}+2\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}\) and Hessian \(2\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\), positive semidefinite by Definition 3.7.
Reader translation. The gradient of \(\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}\) is \((A+A^\top)\mathbf{x}\), the symmetrized matrix times \(\mathbf{x}\) (shape check: \(A+A^\top\) is \(n\times n\), \(\mathbf{x}\) is \(n\times 1\), so the gradient is \(n\times 1\), the same shape as \(\mathbf{x}\), as denominator layout demands). Setting this to zero is what produces the normal equations \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\); the Hessian \(2\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) being positive semidefinite is what certifies that solution is a minimum, not a saddle. This one identity is the entire analytic content of least squares.

Example B.3 (A quadratic gradient two ways) Let \(q(\mathbf{x})=3x_1^2+2x_1x_2+x_2^2\). Writing \(q(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}\) with the symmetric \(A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}3&1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) checks out, since \(\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}=3x_1^2+2\cdot 1\cdot x_1x_2+x_2^2\). Entrywise, \(\partial q/\partial x_1
=6x_1+2x_2\) and \(\partial q/\partial x_2=2x_1+2x_2\), so \(\nabla q=(6x_1+2x_2,\;2x_1+2x_2)\). By the formula Equation B.6, \(\nabla q=2A\mathbf{x}
=2\left(\begin{smallmatrix}3&1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\mathbf{x}
=(6x_1+2x_2,\;2x_1+2x_2)\), in agreement. At \(\mathbf{x}=(1,1)\) both give \(\nabla q=(8,4)\), and the Hessian is \(2A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}6&2\\2&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). The theorem also tolerates a nonsymmetric representation: taking instead \(A'=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}3&2\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) (which also gives \(q\)) yields the same gradient because \(A'+A'^\top=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}6&2\\2&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\); this is exactly why the symmetrization \(A+A^\top\) appears in Equation B.6.


Theorem B.3 (Derivative of a bilinear form) Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be constant and \(\beta(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{x}^\top
A\mathbf{y}\) for \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\), \(\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\). Then \[
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\beta=A\mathbf{y},
\qquad
\nabla_{\mathbf{y}}\beta=A^\top\mathbf{x}.
\] Regarded instead as a function of the matrix \(A\) with \(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\) fixed, \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial A}\bigl(\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{y}\bigr)=\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}^\top .
\]


Proof. Fix \(\mathbf{y}\). Then \(\beta(\cdot,\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{x}^\top(A\mathbf{y})=(A\mathbf{y})^\top\mathbf{x}\) is a linear form in \(\mathbf{x}\) with coefficient vector \(A\mathbf{y}\), so \(\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\beta=A\mathbf{y}\) by Theorem B.1(1). Fix \(\mathbf{x}\). Then \(\beta(\mathbf{x},\cdot)=(A^\top\mathbf{x})^\top\mathbf{y}\) is a linear form in \(\mathbf{y}\) with coefficient \(A^\top\mathbf{x}\), so \(\nabla_{\mathbf{y}}\beta=A^\top\mathbf{x}\). For the derivative in \(A\), write \(\beta=\sum_{i,j}x_i A_{ij}y_j\); then \(\partial\beta/\partial A_{ij}=x_i y_j\), which is the \((i,j)\) entry of the outer product \(\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}^\top\). Equivalently, by the differential, \(\beta(A+H)-\beta(A)=\mathbf{x}^\top H\mathbf{y}=\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{y}\mathbf{x}^\top H)
=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}^\top)^\top H\bigr)\), and Lemma B.1 gives \(\partial\beta/\partial A=\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}^\top\). \(\square\)

Reader translation. Read left to right, \(\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{y}\) is linear in each of its three arguments, so each gradient is just the “other” object: differentiating in \(\mathbf{x}\) leaves \(A\mathbf{y}\), in \(\mathbf{y}\) leaves \(A^\top\mathbf{x}\), and in the matrix \(A\) leaves the outer product \(\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}^\top\) (shape check: \(\mathbf{x}\) is \(m\times 1\) and \(\mathbf{y}^\top\) is \(1\times n\), so \(\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}^\top\) is \(m\times n\), the shape of \(A\)). The outer-product rule \(\partial(\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{y})/\partial A=\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}^\top\) is the seed from which the trace derivatives of the next section grow.

title: Appendix B — Matrix Calculus
text:
B.5 Trace, inverse, and log-determinant
These identities power the restricted-likelihood computations of Chapters 8 and 13, where one must differentiate \(\log\det\mathbf{V}\) and \(\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{a}\) with respect to variance parameters that enter \(\mathbf{V}\).
Why these two expressions, and not others. It is worth seeing, before the algebra, exactly where \(\log\det\mathbf{V}\) and the inverse-quadratic form come from, because they are not arbitrary. A multivariate normal model with mean \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\) and covariance \(\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{V}(\boldsymbol\vartheta)\) (the covariance depending on variance parameters \(\boldsymbol\vartheta\), for instance a between-study variance \(\tau^2\)) has log-likelihood \[
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\vartheta)
=-\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det\mathbf{V}(\boldsymbol\vartheta)
-\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{V}(\boldsymbol\vartheta)^{-1}\mathbf{r}
+\text{const},
\qquad \mathbf{r}=\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta,
\tag{B.7}\] where \(\mathbf{r}\) is the residual vector. This is the single formula that makes the whole section relevant: to fit the model one maximizes Equation B.7, and to maximize it one needs its derivative with respect to \(\boldsymbol\vartheta\), which by the chain rule requires the derivatives of exactly \(\log\det\mathbf{V}\) and \(\mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}\). The restricted (REML) log-likelihood of Chapters 8 and 13 adds one more log-determinant term of the same kind. So the two identities below are precisely the pieces a health researcher needs to differentiate a random-effects meta-analysis or mixed model likelihood; we assemble the resulting score explicitly at the end of Section B.7.

Theorem B.4 (Derivative of the trace of a product) For constant \(A\) and a matrix variable \(X\) of conformable shape, \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial X}\operatorname{tr}(AX)=A^\top,\qquad
\frac{\partial}{\partial X}\operatorname{tr}(X^\top A)=A,\qquad
\frac{\partial}{\partial X}\operatorname{tr}(X^\top A X)=(A+A^\top)X,
\] and in particular \(\dfrac{\partial}{\partial X}\operatorname{tr}(X)=I\).


Proof. We use Lemma B.2 and Lemma B.3, then Lemma B.1.
For \(\operatorname{tr}(AX)\): \(d\operatorname{tr}(AX)=\operatorname{tr}(A\,dX)
=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((A^\top)^\top dX\bigr)\), so the derivative is \(A^\top\).
For \(\operatorname{tr}(X^\top A)\): \(d\operatorname{tr}(X^\top A)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((dX)^\top A\bigr)
=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(((dX)^\top A)^\top\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}(A^\top\,dX)\), so the derivative is \(A\).
For \(\operatorname{tr}(X^\top A X)\), the product and trace rules give \[
d\operatorname{tr}(X^\top A X)
=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((dX)^\top A X\bigr)+\operatorname{tr}\bigl(X^\top A\,dX\bigr).
\] The first term equals \(\operatorname{tr}\bigl((AX)^\top dX\bigr)\) by transposing inside the trace, since \(((dX)^\top AX)^\top=X^\top A^\top\,dX\) has the same trace and \(X^\top A^\top=(AX)^\top\). The second term is already \(\operatorname{tr}\bigl((A^\top X)^\top dX\bigr)\) because \((A^\top X)^\top=X^\top A\). Adding, \(d\operatorname{tr}(X^\top A X)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(((A+A^\top)X)^\top dX\bigr)\), so the derivative is \((A+A^\top)X\). Setting \(A=I\) in the first identity gives \(\partial\operatorname{tr}(X)/\partial X=I\). \(\square\)

Reader translation. These are the workhorse trace derivatives. Notice the last one, \(\partial\operatorname{tr}(X^\top A X)/\partial X=(A+A^\top)X\), is the matrix twin of the quadratic-form gradient \((A+A^\top)\mathbf{x}\); the same symmetrization appears for the same reason. It is instructive to appreciate what the differential method saved us: done entrywise one writes \(\operatorname{tr}(X^\top A X)
=\sum_{i,j,k}X_{ji}A_{jk}X_{ki}\), differentiates this triple sum in a generic entry \(X_{ab}\) (two terms, by the product rule on the two factors of \(X\)), and reassembles the pieces into a matrix; the proof above reached \((A+A^\top)X\) in three clean lines with no indices at all. That contrast is the entire argument for adopting differentials.
To differentiate the determinant and the inverse we first record how the inverse responds to a perturbation. Two classical objects appear, and we define them here at first use rather than assume them. The minor \(M_{ij}\) of a square matrix \(X\) is the determinant of the submatrix obtained by striking out row \(i\) and column \(j\). The cofactor is the signed minor \(C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}\), and the adjugate \(\operatorname{adj}(X)\) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix, \(\operatorname{adj}(X)=C^\top\). The one fact we borrow (from Strang (2016)) is Cramer’s rule in the form \(X^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(X)/\det(X)\), valid whenever \(\det(X)\ne 0\). The proof below needs that the entries of \(X^{-1}\) are differentiable functions of the entries of \(X\); Cramer’s rule exhibits each entry of \(X^{-1}\) as a ratio of polynomials in the entries of \(X\) whose denominator \(\det(X)\) does not vanish on the open set of invertible matrices, so each entry is differentiable there (Strang 2016).

Theorem B.5 (Derivative of the inverse) Let \(X\) range over invertible matrices. As a differential, \[
d\bigl(X^{-1}\bigr)=-X^{-1}\,(dX)\,X^{-1}.
\tag{B.8}\] Componentwise, \(\dfrac{\partial (X^{-1})_{kl}}{\partial X_{ij}}=-(X^{-1})_{ki}\,(X^{-1})_{jl}\). If \(X(t)\) depends differentiably on a scalar \(t\), then \(\dfrac{d}{dt}X(t)^{-1}=-X(t)^{-1}\dot X(t)\,X(t)^{-1}\).


Proof. Differentiate the identity \(X X^{-1}=I\). The right side is constant, so \(d(X X^{-1})=0\); the product rule of Lemma B.2 gives \((dX)X^{-1}+X\,d(X^{-1})=0\). Left-multiplying by \(X^{-1}\) and solving, \[
d(X^{-1})=-X^{-1}(dX)X^{-1},
\] which is Equation B.8. For the componentwise form take \(dX=E_{ij}\); then \(d(X^{-1})=-X^{-1}E_{ij}X^{-1}\), and \[
\bigl(X^{-1}E_{ij}X^{-1}\bigr)_{kl}
=\sum_{p,q}(X^{-1})_{kp}(E_{ij})_{pq}(X^{-1})_{ql}
=(X^{-1})_{ki}(X^{-1})_{jl},
\] where the double sum collapses because \(E_{ij}=\mathbf{e}_i\mathbf{e}_j^\top\) has a single nonzero entry, \((E_{ij})_{pq}=1\) only when \(p=i\) and \(q=j\); every other term is zero. Hence \(\partial(X^{-1})_{kl}/\partial X_{ij}=-(X^{-1})_{ki}(X^{-1})_{jl}\). The scalar-parameter statement is the same computation with \(dX\) replaced by \(\dot X(t)\,dt\). \(\square\)

Reader translation. The rule \(d(X^{-1})=-X^{-1}(dX)X^{-1}\) is the matrix version of the scalar fact \(d(1/x)=-x^{-2}\,dx\); the two copies of \(X^{-1}\), one on each side of \(dX\), are the price of noncommutativity, and their order cannot be swapped. This is exactly the identity that produces the \(-\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}(\partial\mathbf{V}/\partial\vartheta)\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{a}\) term in a variance-component score: it says how the inverse covariance changes when a variance parameter nudges \(\mathbf{V}\). We use it in that form in Section B.7 and Chapters 8 and 13.
Next, the differential of the determinant, classically Jacobi’s formula. It rests on the cofactor (Laplace) expansion and the adjugate identity \(X\,\operatorname{adj}(X)=\det(X)\,I\), both standard (Strang 2016). A reader who only needs the log-determinant derivative below (which is what the likelihood of Equation B.7 requires) may accept this lemma on first reading and skip its proof; the cofactor machinery is used only to prove it, not to apply it.

Lemma B.4 (Jacobi’s formula for the determinant) For any square \(X\), writing \(C=\operatorname{cof}(X)\) for the matrix of cofactors \(C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}\) (with \(M_{ij}\) the minor deleting row \(i\) and column \(j\)), \[
\frac{\partial \det(X)}{\partial X_{ij}}=C_{ij},
\qquad
d\det(X)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\operatorname{adj}(X)\,dX\bigr).
\] If in addition \(X\) is invertible, then \(\operatorname{adj}(X)=\det(X)\,X^{-1}\) and \[
\frac{\partial \det(X)}{\partial X}=\det(X)\,X^{-\top},
\qquad
d\det(X)=\det(X)\,\operatorname{tr}\bigl(X^{-1}\,dX\bigr).
\tag{B.9}\]


Proof. Fix a row index \(i\). The Laplace expansion along row \(i\) reads \(\det(X)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}X_{ik}\,C_{ik}\), and crucially each cofactor \(C_{ik}\) is built from the minor that deletes row \(i\), so \(C_{ik}\) does not depend on any entry of row \(i\). To see this last point plainly: the minor \(M_{ik}\) is by definition the determinant of the submatrix obtained by striking out row \(i\) and column \(k\), so not a single entry \(X_{i1},\dots,X_{in}\) of row \(i\) survives in it; therefore \(\partial C_{ik}/\partial X_{ij}=0\) for every \(j\). Differentiating \(\det(X)=\sum_k X_{ik}C_{ik}\) in \(X_{ij}\), only the explicit factor \(X_{ik}\) can contribute, and it does so only when \(k=j\), giving \(\partial\det(X)/\partial X_{ij}=C_{ij}\). Assembling the differential, \[
d\det(X)=\sum_{i,j}C_{ij}\,dX_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(C^\top\,dX\bigr)
=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\operatorname{adj}(X)\,dX\bigr),
\] since the adjugate is the transpose of the cofactor matrix, \(\operatorname{adj}(X)=C^\top\). When \(X\) is invertible, the adjugate identity \(X\,\operatorname{adj}(X)=\det(X)\,I\) gives \(\operatorname{adj}(X)=\det(X)\,X^{-1}\); substituting yields \(d\det(X)=\det(X)\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}dX)\), and because \(\operatorname{adj}(X)=C^\top\) we get \(C=\det(X)(X^{-1})^\top\), that is \(\partial\det(X)/\partial X=\det(X)X^{-\top}\). \(\square\)

Reader translation. Jacobi’s formula says the determinant changes, to first order, in proportion to \(\det(X)\) times the inverse transpose: \(d\det(X)=\det(X)\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}\,dX)\). We almost never need the raw determinant derivative; we need its logarithm, obtained next by one application of the chain rule, because it is \(\log\det\mathbf{V}\) (not \(\det\mathbf{V}\)) that appears in every Gaussian log-likelihood Equation B.7.

Theorem B.6 (Derivative of the log-determinant) Let \(X\) range over matrices with \(\det(X)>0\). Then \[
d\log\det(X)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(X^{-1}\,dX\bigr),
\qquad
\frac{\partial}{\partial X}\log\det(X)=X^{-\top}=(X^{-1})^\top .
\tag{B.10}\] If \(X\) is symmetric and invertible, \(\partial\log\det(X)/\partial X=X^{-1}\).


Proof. The map \(X\mapsto\log\det(X)\) is the composition of \(t\mapsto\log t\) with \(X\mapsto\det(X)\), both differentiable where \(\det(X)>0\). The ordinary chain rule for the outer scalar function gives \[
d\log\det(X)=\frac{1}{\det(X)}\,d\det(X)
=\frac{1}{\det(X)}\,\det(X)\operatorname{tr}\bigl(X^{-1}\,dX\bigr)
=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(X^{-1}\,dX\bigr),
\] using Equation B.9. Writing this as \(\operatorname{tr}\bigl((X^{-\top})^\top dX\bigr)\) and applying Lemma B.1 gives \(\partial\log\det(X)/\partial X=X^{-\top}\). For symmetric invertible \(X\) the inverse is symmetric, so \(X^{-\top}=X^{-1}\). \(\square\)

Reader translation. This is one of the two identities the whole section was aiming at. In words: the derivative of \(\log\det\) is the inverse (transposed, but for a symmetric covariance matrix the transpose does nothing). Combined with the inverse-derivative rule for the \(\mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}\) term, it delivers the gradient of the Gaussian log-likelihood Equation B.7 with respect to a variance parameter, hence the restricted-likelihood score of random-effects meta-analysis. The next remark records a layout subtlety that matters precisely because covariance matrices are symmetric.

Remark. The symmetric case hides a layout subtlety worth stating, because covariance and precision matrices are symmetric. There are two different questions, and they have different answers.
Question one: all entries free. If one differentiates \(f(X)=\log\det X\) treating all \(n^2\) entries as independent, the answer is \(X^{-\top}\) as proved above. This is the derivative reported by the theorem.
Question two: only the free parameters of a symmetric matrix. If instead \(X\) is constrained symmetric and one differentiates with respect to the \(\binom{n+1}{2}\) genuinely free parameters (the diagonal and one triangle), then a diagonal parameter \(X_{ii}\) moves one entry, but an off-diagonal free parameter \(X_{ij}\) with \(i<j\) moves two entries at once, \(X_{ij}\) and \(X_{ji}\). By the chain rule the derivative with respect to that one parameter is \(\partial f/\partial X_{ij}+\partial f/\partial X_{ji}
=2(X^{-1})_{ij}\): the off-diagonal derivatives are doubled.
A \(2\times 2\) example makes the doubling concrete. Let \(X=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ b&c\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) with free parameters \(a,b,c\), so \(\det X=ac-b^2\) and \(X^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{ac-b^2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}c&-b\\ -b&a\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Differentiating \(f=\log(ac-b^2)\) directly, \[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial a}=\frac{c}{ac-b^2}=(X^{-1})_{11},
\qquad
\frac{\partial f}{\partial c}=\frac{a}{ac-b^2}=(X^{-1})_{22},
\qquad
\frac{\partial f}{\partial b}=\frac{-2b}{ac-b^2}=2\,(X^{-1})_{12}.
\] The diagonal parameters reproduce single entries of \(X^{-1}\), while the off-diagonal parameter \(b\) picks up a factor \(2\) because it sits in both off-diagonal slots. Arranging these into a symmetric matrix gives \[
\begin{pmatrix}(X^{-1})_{11}&2(X^{-1})_{12}\\ 2(X^{-1})_{12}&(X^{-1})_{22}\end{pmatrix}
=2X^{-1}-\operatorname{diag}(X^{-1}),
\] the “symmetric gradient” with off-diagonal entries doubled. This is a genuine chain-rule consequence, not a trap, once one is clear about which variables are being held free.
In the restricted-likelihood applications of Chapters 8 and 13 this subtlety does not arise: one differentiates with respect to a scalar variance parameter \(\vartheta\) that enters \(\mathbf{V}(\vartheta)\), and the chain rule of Section B.7 gives the unambiguous \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\vartheta}\log\det\mathbf{V}(\vartheta)
=\operatorname{tr}\!\Bigl(\mathbf{V}^{-1}\frac{\partial\mathbf{V}}{\partial\vartheta}\Bigr),
\qquad
\frac{\partial}{\partial\vartheta}\bigl(\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{a}\bigr)
=-\,\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\frac{\partial\mathbf{V}}{\partial\vartheta}\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{a},
\] the second equality from Theorem B.5. These are the two pieces of the restricted-likelihood score. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: Appendix B — Matrix Calculus
text:
B.6 The Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity
A recurring computational need is to invert a matrix that differs from an easily inverted one by a low-rank correction.
