In random-effects meta-analysis and in mixed models the marginal covariance has the form \(\mathbf{V}=A+UCV\) with \(A\) diagonal (so trivially inverted) and \(UCV\) of small rank; the Woodbury identity reduces the inversion of \(\mathbf{V}\) to that of a small matrix.
A warning about the letter \(V\). In the identity below, \(V\) (plain, unbolded) is a generic rectangular factor, one of the four matrices \(A,U,C,V\) that build the low-rank update. It is not the covariance matrix \(\mathbf{V}\) (bold) of the likelihood Equation B.7, and it is not a vector space. The clash is unfortunate but the notation \(A+UCV\) is universal, so we keep it and simply flag it here.
What the four matrices are, concretely. It helps to have a picture before the algebra. Think of a mixed model or a random-effects meta-analysis whose marginal covariance is \(\mathbf{V}=A+UCV\). Here \(A\) is the easy diagonal part (within-study or residual variances, one per observation); \(U\) is a tall thin matrix that maps a few random effects to the many observations they influence; \(C\) is the small covariance of those random effects (often just a single between-study variance \(\tau^2\)); and \(V=U^\top\) closes the low-rank correction. Inverting the big \(n\times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{V}\) directly is expensive, but Woodbury turns it into inverting the tiny \(k\times k\) capacitance matrix \(C^{-1}+VA^{-1}U\), where \(k\) is the number of random effects. The compound-symmetry example of Section B.8 is the smallest instance, with \(k=1\): a single shared random effect, \(U=V^\top=\mathbf{1}_n\) and \(C=[\tau^2]\). The same low-rank structure appears in the marginal likelihood of ML-NMR (Chapters 20 to 25), where integrating out individual-level variation leaves a diagonal-plus-low-rank covariance of exactly this kind, and Woodbury is what keeps the likelihood computable.
We build up from the rank-one case.

Lemma B.5 (Sherman-Morrison rank-one update) Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be invertible and \(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\). If \(1+\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{u}\ne 0\), then \(A+\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top\) is invertible and \[
\bigl(A+\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top\bigr)^{-1}
=A^{-1}-\frac{A^{-1}\mathbf{u}\,\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}}{1+\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{u}} .
\tag{B.11}\]


Proof. Write \(c=\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{u}\) (a scalar) and \(s=1+c\ne 0\), and let \(B\) denote the proposed right-hand side of Equation B.11. Multiply on the left by \(A+\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top\): \[
\bigl(A+\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top\bigr)B
=AB+\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top B.
\] Compute each piece. First \[
AB=A A^{-1}-\frac{A A^{-1}\mathbf{u}\,\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}}{s}
=I-\frac{\mathbf{u}\,\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}}{s}.
\] Second, using \(\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{u}=c\), \[
\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top B
=\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}
-\frac{\mathbf{u}\,(\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{u})\,\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}}{s}
=\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\Bigl(1-\frac{c}{s}\Bigr)
=\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\,\frac{s-c}{s}
=\frac{\mathbf{u}\,\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}}{s},
\] since \(s-c=1\). Adding the two pieces, the corrections cancel and \(\bigl(A+\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top\bigr)B=I\). A square matrix with a right inverse is invertible, with that right inverse equal to the inverse (Theorem 1.6), so \(\bigl(A+\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top\bigr)^{-1}=B\). \(\square\)

Reader translation. Sherman-Morrison says: when you add a rank-one bump \(\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top\) to a matrix you can already invert, the new inverse is the old inverse minus a rank-one correction, and the only new scalar you must compute is the denominator \(1+\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{u}\). No new matrix is inverted at all. It is worth verifying once on numbers before trusting the general case.

Example B.4 (Sherman-Morrison on a \(2\times 2\) matrix) Take \(A=I_2\) and \(\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{1}_2=(1,1)^\top\), so \(A+\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top=I_2+\mathbf{1}_2\mathbf{1}_2^\top
=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\ 1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Here \(A^{-1}=I_2\) and the denominator is \(1+\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{u}=1+\mathbf{1}_2^\top\mathbf{1}_2=1+2=3\), so Equation B.11 gives \[
\bigl(I_2+\mathbf{1}_2\mathbf{1}_2^\top\bigr)^{-1}
=I_2-\tfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{1}_2\mathbf{1}_2^\top
=\frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\ -1&2\end{pmatrix}.
\] Direct check: \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\ 1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\cdot
\tfrac{1}{3}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-1\\ -1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) has first row \(\tfrac{1}{3}(2\cdot 2+1\cdot(-1),\ 2\cdot(-1)+1\cdot 2)=\tfrac{1}{3}(3,0)=(1,0)\), and similarly the second row is \((0,1)\), confirming the identity. This is the \(n=2\) case of the compound-symmetry inverse computed in full in Section B.8.


Theorem B.7 (Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity) Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}\) be invertible, and let \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}\), \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}\). If the capacitance matrix \(S:=C^{-1}+VA^{-1}U\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}\) is invertible, then \(A+UCV\) is invertible and \[
\bigl(A+UCV\bigr)^{-1}
=A^{-1}-A^{-1}U\bigl(C^{-1}+VA^{-1}U\bigr)^{-1}VA^{-1}.
\tag{B.12}\] The rank-one identity Equation B.11 is the case \(k=1\), \(C=[1]\), \(U=\mathbf{u}\), \(V=\mathbf{v}^\top\).


Proof. Let \(B\) denote the right-hand side of Equation B.12 and let \(M:=VA^{-1}U\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}\), so \(S=C^{-1}+M\). Multiply on the left by \(A+UCV\) and expand: \[
(A+UCV)B=AB+UCVB.
\] The first term is \[
AB=I-US^{-1}VA^{-1}.
\] For the second term, factor \(VA^{-1}\) on the right: \[
UCVB=UCVA^{-1}-UCVA^{-1}U S^{-1}VA^{-1}
=UC\bigl(I-M S^{-1}\bigr)VA^{-1}.
\] Adding and collecting the common right factor \(VA^{-1}\) and left factor \(U\), \[
(A+UCV)B
=I+U\Bigl\{-S^{-1}+C-CM S^{-1}\Bigr\}VA^{-1}.
\] The braced \(k\times k\) matrix vanishes: \[
-S^{-1}+C-CM S^{-1}
=C-(I+CM)S^{-1}
=C-C\bigl(C^{-1}+M\bigr)S^{-1}
=C-C S S^{-1}
=C-C=0,
\] using \(I+CM=C(C^{-1}+M)=CS\). Hence \((A+UCV)B=I\). A square matrix with a right inverse is invertible (Theorem 1.6), so \((A+UCV)^{-1}=B\). \(\square\)

Reader translation. Woodbury is Sherman-Morrison for a rank-\(k\) (rather than rank-one) correction: the \(n\times n\) inversion of \(A+UCV\) collapses to the \(k\times k\) inversion of the capacitance matrix \(C^{-1}+VA^{-1}U\), a huge saving when \(k\ll n\). The name “capacitance” is borrowed from electrical network theory, where this Schur-complement matrix arises; in this book it carries no electrical meaning and is simply the small matrix you end up inverting. This is the identity that makes the marginal likelihood of a mixed model, a random-effects meta-analysis, or ML-NMR computable at scale.
A companion identity handles the determinant, which is what the log-determinant term of a restricted likelihood requires. We first record the Schur-complement determinant formula, then specialize.

Lemma B.6 (Block determinant via the Schur complement) Let \(P=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\ C&D\end{pmatrix}\) be a square block matrix with \(A\) square and invertible. Then \[
\det P=\det(A)\,\det\bigl(D-CA^{-1}B\bigr).
\]


Proof. Verify the block factorization \[
\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\ C&D\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\ CA^{-1}&I\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\ 0&D-CA^{-1}B\end{pmatrix},
\] by multiplying the right side block by block. All four blocks check out: the \((1,1)\) block is \(I\cdot A+0\cdot 0=A\); the \((1,2)\) block is \(I\cdot B+0\cdot(D-CA^{-1}B)=B\); the \((2,1)\) block is \(CA^{-1}\cdot A+I\cdot 0=C\); and the \((2,2)\) block is \(CA^{-1}B+I\cdot(D-CA^{-1}B)=D\). So the factorization holds exactly. The first factor is block lower triangular with identity diagonal blocks, so its determinant is \(1\); the second is block upper triangular, so its determinant is the product \(\det(A)\det(D-CA^{-1}B)\) of the diagonal blocks (Strang 2016). Multiplicativity of the determinant gives the claim. \(\square\)


Corollary B.1 (Matrix determinant lemma) With \(A,C,U,V\) as in Theorem B.7 and \(A,C\) invertible, \[
\det\bigl(A+UCV\bigr)=\det(A)\,\det(C)\,\det\bigl(C^{-1}+VA^{-1}U\bigr).
\tag{B.13}\] In particular, for the rank-one update, \(\det\bigl(A+\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top\bigr)=\det(A)\,\bigl(1+\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{u}\bigr)\).


Proof. Apply Lemma B.6 to the block matrix \(P=\begin{pmatrix}A&U\\ -V&C^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\) in two ways. This particular block matrix is not pulled from nowhere: it is built so that eliminating one diagonal block produces the small capacitance matrix \(C^{-1}+VA^{-1}U\), while eliminating the other produces the large matrix \(A+UCV\). Computing \(\det P\) both ways and equating the results is what links the two determinants. Taking first the Schur complement of the invertible top-left block \(A\), \[
\det P=\det(A)\,\det\bigl(C^{-1}-(-V)A^{-1}U\bigr)=\det(A)\,\det\bigl(C^{-1}+VA^{-1}U\bigr).
\] Taking instead the Schur complement of the invertible bottom-right block \(C^{-1}\) (the same formula applied to the block matrix after swapping the roles of the two diagonal blocks), \[
\det P=\det\bigl(C^{-1}\bigr)\,\det\bigl(A-U\,(C^{-1})^{-1}(-V)\bigr)
=\det\bigl(C^{-1}\bigr)\,\det\bigl(A+UCV\bigr).
\] Equating the two expressions and using \(\det(C^{-1})=1/\det(C)\) gives Equation B.13. The rank-one case is \(k=1\), \(C=[1]\), where \(\det(C)=1\) and \(C^{-1}+\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{u}
=1+\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{u}\). \(\square\)

Reader translation. The matrix determinant lemma is Woodbury for determinants: the determinant of the big matrix \(A+UCV\) factors through the small capacitance determinant, so the \(\log\det\mathbf{V}\) term of a likelihood (Equation B.7) is computed from a \(k\times k\) determinant instead of an \(n\times n\) one. The rank-one case \(\det(A+\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top)=\det(A)(1+\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{u})\) is the one used in the compound-symmetry determinant of Section B.8.

title: Appendix B — Matrix Calculus
section: B.7 The chain rule for matrix functions
text:
B.7 The chain rule for matrix functions
Finally, the rule that lets all of the above be composed. We state it for vector compositions, where it is the workhorse of the delta method (Theorem 5.3), and for a scalar parameter passing through a matrix, which is the form used for likelihood scores.

Theorem B.8 (Chain rule)  

(Vector composition.) Let \(\mathbf{f}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}\) be differentiable at \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{g}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{p}\) differentiable at \(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\). Then \(\mathbf{g}\circ\mathbf{f}\) is differentiable at \(\mathbf{x}\) with \[
J_{\mathbf{g}\circ\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x})
=J_{\mathbf{g}}\bigl(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)\,J_{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x}).
\tag{B.14}\] For a scalar outer function \(\phi:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}\), \(\nabla(\phi\circ\mathbf{f})(\mathbf{x})=J_{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x})^\top\,
\nabla\phi\bigl(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)\).
(Scalar parameter through a matrix.) Let \(X:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be differentiable at \(t\) and \(f:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}\) differentiable at \(X(t)\). Then \(\phi(t)=f(X(t))\) is differentiable at \(t\) with \[
\phi'(t)=\Big\langle \tfrac{\partial f}{\partial X}\big(X(t)\big),\,\dot X(t)\Big\rangle_F
=\operatorname{tr}\!\Bigl(\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial X}\big(X(t)\big)^{\!\top}\dot X(t)\Bigr).
\tag{B.15}\]



Proof. (1). Differentiability of \(\mathbf{f}\) gives \(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h})=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{k}\) with \(\mathbf{k}=J_{\mathbf{f}}\mathbf{h}+o(\|\mathbf{h}\|)\), so \(\|\mathbf{k}\|=O(\|\mathbf{h}\|)\) and \(\mathbf{k}\to\mathbf{0}\) as \(\mathbf{h}\to\mathbf{0}\). Differentiability of \(\mathbf{g}\) at \(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\) gives \[
\mathbf{g}\bigl(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{k}\bigr)
=\mathbf{g}\bigl(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)+J_{\mathbf{g}}\,\mathbf{k}+o(\|\mathbf{k}\|)
=\mathbf{g}\bigl(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)
+J_{\mathbf{g}}J_{\mathbf{f}}\,\mathbf{h}
+\underbrace{J_{\mathbf{g}}\,o(\|\mathbf{h}\|)+o(\|\mathbf{k}\|)}_{o(\|\mathbf{h}\|)}.
\] The error is \(o(\|\mathbf{h}\|)\) because \(J_{\mathbf{g}}\,o(\|\mathbf{h}\|)=o(\|\mathbf{h}\|)\) and \(o(\|\mathbf{k}\|)=o(O(\|\mathbf{h}\|))=o(\|\mathbf{h}\|)\). By Equation B.3 the Jacobian of the composition is \(J_{\mathbf{g}}J_{\mathbf{f}}\). The scalar case is Equation B.4 applied to \(\phi\circ\mathbf{f}\): \(\nabla(\phi\circ\mathbf{f})=J_{\phi\circ\mathbf{f}}^\top
=(J_\phi J_{\mathbf{f}})^\top=J_{\mathbf{f}}^\top\,\nabla\phi\).
(2). This is part (1) after flattening the matrix into a vector: identify \(\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) with \(\mathbb{R}^{mn}\) by stacking columns, under which the Frobenius inner product becomes the Euclidean inner product. The choice of stacking order does not matter: the conclusion Equation B.15 is written invariantly as a Frobenius inner product (equivalently a trace), and a trace is unchanged by any consistent relabeling of the entries, so every flattening gives the same scalar \(\phi'(t)\). Concretely, \(X(t+\delta)=X(t)+\delta\,\dot X(t)+o(\delta)\), so by Equation B.5 \[
\phi(t+\delta)=f\bigl(X(t)+\delta\dot X(t)+o(\delta)\bigr)
=f(X(t))+\Big\langle\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial X},\,\delta\dot X(t)\Big\rangle_F+o(\delta),
\] and dividing by \(\delta\) and letting \(\delta\to0\) gives Equation B.15. \(\square\)

Reader translation. The chain rule is what lets all the identities above be composed. Part (1) is the familiar “multiply the Jacobians” rule that powers the delta method (Theorem 5.3): to move a variance through a chain of transformations, multiply the local linear maps. Part (2) is the version used for likelihood scores: when a scalar parameter \(t\) (a variance component, say) enters a matrix, the derivative of any scalar function of that matrix is a single trace, \(\operatorname{tr}((\partial
f/\partial X)^\top\dot X)\). The next remark applies it to exactly the two functions the Gaussian log-likelihood needs.

Remark. Two specializations of Equation B.15 were used in Section B.5. With \(f(X)=\log\det X\) and \(\partial f/\partial X=X^{-\top}\), Equation B.15 gives \(\frac{d}{dt}\log\det X(t)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((X^{-\top})^\top\dot X\bigr)
=\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}\dot X)\). With \(f(X)=\mathbf{a}^\top X^{-1}\mathbf{a}\) one combines Theorem B.5 with the chain rule to get \(\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\mathbf{a}^\top X^{-1}\mathbf{a}\bigr)
=-\mathbf{a}^\top X^{-1}\dot X X^{-1}\mathbf{a}\). These are exactly the building blocks of the restricted-likelihood score in Chapters 8 and 13. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Rather than leave those building blocks unassembled, we now build the score, since assembling it is the single computation this whole section exists to enable.

Example B.5 (Assembling a variance-component score) Consider the Gaussian log-likelihood Equation B.7 with residual \(\mathbf{r}\) held fixed and a covariance \(\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{V}(\vartheta)\) depending on a single variance parameter \(\vartheta\) (for instance the between-study variance \(\tau^2\)): \[
\ell(\vartheta)=-\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det\mathbf{V}(\vartheta)
-\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{V}(\vartheta)^{-1}\mathbf{r}+\text{const}.
\] Write \(\mathbf{V}_\vartheta:=\partial\mathbf{V}/\partial\vartheta\). Differentiate term by term. The first term uses Theorem B.6 through the chain rule Equation B.15, \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\vartheta}\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det\mathbf{V}\Bigr)
=-\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{V}_\vartheta\bigr).
\] The second term uses the inverse-derivative rule Theorem B.5, which supplies \(\partial\mathbf{V}^{-1}/\partial\vartheta=-\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{V}_\vartheta\mathbf{V}^{-1}\), so \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\vartheta}\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}\Bigr)
=+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{V}_\vartheta\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}.
\] Adding the two pieces gives the score for the variance parameter, \[
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\vartheta}
=-\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{V}_\vartheta\bigr)
+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{V}_\vartheta\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r},
\tag{B.16}\] and setting it to zero yields the estimating equation \(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{V}_\vartheta)
=\mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{V}_\vartheta\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}\). The restricted (REML) log-likelihood adds a further term \(-\tfrac12\log\det(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X})\), whose derivative is again a trace of the same shape by Theorem B.6 and Theorem B.5; the mechanics are identical.

Reader translation. Equation Equation B.16 is the payoff of the appendix for meta-analysis: it is the exact gradient that a random-effects model solves to estimate heterogeneity. Every symbol in it came from an identity proved above, the log-determinant derivative and the inverse derivative, glued by the chain rule. In the next section we evaluate every piece of it in closed form for the compound-symmetry covariance, where \(\mathbf{V}_\vartheta=\mathbf{1}_n\mathbf{1}_n^\top\).

title: Appendix B — Matrix Calculus
section: B.8 A worked example: the compound-symmetry covariance
text:
B.8 A worked example: the compound-symmetry covariance
We assemble the rank-one inverse, the matrix determinant lemma, and the log-determinant derivative on the covariance matrix that governs the balanced one-way random-effects model and the random-effects meta-analysis of Chapter 13. Let \[
\mathbf{V}=\sigma^2 I_n+\tau^2\,\mathbf{1}_n\mathbf{1}_n^\top,
\] the compound-symmetry (equicorrelation) matrix, with \(\sigma^2>0\) and \(\tau^2\ge 0\). We compute its inverse, its determinant, and the derivative of \(\log\det\mathbf{V}\) with respect to the between-study variance \(\tau^2\), all in closed form, and then verify the formulas numerically.
What each symbol means for a meta-analysis. This covariance is not an abstract choice; it is the exact marginal covariance of the estimates from \(n\) studies in a random-effects meta-analysis, so it is worth translating every symbol. Here \(n\) is the number of studies; \(\sigma^2\) is the within-study (residual, sampling) variance, assumed common across studies in this balanced illustration; and \(\tau^2\) is the between-study variance, the heterogeneity, the extra variability because the true effect differs from study to study. The vector \(\mathbf{1}_n=(1,\dots,1)^\top\) is the \(n\)-vector of ones, and the matrix \(\mathbf{1}_n\mathbf{1}_n^\top\) (a matrix of all ones) encodes a single shared random effect: it says every study’s estimate is shifted by the same common random deviation, so all pairs of studies share the \(\tau^2\) component of variance. That matrix has rank one, because it is the outer product of one vector with itself, and the rank-one structure is exactly what lets Sherman-Morrison and the matrix determinant lemma reduce an \(n\times n\) inverse and determinant to scalars. The reason we care about the derivative with respect to \(\tau^2\) is that estimating heterogeneity means solving the variance-component score Equation B.16, and that score is built from precisely \(\partial\log\det\mathbf{V}/\partial\tau^2\) and the inverse-quadratic derivative computed below.
Inverse. Apply Lemma B.5 with \(A=\sigma^2 I_n\), \(\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{1}_n\), and \(\mathbf{v}=\tau^2\mathbf{1}_n\), so that \(\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top=\tau^2\mathbf{1}_n\mathbf{1}_n^\top\). Here \(A^{-1}=\sigma^{-2}I_n\) and \(\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{u}=\tau^2\sigma^{-2}\mathbf{1}_n^\top\mathbf{1}_n=n\tau^2/\sigma^2\), so Equation B.11 gives \[
\mathbf{V}^{-1}
=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}I_n-\frac{\tau^2/\sigma^4}{1+n\tau^2/\sigma^2}\,\mathbf{1}_n\mathbf{1}_n^\top
=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\Bigl(I_n-\frac{\tau^2/\sigma^2}{1+n\tau^2/\sigma^2}\,\mathbf{1}_n\mathbf{1}_n^\top\Bigr).
\tag{B.17}\]
Determinant. The rank-one case of Corollary B.1 gives \[
\det\mathbf{V}=\det(\sigma^2 I_n)\,\bigl(1+\tau^2\,\mathbf{1}_n^\top(\sigma^2 I_n)^{-1}\mathbf{1}_n\bigr)
=\sigma^{2n}\Bigl(1+\frac{n\tau^2}{\sigma^2}\Bigr).
\tag{B.18}\]
Derivative of the log-determinant. From Equation B.18, \(\log\det\mathbf{V}=n\log\sigma^2+\log\!\bigl(1+n\tau^2/\sigma^2\bigr)\), so directly \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau^2}\log\det\mathbf{V}=\frac{n/\sigma^2}{1+n\tau^2/\sigma^2}.
\] The chain rule Equation B.15 with Theorem B.6 must agree. Since \(\partial\mathbf{V}/\partial\tau^2=\mathbf{1}_n\mathbf{1}_n^\top\), \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau^2}\log\det\mathbf{V}
=\operatorname{tr}\!\Bigl(\mathbf{V}^{-1}\frac{\partial\mathbf{V}}{\partial\tau^2}\Bigr)
=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{1}_n\mathbf{1}_n^\top\bigr)
=\mathbf{1}_n^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{1}_n.
\] Using Equation B.17 and \(\mathbf{1}_n^\top\mathbf{1}_n=n\), \[
\mathbf{1}_n^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{1}_n
=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\Bigl(n-\frac{\tau^2/\sigma^2}{1+n\tau^2/\sigma^2}\,n^2\Bigr)
=\frac{n}{\sigma^2}\cdot\frac{1}{1+n\tau^2/\sigma^2}
=\frac{n/\sigma^2}{1+n\tau^2/\sigma^2},
\] in agreement.
Numerical check. Take \(n=3\), \(\sigma^2=1\), \(\tau^2=2\), so \(\mathbf{V}=I_3+2\,\mathbf{1}_3\mathbf{1}_3^\top=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}3&2&2\\2&3&2\\2&2&3\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Formula Equation B.17 gives \(\mathbf{V}^{-1}=I_3-\tfrac{2}{7}\mathbf{1}_3\mathbf{1}_3^\top\), that is \[
\mathbf{V}^{-1}=\frac{1}{7}\begin{pmatrix}5&-2&-2\\-2&5&-2\\-2&-2&5\end{pmatrix}.
\] Direct multiplication confirms it: the first row of \(\mathbf{V}\) dotted with the first column of \(\mathbf{V}^{-1}\) is \((3\cdot5+2\cdot(-2)+2\cdot(-2))/7=(15-4-4)/7=1\), and with the second column is \((3\cdot(-2)+2\cdot5+2\cdot(-2))/7=(-6+10-4)/7=0\). Formula Equation B.18 gives \(\det\mathbf{V}=1^3(1+3\cdot2)=7\), matching the eigenvalue count: \(\mathbf{1}_3\mathbf{1}_3^\top\) has eigenvalues \(3,0,0\), so \(\mathbf{V}=I_3+2\,\mathbf{1}_3\mathbf{1}_3^\top\) has eigenvalues \(7,1,1\) with product \(7\). Finally \(\partial\log\det\mathbf{V}/\partial\tau^2=\frac{3}{1+6}=\frac{3}{7}\), which equals \(\mathbf{1}_3^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{1}_3=\) (sum of all entries of \(\mathbf{V}^{-1}\)) \(=(3\cdot5+6\cdot(-2))/7=(15-12)/7=\frac{3}{7}\). All three routes agree.
This is precisely the arithmetic that makes the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimating equations for \(\tau^2\) tractable in closed form for balanced designs, as used in Chapters 8 and 13: the Woodbury inverse and the matrix determinant lemma reduce an \(n\times n\) problem to scalars, and the log-determinant and inverse derivatives produce the score.

title: Appendix B — Matrix Calculus
section: B.9 A second worked example: the score of a logistic log-likelihood
text:
B.9 A second worked example: the score of a logistic log-likelihood
The previous example served the variance-component side of the book. This one serves the side the target reader most often needs: the likelihood derivatives behind logistic regression, which underpin the binary-outcome likelihood of ML-NMR (Chapters 20 to 25) and the outcome model of an anchored indirect comparison. The phrase “the MAIC, STC, and ML-NMR derivations just follow from differentiating a likelihood” means, concretely, the computation below.
Let \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) be binary outcomes for \(i=1,\dots,n\), with covariate rows \(\mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb{R}^p\) stacked into the design matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) (rows \(\mathbf{x}_i^\top\)). Logistic regression sets the linear predictor \(\eta_i=\mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta\) and the success probability \(p_i=\operatorname{expit}(\eta_i)=1/(1+e^{-\eta_i})\). The log-likelihood is \[
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl[y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\bigr]
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl[y_i\,\eta_i-\log(1+e^{\eta_i})\bigr].
\]
Score (gradient). Differentiate term by term in \(\boldsymbol\beta\). By the linear-form derivative Theorem B.1, \(\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}\eta_i=\mathbf{x}_i\); and by the chain rule (Theorem B.8), \(\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}\log(1+e^{\eta_i})
=\dfrac{e^{\eta_i}}{1+e^{\eta_i}}\,\mathbf{x}_i=p_i\,\mathbf{x}_i\). Hence \[
\mathbf{s}(\boldsymbol\beta)=\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ell
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-p_i)\,\mathbf{x}_i=\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p}),
\qquad \mathbf{p}=(p_1,\dots,p_n)^\top.
\tag{B.19}\] The score is the design matrix transpose times the residual vector \(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p}\) (shape check: \(\mathbf{X}^\top\) is \(p\times n\), \(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p}\) is \(n\times 1\), so the score is \(p\times 1\), matching \(\boldsymbol\beta\)).
Hessian (curvature) and Fisher information. The score is a sum of \(-p_i\mathbf{x}_i\) plus constants; using \(\partial p_i/\partial\boldsymbol\beta^\top=p_i(1-p_i)\,\mathbf{x}_i^\top\) (chain rule again, since \(\operatorname{expit}'=\operatorname{expit}(1-\operatorname{expit})\)), \[
\nabla^2_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ell
=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i(1-p_i)\,\mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i^\top
=-\mathbf{X}^\top W\mathbf{X},
\qquad W=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(p_i(1-p_i)\bigr).
\tag{B.20}\] Because \(W\succeq 0\), the Hessian is negative semidefinite, so \(\ell\) is concave and its stationary point is the maximum likelihood estimator. The Fisher information is the negative Hessian, \(\mathcal{I}(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf{X}^\top W\mathbf{X}\), exactly the matrix inverted at each iteration of iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) in the GLM chapter; the weights \(W\) are why it is reweighted.
Numerical instance. Take \(n=2\), \(p=2\), design rows \(\mathbf{x}_1=(1,0)^\top\) and \(\mathbf{x}_2=(1,1)^\top\) (an intercept and one covariate), outcomes \(\mathbf{y}=(1,0)^\top\), evaluated at \(\boldsymbol\beta=(0,0)^\top\). Then \(\eta_1=\eta_2=0\) and \(p_1=p_2=\tfrac12\), so the residual is \(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p}=(\tfrac12,-\tfrac12)^\top\) and Equation B.19 gives \[
\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p})
=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac12\\ -\tfrac12\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ -\tfrac12\end{pmatrix}.
\] The weight matrix is \(W=\operatorname{diag}(\tfrac14,\tfrac14)\), so Equation B.20 gives the Fisher information \[
\mathcal{I}=\mathbf{X}^\top W\mathbf{X}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac14&0\\ 0&\tfrac14\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 1&1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac12&\tfrac14\\ \tfrac14&\tfrac14\end{pmatrix},
\] and the Hessian is \(-\mathcal{I}\). One Newton (Fisher scoring) step from \(\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf{0}\) is \(\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto\boldsymbol\beta+\mathcal{I}^{-1}\mathbf{s}\), the same update that drives the maximum likelihood fits in the GLM, MAIC, and ML-NMR chapters. This is the derivative computation the target reader came to this appendix for; it uses only Theorem B.1 and Theorem B.8.

title: Appendix B — Matrix Calculus
text:
B.11 Notes and references
The conventions and identities of this appendix are standard matrix calculus. The differential method, which we adopted as the organizing principle, isolates the derivative as the unique matrix appearing in the canonical form \(\operatorname{tr}(G^\top\,dX)\) (Lemma B.1); it is the systematic development of Magnus and Neudecker, Matrix Differential Calculus with Applications in Statistics and Econometrics, and the same identities are cataloged, without proof, in Petersen and Pedersen, The Matrix Cookbook, and in Harville, Matrix Algebra from a Statistician’s Perspective. The linear-algebra prerequisites we invoked, namely the determinant, the cofactor expansion, the adjugate and Cramer’s rule, the multiplicativity of the determinant, the block-triangular determinant, and the characterization of invertibility, are developed in Strang (2016) and, in this book, in Theorem 1.6, Definition 3.6, and Definition 3.7.
The Sherman-Morrison formula (Lemma B.5) and its generalization (Theorem B.7) are named for Sherman and Morrison (1950) and for Woodbury (1950); the matrix determinant lemma (Corollary B.1) is sometimes attributed to Sylvester. The proofs given here are by direct verification, which is the most transparent route and is self-checking. The compound-symmetry worked example of Section B.8 is the elementary case underlying the closed-form restricted maximum likelihood estimators of the balanced one-way random-effects model; the general restricted likelihood, built from \(\log\det\mathbf{V}\) and \(\mathbf{V}^{-1}\), appears in Dias et al. (2018) and is differentiated using exactly Theorem B.6 and Theorem B.5.
These identities have no separate counterpart in the companion ITC_Coq development, whose formalized results sit at the statistical and causal layer rather than at the level of matrix differentiation; accordingly, none carries a machine-checked tag. The downstream uses are pervasive: the gradient and Hessian of the least-squares objective (Theorem B.2) drive the normal equations and the Gauss-Markov theory of the regression chapter; the Jacobian and the chain rule (Theorem B.8) are the analytic content of the delta method (Theorem 5.3) and of the variance propagation in the population-adjustment chapters; and the trace, inverse, and log-determinant derivatives are the engine of the restricted-likelihood score equations in the hierarchical and meta-analytic models.




Dias, Sofia, A. E. Ades, Nicky J. Welton, Jeroen P. Jansen, and Alexander J. Sutton. 2018. Network Meta-Analysis for Decision-Making. Statistics in Practice. Wiley.


Strang, Gilbert. 2016. Introduction to Linear Algebra. 5th ed. Wellesley-Cambridge Press.

title: Appendix C — Probability Distributions
text:
C.1 How to read this appendix
This appendix is a reference catalogue of the probability distributions used in the book. For each family we record the support, the probability mass or density function, the mean, the variance, and the moment generating function where it exists. The discrete families (Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson binomial, Poisson) and the normal, multivariate normal, and standard normal are defined and their moments derived in Section 4.11 and Section 4.12 of Chapter 4; this appendix collects those results and adds the further families (exponential, gamma, beta, Weibull, Dirichlet) that appear later as survival baselines in Chapters 25 and 26 and as conjugate priors in Chapter 8. Nothing here is proved that is not proved in the chapters or that does not follow by a one-line calculation; the value of the appendix is a single place to look up a defining formula. For the symbols used throughout, see Notation.
The fastest way to use this catalogue is to first name the modeling role you are in, then look up the family. Every distribution in the book plays one of six roles:
Table C.1 maps each family to the clinical object it typically models and to the chapters that use it. A reader browsing this appendix should start there, identify the role, and then read only the relevant catalogue entry.

title: Appendix C — Probability Distributions
text:

a prior, the distribution placed on an unknown parameter before seeing data (a beta on a response probability, a gamma on a rate, a normal on a treatment effect);
a covariate model, the distribution of baseline patient characteristics (a multivariate normal for correlated covariates);

a survival baseline, the model for a time-to-event outcome (exponential, Weibull); or
a numerical integration device, used to average an individual likelihood over a covariate distribution (the standard normal and the Gaussian copula in the ML-NMR integration of Chapter 22).

title: Appendix C — Probability Distributions
text:
C.2 Conventions
Three plain-language reminders precede the formulas, because the tables below mix objects of different kinds. The support of a distribution is the set of values the random variable can actually take, that is, the values where the mass or density is positive; everything outside the support has probability zero (for a binomial the support is \(\{0,1,\dots,n\}\), for a Weibull survival time it is \((0,\infty)\)). A mass function \(P(X=k)\) gives a genuine probability at each point of a discrete support and never exceeds \(1\). A density \(f(x)\) does not: it is a rate of probability per unit length, and an actual probability is recovered only by integrating \(f\) over an interval, so a density can exceed \(1\) (a tightly concentrated normal has a peak above \(1\)) even though no probability ever does. This is why a density value is not itself a probability.
The moment generating function (MGF) of a random vector \(X\) is \(M_X(\mathbf{t})=\mathbb{E}[e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}X}]\), written \(M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]\) in the scalar case (Definition 4.7). We say the MGF exists when it is finite for all \(\mathbf{t}\) in an open neighborhood of the origin; in that case it determines all moments by differentiation at the origin (Theorem 4.10) and determines the law uniquely (Theorem 4.11). Intuitively the MGF is a bookkeeping device: because \(\frac{d}{dt}e^{tX}=X e^{tX}\), each derivative evaluated at \(t=0\) pulls down one extra factor of \(X\), so \(M_X^{(r)}(0)=\mathbb{E}[X^{r}]\) and the entire sequence of moments is stored in one function. That is the only reason the MGF earns a column in the tables below: given the MGF, the mean and variance are two derivatives away. For some families with a finite MGF the function has no elementary closed form; for the beta and Weibull families this is noted in the catalogue, and for the Dirichlet the joint MGF on the ambient space is degenerate.
(Advanced; skip on a first pass.) “Degenerate on the ambient space” means the following. When the support lies in a hyperplane, as it does for the Dirichlet whose components satisfy \(\sum_k x_k=1\), one coordinate is fixed by the others, namely \(x_K=1-\sum_{k<K}x_k\). The joint MGF on \(\mathbb{R}^{K}\) is then really a function of only \(K-1\) free arguments and cannot characterize the law in the usual full-rank way, so we describe such a family by its moments instead of by an MGF. This is why the Dirichlet row lists moments rather than an MGF.
Two special functions recur. The gamma function is \[
\Gamma(s)=\int_0^{\infty} u^{s-1}e^{-u}\,du,\qquad s>0,
\tag{C.1}\] which satisfies \(\Gamma(s+1)=s\,\Gamma(s)\) and \(\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!\) for positive integers \(n\); it is the continuous interpolation of the factorial and appears in the normalizing constants of the gamma, beta, Weibull, and Dirichlet densities. The beta function is \[
B(a,b)=\int_0^1 u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}\,du=\frac{\Gamma(a)\,\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)},\qquad a,b>0,
\tag{C.2}\] and its multivariate form, used by the Dirichlet density, is \(B(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\prod_{k=1}^K\Gamma(\alpha_k)\big/\Gamma\!\big(\sum_{k=1}^K\alpha_k\big)\); the scalar \(B(a,b)\) is the \(K=2\) case of the vector \(B(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\), so the two share a symbol on purpose. The numerical evaluation of these functions, together with the error function below, is treated in Appendix D.
We fix two parametrization conventions that are sources of confusion across the literature. The gamma and exponential families are parametrized by a rate, so that \(\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta)\) has shape \(\alpha\), rate \(\beta\), and mean \(\alpha/\beta\); this matches the convention of Proposition 8.1 in Chapter 8. The Weibull family is parametrized by a shape and a scale, related to the proportional-hazards parametrization of Chapter 25 as recorded below. A rate has units of events per unit of the variable, so a larger rate means shorter times; a scale has the units of the variable itself, so a larger scale means longer times. Because closely related survival families are written with a rate, a scale, or a hazard depending on the chapter, Table C.2 gathers the three side by side.

The gamma and exponential use a rate (events per unit, larger means shorter times); the Weibull table uses a scale (a typical time, larger means longer times); Chapter 25 rewrites the Weibull through its hazard with shape \(\nu=k\) and coefficient \(\lambda(\mathbf{x})=\lambda^{-\nu}\). All three describe the same families with different symbols. A Bayesian precision means the reciprocal of a variance, \(1/\sigma^{2}\); the normal conjugacy of Section C.8 adds precisions rather than variances.

Each family models a distinct kind of health data.
Bernoulli. A single yes/no outcome with success probability \(p\): one patient, responder (\(X=1\)) or non-responder (\(X=0\)). It is the atom from which the binary-outcome likelihoods of the book are built.
Binomial. The number of successes in \(n\) independent, identical yes/no trials, each with the same probability \(p\): the count of responders out of \(n\) randomized patients. This is the workhorse likelihood for aggregate binary endpoints in meta-analysis (Chapter 13) and network meta-analysis, where each arm reports “\(r\) responders out of \(n\).”
Poisson binomial. The number of successes in \(n\) independent trials whose success probabilities \(p_1,\dots,p_n\) are allowed to differ. The mass function looks forbidding but says something simple: to get exactly \(k\) successes, sum over every way of choosing which \(k\) of the \(n\) trials succeed, and for each such choice multiply the success probabilities of the chosen trials by the failure probabilities of the rest. It is the natural law for an aggregate event count when a model assigns each patient a different predicted risk, which is exactly the situation in covariate-adjusted binary outcomes; it drives the discrete aggregation results of Section 21.5 in Chapter 21.
Poisson. The count of events when events arrive independently at a constant average, for example the number of relapses in a fixed follow-up window. In practice the Poisson mean is a rate times an exposure: if events occur at rate \(\rho\) per person-year and a patient is followed for time \(E\), then the event count is \(\mathrm{Poi}(\rho E)\), so \(\lambda=\rho E\). This is how Poisson models describe events per person-time rather than bare counts.
The families nest. A Bernoulli variable is \(\mathrm{Bin}(1,p)\); a binomial is the Poisson binomial with all \(p_i\) equal to a common \(p\), in which case every entry of the Poisson binomial row reduces to its binomial counterpart. The Poisson is the law of rare events: if \(X_n\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,\lambda/n)\) then \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\) (Theorem 4.13), so a Poisson is the limit of a binomial with many trials each individually rare; a quantitative total-variation form of this approximation drives the discrete aggregation results of Part V. Sums of independent Poisson variables are Poisson, with rates adding, by the product rule for moment generating functions (Theorem 4.12).

Remark. For a fixed mean \(\sum_i p_i\), the Poisson binomial variance \(\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)=\sum_i p_i-\sum_i
p_i^2\) is largest when the \(p_i\) are equal, by convexity of \(p\mapsto p^2\). (Convexity means \(\sum_i p_i^2\) is smallest when the \(p_i\) are all equal, hence the variance \(\sum_i p_i-\sum_i p_i^2\) is largest there; pulling the risks apart only lowers the aggregate variance.) Heterogeneous individual risks therefore produce a less dispersed aggregate count than a binomial with the same expected number of events, a fact used when an aggregate event count is modeled under covariate-adjusted risks. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Example C.1 (Aggregating three unequal risks) Suppose three patients have predicted event probabilities \(p_1=0.1\), \(p_2=0.3\), \(p_3=0.6\), and we want the distribution of the total number of events \(X\sim\mathrm{PoBin}(0.1,0.3,0.6)\). Reading the Poisson binomial mass function one value of \(k\) at a time, \[
\begin{aligned}
P(X=0)&=(0.9)(0.7)(0.4)=0.252,\\
P(X=1)&=(0.1)(0.7)(0.4)+(0.9)(0.3)(0.4)+(0.9)(0.7)(0.6)=0.514,\\
P(X=2)&=(0.1)(0.3)(0.4)+(0.1)(0.7)(0.6)+(0.9)(0.3)(0.6)=0.216,\\
P(X=3)&=(0.1)(0.3)(0.6)=0.018,
\end{aligned}
\] which sum to \(1\). The mean is \(\mathbb{E}[X]=0.1+0.3+0.6=1.0\) and the variance is \(\mathrm{Var}(X)=0.1(0.9)+0.3(0.7)+0.6(0.4)=0.54\). Compare a binomial with the same mean, namely \(\mathrm{Bin}(3,\tfrac13)\), whose variance is \(3\cdot\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac23=\tfrac23\approx0.667\). The heterogeneous risks give the smaller variance \(0.54<0.667\), exactly the effect of the remark above: when predicted risks differ across patients the aggregate event count is less dispersed than a binomial with the same expected number of events. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

When there are more than two response categories, the binomial generalizes to the multinomial, which the appendix uses only as the likelihood conjugate to the Dirichlet of Section C.6.

Definition C.1 (Multinomial distribution) Fix \(N\in\{1,2,\dots\}\) and a probability vector \(\mathbf{p}=(p_1,\dots,p_K)\) with \(p_k\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_k=1\). The count vector \(\mathbf{n}=(n_1,\dots,n_K)\) of the outcomes of \(N\) independent trials, each landing in category \(k\) with probability \(p_k\), has the multinomial distribution \(\mathrm{Multinomial}(N,\mathbf{p})\), with mass function \[
P(\mathbf{n})=\binom{N}{n_1,\dots,n_K}\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_k^{\,n_k}
=\frac{N!}{n_1!\cdots n_K!}\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_k^{\,n_k},
\qquad \sum_{k=1}^{K}n_k=N,
\tag{C.3}\] on the set of nonnegative integer vectors summing to \(N\).

The multinomial is the count of how many of \(N\) patients fall into each of \(K\) response categories, for example none, partial, or complete response. It records the joint distribution of category counts, so a single component \(n_k\) is \(\mathrm{Bin}(N,p_k)\) and at \(K=2\) the whole family reduces to \(\mathrm{Bin}(N,p_1)\). Its first two moments are \[
\mathbb{E}[n_k]=N p_k,\qquad \mathrm{Var}(n_k)=N p_k(1-p_k),\qquad
\mathrm{Cov}(n_j,n_k)=-N p_j p_k\ (j\neq k),
\] the negative covariance reflecting that the counts must sum to \(N\), so a surplus in one category forces a deficit in another. This is the likelihood in the Dirichlet-multinomial conjugate pair of Table C.7.

The gamma function \(\Gamma\) and beta function \(B\) are those of Equation C.1 and Equation C.2.

Several entries deserve comment. In modeling terms the four non-normal families split cleanly by role: the exponential and Weibull model time-to-event outcomes (overall or progression-free survival), the gamma is a prior on a positive rate or precision, and the beta is a prior on a probability; the normal models a continuous endpoint and, on the log scale, an estimated relative effect.
Exponential and gamma. The exponential is the gamma of unit shape, \(\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)=
\mathrm{Gamma}(1,\lambda)\), as the densities and moment generating functions show. It is the simplest time-to-event model, the one with a constant hazard: the instantaneous event rate does not change over time, so the exponential is memoryless, meaning a patient who has survived to time \(s\) has the same remaining-life distribution as a fresh patient (\(P(X>s+u\mid X>s)=P(X>u)\)). Because independent moment generating functions multiply (Theorem 4.12), a sum of \(n\) independent \(\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)\) variables has MGF \((1-t/\lambda)^{-n}\), hence is \(\mathrm{Gamma}(n,\lambda)\); more generally gammas with a common rate add in shape. The chi-square law with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom is \(\mathrm{Gamma}(\nu/2,\,1/2)\). The gamma is the book’s default prior on a positive quantity such as a Poisson rate (Proposition 8.1) or a precision; its shape parameter \(\alpha\) sets the shape of the density, with \(\alpha<1\) giving a density that diverges at the origin and decreases, \(\alpha=1\) the exponential, and \(\alpha>1\) a unimodal density that starts at zero, rises to a peak, and decays. The MGF \((1-t/\beta)^{-\alpha}\) is finite precisely for \(t<\beta\) and diverges as \(t\uparrow\beta\), the right tail being too heavy to integrate against \(e^{tx}\) beyond that point (for \(t\ge\beta\) the defining integral \(\int_0^\infty e^{tx}f(x)\,dx\) diverges because \(e^{tx}e^{-\beta x}\) no longer decays); all moments are nonetheless finite, with \(\mathbb{E}[X^{r}]=\Gamma(\alpha+r)/\big(\beta^{r}\Gamma(\alpha)\big)\) for \(r>-\alpha\).
Beta. The single most useful fact for a health researcher is that the beta puts a flexible distribution on a probability: because its support is \((0,1)\), it is the natural prior on a response rate, and it is the conjugate prior for the binomial (Theorem 8.4). Its two parameters read as pseudo-counts: \(a\) behaves like a number of prior successes and \(b\) like a number of prior failures, so the prior mean \(a/(a+b)\) is the prior success fraction and larger \(a+b\) means a more concentrated, more confident prior. As a shape guide: \(a=b=1\) is the uniform law on \((0,1)\) (no prior information); \(a=b>1\) is symmetric and unimodal at \(\tfrac12\); \(a>b\) leans toward \(1\) and \(a<b\) toward \(0\); and \(a,b<1\) is U-shaped, piling mass near the two endpoints. The density is bounded with compact support, so the MGF is finite for every \(t\), but it has no elementary closed form. (Advanced; you will not use the beta MGF in practice, since the moments below are elementary and are what the book uses.) The MGF equals the confluent hypergeometric function \[
M_X(t)={}_1F_1(a;a+b;t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_n}{(a+b)_n}\frac{t^{n}}{n!},\qquad
(c)_n:=c(c+1)\cdots(c+n-1),
\tag{C.4}\] where \((c)_n\) is the rising factorial (Pochhammer symbol). Moments are elementary even though the MGF is not: \(\mathbb{E}[X^{r}]=B(a+r,b)/B(a,b)=\Gamma(a+r)\Gamma(a+b)\big/\big(\Gamma(a)\Gamma(a+b+r)\big)\) for \(r>-a\), which gives the mean and variance in Table C.4. The case \(a=b=1\) is the uniform law on \((0,1)\).
Weibull. The survival function is \(S(x)=\exp(-(x/\lambda)^{k})\) and the hazard is \(h(x)=\frac{k}{\lambda}(x/\lambda)^{k-1}\), a power law in \(x\). The shape parameter \(k\) controls whether risk rises or falls over time, which is exactly what a clinician chooses a survival model to capture: \(k<1\) gives a decreasing hazard (early high risk that wanes, the “infant mortality” pattern), \(k=1\) gives a constant hazard (the exponential), and \(k>1\) gives an increasing hazard (risk that grows with time, the “aging” or wear-out pattern). The \(r\)-th moment is \(\mathbb{E}[X^{r}]=\lambda^{r}\Gamma(1+r/k)\), from which the tabulated mean and variance follow. With \(k=1\) the hazard is constant and the Weibull is the exponential with rate \(1/\lambda\). The moment generating function has no elementary closed form and, more sharply, is finite on a neighborhood of the origin only when \(k\ge 1\): for \(k<1\) the tail \(\exp(-(x/\lambda)^{k})\) decays slower than any exponential, so \(\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]=\infty\) for every \(t>0\) and the MGF does not exist, though all polynomial moments remain finite. (The reason \(k<1\) makes the tail slow is that the exponent \((x/\lambda)^{k}\) then grows sub-linearly in \(x\), so \(e^{-(x/\lambda)^{k}}\) falls off more slowly than \(e^{-cx}\) for any \(c>0\).)

Example C.2 (How the Weibull shape bends the hazard) Fix the scale \(\lambda=1\) and read the hazard \(h(x)=k\,x^{k-1}\) at three follow-up times for three shapes. The table gives \(h(x)\) at \(x=0.25,\ 1,\ 4\).

With \(k=0.5\) the event rate is highest just after baseline and falls; with \(k=1\) it never changes; with \(k=2\) it climbs steadily. All three curves pass through \(h=1\) at \(x=\lambda=1\), so the scale sets the time at which the hazard equals the reference level \(1/\lambda\) and the shape sets the tilt. This is the single most important reading of a Weibull survival model: the shape \(k\) is chosen to match whether a clinical hazard rises or falls with time. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Hazard parametrization. Chapter 25 writes the Weibull through its hazard, \(h(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\lambda(\mathbf{x})\,\nu\,t^{\nu-1}\), giving the survival function \(S(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\exp(-\lambda(\mathbf{x})\,t^{\nu})\) (see Section 25.3). This is the shape-scale form above with shape \(k=\nu\) and scale \(\lambda=\lambda(\mathbf{x})^{-1/\nu}\), equivalently \(\lambda(\mathbf{x})=\lambda^{-\nu}\). The two parametrizations describe the same family; the hazard form places the covariate structure on the rate-type coefficient \(\lambda(\mathbf{x})\), which is convenient for proportional-hazards regression. See Table C.2 for the three survival parametrizations side by side. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

title: Appendix C — Probability Distributions
text:
C.5 The multivariate normal
The multivariate normal \(\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) is defined in Definition 4.13 through its moment generating function and is developed in full in Section 4.12 of Chapter 4. We restate the core formulas and point to the chapter for proofs. In this book the family plays four roles: it models a vector of correlated baseline covariates in a trial population (Chapters 12 and 20); it is the prior for a vector of random effects in a hierarchical model (Chapter 8); it is the approximate sampling distribution of a vector of estimated log-effects fed into network meta-analysis (Chapters 13 and 15); and, through the Gaussian copula, it is the engine that ties marginal covariate distributions together for the ML-NMR numerical integration of Chapter 22 (Section 22.9). Throughout, \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ 0\) means \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is positive definite, which is the condition under which the covariance is invertible and a density exists.

The family is closed under the operations that drive normal-theory inference, proved in Chapter 4.

Affine maps. If \(\mathbf{X}\sim\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) and \(\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{b}+B\mathbf{X}\), then \(\mathbf{Y}\sim\mathcal{N}_q(\mathbf{b}+B\boldsymbol{\mu},\,B\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{\top})\) (Theorem 4.14). In particular every subvector is multivariate normal and every linear combination \(\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\) is univariate normal.
Uncorrelated implies independent. Jointly normal blocks with zero cross-covariance are independent (Lemma 4.3), a property special to the normal family.
Conditioning. With \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\succ 0\), \[

\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}\Big),
\] the conditional mean affine in \(\mathbf{x}_2\) and the conditional covariance, the Schur complement of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\), free of \(\mathbf{x}_2\) (Theorem 4.15, Equation 4.15).

The conditioning formula is best read as a linear regression of \(\mathbf{X}_1\) on \(\mathbf{X}_2\): the conditional mean is the prediction \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}
(\mathbf{x}_2-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2)\) with regression-coefficient matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\), and the conditional covariance (the term some readers know as the Schur complement, which you may take as a name on a first pass) does not depend on the observed value \(\mathbf{x}_2\), so observing \(\mathbf{X}_2\) shifts the center of \(\mathbf{X}_1\) but does not change its spread. This is precisely what one needs to impute an unreported baseline covariate from reported ones in a population-adjustment problem.

Example C.3 (Predicting a missing covariate from an observed one) Let \((X_1,X_2)\) be bivariate normal with means \(\mu_1=\mu_2=0\), unit variances, and correlation \(\rho=0.6\), so \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}=\rho=0.6\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}=1\). Suppose \(X_1\) (say a baseline covariate not reported by a study) is unknown but the correlated covariate \(X_2=2\) is observed. The conditioning formula gives \[
X_1\mid X_2=2\ \sim\ \mathcal{N}\big(\rho\cdot 2,\ 1-\rho^{2}\big)=\mathcal{N}(1.2,\ 0.64).
\] The predicted mean \(1.2\) is the regression of \(X_1\) on \(X_2\) with slope \(\rho=0.6\), and the conditional variance \(0.64\) is smaller than the marginal variance \(1\): knowing the correlated covariate sharpens the prediction. The conditional variance \(1-\rho^{2}\) would be the same whatever value of \(X_2\) we had observed. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

The univariate normal is the case \(p=1\), and the standard normal \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), with density \(\phi\) and distribution function \(\Phi\), is treated in Section C.7.

title: Appendix C — Probability Distributions
text:
C.6 The Dirichlet distribution
The Dirichlet is the distribution of a random probability vector and is the multivariate generalization of the beta. In one line: it is a prior for a list of probabilities that must add up to one, such as the probabilities of the response categories none, partial, and complete. It is the natural conjugate prior for the cell probabilities of a categorical or multinomial outcome (Definition C.1), generalizing the beta-binomial pair of Theorem 8.4.

Definition C.2 (Dirichlet distribution) Let \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_K)\) with each \(\alpha_k>0\), and write \(\alpha_0=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\alpha_k\). A random vector \(\mathbf{X}=(X_1,\dots,X_K)\) supported on the open simplex \(\Delta^{K-1}=\{\mathbf{x}:x_k>0,\ \sum_{k=1}^{K}x_k=1\}\) has the Dirichlet distribution \(\mathrm{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\) if it has density \[
f(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{B(\boldsymbol{\alpha})}\prod_{k=1}^{K}x_k^{\alpha_k-1},
\qquad B(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\frac{\prod_{k=1}^{K}\Gamma(\alpha_k)}{\Gamma(\alpha_0)},
\tag{C.5}\] with respect to Lebesgue measure on the \((K-1)\)-dimensional simplex, taking \(x_1,\dots,x_{K-1}\) as free coordinates and \(x_K=1-\sum_{k<K}x_k\).

The simplex \(\Delta^{K-1}\) is just the set of valid probability vectors: \(K\) nonnegative numbers that add to one. (Advanced; skip on a first pass.) The phrase “density with respect to Lebesgue measure on the \((K-1)\)-dimensional simplex, taking \(x_1,\dots,x_{K-1}\) as free coordinates” means only that we treat \(x_1,\dots,x_{K-1}\) as the free variables, with the last coordinate forced to be \(x_K=1-\sum_{k<K}x_k\), and integrate over those \(K-1\) free variables. The normalizing constant \(B(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\) is the multivariate beta function of Equation C.2, the product-of-gammas generalization of the scalar \(B(a,b)\).
The simplex constraint \(\sum_k X_k=1\) forces the components to be negatively associated and makes the joint moment generating function on \(\mathbb{R}^{K}\) degenerate, so the Dirichlet is described by its moments rather than by an MGF (this is the hyperplane degeneracy explained in Section C.2). The mixed moments are \[
\mathbb{E}\!\Big[\prod_{k=1}^{K}X_k^{r_k}\Big]
=\frac{B(\boldsymbol{\alpha}+\mathbf{r})}{B(\boldsymbol{\alpha})}
=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_0)}{\Gamma(\alpha_0+\textstyle\sum_k r_k)}\prod_{k=1}^{K}
\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_k+r_k)}{\Gamma(\alpha_k)},
\tag{C.6}\] from which the first two moments follow.



Table C.6: The Dirichlet distribution \(\mathrm{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\) on the simplex \(\Delta^{K-1}\), with \(\alpha_0=\sum_k\alpha_k\).

With \(K=2\) and \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}=(a,b)\) the first coordinate \(X_1\) is \(\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)\), so the beta entries of Table C.4 are the \(K=2\) case of Table C.6. The parameters read as pseudo-counts, exactly as for the beta: \(\alpha_k\) is a prior count for category \(k\), and the total \(\alpha_0=\sum_k\alpha_k\) is a concentration. The mean is \(\alpha_k/\alpha_0\) regardless of \(\alpha_0\), while the variances and covariances shrink as \(\alpha_0\) grows. The picture: a small \(\alpha_0\) spreads the random probability vector out toward the corners of the simplex (nearly all mass on one category, but which one varies), while a large \(\alpha_0\) clusters it tightly around the mean vector \((\alpha_1/\alpha_0,\dots,\alpha_K/\alpha_0)\). Concentration is thus the multivariate reading of “how confident is the prior,” the same role \(a+b\) plays for the beta.

title: Appendix C — Probability Distributions
section: C.7 The standard normal function and density
text:
C.7 The standard normal function and density
The standard normal \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) is the case \(\mu=0,\ \sigma^{2}=1\) of Definition 4.12. Its density and distribution function carry the dedicated symbols \(\phi\) and \(\Phi\): \[
\phi(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-z^{2}/2},\qquad
\Phi(z)=\int_{-\infty}^{z}\phi(u)\,du,\qquad z\in\mathbb{R}.
\tag{C.7}\] The density \(\phi\) is even and satisfies the differential identities \[
\phi'(z)=-z\,\phi(z),\qquad \phi''(z)=(z^{2}-1)\,\phi(z),\qquad \Phi'(z)=\phi(z),
\tag{C.8}\] and the distribution function satisfies \(\Phi(0)=\tfrac12\), the reflection identity \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\), and the limits \(\Phi(z)\to 1\) as \(z\to\infty\) and \(\Phi(z)\to 0\) as \(z\to-\infty\). The mean and variance are \(\mathbb{E}[Z]=0\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Z)=1\), the moment generating function is \(M_Z(t)=e^{t^{2}/2}\), finite for all \(t\), and the moments are \[
\mathbb{E}[Z^{2m-1}]=0,\qquad \mathbb{E}[Z^{2m}]=\frac{(2m)!}{2^{m}m!}=(2m-1)!!,\qquad m=1,2,\dots,
\tag{C.9}\] read off as the Taylor coefficients of \(e^{t^{2}/2}=\sum_{m\ge 0}t^{2m}/(2^{m}m!)\) through Theorem 4.10.
There is no elementary closed form for \(\Phi\). It is expressed through the error function \(\mathrm{erf}(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_0^{x}e^{-u^{2}}\,du\) and its complement \(\mathrm{erfc}=1-\mathrm{erf}\) by \[
\Phi(z)=\tfrac12\Big[1+\mathrm{erf}\!\big(z/\sqrt{2}\big)\Big],\qquad
1-\Phi(z)=\tfrac12\,\mathrm{erfc}\!\big(z/\sqrt{2}\big),
\tag{C.10}\] whose numerical evaluation is treated in Appendix D. (Advanced; optional on a first pass.) For the upper tail the Mills ratio gives the two-sided bound, valid for \(z>0\), \[
\Big(\frac{1}{z}-\frac{1}{z^{3}}\Big)\phi(z)\ <\ 1-\Phi(z)\ <\ \frac{\phi(z)}{z},
\tag{C.11}\] so that \(1-\Phi(z)\sim \phi(z)/z\) as \(z\to\infty\). This bound matters because \(1-\Phi(z)\) is the tail probability of a standardized effect, so it controls how fast \(p\)-values and normal-approximation tail probabilities for large standardized effects decay; a novice can note the asymptotic \(1-\Phi(z)\sim\phi(z)/z\) and move on.
The function \(\Phi\) also feeds two constructions the book uses later. It is the inverse link of the probit regression model (Chapter 7), the model in which a binary probability is written \(P(Y=1)=\Phi(\eta)\) for a linear predictor \(\eta\). And its inverse \(\Phi^{-1}\) is the normal quantile transform at the heart of the Gaussian copula \(C_\Omega(\mathbf{u})=\Phi_\Omega\big(\Phi^{-1}(u_1),\dots,\Phi^{-1}(u_d)\big)\) used in ML-NMR numerical integration: given a uniform variable \(u\in(0,1)\), the value \(\Phi^{-1}(u)\) is the standard-normal score with that lower-tail probability, so \(\Phi^{-1}\) turns the uniform points of a quasi-Monte Carlo rule into correlated normal covariate draws over which an individual likelihood is averaged (Section 22.7, Section 22.9). See Notation for the copula symbol.

title: Appendix C — Probability Distributions
text:
C.8 Conjugate pairs
A prior family is conjugate to a likelihood when the posterior stays in the family with updated hyperparameters. Conjugacy is an algebraic convenience, not a requirement of Bayesian modeling: it makes the update a closed-form parameter change instead of a numerical integration, but a valid Bayesian analysis may use any proper prior (and the book’s hierarchical models in Chapter 8 and Chapter 24 mostly use non-conjugate priors sampled by Markov chain Monte Carlo). Chapter 8 proves the three pairs of Section 8.4 in full and uses them to build the shrinkage estimator and the Gibbs updates of its samplers. Table C.7 collects those pairs, together with the Dirichlet-multinomial pair that generalizes the beta-binomial; throughout, the gamma prior uses the shape-rate parametrization, so \(\mathrm{Gamma}(a,b)\) has mean \(a/b\).

In each row the posterior hyperparameters combine prior information with data additively. For the normal-normal pair precisions (the reciprocals of the variances) add, and the posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of prior mean and data (Equation 8.5): if the prior says the effect is about \(\mu_0\) and the data say about \(y\), the posterior mean sits between them, pulled toward whichever is more precise. For the beta-binomial and Dirichlet-multinomial pairs the prior hyperparameters act as pseudo-counts that are incremented by the observed counts (Equation 8.6); and for the gamma-Poisson pair the shape is incremented by the total count and the rate by the number of observations. The posterior mean is in every case a convex combination of the prior mean and the maximum likelihood estimate, the analytic form of shrinkage that Chapter 8 develops.

Example C.4 (A beta-binomial update with numbers) Put a uniform prior \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\) on a response probability \(p\) (the flat prior: every value in \((0,1)\) equally likely, prior mean \(\tfrac12\)). Observe \(y=7\) responders out of \(n=10\) patients. By the beta-binomial row of Table C.7 the posterior is \[
p\mid y\ \sim\ \mathrm{Beta}(1+7,\ 1+10-7)=\mathrm{Beta}(8,4),
\] with posterior mean \(8/(8+4)=8/12=2/3\approx0.667\). The two prior pseudo-counts \(a=b=1\) have been incremented by the \(7\) observed successes and \(3\) observed failures. Contrast the maximum likelihood estimate \(\hat p=7/10=0.7\) and the prior mean \(0.5\): the posterior mean \(0.667\) lies between them, and is in fact their convex combination \[
\frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\cdot\frac12+\frac{n}{a+b+n}\cdot\frac{y}{n}
=\frac{2}{12}\cdot 0.5+\frac{10}{12}\cdot 0.7=0.667,
\] weighted toward the data because the flat prior carries only \(a+b=2\) pseudo-observations against \(n=10\) real ones. This is the shrinkage reading of the closing paragraph, made concrete. \(\blacktriangleleft\)


Remark. Why the inverse-gamma is not cataloged. The classical conjugate prior for the variance \(\sigma^{2}\) of a normal likelihood with known mean is the inverse-gamma (a gamma law on the precision \(1/\sigma^{2}\)). This book does not use it: for the between-study variance of a hierarchical model the text follows modern practice and places a half-normal or half-\(t\) prior on the between-study standard deviation (Chapter 8; Dias et al. (2018)), which behaves better when the variance may be near zero, where an inverse-gamma prior is unstable. The inverse-gamma is therefore mentioned here only so a reader does not search the tables for it. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

C.9 Notes and references
The catalogue draws on the following sources; each family points back to where it is derived or used.

Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson binomial, Poisson, normal, and multivariate normal: mass functions, densities, means, variances, and moment generating functions, with derivations, are in Section 4.11 and Section 4.12 of Chapter 4.
Moment generating function properties that justify the MGF columns are Theorem 4.10 (moments by differentiation) and Theorem 4.11 (the MGF determines the law), the latter relying on the inversion of the characteristic function (Billingsley (1995), §29 to §30).
Gamma, beta, exponential, Weibull, Dirichlet, multinomial and the gamma and beta special functions are standard; a measure-theoretic treatment is Billingsley (1995), and the special-function evaluations are collected in Appendix D.

Hazard parametrization of the Weibull and exponential, used for survival baselines, is that of Section 25.3 in Chapter 25 and of Phillippo et al. (2025).

title: Appendix D — Special Functions for Numerical Integration
text:
D.1 How to use this appendix
The numerical machinery of multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR) rests on a small library of special functions, and the analytic shortcuts that occasionally rescue a closed form rest on the same library. This appendix is the proved reference for those functions. It collects, in one place and with full derivations, the four objects that Part V calls on repeatedly: the moment generating function of the normal, which closes the log-link aggregation integral of Theorem 20.4; the error function, the analyst’s name for the normal distribution function and the gateway to its series and tail expansions; Owen’s \(T\) function, which evaluates bivariate normal probabilities and, through them, the expected squared probit needed for probit-link aggregation; and the radical-inverse function, the arithmetic atom of the Sobol’ sequences that drive the quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) integration of Theorem 22.6. Two further functions that arise in this circle of ideas, the one-probit and two-probit approximations to the logistic function, are derived here because they turn the otherwise non-elementary logit aggregation integral of Theorem 20.5 into an explicit, fast, and surprisingly accurate closed form.
Everything is proved or derived. Where a result is established in the main text we cite it by slug and, when it sharpens the reference to restate the derivation, reprove it self-contained. Symbols follow Notation: \(\Phi\) and \(\phi\) are the standard normal distribution and density functions, \(\mathrm{expit}(z)=e^{z}/(1+e^{z})\) is the inverse logit (also called the logistic sigmoid), \(\Phi^{-1}\) is the normal quantile function, and \(M_X(\mathbf{t})=\mathbb{E}[e^{\mathbf{t}^\top X}]\) is the moment generating function of Definition 4.7. Two standard facts of real analysis are used without proof: the Gaussian normalization \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-t^{2}}\,dt=\sqrt{\pi}\) (equivalently \(\int\phi=1\)), proved by the polar- coordinates evaluation of its square, and differentiation under the integral sign, justified by dominated convergence (Theorem 4.2) whenever a dominating integrable envelope is exhibited, which we do at each use.
Scope, and what is deliberately left out. This appendix is the proved reference for the five objects that the Part V integration machinery calls on: the normal moment generating function, the error function, Owen’s \(T\) function, the one- and two-probit approximations to the logistic, and the radical inverse behind the Sobol’ point set. It is not a general catalogue of the special functions of statistics. The gamma function, its logarithm, the digamma function, and the beta function do appear in Part V, but only as the fixed normalizing constants of standard likelihoods, for example the log-gamma terms in the Poisson and binomial log-likelihoods of Chapters 21 and 25; they are classical, are not special to indirect comparison, and are not reproved here. Everything below, by contrast, is tied to a concrete ML-NMR integration task and is proved in full.
A concrete task to keep in mind. Picture the setting the whole appendix serves. An aggregate-data (AgD) study arm reports an event count and a summary of its patients, say a mean and variance of age, but no individual records. The model has a link function \(g\), and to predict this arm’s event probability the model must average the individual probability \(g^{-1}(\eta)\) over the arm’s covariate distribution. The three regimes below are exactly the three ways that average can be computed, and each is the job of one group of functions in this appendix.
Read the table as a decision tree for the averaging task: the log link is a closed form (the MGF); the probit link has a closed form for the first moment and an Owen’s \(T\) closed form for the second; the logit link has no closed form but an accurate explicit probit approximation; and every remaining case, including the survival and ordinal likelihood kernels of Chapter 25, is handled by Sobol’ quasi-Monte Carlo, whose points are built from the radical inverse and pushed onto the covariate scale through \(\Phi^{-1}\), that is, through \(\operatorname{erf}^{-1}\). The sections are ordered from the easiest regime to the most general, and they rise in difficulty: the MGF section is short and gentle, the error-function section is moderate, Owen’s \(T\) is the hardest section and carries the Plackett partial differential equation, and the Sobol’ section is moderate but dense with quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) vocabulary. A reader who wants only the applied picture can take the closed forms and the worked examples from each section and leave the digital-net algebra of Section D.6 to software.

title: Appendix D — Special Functions for Numerical Integration
section: D.2 The moment generating function of the normal
text:
D.2 The moment generating function of the normal
The moment generating function (MGF) of Definition 4.7 turns the average of an exponential into an algebraic expression. Because the log link sends a linear predictor \(\eta\) to the mean \(e^{\eta}\), and because a linear predictor in jointly normal covariates is itself normal, the aggregate mean on the log scale is the expectation of an exponential of a normal, that is, a normal MGF evaluated at \(t=1\). This is the one nonlinear link for which ML-NMR has an exact closed form, and the MGF is the reason.
The name “moment generating” comes from a fact we do not actually use but which explains the terminology: differentiating \(M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]\) a total of \(k\) times and setting \(t=0\) returns the \(k\)-th moment \(\mathbb{E}[X^{k}]\), because each derivative brings down one factor of \(X\). We exploit the MGF for a different reason. The log link sets the mean equal to \(e^{\eta}\), so an aggregate mean on the log scale is literally \(\mathbb{E}[e^{W}]\) for the (normal) linear predictor \(W\); that is the MGF evaluated at \(t=1\), not a derivative at \(t=0\). This is why the log link, alone among the common nonlinear links, yields a closed form: its inverse link is the exponential, and the exponential of a normal is exactly what the normal MGF integrates.

Theorem D.1 (Moment generating function of the normal) Let \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})\) be univariate normal. Then the MGF of \(X\) is finite for every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\) and \[
M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}\big[e^{tX}\big]=\exp\!\Big(\mu t+\tfrac12\sigma^{2}t^{2}\Big).
\tag{D.1}\] More generally, let \(\mathbf{X}\sim\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) be \(p\)-variate normal with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succeq 0\) (positive semidefinite). Then for every \(\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\), \[
M_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{t})=\mathbb{E}\big[e^{\mathbf{t}^\top\mathbf{X}}\big]
=\exp\!\Big(\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\mu}+\tfrac12\,\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{t}\Big).
\tag{D.2}\]


Proof. Univariate case. Fix \(t\in\mathbb{R}\). Writing the density of \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})\) and collecting the exponent, \[
\mathbb{E}\big[e^{tX}\big]
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{tx}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\,
e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}}\,dx
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\exp\!\Big(-\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}-2\sigma^{2}tx}{2\sigma^{2}}\Big)\,dx .
\] Complete the square in \(x\). The numerator of the exponent is \[
(x-\mu)^{2}-2\sigma^{2}tx
=\big(x-(\mu+\sigma^{2}t)\big)^{2}-2\sigma^{2}t\mu-\sigma^{4}t^{2},
\] which one verifies by expanding the completed square, \(\big(x-(\mu+\sigma^{2}t)\big)^{2}=x^{2}-2\mu x-2\sigma^{2}tx+\mu^{2}+2\mu\sigma^{2}t+\sigma^{4}t^{2}\): then subtracting the two constants \(2\sigma^{2}t\mu\) and \(\sigma^{4}t^{2}\) cancels the final two terms and leaves \(x^{2}-2\mu x-2\sigma^{2}tx+\mu^{2}=(x-\mu)^{2}-2\sigma^{2}tx\), the left side. Substituting and factoring out the constant terms, \[
\mathbb{E}\big[e^{tX}\big]
=e^{\mu t+\frac12\sigma^{2}t^{2}}\cdot
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
e^{-\frac{(x-(\mu+\sigma^{2}t))^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}}\,dx
=e^{\mu t+\frac12\sigma^{2}t^{2}},
\] the remaining integral being that of a \(\mathcal{N}(\mu+\sigma^{2}t,\sigma^{2})\) density, which equals \(1\). The expectation is finite for every \(t\) because the integrand is a positive constant times a Gaussian density. This is Equation D.1.
Multivariate case. The law \(\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) is defined in Definition 4.13 through exactly the MGF Equation D.2, so the statement is the consistency of that definition, which we reprove for reference. Let \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\) be the symmetric positive semidefinite square root of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) (Theorem 3.2), let \(\mathbf{Z}=(Z_1,\dots,Z_p)^\top\) have independent standard normal entries, and set \(\mathbf{X}=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}\), which has mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and, since \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\) is symmetric with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}I_p\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). By independence and the univariate MGF \(\mathbb{E}[e^{sZ_i}]=e^{s^{2}/2}\) from Equation D.1, \[
\mathbb{E}\big[e^{\mathbf{t}^\top\mathbf{X}}\big]
=e^{\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\mu}}\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{E}\big[e^{(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{t})_i Z_i}\big]
=e^{\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\mu}}\exp\!\Big(\tfrac12\big\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{t}\big\|_2^{2}\Big)
=\exp\!\Big(\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\mu}+\tfrac12\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{t}\Big),
\] using \(\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{t}\|_2^{2}=\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{t}\). This is Equation D.2, identical to Equation 4.13. \(\square\)

Reader’s translation. Equation D.1 says the average of \(e^{tX}\) over a normal \(X\) is itself an exponential, with the variance entering through the quadratic \(\tfrac12\sigma^{2}t^{2}\). That single formula is the entire reason the log-link aggregate mean has a closed form; the next corollary reads it off at \(t=1\).
The aggregation payoff is immediate. An aggregate mean on the log scale is the expectation of an exponential of a linear predictor; when the covariates are jointly normal the linear predictor is normal, and Equation D.1 evaluates the expectation at \(t=1\).

Corollary D.1 (Closed-form log-link aggregation) Let the inverse link be \(g^{-1}(z)=e^{z}\) (the log link) and let the covariates in study \(j\) be jointly normal, \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)\). Write \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}=\boldsymbol{\beta}_1+\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,k}\) for the total slope on arm \(k\) and \(W=\eta_{jk}(X)=\mu_j+\gamma_k+X^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}\) for the linear predictor. Then \(W\sim\mathcal{N}(m,v)\) with \[
m=\mu_j+\gamma_k+\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k},
\qquad
v=\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\,\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k},
\] and the aggregate mean is \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\mathbb{E}\big[e^{W}\big]=M_W(1)=\exp\!\Big(m+\tfrac12 v\Big)
=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\cdot e^{\,v/2},
\qquad
\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}=e^{m}.
\tag{D.3}\] This is the closed form Equation 20.12 of Theorem 20.4; the multiplicative correction \(e^{v/2}\ge 1\) is the exact downward bias of the plug-in mean, with equality if and only if \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}=\mathbf{0}\).


Proof. The linear predictor \(W\) is an affine function of the normal vector \(X\), hence univariate normal by the affine-image theorem Theorem 4.14, with the stated mean \(m\) and variance \(v=\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}\). The aggregate mean of Definition 20.2 is \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=\mathbb{E}[g^{-1}(W)]=\mathbb{E}[e^{W}]\), which is \(M_W(1)\) by Definition 4.7. Evaluating Equation D.1 at \(t=1\) gives \(M_W(1)=\exp(m+\tfrac12 v)\). Finally \(e^{m+v/2}=e^{m}e^{v/2}=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}e^{v/2}\), and \(v\ge 0\) because \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\succeq 0\) (Theorem 4.9), with \(v=0\) exactly when \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}\) lies in the null space of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\). \(\square\)


Example D.1 (A multivariate log-link aggregate by hand) Take two covariates, \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)\) with \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j=(2,1)^\top\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0.5\\0.5&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), total slope \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}=(0.4,0.3)^\top\), and intercept-plus-treatment \(\mu_j+\gamma_k=-1\). The mean linear predictor is \(m=-1+\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}=-1+(2)(0.4)+(1)(0.3)=0.1\). The variance is the quadratic form \[
v=\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}
=(0.4,0.3)\begin{pmatrix}0.55\\0.80\end{pmatrix}=(0.4)(0.55)+(0.3)(0.80)=0.46,
\] where \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}=(0.55,0.80)^\top\). By Equation D.3 the exact aggregate rate is \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=e^{0.1+0.23}=e^{0.33}=1.3910\), against the plug-in \(\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}=e^{0.1}=1.1052\). The covariance off-diagonal enters only through \(v\): the same margins with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\) diagonal would give \(v=(0.16)(1)+(0.09)(2)=0.34\) and \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=e^{0.27}=1.3100\), so the positive covariance inflates the aggregate by the factor \(e^{(0.46-0.34)/2}=e^{0.06}=1.0618\). The MGF makes the dependence on the full covariance matrix exact and explicit. \(\blacktriangleleft\)
