text:
F.10 Chapter 10: Adjustment Methods

F.10.1 Solution to Exercise 10.5: Stabilized inverse-probability weights have mean one
This Chapter 10 exercise verifies that stabilized inverse-probability weights average to one and explains why stabilizing lowers the variance of the weighted estimator without changing its target.
Uses. The propensity definition \(\mathbb E[T\mid X]=e(X)\) and the worked example Example 10.3.
Let \(sw=T\,p_1/e(X)+(1-T)\,p_0/(1-e(X))\) with \(p_1=P(T=1)\), \(p_0=P(T=0)=1-p_1\).
(a) Condition on \(X\) and use \(\mathbb E[T\mid X]=e(X)\), \(\mathbb E[1-T\mid X]=1-e(X)\): \[
\mathbb E[sw\mid X]=\frac{p_1}{e(X)}\,\mathbb E[T\mid X]+\frac{p_0}{1-e(X)}\,\mathbb E[1-T\mid X]
=\frac{p_1}{e(X)}e(X)+\frac{p_0}{1-e(X)}(1-e(X))=p_1+p_0=1
\] pointwise in \(X\). Taking expectations, \(\mathbb E[sw]=1\).
(b) In Example 10.3, \(e(0)=0.2\), \(e(1)=0.6\), \(P(X=0)=P(X=1)=\tfrac12\), and \(p_1=P(T=1)=\tfrac12(0.2)+\tfrac12(0.6)=0.4\), \(p_0=0.6\). The four cell values of \(sw\) are \[
\begin{aligned}
(T=1,x=0):\ &\tfrac{0.4}{0.2}=2.0, & (T=1,x=1):\ &\tfrac{0.4}{0.6}=0.6\overline{6},\\
(T=0,x=0):\ &\tfrac{0.6}{0.8}=0.75, & (T=0,x=1):\ &\tfrac{0.6}{0.4}=1.5 .
\end{aligned}
\] The cell probabilities are \(P(T=1,x=0)=\tfrac12(0.2)=0.1\), \(P(T=1,x=1)=\tfrac12(0.6)=0.3\), \(P(T=0,x=0)=\tfrac12(0.8)=0.4\), \(P(T=0,x=1)=\tfrac12(0.4)=0.2\). The \(P\)-weighted average is \[
0.1(2.0)+0.3(0.6\overline 6)+0.4(0.75)+0.2(1.5)=0.2+0.2+0.3+0.3=1.0,
\] confirming \(\mathbb E[sw]=1\).
(c) The stabilized weight multiplies the raw weight \(T/e(X)\) by the constant \(p_1\) (and the control weight by \(p_0\)); rescaling by the marginal treatment probability brings the weights nearer to one, so they vary less around their common mean of \(1\). Their reduced dispersion lowers the variance of the inverse-probability estimator while leaving its target unchanged, because the numerator and denominator of the Hajek-form estimand are scaled by the same constant. Here the Hajek-form estimator is the one that divides the weighted sum of outcomes by the weighted sum of weights (a self-normalizing ratio), rather than by the fixed sample size \(n\); the latter, unnormalized version is the Horvitz-Thompson estimator. The two differ only by whether the weights are renormalized to sum to one, and it is precisely because the Hajek form renormalizes that scaling every weight by a common constant \(p_1\) cancels top and bottom and leaves the point estimate untouched while shrinking the weight dispersion. \(\square\)


F.10.2 Solution to Exercise 10.9: Efficient influence function and efficiency bound for the control mean
This Chapter 10 exercise writes down the efficient influence function and the semiparametric efficiency bound for the control-arm mean \(\psi_0=\mathbb E[Y(0)]\), mirroring the treated-arm result, and evaluates the bound on the worked example.
Uses. The treated-arm efficient influence function and bound Theorem 10.6, mirrored by the symmetry \(T\mapsto 1-T\).
An efficiency bound is the smallest asymptotic variance any regular estimator of the target can achieve; it is the semiparametric analogue of the Cramer-Rao lower bound, and the variance of the efficient influence function is that bound. The efficient influence function itself is the mean-zero random variable whose variance an efficient estimator’s error tracks, so reading off its form and squaring it gives the bound. Mirroring Theorem 10.6, which gives the treated-arm influence function \(\varphi_1=T(Y-m_1(X))/e(X)+m_1(X)-\psi_1\), the control-arm version swaps the treatment indicator and the propensity for their complements.
By the symmetry \(T\mapsto 1-T\), the efficient influence function for \(\psi_0=\mathbb E[Y(0)]\) is \[
\varphi_0=\frac{(1-T)\bigl(Y-m_0(X)\bigr)}{1-e(X)}+m_0(X)-\psi_0,
\] and the semiparametric efficiency bound (the mirror of Theorem 10.6) is its variance, \[
V_0^\ast=\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid T=0,X)}{1-e(X)}\right]+\operatorname{Var}\bigl(\mu_0(X)\bigr).
\]
In Example 10.3, \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid T=0,X=x)=4\), \(1-e(0)=0.8\), \(1-e(1)=0.4\), \(\mu_0(0)=0\), \(\mu_0(1)=2\), \(P(X=0)=P(X=1)=\tfrac12\). The first term is \[
\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{4}{1-e(X)}\right]=\tfrac12\frac{4}{0.8}+\tfrac12\frac{4}{0.4}=\tfrac12(5)+\tfrac12(10)=7.5 .
\] The regression variance is \(\operatorname{Var}(\mu_0(X))=\tfrac12(0-1)^2+\tfrac12(2-1)^2=1\) (mean \(\mathbb E[\mu_0(X)]=1\)). Hence \[
V_0^\ast=7.5+1=8.5 .
\] For the treated mean the analogous computation gives \(V^\ast=\mathbb E[4/e(X)]+\operatorname{Var}(\mu_1(X))=(\tfrac12\cdot 20+\tfrac12\cdot 6.6\overline 6)+1
=13.3\overline 3+1=14.333\), as in the text. The control bound is the smaller of the two, \(8.5<14.333\). The reason is the inverse-propensity inflation factor: the treated term weights each stratum’s conditional variance by \(1/e(x)\), which is large (\(1/0.2=5\)) in stratum \(x=0\) where treatment is scarce, whereas the control term weights by \(1/(1-e(x))\), which is moderate there (\(1/0.8=1.25\)) because controls are plentiful in \(x=0\). Better control-arm overlap in the low-propensity stratum makes \(V_0^\ast<V^\ast\). \(\square\)

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Selected Exercises
section: F.11 Chapter 11: Effect Modification, Interaction, and Collapsibility
text:
F.11 Chapter 11: Effect Modification, Interaction, and Collapsibility

F.11.1 Solution to Exercise 11.6: Odds-ratio attenuation via a tilted-measure argument
This Chapter 11 exercise re-derives the odds-ratio non-collapsibility bound \(1<\omega^{\mathrm M}<\omega\) using the same tilting machinery as the Chapter 7 solution to Exercise 7.12, now framed through an explicit change of measure.
Strategy. Express the marginal odds at tilt level \(a\) as a mean \(A(a)/a=\mathbb E_{Q_a}[W]\) under a tilted probability \(Q_a\), then differentiate that tilted mean; the derivative is a covariance that is negative because two increasing functions are involved.
Uses. The change-of-measure identity Equation 11.10 and the covariance inequality for like-monotone functions.
The identity we lean on is the standard rule for differentiating an expectation under a parametric tilt: if \(\mathrm dQ_a/\mathrm dP\propto h(a,W)\), then \[
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm da}\,\mathbb E_{Q_a}[\varphi(W)]
=\operatorname{Cov}_{Q_a}\!\Bigl(\varphi(W),\ \partial_a\log h(a,W)\Bigr),
\] the derivative of a tilted mean equals the covariance of the integrand with the tilt’s score. This is what Equation 11.10 records, and below we apply it with \(h(a,W)=1/(1+aW)\), whose score is \(\partial_a\log h=-W/(1+aW)\).
Under the hypotheses of Theorem 11.2(a), write the baseline odds as the random variable \(W=\mu_0(X)/(1-\mu_0(X))\ge 0\), non-degenerate, so that \(\mu_0(X)=W/(1+W)\) and \(\mu_1(X)=\omega W/(1+\omega W)\) under a constant conditional odds ratio \(\omega\). With \(A(a)=\mathbb E[aW/(1+aW)]/\mathbb E[1/(1+aW)]\) the marginal odds ratio is \(\omega^{\mathrm M}=A(\omega)/A(1)\).
(a) \(A\) is strictly increasing, so \(\omega^{\mathrm M}>1\) when \(\omega>1\). Using \(aW/(1+aW)=1-1/(1+aW)\) and writing \(D(a)=\mathbb E[1/(1+aW)]\), \[
A(a)=\frac{1-D(a)}{D(a)}=\frac{1}{D(a)}-1 .
\] For each fixed outcome the map \(a\mapsto 1/(1+aW)\) is strictly decreasing on \(\{W>0\}\), an event of probability one, so \(D\) is strictly decreasing, \(1/D\) is strictly increasing, and \(A\) is strictly increasing. Since \(A(1)>0\) and \(\omega>1\), \(\omega^{\mathrm M}=A(\omega)/A(1)>1\).
(b) \(a\mapsto A(a)/a\) is strictly decreasing, so \(\omega^{\mathrm M}<\omega\) when \(\omega>1\). Note \[
\frac{A(a)}{a}=\frac{\mathbb E[W/(1+aW)]}{\mathbb E[1/(1+aW)]}=\mathbb E_{Q_a}[W],
\] the mean of \(W\) under the tilt \(\mathrm dQ_a/\mathrm dP\propto 1/(1+aW)\). The change-of-measure identity Equation 11.10 is exactly \(\omega^{\mathrm M}=\omega\,\mathbb E_{Q_\omega}[W]/\mathbb E_{Q_1}[W]\). Differentiating the tilt mean, \[
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm da}\mathbb E_{Q_a}[W]
=\operatorname{Cov}_{Q_a}\!\Bigl(W,\ \tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm da}\log\tfrac{1}{1+aW}\Bigr)
=-\operatorname{Cov}_{Q_a}\!\Bigl(W,\ \tfrac{W}{1+aW}\Bigr).
\] The functions \(w\mapsto w\) and \(w\mapsto w/(1+aw)\) are both strictly increasing, so by the covariance inequality for like-monotone functions their covariance is strictly positive (strict because \(W\) is non-degenerate), and the derivative is strictly negative. Hence \(A(a)/a\) is strictly decreasing, and with \(\omega>1\), \[
\omega^{\mathrm M}=\omega\cdot\frac{\mathbb E_{Q_\omega}[W]}{\mathbb E_{Q_1}[W]}<\omega .
\]
Combining (a) and (b), \(1<\omega^{\mathrm M}<\omega\) for \(\omega>1\). The covariance vanishes if and only if \(W\) is degenerate, which is the agreement-iff-degenerate clause of Corollary 11.1: \(\omega^{\mathrm M}=\omega\) exactly when there is a single baseline stratum and no prognostic variation to average over. \(\square\)


F.11.2 Solution to Exercise 11.8: Prognostic variables cancel when anchored, bias when not
This Chapter 11 exercise shows that a purely prognostic covariate cancels from an anchored (comparator-based) contrast but biases an unanchored (single-arm) estimand, which is why unanchored comparisons need a far larger adjustment set.
Uses. The anchored-cancellation lemma Lemma 11.3 and the effect-modifier / prognostic-variable distinction Theorem 11.1.
Split the covariate vector as \((X,W)\) with \(X\) measured and \(W\) possibly unmeasured.
(a) Anchored cancellation of a purely prognostic \(W\). Suppose \(W\) is purely prognostic for the contrast, \(\mu_A(x,w)-\mu_C(x,w)\) free of \(w\) on the identity scale (so \(W\) is not an effect modifier of \(A\) versus \(C\)). By Lemma 11.3 the conditional contrast \(\tau^{\mathrm{id}}_{AC}(x,w)\) does not depend on \(w\), hence equals a function \(\tau^{\mathrm{id}}_{AC}(x)\) of \(x\) alone. For any two populations \(\mathcal P_1,\mathcal P_2\) with the same marginal law of \(X\) but different conditional laws of \(W\mid X\), \[
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond,id}}_{AC}(\mathcal P_\ell)
=\int\!\!\int\tau^{\mathrm{id}}_{AC}(x)\,f_\ell(w\mid x)\,f(x)\,\mathrm dw\,\mathrm dx
=\int\tau^{\mathrm{id}}_{AC}(x)\,f(x)\,\mathrm dx,\qquad \ell=1,2,
\] the inner integral over \(w\) giving one because \(\tau^{\mathrm{id}}_{AC}(x)\) is constant in \(w\) and \(f_\ell(\cdot\mid x)\) integrates to one. Thus the anchored contrast is identical in the two populations and \(W\) need not be balanced.
(b) An imbalanced prognostic \(W\) biases the unanchored estimand. Take scalar \(X\in\{0,1\}\) with \(P(X=1)=\tfrac12\) common to source and target, \(W\in\{0,1\}\), and the purely prognostic arm mean \(\mu_A(x,w)=w\) (so \(\mu_A\) depends on \(w\) but the \(A\)-versus-\(C\) contrast does not, provided \(\mu_C(x,w)=w-c\) for a constant \(c\)). Let the conditional law of \(W\mid X\) differ between source and target while \(f_X\) agrees: in the source \(\Pr_{\mathrm{src}}(W=1\mid X=x)=0.2\), in the target \(\Pr_{*}(W=1\mid X=x)=0.8\), for both \(x\). The unanchored target is the absolute arm mean \[
\mathbb E_{f_*}[\mu_A(X,W)]=\Pr_{*}(W=1)=0.8,
\qquad
\mathbb E_{f_{\mathrm{src}}}[\mu_A(X,W)]=\Pr_{\mathrm{src}}(W=1)=0.2,
\] which differ by \(0.6\) even though \(f_X\) is the same and \(W\) is purely prognostic. The anchored contrast cancels this difference, but the unanchored arm mean does not, because there is no comparator term to subtract the common \(W\)-effect. Hence an imbalanced purely prognostic variable biases the unanchored estimand while leaving the anchored one untouched. This is precisely the logical distinctness of effect modifiers and prognostic variables in Theorem 11.1(1): purely prognostic covariates are real influences on each arm whose effect on the link-scale contrast is nil, so they matter for unanchored absolute means but cancel in anchored contrasts. \(\square\)

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Selected Exercises
section: F.12 Chapter 12: Transportability: The Estimand-Based Theory
text:
F.12 Chapter 12: Transportability: The Estimand-Based Theory

F.12.1 Solution to Exercise 12.7: Marginal log odds ratios attenuate and are population-dependent
This Chapter 12 exercise shows that a constant conditional log odds ratio \(c\), marginalized over the covariate, produces a marginal log odds ratio strictly between \(0\) and \(c\), with a gap that grows as the covariate spreads out. The upshot is that the marginal odds ratio is a property of the population, not of the treatments.
Strategy. The map \(\varphi\) that sends the control risk to the treated risk (add \(c\) on the logit scale) is strictly increasing and strictly concave; Jensen’s inequality applied to \(\varphi\) then forces the marginal risk below \(\varphi\) of the mean, which is exactly the attenuation.
Uses. Jensen’s inequality Theorem 4.6, and the chain rule for \(\operatorname{expit}\) and \(\operatorname{logit}\).
Let the conditional log odds ratio be the constant \(c>0\), so \(\mu_B(x)=\varphi(\mu_C(x))\) with \(\varphi(p)=\operatorname{expit}(\operatorname{logit}p+c)\).
(a) Monotonicity and concavity of \(\varphi\). Write \(\ell=\operatorname{logit}p\), so \(\varphi(p)=\operatorname{expit}(\ell+c)\) and \(p=\operatorname{expit}(\ell)\). Since \(\mathrm d\ell/\mathrm dp=1/(p(1-p))>0\) and \(\operatorname{expit}'=\operatorname{expit}(1-\operatorname{expit})>0\), \[
\varphi'(p)=\frac{\varphi(p)(1-\varphi(p))}{p(1-p)}>0,
\] so \(\varphi\) is strictly increasing. For the second derivative it is cleanest to differentiate the logarithm of \(\varphi'\) (logarithmic differentiation turns the product/quotient in \(\varphi'\) into a sum). Taking logs of \(\varphi'=\varphi(1-\varphi)/[p(1-p)]\), \[
\log\varphi'=\log\varphi+\log(1-\varphi)-\log p-\log(1-p),
\] and differentiating each term in \(p\) (using \(\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dp}\log\varphi=\varphi'/\varphi\) and \(\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dp}\log(1-\varphi)=-\varphi'/(1-\varphi)\) by the chain rule), \[
\frac{\varphi''}{\varphi'}
=\frac{\varphi'}{\varphi}-\frac{\varphi'}{1-\varphi}-\frac1p+\frac{1}{1-p}
=\varphi'\Bigl(\tfrac1\varphi-\tfrac{1}{1-\varphi}\Bigr)-\Bigl(\tfrac1p-\tfrac{1}{1-p}\Bigr).
\] Combine each pair of reciprocals over a common denominator, \(\tfrac1\varphi-\tfrac1{1-\varphi}
=(1-2\varphi)/[\varphi(1-\varphi)]\) and \(\tfrac1p-\tfrac1{1-p}=(1-2p)/[p(1-p)]\), so \[
\frac{\varphi''}{\varphi'}=(1-2\varphi)\frac{\varphi'}{\varphi(1-\varphi)}-(1-2p)\frac{1}{p(1-p)} .
\] Now substitute \(\varphi'/[\varphi(1-\varphi)]=1/[p(1-p)]\) (which is just \(\varphi'=\varphi(1-\varphi)/[p(1-p)]\) rearranged), so both terms share the denominator \(p(1-p)\): \[
\frac{\varphi''}{\varphi'}=\frac{(1-2\varphi)-(1-2p)}{p(1-p)}=\frac{2(p-\varphi)}{p(1-p)} .
\] Since \(c>0\) gives \(\varphi(p)>p\) on \((0,1)\), the numerator \(2(p-\varphi)\) is negative while \(\varphi'>0\) and \(p(1-p)>0\), so \(\varphi''<0\): \(\varphi\) is strictly concave on \((0,1)\).
(b) Strict attenuation. The marginal risks are \(m_C=\mathbb E[\mu_C(X)]\) and \(m_B=\mathbb E[\varphi(\mu_C(X))]\). By Jensen’s inequality (Theorem 4.6) applied to the strictly concave \(\varphi\) with the non-degenerate \(\mu_C(X)\), \[
m_B=\mathbb E[\varphi(\mu_C(X))]<\varphi(\mathbb E[\mu_C(X)])=\varphi(m_C),
\] strictly. Since \(\operatorname{logit}\) is increasing and \(\operatorname{logit}\varphi(m_C)=\operatorname{logit}m_C+c\), \[
\operatorname{logit}m_B<\operatorname{logit}\varphi(m_C)=\operatorname{logit}m_C+c,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad \operatorname{logit}m_B-\operatorname{logit}m_C<c .
\] The lower bound is positive: \(\varphi(p)>p\) pointwise gives \(m_B=\mathbb E[\varphi(\mu_C(X))]>\mathbb E[\mu_C(X)]=m_C\), so \(\operatorname{logit}m_B>\operatorname{logit}m_C\). Hence \(0<\operatorname{logit}m_B-\operatorname{logit}m_C<c\).
(c) The gap grows with spread. For a point mass at \(p_0\), Jensen holds with equality and the gap \(c-(\operatorname{logit}m_B-\operatorname{logit}m_C)\) is zero; for any non-degenerate law of \(\mu_C(X)\) the strict concavity makes the Jensen inequality strict and the gap positive. The more dispersed \(\mu_C(X)\) is, the larger the Jensen deficit \(\varphi(\mathbb E[\mu_C])-\mathbb E[\varphi(\mu_C)]\), and so the larger the attenuation gap. Because this deficit depends on the distribution of \(\mu_C(X)\), the marginal log odds ratio \(\operatorname{logit}m_B-\operatorname{logit}m_C\) is population-dependent: it is not a property the treatments carry from one population to another.
(d) Numerical check. In Section 12.8.2 the conditional log odds ratio is \(c=2\). In \(\mathcal P_1\) (\(P(X=1)=0.1\)), \(m_C=0.137941\) and \(m_B=0.341378\), so the marginal log odds ratio is \(\operatorname{logit}(0.341378)-\operatorname{logit}(0.137941)=1.17534\), strictly between \(0\) and \(2\). In \(\mathcal P_2\) (\(P(X=1)=0.9\)), \(m_C=0.862060\), \(m_B=0.920871\), giving \(0.62173\), again in \((0,2)\). Both lie strictly between \(0\) and \(c=2\), and they differ (\(1.18\) versus \(0.62\)) because the spread of \(\mu_C(X)\) differs between the two populations, confirming (b) and (c). \(\square\)


F.12.2 Solution to Exercise 12.8: Scale misalignment manufactures effect modification
This Chapter 12 exercise shows that reporting a logit-scale model on the risk-difference scale turns a covariate-free conditional structure into a covariate-varying, population-dependent risk difference: the effect modification is an artifact of the mismatched scales, not of the biology.
Uses. The scale-alignment theorem Theorem 12.4 and the collapsibility of the risk difference.
Take a logistic model with no interactions, \(\eta_k(x)=\alpha+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_k\), so SEMA holds trivially (\(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,C}=\mathbf 0\)), and report the effect as a risk difference, \(h=\mathrm{id}\) with \(g=\operatorname{logit}\).
(a) Here \(\psi=h\circ g^{-1}=\operatorname{id}\circ\operatorname{expit}=\operatorname{expit}\), which is not affine. The conditional reported contrast is \[
\operatorname{expit}(\eta_B(x))-\operatorname{expit}(\eta_C(x))
=\operatorname{expit}(\alpha+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_B)-\operatorname{expit}(\alpha+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_C).
\] Both arms share the same covariate term \(x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1\), but they enter \(\operatorname{expit}\) at different levels \(\gamma_B\neq\gamma_C\). Writing \(u(x)=\alpha+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1\), the contrast is \(\operatorname{expit}(u+\gamma_B)-\operatorname{expit}(u+\gamma_C)\), whose derivative in \(u\) is \(\operatorname{expit}'(u+\gamma_B)-\operatorname{expit}'(u+\gamma_C)\), generically nonzero because \(\operatorname{expit}'\) is non-constant. So whenever \(\boldsymbol\beta_1\neq\mathbf 0\), the term \(u(x)\) varies with \(x\) and the risk difference is a non-constant function of \(x\), instantiating Theorem 12.4(ii): a shared effect-modifier structure on the logit scale does not make the risk-difference contrast constant in the covariates.
(b) With scalar \(x\in\{0,1\}\), \(\alpha=-2\), \(\beta_1=3\), \(\gamma_C=0\), \(\gamma_B=1.5\): \[
\begin{aligned}
x=0:\ &\eta_C=-2,\ \eta_B=-0.5;\quad \operatorname{expit}(-2)=0.119203,\ \operatorname{expit}(-0.5)=0.377541;\\
&\text{risk difference }=0.377541-0.119203=0.258338.\\
x=1:\ &\eta_C=1,\ \eta_B=2.5;\quad \operatorname{expit}(1)=0.731059,\ \operatorname{expit}(2.5)=0.924142;\\
&\text{risk difference }=0.924142-0.731059=0.193083 .
\end{aligned}
\] The conditional risk difference is \(0.2583\) at \(x=0\) and \(0.1931\) at \(x=1\): non-constant, as predicted. The marginal risk differences are population-weighted averages of these two values. With \(P(X=1)=0.2\), \[
0.8(0.258338)+0.2(0.193083)=0.245287;
\] with \(P(X=1)=0.8\), \[
0.2(0.258338)+0.8(0.193083)=0.206134 .
\] The marginal risk difference depends on the covariate distribution, \(0.2453\) versus \(0.2061\).
(c) The risk difference is a collapsible measure (the marginal risk difference equals the average of the conditional risk differences within any one population, by linearity). Collapsibility, however, concerns averaging across strata at fixed conditional contrasts; it does not make those conditional contrasts constant in \(x\). Here the failure is upstream of collapsibility: the misaligned map \(\psi=\operatorname{expit}\) turns a constant logit-scale contrast into a covariate-varying risk-difference contrast, so the very conditional effect being averaged depends on \(x\). A population shift then reweights those differing conditional values and changes the marginal risk difference. Scale misalignment, not non-collapsibility, is what manufactures the effect modification and the population dependence here. \(\square\)

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Selected Exercises
text:
F.13 Chapter 13: Pairwise Meta-Analysis

F.13.1 Solution to Exercise 13.3: A full fixed- and random-effects meta-analysis by hand
This Chapter 13 exercise runs a three-trial meta-analysis end to end: inverse-variance fixed-effect pooling, Cochran’s \(Q\) and \(I^2\), the DerSimonian-Laird between-study variance, and the random-effects recomputation. Every arithmetic step is shown so the calculation can be checked line by line.
Uses. Inverse-variance weighting Equation 15.17, the expected-\(Q\) constant Equation 13.5, and the DerSimonian-Laird truncation Equation 13.11.
The three trials are \(\hat\theta_1=1.2\ (s_1^2=0.16)\), \(\hat\theta_2=0.8\ (s_2^2=0.09)\), \(\hat\theta_3=1.5\ (s_3^2=0.25)\).
(a) Fixed-effect estimate. The inverse-variance weights are \(w_i=1/s_i^2\): \(w_1=6.25\), \(w_2=11.1111\), \(w_3=4\), with total \(W=\sum_i w_i=21.3611\). Then \[
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}=\frac{\sum_i w_i\hat\theta_i}{W}
=\frac{6.25(1.2)+11.1111(0.8)+4(1.5)}{21.3611}=\frac{22.3889}{21.3611}=1.04812,
\] with standard error \(\operatorname{SE}(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}})=1/\sqrt W=1/\sqrt{21.3611}=0.21636\).
(b) Cochran’s \(Q\) and \(I^2\). With deviations \(\hat\theta_i-\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}\), \[
Q=\sum_i w_i(\hat\theta_i-\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}})^2
=6.25(0.15188)^2+11.1111(-0.24812)^2+4(0.45188)^2=0.1442+0.6840+0.8168=1.6450 .
\] Under homogeneity \(Q\sim\chi^2_{k-1}=\chi^2_2\), with mean \(k-1=2\). Since the observed \(Q=1.645\) is below its null expectation, \(I^2=\max\{0,(Q-(k-1))/Q\}=\max\{0,-0.216\}=0\).
(c) DerSimonian-Laird. The constant of Equation 13.5 is \[
c=W-\frac{\sum_i w_i^2}{W}=21.3611-\frac{6.25^2+11.1111^2+4^2}{21.3611}
=21.3611-\frac{178.5193}{21.3611}=21.3611-8.3563=13.0048 .
\] Then \(\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}=\max\{0,(Q-(k-1))/c\}=\max\{0,(1.645-2)/13.0048\}=\max\{0,-0.0273\}=0\).
(d) Random-effects recomputation. Because \(\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}=0\), the random-effects weights \(\tilde w_i=1/(s_i^2+\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}})\) equal the fixed-effect weights, so the random-effects pooled estimate and standard error coincide with the fixed-effect values, \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{RE}}=1.04812\) and \(\operatorname{SE}=0.21636\). The data show no detectable heterogeneity: the between-study spread is smaller than sampling noise alone would produce, so the truncation in Equation 13.11 returns \(\hat\tau^2=0\) and the two analyses agree. \(\square\)


F.13.2 Solution to Exercise 13.6: REML heterogeneity variance with equal within-study variances
This Chapter 13 exercise solves the REML estimating equation for the between-study variance \(\tau^2\) in the special case of equal within-study variances, recovering the \(k-1\) divisor that maximum likelihood misses.
Uses. The REML estimating equation Equation 13.13 and the one-sample REML correction Theorem 8.8.
Suppose all within-study variances are equal, \(s_i^2\equiv s^2\). Then the random-effects weights are equal, \(\tilde w_i\equiv\tilde w=1/(s^2+\tau^2)\), and the weighted mean \(\hat\theta_R=\sum_i\tilde w_i\hat\theta_i/\sum_i\tilde w_i\) reduces to the unweighted mean \(\bar{\hat\theta}=\tfrac1k\sum_i\hat\theta_i\). The REML estimating equation Equation 13.13 is \[
\sum_{i=1}^k\tilde w_i^2(\hat\theta_i-\hat\theta_R)^2=\sum_{i=1}^k\tilde w_i-\frac{\sum_i\tilde w_i^2}{\sum_i\tilde w_i}.
\] With \(\tilde w_i\equiv\tilde w\) the left side is \(\tilde w^2\sum_i(\hat\theta_i-\bar{\hat\theta})^2\), and the right side is \(k\tilde w-(k\tilde w^2)/(k\tilde w)=k\tilde w-\tilde w=(k-1)\tilde w\). Equating and dividing by \(\tilde w\), \[
\tilde w\sum_{i=1}^k(\hat\theta_i-\bar{\hat\theta})^2=k-1,
\qquad\text{that is}\qquad
\frac{1}{s^2+\tau^2}\sum_{i=1}^k(\hat\theta_i-\bar{\hat\theta})^2=k-1 .
\] Solving, \(s^2+\tau^2=\tfrac{1}{k-1}\sum_i(\hat\theta_i-\bar{\hat\theta})^2\), hence \[
\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{REML}}=\frac{1}{k-1}\sum_{i=1}^k(\hat\theta_i-\bar{\hat\theta})^2-s^2
\] (truncated at \(0\)). The maximum likelihood counterpart divides the same sum of squares by \(k\) rather than \(k-1\), giving \(\tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{ML}}=\tfrac1k\sum_i(\hat\theta_i-\bar{\hat\theta})^2-s^2\). The discrepancy is the single degree of freedom spent on estimating the common mean \(\theta\): REML forms the likelihood from the \(k-1\) contrasts orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1_k\), dividing by \(k-1\), whereas maximum likelihood treats \(\bar{\hat\theta}\) as if known and divides by \(k\), underestimating \(\tau^2\). This is the balanced-data instance of the one-sample variance correction of Theorem 8.8. \(\square\)

section: F.14 Chapter 14: Indirect Comparison and Bucher’s Theorem
text:
F.14 Chapter 14: Indirect Comparison and Bucher’s Theorem

F.14.1 Solution to Exercise 14.8: Bucher variance with correlated within-trial contrasts
This Chapter 14 exercise works out the Bucher indirect-comparison variance when the two contrasts share a trial arm, and shows the shared-comparator correlation is exactly \(\tfrac12\), recovering the direct within-trial contrast.
Uses. The Bucher variance formula Theorem 14.2 and the homoskedastic random-effects correlation Theorem 15.4.
The Bucher estimator is \(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}\), and by the general variance formula of Theorem 14.2, \[
\operatorname{Var}\bigl(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\bigr)=v_{AC}+v_{BC}-2\operatorname{Cov}(\hat d_{AC},\hat d_{BC})
=v_{AC}+v_{BC}-2\rho\sqrt{v_{AC}v_{BC}} .
\] For \(\rho>0\) the subtracted term is positive, so the variance is strictly smaller than \(v_{AC}+v_{BC}\): treating correlated contrasts from one trial as independent overstates the variance and is conservative for this comparison.
Homoskedastic three-arm structure. Let arms \(A,B,C\) of a single trial have independent arm-level estimates \(\hat y_A,\hat y_B,\hat y_C\), each of variance \(\sigma^2\), with \(C\) the shared comparator. Then \(\hat d_{AC}=\hat y_A-\hat y_C\) and \(\hat d_{BC}=\hat y_B-\hat y_C\), so \[
v_{AC}=v_{BC}=2\sigma^2,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\hat d_{AC},\hat d_{BC})=\operatorname{Var}(\hat y_C)=\sigma^2,
\] the covariance coming only from the shared \(C\) arm. Hence \(\rho=\sigma^2/\sqrt{(2\sigma^2)(2\sigma^2)}=\sigma^2/(2\sigma^2)=\tfrac12\). The Bucher variance is \[
\operatorname{Var}\bigl(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\bigr)=2\sigma^2+2\sigma^2-2\sigma^2=2\sigma^2,
\] which equals \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat y_A-\hat y_B)=\operatorname{Var}(\hat y_A)+\operatorname{Var}(\hat y_B)=2\sigma^2\), the variance of the direct within-trial \(A\)-versus-\(B\) contrast. The shared-comparator correlation \(\rho=\tfrac12\) is exactly the value derived for the homoskedastic random-effects network in Theorem 15.4, and it makes the Bucher subtraction recover the direct within-study contrast with no loss. \(\square\)


F.14.2 Solution to Exercise 14.9: Effect-modifier imbalance breaks Bucher’s transitivity
This Chapter 14 exercise puts numbers to the transitivity failure of an unadjusted indirect comparison: an effect modifier distributed differently in the \(BC\) trial and the target population biases the Bucher estimand, and the bias is exactly the reweighting that population adjustment later corrects.
Uses. Network additivity of contrasts and the effect-modifier reweighting introduced from Chapter 17.
The binary effect modifier \(Z\) acts on the \(B\)-versus-\(C\) contrast with conditional values \(d_{BC}(Z=0)=0.2\), \(d_{BC}(Z=1)=0.8\) (treated as collapsible). Study \(BC\) has \(\Pr(Z=1)=0.7\); the target population \(\mathcal P_{AB}\) has \(\Pr(Z=1)=0.3\). The \(A\)-versus-\(C\) contrast is unmodified, \(d_{AC}=0.6\) in every population.
Marginal \(B\)-versus-\(C\) contrasts. Averaging over \(Z\), \[
d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=0.3(0.2)+0.7(0.8)=0.62,
\qquad
d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})}=0.7(0.2)+0.3(0.8)=0.38 .
\]
True target contrast. In the target population, by network additivity, \[
d_{AB}=d_{AC}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})}=0.6-0.38=0.22 .
\]
Bucher estimand and its bias. Bucher subtracts the contrast as reported by trial \(BC\): \[
d_{AC}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=0.6-0.62=-0.02,
\] so the bias of the unadjusted indirect comparison is \[
\bigl(d_{AC}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}\bigr)-d_{AB}=-0.02-0.22=-0.24 .
\] The bias arises entirely because the \(B\)-versus-\(C\) contrast must be reweighted from the \(BC\)-study modifier distribution \(\Pr(Z=1)=0.7\) to the target distribution \(\Pr(Z=1)=0.3\); the effect-modifier adjustment of Chapter 17 onward is precisely the reweighting of \(d_{BC}\) to the target marginal. A purely prognostic variable, which shifts the baseline of both arms equally and leaves the conditional contrast \(d_{BC}(z)\) constant in \(z\), would make \(d_{BC}\) population-free and produce no bias at all. \(\square\)

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Selected Exercises
section: F.15 Chapter 15: Network Meta-Analysis: Models and Identifiability
text:
F.15 Chapter 15: Network Meta-Analysis: Models and Identifiability

F.15.1 Solution to Exercise 15.9: Network pooling is inverse-variance blending of direct and indirect
This Chapter 15 exercise shows that combining a direct and an indirect estimate of the same contrast through generalized least squares reduces to the familiar inverse-variance-weighted average, the algebra behind node-splitting.
Uses. The network generalized-least-squares estimator Equation 15.13 and the definition of node-splitting Definition 15.4.
Take a contrast \(d_{AB}\) informed by two independent unbiased sources, a direct estimate \(\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{AB}\) with variance \(v_{\mathrm{dir}}\) and an indirect estimate \(\hat d^{\mathrm{ind}}_{AB}\) with variance \(v_{\mathrm{ind}}\). Stack them as a one-parameter generalized-least-squares problem with design \(\mathbf X=\binom{1}{1}\), response \(\mathbf y=(\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{AB},\hat d^{\mathrm{ind}}_{AB})^\top\), and covariance \(\mathbf V=\operatorname{diag}(v_{\mathrm{dir}},v_{\mathrm{ind}})\). The GLS estimator Equation 15.13 is \(\hat d^{\mathrm{net}}_{AB}=(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf y\). Here, with \(w_{\mathrm{dir}}=1/v_{\mathrm{dir}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{ind}}=1/v_{\mathrm{ind}}\), \[
\mathbf X^\top\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf X=w_{\mathrm{dir}}+w_{\mathrm{ind}},
\qquad
\mathbf X^\top\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf y=w_{\mathrm{dir}}\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{AB}+w_{\mathrm{ind}}\hat d^{\mathrm{ind}}_{AB},
\] so \[
\hat d^{\mathrm{net}}_{AB}=\frac{w_{\mathrm{dir}}\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{AB}+w_{\mathrm{ind}}\hat d^{\mathrm{ind}}_{AB}}{w_{\mathrm{dir}}+w_{\mathrm{ind}}},
\] the inverse-variance-weighted mean Equation 15.17, with variance \((\mathbf X^\top\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf X)^{-1}=1/(w_{\mathrm{dir}}+w_{\mathrm{ind}})\). This is the best linear unbiased combination of the two sources (the \(k=2\) fixed-effect meta-analysis). In a larger network, any contrast whose only evidence separates into one direct stream (studies comparing \(A\) and \(B\) directly) and one indirect stream (the rest of the network with the direct \(AB\) evidence removed), the two streams being independent, reduces to exactly this two-source blend; this is the construction behind node-splitting (Definition 15.4), where the network estimate of the contrast is the inverse-variance blend of its direct and indirect parts. \(\square\)


F.15.2 Solution to Exercise 15.10: Between-study-only covariates are confounded with baselines
This Chapter 15 exercise shows that when a covariate varies only between studies (constant within each study), its prognostic effect cannot be separated from the study baselines, the individual-level seed of ecological bias.
Uses. The IPD network meta-regression identifiability theorem Theorem 15.5 and the definition of ecological bias Definition 16.2.
In the IPD network meta-regression Equation 15.20 with a single scalar covariate \(x\), \[
g\bigl(\mathbb E[Y_{ijk}]\bigr)=\mu_j+x_{ijk}\beta_1+d_k+x_{ijk}\beta_{2,k},
\] suppose \(x\) is constant within each study, \(x_{ijk}=x_j\) for all individuals and arms of study \(j\).
Identifiability condition (iii) fails. Condition (iii) of Theorem 15.5 requires the within-study covariate covariance to be nonsingular. When \(x\) takes a single value \(x_j\) in study \(j\), the within-study variance of \(x\) is zero, so the covariance is singular and (iii) is violated.
Confounding of \(\beta_1\) with the baselines. On arm \(k\) of study \(j\) the linear predictor is \(\eta_{jk}=\mu_j+x_j\beta_1+d_k+x_j\beta_{2,k}\). For any scalar \(t\), define the alternative parameters \[
\mu_j'=\mu_j+t\,x_j,\qquad \beta_1'=\beta_1-t,
\] leaving \(d_k\) and \(\beta_{2,k}\) unchanged. Then \[
\mu_j'+x_j\beta_1'+d_k+x_j\beta_{2,k}=\mu_j+t x_j+x_j(\beta_1-t)+d_k+x_j\beta_{2,k}=\mu_j+x_j\beta_1+d_k+x_j\beta_{2,k}=\eta_{jk},
\] so every arm of every study has the identical conditional mean. The one-parameter family \((\boldsymbol\mu+t\,\mathbf x_{\mathrm{study}},\,\beta_1-t,\,\mathbf d,\,\{\beta_{2,k}\})\), \(t\in\mathbb R\), gives indistinguishable conditional-mean functions, so the prognostic main effect \(\beta_1\) is confounded with the study baselines \(\mu_j\) and is not identified.
This is the individual-level seed of ecological bias (Definition 16.2): with only between-study variation in \(x\), a study-level association between \(x_j\) and the outcome can be explained equally by a prognostic effect \(\beta_1\) or by differences in the baselines \(\mu_j\), and the two cannot be separated. Within-study covariate variation rescues identifiability because then \(x_{ijk}\beta_1\) varies across individuals within a study and can no longer be absorbed into a single per-study intercept, so \(\beta_1\) is pinned down by the within-study covariate-outcome relationship. \(\square\)

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Selected Exercises
section: F.16 Chapter 16: The Limits of Standard Network Meta-Analysis
text:
F.16 Chapter 16: The Limits of Standard Network Meta-Analysis

F.16.1 Solution to Exercise 16.8: Anchored bias depends only on effect-modifier marginals
This Chapter 16 exercise shows the Bucher bias of an anchored comparison depends only on the marginal distributions of the effect modifiers, so balancing those marginals alone removes it, while an unanchored comparison reinstates the prognostic variables.
Uses. The failure-of-Bucher bias formula Theorem 16.1.
Split \(X=(V,W)\) with \(V\) an effect modifier and \(W\) purely prognostic for the anchored contrast on scale \(g\), so \(\tau^g_{tC}(v,w)=\tau^g_{tC}(v)\) for \(t\in\{A,B\}\), depending on \(v\) but not \(w\). By Theorem 16.1 the Bucher bias is \(b_{AC}-b_{BC}\) with \(b_{tC}=\int\tau^g_{tC}(x)[f_{tC}(x)-f_{*}(x)]\,\mathrm dx\). Substituting \(\tau^g_{tC}(v,w)=\tau^g_{tC}(v)\) and integrating out \(w\), \[
b_{tC}=\int\!\!\int\tau^g_{tC}(v)\,[f_{tC}(v,w)-f_{*}(v,w)]\,\mathrm dw\,\mathrm dv
=\int\tau^g_{tC}(v)\,[f^V_{tC}(v)-f^V_{*}(v)]\,\mathrm dv,
\] where \(f^V_{tC}\) and \(f^V_{*}\) are the \(V\)-marginals of \(f_{tC}\) and \(f_{*}\). Thus each \(b_{tC}\), and hence the total Bucher bias \(b_{AC}-b_{BC}\), depends only on the marginal distributions of \(V\) in \(\mathcal P_{AC}\), \(\mathcal P_{BC}\), and \(\mathcal P^{*}\). It is invariant to every feature of the distribution of \(W\), including the conditional law of \(W\) given \(V\) and any difference in the \(V\)-\(W\) dependence across the three populations, since \(W\) has been integrated out against densities that each integrate to one in \(w\).
Consequently an anchored adjustment that balances the marginal distribution of \(V\) alone removes the bias: once \(f^V_{AC}=f^V_{BC}=f^V_{*}\), every \(b_{tC}=0\). The argument breaks for an unanchored comparison built from absolute arm means \(\mathbb E_{f_*}[\mu_A(V,W)]\): there \(\mu_A\) depends on the prognostic \(W\), so the integral over \(w\) does not collapse to a \(V\)-marginal statement, and an imbalance in the conditional law of \(W\) given \(V\) shifts the absolute mean with no comparator term to cancel it. Anchoring is what confines the adjustment set to effect modifiers; unanchoring reinstates prognostic variables. \(\square\)


F.16.2 Solution to Exercise 16.9: Ecological attenuation of the effect-modifier slope
This Chapter 16 exercise quantifies how within-study covariate variation attenuates the effect-modification slope seen at the aggregate (ecological) level, gives the exact probit answer, and explains why global convexity of the inverse link is not enough to guarantee attenuation toward zero.
Strategy. Expand the inverse link to second order in the within-study spread \(\sigma^2\); the leading correction to the aggregate slope is a curvature term. For the probit the integral is exact, so the approximation becomes an identity; for a general link the sign of the correction is not fixed, which is the point of the last part.
Uses. The delta-method-style Taylor expansion of Chapter 4 and the Gaussian integral identity for \(\mathbb E[\Phi(a+\rho X)]\) derived in part (b).
We organize the solution as (a) the general-link expansion, (b) the exact probit specialization, and (c) why convexity alone does not force attenuation.
(a) General-link Taylor expansion. Let each trial have \(X\sim\mathcal N(\bar x,\sigma^2)\) and arm linear predictors \(\eta_t(x)=a_t+\rho_t x\). Write \(m_t=a_t+\rho_t\bar x\) for the linear predictor at the trial mean and let \(\psi=g^{-1}\). Expand \(\psi\) to second order about \(m_t\): \[
\psi(a_t+\rho_t X)=\psi(m_t)+\psi'(m_t)\rho_t(X-\bar x)+\tfrac12\psi''(m_t)\rho_t^2(X-\bar x)^2+R_t,
\] with \(R_t\) collecting the remainder. Taking expectations and using \(\mathbb E[X-\bar x]=0\), \(\mathbb E[(X-\bar x)^2]=\sigma^2\), \[
\bar\mu_t(\bar x)=\mathbb E[\psi(a_t+\rho_t X)]=\psi(m_t)+\tfrac12\psi''(m_t)\rho_t^2\sigma^2+O(\sigma^4).
\] Apply \(g\) and expand again, using \(g'(\psi(m))=1/\psi'(m)\): \[
g(\bar\mu_t(\bar x))=m_t+g'(\psi(m_t))\cdot\tfrac12\psi''(m_t)\rho_t^2\sigma^2+O(\sigma^4)
=m_t+\tfrac12\rho_t^2\sigma^2\frac{\psi''(m_t)}{\psi'(m_t)}+O(\sigma^4).
\] Therefore the aggregate link-scale contrast is \[
D(\bar x)=g(\bar\mu_1(\bar x))-g(\bar\mu_0(\bar x))
=(m_1-m_0)+\tfrac12\sigma^2\!\left[\rho_1^2\frac{\psi''(m_1)}{\psi'(m_1)}-\rho_0^2\frac{\psi''(m_0)}{\psi'(m_0)}\right]+O(\sigma^4),
\] and differentiating in \(\bar x\) (note \(\mathrm dm_t/\mathrm d\bar x=\rho_t\)), \[
D'(\bar x)=(\rho_1-\rho_0)+\tfrac12\sigma^2\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\bar x}\!\left[\rho_1^2\frac{\psi''(m_1)}{\psi'(m_1)}-\rho_0^2\frac{\psi''(m_0)}{\psi'(m_0)}\right]+O(\sigma^4).
\] To zeroth order in \(\sigma^2\), \(D'(\bar x)=\rho_1-\rho_0=\beta_2\), the individual effect-modification coefficient. The \(O(\sigma^2)\) correction is governed by the curvature \(\psi''=(g^{-1})''\) and, through the \(\bar x\)-derivative, the third derivative \(\psi'''=(g^{-1})'''\).
(b) Probit specialization (exact). For \(g=\Phi^{-1}\), \(\psi=\Phi\) and the integral is exact (no remainder). The identity we need is \(\mathbb E[\Phi(a+\rho X)]=\Phi\bigl((a+\rho\bar x)/\sqrt{1+\rho^2\sigma^2}\bigr)\) for \(X\sim\mathcal N(\bar x,\sigma^2)\), and it is worth deriving rather than quoting, because a beginner cannot check it otherwise. Introduce an auxiliary standard normal \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) independent of \(X\). Then \(\Phi(a+\rho X)=P(Z\le a+\rho X\mid X)\), so taking the expectation over \(X\), \[
\mathbb E[\Phi(a+\rho X)]=P(Z-\rho X\le a).
\] Now \(Z-\rho X\) is a linear combination of independent normals, hence normal, with mean \(\mathbb E[Z-\rho X]=-\rho\bar x\) and variance \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)+\rho^2\operatorname{Var}(X)=1+\rho^2\sigma^2\). Standardizing, \[
P(Z-\rho X\le a)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{a-(-\rho\bar x)}{\sqrt{1+\rho^2\sigma^2}}\right)
=\Phi\!\left(\frac{a+\rho\bar x}{\sqrt{1+\rho^2\sigma^2}}\right),
\] the stated identity (this is the standard Gaussian convolution of Chapter 4, obtained here by the auxiliary normal rather than by completing the square). Applying it to each arm, \(\bar\mu_t(\bar x)=\mathbb E[\Phi(a_t+\rho_t X)]=\Phi\bigl((a_t+\rho_t\bar x)/\sqrt{1+\rho_t^2\sigma^2}\bigr)\), so \(g(\bar\mu_t)=(a_t+\rho_t\bar x)/\sqrt{1+\rho_t^2\sigma^2}\) and \[
D'(\bar x)=\frac{\rho_1}{\sqrt{1+\rho_1^2\sigma^2}}-\frac{\rho_0}{\sqrt{1+\rho_0^2\sigma^2}}=b_2,
\] the exact slope Equation 16.12. Expanding \(1/\sqrt{1+\rho^2\sigma^2}=1-\tfrac12\rho^2\sigma^2+O(\sigma^4)\) gives \[
b_2=(\rho_1-\rho_0)-\tfrac12\sigma^2(\rho_1^3-\rho_0^3)+O(\sigma^4),
\] the leading-order term: the slope equals \(\beta_2\) corrected at order \(\sigma^2\).
(c) Why global convexity is not enough. The probit attenuation \(0<b_2<\beta_2\) holds for every parameter configuration because the exact factor \(\rho/\sqrt{1+\rho^2\sigma^2}\) is a strictly increasing odd contraction of \(\rho\). For a general link the \(O(\sigma^2)\) correction depends on the signed combination \(\rho_1^2\psi''(m_1)/\psi'(m_1)-\rho_0^2\psi''(m_0)/\psi'(m_0)\) and its \(\bar x\)-derivative, which involve the levels \(m_0,m_1\) and the slopes \(\rho_0,\rho_1\) with both signs. A globally convex \(g^{-1}\) fixes the sign of \(\psi''\) but not the sign of the difference, so the correction can push the ecological slope either toward or away from zero depending on the configuration. Global convexity therefore does not guarantee attenuation toward zero, in contrast to the exact, configuration-free probit result. \(\square\)

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Selected Exercises
text:
F.17 Chapter 17: Population Adjustment Theory

F.17.1 Solution to Exercise 17.8: The unanchored adjustment set must include prognostic variables
This Chapter 17 exercise derives the omitted-covariate bias of an unanchored (single-arm) population adjustment and shows it is nonzero for imbalanced prognostic variables, which cancel in the anchored case. The moral is that unanchored comparisons need every imbalanced prognostic variable in the adjustment set, not just effect modifiers.
Uses. The unanchored bias formula Equation 17.17 and the prognostic-cancellation lemma Lemma 17.1.
The bias formula. The unanchored estimand standardizes each arm’s conditional mean to the target, \(m_t(\mathcal P^{*})=\int\mu_t(x)f_{*}(x)\,\mathrm dx\). Suppose the true conditional mean depends on \((X,W)\) with \(W\) omitted from the adjustment set, \(\mu_A=\mu_A(x,w)\). Standardizing only over \(X\) uses the source conditional law of \(W\) given \(X\), \(f_{\mathrm{src},A}(w\mid x)\), whereas the target uses \(f^{*}(w\mid x)\). The \(A\)-arm bias is the difference between the source-plugged and target arm means, \[
\int\!\!\int\mu_A(x,w)\,f_{\mathrm{src},A}(w\mid x)\,f_{*}(x)\,\mathrm dw\,\mathrm dx
-\int\!\!\int\mu_A(x,w)\,f^{*}(w\mid x)\,f_{*}(x)\,\mathrm dw\,\mathrm dx
=\int\!\!\int\mu_A(x,w)\,[f_{\mathrm{src},A}(w\mid x)-f^{*}(w\mid x)]\,f_{*}(x)\,\mathrm dw\,\mathrm dx,
\] which is Equation 17.17. It is nonzero precisely when \(\mu_A\) depends on the omitted \(w\) (prognostic) and the conditional law of \(W\) given \(X\) differs between source and target (imbalance), and there is no comparator arm to cancel it.
Binary specialization. Take \(\mu_A(x,w)=\alpha(x)+\rho w\) with binary \(W\), \(\Pr_{\mathrm{src}}(W=1)=p\), \(\Pr_{*}(W=1)=q\), with \(W\) independent of \(X\) for transparency. The bias of the \(A\) marginal mean is \[
\int\!\!\int(\alpha(x)+\rho w)\,[f_{\mathrm{src}}(w)-f^{*}(w)]\,f_{*}(x)\,\mathrm dw\,\mathrm dx
=\rho\int w\,[f_{\mathrm{src}}(w)-f^{*}(w)]\,\mathrm dw
=\rho\,(p-q),
\] the \(\alpha(x)\) term integrating to zero because \(f_{\mathrm{src}}(\cdot)\) and \(f^{*}(\cdot)\) each integrate to one in \(w\). So an imbalanced purely prognostic \(W\) biases the unanchored \(A\) mean by \(\rho(p-q)\).
Why the anchored comparison is multiplied by zero. In an anchored comparison the same \(W\) contributes to both the \(A\) arm and the comparator arm through the contrast \(\mu_A(x,w)-\mu_C(x,w)\). If \(W\) is purely prognostic, this contrast is free of \(w\), so the \(\rho w\) term cancels and the corresponding bias coefficient is zero: the imbalance \(p-q\) is multiplied by the contrast’s \(w\)-derivative, which vanishes. This is Lemma 17.1. Consequently the unanchored adjustment set of Theorem 17.2 must contain every imbalanced prognostic variable and every imbalanced effect modifier, whereas the anchored set needs only effect modifiers. The unanchored requirement is therefore far harder to satisfy in practice, since prognostic variables are typically far more numerous than effect modifiers and need not even be suspected in advance. \(\square\)


F.17.2 Solution to Exercise 17.9: The marginal odds ratio depends on the target population
This Chapter 17 exercise computes how the marginal odds ratio of \(A\) versus \(B\) changes across target populations that differ only in covariate prevalence, isolating the non-collapsibility (Jensen) gap even though every conditional risk is held fixed.
Uses. The anchored consistency theorem Theorem 17.1 and the SEMA-insufficiency obstruction Theorem 12.6.
Use the conditional risks of Example 17.2: \(\mu_A(0)=0.20\), \(\mu_A(1)=0.50\), \(\mu_B(0)=\mu_B(1)=0.30\), the same functions in every population. We compute the marginal odds ratio of \(A\) versus \(B\) as the covariate prevalence \(\Pr(X=1)=p\) varies over \(\{0.25,0.50,0.75\}\).
Marginal risks and log odds ratios. Since \(\mu_B\) is constant, \(m_B(p)=0.30\) for all \(p\), while \(m_A(p)=(1-p)(0.20)+p(0.50)=0.20+0.30p\). The marginal log odds ratio is \(\operatorname{logit}m_A(p)-\operatorname{logit}(0.30)\) with \(\operatorname{logit}(0.30)=-0.847298\): \[
\begin{aligned}
p=0.25:\ & m_A=0.275,\ \operatorname{logit}=-0.969401,\ \text{log OR}=-0.122103;\\
p=0.50:\ & m_A=0.350,\ \operatorname{logit}=-0.619039,\ \text{log OR}=\phantom{-}0.228259;\\
p=0.75:\ & m_A=0.425,\ \operatorname{logit}=-0.302280,\ \text{log OR}=\phantom{-}0.545018 .
\end{aligned}
\] The marginal log odds ratio changes across the three populations, from \(-0.122\) to \(+0.545\), even though the conditional risks (and therefore the conditional odds ratios at each \(x\)) are identical in all three: no conditional parameter has changed, only \(\Pr(X=1)\).
Isolating the non-collapsibility component. The population-standardized conditional log odds ratio is \(\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{AB}(p)=(1-p)\,\delta(0)+p\,\delta(1)\) with \(\delta(x)=\operatorname{logit}\mu_A(x)-\operatorname{logit}\mu_B(x)\), that is \(\delta(0)=-0.538997\) and \(\delta(1)=0.847298\): \[
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{AB}(0.25)=-0.192423,\quad
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{AB}(0.50)=0.154151,\quad
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{AB}(0.75)=0.500724 .
\] The difference between the marginal log odds ratio and this population-standardized conditional value is the non-collapsibility (Jensen) gap, “logit of the average minus average of the logit.” Showing the subtraction at each prevalence, \[
\begin{aligned}
p=0.25:\ &-0.122103-(-0.192423)=0.070320,\\
p=0.50:\ &\phantom{-}0.228259-\phantom{-}0.154151=0.074108,\\
p=0.75:\ &\phantom{-}0.545018-\phantom{-}0.500724=0.044294.
\end{aligned}
\] This gap is a pure non-collapsibility effect: it is nonzero, and population-dependent, even though every conditional risk is held fixed across the three populations. (In this particular table the \(A\)-versus-\(B\) contrast is itself modified by \(X\), so the conditional standardized value also moves; the clean case where the conditional log odds ratio is held constant across \(x\) and only the baseline varies is the SEMA worked example of Section 12.8.2, which exhibits the non-collapsibility attenuation in isolation.)
Conclusion. On the odds-ratio scale the marginal effect is a property of the population, not of the two treatments: even a fully adjusted anchored comparison, which recovers the conditional contrast exactly (part (a) of Theorem 17.1), does not deliver a population-free marginal odds ratio (part (c)). This is exactly the obstruction of Theorem 12.6: SEMA and scale alignment pin down the conditional effect but cannot make the non-collapsible marginal odds ratio transport. \(\square\)

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Selected Exercises
text:
F.18 Chapter 18: Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison

F.18.1 Solution to Exercise 18.8: Why MAIC is exact on the identity scale but not the logit scale
This Chapter 18 exercise shows that on the identity scale, with a benefit linear in the covariates, any first-moment-balancing weight gives the same (correct) MAIC point estimate, so the choice of balancing objective affects only the variance; and that this exactness fails on the noncollapsible logit scale.
Uses. First-moment balance of the MAIC weights and the non-collapsibility gap Definition 7.7.
Generalize Example 18.3 by replacing the conditional benefit \(4+x_1\) with \(b_0+b_1x_1+b_2x_2\) and the comparator mean by a general target \((\bar x_1,\bar x_2)\). The MAIC-adjusted benefit is the weighted index mean of the conditional benefit, \[
\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=\sum_i w_i\,(b_0+b_1x_{i1}+b_2x_{i2})\Big/\sum_i w_i
=b_0+b_1\frac{\sum_i w_i x_{i1}}{\sum_i w_i}+b_2\frac{\sum_i w_i x_{i2}}{\sum_i w_i}.
\] Any weights achieving first-moment balance satisfy \(\sum_i w_i x_{i\ell}/\sum_i w_i=\bar x_\ell\) for \(\ell=1,2\), by definition of moment balance. Substituting, \[
\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=b_0+b_1\bar x_1+b_2\bar x_2,
\] which is exactly the true comparator-population benefit. The derivation used only that the weights match the two covariate means; it did not use that the weights are the entropy (exponential-tilting) weights. Hence on the identity scale with a benefit linear in the covariates, every moment-balancing weight vector gives the same point estimate, and the choice of balancing objective (entropy, empirical likelihood, or any other) affects only the effective sample size, and through it the variance, not the point estimate.
This exactness fails on the logit scale. There the adjusted contrast is \(\operatorname{logit}(\sum_i w_i\mu_A(x_i)/\sum_i w_i)-\operatorname{logit}(\sum_i w_i\mu_C(x_i)/\sum_i w_i)\), and because \(\operatorname{logit}\) is nonlinear, balancing the first moments of the covariates does not make the weighted average risk equal the target-population risk. The discrepancy is governed by higher moments of the covariate distribution under the weights, which is why MAIC on a noncollapsible scale must consider second-moment balancing (Section 18.4), and why even exact moment balance leaves a residual non-collapsibility gap (Definition 7.7). \(\square\)


F.18.2 Solution to Exercise 18.9: Sandwich versus naive variance for the MAIC weighted mean
This Chapter 18 exercise compares the honest (sandwich) variance of a MAIC weighted mean with the naive fixed-weight variance \(\sigma^2/\mathrm{ESS}\), and identifies exactly the extra term the naive analysis drops by pretending the balancing weights are known.
Strategy. Stack the balancing equation and the weighted mean into one estimating function, read its asymptotic variance off the M-estimation sandwich, and isolate the correction that estimating \(\beta\) adds.
Uses. The MAIC estimating function Equation 18.24 and the sandwich variance Definition 5.11.
Two definitions first, since this is the densest notation in the appendix. For an M-estimator solving \(\sum_i\boldsymbol\psi(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta)=\mathbf 0\), the bread is the expected Jacobian \(A=\mathbb E[\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\boldsymbol\psi]\) and the meat is the outer-product matrix \(B=\mathbb E[\boldsymbol\psi\boldsymbol\psi^\top]\); the influence function of the estimator is the random vector \(-A^{-1}\boldsymbol\psi\) whose (co)variance gives the estimator’s asymptotic variance, because the first-order expansion of an M-estimator is \[
\sqrt n\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\boldsymbol\theta)=-A^{-1}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\boldsymbol\psi(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta)+o_p(1),
\] so \(\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\boldsymbol\theta)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,A^{-1}BA^{-\top})\). A matrix is block lower-triangular when its upper-right block is zero, which here means the balance equation does not involve \(\mu_A\); that zero block is what lets us extract one component’s variance cleanly.
Drop the comparator block of Equation 18.24 and consider the single-arm weighted mean with scalar covariate. Stack \(\boldsymbol\theta=(\beta,\mu_A)\) and per-unit estimating function \[
\boldsymbol\psi(x,Y;\boldsymbol\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}e^{\beta\Delta}\,\Delta\\ e^{\beta\Delta}\,(Y-\mu_A)\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \Delta=x-\bar x_{\mathrm{target}} .
\]
The Jacobian and its inverse. With \(A=\mathbb E[\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\boldsymbol\psi]\), \[
A=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb E[e^{\beta\Delta}\Delta^2] & 0\\[2pt]
\mathbb E[e^{\beta\Delta}\Delta(Y-\mu_A)] & -\mathbb E[e^{\beta\Delta}]\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}&0\\ a_{21}&a_{22}\end{pmatrix},
\] block lower-triangular because the balance equation does not involve \(\mu_A\). Its inverse is \[
A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/a_{11}&0\\ -a_{21}/(a_{11}a_{22})&1/a_{22}\end{pmatrix}.
\] Now apply the M-estimator expansion. The influence function of the pair \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}=(\hat\beta,\hat\mu_A)\) is \(-A^{-1}\boldsymbol\psi\), and we want its second component, the one for \(\hat\mu_A\). Multiplying out, \[
-A^{-1}\boldsymbol\psi
=-\begin{pmatrix}1/a_{11}&0\\ -a_{21}/(a_{11}a_{22})&1/a_{22}\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\psi_1\\\psi_2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-\psi_1/a_{11}\\[2pt] \dfrac{a_{21}\psi_1}{a_{11}a_{22}}-\dfrac{\psi_2}{a_{22}}\end{pmatrix},
\] so the second row (the influence function of \(\hat\mu_A\)) is \[
\mathrm{IF}_{\mu_A}=\frac{a_{21}\psi_1}{a_{11}a_{22}}-\frac{\psi_2}{a_{22}}
=\frac{1}{-a_{22}}\Bigl(\psi_2-\frac{a_{21}}{a_{11}}\psi_1\Bigr).
\] The block lower-triangular structure is what makes this clean: because the upper-right entry of \(A\) (hence of \(A^{-1}\)) is zero, the \(\hat\mu_A\) row picks up only \(\psi_2\) and a single correction proportional to \(\psi_1\), not a full mixing of both. Its asymptotic variance is \[
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_A)=\frac{1}{n\,a_{22}^2}\operatorname{Var}\!\Bigl(\psi_2-\frac{a_{21}}{a_{11}}\psi_1\Bigr)
=\frac{1}{n\,a_{22}^2}\Bigl[B_{22}-2\frac{a_{21}}{a_{11}}B_{12}+\frac{a_{21}^2}{a_{11}^2}B_{11}\Bigr],
\] with \(B=\mathbb E[\boldsymbol\psi\boldsymbol\psi^\top]\).
Fixed-weight term plus a correction. Had \(\beta\) been known, only \(\psi_2\) would enter, giving the fixed-weight variance \(B_{22}/(n\,a_{22}^2)\). With \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid x)=\sigma^2\) this is \(\sigma^2\mathbb E[e^{2\beta\Delta}]/(n\,\mathbb E[e^{\beta\Delta}]^2)=\sigma^2/\mathrm{ESS}\), the variance of a weighted mean with effective sample size \(\mathrm{ESS}=(\sum_i w_i)^2/\sum_i w_i^2\). Estimating \(\beta\) adds the extra terms \[
\frac{1}{n\,a_{22}^2}\Bigl[\frac{a_{21}^2}{a_{11}^2}B_{11}-2\frac{a_{21}}{a_{11}}B_{12}\Bigr],
\] the correction attributable to fitting the balancing parameter.
When the correction vanishes. The correction is zero precisely when \(a_{21}=\mathbb E[e^{\beta\Delta}
\Delta(Y-\mu_A)]=0\). Taking the conditional expectation over \(Y\) given \(x\), \(a_{21}=\mathbb E[w(x)\Delta(x)
(\mu(x)-\mu_A)]\), the weighted covariance between the balancing covariate \(\Delta\) and the conditional outcome mean. It vanishes exactly when, within the weighting, the outcome is uncorrelated with the balancing covariate, that is when the covariate carries no prognostic information about the outcome under the weights. In that case the naive fixed-weight variance \(\sigma^2/\mathrm{ESS}\) equals the sandwich variance. Generically \(a_{21}\neq 0\), so the two differ; as the remark following Theorem 18.9 notes, the off-diagonal coupling that the naive analysis drops is usually positively correlated noise, so fixed-weight standard errors are typically anticonservative, though the sign is not universal, which is why the full sandwich is required. \(\square\)
Common mistake (naive versus sandwich MAIC variance). It is tempting to report the standard error of a MAIC estimate as if the matching weights were fixed constants, giving the tidy formula \(\sigma^2/\mathrm{ESS}\). That treats the estimated balancing parameter \(\beta\) as known, dropping the correction term derived above. Because that term is usually of the anticonservative sign, the fixed-weight standard error tends to be too small, understating the uncertainty of an indirect comparison. For a health technology assessment the safe default is the sandwich (robust) standard error, or a bootstrap that resamples and re-estimates the weights; reporting \(\sigma^2/\mathrm{ESS}\) alone can make a MAIC look more precise than it is.

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Selected Exercises
text:
F.19 Chapter 19: Simulated Treatment Comparison

F.19.1 Solution to Exercise 19.8: The log link makes the plug-in STC contrast collapsible
This Chapter 19 exercise shows that on the log link the marginal and conditional (plug-in) STC contrasts differ by a term that cancels when there is no effect modification, so the log-scale rate ratio is collapsible even though each arm separately carries a nonzero plug-in gap; the logit scale is different.
Uses. The Gaussian moment generating function (Chapter 4) and the logit non-collapsibility counterexample Theorem 19.4.
Work under Example 19.1: \(g=\log\), \(g^{-1}(\eta)=e^{\eta}\), with \(X\sim\mathcal N(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC},
\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC})\) in the comparator population, control-arm slope \(\boldsymbol\beta_1\) and active-arm slope \(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2\). The conditional plug-in STC effect is the link contrast at the mean, \(d^{\mathrm{cond}}=\eta_A(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})-\eta_C(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})\). The marginal effect is \(d^{\mathrm{marg}}=\log\mathbb E[e^{\eta_A(X)}]-\log\mathbb E[e^{\eta_C(X)}]\). By the Gaussian moment generating function (Chapter 4), \[
\mathbb E[e^{\eta_k(X)}]=\exp\!\Bigl(\eta_k(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})+\tfrac12\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}\Bigr),
\] with \(\boldsymbol\beta_{(C)}=\boldsymbol\beta_1\) and \(\boldsymbol\beta_{(A)}=\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2\). Hence \[
d^{\mathrm{marg}}-d^{\mathrm{cond}}
=\tfrac12\boldsymbol\beta_{(A)}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_{(A)}-\tfrac12\boldsymbol\beta_{(C)}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_{(C)} .
\] Expand the difference of quadratic forms with \(\boldsymbol\beta_{(A)}=\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2\) and \(\boldsymbol\beta_{(C)}=\boldsymbol\beta_1\), using the symmetry of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\) (so \(\boldsymbol\beta_1^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_2=\boldsymbol\beta_2^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_1\)): \[
(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2)^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2)-\boldsymbol\beta_1^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_1
=2\,\boldsymbol\beta_1^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_2+\boldsymbol\beta_2^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_2 .
\] Halving, \[
d^{\mathrm{marg}}-d^{\mathrm{cond}}
=\boldsymbol\beta_1^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_2+\tfrac12\boldsymbol\beta_2^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_2 .
\] Therefore the conditional plug-in is unbiased for the marginal effect (\(d^{\mathrm{cond}}=d^{\mathrm{marg}}\)) if and only if \[
\boldsymbol\beta_1^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_2+\tfrac12\boldsymbol\beta_2^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_2=0 .
\] In particular this holds whenever \(\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf 0\) (no effect modification): then the two arm slopes are equal, the two Gaussian variance corrections coincide, and they cancel in the contrast, so the log-link contrast is collapsible even though each arm separately suffers a nonzero plug-in gap. Contrast the logit link, where Theorem 19.4 shows the plug-in is biased for the marginal log odds ratio even with \(\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf 0\). The cancellation is therefore a property of the link: the log scale makes the rate ratio collapsible (as the risk ratio is in Chapter 11), while the logit scale makes the odds ratio non-collapsible. \(\square\)


F.19.2 Solution to Exercise 19.9: Delta-method variance of the marginal STC contrast
This Chapter 19 exercise derives the asymptotic variance of the marginal STC contrast by the delta method, connects it to the Bayesian g-computation posterior, and states what changes under model misspecification.
Uses. The STC functional Equation 19.19, the outcome-MLE limit law Theorem 19.1, the delta method Theorem 5.3, and the sandwich variance Definition 5.11.
Let \(\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi)\) be the STC functional Equation 19.19, \(\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi)=g(\int\mu_C(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)f_{BC})-g(\int\mu_A(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)f_{BC})\) with \(\mu_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)=g^{-1}(\eta_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi))\). By Theorem 19.1 the outcome MLE satisfies \(\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}-\boldsymbol\xi_0)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,
\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\xi_0)^{-1})\). Since \(\Psi\) is continuously differentiable in \(\boldsymbol\xi\), the delta method (Theorem 5.3) gives \[
\sqrt n\bigl(\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}-d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\bigr)
=\sqrt n\bigl(\Psi(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})-\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi_0)\bigr)
\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N\!\bigl(0,\ \nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi_0)^\top\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\xi_0)^{-1}\nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi_0)\bigr).
\]
The gradient. Writing \(\bar\mu_k=\int\mu_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi_0)f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,\mathrm d\mathbf x\) and differentiating under the integral, \[
\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial\xi_j}
=g'(\bar\mu_C)\!\int (g^{-1})'(\eta_C(\mathbf x))\frac{\partial\eta_C}{\partial\xi_j}(\mathbf x)\,f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,\mathrm d\mathbf x
-g'(\bar\mu_A)\!\int (g^{-1})'(\eta_A(\mathbf x))\frac{\partial\eta_A}{\partial\xi_j}(\mathbf x)\,f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,\mathrm d\mathbf x,
\] so each coordinate of \(\nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi_0)\) is an integral of \((g^{-1})'\), weighted by the corresponding linear-predictor derivative, against the comparator density \(f_{BC}\), scaled by the outer \(g'\) at the marginal mean.
Bayesian g-computation. By the Bernstein-von Mises theorem (part 2 of Theorem 19.5) the posterior of \(\boldsymbol\xi\) is asymptotically \(\mathcal N(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi},n^{-1}\mathcal I^{-1})\), and pushing it through the smooth map \(\Psi\) gives a posterior for the target effect asymptotically \(\mathcal N(\Psi(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}),n^{-1}\nabla\Psi^\top\mathcal I^{-1}\nabla\Psi)\), the same variance as the delta method. The Bayesian route avoids computing \(\nabla\Psi\) because it draws posterior samples \(\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)}\) and forms \(\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\) directly; the spread of the pushed-forward draws estimates the variance without any explicit derivative.
Under misspecification. If the outcome model is misspecified, \(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}\) converges to the pseudo-true value \(\boldsymbol\xi^\ast\) minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence, and the M-estimation limit law replaces \(\mathcal I^{-1}\) by the sandwich \(A^{-1}BA^{-\top}\) of Definition 5.11, so the asymptotic variance becomes \(\nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi^\ast)^\top A^{-1}BA^{-\top}\nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi^\ast)\). The point estimand is then \(\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi^\ast)\), the marginal STC contrast induced by the best-fitting (Kullback-Leibler-projected) parameter, which need not equal the true marginal effect when the working outcome surface is wrong. \(\square\)

text:
F.20 Chapter 20: Multilevel Network Meta-Regression I: The Aggregation Principle

F.20.1 Solution to Exercise 20.3: Aggregation bias of the logit contrast, computed by hand
This Chapter 20 exercise recomputes the integrated (ML-NMR) aggregate risks and the naive plug-in risks for a two-point covariate, and reads off the ecological (aggregation) bias arm by arm. Every number is shown so the aggregation identity can be checked with a calculator.
Uses. The no-closed-form logit aggregation theorem Theorem 20.5 and the ecological-bias definition Definition 16.2.
Repeat Example 20.1 with effect-modifier prevalence \(q=P(x=1)=0.3\), keeping \(\mu_j=-1\), \(\beta_1=0.5\), \(\beta_{2,B}=1.0\), \(\gamma_B=0.8\), so \(\eta_C(x)=-1+0.5x\), \(\eta_B(x)=-0.2+1.5x\). The conditional risks do not depend on \(q\): \(\operatorname{expit}(\eta_C(0))=0.26894\), \(\operatorname{expit}(\eta_C(1))=0.37754\), \(\operatorname{expit}(\eta_B(0))=0.45017\), \(\operatorname{expit}(\eta_B(1))=0.78583\).
(a) Integrated aggregate risks. With weights \((1-q,q)=(0.7,0.3)\), \[
\theta_{\bullet C}=0.7(0.26894)+0.3(0.37754)=0.30152,
\qquad
\theta_{\bullet B}=0.7(0.45017)+0.3(0.78583)=0.55087 .
\]
(b) Plug-in risks at \(\bar x_j=q=0.3\). Here \(\eta_C(0.3)=-0.85\), \(\eta_B(0.3)=0.25\), so \[
\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet C}=\operatorname{expit}(-0.85)=0.29943,
\qquad
\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet B}=\operatorname{expit}(0.25)=0.56218 .
\]
(c) Plug-in marginal log odds ratio. Because \(\operatorname{logit}\circ\operatorname{expit}\) is the identity, the plug-in contrast telescopes to the conditional contrast at the mean, \[
\operatorname{logit}\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet B}-\operatorname{logit}\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet C}
=\eta_B(0.3)-\eta_C(0.3)=0.25-(-0.85)=1.10,
\] which equals \(\gamma_B+\beta_{2,B}\bar x_j=0.8+1.0(0.3)=1.10\) exactly. The integrated (ML-NMR) marginal log odds ratio is \[
\operatorname{logit}(0.55087)-\operatorname{logit}(0.30152)=0.20420-(-0.84002)=1.04421,
\] so the ecological bias of the contrast is \(1.10-1.04421=+0.05579\).
(d) Effect of decreasing \(q\). Decreasing \(q\) from \(0.5\) to \(0.3\) shifts both arms’ mean linear predictors downward, since \(\eta_k\) increases in \(x\) and less weight falls on \(x=1\): the reference arm has \(m_C=\eta_C(0.3)=-0.85<0\) and the active arm \(m_B=\eta_B(0.3)=0.25>0\). By Theorem 20.5(c) the sign of each arm’s bias follows the curvature of \(\operatorname{expit}\) at its mean linear predictor: \(\operatorname{expit}\) is convex where the argument is negative, so the reference arm is underestimated (\(\mathrm{EB}_C=0.29943-0.30152=-0.00209<0\)), and concave where positive, so the active arm is overestimated (\(\mathrm{EB}_B=0.56218-0.55087=+0.01131>0\)). As \(q\) decreases further, \(m_B\) falls toward and through zero, at which point the active-arm bias would change sign; the biases do not cancel across arms but combine in the contrast. \(\square\)


F.20.2 Solution to Exercise 20.4: Exact aggregation characterizes the identity link
This Chapter 20 exercise proves that the plug-in-at-the-mean shortcut is exact for every covariate distribution if and only if the link is the identity (up to affine reparameterization); on any nonlinear scale, aggregation bias is unavoidable.
Uses. The identity-link exactness result Theorem 20.3 and the fact that a continuous midpoint-affine function is affine.
We show a twice-differentiable link \(g\) satisfies \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\) for every nondegenerate covariate distribution and every total slope \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}\) if and only if \(g^{-1}(z)=a+bz\) for constants \(a,b\) with \(b\neq 0\) (the identity link up to affine reparameterization).
Sufficiency. If \(g^{-1}(z)=a+bz\), then for the linear predictor \(\eta(\mathbf x)\), \[
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\int g^{-1}(\eta(\mathbf x))f_j(\mathbf x)\,\mathrm d\mathbf x
=a+b\,\mathbb E[\eta(X)]=a+b\,\eta(\bar{\mathbf x}_j)=g^{-1}(\eta(\bar{\mathbf x}_j))=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk},
\] using linearity of \(g^{-1}\) and of \(\eta\) together with linearity of expectation (this is Theorem 20.3).
Necessity. Suppose \(\theta_{\bullet jk}=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\) for every nondegenerate covariate law and every total slope. Fix any open interval \(I\subseteq\mathbb R\). Choosing a slope and a covariate law so that the linear predictor \(W=\eta(X)\) takes its values in \(I\), the equality reads \(g^{-1}(\mathbb E[W])=\mathbb E[g^{-1}(W)]\) for every distribution of \(W\) supported in \(I\). Apply it to the two-point law placing mass \(\tfrac12\) at each of \(w_1,w_2\in I\): with \(\psi=g^{-1}\), \[
\psi\!\Bigl(\frac{w_1+w_2}{2}\Bigr)=\tfrac12\psi(w_1)+\tfrac12\psi(w_2),
\] the midpoint-affine (Jensen) equation. A continuous function satisfying the midpoint-affine identity for every pair in an interval is affine on that interval; since \(g\) is twice differentiable, so is \(\psi\), and twice differentiating the midpoint identity (or invoking the classical result for measurable midpoint-affine functions) gives \(\psi''\equiv 0\) on \(I\), hence \(\psi(z)=a_I+b_I z\) on \(I\). Because \(I\) was an arbitrary open interval and the affine pieces must agree on overlaps, \(\psi=g^{-1}\) is globally affine, \(g^{-1}(z)=a+bz\). The slope \(b\neq 0\) because \(g^{-1}\) is a strictly monotone inverse link. Translating to \(g\), the relation \(\mu=a+b\,g(\mu)\) gives \(g(\mu)=(\mu-a)/b\), also affine: \(g\) is the identity link up to an affine reparameterization.
Conclusion. Exact aggregation for all covariate distributions characterizes the identity link. Equivalently, on any genuinely nonlinear scale, including the logit, log, probit, and complementary log-log, there exist covariate distributions for which \(\theta_{\bullet jk}\neq\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\), so aggregation bias is unavoidable. \(\square\)

text:
F.21 Chapter 21: Multilevel Network Meta-Regression II: Discrete Outcomes and Approximation

F.21.1 Solution to Exercise 21.6: Le Cam’s Poisson approximation by coupling
This Chapter 21 exercise proves Le Cam’s total-variation bound between a Poisson-binomial sum and a Poisson, using an explicit coupling of a Bernoulli with a Poisson, and recovers the classical Poisson limit theorem as a corollary.
Uses. The coupling inequality Equation 21.13 (\(\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le P(X\ne Z)\) for any coupling) and a union bound.
(a) Marginals and disagreement of the single pair. The coupling Equation 21.15 assigns \(P(B_i=0,P_i=0)=1-p\), \(P(B_i=1,P_i=1)=pe^{-p}\), \(P(B_i=1,P_i=0)=e^{-p}-(1-p)\), and \(P(B_i=1,P_i=k)=e^{-p}p^k/k!\) for \(k\ge 2\). The \(B_i\)-marginal is \(P(B_i=0)=1-p\) and \(P(B_i=1)=p\) (summing the row), so \(B_i\sim\mathrm{Ber}(p)\); the \(P_i\)-marginal at \(0\) is \((1-p)+(e^{-p}-(1-p))=e^{-p}\), at \(1\) is \(pe^{-p}\), and at \(k\ge 2\) is \(e^{-p}p^k/k!\), so \(P_i\sim\mathrm{Poi}(p)\). The pair agrees only on \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\), so \[
P(B_i\ne P_i)=1-(1-p)-pe^{-p}=p-pe^{-p}=p(1-e^{-p}).
\]
(b) Coupling inequality and the bound. For any coupling \((X,Z)\) of \(\mu,\nu\) and any event \(A\), \(\mu(A)-\nu(A)=P(X\in A,Z\notin A)-P(Z\in A,X\notin A)\le P(X\ne Z)\); by symmetry \(|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|\le P(X\ne Z)\), and taking the supremum over \(A\) gives the coupling inequality Equation 21.13, \(\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le P(X\ne Z)\). Now take the single-pair couplings independent across \(i=1,\dots,n\), set \(Y_\bullet=\sum_i B_i\sim\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf p)\) and \(Z=\sum_i P_i\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\) (a sum of independent Poissons, \(\lambda=\sum_i p_i\)). Then \(\{Y_\bullet\ne Z\}\subseteq\bigcup_i\{B_i\ne P_i\}\), so by the coupling inequality and a union bound, \[
\|\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf p)-\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le P(Y_\bullet\ne Z)
\le\sum_{i=1}^n P(B_i\ne P_i)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i(1-e^{-p_i})\le\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^2,
\] the last step by \(1-e^{-p}\le p\). This is Equation 21.14.
(c) Equal-risk case. With \(p_i\equiv p\) and \(n\) terms, \(\lambda=np\) and the bound is \(\sum_i p_i^2=np^2\), so \(\|\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)-\mathrm{Poi}(np)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le np^2\). Holding \(np=\lambda\) fixed and letting \(n\to\infty\), \(p=\lambda/n\) gives \(np^2=\lambda^2/n\to 0\), so \(\mathrm{Bin}(n,\lambda/n)\to\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\) in total variation, recovering the Poisson limit theorem Theorem 4.13.
(d) Sharpness to leading order. Expanding \(1-e^{-p}=p-\tfrac12p^2+O(p^3)\), the per-pair disagreement is \(p(1-e^{-p})=p^2-\tfrac12p^3+O(p^4)\). The bound replaces this by \(p^2\), an overstatement of order \(\tfrac12p^3\); relative to the leading \(p^2\) term the error is \(O(p)\), so for small risks \(\sum_i p_i(1-e^{-p_i})=\sum_i p_i^2-\tfrac12\sum_i p_i^3+O(\sum_i p_i^4)\) and the bound \(\sum_i p_i^2\) is tight to leading order. \(\square\)


F.21.2 Solution to Exercise 21.8: The adjusted binomial matches two moments but not three
This Chapter 21 exercise computes the third central moment of a Poisson-binomial sum and shows that the moment-matched adjusted binomial, fixed by the first two moments, generically misses the third, so it is a genuinely two-moment surrogate with no total-variation guarantee.
Uses. The Poisson-binomial generating function Equation 21.8 and the adjusted-binomial construction Theorem 21.4.
(a) The Poisson binomial third central moment. Write \(Y_\bullet=\sum_i B_i\) with independent \(B_i\sim\mathrm{Ber}(p_i)\). For a single Bernoulli, \(B_i-p_i\) takes value \(1-p_i\) with probability \(p_i\) and \(-p_i\) with probability \(1-p_i\), so \[
\mathbb E[(B_i-p_i)^3]=p_i(1-p_i)^3+(1-p_i)(-p_i)^3=p_i(1-p_i)\bigl[(1-p_i)^2-p_i^2\bigr]=p_i(1-p_i)(1-2p_i).
\] The third central moment is additive over independent summands (the third cumulant of a sum of independent variables is the sum of their third cumulants; equivalently, expanding \(\mathbb E[(\sum_i(B_i-p_i))^3]\) all cross terms vanish by independence and mean-zero centering), so \[
\mathbb E[(Y_\bullet-\lambda)^3]=\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)(1-2p_i),
\] as claimed, which also follows from the third derivative of the generating function Equation 21.8 at \(z=1\).
(b) The example. For \(\mathbf p=(0.1,0.3,0.4,0.5,0.7)\) of Example 21.5, \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)(1-2p_i)&=0.1(0.9)(0.8)+0.3(0.7)(0.4)+0.4(0.6)(0.2)+0.5(0.5)(0)+0.7(0.3)(-0.4)\\
&=0.072+0.084+0.048+0-0.084=0.120 .
\end{aligned}
\] The matched adjusted binomial is \(\mathrm{Bin}(N^\ast,\pi^\ast)=\mathrm{Bin}(4,0.5)\) (since \(\lambda=2\), \(\nu=\sum_i p_i^2=1\), so \(\pi^\ast=\nu/\lambda=0.5\) and \(N^\ast=\lambda^2/\nu=4\)). Its third central moment is \(N^\ast\pi^\ast(1-\pi^\ast)(1-2\pi^\ast)=4(0.5)(0.5)(0)=0\): the adjusted binomial is symmetric and misses the Poisson binomial’s right skew \(0.120>0\). Hence no binomial can match three moments of a generic Poisson binomial: once \((N,\pi)\) are fixed to match the mean and variance, the third moment is determined and generically differs (here it is forced to zero by \(\pi^\ast=\tfrac12\)). The adjusted binomial is genuinely a two-moment surrogate, consistent with the remark after Theorem 21.4 that it carries no total-variation guarantee. \(\square\)

text:
F.22 Chapter 22: Multilevel Network Meta-Regression III: Numerical Integration Theory

F.22.1 Solution to Exercise 22.7: The latent correlation is not the covariate correlation
This Chapter 22 exercise shows that the Gaussian-copula parameter \(\boldsymbol\Omega\) is the correlation of the latent normals, which equals the covariate Pearson correlation only when the margins are normal; a nonlinear margin shrinks the observed Pearson correlation while preserving the rank correlation.
Uses. The NORTA map \(X_j=F_j^{-1}(\Phi(Z_j))\) and the maximal-correlation property of the bivariate normal.
Standard-normal margins. With both margins standard normal and a Gaussian copula at latent correlation \(\rho\), the NORTA map \(X_j=\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(Z_j))=Z_j\) is the identity, so \((X_1,X_2)=(Z_1,Z_2)\sim\mathcal N_2\) with correlation \(\rho\). The covariate Pearson correlation therefore equals the latent correlation \(\rho\) exactly: for standard-normal margins the Gaussian-copula parameter and the covariate correlation coincide.
Exponential first margin. Now replace the first margin by an exponential, keeping the Gaussian copula at latent correlation \(\rho\), so \(X_1=F_1^{-1}(\Phi(Z_1))\) with \(F_1\) exponential and \(X_2=Z_2\). The covariate Pearson correlation is \(\operatorname{corr}(X_1,X_2)\). The transform \(u\mapsto F_1^{-1}(\Phi(u))\) is a nonlinear, strictly increasing reshaping of \(Z_1\); Pearson correlation is not invariant under nonlinear monotone transforms, and for a Gaussian vector a strictly increasing nonlinear transform of one coordinate strictly shrinks the magnitude of the Pearson correlation toward zero (this is the content of the maximal-correlation property of the bivariate normal, which is attained only by linear, that is affine, transforms). Hence \(|\operatorname{corr}(X_1,X_2)|<|\rho|\) for \(\rho\neq 0\). By contrast, the Spearman rank correlation depends only on the copula, and applying the strictly increasing map \(F_1^{-1}\circ\Phi\) to a coordinate leaves all ranks unchanged, so the Spearman correlation is exactly the same as in the standard-normal case.
This is precisely the remark in Section 22.9 that \(\boldsymbol\Omega\) is the correlation of the latent normals \(Z\), not of the covariates \(X\): only for normal margins do the two coincide; a nonlinear margin attenuates the covariate Pearson correlation while preserving the rank correlation. \(\square\)
Common mistake (latent versus observed correlation). When specifying the Gaussian copula for ML-NMR integration, it is tempting to plug the observed covariate correlation matrix directly in as \(\boldsymbol\Omega\). That is wrong whenever any margin is non-normal (a skewed biomarker, a binary indicator): the latent correlation that reproduces a target covariate correlation is generally larger in magnitude, because the nonlinear margin shrinks correlation on the way out. Feeding the observed correlation in as the latent one understates the dependence among the integrated covariates and biases the aggregate mean. The fix is to match on the rank (Spearman) correlation, which the copula preserves, or to invert the NORTA relationship numerically to recover the latent \(\boldsymbol\Omega\) that yields the desired covariate correlation.


F.22.2 Solution to Exercise 22.8: A four-point quasi-Monte Carlo aggregation, and its copula dependence
This Chapter 22 exercise traces four Sobol’ points through the full NORTA / Gaussian-copula pipeline to a quasi-Monte Carlo estimate of an aggregate logistic mean, and shows the estimate depends on the copula correlation through the variance of the linear predictor.
Uses. The QMC pipeline Equation 22.17, the Cholesky factor of the copula correlation, and the aggregation/ecological dependence on covariance Theorem 20.2.
Extend Example 22.3 to two standard-normal margins with Gaussian-copula correlation \(\rho=0.5\) and linear predictor \(\eta(\mathbf x)=0.5+x_1+0.5x_2\) on the logit scale. With standard-normal margins the pipeline Equation 22.17 reduces to \(\mathbf x=L\,\Phi^{-1}(\mathbf u)\), where \(L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0.5&0.8660\end{pmatrix}\) is the Cholesky factor of \(\boldsymbol\Omega=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.5\\0.5&1\end{pmatrix}\) (the two normal transforms \(\Phi\) and \(F^{-1}=\Phi^{-1}\) cancel). Using \(\Phi^{-1}(\tfrac12)=0\), \(\Phi^{-1}(\tfrac14)=-0.6745\), \(\Phi^{-1}(\tfrac34)=0.6745\), \(\Phi^{-1}(\tfrac18)=-1.1503\), \(\Phi^{-1}(\tfrac58)=0.3186\), the four Sobol’ points trace to
