The four-point QMC estimate at \(\rho=0.5\) is \[
\widehat\theta_{\bullet}=\tfrac14(0.62246+0.48724+0.74102+0.31005)=\tfrac14(2.16077)=0.54019 .
\] Setting \(\rho=0\) makes \(L=I\), so \(\mathbf x=\mathbf z\) and the same four points give \(\operatorname{expit}(\eta)\) equal to \(0.62246\), \(0.54060\), \(0.69788\), \(0.37966\), with estimate \[
\widehat\theta_{\bullet}=\tfrac14(0.62246+0.54060+0.69788+0.37966)=\tfrac14(2.24060)=0.56015 .
\] The estimate changes (\(0.540\) versus \(0.560\)) even though the margins are unchanged, because the aggregate mean \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{expit}(\eta(X))]\) of a nonlinear link depends on the joint distribution through the variance of the linear predictor. Using \(\operatorname{Var}(aX_1+bX_2)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X_1)
+b^2\operatorname{Var}(X_2)+2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)\) with \(a=1\), \(b=0.5\), standard-normal margins (\(\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=\operatorname{Var}(X_2)=1\)), and \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=\rho\), \[
\operatorname{Var}(\eta)=\operatorname{Var}(X_1+0.5X_2)=1+0.25+2(1)(0.5)\rho=1.25+\rho,
\] which is \(1.75\) at \(\rho=0.5\) and \(1.25\) at \(\rho=0\). The mean linear predictor is \(0.5>0\), where \(\operatorname{expit}\) is concave, so larger variance pulls the aggregate mean further below \(\operatorname{expit}(0.5)=0.622\); the higher-correlation case therefore has the smaller aggregate risk. This is the aggregation/ecological dependence on the covariate covariance of Theorem 20.2 and Definition 16.2: the correlation enters the integrated mean through the spread of \(\eta\), not through the margins. \(\square\)

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Selected Exercises
section: F.23 Chapter 23: Multilevel Network Meta-Regression IV: Estimands, Identifiability, and Reduction
text:
F.23 Chapter 23: Multilevel Network Meta-Regression IV: Estimands, Identifiability, and Reduction

F.23.1 Solution to Exercise 23.7: SEMA fixes the conditional contrast but not the marginal one
This Chapter 23 exercise writes the non-collapsibility gap between the conditional and marginal \(A\)-versus-\(B\) log odds ratios in closed form under the shared effect-modifier assumption (SEMA), identifies when it vanishes, and checks it numerically. The point is that SEMA pins the conditional contrast to a constant but cannot make the marginal contrast population-free.
Strategy. Compute each arm’s marginal risk as a two-point average, take the logit difference for the marginal contrast, and subtract from the SEMA conditional constant. The gap is “logit of an average minus an average of logits,” the Jensen discrepancy, so it vanishes exactly when there is nothing to average over.
Uses. The aggregation-bias theorem Theorem 20.2 and the two-point marginal-mean construction.
(a) Setup. Single binary effect modifier \(X\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\Pr(X=1)=q\), logit link, SEMA. The arm linear predictors in a population with reference baseline \(\mu_{*}\) are \(\eta_C(x)=\mu_{*}+\boldsymbol\beta_1 x\) and, for \(k\in\{A,B\}\), \(\eta_k(x)=\mu_{*}+(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2)x+\gamma_k\) (taking \(\gamma_C=0\)). The conditional \(A\)-versus-\(B\) contrast is the SEMA constant \(\gamma_A-\gamma_B\) (the interaction cancels). Evaluating each arm’s linear predictor at the two covariate values, \(\eta_k(0)=\mu_{*}+\gamma_k\) and \(\eta_k(1)=\mu_{*}+\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2+\gamma_k\).
(b) The closed-form gap. Rather than write one three-line formula, name the pieces. The marginal risk under each arm is the two-point average \[
\bar\theta_A=(1-q)\operatorname{expit}(\mu_{*}+\gamma_A)+q\operatorname{expit}(\mu_{*}+\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2+\gamma_A),
\] \[
\bar\theta_B=(1-q)\operatorname{expit}(\mu_{*}+\gamma_B)+q\operatorname{expit}(\mu_{*}+\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2+\gamma_B),
\] the marginal contrast is the logit difference \(\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})=\operatorname{logit}\bar\theta_A-\operatorname{logit}\bar\theta_B\), and the non-collapsibility gap is the conditional minus the marginal, \[
\text{gap}=(\gamma_A-\gamma_B)-\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})
=(\gamma_A-\gamma_B)-\bigl(\operatorname{logit}\bar\theta_A-\operatorname{logit}\bar\theta_B\bigr).
\] Substituting \(\bar\theta_A,\bar\theta_B\) gives the single closed-form expression, now assembled from four readable ingredients rather than presented as one wall of symbols.
(c) Degenerate cases. If \(q\in\{0,1\}\) the covariate is degenerate: at \(q=0\), \(\bar\theta_k=\operatorname{expit}(\mu_{*}+\gamma_k)\) and \(\operatorname{logit}\bar\theta_A-\operatorname{logit}\bar\theta_B=\gamma_A-\gamma_B\), so the gap is zero; the same holds at \(q=1\). If \(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2=0\), the active-arm linear predictors \(\eta_A,\eta_B\) are constant in \(x\) (no spread), so again \(\bar\theta_k=\operatorname{expit}(\mu_{*}+\gamma_k)\) and the gap is zero. Both vanishing conditions are exactly those of Theorem 20.2: a degenerate covariate or no spread in the active-arm linear predictors leaves nothing to average over.
(d) Numerical check. At the inputs of Example 23.3 (\(\mu_{*}=-0.5\), \(\boldsymbol\beta_1=0.4\), \(\boldsymbol\beta_2=0.5\), \(\gamma_A=0.8\), \(\gamma_B=0.3\), \(q=0.6\)), \(\bar\theta_A=0.4\operatorname{expit}(0.3)+0.6\operatorname{expit}(1.2)=0.690892\) and \(\bar\theta_B=0.4\operatorname{expit}(-0.2)+0.6\operatorname{expit}(0.7)=0.580979\), so \(\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})=\operatorname{logit}(0.690892)-\operatorname{logit}(0.580979)=0.804292-0.326794=0.477498\), and the gap is \((\gamma_A-\gamma_B)-0.477498=0.5-0.477498=0.022502\), matching the chapter. SEMA cannot eliminate the gap because it pins the conditional contrast to a constant but the marginal contrast involves logit-of-average minus average-of-logit, the non-collapsibility (Jensen) discrepancy, which persists whenever the covariate has spread and \(q\in(0,1)\). \(\square\)


F.23.2 Solution to Exercise 23.8: Marginal STC is a special case of ML-NMR
This Chapter 23 exercise shows that marginal STC is exactly ML-NMR restricted to fitting on the IPD alone and fixing the target to the comparator population; the extra aggregate-data information and the free choice of target population are what a full ML-NMR fit adds.
Uses. The ML-NMR aggregate arm mean Equation 23.2, the aggregation identity Theorem 20.1, and STC consistency Theorem 19.6.
Fix a logistic outcome family with linear predictor \(\eta_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)\) and inverse link \(g^{-1}=\operatorname{expit}\). Marginal STC (Chapter 19) for an IPD trial on \(\{A,C\}\) standardized to the comparator covariate distribution \(f_{BC}\) predicts the arm means \[
\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{STC}}=\int \operatorname{expit}\!\bigl(\eta_k(\mathbf x;\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})\bigr)\,f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,\mathrm d\mathbf x,\qquad k\in\{A,C\},
\] and reports \(g(\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{STC}})-g(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}})\). The ML-NMR aggregate arm mean Equation 23.2 over the same target \(f_{BC}\) using the same fitted linear predictor is \[
\bar\theta_{\bullet k}=\int \operatorname{expit}\!\bigl(\eta_k(\mathbf x;\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})\bigr)\,f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,\mathrm d\mathbf x .
\] These are the identical functional of \(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}\): both integrate \(\operatorname{expit}(\eta_k)\) against \(f_{BC}\) and contrast on the link scale. Hence marginal STC is ML-NMR restricted to (i) fitting the outcome surface on the IPD alone and (ii) fixing the target population to the comparator \(f_{BC}\).
Two things distinguish a full ML-NMR fit from this restriction. First, ML-NMR’s likelihood incorporates the aggregate-data outcomes through the aggregation identity Theorem 20.1: the AgD arm contributes its observed event summary to the likelihood, so the fitted \(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}\) uses information that STC (fitting on the IPD only) ignores. Second, ML-NMR’s estimand Theorem 23.1 admits any target population, not only \(f_{BC}\), so it can report the contrast standardized to a decision population different from the comparator trial.
Therefore STC is the special case of ML-NMR obtained by fitting on the IPD alone and fixing the target to \(f_{BC}\). The extra information ML-NMR uses changes the answer when the AgD outcomes are informative about shared parameters, for instance when the comparator arm’s observed event rate sharpens the prognostic or baseline parameters that also enter the IPD arms, shifting \(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}\) and hence the contrast. It does not change the answer when the IPD already identifies \(\boldsymbol\xi\) and the target is the comparator population with no extrapolation, the no-extrapolation regime of Chapter 18, in which STC is consistent (Theorem 19.6) and the AgD outcomes add precision but not a different limit. \(\square\)

text:
F.24 Chapter 24: Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics

F.24.1 Solution to Exercise 24.4: The algebraic floor of the potential scale reduction factor
This Chapter 24 exercise shows that the split-\(\widehat R\) convergence diagnostic has a hard lower bound \(\sqrt{(N-1)/N}\) set by the number of iterations, is centered at \(1\) at convergence, and is pushed above \(1\) by autocorrelation-inflated between-chain variance.
Uses. The between/within variance definitions Equation 24.6, Equation 24.7 and the expectation lemmas Lemma 24.4, Lemma 24.5.
The algebraic floor. From the definitions Equation 24.6 and Equation 24.7, \(\widehat V=(1-\tfrac1N)W+\tfrac1N B\), so dividing by \(W>0\), \[
\frac{\widehat V}{W}=\Bigl(1-\frac1N\Bigr)+\frac1N\frac{B}{W}=\frac{N-1}{N}+\frac{B}{NW}.
\] Since \(B\ge 0\), \(\widehat V/W\ge (N-1)/N\), hence \(\widehat R=\sqrt{\widehat V/W}\ge\sqrt{(N-1)/N}\) always. This floor is a striking practical fact for short chains: at \(N=4\) draws it is \(\sqrt{3/4}=0.866\), at \(N=100\) draws it is \(\sqrt{99/100}=0.995\), and it rises to \(1\) as \(N\to\infty\). So with only four iterations per chain the diagnostic can never read below \(0.866\) no matter how perfectly the chains agree; the floor reflects the estimator’s construction, not convergence. Moreover \(\widehat R\ge 1\) if and only if \(\widehat V/W\ge 1\), that is \((N-1)/N+B/(NW)\ge 1\), that is \(B/(NW)\ge 1/N\), that is \(B\ge W\).
Centering at convergence. In the iid-within-chain idealization a single chain mean of \(N\) independent draws has variance \(v_N=\sigma^2/N\). By Lemma 24.4, \(\mathbb E[W]=\tfrac{N}{N-1}(\sigma^2-v_N)=\tfrac{N}{N-1}\sigma^2\tfrac{N-1}{N}=\sigma^2\), and by Lemma 24.5, \(\mathbb E[B]=Nv_N=\sigma^2\). Thus \(\mathbb E[B]=\mathbb E[W]=\sigma^2\), so \(\widehat V/W\) is centered at \((N-1)/N+\sigma^2/(N\sigma^2)=(N-1)/N+1/N=1\) and \(\widehat R\) is centered at \(1\) at convergence.
What pushes \(\widehat R\) above \(1\). The term that lifts \(\widehat R\) above one is the between-chain term \(B\), through \(B/(NW)\). When the chains are positively autocorrelated but share a common stationary law, the variance of a chain mean is inflated by the integrated autocorrelation time \(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=1+2\sum_{k\ge 1}\rho_k>1\), namely \(v_N\approx(\sigma^2/N)\tau_{\mathrm{int}}\), so \(\mathbb E[B]=Nv_N\approx\sigma^2\tau_{\mathrm{int}}>\sigma^2\) while \(\mathbb E[W]\) stays near \(\sigma^2\). Then \(\widehat V/W\approx(N-1)/N+\tau_{\mathrm{int}}/N=1+(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}-1)/N\) and \(\widehat R\approx\sqrt{1+(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}-1)/N}>1\). The excess of the autocorrelation-inflated between-chain variance over the within-chain variance, captured by \(B/(NW)\), is what holds \(\widehat R\) above one until the chains mix. \(\square\)


F.24.2 Solution to Exercise 24.10: Generalized Pareto tail moments and the PSIS-LOO shape thresholds
This Chapter 24 exercise finds which moments of a generalized Pareto tail are finite as a function of its shape parameter \(k\), then reads those thresholds as the reliability tiers of the Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS) leave-one-out diagnostic.
Strategy. A power-law tail \(f(x)\sim Cx^{-1/k-1}\) has a finite \(m\)-th moment exactly when the integrand \(x^m f(x)\) decays fast enough to integrate at infinity; the threshold is a one-line exponent comparison.
Uses. The generalized Pareto moment lemma Lemma 24.7 and the PSIS reliability theorem Theorem 24.4. As a reminder of the vocabulary, PSIS-LOO is leave-one-out cross-validation carried out by importance sampling: each held-out point is scored by reweighting the full-data posterior draws with importance ratios \(r_i\) (the ratio of the leave-one-out to the full posterior density), and the predictive quantity is a self-normalized importance estimator (a weighted average with weights \(r_i\) divided by their sum). PSIS stabilizes the largest of these ratios by fitting a generalized Pareto distribution to their upper tail, whose estimated shape \(\widehat k\) is the diagnostic below.
Moments of the generalized Pareto tail. Let \(\bar F(x)=(1+kx/\sigma)^{-1/k}\) for \(x\ge 0\) with \(k>0\), density \(f(x)=\sigma^{-1}(1+kx/\sigma)^{-1/k-1}\). To read off the tail behavior, factor out the dominant power inside the bracket: \(1+kx/\sigma=(kx/\sigma)\bigl(1+\sigma/(kx)\bigr)\), so \[
f(x)=\sigma^{-1}\Bigl(\tfrac{kx}{\sigma}\Bigr)^{-1/k-1}\Bigl(1+\tfrac{\sigma}{kx}\Bigr)^{-1/k-1}
\xrightarrow[x\to\infty]{}\ \sigma^{-1}\Bigl(\tfrac{k}{\sigma}\Bigr)^{-1/k-1}x^{-1/k-1}=C\,x^{-1/k-1},
\] since \((1+\sigma/(kx))^{-1/k-1}\to 1\), with \(C=\sigma^{-1}(k/\sigma)^{-1/k-1}>0\). Hence \(x^m f(x)\sim C x^{m-1/k-1}\). The tail integral \(\int^{\infty}x^{m-1/k-1}\,\mathrm dx\) converges if and only if the exponent is below \(-1\), that is \(m-1/k-1<-1\), that is \(m<1/k\). Hence \(\mathbb E[X^m]<\infty\) if and only if \(m<1/k\) (Lemma 24.7). Setting \(m=1\) gives a finite mean iff \(k<1\); setting \(m=2\) gives a finite variance iff \(k<1/2\).
Relation to PSIS-LOO reliability. The importance ratios \(r_i\) in PSIS-LOO have a generalized Pareto upper tail with estimated shape \(\widehat k_i\). By the moment thresholds: if \(\widehat k_i<\tfrac12\) the ratios have finite variance, so the self-normalized importance estimator obeys a \(\sqrt S\) central limit theorem and the estimate is reliable; if \(\tfrac12\le\widehat k_i<1\) the mean is finite but the variance is infinite, so the law of large numbers still gives convergence to the right value but without a Gaussian error rate; if \(\widehat k_i\ge 1\) even the mean is infinite and the estimate does not converge, so the point must be evaluated by refitting. This is Theorem 24.4.
Why the alarm is at \(0.7\) rather than \(0.5\). The theoretical variance-finiteness threshold is \(k=\tfrac12\), but for \(\tfrac12\le k<1\) the estimator still converges to the correct value by the law of large numbers, and PSIS replaces the offending upper tail of the ratios by a smooth generalized Pareto fit, truncating and stabilizing the largest weights. Empirically this smoothing keeps the bias and variance small enough to be usable up to about \(\widehat k\approx 0.7\). The operational alarm is therefore set at the practical \(0.7\), where the smoothed estimate begins to degrade, rather than at the theoretical variance threshold \(0.5\), below which a central limit theorem holds but above which the estimate is often still acceptable. \(\square\)

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Selected Exercises
section: F.25 Chapter 25: General Likelihoods: Survival and Ordered Categorical Outcomes
text:
F.25 Chapter 25: General Likelihoods: Survival and Ordered Categorical Outcomes

F.25.1 Solution to Exercise 25.7: The marginal hazard ratio drifts away from the conditional one
This Chapter 25 exercise shows that under a mixed (frailty) population the marginal hazard ratio departs from the constant conditional hazard ratio \(\psi\) over time, because the two arms shed high-frailty individuals from their risk sets at different rates.
Strategy. The marginal hazard ratio is \(\psi\) times a ratio of survivor-weighted frailty means; the key identity is that the derivative of such a tilted mean is a negative variance, which makes the mean strictly decreasing and forces the ratio above one.
Uses. The time-varying marginal hazard ratio theorem Theorem 25.3 and the survivor-weighted mean Equation 25.9.
A word on the survival vocabulary first. Among individuals still alive (still at risk) at time \(s\), the frailty distribution is no longer the population one: high-frailty individuals die faster, so the survivors are enriched for low frailty. Because surviving to \(s\) under hazard \(\rho\) has probability \(e^{-\rho s}\), the risk-set or survivor-weighted mean of \(\rho\) at time \(s\) tilts the population law by the weight \(e^{-\rho s}\), giving \(\mathbb E[\rho\mid\text{alive at }s]=\mathbb E[\rho\,e^{-\rho s}]/\mathbb E[e^{-\rho s}]\). This tilted average is what the notation \(\mathbb E_{\tilde f_a(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho]\) denotes.
Binary frailty \(\rho(X)\in\{\rho_0,\rho_1\}\) with \(\rho_0<\rho_1\), \(P(X=1)=q\), constant baseline \(h_{a0}(s)=1\), constant conditional hazard ratio \(\psi\in(0,1)\). The control survival is \(S_a(s\mid x)=e^{-\rho(x)s}\) and the treated survival \(S_b(s\mid x)=e^{-\psi\rho(x)s}\). By Theorem 25.3, \(\mathrm{mHR}(s)=\psi\,R(s)\) with \(R(s)=\mathbb E_{\tilde f_b(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho]/\mathbb E_{\tilde f_a(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho]\), the ratio of survivor-weighted frailty means Equation 25.9.
Closed form. The risk-set (survivor-weighted) mean of \(\rho\) under arm \(a\) at time \(s\) is \(g(s):=\mathbb E_{\tilde f_a(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho]=\dfrac{(1-q)\rho_0 e^{-\rho_0 s}+q\rho_1 e^{-\rho_1 s}}{(1-q)e^{-\rho_0 s}+q e^{-\rho_1 s}}\), and under arm \(b\) the survival weights are \(e^{-\psi\rho(x)s}\), replacing \(s\) by \(\psi s\): \(\mathbb E_{\tilde f_b(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho]=g(\psi s)\). Hence \[
R(s)=\frac{g(\psi s)}{g(s)},\qquad
g(c)=\frac{(1-q)\rho_0 e^{-\rho_0 c}+q\rho_1 e^{-\rho_1 c}}{(1-q)e^{-\rho_0 c}+q e^{-\rho_1 c}},
\qquad \mathrm{mHR}(s)=\psi\,\frac{g(\psi s)}{g(s)}.
\]
Monotonicity of \(g\) and the bound \(R(s)\ge 1\). The map \(g(c)=\mathbb E[\rho\,e^{-\rho c}]/\mathbb E[e^{-\rho c}]\) is the mean of \(\rho\) under the tilt \(\propto e^{-\rho c}\). Its derivative is the key identity, so we derive it. Write \(N(c)=\mathbb E[\rho\,e^{-\rho c}]\) and \(D(c)=\mathbb E[e^{-\rho c}]\), so \(g=N/D\), and note \(N'(c)=-\mathbb E[\rho^2 e^{-\rho c}]\) and \(D'(c)=-\mathbb E[\rho\,e^{-\rho c}]=-N(c)\). By the quotient rule, \[
g'(c)=\frac{N'D-ND'}{D^2}=\frac{-\mathbb E[\rho^2 e^{-\rho c}]\,D+N^2}{D^2}
=-\frac{\mathbb E[\rho^2 e^{-\rho c}]}{D}+\Bigl(\frac{N}{D}\Bigr)^2
=-\bigl(\mathbb E_c[\rho^2]-\mathbb E_c[\rho]^2\bigr)=-\operatorname{Var}_c(\rho),
\] where \(\mathbb E_c[\cdot]\) is expectation under the tilt (so \(\mathbb E_c[\rho^2]=\mathbb E[\rho^2 e^{-\rho c}]/D\) and \(\mathbb E_c[\rho]=N/D\)). Thus \(g'(c)=-\operatorname{Var}_c(\rho)\le 0\), strictly negative for \(c\in(0,\infty)\) because \(\rho\) is non-degenerate (\(\rho_0\neq\rho_1\), \(q\in(0,1)\)). So \(g\) is strictly decreasing. Since \(\psi<1\), \(\psi s<s\), hence \(g(\psi s)\ge g(s)\) and \(R(s)\ge 1\), that is \(\mathrm{mHR}(s)\ge\psi\). At \(s=0\) both tilts equal the population law, \(g(0)=(1-q)\rho_0+q\rho_1\), so \(R(0)=1\); as \(s\to\infty\) the risk set in both arms is dominated by the low-frailty stratum, \(g(c)\to\rho_0\), so \(R(\infty)=\rho_0/\rho_0=1\). For every \(s\in(0,\infty)\) the strict monotonicity gives \(g(\psi s)>g(s)\), so \(R(s)>1\) and \(\mathrm{mHR}(s)>\psi\). Thus \(\mathrm{mHR}(s)>\psi\) on \((0,\infty)\) with \(\lim_{s\to 0^+}\mathrm{mHR}(s)=\lim_{s\to\infty}\mathrm{mHR}(s)=\psi\).
Time of maximal attenuation. Setting \(\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm ds}R(s)=0\) gives, since \(R=g(\psi s)/g(s)\), \[
\psi\,\frac{g'(\psi s)}{g(\psi s)}=\frac{g'(s)}{g(s)},
\] that is, the survivor-selection rate \(\mathrm d\log g/\mathrm dc=-\operatorname{Var}_c(\rho)/g(c)\), scaled by \(\psi\) in the treated arm, matches that of the control arm. At this \(s\) the differential rate at which the two arms shed high-frailty individuals from their risk sets is balanced; it is the moment of maximal survivor selection, where the frailty composition of the two risk sets differs most and the marginal hazard ratio departs furthest from the conditional \(\psi\). With \(\rho_0=1,\rho_1=3,q=\tfrac12,
\psi=\tfrac12\) this reproduces the table of Example 25.3, for instance \(\mathrm{mHR}(1)=\tfrac12\,g(0.5)/g(1)=\tfrac12(1.537883/1.238399)=0.62092\). \(\square\)


F.25.2 Solution to Exercise 25.8: RMST is collapsible but not transportable
This Chapter 25 exercise shows that the restricted mean survival time (RMST) contrast is collapsible within each population yet differs across populations with different covariate mixes, so collapsibility does not imply transportability.
Uses. The RMST collapsibility theorem Theorem 25.4 and the shared-hazard (SEMA) assumption.
Two populations \(\mathcal P,\mathcal P^{*}\) share the binary covariate \(X\) but have prevalences \(q\neq q^{*}\), with the exponential proportional-hazards model of Example 25.3: conditional control hazard \(\lambda_x\) and treated hazard \(\psi\lambda_x\), shared across populations (SEMA on the log-hazard scale). The conditional RMST at horizon \(\tau\) is \(\operatorname{RMST}_t(\tau\mid x)=(1-e^{-\lambda_x^{(t)}\tau})/\lambda_x^{(t)}\) with \(\lambda_x^{(C)}=\lambda_x\), \(\lambda_x^{(A)}=\psi\lambda_x\).
Collapsibility within a population. By Theorem 25.4 the marginal RMST contrast is the covariate average of the conditional contrasts, \(\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AC}(\tau\mid\mathcal P)=\mathbb E_{X\sim\mathcal P}[d(X)]\) with \(d(x)=\operatorname{RMST}_A(\tau\mid x)-\operatorname{RMST}_C(\tau\mid x)\). For binary \(X\) this is \((1-q)d(0)+q\,d(1)\) in \(\mathcal P\).
Difference between populations. Since the conditional contrasts \(d(0),d(1)\) are the same functions in both populations (shared hazards), \[
\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AC}(\tau\mid\mathcal P)-\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AC}(\tau\mid\mathcal P^{*})
=\bigl[(1-q)d(0)+q\,d(1)\bigr]-\bigl[(1-q^{*})d(0)+q^{*}d(1)\bigr]
=(q-q^{*})\bigl[d(1)-d(0)\bigr].
\] This is nonzero whenever \(d(1)\neq d(0)\), that is whenever the conditional RMST contrast is modified by \(X\). It is, because RMST is a nonlinear function of the hazard: with \(\lambda_0=1,\lambda_1=3,\psi=\tfrac12,\tau=2\), \[
d(0)=\operatorname{RMST}_A(2\mid 0)-\operatorname{RMST}_C(2\mid 0)=1.2642-0.8647=0.3995,
\qquad
d(1)=0.6335-0.3325=0.3010,
\] so \(d(1)-d(0)=-0.0985\) and the two populations’ RMST contrasts differ by \((q-q^{*})(-0.0985)\); for example \(q=\tfrac12,q^{*}=0.3\) gives a difference of \(0.2(-0.0985)=-0.0197\) years.
Conclusion. RMST is collapsible (the within-population marginal equals the average conditional) yet not transportable (the marginal differs across populations with different covariate mixes), because the shift in the covariate distribution acts on the effect-modified conditional RMST contrast. This is unlike the conditional log-hazard model, which is the single shared number \(\log\psi\) in both populations by assumption, hence trivially population-free. The distinction is the scale-misalignment remark following Theorem 25.4: collapsibility is a within-population identity and does not confer the cross-population identity of transportability, exactly the phenomenon carried into Chapter 26 (Theorem 26.4). \(\square\)
Common mistake (collapsibility versus transportability). These two properties are easy to conflate but are different guarantees. Collapsibility is a within-population statement: the marginal effect equals a straight average of the conditional effects, with no Jensen gap (risk difference and RMST are collapsible; the odds ratio and hazard ratio are not). Transportability is a between-population statement: the same effect number holds in a new population with a different covariate distribution. A measure can be collapsible yet not transportable, as RMST is here, because averaging an effect-modified conditional contrast over a different covariate mix changes the marginal value. Do not treat “collapsible” as a license to carry a marginal effect from a trial population to a decision population; only a conditional effect that is genuinely constant across the relevant covariates, or an explicit standardization to the target, transports.

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Selected Exercises
text:
F.26 Chapter 26: Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression

F.26.1 Solution to Exercise 26.5: Identifying the comparator intercept in unanchored ML-UMR
This Chapter 26 exercise solves the two-point aggregation equation for the comparator-arm intercept \(\alpha_B\) from an observed aggregate response, then computes the conditional and marginal log odds ratios, exhibiting the non-collapsibility gap.
Uses. The aggregation-equation monotonicity Lemma 23.2 and the shared prognostic-factor assumption (SPFA).
Logit link, SPFA prognostic slope \(\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}=0.8\), single binary covariate with comparator prevalence \(\bar x_B=P(X=1)=0.4\), observed comparator response proportion \(\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}=0.30\). The two-point aggregation equation Equation 26.9 is \[
\Theta_B(\alpha_B)=(1-0.4)\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B)+0.4\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B+0.8)=0.30 .
\]
Solving by bracketing. \(\Theta_B\) is strictly increasing in \(\alpha_B\) (Lemma 23.2), so the root is unique. Evaluating: \[
\Theta_B(-1.3)=0.6(0.21417)+0.4(0.37754)=0.27952,\qquad
\Theta_B(-1.2)=0.6(0.23148)+0.4(0.40131)=0.29941 .
\] Since \(\Theta_B(-1.3)<0.30<\Theta_B(-1.19)=0.30144\), linear interpolation between \(-1.20\) and \(-1.19\) places the root at \(\alpha_B\approx-1.20\) (to two decimals; more precisely \(\alpha_B\approx-1.197\)).
Comparator-population marginal response. By construction \(\Theta_B(\alpha_B)=0.30\), so the comparator-population marginal response under arm \(B\) is \(0.30\), as required.
Log odds ratios with the index fit \(\alpha_A=-0.2\). Under SPFA the conditional log odds ratio of \(A\) versus \(B\) is the covariate-free constant \[
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{AB}=\alpha_A-\alpha_B=-0.2-(-1.197)=0.997\approx 1.00 .
\] The comparator-population marginal response under arm \(A\) is \[
\Theta_A=(1-0.4)\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_A)+0.4\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_A+0.8)
=0.6\operatorname{expit}(-0.2)+0.4\operatorname{expit}(0.6)=0.6(0.45017)+0.4(0.64566)=0.52836,
\] so the comparator-population marginal log odds ratio is \[
\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg}}_{AB}=\operatorname{logit}(0.52836)-\operatorname{logit}(0.30)=0.11352-(-0.84730)=0.96082 .
\] The marginal log odds ratio \(0.96\) is smaller in magnitude than the conditional \(1.00\), a non-collapsibility gap of about \(0.04\): averaging the logistic model over the comparator covariate distribution attenuates the contrast toward the null, exactly as in the anchored ML-NMR computation. \(\square\)


F.26.2 Solution to Exercise 26.10: Population-specific RMST from an unanchored ML-UMR survival fit
This Chapter 26 exercise computes the RMST contrast at two target covariate distributions from an exponential proportional-hazards fit, again showing the RMST contrast is collapsible within a population but differs between populations, while the conditional log hazard ratio is a single population-free scalar.
Uses. The RMST collapsibility theorem Theorem 25.4 and the ML-UMR time-to-event result Theorem 26.4.
For the exponential proportional-hazards survival coda, \(h_k(t\mid x)=\lambda_k e^{\beta x}\) with \(\beta=\log 2\), \(\lambda_A=0.10\), \(\lambda_B=0.15\), so \[
\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid x)=\frac{1-\exp(-\lambda_k e^{\beta x}\tau)}{\lambda_k e^{\beta x}}.
\] The population RMST contrast at \(P(X=1)=\pi^{*}\) is, by collapsibility (Theorem 25.4), the two-point average \[
\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AB}(\tau\mid\mathcal P^{*})=(1-\pi^{*})\,d(0)+\pi^{*}d(1),
\qquad d(x)=\operatorname{RMST}_A(\tau\mid x)-\operatorname{RMST}_B(\tau\mid x).
\]
Conditional contrasts at \(\tau=10\). With \(e^{\beta\cdot 0}=1\), \(e^{\beta\cdot 1}=2\), \[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{RMST}_A(10\mid 0)&=\tfrac{1-e^{-1}}{0.10}=6.32121, & \operatorname{RMST}_A(10\mid 1)&=\tfrac{1-e^{-2}}{0.20}=4.32332,\\
\operatorname{RMST}_B(10\mid 0)&=\tfrac{1-e^{-1.5}}{0.15}=5.17913, & \operatorname{RMST}_B(10\mid 1)&=\tfrac{1-e^{-3}}{0.30}=3.16738,
\end{aligned}
\] so \(d(0)=6.32121-5.17913=1.14208\) and \(d(1)=4.32332-3.16738=1.15594\), with \(d(1)-d(0)=0.01387\).
Collapsible but not transportable. Within each population the marginal contrast is the average of these conditional contrasts (collapsibility). Across populations, \[
\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AB}(10\mid \pi^{*}=0.5)=0.5(1.14208)+0.5(1.15594)=1.14901,
\qquad
\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AB}(10\mid \pi^{*}=0.3)=0.7(1.14208)+0.3(1.15594)=1.14624,
\] which differ by \((0.5-0.3)(d(1)-d(0))=0.2(0.01387)=0.00277\) years. So the RMST contrast is collapsible within each population yet differs between the two populations: collapsibility does not imply transportability. By contrast the conditional log hazard ratio of \(A\) versus \(B\) is the single number \(\log(\lambda_B/\lambda_A)=\log(0.15/0.10)=\log 1.5\) in every population, covariate-free and time-invariant. This is Theorem 26.4(e): an unanchored ML-UMR analysis can report the population-specific RMST contrast at any target \(\pi^{*}\), but only the conditional log hazard ratio is a single population-free scalar. \(\square\)

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Selected Exercises
text:
F.27 Chapter 27: Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching

F.27.1 Solution to Exercise 27.6: Mahalanobis distance is affine-invariant, Euclidean is not
This Chapter 27 exercise proves the Mahalanobis distance between covariate means is unchanged by any invertible affine reparameterization of the covariates, whereas the standardized Euclidean distance can even reverse rankings, because it discards the off-diagonal covariance.
Uses. The Mahalanobis distance definition Definition 27.3 and the whitening interpretation (Mahalanobis is Euclidean distance after standardizing by the covariance).
Let the covariates be reparameterized by an invertible affine map \(\mathbf x\mapsto A\mathbf x+\mathbf c\), with the covariance transformed accordingly to \(A\boldsymbol\Sigma A^\top\). A gap between two means \(\boldsymbol\delta=\bar{\mathbf x}_0-\bar{\mathbf x}_j\) transforms to \(A\boldsymbol\delta\) (the constant \(\mathbf c\) cancels in the difference). The Mahalanobis distance (Definition 27.3) becomes \[
d_M^2=(A\boldsymbol\delta)^\top(A\boldsymbol\Sigma A^\top)^{-1}(A\boldsymbol\delta)
=\boldsymbol\delta^\top A^\top A^{-\top}\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}A^{-1}A\boldsymbol\delta
=\boldsymbol\delta^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol\delta,
\] using \((A\boldsymbol\Sigma A^\top)^{-1}=A^{-\top}\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}A^{-1}\) and \(A^\top A^{-\top}=I\), \(A^{-1}A=I\). So the Mahalanobis distance is unchanged under every invertible affine reparameterization. The standardized Euclidean distance uses only the diagonal of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) as scales; under \(\mathbf x\mapsto A\mathbf x+\mathbf c\) the scales become the diagonal of \(A\boldsymbol\Sigma A^\top\), which for a nondiagonal \(A\) mixes the coordinates and is not the coordinatewise rescaling of the original scales. For diagonal \(A=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_p)\) each coordinate is scaled by \(a_\ell\) and its standard deviation by \(|a_\ell|\), so the ratio \(\delta_\ell/s_\ell\) is unchanged in magnitude and the standardized Euclidean distance is invariant; for nondiagonal \(A\) it generally is not.
A reversing example. Work in \(\mathbb R^2\) with original covariance \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=I\), so initially Mahalanobis and standardized Euclidean both equal ordinary Euclidean distance. Take the two candidate gaps \(\boldsymbol\delta_a=(1.4,0)\) and \(\boldsymbol\delta_b=(0,1)\), so Mahalanobis ranks \(a\) as the more distant (\(1.4>1\)). Apply the nondiagonal shear \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), giving \(\boldsymbol\delta_a'=A\boldsymbol\delta_a=(1.4,0)\), \(\boldsymbol\delta_b'=A\boldsymbol\delta_b=(1,1)\), and covariance \(\boldsymbol\Sigma'=AA^\top=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) with \((\boldsymbol\Sigma')^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\). The Mahalanobis distances are preserved, \(d_M(\boldsymbol\delta_a')^2=(1.4,0)(\boldsymbol\Sigma')^{-1}(1.4,0)^\top=1.96\) and \(d_M(\boldsymbol\delta_b')^2=(1,1)(\boldsymbol\Sigma')^{-1}(1,1)^\top=1\), so \(a\) remains more distant (\(1.4>1\)). But the standardized Euclidean distance now uses the new scales \(\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\Sigma')=(2,1)\): \[
d_{SE}(\boldsymbol\delta_a')^2=\frac{1.4^2}{2}+\frac{0^2}{1}=0.98,
\qquad
d_{SE}(\boldsymbol\delta_b')^2=\frac{1^2}{2}+\frac{1^2}{1}=1.5,
\] so the standardized Euclidean ranking is reversed: it now calls \(b\) the more distant candidate (\(\sqrt{1.5}>\sqrt{0.98}\)), whereas before the reparameterization it agreed with Mahalanobis that \(a\) was farther. The Mahalanobis ranking is preserved throughout. This is the precise sense in which Mahalanobis distance is the coordinate-free member of the family: it depends only on the geometry of the covariate cloud (it is the Euclidean distance after whitening), so any invertible affine relabeling leaves it and its rankings intact, while standardized Euclidean distance, which discards the off-diagonal covariance, is tied to the chosen coordinates. \(\square\)


F.27.2 Solution to Exercise 27.7: A small moment distance does not certify an unbiased comparison
This Chapter 27 exercise builds two covariate distributions with identical first and second moments but different target effects under a nonlinear (quartic) contrast, showing that matching a finite set of moments leaves a residual bias for contrasts whose curvature reaches beyond those moments.
Uses. The diagnostic-not-validity proposition Proposition 27.4 and the second-moment MAIC balancing of Chapter 18.
Construct two scalar covariate distributions with identical first and second moments but different target effects under a nonlinear contrast, strengthening Proposition 27.4. Let \(\mathcal P_0\) put mass \(\tfrac12\) at each of \(\pm 1\), and \(\mathcal P_1\) put mass \(\tfrac34\) at \(0\) and mass \(\tfrac18\) at each of \(\pm 2\).
Equal first two moments. Both are symmetric about \(0\), so each has mean \(0\). Their variances are \[
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal P_0}=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(1)=1,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal P_1}=\tfrac34(0)+\tfrac18(4)+\tfrac18(4)=1 .
\] So any diagnostic built from the first two moments (mean and variance, hence standardized Euclidean or Mahalanobis distance between the two distributions’ moment summaries) reports zero distance.
Different target effect under a quartic contrast. Take \(\tau(x)=x^4\). The target effects are \[
\mathbb E_{\mathcal P_0}[\tau(X)]=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(1)=1,
\qquad
\mathbb E_{\mathcal P_1}[\tau(X)]=\tfrac34(0)+\tfrac18(16)+\tfrac18(16)=4 .
\] The two target effects are \(1\) and \(4\), so the bias from treating the two populations as exchangeable under this contrast is \(4-1=3\), despite zero distance under any first-two-moment diagnostic.
Implication for MAIC second-moment balancing. Matching through any fixed finite set of moments controls only the corresponding low-order features of the covariate distribution. A sufficiently nonlinear contrast (here a quartic, sensitive to the fourth moment) responds to features the matched moments do not constrain, leaving a residual bias. Balancing means and variances is therefore not enough in general: MAIC weights that equate the first two moments still leave a target-effect discrepancy for contrasts whose curvature reaches beyond those moments, which is why a small moment distance is a diagnostic of similarity, not a certificate of validity. Concretely, a regulator reviewing a submitted MAIC should not accept a small Mahalanobis distance, or a report that “all covariate means and variances are balanced,” as evidence that the indirect comparison is unbiased. The example above has zero first-two-moment distance yet a target-effect bias of \(3\); the missing ingredient is the shape of the outcome-covariate relationship, which no fixed number of matched moments can guarantee. The right posture is to treat moment balance as necessary housekeeping and to argue separately, from subject-matter knowledge, that the outcome model is not so nonlinear in the unbalanced higher moments that a residual bias survives. \(\square\)

F.28 Chapter 28: Quantitative Bias Analysis for Indirect Comparisons

F.28.1 Solution to Exercise 28.6: The E-value for an indirect comparison, and when it is infinite
This Chapter 28 exercise recomputes the sensitivity curve and E-value for an indirect comparison under a stronger unreported covariate, and shows the E-value can be infinite, a certificate that no single-covariate imbalance can explain away the observed effect.
Strategy. The adjusted effect is linear in the unreported covariate’s mean, \(\Delta(m)=K+\beta_U m\); the whole analysis rests on the constant \(K\), which is a Gaussian-MGF integral of the log-linear model. Derive \(K\) once, then read the bias factor and E-value off the standard formulas.
Uses. The indirect-comparison E-value proposition Proposition 28.1 and the lognormal (Gaussian moment-generating-function) mean of a log-linear model.
(a) Recomputed constants. First, where \(K\) comes from. The worked-example model is log-linear, \(\log\mu(R,U)=\beta_0+\beta_R R+\beta_U U\), with independent Gaussian covariates \(R\sim\mathcal N(m_R,\sigma_R^2)\) and \(U\sim\mathcal N(m,\sigma_U^2)\). Taking the marginal mean by the Gaussian moment generating function (\(\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]=e^{tm_Z+t^2\sigma_Z^2/2}\) for \(Z\sim\mathcal N(m_Z,\sigma_Z^2)\)), \[
\log\mathbb E[Y]=\beta_0+\beta_R m_R+\tfrac12\beta_R^2\sigma_R^2+\beta_U m+\tfrac12\beta_U^2\sigma_U^2 .
\] The adjusted effect \(\Delta(m)\) is this marginal log-mean minus the observed baseline \(\log\mu_0\), so grouping every term that does not involve \(m\) into a single constant, \[
\Delta(m)=\underbrace{\bigl(\beta_0+\beta_R m_R+\tfrac12\beta_R^2\sigma_R^2+\tfrac12\beta_U^2\sigma_U^2-\log\mu_0\bigr)}_{K}+\beta_U m,
\] which is the sensitivity curve and defines \(K\). Now use \(\beta_0=-1.0\), \(\beta_R=0.4\), \(m_R=1.0\), \(\sigma_R=0.5\), \(\sigma_U=1.0\), \(\mu_0=0.47\), \(\bar x_U=2.0\), but now a stronger unreported covariate \(\beta_U=-0.8\): \[
K=\beta_0+\beta_R m_R+\tfrac12\beta_R^2\sigma_R^2+\tfrac12\beta_U^2\sigma_U^2-\log\mu_0
=-1.0+0.4+\tfrac12(0.16)(0.25)+\tfrac12(0.64)(1)-\log(0.47),
\] that is \(K=-1.0+0.4+0.02+0.32+0.75502=0.49502\). The sensitivity curve is \(\Delta(m)=K+\beta_U m=0.49502-0.8m\), so the adjusted effect at the IPD value is \(\Delta(2.0)=0.49502-1.6=-1.10498\). The observed bias factor is \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\exp(|\Delta(2.0)|)=\exp(1.10498)=3.0192\), and the outcome association is \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=\exp(|\beta_U|)=\exp(0.8)=2.2255\).
(b) The E-value. By Proposition 28.1 the indirect-comparison E-value is finite only when \(1<\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}<\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\). Here \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=2.2255<3.0192=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\), so \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\le\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=+\infty\): no across-arm imbalance of the single covariate, however extreme, can manufacture a bias factor as large as the observed one, given that the outcome association is pinned at \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=2.2255\). This is a robustness certificate. As a check of the finite formula on the artificial pair \(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=1.5\), \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=2.5\) (where \(1<1.5<2.5\)), \[
E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=\frac{\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)}{\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}}
=\frac{1.5(2.5-1)}{2.5-1.5}=\frac{2.25}{1}=2.25 .
\]
(c) The certificate. For fixed \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=y>1\), the bias factor \(\mathrm{BF}_U(x,y)=\dfrac{xy}{x+y-1}=\dfrac{y}{1+(y-1)/x}\) as a function of \(x=\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\) has derivative \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{xy}{x+y-1}=\frac{y(x+y-1)-xy}{(x+y-1)^2}=\frac{y(y-1)}{(x+y-1)^2}>0,
\] so it is strictly increasing in \(x\). Moreover \(1+(y-1)/x>1\) for all finite \(x>0\), so \(\mathrm{BF}_U(x,y)<y=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\), and as \(x\to\infty\), \((y-1)/x\to 0\) and \(\mathrm{BF}_U(x,y)\uparrow y\). Hence the bias factor is strictly increasing in \(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\) and bounded above by \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\), the bound approached but never attained. Consequently, when \(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\le\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\), the target is unreachable for every finite imbalance and the result cannot be explained away by imbalance of this one covariate, which is the meaning of \(E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=+\infty\). \(\square\)


F.28.2 Solution to Exercise 28.8: NORTA marginal recovery, copula non-uniqueness, and Pearson drift
This Chapter 28 exercise checks three facts about the NORTA (normal-to-anything) construction: (a) it recovers a discrete Bernoulli margin exactly, (b) for discrete margins the copula is not uniquely determined by the joint law (Sklar non-uniqueness), and (c) for continuous margins the covariate Pearson correlation need not equal the latent normal correlation.
Strategy. Separate the two questions the exercise mixes together: marginal recovery uses only that \(\Phi(Z)\) is uniform, while the dependence questions are about the copula. Keep the identification of the Gaussian parameter distinct from the Sklar non-uniqueness of the copula function.
Uses. The NORTA/Gaussian-copula theorem Theorem 28.2 and the Gaussian moment generating function.
Some copula vocabulary, since the exercise leans on it. The Frechet (Frechet-Hoeffding) bounds say every joint distribution with given margins lies between two extremes: the countermonotone coupling (perfect negative dependence, each variable a decreasing function of the other) below and the comonotone coupling (perfect positive dependence) above. Sklar’s theorem guarantees a copula \(C\) with \(F(x_1,x_2)=C(F_1(x_1),F_2(x_2))\); this \(C\) is unique on the set \(\operatorname{Range}(F_1)\times\operatorname{Range}(F_2)\), which is all of \([0,1]^2\) for continuous margins (so \(C\) is unique) but only a coarse grid for discrete margins (so \(C\) is free between grid points). That grid-only determination is the Sklar non-uniqueness of part (b).
Let \(F\) be the \(\mathrm{Ber}(\pi)\) distribution function and \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\).
(a) Discrete margin recovery. The generalized inverse of the Bernoulli distribution function is \[
F^{-1}(u)=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge u\}=\begin{cases}0,& 0<u\le 1-\pi,\\ 1,& 1-\pi<u\le 1.\end{cases}
\] Since \(\Phi(Z)\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)\) (the probability integral transform), \(X=F^{-1}(\Phi(Z))\) equals \(1\) exactly when \(\Phi(Z)>1-\pi\), an event of probability \(1-(1-\pi)=\pi\), and equals \(0\) otherwise. Hence \(X\sim\mathrm{Ber}(\pi)\), confirming Theorem 28.2(1) for a discrete margin, with no continuity needed.
(b) Non-uniqueness of the copula for discrete margins. It is important to separate two claims that are easy to run together. Take two such Bernoulli variables \(X_1=F^{-1}(\Phi(Z_1))\), \(X_2=F^{-1}(\Phi(Z_2))\) with \((Z_1,Z_2)\) bivariate normal of correlation \(\rho^N\). The joint law of \((X_1,X_2)\) is determined by the single cell probability \[
P(X_1=1,X_2=1)=P\bigl(\Phi(Z_1)>1-\pi,\ \Phi(Z_2)>1-\pi\bigr)=P(Z_1>z_\pi,Z_2>z_\pi),\qquad z_\pi=\Phi^{-1}(1-\pi),
\] which is a continuous, strictly increasing function of \(\rho^N\) on \([-1,1]\) for fixed \(\pi\in(0,1)\).
First claim (the Gaussian parameter is identified). Because this cell probability is strictly increasing in \(\rho^N\), it is injective: distinct latent correlations \(\rho^N\) give distinct cell probabilities and hence distinct bivariate Bernoulli laws. So within the Gaussian (NORTA) family the parameter \(\rho^N\) is recovered from the joint law; there is no ambiguity of the Gaussian parameter in the nondegenerate case.
Second claim (the copula function is not unique). The non-uniqueness the exercise is after is a different, Sklar-level statement, and it is not about \(\rho^N\) at all. Sklar’s theorem determines the copula only on \(\operatorname{Range}(F_1)\times\operatorname{Range}(F_2)\); for a Bernoulli margin that range is the finite set \(\{0,\,1-\pi,\,1\}\), so the copula \(C\) is pinned only at those grid points and is free to be interpolated in infinitely many ways between them. Many distinct copula functions, most of them not Gaussian at all, reproduce the same bivariate Bernoulli law, because a discrete margin can only “see” the copula on its coarse grid. That is the sense in which the copula is non-unique for discrete margins: not that two Gaussian parameters collide, but that the copula function is underdetermined once the margins are discrete. The range of attainable cell probabilities is itself limited by the Frechet bounds, with the comonotone and countermonotone couplings as the extremes; a target joint law outside that attainable interval has no Gaussian \(\rho^N\) realizing it. Marginal recovery in (a), by contrast, holds for every \(\rho^N\), because it used only that \(\Phi(Z_j)\) is uniform, irrespective of the dependence.
(c) Pearson correlation need not equal \(\rho^N\) for continuous margins. Take \(F_1=F_2\) a lognormal margin, \(X_j=\exp(\sigma Z_j)\) with \((Z_1,Z_2)\) standard bivariate normal of correlation \(\rho^N\). The degenerate value \(\rho^N=1\) is not informative here: then \(Z_1=Z_2\), so \(X_1=X_2\) and trivially \(\operatorname{corr}(X_1,X_2)=1=\rho^N\), which cannot exhibit strict inequality. So take a genuinely dependent case, \(\rho^N\in(-1,1)\), and compute the covariate Pearson correlation in closed form from the Gaussian moment generating function. With \(\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]=e^{t^2/2}\) for a standard normal and \(Z_1+Z_2\sim\mathcal N(0,\,2+2\rho^N)\), \[
\mathbb E[X_j]=e^{\sigma^2/2},\qquad \mathbb E[X_j^2]=e^{2\sigma^2},\qquad
\mathbb E[X_1X_2]=\mathbb E\bigl[e^{\sigma(Z_1+Z_2)}\bigr]=e^{\sigma^2(1+\rho^N)} .
\] Hence \(\operatorname{Var}(X_j)=e^{2\sigma^2}-e^{\sigma^2}=e^{\sigma^2}(e^{\sigma^2}-1)\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=e^{\sigma^2(1+\rho^N)}-e^{\sigma^2}=e^{\sigma^2}(e^{\sigma^2\rho^N}-1)\), so the \(e^{\sigma^2}\) factors cancel and \[
\operatorname{corr}(X_1,X_2)=\frac{e^{\sigma^2\rho^N}-1}{e^{\sigma^2}-1} .
\] For \(\sigma=1\) and \(\rho^N=0.5\) this is \((e^{0.5}-1)/(e-1)=0.64872/1.71828=0.37752\neq 0.5\). The Pearson correlation of the lognormal covariates (\(0.3775\)) differs from the latent normal correlation (\(0.5\)), because the nonlinear exponential margin reshapes the dependence; only the rank correlation is preserved. This is exactly why \(\boldsymbol\Omega\) in the NORTA and Gaussian-copula construction is the correlation of the latent normals, not of the covariates. \(\square\)

F.29 Chapter 29: Simulation Study Theory

F.29.1 Solution to Exercise 29.7: Sample size, power, and the test-interval duality
This Chapter 29 exercise computes the standardized signal and the sample size for a target power, checks that the wrong-side rejection term is negligible, and shows the power calculation and the confidence-interval-width calculation are two readings of the same inequality.
Uses. The simulation power formula Theorem 29.3 and its exact two-term version Equation 29.17.
A study targets a true contrast \(\theta=0.4\) against \(\theta_0=0\) at level \(\alpha=0.05\), with standard error \(\sigma_n=c/\sqrt n\), \(c=2.0\).
(a) Standardized signal. By Theorem 29.3 the standardized signal is \[
\Delta_n=\frac{\theta-\theta_0}{\sigma_n}=\frac{0.4}{2.0/\sqrt n}=\frac{0.4}{2.0}\sqrt n=0.2\sqrt n .
\]
(b) Sample size for power \(0.80\). Using the one-sided approximation \(\mathrm{Power}\approx\Phi(\Delta_n-z_{\alpha/2})\) with \(z_{\alpha/2}=z_{0.025}=1.95996\) and \(\Phi^{-1}(0.80)=0.84162\), set \(\Delta_n-1.95996=0.84162\), so \(\Delta_n=2.80158\). Then \(0.2\sqrt n=2.80158\), \(\sqrt n=14.0079\), and \(n=196.2\), rounded up to \(n=197\).
(c) The dropped term is negligible. The exact two-term power Equation 29.17 is \(\Phi(\Delta_n-z_{\alpha/2})+\Phi(-\Delta_n-z_{\alpha/2})\). At \(\Delta_n=2.80158\) the dropped term is \[
\Phi(-\Delta_n-z_{\alpha/2})=\Phi(-2.80158-1.95996)=\Phi(-4.7615)\approx 9.6\times 10^{-7},
\] below one part in a million, so the one-term and two-term power formulas agree to far more than the precision of any simulation; the second term is the probability of rejecting on the wrong side and is negligible for a signal this large.
(d) Test-interval duality. The Wald test rejects \(\theta_0\) exactly when \(\theta_0\) lies outside the interval \(\hat\theta_n\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sigma_n\). Power \(0.80\) to reject \(\theta_0=0\) when the truth is \(\theta=0.4\) is therefore the probability \(0.80\) that the \(95\%\) confidence interval of half-width \(z_{\alpha/2}\sigma_n\) excludes \(0\), which holds when \(|\theta-\theta_0|\ge(z_{\alpha/2}+z_{0.20})\sigma_n\), the same standardized-signal condition \(\Delta_n\ge z_{\alpha/2}+\Phi^{-1}(0.80)\) and hence the same \(n\). The power calculation and the confidence-interval-width calculation are two readings of one inequality. \(\square\)


F.29.2 Solution to Exercise 29.8: When balancing fewer covariates lowers mean squared error
This Chapter 29 exercise sets up the bias-variance trade-off of covariate balancing: dropping a covariate saves effective sample size (variance) at the cost of some bias, and balancing the smaller set wins on mean squared error exactly when that bias is below a variance-set threshold.
Uses. The bias-variance (mean-squared-error) decomposition Theorem 29.1 and the MAIC effective sample-size bound Theorem 18.6.
In the geometry of Example 29.1, compare two adjusted estimators: balancing only the effect modifier \(x_1\) leaves a small omitted-covariate bias \(\beta\) on a non-collapsible scale but retains effective sample size \(\mathrm{ESS}_1\), with variance \(\sigma^2 n/\mathrm{ESS}_1\); balancing both \(x_1\) and the prognostic \(x_2\) removes the bias but lowers the effective sample size to \(\mathrm{ESS}_2<\mathrm{ESS}_1\), with variance \(\sigma^2 n/\mathrm{ESS}_2\).
(a) Mean squared errors. By the bias-variance decomposition Theorem 29.1, \(\mathrm{MSE}=\mathrm{bias}^2+\mathrm{variance}\): \[
\mathrm{MSE}_1=\beta^2+\frac{\sigma^2 n}{\mathrm{ESS}_1},
\qquad
\mathrm{MSE}_2=0+\frac{\sigma^2 n}{\mathrm{ESS}_2}.
\]
(b) When balancing only \(x_1\) wins. \(\mathrm{MSE}_1<\mathrm{MSE}_2\) if and only if \[
\beta^2+\frac{\sigma^2 n}{\mathrm{ESS}_1}<\frac{\sigma^2 n}{\mathrm{ESS}_2},
\qquad\text{that is}\qquad
\beta^2<\sigma^2 n\Bigl(\frac{1}{\mathrm{ESS}_2}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{ESS}_1}\Bigr)
=\sigma^2 n\,\frac{\mathrm{ESS}_1-\mathrm{ESS}_2}{\mathrm{ESS}_1\,\mathrm{ESS}_2}.
\] Equivalently \(|\beta|<\sigma\sqrt{n(\mathrm{ESS}_1-\mathrm{ESS}_2)/(\mathrm{ESS}_1\mathrm{ESS}_2)}\): the smaller-set estimator achieves the lower mean squared error exactly when its bias is below the threshold set by the variance saved through the larger effective sample size.
(c) Relation to ESS and the identity scale. Balancing the additional covariate \(x_2\) adds a moment constraint to the weights, which by Theorem 18.6 can only lower the effective sample size, \(\mathrm{ESS}_2\le\mathrm{ESS}_1\), raising the variance; this is the variance cost on the right-hand side of the condition. The trade-off in (b) is the bias-variance balance of the remark following Lemma 29.4: balancing a covariate is worthwhile only when the bias it removes exceeds the variance it costs. On the identity scale a purely prognostic covariate carries no bias, \(\beta=0\), because it cancels in the contrast (it shifts both arms equally); then the condition \(\beta^2=0<\sigma^2 n(\cdots)\) holds automatically, so balancing \(x_2\) removes no bias while strictly lowering the effective sample size, and it can only hurt. \(\square\)

text:
F.30 Chapter 30: Machine-Checked Foundations: The Coq Formalization

F.30.1 Solution to Exercise 30.8: Why one Coq theorem needs no premise and another carries one
This Chapter 30 exercise contrasts two machine-checked results and explains why the discrete balancing theorem is proved outright while the continuous inverse-probability-weighting identity must carry a named, unproved premise.
A reminder on the tiers (for readers who jumped straight here). The formalization sorts theorems by how much they assume. A tier F (“fully proved”) theorem is proved from first principles inside Coq with no unproved input. A tier P (“proved given a premise”) theorem is a complete Coq proof of an implication whose hypothesis is a named premise: an abstract, explicitly stated proposition that the current libraries cannot yet discharge, made visible in the theorem’s own statement rather than hidden. Schematically the two shapes are
(* tier F: proved outright, no probabilistic hypothesis *)
Theorem propensity_score_is_balancing :
  forall x, balancing_property x.

(* tier P: a complete proof of an implication whose premise Hipw1 is stated, not proved *)
Theorem mu1_IPW_unbiased :
  Hipw1 -> estimator_IPW = mu1_true.
The point of the exercise is to explain why the first needs nothing to the left of its conclusion while the second must display Hipw1.
Contrast propensity_score_is_balancing, a tier-F result with no probabilistic premise, against mu1_IPW_unbiased, a tier-P result carrying the named premise Hipw1.
Why the discrete balancing theorem needs no premise. The Rosenbaum-Rubin balancing property is proved over a finite discrete model, a joint probability mass function over finite types, with conditional independence written in the cross-multiplied form Equation 30.1, \(q_{XYZ}(x,y,z)\,q_Z(z)=q_{XZ}(x,z)\,q_{YZ}(y,z)\). In this multiplicative form the statement needs no positivity hypothesis: when a conditioning mass is zero, both sides vanish by marginal monotonicity (every joint marginal is dominated by the conditioning mass), so the identity holds trivially at zero-mass covariate points rather than requiring a nonzero denominator. There is therefore no division to justify and no probabilistic fact to admit; the proof goes through outright in Coq for every covariate value, including those of measure zero, and the theorem is tier F.
Why the continuous IPW identity defers to Hipw1. The inverse-probability-weighting unbiasedness mu1_IPW_unbiased is a statement in the continuous kernel model, and its proof needs the tower property (law of total expectation) for conditional expectations under a continuous covariate law. As Section 30.9 explains, the development is built on mathcomp-analysis, which does not yet supply the conditional-expectation and disintegration library needed to discharge that step inside Coq. So rather than hide the gap, the tower-property consequence is admitted as the visible named premise Hipw1, and the theorem is tier P: a fully proved Coq object given Hipw1, but resting on a stated, unproved probabilistic input.
What would close the gap, and where the paper proof lives. Discharging Hipw1 inside Coq requires developing, on top of mathcomp-analysis, a measure-theoretic conditional-expectation theory with the tower property and a disintegration (regular conditional distribution) library for the kernel model. Until that exists, the paper proof of the premise is supplied by the potential-outcomes and adjustment chapters: the IPW unbiasedness identity is proved there (Theorem 10.3 in Chapter 10, resting on the identification results of Chapter 9), which is exactly the tower-property argument that Hipw1 abbreviates. \(\square\)


F.30.2 Solution to Exercise 30.9: The placeholder trap and statement faithfulness
This Chapter 30 exercise shows how a formalization can type-check yet certify nothing, if a modeling assumption is replaced by the trivially true proposition, and explains the structural policy that guards against it.
Uses. The statement-faithfulness guarantee Section 30.5 and the visible-premise policy Section 30.9.
Suppose a developer had defined a modeling assumption as the trivially true proposition, Definition conditional_constancy : Prop := True, instead of as an abstract named proposition with real content.
The placeholder trap. A “consistency theorem” of the shape conditional_constancy -> (estimator = truth) then unfolds to True -> (estimator = truth), which is logically equivalent to estimator = truth. If, as is typical of a placeholder development, the estimator and truth terms are wired to be definitionally or provably equal (for instance both reduce to the same standardized integral), the implication is discharged by intros; reflexivity with no mathematical content: the premise contributes nothing because every proof of True is vacuous, and the conclusion was already provable on its own. The theorem type-checks and the kernel certifies it, yet it certifies nothing about the substantive assumption its name advertises.
Which guarantee is violated. This is precisely the statement faithfulness gap of Section 30.5: the kernel checks that the proof proves the stated theorem, but it cannot check that the stated theorem is the one the mathematician meant. A formalization with an unintended hypothesis that renders the proposition vacuous type-checks just as readily as the intended one. Replacing a real modeling restriction by True substitutes a vacuous proposition for the intended conditional-constancy assumption, so the certified statement is no longer a faithful formalization of “under conditional constancy, the estimator is consistent,” even though it compiles.
The structural defense. The development’s stated policy, recorded in MAIC.v and STC.v, is to refuse True-valued assumption definitions and instead make every modeling assumption a visible, abstract named premise that appears in the theorem’s own statement (Section 30.9). Because such a premise is a genuine, non-trivial Prop that the conclusion actually consumes, a vacuous proof is impossible: the theorem cannot be discharged without using the assumption, and a human reading the statement can confirm that the premise says what the book says. Making each assumption a load-bearing visible premise is the structural guard against the placeholder trap, since it converts the unprovable question “is this the intended theorem?” into the checkable question “is this premise the intended assumption?”, which a reader can answer by inspection. \(\square\)

title: Appendix G — Reading the Coq Proofs
text:
G.1 Why read the Coq development, and what success looks like
Chapter 30 (Section 30.1) tells the story of the companion ITC_Coq development: what a proof assistant guarantees, the proof-status vocabulary (Definition 30.1), the three active axioms (Definition 30.2), and the map from the book’s tagged theorems to the Coq lemmas that machine-check them (Section 30.10). This appendix is the operational counterpart: a hands-on guide for a reader who wants to obtain the development, install the toolchain, compile every file, read the proof scripts, and query the kernel for the axioms a theorem uses. Nothing here re-argues the mathematics; the chapters do that. What follows is precise enough to be typed at a shell and a Coq prompt. Symbols follow Notation; in particular the abstract expectation operator written E in the Coq source plays the role of \(\mathbb{E}\).
The development is fifteen Coq source files in a directory theories/, built against the Mathematical Components and mathcomp-analysis libraries, compiling with zero project axioms and zero admitted proofs. It is released under the GPL-3 license and lives in the repository https://github.com/choxos/ITC_Coq, whose theories/AXIOMS.md is the canonical assumption inventory and whose manuscript/16_coq.md is the file-by-file walk-through on which Chapter 30 is based.
If you run meta-analyses in R or Stan, a fair first question is why you would spend an afternoon installing a proof assistant to read files you will never execute in an analysis. The payoff is specific to indirect comparison. Every method in this book rests on assumptions that are easy to state in prose and easy to lose in prose: constancy of relative effects for a Bucher comparison (Definition 14.3), positivity and conditional exchangeability for weighting (Definition 9.8, Definition 9.7), the absence of effect modification on the scale that would otherwise bias an unanchored comparison (Definition 11.3). In a machine-checked proof these assumptions cannot be smuggled into a sentence: each one appears as a named Hypothesis that the final theorem carries in its statement, and the proof will not close if the algebra leans on an assumption that was never declared. Three concrete guarantees follow.
What the machine does not do matters just as much, and a health researcher should hold onto it: Coq verifies that the conclusions follow from the stated premises by valid logic and algebra. It does not verify that those premises hold in your trials. Whether relative effects really are constant across the \(AC\) and \(BC\) populations, whether positivity holds in your data, whether you have measured the effect modifiers: those are scientific questions the machine leaves to you. Machine-checking moves the argument from “trust the author’s algebra and the author’s assumption bookkeeping” to “trust the author’s science”; it does not remove the science. For a health technology assessment that shift is worth having, because a reviewer can see the exact assumption ledger behind a comparative-effect estimate.
Reader goal. You do not need to become a Coq developer, and this appendix does not try to teach you to write proofs. A realistic goal is narrower: install the toolchain, rebuild the development so you have watched the kernel accept every theorem, open one file, read the statement of a theorem the book tags as machine-checked, identify the assumptions written into that statement, and run one command that reports the foundational axioms the proof uses. If at the end you can do that for bucher_unbiased, you can do it for any tagged theorem in the book, and you have gained the ability to audit a machine-checked claim rather than take it on trust.

title: Appendix G — Reading the Coq Proofs
text:
Assumptions are auditable. You can read exactly which premises a result needs, in one place, and you can query the proof mechanically for the foundational axioms it rests on (Section G.11).
The algebra cannot be fudged. The subtraction that cancels the common comparator in Bucher (Theorem 14.1), the exponential tilt defining the MAIC weights (Theorem 18.1), and the effective-sample-size bound (Theorem 18.6) are each checked symbol by symbol by a small trusted program, so a sign error or a dropped term cannot slip through.
The certificate is reproducible. Anyone can rebuild the development and re-verify every tagged theorem on their own machine; the check is a command you run, not a claim you accept.

title: Appendix G — Reading the Coq Proofs
text:
G.2 The minimal path
Before the step-by-step detail, here is the whole journey in a handful of commands, so you can see its shape. The sections that follow expand each step, and Section G.6 says what to do when one fails. First, at an ordinary shell:
git clone https://github.com/choxos/ITC_Coq.git       # 1. get the source
cd ITC_Coq
opam install 'coq>=9.1' 'coq-mathcomp-analysis>=1.9'   # 2. install the toolchain (full list below)
make                                                   # 3. compile and kernel-check every file
Then, at a Coq prompt started with the project’s load path (coqtop -R theories ITC, explained in Section G.11):
Require Import ITC.Bucher.          (* 4. load the compiled Bucher module *)
Check bucher_unbiased.              (* 5. print the theorem's statement, assumptions included *)
Print Assumptions bucher_unbiased.  (* 6. report the foundational axioms the proof uses *)
What success looks like. Step 3 ends without an error and leaves fifteen .vo files in theories/, one per source file; that clean exit is itself the verification that the kernel accepted every theorem (Section G.5). Step 5 prints the premises and the conclusion, so you can read the theorem’s assumptions (Section G.10). Step 6 prints exactly three axioms and nothing else (Section G.11). The companion “nothing was left unproved” check is one more shell command, grep -nE "Admitted|^Axiom|admit\." theories/*.v, which should print nothing at all. If every one of these signals appears, you have reproduced the book’s central machine-checked claim yourself; the rest of this appendix explains what each step means and how to read what it prints.

title: Appendix G — Reading the Coq Proofs
text:
G.3 Getting the development
Clone the repository and enter it:
git clone https://github.com/choxos/ITC_Coq.git
cd ITC_Coq
The pieces relevant to this appendix are the build files _CoqProject and Makefile at the root, the fifteen .v source files in theories/, and theories/AXIOMS.md. The sibling directories proofs/ (the Markdown proof catalogue, Parts A through O) and manuscript/ (a self-contained pedagogical text) are reference prose and are not part of the Coq build.

title: Appendix G — Reading the Coq Proofs
text:
G.4 Installing the toolchain
The development is built and checked by Coq, the proof assistant renamed the Rocq Prover in 2025, together with three libraries: Mathematical Components (mathcomp, the SSReflect proof language plus the algebra hierarchy), mathcomp-analysis (classical real analysis, measure theory, Lebesgue integration, probability measures, and transition kernels), and Hierarchy Builder (the tool that generates mathcomp’s structure hierarchy). The required versions, as declared in _CoqProject and the project README, are collected in Table G.1.



Table G.1: Toolchain for the ITC_Coq development, from _CoqProject and the project README. The development was checked with the Rocq Prover 9.1.0 and mathcomp-analysis 1.9.





Component
opam package
Minimum version




Coq (Rocq Prover)
coq
9.1


MathComp SSReflect
coq-mathcomp-ssreflect
2.0


MathComp Algebra
coq-mathcomp-algebra
(with ssreflect)


mathcomp-analysis
coq-mathcomp-analysis
1.9


Hierarchy Builder
coq-hierarchy-builder
1.6






These libraries form a stack, each layer resting on the one below. mathcomp-ssreflect is the base: the SSReflect proof language and the library of finite objects. mathcomp-algebra adds the algebraic hierarchy on top of it, and mathcomp-analysis adds real analysis, measure theory, and probability on top of that. Hierarchy Builder is not a mathematical layer but the tool that generates the hierarchy itself, the layered tower of algebraic structures (from monoid up to ring up to field) that lets a theorem proved for rings apply automatically to the real numbers. For reading Bucher.v you need only the base and the algebra layer; the analysis layer matters for the measure-theoretic files.
The supported way to obtain these is opam, the OCaml package manager. Install opam from your operating system’s package manager, then create an isolated switch (an opam switch is a self-contained OCaml compiler together with its own installed packages, analogous to a Python virtual environment or a separate R library tree, but covering the whole toolchain rather than one language’s add-on packages), add the Coq released-packages repository, and install the libraries; opam resolves the prover and the remaining mathcomp packages as dependencies:
opam init --bare                                   # first-time opam setup
opam switch create itc-coq 4.14.2                  # a fresh switch with an OCaml compiler
eval $(opam env)                                   # point the shell at the new switch

opam repo add coq-released https://coq.inria.fr/opam/released

opam install 'coq>=9.1' 'coq-mathcomp-ssreflect>=2.0' coq-mathcomp-algebra \
             'coq-mathcomp-analysis>=1.9' 'coq-hierarchy-builder>=1.6'
opam will select a mutually compatible set of versions satisfying the constraints; installing coq-mathcomp-analysis alone would pull in coq-mathcomp-ssreflect, coq-mathcomp-algebra, and coq-hierarchy-builder transitively, but listing them documents the intent and lets opam report a clear error if any constraint cannot be met.
One practical point the commands above hide: eval $(opam env) updates only the current shell so that coqc, make, and the libraries resolve to the new switch. It is not permanent. Open a fresh terminal, or reboot, and you must run eval $(opam env) again before building, or the shell will not find the switch’s tools (Section G.6). Some opam installations add a startup hook that does this for you; when in doubt, run it.

Remark. The Coq to Rocq rename. At version 9.x the prover’s opam package may appear as rocq-prover, with coq retained as a transitional alias, and the libraries may also be published under rocq-mathcomp-*. If the coq package is unavailable on your opam repository snapshot, substitute rocq-prover for coq in the install command; the source files and build are unaffected, since they refer to the libraries by their logical module names, not their opam package names.
In practice, try the coq-named commands first; if your shell reports that coqc or coqtop is not found, the Rocq 9 equivalents are rocq (for example rocq --version in place of coqc --version) and rocqtop in place of coqtop. The two naming families drive the same prover, read the same source files, and take the same -R theories ITC load-path flag, so anywhere this appendix writes coqc or coqtop you may read rocq or rocqtop with no other change. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Verify the installation before building:
coqc --version                 # or: rocq --version
opam list | grep mathcomp      # should list ssreflect, algebra, analysis
To read and step through the proofs interactively, any of the standard front ends works: VsCoq (the Visual Studio Code extension), Proof General (the Emacs mode), or the bundled graphical interface CoqIDE, called RocqIDE from version 9. Each lets you place the cursor mid-proof and inspect the goal and context after every tactic, which is the natural way to read a Coq proof for the first time.

title: Appendix G — Reading the Coq Proofs
section: G.5 The _CoqProject file and the build
text:
G.5 The _CoqProject file and the build
_CoqProject is the single source of build configuration. It declares one logical mapping and lists the source files in dependency order:
-R theories ITC

theories/Axioms.v
theories/BasicTypes.v
...
theories/EffectModifiers.v
The line -R theories ITC maps the physical directory theories/ to the logical module prefix ITC (recursively); a logical name here is simply the name Coq uses to locate a compiled module, independent of where the file sits on disk, so that the module compiled from theories/Bucher.v is addressed as ITC.Bucher, theories/MAIC.v as ITC.MAIC, and so on. This is the path you will use in Require Import (Section G.11).
Building is driven by make from the repository root:
make
The top-level Makefile is a thin wrapper: if Makefile.coq is missing or out of date it regenerates it from _CoqProject with coq_makefile, namely
coq_makefile -f _CoqProject -o Makefile.coq        # rocq makefile -f ... on Rocq 9
and then delegates the actual compilation to that generated makefile. To compile a file here means more than to translate it. coqc runs the file’s proof scripts to build a proof term for each theorem and submits every one to the kernel, Coq’s small trusted checking core (the kernel is explained in Section G.8). The resulting theories/X.vo is the compiled, kernel-checked file: an artifact that exists only because the kernel accepted every proof in X.v. So a run that ends without error, producing fifteen .vo files, is not merely a successful build; it is the verification that every theorem in the tree is accepted by the kernel. A clean rebuild is
make clean && make
which deletes the .vo files and the generated Makefile.coq and recompiles from scratch.
The inventory claims of Chapter 30 are reproducible at the shell. That the development declares no axioms of its own and admits no proof is confirmed by a search that returns nothing across the fifteen files:
grep -nE "Admitted|^Axiom|admit\." theories/*.v        # no output
Two flaws would undermine the claim that the tree is fully proved, and this one command looks for both. An Admitted proof is a hole the kernel is told to accept with no proof term, so the theorem above it is not actually checked; an Axiom (or an admit. inside a proof) is an extra unproved assumption that every result downstream silently inherits. Fewer of both means more of the mathematics is genuinely verified, which is why “zero admits, zero project axioms” is a guarantee, not a boast. The grep prints one line per match; finding none, it prints nothing and returns you to the prompt. Had it printed a line, that line would name the file and the offending Admitted or Axiom, and the tree would not be fully proved. The search deliberately scans only the project’s own theories/*.v: the three classical axioms the proofs rely on live in the mathcomp-analysis library, not in these files, so they never appear here. That is exactly why the complementary per-theorem check below, Print Assumptions, exists; it reports the inherited library axioms that grep cannot see.
Per-theorem axiom closure is queried with Print Assumptions, described next.

title: Appendix G — Reading the Coq Proofs
text:
G.6 Troubleshooting the build
When the minimal path of Section G.2 stops at an error, the cause is almost always one of a short list. The fixes are in plain terms.

opam install cannot find a compatible set of versions. Refresh opam’s index with opam update, confirm the released-packages repository is present (opam repo list should show coq-released), and re-run the install. On an older switch, opam upgrade may be needed first.
coqc --version reports a version below 9.1, or an old mathcomp. The shell is using a system-wide Coq rather than the switch you built. Run eval $(opam env) in that terminal and check again; opam switch list shows which switch is active.
coqc: command not found. Same cause: the switch is not active in this shell. Run eval $(opam env); if you have only just installed opam, open a new terminal so its startup hook runs.
make reports coq_makefile: command not found. Coq itself is not on the path, so the switch is not active, or the libraries installed but the prover did not. Activate the switch and confirm coqc --version works before running make. On Rocq 9 the tool is rocq makefile, which make invokes automatically once the switch is active.
Require Import ITC.Bucher fails with the module not found. The load path is missing. Interactive sessions and scratch files need the -R theories ITC flag (coqtop -R theories ITC), the same mapping that turns theories/Bucher.v into the name ITC.Bucher (Section G.5). Inside the build, make supplies it from _CoqProject; outside the build you must pass it yourself.
A scratch file breaks make. If you place a scratch .v file inside theories/ or list it in _CoqProject, make will try to compile it. Keep scratch files at the repository root and out of _CoqProject, and run them directly with coqc -R theories ITC scratch.v (Section G.11).
You are on Windows without a Unix-like shell. opam and the sh/make workflow assume a Unix-like environment. The Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) provides one: install opam inside WSL and follow the instructions unchanged.

title: Appendix G — Reading the Coq Proofs
section: G.7 Dependency order of the theories
text:
G.7 Dependency order of the theories
The fifteen files are grouped into five phases in _CoqProject, each phase building only on the ones before it. The grouping is pedagogical; the binding constraint is the set of Require Import lines at the top of each file, which the build resolves into a topological order.

Phase 1, foundations: Axioms.v, BasicTypes.v, PotentialOutcomes.v, CausalAssumptions.v.
Phase 2, conditional independence and balancing scores: ConditionalIndep.v, BalancingScore.v, PropensityScore.v.
Phase 3, estimators: IPWEstimator.v, OutcomeRegression.v, DoublyRobust.v.
Phase 4, indirect-comparison methods: MAIC.v, STC.v, Comparison.v.
Phase 5, indirect-comparison algebra: Bucher.v, EffectModifiers.v.

The actual import edges are tighter than the linear phase order suggests. Axioms.v imports only the mathcomp libraries; BasicTypes.v imports Axioms; PotentialOutcomes imports Axioms BasicTypes; CausalAssumptions adds PotentialOutcomes; ConditionalIndep adds CausalAssumptions. The balancing and estimator layers chain on top: PropensityScore imports through ConditionalIndep and BalancingScore; IPWEstimator, OutcomeRegression, and DoublyRobust import PropensityScore (and, for DoublyRobust, the two estimator files); Comparison imports all of MAIC, STC, and the estimator layer.
Table G.2 gives the literal dependency: the modules named on each file’s Require Import line(s) at its head, read from the source.
